records.definition: Frozen, rigid, unresponsive; feminine adjective for a completely sexually frigid or wholly inert woman.
records.notes: Feminine of جامد (frozen/solid/rigid); stronger and more contemptuous than خاملة; implies total absence of sexual feeling or arousal response; a commonly deployed colloquial insult for a sexually unresponsive woman; higher crude score than other frigidity terms due to its insulting edge.

records.definition: Does not respond; colloquial phrase for a woman who fails to react to sexual stimulation or show any sign of arousal.
records.notes: A phrase rather than a single lexeme; the feminine verb form (tastajīb) marks this as gendered toward describing women; used descriptively to denote failure of arousal response; less openly insulting in tone than جامدة; implies a physiological or psychological block more than a character flaw.

records.definition: Homosexual; the standard Modern Standard Arabic clinical and journalistic term for a person attracted to the same sex.
records.notes: Literally 'same-sex [person]'; a calque from Western clinical terminology; dominant in MSA journalism, law, and public health contexts; gender-neutral in form; preferred in formal writing over colloquial slurs; heavily stigmatized as a topic in most Arabic-speaking societies despite the clinical register of the term itself.

records.definition: Homosexuality; the abstract MSA noun for same-sex sexual orientation as a concept or phenomenon.
records.notes: Abstract noun form distinguishing the orientation concept from مثلي الجنس (the person); mithliyya = sameness + jinsiyya = sexual; rated approximate rather than direct because 'homosexuality' maps the orientation concept while this term straddles orientation and identity as used in Arabic academic, medical, and legal discourse.

records.definition: Lesbian; a woman sexually and romantically attracted to other women; derived etymologically from the verb meaning to grind or rub.
records.notes: Derived from سحاق (grinding/rubbing), referencing the sexual act of tribadism; higher crude score than مثلي الجنس because the etymological root is a sexual act rather than a neutral descriptor; used in both clinical and everyday Arabic but carries the weight of its anatomical etymology in ways the English 'lesbian' does not.

records.definition: Lesbianism; etymologically refers to tribadism (vulva-to-vulva sexual friction); the root noun from which سحاقية is derived, used for both the sexual act and lesbian orientation.
records.notes: From the verb سحق (to grind, crush, or rub); historically denoted the sexual act specifically but has generalized to denote lesbian identity and orientation; the Arabic cognate of the clinical English term 'tribadism'; retains more of its act-based etymology than سحاقية, which is why it maps primarily to tribadism despite its broader usage.

records.definition: Clinical Modern Standard Arabic phrase for bisexual, literally 'dual of sex/gender'; used in formal health and human-rights discourse about sexual orientation.
records.notes: Calque construction; competes with مزدوج الميل الجنسي in formal academic writing; recognition limited to educated and LGBTQ+-informed speakers.

records.definition: Clinical MSA phrase for heterosexual, literally 'contrary/different of sex'; used mainly in LGBTQ+ and medical contexts where heterosexuality must be explicitly named rather than assumed as default.
records.notes: Arabic discourse rarely needs to name heterosexuality explicitly because it is the unmarked norm; this clinical phrase appears almost exclusively in texts that must enumerate orientation categories.

records.definition: Clinical MSA phrase for asexual, literally 'non-sexual'; describes a person who experiences little or no sexual attraction to others.
records.notes: Asexuality as a named identity category is poorly represented in Arabic-language discourse; recognition essentially limited to highly educated LGBTQ+-informed speakers; competes with the calque لاجنسي.

records.definition: Clinical MSA calque of 'transgender', literally 'crossing/transcending sex-gender'; the preferred neutral identity term in Arabic LGBTQ+ advocacy and human-rights writing.
records.notes: Foregrounds identity and gender crossing rather than medical transition; distinguishable from متحول جنسياً which emphasizes bodily change; preferred by activists but uncommon in mainstream Arabic media.

records.definition: Classical Arabic and Islamic jurisprudence term for a person with ambiguous or mixed sex characteristics; codified in fiqh to govern inheritance, dress, and ritual obligations; in modern colloquial use can be repurposed as a slur for effeminate men.
records.notes: The classical fiqh category distinguishes khunthā wāḍiḥ (unambiguous hermaphrodite) from khunthā mushkil (ambiguous); the term predates the modern intersex concept and carries no malice in religious-legal discourse but has acquired a derogatory colloquial register when applied to men without ambiguous biology.

records.definition: Formal MSA phrase for bisexual, literally 'dual/double of sexual inclination'; the more verbose academic variant used in psychology, sexology, and public-health writing.
records.notes: More technically precise than ثنائي الجنسية by naming 'inclination' (mayl) rather than 'sex/gender' as the doubled element; found primarily in academic texts and formal health communications; low recognition outside specialist contexts.

records.definition: MSA clinical phrase for transsexual or transgender, literally 'sexually/gender-transformed'; emphasizes bodily or social transition and is the most common term in Arabic news coverage and medical discourse about trans people.
records.notes: More widely used than عابر الجنس in mainstream Arabic media; carries stronger connotation of medical transition (surgery, hormones) than identity alone; the adverb جنسياً can imply sexual deviance to conservative readers, giving the phrase a slightly loaded quality absent from the activist-preferred عابر الجنس.

records.definition: Clinical MSA noun phrase for 'sexual attraction' as an abstract orientation-framework concept; used to name the phenomenon of being drawn to others sexually, independent of direction, in academic and LGBTQ+-discourse contexts.
records.notes: Proposed slug: sexual_attraction_concept. The registry has no generic 'sexual attraction as orientation concept' entry distinct from states of arousal or specific same-sex attraction categories; this term functions as the Arabic equivalent of 'sexual attraction' when used abstractly in orientation definitions such as 'same-sex attraction' (الانجذاب الجنسي المثلي).

records.definition: Arabic phonetic transliteration of the English 'pansexual'; used exclusively in LGBTQ+-informed Arabic social-media and activist contexts to describe attraction regardless of gender.
records.notes: Very recent borrowing with no established MSA calque alternative; virtually absent outside online Arabic LGBTQ+ communities; low recognition even among educated speakers unfamiliar with queer-identity discourse.

records.definition: Arabic calque of 'asexual' formed with the negative prefix لā; describes a person experiencing little or no sexual attraction; used primarily in online Arabic LGBTQ+ spaces.
records.notes: The morphological structure (لا + جنسي) mirrors the English 'a-' + 'sexual' prefix logic, making it community-coined rather than formally adopted; competes with غير جنسي in the same semantic space; recognition negligible outside identity-aware speakers.

records.definition: The primary Islamic condemnatory term for a gay man or sodomite, derived from the Prophet Lūṭ (Lot) whose people in Sodom practiced anal intercourse between men; carries severe religious-moral condemnation across all Arabic-speaking societies.
records.notes: Cognate with the act-noun liwāṭ (اللواط, sodomy); one of the oldest and most universally recognized Arabic terms for homosexuality; simultaneously a formal religious-legal category and a devastating street-level slur; deeply embedded in Islamic jurisprudence (the act is a ḥadd offense under some schools).

records.definition: Derogatory MSA phrase for a homosexual person, literally 'sexually abnormal/deviant'; used in conservative religious discourse and mainstream Arabic media to pathologize homosexuality as a biological or moral aberration.
records.notes: شاذ (shādhdh) means irregular, exceptional, anomalous; applied to sexuality it frames same-sex attraction as a deviation from natural and divine order; widely used in Arabic-language religious fatwas, state media, and conservative commentary; its register is semi-formal rather than street-slang, lending it the air of authoritative condemnation.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term for a man who imitates women in appearance, speech, and mannerism; explicitly cursed in hadith literature; used in both classical Islamic texts and contemporary discourse as a slur for effeminate gay men.
records.notes: The Prophet's curse of al-mutakhannithīn (men who imitate women) and al-mutarajjilāt (women who imitate men) is widely cited in Islamic literature; the Form V verb form takhannatha implies habitual self-directed feminization; the term predates modern homosexual identity categories but is routinely applied to gay men.

records.definition: Extremely vulgar Egyptian colloquial slur for an effeminate or passive gay man; one of the most offensive Arabic terms for a male who adopts the feminized or receptive role; widely exported via Egyptian cinema and television.
records.notes: Egyptian dialectal in origin but broadly understood across the Arab world due to Egypt's cultural dominance in film and media; used both as a specific homosexuality slur and as a general-purpose insult disconnected from sexual context, similarly to how 'faggot' functions in colloquial English; considered maximally offensive in formal contexts.

records.definition: Classical and medieval Arabic term for a man who habitually submits to anal penetration; attested in pre-modern poetry and medical literature as a marker of sexual passivity and extreme social dishonor.
records.notes: Has attestation in classical Arabic erotic poetry (adab al-jins), medieval medical texts, and adab literature; specifically marks the receptive-passive sexual role as a fixed character type rather than homosexuality in the modern identity sense; recognized by educated speakers but less common in everyday colloquial use than منيوك or خَوَل.

records.definition: Extremely vulgar colloquial Arabic slur for a man who receives anal penetration; passive participial form of nayk (to fuck), marking the recipient of intercourse; among the most offensive Arabic insults for a passive or gay male.
records.notes: Derived from نيك (nayk), widely considered the most obscene Arabic verb for sexual intercourse; the passive-participial form (mafʿūl pattern) grammatically positions the target as the acted-upon party; also deployed as a general-purpose insult analogous to 'fucker' but with explicit passivity connotation.

records.definition: Vulgar colloquial slur for a man who is anally penetrated, derived from qāʿ/qaʿr meaning the bottom or depth of a vessel; marks the receptive sexual role as social-shame category and general insult.
records.notes: قعر (qaʿr) means the bottom, floor, or pit of a container; applying it to a person implies he is the lowest point, the receptive base; common in Levantine and Gulf colloquial Arabic; shares semantic territory with منيوك but the root imagery emphasizes being at the 'bottom' rather than the act of being penetrated.

records.definition: Vulgar colloquial Arabic slur for a passive homosexual, derived from daʿaka meaning to rub, grind, or crush; implies the person is physically ground down or worked over in the receptive sexual role.
records.notes: دعك (daʿk) denotes vigorous rubbing or grinding friction; the passive-participle formation designates the recipient of this action; somewhat regionally variable in distribution compared to منيوك; found across Levantine and North African colloquial Arabic; less widely recognized than the other passive-role slurs in this set.

records.definition: Colloquial Arabic slur that calls an effeminate or passive gay man a 'bride' or 'daughter-in-law', imposing the feminine-marital role on the target to mark sexual and social shame.
records.notes: كنّة (kanna) literally means daughter-in-law or bride in various regional dialects; applied to a man it lexically forces him into the feminine-receptive marital role; the insult's force derives from the Arab honor-shame system in which a man occupying a woman's role is profoundly dishonored; regional distribution variable.

records.definition: Colloquial Arabic slur for an effeminate or nagging gay man, derived from zanna meaning to buzz, drone, or whine; evokes a stereotyped image of an effeminate man who chatters or complains in a high-pitched, womanish manner.
records.notes: زنّ (zann) denotes the continuous buzzing of an insect or the persistent nagging whine of a person; the intensive form زنّانة amplifies both effeminacy and irritating persistence; particularly common in Egyptian and Levantine colloquial Arabic; the onomatopoeic root adds a quality of contemptuous mockery absent from purely anatomical slurs.

records.definition: Literally 'feminized' or 'made feminine'; the standard Arabic grammatical term for the feminine gender, repurposed as a mild-to-moderate personal insult for an effeminate man when applied to a person rather than a noun.
records.notes: Sharply dual-register: in grammatical contexts (الاسم المؤنث, feminine noun) it is entirely neutral and high-frequency; applied to a man as a character descriptor it becomes a derogatory label of effeminacy; crude score reflects the derogatory personal-insult usage; the low crude relative to other slurs in this set reflects the word's overwhelming association with grammar rather than sexuality.

records.definition: Figurative insult meaning 'spiritually or soulfully castrated'; applies the image of physical castration to a man's inner character to condemn total emasculation of will, courage, and masculine agency.
records.notes: مخصي = castrated (from khaṣā, to castrate); بالروح = in/of the soul/spirit; weaponizes the extreme dishonor of physical castration and displaces it onto character rather than anatomy; no direct English idiom equivalent; the compound is creative colloquial Arabic rather than a fixed lexical item.

records.definition: Classical and semi-formal Arabic term for a man who voluntarily adopts feminine characteristics or demeanor; from the Form X verb istaʾnatha, 'to make oneself feminine'; implies deliberate gender-norm transgression.
records.notes: Form X (istaFʿaLa) morphology encodes deliberate self-directed action, distinguishing it from مؤنث (passively feminized) and متخنث (habitually imitating women): the target is actively choosing femininity; attested in classical texts and survives in formal written Arabic; more literary in register than متخنث.

records.definition: Extreme Arabic insult branding a man as 'permissible/lawful of the anus'; inverts Islamic halal/haram legal language to declare that his rectum is sexually available to anyone, combining maximal sexual violation with religious desecration.
records.english_term: one whose ass is open to all (extreme gay slur)
records.notes: حلال = religiously permissible (halal); الدبر = the back/anus (the classical anatomical term, used in Quranic commentary on the prohibition of anal intercourse); the phrase is specifically Arabic-Islamic in construction, weaponizing the central halal/haram binary as a sexual insult; no English idiom captures the simultaneous attack on sexual honor and religious standing.

records.definition: Literally 'son of a whore/slut'; شرموطة is one of the most vulgar Arabic terms for a sexually promiscuous woman, so the compound attacks the target's honor through his mother's sexual reputation — the most powerful shaming vector in Arab honor culture.
records.notes: شرموطة (sharmūṭa) is itself one of the most sexually explicit and offensive Arabic terms for a woman, making this compound substantially more vulgar than its English functional equivalent 'son of a bitch'; strikes at sharaf (honor) via maternal sexual shame, which carries far greater cultural weight in Arab honor-shame systems than in contemporary Western contexts; universal recognition across all Arabic dialects.

records.definition: 'Son of a whore'; severe maternal-lineage insult invoking the mother's alleged prostitution, functionally equivalent to English 'son of a bitch' but more sexually explicit due to the explicit prostitution lexeme.
records.notes: القحبة (prostitute) is itself highly offensive; the compound attacks maternal honor via sexual accusation; القحبة is more explicitly sexual than English 'bitch'; pan-Arabic recognition across all dialects.

records.definition: 'Son of a female dog/bitch'; the most literal Arabic equivalent of English 'son of a bitch,' attacking the mother's honor through animal comparison rather than sexual accusation.
records.notes: Structurally and semantically the closest Arabic analog to English SOB; كلبة (female dog) maps directly to 'bitch'; somewhat less sexually loaded than ابن القحبة because the insult is animal-based rather than prostitution-based.

records.definition: 'Son of a fornicatress/adulteress'; insult invoking the mother's alleged commission of zinā — the Islamic legal category for all unlawful sexual intercourse — compounding sexual slur with religious-moral condemnation.
records.notes: الزانية is the feminine active participle of زنا (zinā); carries heavier religious-legal weight than القحبة because zinā is a Quranic concept and a ḥadd offense in classical Islamic law; deployed when the speaker wants a religiously-framed insult rather than a purely crude one.

records.definition: 'Son of a prostitute'; maternal-lineage insult using مومس, a slightly more literary or formal register term for a prostitute or sexually loose woman.
records.notes: مومس is a step more elevated in register than قحبة, making this compound marginally less raw but still severe; more likely to appear in written or literary invective; recognition lower than ابن القحبة because مومس is a less everyday lexeme.

records.definition: 'You who has been fucked/sodomized'; passive participle of نيك (to fuck) used as a severe insult implying the addressee has been used as a passive sexual object, with strong connotations of homosexual receptive role and profound emasculation.
records.notes: In Arabic honor culture the passive-receptive sexual role is deeply stigmatizing; the insult attacks both sexual identity and masculine honor simultaneously; stronger than most English gay slurs because it combines a sexual-act accusation with an honor violation encoded in grammatical voice (passive participle = acted upon, not acting).

records.definition: 'O fornicator/whoremonger' (masculine form); insult from the root عهر denoting habitual illicit sexual conduct, applied to men who engage in or facilitate sexual immorality.
records.notes: Masculine counterpart to عاهرة (item 25); the word straddles moral condemnation and crude insult — carries Quranic-register gravity but is deployed conversationally; less common as a pure insult than its feminine form because female sexual transgression is more heavily stigmatized.

records.definition: 'Your mother's clitoris'; extreme honor-attack insult that names a female relative's genitalia by anatomical term as a form of maximal disrespect; the clitoris-specific variant of Arabic maternal genital cursing.
records.notes: بظر is the semi-anatomical term for clitoris (relatively specific vs. the broader كس); the insult's mechanism is unique to the Arabic honor-shame framework — verbal exposure of maternal anatomy constitutes a grave attack on the family's honor; no English equivalent combines the maternal framing with specific anatomical naming as an insult genre; less universal than كس أمك but still widely recognized.

records.definition: 'Your mother's vagina/cunt'; the single most recognized and most offensive maternal genital insult in Arabic, invoking the mother's vagina as a catastrophic honor violation and general expletive.
records.notes: كس is the most taboo sexual lexeme in Arabic; this two-word construction is likely the most widely recognized profanity across the entire Arabic-speaking world, understood universally across all dialects; used both as a directed insult and as a free-floating expletive of shock or frustration; recognition effectively 100% among adult Arabic speakers regardless of education or region.

records.definition: 'A penis in your mother'; extreme honor-attack curse phrased as a declarative verbless sentence invoking someone penetrating the addressee's mother, functionally equivalent to calling someone a motherfucker but structurally framed as a curse rather than a label.
records.notes: أير is a crude colloquial term for penis; the verbless-sentence construction (noun phrase as curse) is distinctly Arabic — it asserts an act rather than labeling the person, making it structurally different from the English 'motherfucker' label; both target the same honor-violation mechanism; common across Levantine and Egyptian dialects.

records.definition: 'Son of a pimp/cuckold'; insult derived from عرص, denoting a man who profits from or is complicit in female family members' sexual dishonor — whether as a pimp, a passive facilitator, or a failed guardian — with the compound attacking the father's honor and virility.
records.notes: عرص is semantically fluid across dialects: Egyptian usage leans toward 'pimp'; Levantine usage toward 'passive homosexual' or 'man dishonored through his women'; the paternal targeting distinguishes it from the maternal-lineage insults above; the concept intersects with dayyūth (item 19) but عرص more explicitly implies active exploitation or a passive-homosexual stigma.

records.definition: 'O sodomite/homosexual'; insult derived from the name of the Prophet Lūṭ (Lot), whose community was destroyed in the Quran for sexual transgression; the standard Islamic-register term for a gay man or sodomite, carrying both legal and theological condemnation.
records.notes: Direct Islamic parallel to the English 'sodomite': both derive from an Abrahamic narrative of divine punishment for homosexual acts; لوطية is the jurisprudential noun for the act in Islamic law; carries more formal-theological weight than يا منيوك; the Quranic backstory is actively part of its meaning in ways that 'sodomite' has largely lost in English secular usage.

records.definition: 'O adulterer/fornicator'; accusation invoking zinā — the Islamic legal category covering all unlawful sexual intercourse — which carries both severe social condemnation and, under classical Islamic law, potential corporal punishment.
records.notes: Zinā in Islamic jurisprudence covers all extra-marital sex regardless of marital status of the parties; the hadd punishment is 100 lashes for an unmarried person or death by stoning for a married person in classical fiqh, giving this insult a gravity the English 'fornicator' has entirely lost; theological weight makes it more potent in religious-conservative contexts than its moderate crude score suggests.

records.definition: 'O depraved/dissolute one'; insult from the root فجور (moral corruption, sexual licentiousness, sinfulness), broadly condemning someone as morally bankrupt with sexual immorality as the primary but not exclusive implication.
records.notes: فاجر is broader than عاهر or زاني — it condemns general moral corruption including but not limited to sexual sins; also used in political and religious rhetoric against moral degeneracy; Quranic usage (البر والفجور) reinforces its gravity but makes it slightly more formal and less street-level crude than the other sexual insults in this section.

records.definition: 'O donkey/ass'; primarily a non-sexual insult meaning idiot or blockhead; listed here because in Arabic folk metaphor the donkey is also associated with large genitalia and unrestrained animal sexuality, giving it a secondary sexual register in some usages.
records.notes: The weakest item in this list by crude score; primarily means 'you fool'; the sexual resonance is secondary and context-dependent; Arabic folk idiom associates the donkey with an oversized penis (أير الحمار), so in explicit sexual contexts the word gains a different valence; one of the most universally recognized insults in Arabic precisely because it is mild enough for semi-public use.

records.definition: 'Billy goat'; applied to a man as an insult meaning sexually voracious, lecherous, or uncontrollably lustful, evoking the male goat's notorious smell, rutting behavior, and indiscriminate sexuality.
records.notes: The goat-as-lechery metaphor is cross-cultural but Arabic تيس carries additional semantic freight: in Islamic ritual context the تيس is an animal of sacrifice, adding a contempt dimension; can alternatively mean 'blockhead' or 'dunce' without sexual connotation depending on context; closer to English 'horny old goat' than to 'satyr' but evokes the same goat-lust archetype.

records.definition: 'O pimp/cuckold'; direct vocative use of عرص labeling the addressee as someone who exploits women sexually (pimp), fails to protect female family members' honor, or occupies the passive-homosexual role; strong connotations of emasculation.
records.notes: Direct usage without the 'son of' frame intensifies the insult as a personal label rather than a lineage attack; in Egyptian Arabic the pimp meaning dominates; in Levantine Arabic the passive-homosexual or dishonored-man-through-women reading is more salient; the word encapsulates the honor-shame economy where male worth derives from controlling female sexuality.

records.definition: 'Fucker'; intensive-pattern active participle of نيك (to fuck), labeling someone as an inveterate or aggressive sexual actor; used as a general crude insult comparable to English 'fucker.'
records.notes: The فعّال pattern in Arabic morphology denotes habitual or excessive agency — nayyāk means 'one who fucks constantly and aggressively'; paradoxically, in a culture that stigmatizes the passive role (منيوك), the active-voice label carries less pure sexual shame and is sometimes wielded with mixed swagger-and-insult connotations; one of the most morphologically transparent sex-derived insults in Arabic.

records.definition: 'Father of an ass/butt'; colorful insult using the Arabic kunya (father-of) construction with طيز (buttocks) to label someone as contemptible or sexually crude via deliberate inversion of the honorific kunya form.
records.notes: طيز refers to buttocks broadly rather than the anus specifically, so the anatomical match to English 'asshole' is imprecise; the kunya construction (أبو X) is culturally honorific — using it with a crude body part creates deliberate comic and offensive inversion; more witty than devastating; more common in Egyptian and Levantine colloquial Arabic than in Gulf or Maghrebi dialects.

records.definition: A man who lacks protective sexual jealousy (ghayra) over his female relatives — wife, daughters, sisters, mother — and either permits, facilitates, or is indifferent to other men's sexual access to them; one of the most condemned categories in Islamic moral theology, barred from paradise in hadith.
records.notes: The concept requires the Arabic honor-shame framework in which a man's worth depends on his exclusive control of his women's sexuality; ديوث is distinct from 'cuckold' (deceived without consent), 'pimp' (commercial exploitation), and 'hotwife husband' (consensual kink): it is specifically the willing or negligent abandonment of ghayra (غيرة, protective jealousy) as a moral-religious failure; cited in multiple hadith as a person Allah will not look upon on Judgment Day; no English word or concept adequately captures the theological and honor-economic weight of the term.

records.definition: 'Girl/daughter of the streets'; a slur for a woman of loose sexual morals or a prostitute, implying she belongs to no respectable household and is sexually available to any man she encounters on the street.
records.notes: The 'streets' framing encodes the honor-shame logic: a proper woman is confined to the domestic sphere under male guardianship; a woman 'of the streets' has escaped that control and is therefore sexually available to all; sits between general promiscuity accusation and explicit prostitution accusation — the ambiguity intensifies the insult.

records.definition: 'Girl of desire/air/whim'; a softer euphemism for a prostitute or sexually loose woman, using الهوى — which means carnal desire, romantic passion, or literally the wind — as a poetic veil over an explicit accusation.
records.notes: الهوى is beautifully ambiguous: it can mean erotic desire (هوى النفس), capricious whim, or simply air/breeze — the term lets speakers imply prostitution with plausible deniability; this makes it suitable for contexts where direct obscenity would be inappropriate; predominantly Egyptian colloquial usage; notably softer than بنت الشوارع while covering similar semantic ground.

records.definition: 'Stray/loose woman'; adjective-as-insult for a woman who is sexually available or promiscuous, derived from سائب (unattached, untethered, free-roaming), implying she lacks proper male guardianship and therefore sexual control.
records.notes: The root image is of an animal let off its leash — سائبة describes stray animals in standard usage; when applied to a woman it frames her sexual autonomy as dangerous freedom from rightful restraint; reflects the honor-shame framework in which female sexuality must be supervised by male guardians; moderate crude score because the animalistic comparison is implicit rather than explicit.

records.definition: 'One who is freely given/offered'; passive participle of بذل (to give or spend liberally), applied to a woman to mean she makes herself sexually available to anyone without restriction, framing her body as a commodity dispensed without cost or gatekeeping.
records.notes: The passive-participle morphology (مفعولة pattern) is linguistically significant: it grammatically positions the woman as the object of action rather than the agent — she is 'given out' rather than actively choosing; slightly more formal or literary register than direct slurs; the commodity metaphor (بذل also applies to spending money freely) encodes the sexual economics implicit in honor-shame vocabulary.

records.definition: 'Female cat'; used as a veiled slur for a promiscuous or sexually available woman, drawing on the cat's associations with nocturnal wandering, sexual heat cycles, and wanton behavior in Arabic folk idiom.
records.notes: The female-cat metaphor for female promiscuity is cross-cultural (cf. English 'pussy' and 'cat' in dated use) but operates somewhat differently in Arabic: the هرة in heat (الشبق) is a specific folk image; mild enough to be used in semi-polite company as a veiled insult where direct terms would be unacceptable; regional variation is significant — more common in Egyptian and Levantine colloquial than Gulf Arabic.

records.definition: 'Whore/prostitute'; the most common and widely recognized Arabic word for a prostitute or sexually promiscuous woman, derived from the root عهر (habitual illicit sexual conduct); used both as a literal descriptor for sex workers and as a maximally offensive general insult.
records.notes: Feminine active participle of عهر; among the most loaded terms in the Arabic lexicon, combining three registers simultaneously: religious (عهر appears in classical Islamic texts on sexual transgression), legal (historically a ḥadd-adjacent concept), and social (maximum female honor violation); the word's power exceeds the English 'whore' because in Arabic cultural context it implicates family honor, religious standing, and legal jeopardy together; ubiquitous as a general female insult well beyond literal application to sex workers.

records.definition: A prostitute or sex worker; an archaic literary term in classical and formal Modern Standard Arabic for a woman who sells sexual services.
records.notes: More literary and dated than colloquial equivalents; appears in formal texts, journalism, and classical literature rather than street speech; less loaded than قحبة or شرموطة.

records.definition: A prostitute or harlot; a Quranic and classical Arabic term for a woman who engages in unlawful sexual relations for pay, carrying strong religious and moral condemnation.
records.notes: Quranic term (24:33) used for a woman forced into or practicing prostitution; retains heavy religious framing in modern MSA usage; moralistic charge absent from clinical equivalents; root بغي connotes transgression and injustice.

records.definition: The most common crude vulgar term for a prostitute or whore across Arabic dialects; used both as a literal designation for sex workers and as a general misogynistic insult targeting any woman.
records.notes: One of the most offensive Arabic words for a woman; crosses freely from literal sex-work reference into general slut-shaming; widely understood across all Arabic-speaking regions regardless of dialect.

records.definition: An extremely crude slur for a promiscuous woman, slut, or whore; among the most intensely offensive Arabic terms for female sexual immorality, deployed both literally and as a maximally derogatory all-purpose insult.
records.notes: Rivals قحبة in vulgarity; somewhat more common in Levantine and Egyptian dialects as a slut-shaming term than a strict sex-work designation; among the harshest things one can call an Arabic-speaking woman; etymology uncertain, possibly Aramaic or Turkish.

records.definition: Prostitution or sex work as a social and legal phenomenon; the standard Modern Standard Arabic clinical and journalistic term for the practice of exchanging sex for money.
records.notes: Default MSA term in law, journalism, and public health; not particularly crude due to formal register, though the subject carries cultural stigma; appears in compounds such as بيت الدعارة (brothel) and شبكة دعارة (prostitution ring).

records.definition: A brothel or house of prostitution; the standard compound noun in Modern Standard Arabic legal, journalistic, and formal contexts for a premises where commercial sex is conducted.
records.notes: Literal translation: 'house of prostitution.' Standard MSA phrase used in legislation, law-enforcement reporting, and journalism throughout the Arab world; clinical register despite referring to an illicit institution.

records.definition: A brothel or house of ill repute; a more literary and classical Arabic compound for a brothel, drawing on the Quranic term بغيّ (harlot) rather than the modern clinical دعارة.
records.notes: More archaic and literary than بيت الدعارة; appears in classical texts and older journalism; carries stronger religious and moral overtones due to the Quranic root بغي; less common in contemporary MSA usage.

records.definition: A pimp or procurer who manages sex workers and profits from their earnings; also used as a general insult for a contemptible, dishonorable, or opportunistic man.
records.notes: Root قاد (to lead) frames this as 'leader of prostitutes'; doubles as a common insult meaning roughly 'dishonorable opportunist' with no strict sex-work implication; widely understood across Arabic dialects.

records.definition: A pimp, procurer, or man who profits from or facilitates prostitution; also a crude insult for an effeminate, passive, or morally debased man, especially one perceived as homosexual.
records.notes: Predominantly Egyptian and Levantine colloquial; carries heavy honor-shame connotations beyond the sex-work meaning; also deployed as a homophobic insult for a passive gay man; extremely offensive on multiple cultural axes simultaneously.

records.definition: A streetwalker or sex worker who solicits clients in public; literally 'snatcher,' evoking the image of a woman who seizes passersby for sexual business.
records.notes: Primarily Egyptian colloquial; the literal meaning 'snatcher/kidnapper' is repurposed as a vivid metaphor for street solicitation; not widely used in formal MSA contexts or outside Egypt and the Levant.

records.definition: A colloquial and derogatory Egyptian Arabic term for a red-light district or neighborhood known for prostitution; literally 'donkey alley,' evoking baseness and animalistic degradation.
records.notes: Highly colloquial Egyptian slang; the donkey (ḥimār) metaphor implies brutishness and sexual availability as degradation; not used in formal or pan-Arabic contexts; name may also reference specific historical Cairo neighborhoods.

records.definition: Pornography or pornographic material; the standard Modern Standard Arabic term for explicit sexual content, derived from the root أباح (to permit), ironically invoking permissibility for content widely considered forbidden.
records.notes: Used in law, journalism, and content regulation; relatively clinical despite its subject matter; the root أباح (to permit/make lawful) creates an interesting semantic tension given that such content is legally and religiously prohibited across most Arab states.

records.definition: Pornographic films; the standard MSA compound noun for filmed sexually explicit content, used in legal, journalistic, and regulatory contexts throughout the Arab world.
records.notes: Literal translation: 'permissive/pornographic films'; standard in legislation and media reporting; less loaded than colloquial alternatives; widely understood across all Arabic-speaking regions; frequently appears in criminal statutes and content-moderation policy.

records.definition: Pornographic material or explicit sexual content in any medium; a broad compound noun used in legal and journalistic contexts to cover films, images, and digital content collectively.
records.notes: The prompt romanizes this as 'mādd' (singular) but the Arabic مواد is plural (mawādd, 'materials/substances'); the plural broadens the term to encompass any medium; standard in Arab-state legislation banning explicit content and in platform content-moderation policy.

records.definition: Commercial sex or the transactional exchange of sexual services for money; a clinical MSA phrase used in public health, human rights, and social-science discourse on sex work.
records.notes: Formal clinical compound that deliberately avoids moral framing; common in UN and NGO reports written in or translated into Arabic; less common in street-level discourse than دعارة; carries a neutral bureaucratic register.

records.definition: Body rental; a euphemistic or polemical phrase describing the purchase of sexual services, framing sex work as the temporary hire of a human body rather than naming the sexual act directly.
records.notes: Not standard terminology; appears in polemical, religious, and feminist Arabic discourse to describe or critique sex work; the commodification framing (rental rather than sale) is rhetorically charged and appears more in opinion writing than in legislation or everyday speech.

records.definition: A sexual broker, procurer, or intermediary who arranges sex work transactions, functioning as a pimp, trafficker, or agent connecting clients with sex workers.
records.notes: سمسار is the standard Arabic word for broker or middleman (real estate, stock market); combining it with جنسي (sexual) creates a formal, somewhat euphemistic compound that appears in legal and journalistic contexts rather than colloquial speech.

records.definition: The sex trade or sex industry as a commercial and social institution; a formal MSA compound for the organized commercial exchange of sexual services.
records.notes: Literal translation: 'commerce of sex'; used in human rights reporting, anti-trafficking legislation, and academic Arabic texts; more neutral in framing than moralistic alternatives like دعارة; common in pan-Arab media coverage of trafficking.

records.definition: Sexual exploitation; a formal legal and human rights term for the coercive use of persons for sexual purposes, encompassing trafficking, forced prostitution, and abuse of power differentials.
records.notes: Standard MSA legal and NGO terminology; broader than sex trafficking alone (which implies transport and recruitment) but mapped there as closest registry concept; appears in UN conventions in Arabic translation, domestic legislation, and regional media covering trafficking and abuse.

records.definition: A male condom; the formal Modern Standard Arabic clinical term for a penile sheath contraceptive, literally meaning 'male protector' or 'male shield.'
records.notes: Preferred in public health communications and medical contexts; واقٍ means 'protector/shield' (active participle of وقى, to protect) and ذكري means 'male'; less common in colloquial speech where loanwords or عازل dominate depending on region.

records.definition: A colloquial loanword for condom, borrowed from French 'capote'; used primarily in North African and Levantine colloquial Arabic among French-influenced Maghrebi speakers.
records.notes: From French 'capote' (literally 'hood'); strongest in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Lebanon due to French colonial linguistic legacy; less familiar in Gulf or Egyptian Arabic where عازل or واقٍ ذكري are preferred; carries a slightly casual or street-level register relative to clinical MSA alternatives.

records.definition: A condom or barrier contraceptive; derived from the Arabic root عزل (to isolate or insulate), used in both clinical and everyday speech as a relatively neutral term for a condom.
records.notes: The root عزل (isolation/insulation) gives this a physical-barrier framing analogous to an electrical insulator; used in health campaigns and colloquial speech; more widely understood across dialects than واقٍ ذكري but less colloquially embedded than كابوت in the Maghreb.

records.definition: Pregnancy; the condition of carrying a developing fetus in the uterus; the standard Modern Standard Arabic term for pregnancy across all registers from clinical to everyday speech.
records.notes: حمل also means 'carrying/bearing' in non-reproductive senses (e.g., carrying a load), giving it a mild euphemistic quality in reproductive contexts; universally understood; no registry equivalent exists, hence novel concept flag despite a direct English translation.

records.definition: Abortion or miscarriage; the termination of a pregnancy whether spontaneous or induced; the standard Modern Standard Arabic clinical and legal term used in medical, religious, and legislative discourse.
records.notes: Arabic إجهاض covers both spontaneous miscarriage and induced abortion without distinguishing them lexically, unlike English; context determines meaning; heavily charged in Islamic jurisprudence and subject to legal restriction across most Arab states; marked novel because no registry entry covers this concept.

records.definition: Contraception or birth control; the standard Modern Standard Arabic compound for methods used to prevent pregnancy, literally 'prevention of pregnancy.'
records.notes: Literal translation: 'prevention of pregnancy'; used in public health, medical, and NGO family-planning contexts; neutral clinical register; widely used across the Arab world in family planning campaigns and reproductive health discourse.

records.definition: Pubic hair removal; the shaving of pubic hair, mandated in Islam as a fitra hygiene practice.
records.notes: One of five fitra practices per hadith; Islamic jurisprudence sets a recommended maximum interval of 40 days; the religious framing reduces secular shame relative to Western discourse; literally 'shaving the pubic region' (العانة = pubic area).

records.definition: Female genital mutilation; the partial or total removal of external female genitalia for cultural or purported religious reasons.
records.notes: Literally 'female circumcision'; the neutral-seeming name functions as a sanitizing euphemism in pro-FGM discourse; human-rights Arabic prefers 'تشويه الأعضاء التناسلية الأنثوية'; prevalence high in Egypt, Somalia, Sudan, parts of Yemen; practice predates Islam and is not mandated by any of the four major Sunni schools.

records.definition: Sadism; sexual gratification derived from inflicting pain, humiliation, or suffering on a partner.
records.notes: Arabized calque of the European psychological term, derived from the Marquis de Sade; known primarily in educated and psychology-literate circles; also used non-sexually in political and social commentary to mean generalized cruelty.

records.definition: Masochism; sexual gratification derived from experiencing pain, humiliation, or subjugation.
records.notes: Arabized transliteration named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch; less commonly known than سادية among general MSA speakers; primarily encountered in psychological literature and internet discourse; sometimes spelled ماسوشية in informal contexts.

records.definition: Sadomasochism; a practice or person combining both sadistic and masochistic elements in sexual activity.
records.notes: Compound of the two Arabized transliterations; found primarily in psychology texts and journalism; the acronym SM is not in common MSA use; recognition limited to educated and internet-connected speakers.

records.definition: Physical restraint; in sexual/kink contexts, the erotic practice of restraining a partner with ropes, cuffs, or other means.
records.notes: General MSA word with broad non-sexual applications (legal confinement, restricted access, document registration); the BDSM meaning is secondary and understood only in kink-aware circles; crude score reflects erotic connotation rather than the base word, which is clinically neutral.

records.definition: Bonds, fetters, or physical restraints; in a sexual context, the binding of a partner for erotic purposes.
records.notes: Classical and Quranic Arabic word for fetters or chains (root و ث ق, 'to bind firmly'); literary register gives it an archaic flavor compared to the more prosaic تقييد; occasionally used in Arabic-language erotica or BDSM writing for its elevated register; recognition lower than تقييد due to literary/archaic character.

records.definition: Sexual deviance or perversion; any behavior or orientation judged to deviate from religiously and socially sanctioned norms, deployed to condemn homosexuality, premarital sex, BDSM, and other non-normative sexuality.
records.notes: Literally 'sexual deviation'; commonly deployed in MSA media, religious fatwas, and legal discourse as a condemnation term; mapped to paraphilia as the nearest clinical concept but انحراف جنسي is inherently pejorative and morally loaded, unlike the neutral DSM term.

records.definition: Sexual deviance or abnormality; the dominant MSA legal and religious term for homosexuality, carrying inherent condemnation and used to criminalize LGBTQ identity across Arab jurisdictions.
records.notes: Literally 'sexual abnormality' (شذوذ = deviation/aberration); the primary official Arabic term used against LGBTQ people in legislation, media, and religious discourse; criminalized under شذوذ جنسي statutes in many Arab countries; broader than 'sodomite' since it encompasses all non-normative sexuality, not only anal sex; mapped to sodomite as the closest registry concept combining legal/religious condemnation.

records.definition: Sexual slavery or sexual submission; used in BDSM contexts for consensual total-power-exchange, and in general MSA discourse for coerced sex slavery or trafficking.
records.notes: Ambiguous between consensual BDSM submission and literal coerced sex slavery; kink-section context maps to bdsm_submission; in Arabic news and legal discourse عبودية جنسية far more commonly refers to trafficking or ISIS-documented enslavement of Yazidi women; the BDSM reading is a Western import known to internet-connected demographics.

records.definition: Dominance and submission; the BDSM dynamic in which one partner exercises consensual authority over the other.
records.notes: Calque of English 'dominance and submission'; used in Arabic-language BDSM and psychology writing; هيمنة (dominance/hegemony) is mainstream MSA while خضوع (submission/compliance) carries Quranic resonance; the pairing in an explicitly sexual-kink context is a modern Western import.

records.definition: A fetish; sexual arousal triggered by a specific object, body part, or scenario not typically considered inherently sexual.
records.notes: Direct phonetic transliteration of English 'fetish'; native alternatives such as 'هوس جنسي' or 'شهوة محددة' appear in clinical texts but فيتيش dominates online discourse; recognition concentrated among younger, internet-exposed demographics.

records.definition: Exhibitionist desire; sexual arousal derived from exposing oneself or performing sexually in front of others.
records.notes: Descriptive compound (شهوة = lust/desire, استعراض = display/showing off) rather than a loanword; the registry concept names the person while this phrase names the desire, hence approximate; alternative phrasing 'شهوة التعري' also used; the concept is less commonly discussed in Arabic psychological and social discourse than in Western contexts.

records.definition: The act of covertly watching others in intimate or sexual situations for sexual gratification; voyeurism or peeping.
records.notes: Verbal noun of laṣṣaṣa (to spy/peep); applies equally to non-sexual spying; the sexual sense is contextually disambiguated; used in both clinical psychiatric texts and everyday speech.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse between close blood relatives; the standard MSA clinical and legal term for incest.
records.notes: Sifāḥ = illicit fornication; qurbā = close kin; strictly legal and clinical in primary usage; carries extreme social and religious stigma; mapped to paraphilia_general as no incest-specific concept exists in the registry.

records.definition: Plural of maḥram: blood relatives with whom marriage and sex are forbidden in Islamic law; repurposed in pornographic slang as a synonym for incest content.
records.notes: The primary meaning is sacred-legal (the maḥram system governs veiling and travel obligations in Islamic practice); profane sexual repurposing is maximally transgressive, which drives the crude score to 90 despite the term itself being mainstream religious vocabulary.

records.definition: Sexual games or sex toys; a broad phrase covering erotic power games, bedroom play, and physical sex devices.
records.notes: Structurally ambiguous: alʿāb can mean both games (activities) and toys (objects); context disambiguates; increasingly common in online health-education and e-commerce discourse; not restricted to BDSM.

records.definition: Sexual role play: consensual erotic enactment of scenarios, personas, or power dynamics between partners.
records.notes: In non-sexual contexts simply means theatrical role play; sexual meaning is entirely contextual; mapped to bdsm_play as the closest registry concept, though sexual roleplay is broader than BDSM and does not inherently imply power exchange.

records.definition: Sexual cross-dressing or erotic costume play; wearing clothing or adopting the persona of another gender for sexual purposes.
records.notes: Tanakkur = disguise or masquerade; the qualifier jinsī (sexual/gender) narrows it to erotic or gender-transgressive dress; recognition is moderate because the compound is a constructed clinical phrase rather than organic colloquial slang.

records.definition: Sexual narcissism: deriving sexual arousal primarily from oneself, or from being admired, watched, or mirrored by others during sexual activity.
records.notes: Academic psychological compound; narjisiyya is borrowed from Greek via English/French Narcissus; low recognition because it is clinical jargon rather than organic slang; mapped to paraphilia_general as the nearest registry concept, though sexual narcissism is a personality-trait framing rather than a discrete paraphilia.

records.definition: Childhood or infantile sexuality; in kink contexts, erotic age regression in which adult participants consensually adopt child-like personas.
records.notes: The phrase literally means 'infantile sexuality' and appears in non-kinky clinical developmental psychology texts; in sexual contexts it denotes ageplay or infantilism; crude is elevated because sexualization of childhood registers as an extreme cultural taboo regardless of whether the participants are adults.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual acts with animals; a softened phrasing using 'love' rather than clinical or crude terminology.
records.notes: Ḥubb (love) substantially softens the phrase; zoophilia chosen over bestiality because ḥubb implies emotional attraction rather than purely behavioral contact; concept is widely recognized even though the topic is severely taboo.

records.definition: A sexual fantasy or erotic illusion; a mentally constructed scenario used for sexual arousal.
records.notes: Wahm = illusion, delusion, or unfounded impression; the sexual fantasy concept has no dedicated registry slot, so mapped to eroticism as the closest available concept; wahm carries a mild pathologizing undertone (delusion/false belief) that distinguishes it from neutral 'fantasy.'

records.definition: The commodification or objectification of the body; treating a person's body as a purchasable or exploitable sexual commodity.
records.notes: Taslīʿ = to turn into a commodity (from silʿa = tradeable good); a feminist critical-theory term more academic and political than kinky in primary usage; included in kink section because it appears in analyses of BDSM, commercial sex, and pornography.

records.definition: Desire or lust for pain; the erotic attraction to experiencing physical or psychological pain.
records.notes: Shahwa = lust/appetite/desire; alam = pain/suffering; a descriptive Arabic compound rather than a borrowed clinical label; default reading is masochistic (receiving pain) but the phrase could theoretically describe sadism depending on context; no explicit BDSM connotation.

records.definition: Sexual relations or intercourse; the most common polite classical Arabic euphemism, derived from the root for 'living together' or 'association.'
records.notes: Quranic usage (Q2:187 muʿāsharat bi-l-maʿrūf) gives it religious sanction and makes it the default register-neutral term for sex in formal MSA; appears in medical, legal, marital-guidance, and religious contexts.

records.definition: Conjugal sexual relations between spouses; the formal Islamic jurisprudential term for marital intercourse.
records.notes: Al-zawjayn = 'the two spouses'; explicitly frames intercourse within the marital contract; extremely low crude because the marital framing carries full Islamic sanction; standard in fiqh literature and fatwa rulings on marital rights and duties.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; a classical Arabic term for lying together in the sexual sense, from the root ḍajaʿa (to lie down).
records.notes: More anatomically direct than al-muʿāshara; the root implies shared horizontal position; appears in classical erotic literature (e.g., Rawḍ al-ʿĀṭir) and modern clinical texts; higher crude than معاشرة because the root is more explicitly physical rather than social.

records.definition: Union or joining; a classical poetic and Sufi-inflected euphemism for sexual union, often connoting emotional and spiritual consummation as well as the physical act.
records.notes: Root waṣala (to join/connect); heavily laden with Sufi mystical connotations (union with God); when applied to human lovers it implies deep intimacy alongside physical joining; near-zero crude because of its elevated poetic register.

records.definition: Seclusion of a man and woman alone together; in Islamic law this is forbidden outside marriage, and within marriage it euphemistically implies that sexual intimacy has occurred.
records.notes: A legal category in Islamic fiqh: a man and a non-maḥram woman alone together constitutes forbidden khalwa; post-marriage khalwa is therefore a euphemism for consummated intercourse; the word itself carries no crude connotation whatsoever, but the sexual implication is universally understood.

records.definition: The wedding night; literally 'the night of entry,' referring to the first night of marriage during which sexual consummation traditionally takes place.
records.notes: Dakhla = entry; an extremely culturally central concept across the Arab world; the night carries enormous social weight around virginity, honor, and consummation; near-universal recognition across all Arabic-speaking populations; minor regional variation in ritual customs but the term itself is universal.

records.definition: Entry or penetration; a widespread MSA euphemism for penile-vaginal intercourse emphasizing the act of physical entry.
records.notes: Literally 'the entering'; in marital and legal contexts specifically denotes first intercourse that consummates a marriage; also used for subsequent acts; recognized across legal, religious, and everyday registers; slightly cruder than al-muʿāshara because the physical image is less abstracted.

records.definition: Touching or contact; a Quranic and classical Arabic term for sexual intercourse drawn from the root massa (to touch).
records.notes: Appears in Q2:237 and Q33:49 ('before you touch them') as a euphemism for consummated intercourse; Quranic sanction makes it entirely non-crude despite its sexual meaning; lower recognition than contemporary terms because of its classical register; used in classical fiqh to determine marriage and divorce rules.

records.definition: Fulfilling the sexual need; a functional religious framing of intercourse as a biological necessity to be satisfied within the sanctioned marital context.
records.notes: Qaḍāʾ al-ḥāja literally means 'meeting a need'; Islamic jurisprudence treats sex within marriage as both a right (ḥaqq) and a duty for both spouses; framing intercourse as a 'need' desexualizes and legitimizes the act, producing very low crude despite explicit subject matter.

records.definition: Physical pleasure or bodily enjoyment; a broad literary euphemism for sexual pleasure.
records.notes: Mutʿa = pleasure/enjoyment/benefit; jasadiyya = bodily/physical; deliberately broad — covers any physical pleasure, though in context implies intercourse; caution: mutʿa alone can denote the Shia temporary marriage contract (zawāj al-mutʿa), but that meaning requires fuller phrasing.

records.definition: Marital life; an extremely common and maximally polite euphemism for the sexual dimension of marriage.
records.notes: Literally 'the married life'; the sexual meaning is fully implied but never named; ubiquitous in media, marriage-counseling, and religious-guidance contexts; receives the lowest crude score in this dataset because the marital framing and total indirection are doubly sanitizing.

records.definition: Bodily pressing or clinging together; a euphemism for intimate physical contact including non-penetrative genital friction between partners.
records.notes: Root laṣaqa (to stick/adhere); implies bodies pressed tightly together; can cover the full range from romantic embrace to explicit non-penetrative genital rubbing; mapped to frottage as the closest registry concept, though the Arabic term is broader and does not necessarily imply genital contact.

records.definition: Fulfilling one's desire; a classical and Quranic euphemism for satisfying sexual need, implying the completion of the sexual act.
records.notes: Appears in Q33:37 (fa-lammā qaḍā Zaydun minhā waṭaran — 'when Zayd had fulfilled his desire from her'); waṭar = deep desire or longing; the Quranic occurrence made this phrase the canonical polite euphemism for consummated intercourse; recognition is lower than contemporary terms and skews toward religiously educated speakers.

records.definition: A literary or elevated phrase meaning 'physical passion' or 'bodily love,' used as a polite or poetic euphemism for sexual desire or carnal intimacy.
records.notes: Composed of ʿishq (intense, often tragic love) and jasadī (bodily/physical); more poetic than clinical, carries less explicit charge than direct sexual vocabulary.

records.definition: Literally 'drawing close' or 'coming together'; used euphemistically to imply sexual intimacy, exploiting the word's primary non-sexual meaning of convergence or rapprochement.
records.notes: Primary meaning is non-sexual (political rapprochement, physical proximity); the sexual inference is entirely contextual.

records.definition: Literally 'the private/special relationship'; a widespread Arabic euphemism for a romantic or sexual relationship, especially one illicit or outside the bounds of marriage.
records.notes: Khāṣṣa ('private/special') carries the euphemistic weight; broadly understood across Arabic-speaking regions.

records.definition: Literally 'physical/bodily love'; a polite euphemistic phrase for sexual love or physical intimacy, using ḥubb (love) rather than the more impassioned ʿishq.
records.notes: Slightly more demotic than al-ʿishq al-jasadī; both function as transparent euphemisms for sexual intimacy while avoiding explicit vocabulary.

records.definition: Literally 'sleeping with'; a common and universally understood Arabic euphemism for sexual intercourse, parallel to the English idiom 'sleeping with.'
records.notes: Near-calque of the English euphemism; understood across all registers and age groups.

records.definition: Classical Arabic phrase meaning 'coming to the wife' or 'approaching the wife'; a jurisprudential euphemism for marital sexual intercourse, used extensively in Islamic fiqh texts concerning conjugal rights and duties.
records.notes: Ityān (coming/approaching) is a classical euphemistic root for intercourse; appears in hadith and fiqh literature; now rare outside religious-legal scholarship.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term for sexual vigor, libido, and potency; the central concept of the 'kutub al-bāh' genre of classical Arabic erotic-medical literature.
records.notes: An entire classical Arabic literary and medical genre — kutub al-bāh — is named after this term; authors include al-Tīfāshī and Ibn Faḍlallāh; now essentially archaic outside academic contexts.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term carrying the dual meaning of 'marriage contract' and 'sexual intercourse'; used in the Quran and throughout classical jurisprudence, with context determining the operative meaning.
records.notes: High recognition because the term appears in Quranic and religious marriage contexts; the intercourse meaning is widely understood but considered crude in modern spoken Arabic; scholars debate which meaning is primary in Quranic usage.

records.definition: Classical Arabic technical term for sexual intercourse or coitus, derived from the root j-m-ʿ (to gather/unite); the standard clinical or jurisprudential equivalent of 'coitus' in classical texts.
records.notes: Appears extensively in classical fiqh, medicine, and erotic literature; more technical and less emotionally charged than colloquial alternatives; recognition higher among educated and religiously literate speakers.

records.definition: Literally 'enjoyment' or 'deriving benefit'; in classical Islamic jurisprudence denotes the sexual enjoyment of a spouse or concubine; in Shia Islam specifically refers to mutʿa (temporary marriage contracted for sexual purposes).
records.notes: General Arabic meaning is simply 'enjoyment' with no sexual connotation; the sexual jurisprudential sense is context-dependent; the Shia concept of zawāj al-mutʿa is sometimes called istimtāʿ alone.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term literally meaning 'to spread out as a bed/mattress'; a legal-literary euphemism for sexually possessing a slave woman or concubine, used in classical jurisprudential texts on the sexual rights of slaveholders.
records.notes: Metaphor treats the enslaved woman as a surface to lie upon; deeply embedded in the classical institution of concubinage; essentially unintelligible to modern Arabic speakers without classical training.

records.definition: Classical Arabic phrase literally meaning 'reaching/hitting the woman'; a jurisprudential euphemism for sexual intercourse with a woman, particularly the consummation of a marriage establishing conjugal cohabitation rights.
records.notes: From root ṣ-w-b (to reach the mark/hit the target); appears in hadith literature and fiqh; the violent-sounding literal meaning is purely etymological in this jurisprudential context.

records.definition: Classical Arabic and Islamic legal term for illicit sexual intercourse outside of marriage or lawful concubinage; a morally condemned category of sexual union contrasted with the licit nikāḥ.
records.notes: Etymologically linked to sifḥ (pouring/spilling), implying unlawful spilling of sexual fluid; distinguished in some classical texts from zinā by scope; carries heavy moral and religious condemnation in Islamic discourse.

records.definition: Classical Arabic and Quranic term for sexual obscenity, lewdness, or gross indecency; covers both immoral sexual behavior and foul speech; one of the most common Quranic terms for moral transgression.
records.notes: The feminine form fahshāʾ is the more common Quranic usage; fuḥsh is the masdar (verbal noun); appears in multiple Quranic injunctions prohibiting indecency.

records.definition: A classical Arabic term and recognized literary genre denoting shameless licentiousness and deliberate transgression of sexual and moral norms; the Abbasid tradition of bawdy, wine-celebrating, homoerotic, and sexually explicit poetry.
records.notes: Famous mujūn poets include Abū Nuwās and Ibn al-Ḥajjāj; the genre performs shamelessness as a literary stance, celebrating sexual transgression with brazen defiance; more culturally specific than any single English equivalent.

records.definition: A classical Arabic literary device referring to the erotic or amatory description of a beloved woman in verse, particularly in the opening section of a qasida; the poet's articulation of youthful passion and erotic longing.
records.notes: Derived from shāb (youth); closely overlaps with nasīb but emphasizes the poet's youthful passion and the erotic portrayal specifically; classical critics distinguished the two but usage was often interchangeable.

records.definition: The conventional amatory prelude of the classical Arabic qasida (ode), in which the poet evokes a departed beloved, describes her beauty, or recalls erotic encounters at an abandoned campsite; a foundational structural element of classical Arabic poetics.
records.notes: One of the defining structural features of the classical qasida; ranges from elegiac longing to explicit erotic description; the convention is so formalized that poets composed nasīb sections even for patron-addressed odes unrelated to actual beloveds.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term for sexual dissolution and moral licentiousness, from the root KH-L-ʿ (to strip off/cast away); metaphorically describes someone who has cast off the garment of propriety and moral restraint.
records.notes: The verb kharaʿa means to remove or cast off; khalāʿa thus implies the deliberate stripping away of social and moral norms; now largely archaic in everyday Arabic usage.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term for verbal or behavioral obscenity and gross vulgarity; covers sexually explicit language, foul speech, and any grossly indecent expression or behavior.
records.notes: More commonly applied to speech than fuḥsh, which encompasses acts as well; badhāʾa emphasizes the coarseness of expression rather than the immorality of the act.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term for a debauchee or dissolute person who indulges excessively in wine, sexual licentiousness, and other forbidden pleasures; a habitual sensualist.
records.notes: Combines connotations of heavy drinking and sexual dissolution; closely associated with the mujūn literary tradition; etymology uncertain, possibly Aramaic or foreign-origin; now essentially archaic.

records.definition: Classical Arabic noun and adjective for a licentious, bawdy, or shameless person; specifically one who practices mujūn — deliberate, defiant transgression of sexual and moral norms as a lifestyle or literary stance.
records.notes: Active participle of majana (to be brazen/shameless); Abū Nuwās is the paradigmatic māijn figure; the term implies not just immorality but a proud, performative rejection of convention; note: source romanization contained a Cyrillic typo.

records.definition: Classical Arabic and Islamic ethical term for moral suspicion, doubt, or the appearance of sexual impropriety; refers to situations or behaviors that generate suspicion of wrongdoing even without a concrete act having occurred.
records.notes: Islamic ethics prohibits placing oneself in situations of rayba; the foundational hadith 'abandon what causes you doubt for what does not' (da' mā yurībuka) anchors this ethical category; concerns social perception and moral precaution, not the act itself.

records.definition: Arabic verbal noun meaning 'nakedness' or 'the act of becoming naked/undressed'; used in classical erotic poetry to describe the nudity of a beloved and in modern contexts for nudity generally, including public nudity.
records.notes: No registry concept covers nudity as a distinct erotic state; taʿarrī encompasses both the state (being naked) and the process (undressing), and appears across classical erotic verse and modern Arabic discourse about public nudity or striptease.

records.definition: Plural of qayna; female slave entertainers in Abbasid-era Islamic civilization trained in music, singing, and poetry who also provided sexual companionship to wealthy male patrons; the Arabic world's closest historical equivalent to the courtesan.
records.notes: The qiyān were educated, artistically accomplished, and culturally influential yet enslaved; they were active contributors to classical Arabic poetry; their institution was distinct from street prostitution and closer to the Japanese geisha, though they were typically enslaved rather than independent.

records.definition: Classical Arabic term for a young male page, servant, or attendant; in classical homoerotic poetry (particularly the mujūn tradition), the waṣīf is a common erotic archetype — the beautiful young male servant who serves as the object of the poet's desire.
records.notes: Primary meaning is simply 'male servant' with no inherent sexual connotation; the erotic reading is specific to classical Arabic homoerotic poetry and the mujūn tradition; female equivalent is waṣīfa; appears alongside ghulām and sāqī as archetypes of the male beloved.

records.definition: A female slave who served as a concubine in classical Islamic society, legally available for her owner's sexual use under the institution of milk al-yamīn (right-hand possession).
records.notes: From the root j-r-y (to flow/run); a jāriya was legally distinct from a wife (zawja) but could be freed and elevated in status by bearing her master's child (umm al-walad). The institution was abolished across the Arab world in the 19th–20th centuries but the term persists in classical literature, Quranic exegesis, and historical fiction.

records.definition: The deliberate savoring of sensual or erotic pleasure; enjoying carnal delight with full conscious awareness.
records.notes: Masdar of Form V verb taladdhadha (to savor/enjoy), from root l-dh-dh (pleasure/delight). Found in classical mujūn literature and medieval medical texts on sexual pleasure. Modern educated readers can parse it; ordinary speakers would understand the word but not produce it in everyday speech.

records.definition: Uncovered, exposed, or naked; in sexual contexts, used to describe nudity or immodest physical exposure that violates norms of propriety.
records.notes: Passive participle of kashafa (to uncover/reveal). The word is common in everyday Arabic with no inherently sexual meaning; sexual and shameful connotations arise entirely from context. In honor-shame cultures, being makshūf carries moral weight beyond mere physical nakedness. No precise single-concept match in registry — mapped to indecency as closest available.

records.definition: One who has been publicly exposed and disgraced, especially for sexual misconduct; a person whose shameful acts have been brought to light before the community.
records.english_term: disgraced / publicly outed for sexual wrongdoing
records.notes: Passive participle of faḍaḥa (to expose/scandalize). Gender-neutral grammatically but applied with heavier social consequences when directed at women in traditional Arabic contexts. Maps only approximately to slut_shaming — mafḍūḥ applies to any public sexual or moral scandal, not specifically to promiscuity stigma. Central concept in honor-shame discourse.

records.definition: Sexual craving or appetite; the intense desire for carnal gratification.
records.notes: Masdar of Form V verb tashahhā (to crave), from root sh-h-w (appetite/desire). The simpler root-form shahwa (carnal desire) is far more common in everyday and religious discourse; al-tashahhī is the elevated literary variant. Appears in classical erotic manuals such as The Perfumed Garden. The definite article in the input (al-) indicates nominal/citation form.

records.definition: The deliberate act of seeking out and savoring erotic or sensual pleasure; the cultivation of carnal delight as an end in itself.
records.notes: Masdar of Form X verb istaladhdha (to seek/find delectable), from root l-dh-dh. More formal and rarer than taladdudh; carries a connotation of intentional, connoisseur-like pursuit of pleasure rather than mere experience of it. Found primarily in classical medical and erotic literature; unlikely to be produced in contemporary speech.

records.definition: Pleasurable intimate companionship; in classical mujūn literature, the shared enjoyment of drink, music, and sexual pleasure in refined erotic company.
records.notes: From ʾanisa (to be intimate/familiar with); the root ʾ-n-s connotes warmth, familiarity, and comfort. Sexual connotations are entirely context-dependent: in religious or neutral contexts the word simply means socializing or conviviality; in mujūn poetry it implies erotic companionship. The registry match intimate_physical_play captures the physical register but loses the social and intellectual dimensions of the classical concept.

records.definition: Playful caressing or erotic fondling of the beloved; intimate foreplay between lovers, described in elevated literary language.
records.notes: Mudāʿaba (Form III masdar of daʿaba, to play/jest) implies reciprocal playful interaction; al-ḥabīb (the beloved) supplies the relational frame. This is a phrase rather than a fixed single-word term. Recognizable to educated Arabic readers of classical love poetry and erotic manuals, but not in active contemporary use.

records.definition: Sex; sexual intercourse; a direct phonological adaptation of English 'sex' that functions as the dominant colloquial and internet term for sexual activity across the Arabic-speaking world.
records.notes: One of the most ubiquitous sexual loanwords in Arabic internet usage. Crude rating is high because even this clinical-in-English concept is strongly taboo in public Arabic speech; the loanword avoids triggering the full shame load of native Arabic terms while retaining high recognizability. Used across search queries, messaging, and social media pan-regionally.

records.definition: Porn; a direct phonological adaptation of English 'porn' used in Arabic internet, messaging, and search contexts.
records.notes: The shortened form coexists with the fuller بورنو (bornū). Both spellings circulate interchangeably; بورن may be the more common in typing-heavy contexts due to fewer keystrokes. Familiar to virtually all Arabic internet users regardless of whether they consume the content.

records.definition: Porno; a phonological adaptation of English 'porno' used in Arabic internet and youth contexts, competing with the shorter بورن.
records.notes: The -o suffix version preserves more of the source word's phonetic shape. No meaningful semantic difference from بورن; choice between them is stylistic or regional. Both terms are well-established in Arabic internet lexicon and appear across Gulf, Levantine, and North African usage.

records.definition: Pornographic; obscene; licentious — the standard Arabic adjective for sexually explicit or pornographic content, used in formal media, news reporting, and casual speech alike.
records.notes: Derived from ibāḥa, an Islamic jurisprudential term for religious permissibility; the word has been repurposed to mean 'licentious/pornographic,' an ironic inversion since pornography is decidedly non-permissible under Islamic law. Lower crude score than loanword alternatives because the Arabic root disguises the referent slightly; used in formal contexts (محتوى إباحي = pornographic content) without the same social charge as بورن.

records.definition: Nude images or photographs; a direct adaptation of English 'nude' used primarily in the context of requesting or sharing naked pictures digitally.
records.notes: Used almost exclusively in messaging and internet contexts to mean naked photographs rather than artistic nudity. The Arabic phonological shape نود is close to the numeral نود (ninety) in some pronunciation contexts, enabling occasional obfuscation in messaging — 'send me a ninety' as code — though this is anecdotal rather than systematic.

records.definition: Sexting; the sending of sexually explicit messages, images, or videos via mobile device, adapted directly from English.
records.notes: The Arabic adaptation appends the English progressive suffix -ing as a phonological element rather than a morphological one. Recognition is lower than basic terms like سكس because the named activity is more specific and carries its own layer of social risk in Arabic contexts. More common among younger, digitally active speakers in Gulf and Levantine communities.

records.definition: Sex video; a sexually explicit video, whether professional pornography or amateur content, using two fully transliterated English loanwords.
records.notes: A compound of two loanwords (video + sex) that functions as the dominant Arabic internet search phrase for pornographic video content. Extremely high search volume on Arabic-language versions of mainstream platforms. Covers both professionally produced pornography and user-generated amateur content.

records.definition: Hentai; Japanese animated or illustrated pornography, borrowed into Arabic from Japanese via English-language global internet culture.
records.notes: Borrowed from Japanese hentai (pervert/perversion) via the global anime and gaming internet communities. Recognition concentrated among Arabic youth with anime or gaming interests; meaningless to older or less internet-exposed speakers. The Arabic rendering هنتاي is phonetically close to the English/Japanese source. Use is pan-Arab but density is highest in Gulf and Levantine online communities.

records.definition: Cam sex; live sexual performance conducted via webcam, either as a commercial transaction or a casual video-call encounter.
records.notes: Compound loanword (cam + sex). Used in Arabic contexts for both commercial webcam sex work and informal video-call sexual exchanges.
