Less common as a search term than فيديو سكس because it implies a live, interactive element rather than recorded content. Well-known in relevant online communities.

records.definition: OnlyFans; the subscription-based content platform, used in Arabic internet contexts almost exclusively as shorthand for online sex work and explicit content creation.
records.notes: The platform name functions as a proper noun but has acquired generic connotations of digital sex work in Arabic public discourse. Awareness grew sharply 2020–2022 following mainstream media coverage of the platform. Recognition highest among Arabic speakers under 35 in Gulf and Levantine regions. Occasionally used by Arabic speakers to describe any subscription-based adult content, not exclusively the OnlyFans platform itself.

records.definition: Sexy; sexually attractive or arousing, borrowed directly from English and used extensively in Arabic internet, pop culture, and youth contexts.
records.notes: One of the most widely adopted English sexual loanwords in Arabic, likely because Arabic lacks a precise single-word colloquial equivalent that is socially tolerable in casual public speech — the native terms for sexual attractiveness (فاتن, مثير) carry heavier formal or religious freight. Crude score is relatively low because exposure through pop music, advertising, and film has partially normalized the term.

records.definition: Hot; sexually or physically attractive, borrowed from English and used in Arabic online and youth slang as a casual descriptor of appeal.
records.notes: Competes with سيكسي as the primary Arabic internet term for sexual attractiveness. هوت feels slightly less explicitly sexual and carries a lower crude rating as a result. Written with initial ه (hā), phonetically distinct from the Arabic word for whale حوت (ḥūt, written with ح), so no orthographic ambiguity in Arabic script. Widely understood across age groups due to saturation of English-language media.

records.definition: Snapchat sex; the exchange of sexual images, videos, or live video via Snapchat, exploiting the platform's ephemeral disappearing-content feature to reduce evidence risk.
records.notes: Compound of Snap (Snapchat abbreviated) + saks (sex). Snapchat's disappearing-message feature made it popular for sexual content exchange in Arabic-speaking markets where digital evidence of sexual behavior poses serious social and sometimes legal risk. Recognition is higher in Gulf Arabic internet communities where Snapchat adoption has been especially strong.

records.definition: Live sexual broadcast; real-time internet streaming of sexual acts using native Arabic vocabulary rather than loanwords.
records.notes: Fully Arabic phrase: bathth (broadcast/streaming) + mubāshir (direct/live) + jinsī (sexual). Represents the formal Arabic description of camming as it appears in news coverage, content moderation policy, and academic discourse, contrasting with the informal loanword term كام سكس. The word jinsī (from jins, sex/gender) is the standard Arabic adjective for 'sexual' across formal registers.

records.definition: Sexual TikTok; provocative or sexually suggestive content posted on TikTok, or the broader genre of such content on the platform.
records.english_term: sexual TikTok content / TikTok thirst trap
records.notes: Hybrid phrase combining the loanword brand name TikTok with the Arabic adjective jinsī (sexual). Functions as a descriptive label rather than a fixed idiom; can refer to anything from suggestive dances to more explicitly sexual videos on the platform. Mapped to thirst_trap as the most representative concept in the registry, though the phrase is broader than that single concept.

records.definition: FWB (Friends with Benefits); a sexual arrangement between friends without romantic commitment, rendered as a letter-by-letter Arabic phonological transliteration of the English acronym.
records.notes: Arabic transliteration of the English acronym, used by younger Arabic speakers with strong English internet fluency. The concept of friends-with-benefits is culturally alien in traditional Arabic social frameworks where non-marital sex is formally prohibited; the term therefore functions as an in-group marker among westernized youth. Recognition is notably lower than basic loanwords because it requires familiarity with the English acronym itself.

records.definition: Friends with benefits; a full phonological transliteration of the English phrase into Arabic script, used when the arrangement is referenced directly rather than by acronym.
records.notes: The spelled-out form coexists with the acronym إف دبليو بي and carries slightly higher recognition because it preserves the full English phonetic signal. Both forms index westernized relationship norms incompatible with traditional Arabic social structures, functioning as markers of cosmopolitan or diasporic Arabic-speaking identity. No known regional variation; usage is distributed across digitally active Arabic-speaking communities globally.

records.definition: Sexual weakness; a general term for diminished sexual function, libido, or performance capacity; encompasses erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, and general loss of sexual drive.
records.notes: Broader and less clinical than عجز جنسي; extremely common in popular health content and supplement advertising; ḍaʿf (weakness) is among the most common MSA lexical items, making this phrase widely accessible.

records.definition: Sexual incapacity; clinical term for the inability to perform sexually, particularly male erectile dysfunction or inability to complete intercourse.
records.notes: Literally 'sexual incapacity/inability'; عجز (ʿajz) means incapacity more broadly; more formal and clinical than ضعف جنسي; used in urology, psychology, and medical literature.

records.definition: Sexual frigidity or coldness; lack of sexual desire or physical responsiveness; applied to both sexes but most commonly discussed in relation to women.
records.notes: Literally 'sexual coldness'; برود (burūd) is the standard Arabic word for physical and emotional coldness; conflates low libido, arousal disorder, and emotional distance; appears in health media, marriage counseling content, and Islamic self-help literature.

records.definition: Sexual insufficiency or deficiency; clinical term for inadequate sexual function, covering erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, and insufficient sexual performance.
records.notes: Literally 'sexual shortcoming/falling short'; قصور (quṣūr) means falling short of a standard; more formal and less common than ضعف جنسي or عجز جنسي; appears primarily in medical and psychological literature.

records.definition: Sexual energy or capacity; the overall level of sexual drive and physical capability for sexual activity; closely related to libido.
records.notes: Literally 'sexual energy/power'; طاقة (ṭāqa) means energy, capacity, or power; ubiquitous in sexual health supplement advertising, popular psychology, and self-help content across the Arab world; used for both sexes.

records.definition: The virile man; a man celebrated for his sexual potency and masculine dominance; literally 'the man who is a stud animal,' used as a stock phrase valorizing idealized masculine sexuality.
records.notes: Definite-article form functioning as a cultural stock phrase; more emphatic than فحل alone; embodies the Arabic cultural ideal of aggressive masculine virility; used in discourse about idealized manhood and sexual capability.

records.definition: A male lover or beloved; a man in a romantic or sexual relationship, often illicit or adulterous; in classical poetry, the worshipful admirer devoted to an idealized beloved.
records.notes: From root ع-ش-ق denoting intense passionate love (ʿishq); in classical Sufi poetry refers to the mystic lover seeking union with the divine; in modern MSA often implies an illicit or extramarital relationship; feminine form عشيقة carries stronger moral condemnation due to the honor-shame double standard.

records.definition: A female lover or mistress; a woman in a romantic or sexual relationship, often illicit or adulterous; carries stronger moral condemnation than the masculine form ʿashīq.
records.notes: Feminine form of عشيق (ʿashīq); higher crude score reflects the honor-shame double standard whereby a woman's sexual transgression is condemned far more severely than a man's; used in news media to describe affairs and in classical Sufi poetry for the soul or divine beloved.

records.definition: An intimate female companion or beloved; in romantic or erotic contexts, a female lover or close intimate partner; more veiled in sexual implication than عشيقة.
records.notes: Feminine form of خليل (khalīl); from root خ-ل-ل denoting closeness and intimacy; can be purely platonic or erotic depending on context; appears in classical and modern poetry; falling out of everyday colloquial use.

records.definition: An intimate male companion; a close friend or, in romantic contexts, a male lover; also the Quranic epithet of the Prophet Ibrahim meaning 'intimate friend of God.'
records.notes: Widely known as a common male given name (e.g. Khalil Gibran); Quranic use as Ibrahim's epithet (خليل الله) gives it a sacred dimension that complicates erotic use; the sexual connotation is secondary and context-dependent; less sexually charged than عشيق.

records.definition: A concubine; a woman held in sexual servitude by a man, typically enslaved, with lower legal status than a wife; a classical institution regulated in Islamic law.
records.notes: Etymologically linked to سر (sirr, secret) or سرور (surūr, joy); in classical Islamic law a surriyya was typically an enslaved woman whose owner had exclusive sexual rights; institution abolished in most Arab states in the 20th century but remains referenced in religious and historical discourse.

records.definition: A co-wife; one of a man's multiple wives in a polygamous marriage; specifically denotes the rival wife from another wife's perspective, with strong connotations of jealousy, competition, and grievance.
records.notes: Derived from ضرر (ḍarar, harm or damage), reflecting inherent enmity between co-wives; English 'co-wife' is a pale equivalent lacking the emotional and cultural weight of ḍurra; Arabic proverbs and folk literature treat the ḍurra relationship as inherently painful and competitive.

records.definition: A secret marriage; a private Islamic marriage contract (nikah) conducted without family or public knowledge, used to religiously legitimize a relationship while concealing it from social oversight.
records.notes: Distinct from cohabitation in that a formal religious marriage contract (nikah) exists; widely practiced among young Arabs seeking a religiously permissible relationship without family involvement; contested in Islamic jurisprudence over whether the requirement for a wali (guardian) and witnesses was properly fulfilled; sometimes exploited to deceive women who believe they are married while the man keeps the union hidden.

records.definition: Temporary marriage; a Shia Islamic contractual marriage for a fixed term (hours to years) with a negotiated dowry, after which the union automatically dissolves; accepted in Shia jurisprudence, forbidden in Sunni Islam.
records.notes: Also called nikāḥ al-mutʿa (pleasure marriage); condemned by Sunni scholars as institutionalized prostitution; in Shia fiqh governed by strict rules covering dowry (mahr), duration, waiting period (ʿidda), and child custody; a major doctrinal flashpoint in Sunni–Shia relations; practiced widely in Iran and Shia-majority communities of Iraq and Lebanon.

records.definition: Boyfriend; a male romantic and/or sexual partner in a non-marital relationship; a phonetic transliteration of English 'boyfriend,' signaling Western-influenced relationship norms.
records.notes: Phonetic Arabic-script rendering of English 'boyfriend'; the absence of a native Arabic equivalent reflects the cultural taboo around non-marital relationships; used primarily by younger, urban, educated Arabic speakers; the concept is borrowed alongside the word, representing a shift in relationship norms; transgressive in conservative contexts despite the neutral register of the loanword itself.

records.definition: Loanword from English 'girlfriend'; an unmarried female romantic partner, implying a non-marital relationship that is often socially transgressive in Arabic cultural contexts.
records.notes: English pronunciation preserved almost unchanged. In conservative Arabic contexts, openly having a 'girlfriend' implies premarital relations; the loanword signals urban modernity and Western influence, which is itself part of the social charge.

records.definition: Literally 'friend' or 'companion'; used contextually as a euphemism for a boyfriend, allowing speakers to reference an unmarried romantic partner while maintaining plausible deniability.
records.notes: Primary meaning is simply 'friend'; the romantic reading depends entirely on context, tone, and audience. Choosing this word rather than a more explicit term signals the speaker's awareness of the social risk in naming the relationship directly.

records.definition: Feminine form of ṣāḥib; literally 'female friend' or 'companion,' used euphemistically to refer to an unmarried female romantic partner.
records.notes: Same deniability function as the masculine form. The ambiguity between 'friend' and 'girlfriend' is the communicative feature, not a flaw. A man mentioning his ṣāḥiba in certain tones unambiguously signals a romantic relationship without ever naming it.

records.definition: A secret romantic or sexual partner; implies a clandestine relationship, either premarital or extramarital, conducted covertly to avoid family or social consequences.
records.notes: ḥabīb means 'beloved' or 'lover'; sirrī means 'secret.' The compound communicates both emotional depth and the shame economy requiring secrecy. Applicable to premarital relationships as well as affairs; the secrecy itself signals that both parties know the relationship violates social norms.

records.definition: Marital betrayal; a spouse engaging in sexual relations outside of marriage; adultery framed explicitly as a breach of honor and trust rather than merely as fornication.
records.notes: Khiyāna means 'betrayal' or 'treason'; zawjiyya means 'marital.' The framing foregrounds breach of contract and honor rather than the sexual act itself. Carries legal implications in most Arabic jurisdictions; in some countries it is a criminal offense or grounds for severe extra-legal punishment.

records.definition: That which is religiously lawful and permitted under Islamic law; in sexual contexts, designates acts and relationships — principally marital sex within a valid nikāḥ contract — that are divinely sanctioned.
records.notes: Forms the positive pole of the Islamic ḥalāl/ḥarām moral binary. Ubiquitous in non-sexual contexts (food, finance, cosmetics); the sexual application is a subset of the general jurisprudential classification. Widely borrowed into English in the food-labeling context, which has stripped most of its sexual moral charge for non-Arabic speakers.

records.definition: That which is religiously forbidden under Islamic law; in sexual contexts, encompasses all sexual acts and relationships outside of a valid marriage contract.
records.notes: Negative pole of the ḥalāl/ḥarām binary. Used in everyday speech as a general expression of moral disapproval extending far beyond formal jurisprudential contexts. Also informally borrowed into English. The term is not inherently crude; charge varies entirely with subject matter.

records.definition: In Islamic law, any sexual intercourse outside of a valid marriage contract, encompassing both premarital sex and adultery; one of the ḥudūd offenses with Quranically prescribed punishments.
records.notes: Broader than English 'fornication,' which typically denotes premarital sex only; zinā covers adultery as well. Quranic prescribed punishment is 100 lashes for unmarried parties (24:2); classical hadith scholarship adds stoning for married adulterers, though this is not explicit in the Quran. The word itself carries heavy moral weight far beyond its technical legal meaning.

records.definition: The Quranically-prescribed fixed punishment for zinā; classically interpreted as 100 lashes for unmarried offenders and stoning (rajm) for married adulterers, with an evidential threshold of four eyewitnesses to penetration.
records.notes: Ḥadd (pl. ḥudūd) means a fixed divine limit. The four-witness threshold makes formal enforcement nearly impossible, functioning historically more as a deterrent than a regularly applied sanction. Nevertheless enforced in Saudi Arabia, Iran, northern Nigeria, and parts of Pakistan. The stoning punishment derives from hadith, not explicitly from the Quran — a point of ongoing theological debate.

records.definition: Sexual immorality, obscenity, or lewd conduct; a Quranic term for any sexually wicked or indecent act, frequently deployed as condemnation of zinā and related sins.
records.notes: Used multiple times in the Quran in condemnation of sexual sin. Also used colloquially as a gendered insult for a promiscuous woman ('she is a fāḥisha'), functioning similarly to English 'slut' in that context — the slippage from theological category to personal insult is culturally significant.

records.definition: The Islamic marriage contract; the formal lawful union between husband and wife that sanctions sexual relations; by classical extension, also the sexual act itself within marriage.
records.notes: Root n-k-ḥ in classical Arabic denotes sexual intercourse; the term for marriage derives from this root, reflecting the right to sexual relations as constitutive of the contract. In colloquial usage, nikāḥ can be deployed crudely to mean 'fuck' — crude score climbs sharply in that register. The crude score here reflects the standard religious/legal register; colloquial sexual usage would score 80+.

records.definition: Temporary marriage contract of fixed duration, practiced in Twelver Shia Islam; a contractual union specifying a set period and financial compensation, functioning as a religiously sanctioned alternative to premarital sex.
records.notes: Explicitly permitted in Shia Islam, explicitly prohibited in Sunni Islam (abrogated per Umar according to Sunni tradition). Sunni critics characterize mutʿa as institutionalized prostitution. Widely practiced in Iran, Iraq, and Lebanese Shia communities. Distinct from nikāḥ dāʾim (permanent marriage) and from misyār.

records.definition: A form of Sunni Islamic marriage in which the wife contractually waives her rights to shared housing, financial maintenance, and equal time allocation with co-wives, typically conducted in secrecy and allowing both parties to maintain separate households.
records.notes: Controversial in Sunni jurisprudence: permitted by Saudi scholars including Ibn Baz and Ibn Uthaymeen, opposed by others as a legal fiction for clandestine affairs. Common in Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia. Often used by already-married men seeking additional partners without full financial obligation. Peak discourse approximately 2003–2007.

records.definition: Moral corruption or depravity, especially the act of corrupting others or spreading sexual immorality through society; carries connotations of active harm beyond one's own sin.
records.notes: Root f-s-d means to spoil, corrupt, or destroy. The Quranic phrase 'ifsād fī al-arḍ' (spreading corruption on earth) is among the gravest offenses in Islamic law and is cited as justification for capital punishment. In sexual contexts implies actively enabling or spreading immorality, not merely committing it oneself.

records.definition: Sexual wickedness, dissolute behavior, and moral dissipation; the habitual state of transgressing divine sexual prohibitions without remorse.
records.notes: Root f-j-r also yields fajr (dawn) from the image of the horizon splitting. Referenced in the Quran (91:8) as one of two paths (taqwā vs. fujūr). Fājir is the person living in fujūr. Used colloquially as a strong insult ('yā fājir' — you dissolute wretch), showing the slide from theological category to personal slur.

records.definition: Sin or moral transgression; in sexual contexts, the guilt and wrongdoing incurred by engaging in any Islamically forbidden sexual act.
records.notes: General Quranic term for moral wrongdoing, not restricted to sexual contexts but frequently applied to them. Contrasted with birr (righteousness). Less viscerally charged than fujūr; more the theological category of 'wrongful act' than a behavioral description. Plural āthām.

records.definition: A major or grave sin in Islamic theology; zinā, sodomy, and adultery are classified among the kabāʾir because they carry specific Quranic or Prophetic condemnation and in some cases prescribed punishments.
records.notes: The kabīra/ṣaghīra (major/minor sin) taxonomy is central to Islamic moral theology; rough analogy to Catholic mortal vs. venial sin, but without exact structural equivalence. Scholars differ sharply on the total number of kabāʾir (Ibn Hajar al-Haytami listed 467). Plural kabāʾir is more common in discourse than the singular form.

records.definition: Repentance from sexual sin; the sincere return to God after committing a forbidden sexual act, requiring cessation of the act, genuine remorse, and firm intention not to repeat it.
records.notes: Tawba (repentance) is a major concept in Islamic theology; jinsiyya (sexual) is a modern qualifier. The compound is more common in contemporary Islamic counseling and online fatwa contexts than in classical texts, which would specify 'al-tawba ʿan al-zinā.' Islamic tawba is conditionally complete only when all required conditions (cessation, remorse, resolve, and if a third party is harmed, making amends) are met.

records.definition: Satanic whispering; the demonic inner voice of temptation attributed to Iblīs that incites believers toward sin, including forbidden sexual acts; the primary mechanism in Islamic theology by which sexual desire for prohibited objects is provoked.
records.notes: Quranic term: Sura 114 (Al-Nās) addresses 'waswās al-khannās' (the slinking whisperer). Conceptually distinct from nafs al-ammāra (the commanding carnal self, which is internal appetite); waswasa is the external demonic instigation. Used in Islamic self-help and religious counseling to explain how believers are tempted toward sexual sin despite sincere faith.

records.definition: Forbidden entertainment or amusement; activities considered sinful in Islamic jurisprudence that arouse sexual desire or serve as pathways toward zinā, including certain music, mixed-gender dance, and sexually suggestive media.
records.notes: Lahw (idle amusement) is referenced negatively in the Quran (31:6, etc.). The compound is jurisprudential shorthand for entertainment crossing into ḥarām territory via its sexual-arousal function. Scholars disagree on which entertainments qualify; the prohibition is most consistently applied to music and dance associated with sexual arousal or intoxication.

records.definition: The mixing of unrelated men and women in the same social space; considered a religious prohibition in conservative Islamic jurisprudence because it creates the conditions of temptation and khalwa risk that may lead to zinā.
records.notes: Major policy issue in Saudi Arabia, where strict sex segregation in workplaces, schools, and public spaces was enforced until Vision 2030 reforms circa 2017. Derives not from explicit Quranic text but from sadd al-dharāʾiʿ (blocking the means to sin). Peak recognition estimated around 2009 when Saudi gender-integration debates received heavy international coverage.

records.definition: The deliberate display of a woman's physical beauty, adornments, or attractions to men who are not her husband or close male relatives; prohibited in Islamic law as fitna-inducing conduct.
records.notes: Quranic term (33:33): 'do not display yourselves as in the former times of ignorance.' Root b-r-j relates to towers and prominence — something that stands out and draws attention. Applied in contemporary Islamic discourse to tight clothing, public makeup, uncovered hair, or any behavior deemed to sexually expose a woman to non-mahram men.

records.definition: The state of a woman going uncovered or unveiled in public, particularly without the hijab; in conservative Islamic discourse, a sexual transgression because female visibility is understood through the lens of fitna.
records.notes: Antonym of ḥijāb (covering). Root s-f-r means to uncover, reveal, or depart on a journey. A woman described as sāfira in conservative religious contexts is implicitly labeled sexually transgressive, because her visible appearance is believed to provoke men. The concept is inseparable from the fitna framework in which female visibility in public is treated as a form of sexual exposure.

records.definition: Trial, temptation, or social disorder; in the context of gender and sexuality, the chaos and moral disruption attributed to unconstrained female beauty, used to justify modesty norms, gender segregation, and restrictions on women's public presence.
records.notes: Fitna has multiple primary meanings: civil war/strife, religious trial, and temptation. Al-fitna al-nisāʾiyya (female fitna) is a recognized theological discourse attributing social destabilization to uncontrolled female sexuality. Central to classical Islamic justifications for veiling, ikhtilāṭ prohibition, and guardianship systems. A hadith attributed to the Prophet: 'I have not left behind any trial more harmful to men than women.' No single English word captures the causal-societal claim embedded in this use of fitna.

records.definition: Forbidden seclusion; the state of an unrelated man and woman being alone together in an enclosed or private space, prohibited in Islamic law because it creates the conditions most likely to lead to zinā.
records.notes: Prophetic hadith: 'No man should be alone with a woman, and no woman should travel except with a mahram' (Bukhari/Muslim). The prohibition applies regardless of intent; the mere condition of privacy triggers the ruling. Historically used to police female movement and restrict mixed-gender professional interaction. Still invoked in conservative fatwas to oppose mixed workplaces and mixed-gender medical care.

records.definition: A shameful act, defect, or social taboo; in sexual contexts, behavior that violates community norms of propriety and brings personal or familial disgrace.
records.notes: Extremely common in everyday Arabic across all registers; used for anything from a social faux pas to serious sexual transgression; the sexual shame application is among its most culturally powerful uses.

records.definition: A public scandal or disgrace, especially the exposure of a woman's sexual transgression that destroys her reputation and her family's honor.
records.notes: While faḍīḥa applies to any public scandal, its most consequential and culturally loaded application is the exposure of a woman's sexual behavior; fear of faḍīḥa is a primary driver of honor-based violence and family control of female sexuality.

records.definition: The parts of the body that Islamic law requires to be covered; for men, the area between navel and knee; for most women, the entire body except face and hands; exposure of ʿawra is a religious violation rather than mere social impropriety.
records.notes: Goes far beyond 'private parts' — ʿawra is a religiously defined category creating legal obligations of concealment that also governs whose nudity any given person may lawfully view, intersecting with maḥram rules; its extent is debated across legal schools.

records.definition: Honor vengeance; retributive violence carried out to restore a family's sexual honor after a female member's transgression or rape, typically by killing her or her sexual partner.
records.notes: Emphasizes the retributive-vengeance framing of honor violence, contrasting with jarīmat al-sharaf which uses neutral crime language; the thaʾr framing positions the killing as a legitimate moral duty rather than a crime, drawing on pre-Islamic blood-vengeance traditions absorbed into Arab honor culture.

records.definition: An honor crime; a violent act, typically the murder of a female family member, committed to restore a family's damaged sexual honor after perceived or actual sexual transgression.
records.notes: The formal Arabic legal-journalistic term, prominent in human rights reporting; English 'honor killing' is a widely-used calque but lacks a canonical registry entry; the crime framing reflects a modern legal lens on a practice that honor culture frames as a legitimate duty.

records.definition: The defilement or pollution of family honor; the state of quasi-ritual disgrace that a woman's sexual transgression inflicts on her family's collective standing.
records.notes: Danas (filth/defilement) combined with sharaf (honor) creates a rhetorically powerful compound evoking ritual contamination; more literary and rhetorical than everyday usage; the pollution framing maps honor damage onto the Islamic concept of najāsa.

records.definition: A woman's reputation, understood in Arabic honor culture as almost entirely determined by her perceived sexual propriety and chastity rather than by personal achievements or character.
records.notes: A noun phrase rather than a single lexeme; in Arabic honor-shame culture sumʿat al-marʾa is structurally coextensive with her sexual virtue — professional or intellectual accomplishments rarely constitute a woman's 'reputation' in this sense.

records.definition: Chastity and sexual virtue in Islamic ethics; the quality of restraining sexual desires within lawful bounds, regarded as a cardinal virtue especially for women but enjoined on all believers.
records.notes: Unlike English 'prudishness' (negative) or 'sexual abstinence' (neutral behavioral description), ʿiffa is an unambiguously positive moral virtue; it also encompasses modesty in speech, gaze, and dress beyond merely refraining from sex.

records.definition: Modesty, bashfulness, and shame-consciousness as a positive Islamic virtue; in sexual contexts, the inhibition of displaying or discussing sexuality beyond prescribed norms, regarded as foundational to moral character.
records.notes: A prophetic hadith states 'al-ḥayāʾ min al-īmān' (modesty is a branch of faith), making it a core theological virtue; the closest English concept is 'prudishness' but that term carries entirely negative connotations that ḥayāʾ does not share.

records.definition: Disgrace, humiliation, or shame; in sexual contexts, the crushing public humiliation that befalls a family or individual as a result of sexual transgression becoming known.
records.notes: More literary and classical than ʿayb; used in Quranic language where it often connotes divine punishment and eternal shame; emphasizes the humiliating and crushing quality of the disgrace rather than the social-taboo dimension alone.

records.definition: The 'touching' or impugnment of someone's honor; behavior, rumors, or accusations that begin to tarnish a family's sexual reputation without necessarily constituting full public scandal.
records.notes: The euphemistic image of 'touching' (mass) implies incipient or partial violation rather than full defilement; appears in legal and journalistic contexts for lesser honor violations that may nonetheless trigger protective or retaliatory violence.

records.definition: The Islamic legal institution of male guardianship over women, granting male relatives authority over women's marriage, mobility, and sexual access; a central pillar of the honor-shame system controlling female sexuality.
records.notes: Formally institutionalized in Saudi Arabia's guardianship system; contested by Muslim feminists; the institution structurally treats a woman's sexuality as a family and male prerogative rather than her own autonomous domain.

records.definition: A male relative so closely related to a woman by blood, nursing, or marriage that marrying her is permanently prohibited; in Islamic law, a maḥram must accompany a woman on travel and serves as her guardian and sexual protector.
records.notes: The prohibition of marriage between a woman and her maḥram defines precisely who may legitimately guard her — an intersection of sexual prohibition and sexual guardianship unique to Islamic jurisprudence; the maḥram list includes father, brother, son, paternal uncle, and men related through nursing.

records.definition: The Islamic principle of concealing one's own and others' sins and sexual transgressions from public view; a positive religious virtue that prioritizes communal privacy over accountability for sexual misconduct.
records.notes: Hadith encourages sitr: 'whoever conceals a Muslim's fault, Allah will conceal his fault on the Day of Judgment'; in practice this virtue has been invoked to suppress reporting of sexual abuse and rape within Muslim communities; related to but distinct from ʿawra (bodily concealment) — sitr is behavioral concealment.

records.definition: A young woman considered sexually chaste and morally pure whose sharaf (honor) is intact and upheld through sexual modesty and adherence to family propriety norms.
records.notes: Sharaf in this context specifically indexes female sexual purity; losing it typically entails loss of marriageability and family status. The phrase is a social designation rather than a legal one.

records.definition: A respectable, chaste woman from a good family who conducts herself according to Islamic norms of sexual propriety; used as high praise indicating she is a lawful and appropriate marriage prospect.
records.notes: Ḥalāl here means 'lawfully permissible'; the antonym 'bint ḥarām' (daughter of the forbidden) implies illegitimacy or sexual misconduct. The phrase endorses both sexual purity and social lineage simultaneously.

records.definition: The sacred sexual inviolability of a woman — especially a wife or female relative — encompassing her bodily sanctity, sexual honor, and the social prohibition against violating or disgracing her.
records.notes: In colloquial dialects, ḥurma also simply means 'wife'; in MSA the root connotes both sacred prohibition and female personhood defined by sexual untouchability. Cognate with ḥarām (forbidden).

records.definition: Idiomatic phrase meaning a woman's sexual honor is in her own hands — she alone is responsible for maintaining or destroying it through her conduct.
records.english_term: her honor is in her own hands
records.notes: Simultaneously empowering and constraining: it places sole moral responsibility on the woman for any sexual dishonor while implicitly absolving external actors (including perpetrators of coercion) of blame.

records.definition: A woman whose sexual honor is publicly doubted or questioned; the social designation of a woman suspected of having engaged in unsanctioned sexual behavior.
records.notes: Social consequences in honor-shame cultures can be severe: ostracism, forced marriage, or honor-based violence. The designation can arise from gossip, association, or actual conduct and is nearly impossible to formally rebut.

records.definition: A woman's departure from the domestic sphere into the public realm; in conservative Islamic discourse, her movement outside the home without a male guardian's permission carries strong implications for sexual propriety and family honor.
records.notes: Implicitly sexualized in conservative jurisprudence because public space is a site of fitna (sexual temptation/social chaos); a woman 'going out' risks both her own honor and her family's. The phrase appears in classical fiqh discussions of female travel and movement.

records.definition: A modest, chaste woman who adheres to norms of sexual decorum in dress and behavior; an adjective of high social praise in conservative Arab and Islamic contexts.
records.notes: From the root ḥ-sh-m, connoting shame, restraint, and decorum. Ḥishma is a cardinal social virtue distinct from Western prudishness in that it is actively valorized rather than mocked; the concept covers dress, gaze, speech, and bodily comportment.

records.definition: A shameless, brazen woman who violates norms of sexual modesty and decorum; used as an insult for a sexually forward or immodest woman who lacks ḥayāʾ.
records.notes: The masculine form is waqiḥ; waqāḥa (shamelessness) applied to a woman is among the most damning insults in the honor-shame framework. The term is not inherently sexual in its root meaning but becomes strongly sexual when applied to women.

records.definition: Excessive modesty or sexual inhibition beyond the culturally expected norm; describes a person so sexually reserved as to be unable to function normally in intimate or marital contexts.
records.notes: Ḥayāʾ (modesty/shame) is a cardinal Islamic virtue; calling it zāʾid (excessive) implies it has crossed from virtue into dysfunction, a distinction rarely drawn in traditional discourse. The phrase appears in contemporary marital counseling contexts more than classical texts.

records.definition: A husband's oath to abstain from sexual intercourse with his wife for a period exceeding four months; in Islamic law, if he does not resume relations after that period the wife may seek a judicial divorce.
records.notes: Addressed in Quran 2:226–227; one of several classical mechanisms for marital dissolution whose trigger is explicitly sexual. Transliterated as 'ila' in Islamic studies literature. The four-month window is the maximum patience Islam grants a wife without recourse.

records.definition: A husband's pronouncement assimilating his wife to his mother's back, thereby rendering conjugal relations temporarily forbidden; in Islamic law it requires expiation (kafāra) before marital relations can resume.
records.notes: A pre-Islamic Arabian divorce formula reinterpreted in Islam as a serious but reversible prohibition (Quran 58:2–4). The comparison to the mother's back evokes both a forbidden body part and the incest taboo; kafāra requires freeing a slave, fasting 60 days, or feeding 60 poor persons.

records.definition: A divorce initiated by the wife in which she returns her mahr or other compensation to the husband in exchange for release from the marriage contract and its conjugal obligations.
records.notes: The word literally means 'removal/undressing'; conceptually the wife removes herself from the marriage garment. Sexual consent is central: khulʿ is most commonly sought to escape an unwanted sexual relationship. Considered a right in most madhhabs though procedural requirements vary.

records.definition: Marital recalcitrance in Islamic jurisprudence; specifically a wife's refusal of her husband's conjugal rights or a husband's failure to fulfill marital obligations, permitting a structured corrective response.
records.notes: Quran 4:34 prescribes a three-stage response to female nushūz (admonition, separate beds, then light physical correction); the sexual dimension is primary, as nushūz classically centers on refusal of the marital bed rather than other forms of disobedience.

records.definition: The husband's conjugal right; specifically the legally and religiously recognized entitlement to sexual access with his wife as part of the Islamic marriage contract.
records.notes: In classical fiqh the right is mutual but asymmetrical: the wife's corresponding ḥaqq exists but carries different legal weight and enforcement mechanisms. The concept is central to contemporary debates about the legal status of marital rape in Islamic jurisprudence.

records.definition: Conjugal obedience; the religious and legal duty of a wife to be sexually available and obedient to her husband within the bounds of the Islamic marriage contract.
records.notes: Grounded in Quran 4:34 and multiple hadiths; classical scholars hold that a wife's refusal of ṭāʿa constitutes nushūz. Contemporary Islamic reformers contest whether the duty encompasses unconditional sexual availability or is constrained by the wife's consent and wellbeing.

records.definition: The mandatory waiting period a Muslim woman must observe after divorce, widowhood, or annulment before she may remarry, requiring sexual abstinence and serving to establish the paternity of any pregnancy.
records.notes: Duration varies: three menstrual cycles after revocable divorce, four months and ten days after widowhood, until childbirth if pregnant. Sexual abstinence is obligatory throughout; violation carries both religious and, in many jurisdictions, legal consequences.

records.definition: Ritual suckling or breastfeeding that in Islamic jurisprudence creates a kinship bond between the nursing woman and the infant, generating sexual prohibitions equivalent to those of blood kinship.
records.notes: Quran 4:23 and multiple hadiths establish raḍāʿa as a category of sexual prohibition (maḥārim). Classical threshold is five or more confirmed sucklings in the first two years of life; the resulting sexual prohibitions are legally equivalent to those from blood relation.

records.definition: The Islamic legal prohibition on marriage and sexual relations arising from shared nursing; the specific subset of forbidden sexual relationships created by the breastfeeding bond rather than blood kinship.
records.notes: Explicitly enumerated in Quran 4:23 alongside blood relatives. A notable contemporary application: Saudi scholars raised concern about hospital breast milk banks creating unknown milk-kinship bonds that could unknowingly prevent future marriages between recipients.

records.definition: A woman who is sexually forbidden to a man by Islamic law, whether through blood kinship, milk kinship, active marriage ties, or other Quranic prohibition categories.
records.notes: The Quranic term for categories of women a man may not marry or have sexual relations with (Quran 4:23). Distinct from ḥarām as a generic prohibition — muḥarrama specifically designates a person who is categorically off-limits as a sexual or marital partner.

records.definition: A woman who serves as the intermediate wife in a tahleel arrangement, marrying and sexually consummating with a man solely to render his triply-divorced ex-wife lawful for remarriage to him; the role is widely condemned as a legal fiction.
records.notes: Literally 'the one made lawful'; her sexual consummation with the intermediate husband is the required condition rendering the first wife licit again. A hadith explicitly curses the muḥallil (intermediate husband) and those who arrange such marriages.

records.definition: A marriage contracted specifically to allow a triply-divorced woman to return to her first husband; requires consummation and subsequent divorce from the intermediate husband before the original couple may remarry.
records.notes: Sexual consummation (al-wuṭʾ) is non-negotiable: without it the intermediate marriage does not achieve its purpose. Hanbali and most Shafi'i scholars consider it absolutely prohibited; Hanafi school permits it if the second marriage is ostensibly genuine in intent.

records.definition: The Islamic jurisprudential requirement of compatibility or equivalence between spouses in religion, lineage, and sometimes occupation or wealth, regarded as a condition for a valid and socially endorsed marriage.
records.notes: Primarily invoked when a marriage is contracted without the guardian's (walī's) consent: a groom of lower kafāʾa gives the walī grounds for annulment. The concept intersects with sexuality insofar as mismatched status is seen as risking the woman's honor and the family's social standing.

records.definition: The obligatory gift of money or property given by a groom to his bride as a condition of the Islamic marriage contract, becoming her exclusive property and legally tied to the sexual consummation of the marriage.
records.notes: If divorce occurs before consummation the bride receives only half the specified mahr; full mahr is due upon consummation, explicitly linking the dower to sexual access. This makes mahr the legal expression of the sexual contract within Islamic marriage.

records.definition: The intense sexual desire or lust of a husband; in Islamic jurisprudential discourse, the husband's sexual appetite that generates the wife's legal duty of availability and underpins the conjugal-rights framework.
records.notes: Shabaq (شبق) denotes intense, urgent sexual craving; in this marital-juridical compound the husband's desire is not condemned but recognized as a natural drive that Islamic law structures around, requiring the wife's sexual availability as the legally responsive mechanism.

records.definition: A wife's withholding of conjugal relations from her husband; in Islamic jurisprudence, sustained refusal without a legitimate excuse constitutes nushūz and may entitle the husband to withhold maintenance and take corrective measures.
records.notes: Legitimate excuses for refusal include illness, menstruation, and prescribed fasting days; refusal on other grounds is generally treated as a legal and religious breach. The term sits at the intersection of sexuality, marital law, and the distribution of power within Islamic marriage.

records.definition: In classical Islamic jurisprudence, a man with congenital gender inversion — naturally effeminate in voice, movement, and manner — legally distinguished from one who deliberately imitates women.
records.notes: The Prophet reportedly tolerated mukhannathun in women's spaces until one was found describing women's bodies to men; the category carries no inherent sin unlike the mutakhannith, making it a genuine third-gender legal status.

records.definition: A man who deliberately adopts feminine mannerisms, clothing, or speech; condemned in multiple hadith traditions and legally distinguished from the naturally effeminate mukhannath.
records.notes: The Arabic Form V verbal pattern (tafaʿʿala) encodes deliberate, volitional action, making the condemnation categorically moral; modern speakers often conflate this term with mukhannath, erasing the jurisprudentially significant natural/deliberate distinction.

records.definition: A woman who deliberately adopts masculine attributes, behavior, or appearance; the female counterpart to the mutakhannith in classical Islamic jurisprudence.
records.notes: Considerably rarer in classical sources than its male counterpart; cursed alongside men who imitate women in the same Sahih al-Bukhari hadith; the Form X verbal root implies actively seeking to appropriate maleness.

records.definition: A face covering or mask associated with mukhannathun in classical Arabic social and performative contexts, marking their liminal gender status and mediating their access to gender-segregated spaces.
records.notes: Attestations are sparse and the term is highly obscure; may also denote a disguise or covering used more broadly in gender-ambiguous performance; root ق-ن-ع shares a semantic field with concealment and satisfaction, suggesting the veil simultaneously hides and resolves gender ambiguity.

records.definition: A descriptive compound noun phrase meaning 'the feminine man' or 'the womanly man,' used in modern standard Arabic to characterize an effeminate male.
records.notes: More descriptive and less formally condemnatory than the classical jurisprudential terms; encountered in MSA journalism, literary criticism, and contemporary social commentary; connotation ranges from neutral description to implicit stigma depending on context.

records.definition: A man who deliberately imitates or resembles women in manner or dress; drawn almost verbatim from hadith texts in which such men are cursed alongside women who imitate men.
records.notes: The phrase is nearly verbatim from Sahih al-Bukhari (hadith 5885); in modern religious discourse it functions primarily as a condemnation formula invoked against gender-nonconforming men; maps only approximately to cross-dressing since the condemnation targets behavioral imitation broadly, not clothing specifically.

records.definition: A woman who deliberately imitates or resembles men in manner or dress; the female counterpart in the same hadith tradition that condemns gender-crossing behavior.
records.notes: Paired symmetrically with the male equivalent in Sahih al-Bukhari; applied in modern contexts to condemn masculine-presenting women, short hair, or trousers on women; carries less social intensity in practice than its male counterpart in most contemporary Arabic-speaking contexts.

records.definition: A classical Arabic literary and cultural tradition of deliberate moral transgression, encompassing bawdy poetry, wine celebration, explicit homoeroticism, and erotic verse, cultivated as an aesthetic and social stance by poets such as Abu Nuwas and al-Akhtal al-Saghir.
records.notes: Mujūn is simultaneously a literary genre, an ethical posture of deliberate irreverence, and a social performance; 'libertinism' is the closest English approximation but misses the specific aesthetic tradition and the playful provocation of religious norms as a compositional strategy.

records.definition: The classical Arabic tradition of amatory and love poetry, ranging from chaste Platonic longing (ʿudhrī ghazal) to explicitly erotic verse (ḥissī ghazal), constituting one of the major classical Arabic poetic genres.
records.notes: Ghazal spans a wide register from spiritualized longing to explicit eroticism; the mapping to erotica applies only to the ḥissī (sensual) subtype; the broader genre category includes non-erotic verse and is better characterized as amatory poetry.

records.definition: An ode or extended poem explicitly treating sexual intercourse, erotic technique, and carnal pleasure, using the archaic Arabic term 'bāh' as a genre marker for sexuality.
records.notes: 'Bāh' (باه) is a classical Arabic synonym for coitus, sexual capacity, and erotic pleasure, now largely archaic; major works bearing this title include encyclopedic sexual manuals framed as verse; the qaṣīdat al-bāh genre overlaps with the broader kutub al-bāh (books of sexuality) tradition.

records.definition: The corpus of classical Arabic bawdy and libertine literature, encompassing erotic poetry, risqué anecdotes, and transgressive prose cultivated as a high-culture aesthetic tradition from the Abbasid period onward.
records.notes: Adab al-mujūn is distinct from pornography in that it is a self-conscious high-culture literary tradition; major contributors include Abu Nuwas, al-Jahiz (in adjacent registers), and numerous Abbasid court poets; the term 'adab' signals literary cultivation, making this learned transgression rather than crude obscenity.

records.definition: The amatory prelude that opens a classical Arabic qasida, in which the poet laments the departure of the beloved and describes her beauty — often in sensual or erotic terms — before transitioning to the ode's main panegyric or other themes.
records.notes: The nasīb is a structurally defined element of the classical Arabic ode with no English literary equivalent; its erotic content varies from mild longing to explicit sensuality; its presence is a formal expectation of the qasida genre such that its omission was itself a rhetorical statement.

records.definition: The classical Arabic genre of wine poetry, celebrating alcohol, beautiful cup-bearers, and sensual pleasure, frequently intertwined with homoerotic themes in the work of Abbasid poets such as Abu Nuwas.
records.notes: Khamriyyāt maps only loosely to erotica; it is a distinct genre in which erotic themes are frequent but not constitutive; 'Bacchic poetry' is used in English scholarship; the genre was theologically transgressive in an Islamic context, lending the eroticism an additional edge of religious provocation.

records.definition: A scholarly-constructed term for poetry treating sexual confinement, erotic repression, or the captivity of desire, extending the classical ḥabsiyyāt (prison poetry) genre into explicitly sexual territory.
records.notes: This appears to be a modern scholarly construction rather than an attested classical genre designation; the ḥabsiyyāt genre proper concerns physical imprisonment; appending al-jins creates a specialized critical term; recognition is extremely low and confined to academic discourse on classical Arabic poetics.

records.definition: A modern analytical term for erotic poetry, using the Greek-derived Arabic loanword 'ʾīrūsī' (from Eros) as a genre descriptor in literary criticism and comparative poetics.
records.notes: A descriptive scholarly label rather than a classical genre name; the loanword 'ʾīrūsī' signals a modern or Western-influenced academic framing; used to discuss both classical Arabic erotic traditions and translated Western erotic literature in Arabic-language literary studies.

records.definition: A theological and literary phrase meaning 'the sinful body' or 'the erring body,' encoding the concept that the physical self is inherently prone to moral transgression, particularly sexual sin.
records.notes: A phrasal construction rather than a fixed lexeme; encountered in Islamic philosophical, Sufi, and ascetic discourse about the nafs (self) and its bodily desires; 'khāṭiʾ' (erring, sinful) implies the body actively errs rather than passively tempting, distinguishing it slightly from concupiscence's theological framing of inherited desire.

records.definition: A theological and literary phrase meaning 'the shame of the body' or 'bodily disgrace,' encoding the concept that the body and its desires are inherently shameful and spiritually dangerous.
records.notes: 'Khizī' denotes disgrace and humiliation rather than merely embarrassment; used in Islamic ascetic and Sufi discourse about the spiritual dangers of bodily appetite; the phrase constructs shame as ontologically attached to the body rather than as a response to specific acts.

records.definition: A theological and literary phrase meaning 'the curse of desire' or 'the curse of lust,' framing sexual appetite as a divine punishment or a condemned affliction of the soul.
records.notes: 'Shahwa' (شهوة) is the standard Quranic word for desire/lust and carries significant theological weight; 'laʿna' (divine curse) adds formal condemnation; the phrase frames lust not merely as a temptation but as a punishment visited upon humanity, paralleling certain Christian readings of concupiscence as a consequence of the Fall.

records.definition: A Quranic term denoting ritual and moral impurity, filth, or abomination; applied to prohibited substances, acts, and behaviors including sexual transgressions of the gravest kind.
records.notes: Appears multiple times in the Quran (e.g., 5:90 on wine and gambling as rijs; 9:125 on hypocrites); 'indecency' substantially understates the term's gravity — rijs designates the most severe category of moral contamination and is closer to 'abomination' in weight; its Quranic authority gives it unique rhetorical force in religious condemnation of sexual transgression.

records.definition: Moral or ritual defilement, pollution, or contamination; describes the spiritual stain left by sexual transgression or contact with morally impure acts and people.
records.notes: Danas occupies the semantic space between ritual impurity (najāsa, addressed by wuḍūʾ) and moral contamination; in sexual discourse it implies the polluting effect of illicit acts on a person's spiritual standing; also used metaphorically for any corrupting moral influence.

records.definition: Filthiness, dirtiness, or moral squalor; used in sexual contexts to characterize obscene acts, language, or people as viscerally repugnant and degrading.
records.notes: Used for both physical uncleanliness and moral depravity; in sexual registers it emphasizes visceral disgust rather than formal jurisprudential impurity; the abstract noun form makes it slightly more literary than the adjective qadhir, though both are common across registers.

records.definition: Dirty, filthy, or morally repugnant; an adjective applied both to physically unclean things and to sexually obscene acts, speech, or people.
records.notes: One of the most common and universally recognized Arabic words for moral-sexual disgust; simultaneously physical and moral in connotation; applied freely to obscene speech, pornographic content, or sexually transgressive people; carries no technical register, making it the default crude condemnation across dialects.

records.definition: Obscene, indecent, or grossly lewd; a Quranic adjective and noun (fāḥisha, فاحشة) denoting grave moral transgression, particularly sexual indecency, fornication, or any act crossing the bounds of propriety.
records.notes: The root ف-ح-ش appears repeatedly in the Quran to condemn sexual misconduct; 'fāḥisha' (the noun) is the standard Quranic term for fornication and indecency (e.g., 4:15, 7:80); fāḥish carries this full jurisprudential and scriptural weight, making it substantially more grave than 'obscene' in English suggests.

records.definition: Vulgar, raucous, or sexually suggestive singing, speech, or behavior; especially associated in classical and colloquial usage with women's lewd, noisy, or sexually brazen conduct.
records.notes: Radaḥ carries gendered connotations, historically framing loud or sexually suggestive female behavior as socially transgressive; the concept overlaps with but is not equivalent to bawdy humor — it implies performative lewdness and social impropriety as much as sexual humor; also used in some modern dialects for noisy, vulgar arguing.

records.definition: Obscene, vulgar, foul-mouthed, or crudely indecent; applied to people, speech, or behavior that transgresses standards of sexual and social decency.
records.notes: Common across all Arabic-speaking regions and registers; frequently used to characterize sexually explicit or crude speech (kalām badhīʾ) and sexually transgressive people; in some contexts slightly stronger in condemnatory force than qadhir, emphasizing moral character over sensory disgust.

records.definition: A morally dissolute, sinful person who commits acts of debauchery and sexual transgression against Islamic law; a reprobate.
records.notes: Quranic term; contrasts with 'barr' (pious). Carries legal weight in classical fiqh — a fājir's testimony is given reduced credibility in court. Used as a general insult for the untrustworthy beyond sexual contexts.

records.definition: A person who knowingly transgresses Islamic religious law through immoral, especially sexual, conduct; a deliberate sinner acting in defiance of divine command.
records.notes: Stronger theological valence than fājir — the fāsiq acts with full knowledge of the prohibition, making the sin more culpable. In classical fiqh, a fāsiq's legal testimony is inadmissible. Quranic term widely used in religious discourse.

records.definition: A lewd, bawdy, licentious person who indulges in ribald humor and sexual immodesty without shame.
records.notes: Mujūn (مجون) is a recognized classical Arabic literary genre pairing ribald wit with sexual licentiousness; mājiн denotes the person embodying it. Distinctively combines erotic transgression with irreverent humor. Rarely used in modern MSA.

records.definition: A shameless, utterly dissolute person who has cast off all moral restraint and social propriety; a debauched reprobate.
records.notes: Root هتك = to tear away or rip off, implying one who has torn away the veil of shame (هتك الستر). Emphasizes the social and honor-shame dimension more than the theological. Primarily literary; less common in everyday modern Arabic.

records.definition: A morally loose, licentious person who has shed all social and religious restraint; one cast off from respectable society due to moral dissolution.
records.notes: Root خلع = to strip off or remove; implies having stripped off moral constraints or been expelled from social belonging. Sometimes implies the family formally disowned the person. Classical term; uncommon in modern MSA.

records.definition: Exciting, arousing, stimulating; describes a person or situation that provokes sexual desire or strong interest.
records.notes: Broad word meaning 'exciting' in non-sexual contexts as well; sexual meaning is activated by context. Common in both MSA and colloquial Arabic. Extremely high frequency. One of the most neutral ways to call something sexually stimulating.

records.definition: Tempting, alluring, seductive; describes a person, object, or situation that draws one in irresistibly, including sexually.
records.notes: Active participle of أغرى (to entice/tempt). Has broad non-sexual use (a tempting offer, an attractive salary) but is commonly applied in sexual and romantic contexts. The nunation orthography (مغرٍ with tanwīn) is phonetically distinctive.

records.definition: Seductive, alluring, provocative; describes content, dress, or behavior calculated to incite sexual desire.
records.notes: Adjectival form of إغراء (enticement/seduction). More specifically sexual in connotation than مغرٍ; often applied to provocative clothing, poses, or media content. Frequently appears in media censorship and religious discourse about indecency.

records.definition: Driven by sexual caprice or whim; impulsively licentious; relating to نزوة, a sudden uncontrolled sexual impulse or passing fancy.
records.notes: Derived from نزوة (caprice, whim, sexual impulse). نزوي emphasizes the impulsive, capricious nature of the urge rather than habitual licentiousness. Literary register; uncommon in everyday speech. Distinct from مثير in that it describes the actor's psychology rather than the object's effect.

records.definition: Charming, captivating, alluring; a person or quality that beguiles and tempts others with strong romantic and sexual undertones.
records.notes: Active participle of فتن (to beguile/tempt/cause fitna). Fitna originally means sedition or trial; فاتن is one who creates that disruptive effect on observers. Commonly used as a compliment for attractive people. Also used as a proper name.

records.definition: Intensely captivating, irresistibly alluring; the intensive form implying one who habitually and powerfully bewitches those around them.
records.notes: Intensive form (فعّال pattern) of فاتن, implying habitual or overwhelming enchantment rather than merely occasional charm. Slightly more literary than فاتن. Can also mean 'inciter of discord' in non-sexual political contexts.

records.definition: Enchanting, bewitching, spellbinding; literally a sorcerer but used metaphorically for someone whose beauty or charm is supernaturally irresistible.
records.notes: Literal meaning is 'magician/sorcerer'; the sexually attractive meaning is purely metaphorical. Widely used and not considered crude. Most common collocations: عيون ساحرة (enchanting eyes), ابتسامة ساحرة (bewitching smile).

records.definition: Appetizing, delectable; when applied to a person, implies they arouse sexual appetite in the way enticing food arouses hunger.
records.notes: Primarily means appetizing for food; when applied to people the sexual connotation is activated by context. Derived from شهوة (appetite/desire/lust). The food-to-sex metaphor is conscious and mildly transgressive; crude level rises significantly if context makes the sexual meaning explicit.

records.definition: Lust-arousing; describes a person, image, or act that directly provokes sexual appetite.
records.notes: Compound phrase: مثيرة (feminine arouser) + للشهوة (of desire/lust). More explicitly sexual than standalone مثير because it names شهوة (lust) directly. Frequently appears in religious rulings about indecency and in public discourse condemning provocative media or dress.

records.definition: Slender, willowy, and upright in posture; describes a person with an elegantly elongated, graceful physique considered sexually attractive.
records.notes: From مشق (to be slender, elongated, to draw out). Classical Arabic beauty descriptor applied to both sexes; implies tall, lean, and upright carriage. Primarily literary; less common in modern colloquial Arabic. Not inherently sexual — crude level rises only with context.

records.definition: A slender-waisted, graceful woman; a classical Arabic feminine beauty ideal emphasizing a narrow waist and elegant, swaying bearing.
records.notes: From هيف = slimness of the waist. Exclusively feminine (فعلاء morphological pattern). A stock epithet in pre-Islamic and classical Arabic erotic poetry for the ideal female figure. Also commonly used as a proper name. Distinct from ممشوق in being exclusively feminine and specifically waist-focused.

records.definition: Slender, lithe, and graceful; describes a well-proportioned, nimble physique considered elegantly attractive.
records.notes: Common in both literary and everyday contexts. Applies to both sexes. More accessible in modern Arabic than ممشوق. Often used to compliment dancers, athletes, or physically attractive figures. Not inherently sexual; crude level rises only with sexual context.

records.definition: Full-bodied, curvaceous, plump in an attractive way; describes a pleasingly rounded physique.
records.notes: Literally 'full/complete/filled'; sexually it signals a pleasingly curvaceous body. Functions as a polite euphemism avoiding more explicit body descriptors. Culturally, fuller body types have traditionally been admired across much of the Arab world, giving this word a positive sexual valence.

records.definition: A woman with large, heavy buttocks who sways conspicuously when walking; a classical Arabic erotic epithet used admiringly in poetry.

Essentially archaic in modern MSA; a reader encountering it today would recognize it as classically poetic. Often paired with other body-size epithets in classical erotica.

records.definition: A sexually transmitted disease or infection; the standard MSA clinical phrase for any illness contracted through sexual contact.

records.definition: Venereal diseases; sexually transmitted infections framed specifically as diseases of the reproductive organs; the formal clinical MSA term used in medical and public health texts.
records.notes: Plural of مرض تناسلي. The adjective تناسلي derives from تناسل (reproduction/procreation), producing a specifically genital-reproductive framing analogous to the Latin etymology of English 'venereal.' More formal register than مرض جنسي; preferred in medical literature.

records.definition: AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome); the phonetic Arabic transliteration of the English acronym, referring to the advanced stage of HIV infection.

records.definition: Syphilis; the standard Arabic clinical and colloquial term for the sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Treponema pallidum.
records.notes: Also an adjective meaning 'rosy, rose-colored' (from زهر, flower/blossom); the association with syphilis likely relates to the rosy rash characteristic of secondary syphilis. Unusual in Arabic in being simultaneously the clinical and colloquial term with no competing slang alternative widely in use.

records.definition: Gonorrhea; the standard Arabic clinical term for the sexually transmitted bacterial infection, named for the characteristic purulent genital discharge.
records.notes: Literally 'flow, flowing, discharge' from the root سيل (to flow); directly parallels the Greek etymology of 'gonorrhea' (seed-flow). Clinical and colloquial simultaneously with no competing common slang term in MSA. Recognition has declined slightly as 'gonorrhea' is sometimes borrowed directly.

records.definition: Sexual dysfunction, especially male impotence; the clinical MSA phrase for inability to perform sexually, most commonly referring to erectile dysfunction.

Less specific than the English 'erectile dysfunction'; mapped to that concept because it is the dominant referent in practice.
