records.definition: Clinical German term for transvestism: the paraphilic disorder or practice of wearing clothing associated with a gender other than one's own, as classified in psychiatric nomenclature.
records.notes: DSM-IV classified as 'transvestic fetishism'; DSM-5 revised framing; the term is increasingly viewed as stigmatizing by LGBTQ+ communities in German-speaking countries, contributing to declining clinical and popular use.

records.definition: An older clinical variant spelling of 'Transvestismus' found in some German-language psychiatric literature, referring to cross-dressing as a paraphilic pattern.
records.notes: Less frequent spelling variant than 'Transvestismus'; both terms appear in German clinical literature with no meaningful semantic distinction; 'Transvestitismus' may reflect slightly older nomenclature conventions in German-speaking psychiatry.

records.definition: Clinical German term for frotteurism: sexual arousal derived from rubbing one's genitals against a non-consenting person, typically in crowded public spaces.
records.notes: Low recognition reflects its niche psychiatric status; the act itself is broadly understood as sexual assault or 'Begrapschen' (groping) in everyday German, but the diagnostic term 'Frotteurismus' is known primarily to mental health professionals and criminologists.

records.definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from secretly watching others in intimate situations; also used metaphorically in German for any compulsive or passive observer.
records.notes: Loanword from French, used identically in German; significantly more broadly known than the clinical 'Voyeurismus'; extended metaphorical use ('politischer Voyeur') is common in German journalism and literary criticism.

records.definition: A German clinical sexological category grouping paraphilias practiced consensually within a partnership, distinguishing them from solitary or non-consensual paraphilic acts.

records.definition: The German clinical term for paraphilia; any persistent atypical pattern of sexual arousal directed at unusual objects, situations, or individuals, classified in DSM-5 and ICD-11.
records.notes: Direct German equivalent of the clinical term; used almost exclusively in psychiatric, psychological, and forensic sexology contexts rather than community vocabulary.

records.definition: The German clinical term for scopophilia; a paraphilia characterized by sexual arousal derived from watching the intimate behavior, nudity, or sexual activity of others, typically without their knowledge.
records.notes: In German clinical sexology essentially synonymous with Voyeurismus; 'Scopophilie' appears in older psychiatric literature and is rarer in contemporary usage than Voyeurismus; derived from Greek skopein (to look).

records.definition: The same acronym used in German as in English, expanding as Bondage/Disziplin, Dominanz/Submission, Sadismus/Masochismus; the umbrella term for consensual power-exchange and pain-play sexual practices and the community around them.

records.definition: German word for 'dominance'; in BDSM contexts refers specifically to the role of holding authority and control over a submissive partner within a consensual power-exchange dynamic.

records.definition: The feminine form of 'Herr' meaning 'mistress, lady, owner'; in BDSM contexts used as a title of address for a female dominant, functionally equivalent to the English BDSM title 'Mistress.'

records.definition: German colloquial term for a threesome; formed from 'drei' (three) plus the colloquial agentive suffix '-er', meaning 'a three-person [sexual encounter].'

records.definition: English loanword for group sex in which one person is sexually engaged by multiple partners sequentially or simultaneously; used without translation in German.

records.definition: German infinitive adapted from English 'to swing'; to participate in the swinging lifestyle, including consensual partner-swapping with other couples.

records.definition: A euphemistic German term for a swinger club; literally 'couples club' (Pärchen = couple), emphasizing the couple-oriented nature over the explicit sexual purpose.

records.definition: German for orgy; a sexual gathering involving multiple participants engaging freely with one another; also used figuratively for any excess (e.g. 'Fressorgie' = eating binge).

records.definition: British-origin kink practice adopted into German vocabulary: having sex in semi-public spaces — typically car parks — while onlookers watch or join in.

records.definition: Euphemistic English loanword used in German BDSM and kink communities for sexual play involving urine; deliberately disguised as an innocuous sports activity term.

records.definition: German euphemistic idiom for having sex; literally 'to drive/pursue it'; the 'es' is the canonical deictic stand-in for the unnamed act.

records.definition: German euphemistic idiom for having sex; literally 'to do it' or 'to make it'; the most semantically vacuous and therefore most neutral German circumlocution for sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Even milder than 'es treiben' because 'machen' (to do, to make) is the most content-free German verb; used by children who have just learned about reproduction, by elderly speakers avoiding explicit language, and in any context requiring maximum indirection; lowest crude score in this batch by design.

records.definition: Literally 'to sleep with each other'; the standard polite German euphemism for having sexual intercourse.
records.notes: The most neutral and widely used German euphemism for sex; appropriate in almost any register outside clinical writing.

records.definition: Literally 'to go to bed'; used with a partner referent ('mit jemandem ins Bett gehen') as a circumlocution for having sex.
records.english_term: to go to bed with someone

records.definition: Literally 'to be together'; primarily denotes being in a romantic partnership, implying an ongoing sexual relationship rather than a single act.
records.english_term: to be together / to be an item

records.definition: Calque of 'to make love'; a romantically framed German euphemism for sexual intercourse emphasizing emotional intimacy.
records.notes: Direct borrowing/calque from the English expression; fully naturalized in German. The romantic connotation is preserved; cruder synonyms are preferred when emotional distance is implied.

records.definition: Literally 'to become intimate'; a polite euphemism for initiating sexual activity, often implying a first sexual encounter between partners.
records.english_term: to get intimate / to become intimate
records.notes: Slightly clinical in tone relative to other euphemisms in this set; common in relationship advice, journalism, and counseling discourse.

records.definition: Reflexive verb meaning 'to enjoy oneself' or 'to amuse oneself'; deployed as a coy, somewhat old-fashioned euphemism for engaging in sexual activity.
records.english_term: to have a good time / to enjoy oneself

records.definition: Literally 'physical love' or 'bodily love'; a formal-register euphemism for sexual intercourse or physical sexual intimacy.
records.notes: Typically contrasted with 'geistige Liebe' (spiritual love) in philosophical or relationship-counseling discourse; more formal than conversational.

records.definition: Literally 'physical closeness' or 'physical proximity'; the mildest German euphemism in this set, implying intimate touch that may or may not include sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Preferred in therapeutic, medical, and relationship-advice contexts precisely because it does not commit to naming intercourse; also used for non-sexual affectionate touch.

records.definition: Phrase meaning 'to exchange tenderness' or 'to exchange caresses'; a delicate euphemism for affectionate erotic contact that stops short of explicitly naming intercourse.
records.notes: 'Zärtlichkeiten' (pl.) encompasses kisses, embraces, and light erotic touch; the phrase is used in both non-sexual affectionate and sexual foreplay contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'shepherd's little hour'; an archaic-flavored German euphemism for a brief, often stolen amorous or sexual tryst.
records.notes: Originates in German pastoral poetry tradition where shepherds enjoyed idle amorous interludes; today it is used with ironic or humorous distance and carries a distinctly old-fashioned charm.

records.definition: Literally 'afternoon nap'; used as a humorous or coy euphemism for an afternoon sexual encounter.
records.notes: The literal meaning (a brief after-lunch sleep) remains the dominant reading; the sexual euphemism is activated entirely by context or a knowing tone.

records.definition: Crude idiom meaning 'to push a number'; colloquial slang for having sex, with 'Nummer' as slang for a sex act and 'schieben' (to push/shove) adding a blunt physical connotation.

records.definition: Idiom 'to do a number'; crude-neutral slang for having sex, slightly less physically blunt than 'eine Nummer schieben' but equally colloquial.
records.english_term: to do it / to get it on
records.notes: Variant of 'eine Nummer schieben'; 'machen' (to make/do) is milder than 'schieben' (to push). Both phrases treat sex as an activity ('Nummer') to be performed.

records.definition: Direct English loanword for a brief, hasty sexual encounter; fully naturalized in German colloquial speech.
records.notes: Appears without quotation marks in German print and conversation; one of the more successful English sexual loanwords in German.

records.definition: Literally 'to lay (someone) flat'; crude German slang for having sex with someone, implying a dominant, conquering perspective.

records.definition: Literally 'to lay (someone) on their back'; a crude idiom for having sex with someone with connotations of overcoming or seducing them.

records.definition: Literally 'relationship maintenance'; a wryly bureaucratic German euphemism for sex within a committed relationship, framing physical intimacy as a household duty or upkeep activity.
records.english_term: keeping the spark alive / relationship maintenance sex

records.definition: Literally 'love play'; a romantic German euphemism for erotic activity between partners, encompassing foreplay and the broader sexual encounter.
records.notes: 'Spiel' (play/game) implies mutual, playful engagement rather than unilateral action; can refer specifically to foreplay or to the entire sexual encounter depending on context.

records.definition: Literally 'night of love'; a romantic and literary German euphemism for a night of sexual intimacy between partners.
records.english_term: a night of love / a passionate night
records.notes: Higher literary register than conversational German; appears frequently in romance novels, song lyrics, and poetry. Less likely in informal spoken use.

records.definition: Literally 'act of love'; a standard German euphemism for the sexual act, especially penetrative intercourse.
records.english_term: the act of love / the sex act
records.notes: More formal and quasi-clinical than 'Liebe machen'; preferred in journalistic, educational, and public-health contexts where a non-crude but non-clinical term is needed.

records.definition: Literally 'to have traffic'; shortened from 'Geschlechtsverkehr haben' (to have sexual intercourse); a formal to semi-clinical German euphemism for sex.
records.english_term: to have intercourse / to have sexual relations

records.definition: Latin phrase for 'caught in the act'; used in German specifically to mean catching someone during sexual intercourse or in a compromising sexual situation.
records.english_term: in flagrante delicto / caught in the act
records.notes: Derived from Latin legal terminology ('in flagrante delicto'); in modern German colloquial use the sexual application dominates over the general criminal law sense. The full Latin form is also used.

records.definition: Literally 'under the duvet/blanket'; a coy German euphemism for sexual activity that implies intimacy by referencing its domestic spatial context.

records.definition: Literally 'between the sheets'; a German euphemism for sexual activity equivalent to the English phrase, implying intercourse by referencing the bed linen.

records.definition: Idiom meaning 'to go on the street' or 'to go out on the rounds'; used in German slang for a sex worker going out to solicit clients, or more loosely for going out to seek casual sexual encounters.

records.definition: Idiomatic phrase for being actively in a phase of pursuing casual sexual encounters; literally 'to be on tour,' implying an ongoing state of sexual seeking.

records.definition: Euphemistic compound for a sexual affair or bedroom episode; can also refer to a boastful account of a sexual conquest; literally 'bed story.'

records.definition: Mildly crude diminutive for a woman regarded primarily as a sexual partner or playmate; literally 'little bed bunny.'

records.definition: A romantic or sentimental love affair, especially one that is fleeting or unofficial; emphasizes the emotional dimension over the purely sexual; from 'Liebe' (love).

records.definition: The standard German term for an (often illicit) love affair or romantic episode; borrowed from French 'affaire.'

records.definition: Euphemism for an ongoing romantic or sexual relationship, especially an illicit or secret one; standard phrase 'ein Verhältnis haben' (to have an affair); literally 'relationship, proportion.'

records.notes: Specifically implies betrayal of a primary relationship; unlike Affäre, emphasizes brevity and the act of stepping out rather than a sustained emotional affair. Registry lacks an 'infidelity' concept; love_affair is the closest available.

records.definition: To cheat on a romantic partner; to have a sexual or romantic encounter outside of a committed relationship; literally 'to go with strangers/foreigners.'
records.notes: The dominant colloquial verb for infidelity in contemporary German; highly transparent etymology (fremd = foreign/stranger, gehen = to go); used as infinitive and participial noun ('das Fremdgehen').

records.definition: Adultery; the violation of marriage vows through extramarital sexual relations; literally 'marriage-breaking'; formerly a criminal offense in West Germany until 1969.
records.notes: More formal and legalistic than Seitensprung; rarely used in everyday speech but well-recognized. Registry lacks an 'adultery' concept; love_affair is the closest available match.

records.definition: Humorous euphemism for sexual intercourse; literally 'bed gymnastics,' treating sex as an athletic or gymnastic activity performed in bed.

records.definition: Humorous mock-formal euphemism for sexual intercourse; literally 'horizontal activity,' referencing the supine position typical of sex.

records.definition: Archaic and formerly legal term for sexual immorality or illicit sexual acts; covered a broad range of non-marital and criminalized sexual conduct; literally 'un-discipline/un-breeding.'

records.definition: Archaic pejorative for prostitution or sexually promiscuous behavior; the abstract noun derived from 'Hure' (whore).

records.definition: Unchastity; the state of failing to adhere to standards of sexual purity; a religious and moral term for sexual licentiousness or immodesty.
records.notes: Abstract noun of 'unkeusch'; primarily found in religious texts, catechisms, sermons, and older moral literature; recognition has declined sharply outside churchgoing populations.

records.definition: Unchaste; adjective describing a person or act as violating sexual purity norms; archaic and primarily used in religious or historical contexts.
records.notes: Adjective form of Unkeuschheit; rarely encountered in contemporary German outside of historical or religious texts; occasionally used in ironic modern contexts.

records.definition: Archaic German for an amorous or illicit romantic relationship; courtship or love affair with erotic overtones; from 'buhlen' (to court, to woo).
records.notes: Very archaic; primarily found in medieval and early modern German texts, poetry, and legal documents; also used in older Bible translations; 'buhlen' as a verb survived somewhat longer than the noun.

records.definition: Archaic German for a beloved, sweetheart, or lover; grammatically both masculine (der Buhle) and feminine (die Buhle); denotes an intimate amorous partner.

records.definition: Archaic German compound for a concubine; a woman cohabiting with a man without the legal status of wife; literally 'concubine-woman.'

records.definition: Archaic German for a concubine; a secondary female partner cohabiting without marital status; shortened form of Kebsweib.
records.notes: Even more archaic and rare than Kebsweib; found primarily in medieval and early modern German religious and legal texts; largely displaced by 'Konkubine' in formal usage.

records.definition: French loanword used in archaic German for the officially acknowledged mistress of a monarch or high noble; implies high social rank and frequently political influence.

records.definition: The Germanized form of French 'maîtresse'; the official mistress of a powerful man, especially a ruler or nobleman in 17th–18th century court society; a kept woman of high social standing.
records.notes: More widely recognized than Mairesse due to use in German-language historical scholarship; specifically connotes the institutionalized royal or noble mistress role (e.g., Madame de Pompadour, Countess Cosel at the Saxon court).

records.definition: A concubine; a woman cohabiting with a man in a long-term sexual union without the legal or social status of a wife; Latin loanword common in historical, biblical, and ecclesiastical contexts.

records.definition: The institution or legal-social practice of concubinage; a cohabitation arrangement in which a man and woman live in a de facto sexual union without legal marriage.
records.notes: Refers to the institution or practice rather than the person (Konkubine); found in historical law, church canon, and anthropology; in older German civil law contexts also used for common-law cohabitation.

records.definition: Archaic/literary German for intense sensual pleasure and desire; voluptuousness or lust; encompasses both the experience of sensual gratification and the carnal appetite for it.

records.definition: The lust of the flesh; carnal desire framed in religious or moral terms as the base appetite of the body opposing the spirit.

records.definition: Carnal, fleshly; of or relating to the body and its desires, especially sexual appetite, as opposed to the spiritual.
records.notes: Adjective; appears in fixed phrases like 'fleischliche Lust' (carnal lust) and 'fleischliche Begierde' (carnal desire); still recognizable from religious and literary contexts.

records.definition: Lewd, unchaste, or indecent; sexually immoral or violating norms of public decency.

records.definition: An offense against public morality or sexual decency; a minor sex crime or indecency offense as classified in the older German penal framework.

records.definition: A serious crime against morality or sexual decency; a felony-level sex crime in the older German legal classification, more severe than a Sittlichkeitsdelikt.

records.definition: Lasciviousness, lustfulness; the quality of being driven by lascivious sexual desire in a morally reproachable or licentious way.
records.notes: Noun form of 'lüstern' (lustful, lascivious); archaic in everyday speech but still encountered in literary and moral-philosophical texts.

records.definition: The male genitalia; an archaic German literary term for the male sex organs, etymologically related to 'machen' (to make/fashion), implying that which is endowed by nature.

records.definition: The genitals; literally 'parts of shame,' an archaic German euphemism for the external sex organs used to avoid direct naming.
records.notes: The 'Scham-' prefix (shame) reflects historical modesty norms; cf. Schamglieder, Schamhaar (pubic hair), Schamlippen (labia). Plural noun.

records.definition: The genitals; literally 'members of shame,' a near-synonym of Schamteile with a slightly more clinical weight, used in older medical and religious German texts.
records.notes: 'Glieder' (members/limbs) gives it a quasi-anatomical register compared to Schamteile; both share the shaming 'Scham-' prefix.

records.definition: A sexually motivated murder; a killing in which sexual gratification is the primary motive; also a celebrated motif in Weimar-era German art and literature.
records.notes: Compound of Lust (desire/pleasure) + Mord (murder). Gained cultural currency through Weimar-era art (Grosz, Dix, Wedekind) and infamous criminal trials (Haarmann, Kürten). 'Lust murder' exists in English criminology but lacks a registry slot; the German term carries specific cultural weight beyond the English gloss.

records.definition: A person who commits a sexually motivated murder; a lust killer.
records.notes: Agent noun of Lustmord; entered German cultural consciousness through the trials of Fritz Haarmann and Peter Kürten ('Vampir von Düsseldorf') in the 1920s–30s.

records.definition: Shamelessness; a total absence of shame, especially in sexual or public behavior; brazen indecency.
records.notes: Schamlos (shameless) + -igkeit; still in active modern German use, so recognition is higher than most items in this section; the moral/sexual connotation is more archaic than the general sense of brazenness.

records.definition: Literally 'boy of pleasure'; an archaic German term for a young male kept for sexual gratification, especially in pederastic contexts; a catamite.
records.notes: The 'Freuden-' prefix echoes 'Freudenmädchen' (prostitute, lit. 'pleasure girl'); the 'Knabe' (boy) component signals an explicitly pederastic character not captured by 'kept_partner' alone. Extremely low recognition today.

records.definition: Literally 'love of boys'; an archaic/literary German term for pederasty, the erotic attraction of adult men to adolescent boys, often idealized through the lens of classical Greek culture.
records.notes: Distinct from clinical 'Pädophilie' in that Knabe implies a pubescent or adolescent male; the classical Greek framing aestheticizes what modern law classifies as child sexual abuse.

records.definition: Pederasty; the sexual relationship between an adult man and a pubescent or adolescent boy, borrowed from the ancient Greek practice.
records.notes: A direct German transliteration of Greek/Latin 'paederastia'; more clinical in register than Knabenliebe; in historical usage often framed as a feature of Greek antiquity rather than a contemporary crime.

records.definition: Literally 'back-staircase novel'; a trashy, sensationalist pulp novel with scandalous romantic or erotic content; the German equivalent of a penny dreadful.
records.notes: The 'Hintertreppe' (back stairs) evokes servants' entrances and clandestine reading — the kind of book hidden under the mattress. Not necessarily explicitly pornographic but reliably salacious; cf. Schundliteratur.

records.definition: Trash literature; low-quality, morally objectionable writing condemned for its sexual, violent, or otherwise corrupting content; the German equivalent of pulp smut.
records.notes: Schund (trash/filth) + Literatur; central to early 20th-century German censorship debates ('Schmutz und Schund' campaigns). A moralistic umbrella term rather than a precise literary genre label.

records.definition: Literally 'pleasure play'; primarily a theatrical comedy or light drama; in archaic erotic usage, an amorous game or playful sexual encounter.
records.notes: The theatrical meaning (comedy) strongly dominates modern usage; its erotic sense is archaic and subordinate. 'Lust' in early German meant pleasure broadly, not exclusively sexual desire; cf. Lustgarten (pleasure garden).

records.definition: A seducer; a man who uses charm, flattery, or deception to persuade someone into sexual activity or moral corruption.
records.notes: Also carries the theological sense of 'tempter' (the devil as Verführer); still in active modern use, hence higher recognition than most terms in this section. 'Debaucher' is the nearest registry slot but 'seducer' is the precise English gloss.

records.definition: A seductress; a woman who uses charm, beauty, or deception to lead someone into sexual activity or moral corruption.
records.notes: Feminine form of Verführer; in literary usage typically coded as a femme fatale archetype. Still in active modern use.

records.definition: Seduction; the act of leading someone into sexual activity or moral transgression through charm, flattery, or deception.
records.notes: Still very common in modern German; in older criminal law, 'Verführung zur Unzucht' (seduction to indecency) was a specific charge. 'Debauchery' is the nearest registry slot but 'seduction' is the precise English gloss.

records.definition: A dirty, sexually perverted, or obscenity-obsessed person; a variant or dialectal form of Schmutzfink, literally 'dirty finch.'
records.notes: The -e suffix likely represents a dialectal or weak-declension variant of Schmutzfink; possibly used as a feminine form in some registers, though non-standard. See also Schmutzfink.

records.definition: Literally 'dirty finch'; a person with a penchant for sexual filth, crude humor, or pornographic material; a dirty pervert or smutty type.
records.notes: Schmutz (dirt/filth) + Fink (finch/sparrow); used both as a mild insult and affectionately depending on context; recognition is higher than most archaic terms in this section because it remains in colloquial use.

records.definition: A male procurer, panderer, or go-between; a man who arranges sexual encounters or facilitates prostitution for others.
records.notes: From kuppeln (to couple/connect); in older German law, Kuppelei (procuring) was a criminal offense. The Kuppler arranged introductions between sex workers and clients.

records.definition: A female procuress or bawd; a woman who arranges sexual encounters or manages the supply of sex workers to clients.
records.notes: Feminine form of Kuppler; historically associated with a discreet matchmaker for illicit assignations or a bawd managing sex workers. Kuppelei (the crime of procuring) was gender-neutral in application.

records.definition: The German legal and moral term for procuring: the criminal facilitation of sexual acts between third parties, encompassing organized prostitution and private pimping.
records.notes: §180 StGB criminalizes Kuppelei in Germany; the term covers both facilitating prostitution and arranging sexual encounters between third parties for profit or immoral purposes.

records.definition: Feminine plural of Kupplerin; women who act as procurers or go-betweens arranging sexual encounters between others, typically for profit.
records.notes: Historically the Kupplerin was a stock figure in German folk tales and bourgeois comedy as the scheming matchmaker who slides into procuress; masculine form is Kuppler.

records.definition: Archaic German slang for a sexually promiscuous or 'easy' woman, derived from the hammock's image of something swinging loosely between different men.
records.notes: Literal meaning is 'hammock'; the sexual slang sense is very dated and recognized only by specialists or through historical literary sources; not in active modern use.

records.definition: The vice police or morality squad; an institutional body charged with enforcing laws against prostitution, obscenity, and sexual immorality in German-speaking lands.
records.notes: Concept match to 'sexual_conservatism' is imprecise — Sittenpolizei is an institutional enforcement mechanism, not a personal quality; active in German cities from the 19th century through the Third Reich; post-war vice squads used different terminology.

records.definition: The condition of being without sexual or moral restraint; licentiousness or moral depravity, especially in the sexual sphere.
records.notes: Compound of Sitten (morals/customs) + Losigkeit (absence of); carries a moralizing, condemning register common in 19th-century social reform and temperance discourse.

records.definition: Sexual and moral dissoluteness; the habitual practice of debauchery, loose living, and sexual immorality combined with general slovenliness and disorder.
records.notes: The term conflates sexual licentiousness with general messiness and irresponsibility; 'liederlicher Lebenswandel' (licentious lifestyle) implies both sexual looseness and a disordered life.

records.definition: Adjective meaning dissolute, morally loose, or of poor sexual character; also describes slovenliness or shoddiness in non-sexual contexts.
records.notes: Unlike English 'dissolute,' liederlich carries an additional connotation of physical slovenliness and untidiness, blurring the distinction between moral and material disorder.

records.definition: Literally 'slippery'; figuratively used to mean risqué, racy, or sexually suggestive, applied to jokes, remarks, or situations with an indecent undertone.
records.notes: Still in active use in modern German, though feels slightly old-fashioned; the slippery metaphor captures how sexual content slides in without being stated directly; also used literally for icy or greasy surfaces.

records.definition: Plural noun for indecent acts or obscenities; sexual violations of public decency, used in both legal condemnation and moral censure.
records.notes: Unzucht (fornication, lewdness) is an archaic legal term found in older German penal codes (e.g. §175 on homosexuality); the plural Unzüchtigkeiten emphasizes multiple distinct acts of indecency.

records.definition: A lewd, dirty, or smutty joke; bawdy humor with explicit sexual content.
records.notes: Still encountered, though felt as slightly old-fashioned; common in compounds such as Zotenerzähler (dirty-joke-teller) and Zotenreißer (serial teller of crude jokes).

records.definition: The habitual or excessive practice of telling lewd jokes; a pattern of crude, sexually suggestive humor.
records.notes: More archaic than Zote (the individual joke); the -erei suffix indicates a habitual or compulsive pattern of behavior and carries a mildly contemptuous connotation.

records.definition: Adjective meaning grossly indecent, obscene, or foul-mouthed; applied to language or conduct that shockingly transgresses social decency norms.
records.notes: Can describe non-sexual crudeness as well; in sexual contexts implies offensive, boundary-violating indecency of speech or behavior; derived from Unflat (filth, mire); unflätige Reden means grossly lewd speech.

records.definition: The quality or instance of being unflätig; gross indecency, obscenity, or foul-mouthed vulgarity in speech or conduct.
records.notes: Closely related to the adjective Unflätig; the noun form is more archaic than the adjective and conveys strong moral reprobation; used in literary and religious condemnation of sexually offensive behavior.

records.definition: The Freudian term for the psychic energy arising from the sexual drive; in everyday German usage now synonymous with sexual desire or sex drive.
records.notes: Borrowed directly from Latin; Freud used it as a technical term for the energy of the Sexualtrieb; now so widespread that it functions both as psychoanalytic jargon and as a common everyday synonym for sex drive; concept match to 'lust' is approximate — libido is energic, lust is affective.

records.definition: Freudian 'drive'; the psychic representative of a somatic source of excitation, most prominently the sexual drive (Sexualtrieb), constituting the core motivating force of human psychic life.
records.notes: The Standard Edition translated Trieb as 'instinct,' but most modern scholars prefer 'drive' to preserve the somatic-psychic duality Freud intended; the word means 'impulse' or 'urge' in everyday German and carries no inherent crudeness.

records.definition: Freud's term for the id; the primitive, unconscious seat of libidinal and aggressive drives, operating entirely on the pleasure principle without moral constraint or reality-testing.
records.notes: Freud chose the everyday German pronoun 'Es' (it) from Georg Groddeck's usage to evoke the alien, impersonal quality of unconscious drives; the Standard Edition rendered it as the Latin 'id,' losing this deliberately colloquial flavor; concept match to 'lust' captures only the libidinal content.

records.definition: Freud's Oedipus complex; the child's unconscious sexual attraction to the opposite-sex parent and hostile rivalry with the same-sex parent, considered by Freud the nucleus of neurosis.
records.notes: Concept match to 'amorous_desire' is imprecise — the Ödipuskomplex is a structured psychodynamic formation involving desire, rivalry, and prohibition, not simply desire; so culturally embedded that it functions as a general idiom in German.

records.definition: The female counterpart to the Oedipus complex, named by Carl Jung; a girl's unconscious sexual desire for her father combined with hostile rivalry toward her mother.
records.notes: Freud explicitly rejected Jung's term, preferring to speak of a female Ödipuskomplex with distinct dynamics; the Elektrakomplex is consequently less recognized than its male counterpart and carries a slightly contested status in psychoanalytic discourse.

records.definition: Freud's concept of 'penis envy'; the theory that girls and women experience unconscious envy of the male organ as a symbol of power, completeness, and social privilege.
records.notes: Concept match to 'emasculation' is imprecise — emasculation is male loss of phallic power, Penisbeneid is female desire for it; one of Freud's most contested concepts, broadly criticized as culturally projective and misogynistic.

records.definition: Freudian 'castration anxiety'; the boy's fear of penile removal as punishment for Oedipal desires, posited as the force that drives resolution of the Oedipus complex and internalization of the law.
records.notes: In Freudian theory, the boy observes that females lack a penis and interprets this as evidence that castration occurs; fear of this fate causes him to renounce incestuous desires and identify with the father's prohibition.

records.definition: Freud's 'pleasure principle'; the governing logic of the id — the drive to seek immediate gratification of libidinal drives and avoid unpleasure, without regard for reality or consequence.
records.notes: Contrasted with the Realitätsprinzip (reality principle), which governs the ego; the Lustprinzip operates through primary process thinking and is superseded (but never eliminated) by the reality principle in psychological development.

records.definition: Freud's 'death drive' (Thanatos); the psychic drive toward entropy, dissolution, and repetition compulsion, counterposed to Eros as the life and sexual drive.
records.notes: Introduced in 'Jenseits des Lustprinzips' (1920); manifests externally as aggression and destruction (approximating sadism, hence the concept match) and internally as masochism or self-destruction; remains the most contested of Freud's major theoretical constructs.

records.definition: The 'primal scene' in Freudian theory; a young child's actual or fantasized observation of parental sexual intercourse, believed to have profound and lasting psychological effects.
records.notes: Famously analyzed in Freud's case of the 'Wolf Man'; Freud debated whether the scene must be actually witnessed or could be a phylogenetically inherited fantasy; concept match to 'intercourse_generic' captures the content of the observed act but not its psychoanalytic significance.

records.definition: Freudian 'sublimation'; the defense mechanism by which libidinal energy is redirected from direct sexual aims toward socially valued, desexualized activities such as art, science, or intellectual work.
records.notes: Distinct from repression: sublimation redirects sexual energy productively rather than suppressing it into the unconscious; Freud considered it the foundation of civilization; concept match to 'sexual_repression' is imprecise since sublimation is a productive redirection, not suppression.

records.definition: Freudian 'repression'; the fundamental defense mechanism by which unacceptable sexual or aggressive impulses are expelled from conscious awareness into the unconscious.
records.notes: Freud's foundational concept; repressed material does not disappear but returns in disguised form as neurotic symptoms, dreams, and parapraxes; so central to psychoanalysis that Verdrängung is sometimes used as a metonym for the entire psychoanalytic project.

records.definition: A wish, typically sexual, that has been pushed into the unconscious by the defense mechanism of repression, where it continues to exert pressure toward conscious expression without the subject's awareness.
records.notes: Core Freudian concept; Verdrängung (repression) was Freud's foundational defense mechanism, applied most commonly to sexual and aggressive Wünsche. Recognized by most educated Germans even without formal psychology training. Maps approximately to sexual_repression, though Freud's Wunsch (wish) is a technical term distinct from a felt emotion.

records.definition: In Freudian theory, any sexual aim or object deviating from genital coitus aimed at reproduction; in everyday German usage, a deviant or morally condemned sexual practice or desire.
records.notes: Freud used Perversion in a clinically neutral descriptive sense and wrote that 'neurosis is the negative of a perversion.' In colloquial German the term carries strong moral condemnation. The current clinical equivalent in DSM/ICD is 'paraphilia,' which is why paraphilia_general is the best registry match.

records.definition: Freud's concept that the infant possesses a diffuse, undifferentiated sexuality capable of erotic pleasure from any body part or zone, prior to organization around genital aims at puberty.
records.notes: Introduced in 'Drei Abhandlungen zur Sexualtheorie' (1905). Adult paraphilias are theorized as fixations at or regressions to this undifferentiated infantile state. Recognized mainly by psychology students and educated readers; essentially unknown outside academic contexts. Concept match is approximate: polymorphous perversion is a specific developmental claim, not a paraphilia per se.

records.definition: The mode of unconscious psychic functioning governed by the pleasure principle, seeking immediate discharge of libidinal tension through wish-fulfillment, displacement, and condensation, as in dreams and parapraxes.
records.notes: Contrasted with the Sekundärprozess (secondary process) of conscious reality-oriented thought. The primary process is the theoretical engine of libidinal drive satisfaction; mapping to 'lust' is approximate — Primärprozess is the mechanism, not the felt desire itself. Recognized only by those with formal psychoanalytic or academic psychology training.

records.definition: Archaic literary term for the vagina or womb; literally 'pleasure grotto' or 'pleasure cavity,' evoking a sheltered erotic interior space.
records.notes: Compound of Lust (pleasure, desire) and Höhle (cave, grotto). Appears in 19th-century erotic literature and early psychoanalytic writing, sometimes as a poetic vaginal term, sometimes metonymically for the womb as a site of libidinal return. Now archaic; reads as literary or ironically ornate in contemporary German. Peak recognition was in the Wilhelmine and Weimar eras.

records.definition: The infant's first object of libidinal attachment, typically the mother's breast or the mother as a whole person; the original target of the sexual drive around which all later object relations are organized.
records.notes: Central to object relations theory (Klein, Winnicott, building on Freud). The relationship to the Primärobjekt is theorized as the template for all subsequent romantic and sexual attachments. Mapping to amorous_desire is approximate: the Primärobjekt is the first object of desire, not the desire itself. Recognized almost exclusively within psychoanalytic and academic communities.

records.definition: In Freudian theory, the arrest of a portion of the libido at an earlier psychosexual stage, predisposing the individual to characteristic neurotic symptoms or atypical sexual interests tied to that stage in adulthood.
records.notes: Oral fixation → dependency and orally-organized traits; anal fixation → obsessionality and control; phallic fixation → exhibitionism or anxiety. In everyday German, Fixierung commonly means 'obsession with' something, giving it significantly higher recognition than other technical Freudian terms. Concept match is approximate: fixation causes paraphilias in Freudian theory but is not itself a paraphilia.

records.definition: In psychoanalytic theory, the defensive return to an earlier psychosexual stage or more primitive mode of gratification when the psyche is overwhelmed by anxiety or frustration.
records.notes: Freud distinguished temporal regression (to earlier libidinal fixation points), topographic regression (to perceptual-system functioning), and formal regression (to primitive modes of representation). Sexually, regression may manifest as attraction to pre-genital activities or previously abandoned aims. Note: Regression (Regression) and repression (Verdrängung) are distinct mechanisms — the shared registry mapping to paraphilia_general is an indexing approximation. Everyday German uses Regression in statistical and behavioral contexts too, boosting recognition.

records.definition: Freud's third stage of psychosexual development (approximately ages 3–6), during which children of both sexes become aware of the phallus as the central sexual symbol, giving rise to castration anxiety in boys and penis envy in girls.
records.notes: The Phallusphase (or phallische Phase) is characterized by the primacy of the phallus as the organizing symbol of sexuality, awareness of genital difference, and the emergence of the Oedipus complex. Freud controversially posited that both sexes initially recognize only one genital organ: the phallus. Mapping to 'erection' is a loose approximation given the phallocentric focus; no registry entry captures a developmental stage concept.

records.definition: Freud's first stage of psychosexual development (birth to approximately 18 months), in which the infant's libido is centered on oral stimulation and feeding as the primary source of erotic pleasure.
records.notes: Adults with oral fixation were theorized to exhibit dependency, passivity, or oral preoccupations including smoking, eating disorders, or preference for oral sex. Mapping to 'oral_sex' is approximate and reductive: the Oralphase concerns infant oral pleasure (sucking, feeding), not adult oral sexual practice. Recognized by most Germans who have taken a secondary psychology course.

records.definition: Freud's second stage of psychosexual development (approximately 18 months to 3 years), in which the infant's libido is centered on anal stimulation and the tension between retention and expulsion, linked to issues of control, autonomy, and power.
records.notes: Anal character traits theorized from fixation at this stage: orderliness (Ordnung), parsimoniousness (Geiz), and obstinacy (Eigensinn) — Freud's classic triad. Mapping to 'anal_sex' is approximate; the Analphase concerns infant anal eroticism and ego development, not adult anal intercourse. Co-recognized alongside Oralphase and Phallusphase for those with any psychology education.

records.definition: Freud's final stage of psychosexual development, beginning at puberty, in which the libido is organized around mature genital sexuality directed toward heterosexual coitus aimed at reproduction.
records.notes: Preceded by the Latenzphase (latency period, ages 6–puberty) during which sexual impulses are sublimated. The genitale Phase is the ideal developmental endpoint; failure to reach it fully was theorized to result in neurosis or perversion. Freud's teleological and heteronormative framing has been widely criticized by later analysts and feminist theorists. Mapping to piv_intercourse is approximate.

records.definition: The sending of sexually explicit text messages, images, or videos via mobile device or digital messaging platform; a direct English loanword used without modification in German.
records.notes: Portmanteau of 'sex' and 'texting' borrowed directly from English. Fully integrated into standard German journalism, youth-protection law discourse, and everyday speech. Particularly prominent in legal and educational contexts addressing minors and digital consent.

records.definition: Nude or sexually explicit photographs shared digitally, typically privately between partners or via online platforms; used as an English-language plural noun within German digital culture.
records.notes: Used as-is from English with no morphological adaptation. Strongly preferred over the native 'Nacktbilder' in youth and online contexts; common in phrases like 'Nudes schicken' (to send nudes). The English plural form is treated as an uninflected German noun.

records.definition: Nude photographs or sexually explicit images; the native German compound for nude pictures, used across registers from journalism to casual conversation.
records.notes: Compound of nackt (naked) and Bilder (pictures/images). More neutral and formal than the loanword 'Nudes'; preferred in legal texts, news reporting, school-based media literacy, and parental guidance. Slightly higher recognition than 'Nudes' due to being native German, but among younger speakers the English loanword is increasingly dominant.

records.definition: The practice of performing sexual or erotic acts live on webcam in exchange for payment or subscriptions; a direct English gerund loanword used in German sex-work discourse.
records.notes: Used in German journalism covering the digital adult industry, in sex-worker self-identification, and on German-language platforms. Less universally recognized by the general population than older sex-work terms, but increasing steadily with the mainstreaming of platforms like OnlyFans.

records.definition: Sexual activity conducted online via text chat, voice, video, or real-time messaging, typically involving mutual erotic exchange and often simultaneous masturbation.
records.notes: Peaked in the late 1990s–early 2000s chat-room era (ICQ, IRC, early video chat); still in use but somewhat dated compared to platform-specific terminology. Higher recognition among speakers who were online in the early internet era. German-specific coinage Netzsex exists as a native-language parallel.

records.definition: German-native compound for cybersex; sexual activity conducted online via chat or messaging; literally 'net sex.'
records.notes: Compound of Netz (net, web) and Sex. The German-language alternative to the English loanword Cybersex, more prevalent in early German internet culture (circa 1997–2006) before English loanwords became dominant in digital sexual vocabulary. Now largely displaced by 'Cybersex' and platform-specific terms; reads as dated.

records.definition: Sexually explicit verbal communication during or around sexual activity, intended to heighten arousal; a direct English loanword used without modification across mainstream and kink contexts in German.
records.notes: Used without translation in German; native alternatives such as 'schmutzige Rede' or 'erotisches Sprechen' exist but are rarely used in practice. Dirty Talk spans mainstream and BDSM contexts; the adjective 'dirty' carries a transgressive sexual charge even for German speakers unfamiliar with English.

records.definition: An online text or video chat session conducted with the explicit purpose of mutual erotic exchange and simultaneous masturbation between participants.
records.notes: Compound of Masturbation and Chat. Peaked during the early internet chat-room era (ICQ, IRC, early webcam platforms circa 1998–2006). Now largely displaced by platform-specific terms, Cybersex, or video-based terminology. The explicit naming of Masturbation in the compound makes it moderately crude despite clinical compound structure.

records.definition: A casual sexual encounter without romantic commitment; a direct English loanword fully integrated into German dating and youth culture.
records.notes: Also spelled 'Hookup' or 'Hook Up' in German texts; orthography is inconsistent. Dominant in dating-app contexts and youth language; recognized across age groups but most natural for speakers under 45. German has no single-word native equivalent of similar currency.

records.definition: A person with whom one has a regular casual sexual relationship without romantic commitment; a friend or acquaintance with ongoing sexual benefits.
records.notes: Borrowed directly from English without morphological modification; the 'fuck' component gives it notably higher crude charge than alternatives like 'Freund mit Vorteilen' (calque of friends with benefits), which is also used. One of the more crude English sexual loanwords in common German youth usage.

records.definition: Casual sex with no emotional commitment or expectation of a continuing relationship; abbreviation of the English phrase 'No Strings Attached' used in German dating and hookup culture.
records.notes: The abbreviation NSA is borrowed directly from English-language personal-ad culture; widely understood in dating-app contexts and hookup forums, but lower general recognition than 'One-Night-Stand' given its abbreviated form. Frequently appears in Grindr and heterosexual hookup app profiles on German-language platforms.

records.definition: A sexual encounter spanning a single occasion between two people with no expectation of meeting again for sex; one of the most thoroughly integrated English loanwords in German sexual vocabulary.
records.notes: Used in German news media, literary fiction, film, and everyday speech without hesitation; German has no single-word native equivalent of equivalent cultural currency. Abbreviated ONS (entry 25). The hyphenated form is standard in German orthography.

records.definition: Abbreviation of One-Night-Stand; a casual single-occasion sexual encounter with no expectation of a continuing relationship.
records.notes: Common in German dating-app profiles, personal ads, and online forum discussions of casual sex. Preferred over the full form in character-limited contexts such as Tinder bios and Grindr profiles. Predominantly used by younger speakers; less universal recognition than the unabbreviated 'One-Night-Stand.'

records.definition: English loanword used in German for a late-night contact made to someone purely for casual sex with no romantic commitment.
records.notes: Fully adopted anglicism in German youth language; used identically to the English source term; appears frequently in German rap lyrics and dating discourse.

records.definition: English loanword for an undefined romantic or sexual relationship that has the emotional qualities of a partnership but lacks explicit labels or mutual commitment.
records.notes: Adopted into German Gen Z social media discourse from approximately 2022; primarily used by speakers under 30; widely discussed in German relationship and dating content on TikTok and Instagram.

records.definition: Japanese animated or illustrated pornography; used in German internet culture as a genre label for sexually explicit anime or manga content.
records.notes: Borrowed into German via English internet culture; itself a Japanese loanword (変態, lit. 'pervert/abnormal') now used globally as a pornographic genre label; recognition boosted by the large German anime fandom.

records.definition: English loanword used in German fanfiction and internet communities for sexually explicit written or illustrated creative content.
records.notes: In German internet usage 'Smut' is strongly associated with explicit fanfiction and amateur creative writing; broader usage can mean any sexually explicit user-generated content; recognition concentrated in fanfic and anime communities.

records.definition: Internet adage stating that sexually explicit content exists for any conceivable subject or character; used identically in German internet communities.
records.notes: Originated on English-language imageboards circa 2006–2007; adopted verbatim into German internet culture; peak recognition was among chan-adjacent communities around 2010–2012; still understood but less actively cited than at peak.

records.definition: English loanword from chan culture for a man who compulsively masturbates to pornography; used in German internet and meme contexts for a degraded porn addict.
records.notes: Derives from the 'Coomer' Wojak meme variant; recognition skews heavily toward young male German-language users of imageboards and gaming forums; peaked as a meme character in 2019–2020; niche even within internet culture.

records.definition: English loanword for a man who is excessively attentive and deferential toward women in hopes of sexual or romantic approval.
records.notes: One of the most rapidly adopted English internet slang terms in German youth language; disseminated via TikTok and YouTube gaming culture in 2020; well understood even by casual social media users; also used as a verb ('simpen').

records.definition: Clipping of 'involuntary celibate'; a man who cannot find a sexual partner and attributes this to societal unfairness rather than his own behavior, often with expressed resentment toward women.
records.notes: Entered German mainstream media discourse around 2018–2019 following high-profile violent incidents; widely covered in German-language journalism, political discussion, and public broadcasting; used without modification.

records.definition: English loanword for a person who voluntarily chooses celibacy; internet subculture counterpart to 'incel,' used in manosphere, NoFap, and monk-mode communities.
records.notes: Niche term primarily known within German communities engaged with manosphere or NoFap discourse; rarely appears in mainstream German media; recognition concentrated among young men active in these online spaces; concept slug 'sexual_abstinence' is broader than the internet-identity usage.

records.definition: Acronym borrowed from English ('Mom I'd Like to Fuck'); objectifying label for a sexually attractive mother, used in German internet culture and pornographic genre labeling.
records.notes: Entered German vernacular via American Pie (1999) and pornographic platform category labels; among the most recognized English sexual acronyms in German; occasionally expanded as 'Mutter, die ich ficken würde' in German media contexts.

records.definition: Acronym borrowed from English ('Dad I'd Like to Fuck'); objectifying label for an attractive father, used in German social media and internet discourse.
records.notes: Less widely recognized than MILF in Germany; primarily circulates in social media and online dating contexts; recognition highest among women aged 20–40 active on Instagram and TikTok.

records.definition: English loanword for an older woman, typically 40+, who pursues sexual or romantic relationships with significantly younger men.
records.notes: Entered German via English-language media and the American TV series Cougar Town (2009); remains in active use but peak popular awareness was in the late 2000s to early 2010s; 'Cougar' is used as-is since the German word 'Puma' is not used in this sense.

records.definition: English loanword from gay subculture for a young, slim, smooth-skinned gay man; used in German LGBTQ+ communities and internet culture as a community body-type label.
records.notes: Gay subculture body-type taxonomy label adopted verbatim into German; no German-origin equivalent exists; 'gay' is the closest registry concept but underdescribes the specific body-type subtype; recognition extends beyond the gay community through mainstream internet culture.

records.definition: English loanword from gay subculture for a large, heavyset, and typically hairy gay man; used in German LGBTQ+ communities as a positive community identity label.
records.notes: Gay subculture body-type label; the German word 'Bär' is not used in this sexual sense — the English loanword 'Bear' is the standard form in German-language gay community spaces; recognition concentrated within the gay community and general internet users.

records.definition: English loanword from gay subculture for a slim, hairy gay man positioned between the twink and bear body types; used in German LGBTQ+ contexts.
records.notes: Niche even within the German gay community; primarily known among men actively engaged with gay subculture taxonomy; the German word 'Otter' (otter/viper) carries no sexual connotation, so the English form is used exclusively.

records.definition: English loanword from gay subculture for a younger, heavier or chubby gay man who presents as the youthful variant of a bear; used in German LGBTQ+ communities.
records.notes: Very niche in German, known mainly within bear-community subgroups; the English loanword dominates over any German alternative in German-language online gay spaces; the 'bear taxonomy' (bear, cub, otter, pup) is used as an integrated system.

records.definition: English loanword used in German internet and LGBTQ+ culture for a sexually dominant, attractive older man; also the caretaker-dominant role in BDSM Daddy Dom/Little dynamics.
records.notes: Distinct from the standard German family term 'Daddy/Papa' meaning father; in sexual contexts the English form 'Daddy' is used to avoid ambiguity; widely understood across German pop culture, BDSM communities, and social media.

records.definition: English loanword for a typically older, wealthy man who provides money, gifts, or lifestyle support to a younger partner in exchange for companionship and sexual access.
records.notes: Fully integrated anglicism in German; recognized across a wide age range; used as a compound noun ('ein Sugar Daddy'); frequently discussed in German media in connection with platforms like Seeking Arrangement.

records.definition: English loanword for a younger person who receives money, gifts, or lifestyle benefits from a wealthier older partner in exchange for companionship and sexual access.
records.notes: Widely recognized in Germany; used as a compound noun ('ein Sugar Baby'); covered extensively in German mainstream media debates about the ethics and legal status of sugar dating arrangements.

records.definition: English loanword for a young man who adopts a feminine aesthetic through clothing, makeup, and demeanor while typically retaining a male gender identity.
records.notes: Used as a self-identifier in German anime, LGBTQ+, and gaming communities; distinct from cross-dressing in that it is a sustained aesthetic identity rather than a discrete behavior; concept slug 'cross_dressing' is the closest registry match but does not fully capture the internet-subculture identity dimension; often used affirmatively by those it describes.

records.definition: English loanword used as an internet slur for a transgender woman or feminine-presenting man who 'traps' straight men into unintentional homosexual attraction.
records.notes: Predominantly used in German anime and chan communities; highly offensive to transgender people; peak usage was in chan and anime meme culture circa 2013–2016; increasingly challenged as a slur even within those communities; the German word 'Falle' (trap) is not used in this sexual sense.

records.definition: English loanword (acronym: 'That Ho Over There') used in German internet slang as a pejorative for a promiscuous or sexually attention-seeking woman.
records.notes: Originated in AAVE and hip-hop culture; adopted into German internet slang primarily via social media and German rap; peak usage in German internet culture was approximately 2015–2018; still used but less dominant; also used as an adjective ('thot-like').

records.definition: English loanword ('electronic thot') for a woman who cynically leverages sexual appeal and flirtatious behavior online to gain followers, donations, or clout.
records.notes: Very niche even in German internet subculture; primarily used in gaming, Twitch streaming, and chan-adjacent communities; differs from 'e-girl' by carrying an explicitly pejorative implication of calculated manipulation rather than just a particular online aesthetic; peaked in German usage approximately 2018–2020.

records.definition: German compound loanword for a woman who produces and sells sexually explicit content on the OnlyFans subscription platform.
records.notes: Hyphenated German compound; recognized across a wide age range due to heavy mainstream media coverage of OnlyFans during and after the COVID-19 pandemic; carries a mild stigma in mainstream German discourse but is increasingly normalized among younger cohorts.

records.definition: English loanword for a woman who performs sexual or erotic acts live on webcam in exchange for payment, tips, or subscriptions.
records.notes: Hyphenated German compound; predates 'OnlyFans-Girl' chronologically as the dominant term for online sex performance; recognized widely across age groups; 'Cam-Boy' exists as a less common male variant; associated platforms include LiveJasmin and Chaturbate in German user discourse.

records.definition: A male sex worker or erotic performer who streams live sexual content via webcam for a paying online audience.
records.notes: The registry defines cam_performer as female; Cam-Boy is the male-specific counterpart but maps to the same functional concept.

records.definition: Pornographic video content in which a real person's face or body is digitally grafted onto explicit footage using AI deepfake technology, typically without that person's knowledge or consent.
records.notes: Legally regulated in Germany under §184k StGB since 2021; distinct from amateur or professional pornography by the non-consensual identity substitution that defines the category.

records.definition: The non-consensual distribution of intimate or sexually explicit images or videos of a person, typically by a former partner as retaliation or control.
records.notes: English loanword preferred in German media and legal discourse alongside the native compounds Racheporno and Rachepornografie; all three terms coexist.

records.definition: German compound noun for revenge pornography; the non-consensual distribution of sexually explicit images to harm or humiliate the depicted person.
records.notes: Native German compound; slightly less formal than Rachepornografie but more immediately accessible; both terms coexist with the English loanword Revenge-Porn.

records.definition: Formal German compound for revenge pornography, framing it as a systematic category rather than a single act; preferred in criminal-code language and journalism.
records.notes: The -grafie suffix signals broader industry or systematic framing; slightly more technical register than Racheporno; used in §184b and related statutes discussions.

records.definition: The act of ejaculating inside a partner's vagina or anus without a condom, or the visible leaking of semen from the orifice afterwards; an English loanword used widely in German pornographic and internet subculture.
records.notes: Fully integrated English loanword in German pornographic taxonomy; no established native German equivalent in common use.

records.definition: Female ejaculation; the expulsion of fluid from the urethral area during intense sexual arousal or orgasm; an English loanword ubiquitous in German sexual and pornographic discourse.
records.notes: German courts briefly attempted to classify the expelled fluid as urine and ban its depiction in pornography; ruling ultimately did not hold. High recognition driven by pornographic prevalence.

records.definition: The sexual practice in which a woman or non-binary person penetrates a male partner anally using a strap-on dildo; English loanword used in German kink and sex-positive communities.
records.notes: Recognition concentrated in kink-aware and internet-active demographics; significantly lower among older or non-internet-using adults.

records.definition: The consensual practice or fantasy in which a person gains sexual arousal from watching or knowing their partner is having sex with another person.
records.notes: Used as both a kink self-identifier and an internet/political insult implying weakness; the kink sense is primary in German sexual subculture contexts.

records.definition: A man whose partner has sex with other men; in kink contexts a consensual fetish role; in pejorative internet use an insult implying weakness and sexual humiliation.
records.notes: Higher recognition than Cuckolding because the noun form circulates more widely as an insult in German-language far-right and manosphere communities, mirroring English usage.

records.definition: A married woman who engages in consensual sexual encounters with men other than her husband, with the husband's full knowledge and enthusiastic participation in the arrangement as a shared erotic practice.
records.notes: Recognition limited to communities engaged with swinging, cuckolding, or ethical non-monogamy discourse; well below general-population awareness.

records.definition: A sexual kink or fantasy centered on the act of ejaculating inside a partner with the explicit goal or intense fantasy of achieving pregnancy; implies condomless penetration and deliberate insemination.
records.notes: Distinct from creampie (focus on visible semen display) and bareback (focus on the absence of a condom); breeding adds the impregnation-fantasy component that marks it as a clinically distinct concept.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse, especially anal sex, performed without a condom; originated in gay male subculture and now used broadly in German sexual discourse.
records.notes: Etymologically from horseback riding without a saddle; entered gay male subculture vocabulary during the 1990s AIDS crisis and has since broadened across gender and orientation contexts.

records.definition: Explicit German compound for condomless sexual intercourse; the appended -Sex removes any ambiguity and makes the referent unambiguous in public health and harm-reduction contexts.
records.notes: Often used in German public health communications because its explicitness eliminates the ambiguity that can attach to the standalone term Bareback or the euphemistic Natursex.

records.definition: German compound meaning 'natural sex'; a euphemistic term for condomless intercourse that frames the absence of a condom as an authentic or unmediated physical experience.
records.notes: The natur- prefix carries an implicit normative claim that condomless sex is more 'real' or intimate; this ideological loading is absent from the neutral term Bareback, marking a distinct register.

records.definition: The subculture practice of having sex or watching sex in semi-public outdoor locations such as car parks or wooded areas, typically with anonymous participants who double as voyeurs or exhibitionists.
records.notes: Term originated in British English slang; awareness in German-speaking contexts is concentrated among internet-active adults; the practice exists in Germany under local German terms but the English loanword is the most recognized label online.

records.definition: The non-consensual act of secretly removing or sabotaging a condom during sex without the partner's knowledge or agreement; legally classified as sexual assault in Germany.
records.notes: Criminalized in Germany under the reformed sexual self-determination law following a 2016 landmark case; intensive media coverage drove recognition; the English loanword is used universally in German legal and journalistic discourse with no competing native German term.

records.definition: The practice of creating a false online identity to deceive someone into a romantic or sexual relationship; an English loanword fully integrated into German internet slang.
A photograph of a penis, typically sent digitally and often unsolicited; an English loanword widely used across German internet and youth culture.
records.notes: Preferred over the native compound Schwanzfoto in everyday usage; frequently discussed in German legal contexts around digital sexual harassment.

records.definition: German compound for a photograph of a penis (Schwanz = crude slang for penis, Foto = photo); the native-German counterpart to the English loanword Dick-Pic.
records.notes: Schwanz carries a mild-to-moderate crude charge on its own; combining it with Foto produces a slightly cruder register than the relatively sanitized English loanword. Significantly less common in actual usage than Dick-Pic.

records.definition: Abbreviation of flexibel; used in German gay and sexual subculture to describe a person who comfortably takes both insertive (top) and receptive (bottom) roles during sexual activity.
records.notes: Recognition concentrated in gay male and kink communities; low among the general population; appears in German dating app profiles and hookup contexts analogously to English 'vers'.

records.definition: To flirt; to engage in playful, suggestive, or lightly provocative romantic and sexual signaling with another person without necessarily pursuing further intimacy.
records.notes: Originally borrowed from French/English flirter; now fully assimilated into standard German as a neutral everyday verb; recognition is near-universal across all age groups and registers.

records.definition: Online sexual harassment; the targeted and unwanted delivery of sexually explicit content, sexual insults, or coercive sexual messages to a person via digital platforms.
records.notes: Standard legal and journalistic term in German; addressed under §184i StGB (sexuelle Belästigung); high recognition driven by sustained media and public-health campaigns.

records.definition: Coordinated mass online harassment in which a group of users floods an individual's digital presence with sexual insults, explicit content, or threatening messages intended to intimidate or silence them.
records.notes: The sexual harassment sense is a specific subset of the broader internet meaning (coordinated harassment for any motive); recognition limited to politically active or highly online users; no native German equivalent in common circulation.

records.definition: The organized German naturist and nudist movement, emphasizing social nudity in communal settings as an expression of bodily freedom, physical health, and egalitarianism; the defining institution of German nudist culture.
records.notes: FKK has a specific cultural-historical character distinct from anglophone naturism, rooted in the German Lebensreform and Wandervogel movements of the early 20th century and institutionalized at mass scale in the DDR; the concept carries strong German national-cultural specificity that 'naturism' does not capture.

records.definition: Abbreviation for Freikörperkultur ('Free Body Culture'), the organized German naturist movement promoting communal non-sexual nudity in designated outdoor and recreational spaces.
records.notes: Culturally iconic in German-speaking countries; especially prominent in former East Germany where it was near-universal. More mainstream and desexualized than comparable nudist movements in Anglophone cultures.

records.definition: A designated beach where nudity is permitted or customary within the Freikörperkultur tradition.
records.notes: Common throughout Germany, Austria, and Scandinavia; usually signposted. Not considered taboo or sexual in mainstream German culture.

records.definition: An organized club or association for the practice of Freikörperkultur, with membership, dedicated facilities, and designated grounds.
records.notes: Reflects German Vereinskultur (associational club culture); many FKK-Vereine date to the early 20th century and were formalized or revived post-WWII.

records.definition: Naturism: the philosophy and practice of communal nudity in natural settings as a wholesome, non-sexual lifestyle emphasizing connection with nature and bodily acceptance.
records.notes: More philosophical register than FKK or Nudismus; emphasizes the back-to-nature and health ideology. Affiliated internationally with the International Naturist Federation.

records.definition: A naturist; a person who practices and advocates for naturism as a lifestyle.
records.notes: Loanword from English/French naturiste; carries slightly more philosophical connotation than Nudist.

records.definition: Nudism: the practice of communal social nudity; used interchangeably with Naturismus but with a more pragmatic and less philosophical emphasis.
records.notes: Nudismus vs. Naturismus: Nudismus refers to the practice itself; Naturismus implies the broader philosophical back-to-nature ideology. Both are non-sexual lifestyle terms.

records.definition: A nudist; a person who practices nudism by participating in communal social nudity.
records.notes: Loanword from English 'nudist'; standard contemporary German usage.

records.definition: Nude bathing; the act of bathing or swimming without clothing, typically at a designated beach or body of water.
records.notes: Highly normalized German compound noun; culturally routine rather than transgressive. Differs from English 'skinny dipping' in that it implies organized or designated-area practice rather than spontaneous activity.

records.definition: Nude camping; camping at designated naturist campsites where clothing is optional or not worn.
records.notes: Compound following standard German pattern; less universal than Nacktbaden but readily understood.

records.definition: Nude culture; the broader cultural movement and lifestyle centered on communal social nudity, encompassing FKK and naturism as expressions of a body-positive worldview.
records.notes: Older or more literary variant of Freikörperkultur; can also refer broadly to a society's cultural attitudes toward the naked body rather than specifically to the FKK movement.

records.definition: Nakedness; the state of being without clothing, applicable across neutral, artistic, medical, and sexual contexts.
records.notes: Semantically neutral; context determines whether the charge is clinical, aesthetic, or erotic. Core everyday German vocabulary with no inherent vulgarity.

records.definition: A beach designated for nude bathing; a naturist beach.
records.notes: More descriptively transparent compound than FKK-Strand (Nacktbaden + Strand); functionally synonymous but more explicit to audiences unfamiliar with the FKK abbreviation.

records.definition: Open-air nudism; naturism practiced specifically in outdoor environments rather than enclosed or indoor venues.
records.notes: Compound of Freiluft (open air/outdoors) + Nudismus; emphasizes the outdoor dimension explicitly. Less common as a standalone term; more likely in advocacy, legal, or documentation contexts than in everyday speech.

records.definition: Sexual enlightenment or sex education; the formal or informal provision of accurate information about human sexuality, reproduction, and relationships to children, adolescents, or the public.
records.notes: Carries the philosophical weight of Aufklärung (Enlightenment); frames sex education as rational emancipation from ignorance. Broader than the parental 'talk'; includes school curricula and public health campaigns.

records.definition: In the context of sexuality, the act of informing a child or young person about sex, reproduction, and relationships; derived from the broader philosophical meaning of 'enlightenment' or 'clarification.'
records.english_term: the birds and the bees talk / sex ed
records.notes: Primary meaning is the 18th-century Enlightenment philosophical movement or generic clarification/briefing; sexual education sense is idiomatic and universally understood. German parents 'klären auf' (enlighten) their children about sex.

records.definition: Sexual education; formal educational instruction covering biological, emotional, and relational aspects of sexuality as implemented in school curricula.
records.notes: Erziehung = upbringing/education (broader than Unterricht/teaching). Standard term in German educational policy and school law. More systemic and formal than Aufklärung.

records.definition: Sexual pedagogy; the academic discipline and professional practice concerned with education and guidance around sexual development across the lifespan.
records.notes: University and professional register; used in educator and social worker training. More specialized than Sexualerziehung; implies a theoretically grounded, lifespan-oriented discipline rather than just school curricula.

records.definition: Sex education as a designated school subject; the biology and health curriculum covering human reproduction, anatomy, and sexuality in German secondary schools.
records.notes: Specifically the named school subject (Sexualkunde-Unterricht). Somewhat dated; modern curricula may integrate content into Biologie or use Sexualerziehung. Strongly associated with generations schooled in the 1970s–2000s.

records.definition: Shame thresholds or shame limits; the individual or culturally defined points at which bodily exposure, nudity, or sexual behavior triggers a shame response.
records.notes: Key term in German Sexualpädagogik; used to describe where individual modesty begins and what triggers shame. Recognizing and respecting Schamgrenzen is a central ethical principle in German sex education curricula.

records.definition: The sense or feeling of shame; in sexual contexts, the emotional experience of embarrassment, exposure, or violation when one's body or sexuality is involved.
records.notes: Not exclusively sexual; core psychological vocabulary. In sex education, Schamgefühl is treated as a natural emotional response to be acknowledged and respected rather than dismissed, forming the basis for boundary-setting education.

records.definition: Intimacy limits or personal boundaries; the lines an individual draws around physical closeness, touch, and sexual contact with others.
records.notes: Standard term in German sexual health education, therapy, and consent education. Often taught alongside Zustimmung and Grenzüberschreitung in school-based programs.

records.definition: Boundary violation or transgression; in sexual contexts, the act of crossing another person's stated or implied bodily, intimate, or sexual limits without consent.
records.notes: General German compound for crossing any limit (border crossing, rule breaking, personal boundary); in sexual and pedagogical discourse specifically denotes unwanted physical or intimate contact. Severity ranges from mild to criminal.

records.definition: Consent or agreement; in sexual contexts, the freely given, informed, and ongoing agreement to engage in sexual activity.
records.notes: General German word for agreement/approval across all domains; in sexual discourse the standard lay and educational term for consent. Less formal than Einwilligung; more common in everyday sex education and activist language.

records.definition: Informed consent; the formal or legal expression of voluntary agreement to a specific act including sexual contact; carries stronger legal weight than Zustimmung.
records.notes: Preferred legal and medical-ethical term; appears in German sexual assault legislation (§177 StGB) and medical ethics discourse. More formal register than Zustimmung; implies a specific, deliberate act of agreement rather than general willingness.
