records.definition: Mutual consent or consensus; in sexual discourse, the shared and ongoing agreement of all parties to engage in sexual activity, emphasizing its collaborative and negotiated character.
records.notes: From Latin consensus; used across political, academic, and social domains. In sexual discourse particularly prominent in BDSM and consent-culture communities ('Konsens-Prinzip') as well as mainstream sex education. Emphasizes mutuality more explicitly than Zustimmung or Einwilligung.

records.definition: The feeling of shame about one's body, sexuality, or sexual behavior; also (archaic/poetic) the genital or pubic region itself.
records.notes: German Scham has a somatic double meaning absent in English: Schamhaare (pubic hair), Schamlippen (labia), Schambein (pubic bone). The shame-emotion and genital-anatomy senses are etymologically fused, giving the word a bodily weight that English 'shame' lacks.

records.definition: Disgrace or scandal resulting from sexual transgression or moral failure; the public dishonor attached to a shameful sexual act.
records.notes: Stronger than Scham (subjective feeling); Schande is the social consequence — being publicly dishonored. 'Das ist eine Schande!' is the standard exclamation of moral outrage. Often frames the community's verdict rather than the offender's inner state.

records.definition: A shameful or outrageous deed, especially a sexual offense or act of moral depravity considered a violation of community standards.
records.notes: Compound: Schand- (shame/scandal) + Tat (act/deed). Often appears in criminal and ecclesiastical contexts for rape, sexual assault, or other acts that bring public disgrace. Slightly archaic in everyday use but still appears in media reporting of crimes.

records.definition: The quality of being naturally bashful or modest about sexual matters; an ingrained sense of sexual shame governing comportment.
records.notes: Less pathological than Prüderie; implies cultivated or instilled sexual modesty rather than excessive neurotic inhibition. The -haftigkeit suffix marks it as a character trait. Fading from active everyday use; more common in literary and psychological discourse.

records.definition: Prudery; excessive or affected modesty about sexual matters, often implying hypocritical or pathological sexual inhibition.
records.notes: Loanword via French 'pruderie'. Almost always used critically or ironically in modern German; the person is called 'prüde' (adjective). High recognition sustained by shared European cultural discourse about sexual openness vs. repression.

records.definition: Moral rigorism; strictness or severity in upholding sexual and social standards of propriety.
records.notes: Compound: Sitten (morals/customs) + Strenge (strictness/severity). Associated with Wilhelmine-era and Victorian social conservatism in German-speaking countries. Somewhat dated; predominantly appears in historical and literary analysis rather than everyday speech.

records.definition: Virtuousness; the positive moral quality of being sexually pure, behaviorally restrained, and ethically upright.
records.notes: The positive pole of the shame-morality axis; unlike Prüderie or Keuschheit carries no ironic loading. Contrasts directly with Lasterhaftigkeit. Somewhat literary and philosophical in contemporary usage; more common in religious or classical educational contexts.

records.definition: Chastity; the sexual virtue of abstaining from intercourse outside of marriage, or from all sexual activity as a religious ideal.
records.notes: Central concept in Catholic and Protestant sexual ethics; Keuschheitsgelübde = vow of chastity. Widely understood but associated primarily with religious rather than secular discourse in contemporary Germany. Appears in youth purity-pledge contexts and theological literature.

records.definition: Sexual abstinence or general temperance; deliberate self-restraint from sexual activity for moral, religious, or health reasons.
records.notes: Slightly broader than Keuschheit; applies to abstinence from any appetite (alcohol, food, sex). The sexual application is dominant in moralistic discourse. Used in sex-education contexts for abstinence-only programs and in health messaging.

records.definition: Abstention or formal restraint; the deliberate act of withholding oneself from sexual activity, framed procedurally or administratively rather than as virtue.
records.notes: More formal and neutral than Enthaltsamkeit; primary modern use is political (Enthaltung bei der Abstimmung = abstention in a vote). Sexual application requires explicit context and tends toward legal or regulatory framing.

records.definition: Modesty, chasteness, and sexual decency; an archaic term for the propriety expected of sexually respectable persons, especially women.
records.notes: From züchtig (see below); largely displaced by Keuschheit and Schamhaftigkeit in active use. Carries a gentle cultivated-virtue connotation rather than harsh religious enforcement. Recognition concentrated in older and educated cohorts; fading in younger generations.

records.definition: Chaste, modest, or decorous; an archaic adjective for sexually proper, restrained, or well-behaved persons.
records.notes: In older German literary tradition applied especially to women; also appears in compound Zucht und Ordnung (discipline and order). Rarely used in contemporary speech outside deliberate archaism or irony. Shares root with züchtigen (to discipline/punish), revealing the coercive dimension of sexual modesty norms.

records.definition: Decency and propriety in behavior, including sexual comportment; the social standard of respectable and non-offensive conduct.
records.notes: Covers all propriety, not exclusively sexual; 'das gehört sich nicht' (that is indecent) is the everyday equivalent. Anstandsregeln = rules of decency. A culturally central concept in German-speaking societies; failing to observe Anstand is a serious social offense.

records.definition: Respectability and decency; the quality of adhering to accepted sexual and social norms in behavior and reputation.
records.notes: Abstract noun from anständig (decent); implies both outward behavior and inner moral character. Slightly more emphatic than Anstand; frequently used in moral evaluation of persons rather than individual acts.

records.definition: Indecency or impropriety; sexually offensive or socially unacceptable behavior or language that violates standards of public decency.
records.notes: Direct antonym of Anständigkeit. Used in both everyday and legal-moral registers; 'grobe Unanständigkeit' (gross indecency) echoes criminal law language. Can describe crude speech, offensive gestures, or explicitly sexual acts in public.

records.definition: Indecent, improper, or dirty; an adjective widely used for anything sexually offensive, crude, or violating social decorum.
records.notes: High-frequency everyday word across all registers; children learn it early ('das ist unanständig!'). Covers a wide range from mildly rude (dirty joke) to explicitly sexual (public nudity, obscene gesture) depending on context.

records.definition: Sin; in religious and moral discourse, any sexual transgression regarded as a violation of divine or natural law.
records.notes: Generic German word for sin; in sexual contexts prototypically denotes fornication, adultery, and other church-condemned acts. Also used hyperbolically in secular speech ('das ist eine Sünde!' = that's a crime/shame). Mapped to fornication as the prototypical religious sexual sin concept.

records.definition: Sinful; describing sexual behavior, desires, or persons regarded as morally transgressive or violating divine law.
records.notes: Adjective form of Sünde. Notably used hyperbolically in secular speech for something intensely pleasurable but supposedly forbidden ('sündhaft lecker' = sinfully delicious, 'sündhaft teuer' = sinfully expensive). This ironic secular use substantially coexists with the serious moral-religious register.

records.definition: Scapegoat; a person designated to bear collective blame or stigma for a community's sexual transgressions or moral failures.
records.notes: Derived from the biblical sin-goat (Leviticus 16) driven into the wilderness bearing communal sin. In sexual discourse applied when one person — often a woman — is made to carry the group's sexual shame. Mapped to slut_shaming as the closest available registry concept for blame-assignment in a sexual moral context; the match is imperfect since Sündenbock is the target, not the act.

records.definition: Vicious, depraved, or dissolute; describing a person or lifestyle marked by habitual indulgence in immoral or sexual excess.
records.notes: Adjective of Laster (vice); implies a habitual, character-defining moral degradation rather than a single transgression. Somewhat literary and dated in active use; more common in historical and theological texts than contemporary speech.

records.definition: Vice or depravity; a habitual moral failing or indulgent engagement in pleasures considered sinful, especially those of a sexual nature.
records.notes: Standard German word for vice; productive in compounds: Lastermaul (foul-mouthed scandalmonger), Lasterhöhle (den of iniquity/vice den), Lotterleben (dissolute life). Sexual vices are the prototypical Laster in religious discourse; term remains well-known through these compounds even as standalone use declines.

records.definition: Immorality or indecency; the general quality of disregarding accepted sexual and social moral codes.
records.notes: Formal compound: un- + Sittlichkeit (morality/ethics). Used in moral-philosophical, legal-historical, and ecclesiastical discourse. Less common in everyday speech than Unanständigkeit; recognition concentrated in educated and older cohorts.

records.definition: Contrary to good morals; a legal-moral adjective for sexual conduct that violates community moral standards, equivalent to the Latin contra bonos mores.
records.notes: Legal term anchored in German civil law: §138 BGB voids contracts that are sittenwidrig (contrary to public morality). In sexual contexts marks behavior as both legally actionable and morally unacceptable. Recognition concentrated in legal, academic, and older educated registers.

records.definition: Immorality or violation of public morals; the legal-philosophical noun for conduct that offends community moral standards, used especially in contract and family law to invalidate transactions.
records.notes: Noun pair to sittenwidrig; central to German legal doctrine under §138 BGB. More technical and formal than Unsittlichkeit; recognition concentrated in legal professionals and older educated cohorts. In sexual contexts encompasses prostitution contracts, coerced marriages, and similar instruments historically voided on moral grounds.

records.definition: A scandalmonger or foul-mouthed person who spreads sexual gossip, shameful insults, or morally defaming speech about others' sexuality.
records.notes: Compound: Schand- (shame/scandal) + Maul (crude: mouth/snout, always pejorative when applied to humans). The Maul component itself contributes significant crudeness. Applied to someone whose speech weaponizes sexual shame; the compound is moderately archaic but widely recognized. Mapped to slut_shaming as the closest blame-distribution concept in the registry.

records.definition: To crack or tell dirty, bawdy, or sexually ribald jokes; an idiomatic phrase for ribald joke-telling.
records.notes: Reißen (to rip/tear) is used idiomatically in the sense of 'to crack' or 'to deliver'; the phrase carries mild moral disapproval and implies a lack of refinement in the speaker.

records.definition: A person who habitually tells dirty, bawdy, or off-color jokes; a ribald raconteur.
records.notes: Agent noun formed directly from the idiom 'Zoten reißen'; implies social disapproval and low refinement rather than moral outrage. Mild enough to appear in published fiction without censorship.

records.definition: The article of the German criminal code (Strafgesetzbuch §175) that criminalized sexual acts between men; enacted 1871, brutally expanded under the Nazis 1935, and not fully repealed until 1994.
records.notes: Over 100,000 men were convicted under this law across its history; approximately 5,000–15,000 were sent to concentration camps with the pink triangle. East Germany abolished its version in 1968; West Germany maintained a modified form until 1994. No direct English-language law analog.

records.definition: Abbreviated citation form of Paragraph 175; the standard shorthand for the German criminal code article criminalizing male homosexual acts from 1871 to 1994.
records.notes: The § symbol (Paragraphenzeichen, section sign) is the standard German legal notation; in spoken language the full form 'Paragraph 175' or 'Hundertfünfundsiebziger' is used. Functionally identical in meaning to the full form but more common in written legal and journalistic contexts.

records.definition: Colloquial and often derogatory label for a man prosecuted or prosecutable under §175 of the German criminal code; broadly used as a stigmatizing term for a gay man.
records.notes: The -er suffix forms an agent noun from the law citation, analogous to English coinages like 'a Section 8.' Used pejoratively by hostile outsiders; partially reclaimed in some activist and memorial contexts. Effectively obsolete since the law's full repeal in 1994. No English concept covers both the legal and social stigma dimensions simultaneously.

records.definition: A criminal offense against public morals or decency (Sittlichkeit); a broad German legal category encompassing sexual crimes from exhibitionism to assault, prominent in 19th and 20th century German law.
records.notes: Compound of Sittlichkeit (morality, decency, good customs) and Delikt (criminal offense). The category has been largely replaced in modern German law (StGB) with offense-specific classifications; the term persists mainly in historical and legal-historical discourse.

records.definition: A criminal offense against moral decency or good customs (Sitten); a variant of Sittlichkeitsdelikt used in legal and journalistic contexts throughout the 20th century.
records.notes: Slightly shorter compound than Sittlichkeitsdelikt; used interchangeably in older statutes and judicial decisions. Sitten (customs, mores) is the root rather than Sittlichkeit. Both terms are largely displaced by modern offense-specific legal language in contemporary German law.

records.definition: Unnatural fornication; the original legal formulation in Paragraph 175 of the German criminal code used to criminalize male homosexual acts as offenses against nature.
records.notes: Widernatürlich (against-natural, contrary-to-nature) carries stronger moral-condemnatory force than unnatürlich (simply unnatural). This formulation appears in the 1871 text of §175 and echoes natural law theory inherited from Roman canon law. The Unzucht (fornication, lewdness, debauchery) component renders the phrase doubly condemnatory.

records.definition: Unnatural lewdness; a variant legal formulation used alongside or in lieu of 'widernatürliche Unzucht' to describe criminalized same-sex or non-procreative sexual acts in German law.
records.notes: Unnatürlich (unnatural) is rhetorically slightly softer than widernatürlich (against nature). Both Unzucht formulations appear in legal documents and judicial decisions across the 19th and 20th centuries; the distinction rarely affected outcomes in practice.

records.definition: A same-sex sexual act; the clinical and legal formulation used in the context of Paragraph 175 and related German legislation to describe the criminalized behavior without naming specific anatomical acts.
records.notes: Gleichgeschlechtlich = same-sex (literally 'same-gendered'), Handlung = act, action. The phrase occupies a fully neutral clinical register despite being consistently deployed in condemnatory legal contexts; the neutrality of the language was itself part of the law's technocratic framing.

records.definition: A homosexual act; the clinical and legal descriptor used in German law and medicine to categorize same-sex sexual activity as a behavioral phenomenon independent of identity.
records.notes: More widely recognized than 'gleichgeschlechtliche Handlung' due to the international familiarity of the root 'homosexuell.' Used in legal, medical, and psychological contexts through the 20th century; the phrase explicitly names the identity category unlike its more circumspect synonym.

records.definition: Homosexuality as a criminal offense; the condition or historical reality of same-sex attraction or acts being legally criminalized and subject to prosecution and imprisonment.
records.notes: Unter Strafe stellen = to criminalize; unter Strafe stehen = to be illegal. A descriptive legal-political phrase rather than a single lexical item; used in historical, journalistic, and activist discourse to describe the Paragraph 175 era. No single English concept term captures the bundled meaning of a specific national criminal status applied to a sexual orientation.

records.definition: Compound collective insult; literally 'whore-rabble' or 'pack of slatterns,' applied derogatorily to a group of women perceived as promiscuous, low-class, or disreputable.
records.notes: Schlampe = slut, whore, slattern (one of the most common German slurs for a promiscuous woman); Pack = rabble, riffraff, mob. The collective noun Pack adds a class-contempt dimension beyond what individual Schlampe conveys; implies the women are also low-status or criminal.

records.definition: Compound exclamatory insult; literally 'whore alarm,' used to announce or mock a woman perceived as sexually provocative or promiscuous.
records.notes: Nutte = whore, prostitute (strongly pejorative; one of the harshest German terms for a sex worker or promiscuous woman). The Alarm component adds theatrical urgency or irony. Can be deployed semi-humorously among close male associates as an exclamation but is derogatory toward the woman regardless of tone.

records.definition: Compound insult; literally 'wanker face,' combining the crude term for a masturbator (Wichser) with Gesicht (face) to produce a severe insult for a contemptible or repulsive person.
records.notes: Wichser = one who masturbates (from wichsen, to wank, itself from Wichs, shoe polish, via polishing-motion metaphor). The -gesicht suffix compounds are a productive German insult pattern (cf. Arschgesicht, Drecksgesicht). More emphatic and crude than plain Wichser.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'cock-sucker'; derived from Schwanz (cock) and lutschen (to suck); a severe general-purpose insult for a contemptible person.
records.notes: Schwanz literally means 'tail' but functions as the most common crude term for penis in colloquial German. Lutscher also denotes a lollipop, lending the compound a faint ironic edge. Functions identically to English 'cocksucker' as a general severe insult rather than a literal accusation.

records.definition: Compound insult combining Votze (cunt, the most vulgar German term for the vulva/vagina) with Gesicht (face); an extremely offensive insult for a disgusting or contemptible person.
records.notes: Votze occupies the same register in German as 'cunt' in American English — the harshest anatomical slur for female genitalia. The -gesicht compound pattern intensifies the base insult. Less common in everyday use than Arschloch or Wichser derivatives, which partly accounts for the lower recognition figure.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'ass-licker'; primarily used to denote a sycophant or obsequious flatterer who metaphorically licks someone's backside to gain favor.
records.notes: Arsch = ass; lecken = to lick. Parallel to English 'ass-kisser' and 'brown-noser' is near-perfect in both literal derivation and figurative sycophancy meaning. Less severe in everyday use than the literal sexual act implies; widely recognized and commonly deployed as a general-purpose sycophancy insult with no particular sexual directedness.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'ass-crawler'; a contemptible sycophant or groveling flatterer who figuratively crawls into someone's backside to curry favor.
records.notes: Arsch = ass; kriechen = to crawl, creep. Slightly more emphatic than Arschlecker in conveying the abject, groveling quality of the sycophancy rather than the mere act of flattery. Both are common and largely interchangeable in practice; Arschkriecher may imply slightly more sustained servility.

records.definition: Compound crude insult; literally 'juice sack,' with Sack also functioning as crude slang for scrotum; used to call someone a disgusting, contemptible, or pathetic idiot.
records.notes: Saft (juice, sap) + Sack (bag, sack; also crude slang for scrotum). The sexual resonance comes from Sack as genital slang; Saftsack thus implies something like 'scrotum full of bodily fluid.' Comparable to English 'douchebag' in that the anatomical literal meaning is deployed as a general contempt marker.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'bundle of disgust'; applied to an extremely repulsive, loathsome, or morally nauseating person.
records.notes: Ekel = disgust, revulsion, nausea; Paket = package, bundle. Lower crude score than most items in this set because it evokes general revulsion rather than explicit sexual grossness, though it is frequently applied when the disgust is sexual in nature. The Paket component suggests a concentrated, self-contained quantity of repugnance.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'piece of filth'; applied to a morally corrupt, despicable, or vile person.
records.notes: Dreck = dirt, filth, garbage, ordure; Stück = piece. Versatile contempt marker applicable to both men and women. Occasionally written Drecksstück with the genitive-s in older usage. The filth framing can encompass moral, sexual, or class-based contempt depending on context.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'grease rag'; applied to a sleazy, morally corrupt, or oily individual, especially one who is sexually predatory or shamelessly dishonest.
records.notes: Schmier = grease, slime, lubricant; Lappen = rag, cloth, wiping material. The metaphor evokes something used to wipe away dirty residue, implying the target is the filth itself. Also extends to corrupt, bribery-prone persons (Schmiergelder = bribe money), so the sleaze can be financial as well as sexual.

records.definition: Intensified compound insult combining Schmierlappen (sleazebag) with Kerl (fellow, man); denotes a particularly sleazy, contemptible, or morally repugnant male individual.
records.notes: Kerl = man, fellow, bloke (neutral to slightly rough register). Adding Kerl makes the insult explicitly male-directed and marginally more emphatic. Considerably rarer than plain Schmierlappen; likely constructed ad hoc rather than fully lexicalized, which accounts for the lower recognition figure.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'wank rag'; literally the cloth used to wipe up semen after masturbation; repurposed as an extreme contemptuous insult for a worthless or disgusting person.
records.notes: Wichsen = to masturbate (from Wichs, shoe polish, via the polishing-motion metaphor); Tuch = cloth, rag. Lower recognition than core crude insults like Wichser or Arschloch suggests it is more a creative compound than a fully conventionalized lexical item; its force comes from vividness rather than familiarity.

records.definition: Literally 'ball-licker' (Eier = eggs/testicles, lecker = licker); a compound insult for a contemptible, servile, or sycophantic person.
records.notes: 'Eier' (eggs) is ubiquitous German slang for testicles; the insult maps functionally to 'ass-kisser' in its servility connotation but deploys explicitly oral-genital imagery instead of the anal euphemism.

records.definition: Literally 'ball-muncher' (Kloten = testicles, Fresser = glutton/eater); an extremely crude compound insult for a despicable or contemptible person.
records.notes: 'Kloten' is primarily Alemannic/Swiss German dialect for testicles (also the name of a municipality near Zürich Airport); the '-fresser' suffix (from fressen, animal-style eating) is a highly productive crude intensifier implying bestial excess.

records.definition: Literally 'pussy-kisser' (Mose/Möse = vulva, Küsser = kisser); a crude compound insult implying servility or contemptibility, derived from the act of cunnilingus.
records.notes: 'Möse' is standard crude German slang for the vulva; the insult parallels English 'ass-kisser' in its sycophancy register but substitutes an explicit vulvar referent for the anal euphemism.

records.definition: Literally 'porn pig/sow' (Porno = pornography, Sau = pig/sow); a crude compound insult for a person degradingly obsessed with pornography or sexual excess.
records.notes: 'Sau' (sow) is one of the most productive German insult suffixes, implying wallowing, dirtiness, and moral degradation; productive in compounds such as 'Drecksau,' 'Arschlochsau,' etc.; the Porno- prefix narrows the excess specifically to pornographic consumption.

records.notes: A near-calque of the English 'pornstache'; mild on the crude scale because it targets physical appearance rather than sexual behavior directly; recognized across generations as cultural shorthand for retro-sleazy male presentation.

records.definition: Literally 'fuck-spoon' (Fick = fuck, Löffel = spoon); a nonsensical but crude compound insult for a contemptible idiot or deeply annoying person.
records.notes: The '-löffel' (spoon) suffix is semantically arbitrary — it functions as a comic intensifier rather than contributing literal meaning; German's compounding morphology enables such creative nonsense-compounds freely, and the absurdity can itself amplify the insult's dismissiveness.

records.definition: Literally 'fuck-mistake' (Fick = fuck, Fehler = mistake/error); an extremely cruel insult for an unwanted or accidentally conceived child, or broadly for any worthless, contemptible person.
records.notes: The primary and most cutting sense is 'accidental conception' — an unwanted child — making it one of the more savage German insults because it attacks a person's right to exist; secondarily used as a generic crude insult stripped of the birth-origin implication.

records.definition: Literally 'wanker-canal' (Wichser = wanker/masturbator, Kanal = canal/channel); a crude compound insult for a pathetically contemptible person conceived as a conduit for masturbatory waste.
records.notes: 'Wichser' alone is already a strong stand-alone insult equivalent to British 'wanker'; appending '-kanal' adds an anatomical dimension — implying the person is essentially a bodily duct for semen — while in internet-native usage it may additionally evoke a sleazy YouTube 'channel' run by a wanker.

records.definition: Literally 'sperm ray' (Sperma = semen, Rochen = manta/stingray); a hyper-creative compound insult evoking a flat, bottom-dwelling aquatic creature wallowing in semen; used as an extremely crude general-purpose insult.
records.notes: An inventive confection typical of German's productive nominal compounding; the ray fish (Rochen) contributes associations of bottom-dwelling flatness and silent predation alongside the semen imagery; technical score nudged above zero because 'Sperma' retains its clinical register even in crude compounds; low recognition reflects creative invention over established slang circulation.

records.definition: Literally 'cream face' (Sahne = cream, a standard euphemism for semen; Gesicht = face); refers to a person who has received a facial ejaculation, or is deployed as a crude insult for a despicable person.
records.notes: 'Sahne' (cream) is a well-established German sexual euphemism for semen, appearing in compounds such as 'Sahneschnitte'; the term functions both as a literal pornographic descriptor of the act/result and as a generalized crude insult whose sexual referent may be only dimly felt by casual users.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis derived from the phallic shape of a magic wand.
records.notes: Less established as a standalone penis term than 'magic wand'; recognition as a penis term specifically is lower than the word's general recognition.

records.definition: Literary euphemism for the penis, common in romance and fantasy fiction.
records.notes: Feels archaic or self-consciously literary; appears in Harlequin-style novels and epic fantasy prose.

records.definition: The penis, especially as a symbol of male generative power; used in clinical, academic, and literary contexts.
records.notes: Greek origin; in art history, anthropology, and religious studies 'phallus' often refers to the symbolic rather than strictly anatomical organ.

records.definition: Crude US slang for the penis, emphasizing size or meat-like quality.
records.notes: Heavily polysemous (argument, complaint, beef as food); the sexual meaning is context-dependent and may be unfamiliar to younger speakers.

records.definition: British mild slang for the penis; now largely archaic in this sense.
records.notes: Rarely used in isolation; survives mainly in regional dialects or older speech.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis playing on the rod or baton shape.
records.notes: Less common than other shape-based euphemisms; appears in comedic writing.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis based on shape resemblance to the vegetable.
records.notes: Common in schoolyard humor and innuendo; 'cool as a cucumber' is an unrelated idiom that adds mild comedic interference.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis based on phallic shape; widely used in innuendo and comedy.
records.notes: One of the most universally recognized shape-based penis euphemisms in English.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis referencing shape and fleshy cylindrical quality.
records.notes: Common in British and American humor; also appears in 'hiding the sausage' as a euphemism for intercourse.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis playing on the joystick gaming or aviation control device.
records.notes: Double entendre; joystick is also a legitimate term for game controllers and aircraft controls.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis referencing the automotive tool used to measure oil levels.
records.notes: Also used as a mild insult in British English meaning a stupid or useless person.

records.definition: Crude slang for the penis referencing its tubular shape; prominent in AAVE and hip-hop.
records.notes: Associated with 'laying pipe' meaning to have vigorous sex; particularly common in US Black slang and hip-hop lyrics.

records.definition: Originally US slang for the penis; now overwhelmingly used as a mild insult for a socially awkward person.
records.notes: The penis meaning has largely been displaced by the nerd/doofus sense; most contemporary speakers are unaware of the sexual etymology.

records.definition: Childish or infantile term for the penis used primarily with young children.
records.notes: Can also refer to urination in child speech; sometimes applied to female genitalia in children's usage; considered infantilizing when used by adults.

records.definition: Mild US slang for the penis, derived from Wiener schnitzel (Vienna sausage).
records.notes: Also the standard American word for a hot dog; primarily used in children's speech or low-key comedic contexts.

records.definition: Mild US slang for the penis; variant spelling of wiener.
records.notes: Also used as a mild insult for a timid or cowardly person; slightly more playful and childish in register than wiener.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis playing on the phallic shape of a hot dog sausage.
records.notes: Associated with bun-based intercourse metaphors ('hotdog in a bun', 'hiding the hotdog').

records.definition: British comic euphemism for the penis comparing it to a police truncheon.
records.notes: Associated with British laddish comedy of the 1980s–90s (Viz magazine, similar venues); recognition has declined significantly outside the UK.

records.definition: British euphemism for the male genitalia collectively (penis and scrotum), treating them as prized equipment.
records.notes: 'Tackle' in British English can mean equipment or gear; the phrase implies the genitals are important possessions, especially in the context of marriage.

records.definition: British euphemism for the male genitalia, comparing them humorously to the treasured regalia of the British monarchy.
records.notes: Widely understood beyond the UK; the literal crown jewels (royal regalia) meaning creates a sustained comic double entendre.

records.definition: British euphemism for the penis and testicles using the traditional meat-and-two-vegetables meal as an analogy.
records.notes: 'Meat' = penis, 'two veg' = testicles; rooted in British working-class culinary culture; recognition has declined along with the meal's cultural ubiquity.

records.definition: Mild British slang for the genitals, used of any gender.
records.notes: Plural; applies to both male and female genitalia; widely used in polite-adjacent conversation as a discreet reference.

records.definition: British slang for the male genitalia; the standalone form of wedding tackle.
records.notes: More recognizable as part of 'wedding tackle' than in isolation; 'tackle' also means fishing equipment or sports gear in standard British English.

records.definition: British variant spelling of knob; slang for the penis, particularly the glans.
records.notes: Also a British class-based noun for an upper-class or aristocratic person (nob = posh person); the two meanings can cause confusion in context.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis comparing it to the cured Italian sausage in shape and appearance.
records.notes: Common in innuendo in both British and American humor; implies thickness as well as length.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis comparing it to Polish kielbasa sausage, often implying notable size.
records.notes: Kielbasa is a thick, coarse-ground Eastern European sausage; the euphemism is most common in the US where kielbasa is a familiar grocery item; size implication stronger than with salami.

records.definition: Slang for the vulva or vagina; extremely common in sexual contexts.
records.notes: Also used non-sexually as slang for a coward; one of the most frequent sexual slang terms in English; polysemous but sexual meaning is primary in adult contexts.

records.definition: Extremely crude term for the vulva or vagina; also deployed as one of the most severe personal insults in English.
records.notes: Considered the most offensive word in American English; significantly less taboo in British and Australian English where it can be used affectionately or casually among friends; taboo asymmetry is cross-culturally significant.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva or vagina.
records.notes: Coexists with the weightlifting term (the snatch lift) and a verb meaning to grab; sexual meaning is unambiguous in context; no notable regional skew.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva or vagina; also used as a personal insult, especially in British English.
records.notes: More common and somewhat less taboo in British than American English; in British everyday speech the insult sense ('you twat') often dominates over the anatomical sense.

records.definition: Slang for the vulva, referencing pubic hair; mildly crude.
records.notes: Likely derives from visual similarity of pubic hair to beaver fur; common in 1970s–80s US slang and feels somewhat dated today; appears in 'beaver shot' (pornographic).

records.definition: Slang for the vulva or pubic-hair region; mildly crude.
records.notes: Possibly derives from the cylindrical fur hand-warmer; appears in the compound 'muff-diving' (cunnilingus); slightly dated in register.

records.definition: Crude anatomical slang for the vulva, referencing its shape as a narrow opening.
records.notes: Carries a mildly clinical edge due to the anatomical shape reference; predominantly appears in pornographic or explicitly sexual contexts; perceived as objectifying.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina.
records.notes: Etymological origin unclear; possibly refers to anatomical cavity or to underwear as a container; appears in pornographic compound terms.

records.definition: Crude and dehumanizing slang for the vagina, framing it purely as an orifice.
records.notes: Widely considered objectifying and dehumanizing; predominantly used in pornographic or misogynistic contexts; the reductive framing (person reduced to orifice) accounts for the elevated crude score.

records.definition: Mild US slang for the vagina, perceived as folksy or rural in register.
records.notes: Predominantly US Southern usage; the same word also refers to a freshwater turtle in Southern US dialect, creating comic potential; not widely used outside North America.

records.definition: Mild US slang for the vagina; a clipped form of 'coochie'.
records.notes: Common in African American Vernacular English (AAVE) and broader US youth slang; popularized via hip-hop; 'coochie' is the fuller form; not widely used outside North America.

records.definition: Casual abbreviation of 'vagina'; mildly crude but carries a semi-clinical feel.
records.notes: Feels more like clipped medical speech than true slang; common in casual body-positive, feminist, or health-education contexts; low taboo load relative to other slang in this set.

records.definition: Playful, childlike euphemism for the vagina, popularized by US network television.
records.notes: Coined or popularized on Grey's Anatomy (c. 2006–2007) by writer Shonda Rhimes as a workaround for network broadcast standards; became a widespread pop-culture term; recognition has declined slightly from its mid-2000s peak.

records.definition: Mild euphemism for the vagina, used in polite or humorous contexts.
records.notes: Has an entirely unrelated common meaning ('commotion, fuss') which dominates in non-sexual contexts; sexual meaning understood only through context; hyphenation varies (hoo ha, hoo-ha).

records.definition: A mild gender-coded euphemism for the female genitalia, used to avoid explicit terms.
records.notes: Common in media, parenting, and polite conversation; criticized in feminist discourse for reinforcing gendered language norms; can refer to the entire vulva/vagina region rather than vagina specifically.

records.definition: A mild British euphemism for the female genitalia.
records.notes: More common in British than American English; used in the same polite/avoidant register as 'lady parts'; 'bits' is a broadly British colloquial term for genitalia of either sex.

records.definition: A literary or poetic euphemism for the vulva, invoking floral imagery of opening and beauty.
records.notes: Found in literary erotica, romance fiction, and Romantic-era poetry; not used in everyday casual speech; visual and conceptual metaphor exploiting the flower's shape and connotations of femininity.

records.definition: A playful euphemism for the vagina invoking sweetness and desirability.
records.notes: Two-word spaced variant; connotes positive desirability rather than crudeness; the same term has an unrelated cybersecurity meaning (a decoy network trap) that may cause disambiguation issues.

records.definition: A playful euphemism for the vagina; single-word orthographic variant of 'honey pot'.
records.notes: Functionally identical to 'honey pot' in meaning and register; one-word form appears more in written/online contexts; cybersecurity meaning (deceptive network trap) is widely known and may reduce sexual disambiguation for tech-literate readers.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva, referencing its coloration.
records.notes: More common in pornographic than everyday speech; appears in the phrase 'show some pink' (genital exposure); slight technical elevation because the reference is anatomically descriptive rather than purely metaphorical.

records.definition: Crude compound slang for the vulva, combining a pubic-hair reference with a bivalve shape metaphor.
records.notes: Two-word compound; 'bearded' references pubic hair, 'clam' references anatomical shape; tone is more humorous than derogatory; associated with crude comedy registers (Austin Powers, etc.).

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva, referencing the bivalve's shape.
records.notes: Shorter form sharing the seafood shape metaphor with 'bearded clam'; also appears in compound 'clam digger' and related expressions; slightly lower crude score than 'bearded clam' due to the absent pubic-hair intensifier.

records.definition: A mildly euphemistic term for the vulva, referencing the bivalve's appearance.
records.notes: Less frequent than 'clam' as vulva slang; carries a slightly more literary or coy connotation; oysters are independently coded as aphrodisiacs in Western culture, reinforcing the erotic association.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva, referencing the folded shape of a taco shell.
records.notes: Food-shape metaphor; predominantly US usage; can carry unintentional racialized overtones given the Mexican-food reference, though typically deployed without ethnic intent; common in crude comedy and pornographic contexts.

records.definition: A mild, playful euphemism for the vagina, sharing the cat metaphor with 'pussy' but in softer register.
records.notes: Diminutive/affectionate form of the same feline metaphor underlying 'pussy'; perceived as gentler and more coy; common in flirtatious, erotic-romance, or non-pornographic sexual speech; primary meaning is still 'kitten/cat', so context is essential.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva, playing on the visual resemblance of pubic hair to a burger bun.
records.notes: Comic rather than aggressively insulting; the '-burger' suffix appears in other compound crude slang; spread through internet culture.

records.definition: British crude slang for the labia, referring to the skin folds of the vulva.
records.notes: Primarily British; in American English 'flaps' carries no sexual connotation.

records.definition: Crude, often derogatory slang for prominent labia, comparing them to hanging flaps of meat.
records.notes: The meat metaphor is deliberately dehumanizing; frequently deployed in body-shaming contexts; spread globally via internet.

records.definition: Euphemistic slang for the vulva or vaginal opening, based on visual resemblance to a smile rotated 90 degrees.
records.notes: Playfully euphemistic rather than aggressively crude; part of a broader pattern of orientational metaphor in sexual slang.

records.definition: Childish British euphemism for the vagina or vulva, used primarily when speaking to or about young children.
records.notes: Pairs with 'back bottom' for the anus; primarily a parenting and early-childhood communication term; very mild register.

records.definition: Generic mild deictic euphemism for the genital region, used to avoid naming specific anatomy.
records.notes: Gender-neutral; context-dependent; universally understood across all English-speaking cultures.

records.definition: Mild, slightly literary euphemism for the genital or groin area, using 'nether' (lower) as a spatial reference.
records.notes: Often used humorously; 'nether' is archaic for 'lower'; also used non-sexually in literary and fantasy contexts.

records.definition: In British English, mild slang for the vagina; in American English, an innocuous informal word for the buttocks with no sexual connotation.

records.definition: British slang for the vagina, attested from at least the 18th century, now considered archaic or dated.
records.notes: Appears frequently in Victorian and Edwardian erotica; etymology uncertain; occasionally revived ironically or in period fiction.

records.definition: British crude slang for the vagina or female pubic region; sometimes also used to refer to pubic hair.
records.notes: Common in British comedy and casual speech; largely unknown in North American English.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina, using the visual metaphor of a slash or wound.

records.definition: Euphemistic slang for the vagina, using a tunnel metaphor that implies penetration.

records.definition: Euphemistic slang for the vagina, using a cave metaphor to imply a hollow or enclosed space.
records.notes: Less common than 'love tunnel'; follows the same productive compound pattern; appears in humorous and erotic contexts.

records.definition: Mild British euphemism for the female pubic region or vulva, with particular reference to pubic hair.
records.notes: Popularized by British media and hair removal advertising campaigns; affectionate and playful in register.

records.definition: British crude slang for the vagina; may allude to pubic hair or the visual appearance of the vulva.
records.notes: Etymology unclear; 'growler' also denotes a small beer keg in the US and historically a hansom cab in British usage, creating polysemy.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina, with origins in Caribbean and AAVE usage, widely spread through hip-hop culture.

records.definition: US crude slang for the vagina; a clipped form of 'poontang.'
records.notes: Common in American English; also used to mean sex or women as sexual objects; the shortening marginally softens the crude register.

records.definition: US crude slang for the vagina or for sex; possibly derived from Louisiana Creole French 'putain' (prostitute).

records.definition: US crude slang for the vagina or for women regarded as sexual objects; can also refer to sex generally.

records.definition: US crude slang for the vagina; etymology uncertain, with possible Dutch or Low German roots.

records.definition: British crude comic slang for the vagina, combining a phallic reference ('sausage' = penis) with a container metaphor ('wallet').

records.definition: Crude slang for female breasts; one of the most common vulgar terms in English.

records.definition: Casual, mildly vulgar slang for female breasts; widely used across demographics.

records.definition: Mild, playful diminutive slang for female breasts.

records.definition: Crude container-metaphor slang for breasts, implying heaviness or volume.

records.definition: Crude slang for breasts, implying motion, weight, or sound.

records.definition: Crude slang for female breasts, particularly emphasizing size or visual prominence.

records.definition: Mild anatomical euphemism for breasts, substituting the broader chest region.

records.definition: Crude food-metaphor slang for large female breasts.
records.notes: Size and roundness metaphor; part of a broad English pattern of fruit/food analogies for breasts; implicitly signals large size.

records.definition: Crude American slang for female breasts.

records.definition: Crude slang for large breasts using a weapon/artillery metaphor.
records.notes: Military metaphor implying impressive or large size; less common than most terms in this set; more likely encountered in written comedy or fiction than spoken slang.

records.definition: Crude, overtly objectifying slang for female breasts, framing them as entertainment objects.

records.definition: Mild, childish-register slang for female breasts.

records.definition: Crude diminutive of 'tits'; slang for female breasts.

records.definition: Australian slang for female breasts.

records.definition: Cockney rhyming slang for breasts: 'Bristol Cities' rhymes with 'titties'.

records.definition: Mild, playful euphemism for female breasts, evoking softness and cuteness.

records.definition: British slang for female breasts.

records.definition: British slang for female breasts.
records.notes: Primarily British usage; 'bangers' also means sausages and old dilapidated cars in British English; breast meaning largely unknown outside the UK.

records.definition: Comic portmanteau of 'chest' and 'testicles' used as humorous slang for breasts.

records.definition: Semi-clinical euphemism for breasts, derived from Latin 'mamma' (breast/mammary gland).

records.definition: Crude, objectifying slang for female breasts; single-word spelling variant of 'fun bags'.

records.definition: Automotive euphemism for visibly protruding nipples or breasts generally.

records.definition: Automotive euphemism specifically for visibly erect nipples, referencing full-beam headlights.

records.definition: Crude container-metaphor slang for female breasts.
records.notes: Container metaphor similar to 'jugs'; also means buttocks in some regional dialects (particularly British), which can cause ambiguity; common in American English.

records.definition: Coy financial euphemism for breasts, framing them as valued physical attributes.

records.definition: Mild slang term for breasts.
records.notes: Less common than most breast slang; mildly dated feel in contemporary usage.

records.definition: Soft euphemism for breasts, evoking their plush, cushiony shape.

records.definition: Very common crude slang for testicles; also metaphorically means courage or audacity.

records.definition: Crude slang for testicles.

records.definition: Crude slang for the scrotum, the skin pouch enclosing the testicles.

records.definition: Shortened slang for gonads, typically used to mean testicles.

records.definition: Semi-clinical term for reproductive glands (testicles or ovaries); informally defaults to meaning testicles.

records.definition: Mild euphemism for testicles, framing them as precious valuables.
records.notes: Often a shortening of 'family jewels'; humor derives from treating anatomy as irreplaceable treasure.

records.definition: Archaic term for testicles, common from Old English through the early modern period.

records.definition: Crude slang for testicles.

records.definition: Spanish loanword literally meaning 'eggs', used in US English slang to mean testicles.

records.definition: Spanish loanword for testicles; used broadly in English to mean courage or audacity.
records.notes: The guts/courage meaning dominates in English-language sports and political journalism; globally recognized via anglophone media.

records.definition: Humorous euphemism for the testicles, framing them as the irreplaceable biological inheritance of the male line.
records.notes: Set phrase; parent expression of the shorthand 'jewels'; broadly recognized across generations.

records.definition: Crude slang for testicles, referencing their pendulous, hanging nature.
records.notes: Descriptive/anatomical coinage; less common than core terms; understood by most adults.

records.definition: British crude slang for testicles; also a general expletive meaning nonsense or expressing frustration.
records.notes: Expletive/nonsense meaning now dominates in British usage over the anatomical; globally recognized through British media export.

records.definition: British and Irish crude slang for testicles.
records.notes: Predominantly British and Irish; 'knacker' separately means a horse slaughterer or abattoir worker, giving the word a second register outside of sexual slang.

records.definition: Mild British euphemism for testicles based on shape and color resemblance.

records.definition: Euphemism for testicles, evoking their round shape.
records.notes: The dominant idiom 'lost one's marbles' (meaning gone crazy) is far more common and may reduce recognition of the testicle meaning.

records.definition: Rare euphemism for testicles based on shape resemblance to small round fruit.
records.notes: Uncommon in contemporary use; context-dependent recognition; more likely to land as understood than as first-choice vocabulary.

records.definition: Literary or poetic euphemism for testicles.
records.notes: Rare in contemporary speech; appears in erotica and pastiche; 'orbs' more commonly refers to eyes in literary usage, causing potential confusion.

records.definition: Crude comic compound slang for testicles, referencing their semen-producing function.
records.notes: 'Spunk' means semen in British English (crude) but courage in American English, so register and vulgarity of this compound vary sharply by region.

records.definition: Common American slang for the buttocks; also used to mean the anus in sexual contexts, and as a general intensifier or insult.

records.definition: British spelling and pronunciation of 'ass'; crude slang for the buttocks or anus.
records.notes: British, Australian, and Irish variant; same dual anatomical and intensifier usage as 'ass'; globally understood due to media crossover.

records.definition: American crude slang for the anus; also one of the most common English insults for a selfish or contemptible person.

records.definition: British crude slang for the anus; also a major insult for a contemptible or stupid person.

records.definition: Common informal term for the anus.

records.definition: Crude slang for the anus, referencing its color.

records.definition: Mild casual slang for the anus, derived from 'poop'.

records.definition: Euphemism for the anus, most commonly in reference to anal sex.

records.definition: British euphemism for the rectum or anus.
records.notes: Primarily British English; quasi-clinical register makes it common among older speakers and in formal-avoidant medical contexts.

records.definition: Crude slang for the anus, combining color and radial-shape imagery.
records.notes: Peak recognition tied to the Limp Bizkit album title (October 2000); combines both the 'browneye' and 'starfish' metaphor families.

records.definition: Mild euphemism for the buttocks.
records.notes: Also used for the back of a vehicle; fully safe for polite company.

records.definition: Slang for the buttocks, frequently carrying an admiring or sexual connotation.
records.notes: Originally AAVE, now fully mainstream; polysemous — also means pirate loot and, in gaming contexts, loot generally.

records.definition: The default casual American English term for the buttocks.
records.notes: Also means the blunt end of an object; effectively a neutral register word in American English despite being slang in origin.

records.definition: Mild term for the buttocks; also denotes the hindquarters of animals.
records.notes: Also a butcher's cut of beef ('rump steak'); slightly old-fashioned in human anatomical use.

records.definition: Plural slang for the buttocks, referencing their rounded shape.
records.notes: Frequently appears in the sexualized compliment 'buns of steel'.

records.definition: The two rounded halves of the buttocks, used metonymically for the buttocks as a whole.
records.notes: Metonymic transfer from facial cheeks; context-dependent — 'cheeks' alone is ambiguous between face and buttocks.

records.definition: Abbreviation of 'gluteal muscles'; denotes the buttocks, primarily in fitness contexts but frequently sexualized.
records.notes: Straddles clinical and colloquial registers; low crude score because the term is anatomical even when the context is sexual.

records.definition: AAVE slang for a large, prominently shaped buttocks; used admiringly.
records.notes: Originated in AAVE; crossed over via the 2005 Trace Adkins country song 'Honky Tonk Badonkadonk'; now somewhat dated but still broadly recognized.

records.definition: Idiomatic phrase for having a large, shapely buttocks; used admiringly.
records.notes: Automotive metaphor comparing the buttocks to a car trunk; originated in AAVE, now widely understood across American English.

records.definition: The most common English slang term for the perineum, the area between the genitals and the anus.
records.notes: Folk etymology: 'taint yer ass and taint yer balls'; the dominant English slang term for this anatomy.

records.definition: Slang for the perineum; more prevalent among younger English speakers.
records.notes: Synonymous with 'taint'; etymology obscure; slightly less widespread than 'taint' nationally.

records.definition: Slang term with two competing meanings: (1) the perineum; (2) a short, wide penis.
records.notes: Unusual polysemy in vulgar slang; which meaning is primary varies by region and speaker cohort.

records.definition: Rare slang variant for the perineum.
records.notes: Very low recognition; one of several obscure or regional alternatives to 'taint' alongside 'grundle' and 'gooch'.

records.definition: Slang for the perineum.
records.notes: Regional/subculture term; less widespread than 'taint' but more recognized than 'twaffle'.

records.definition: The canonical clinical term for penetrative sex between partners, prototypically denoting penis-vagina coitus.
records.notes: Appears in legal statutes, medical literature, and formal journalism; prototypically heterosexual in common usage though not definitionally restricted.

records.definition: Penis-in-vagina sexual intercourse; from Latin coitus (a coming together).
records.notes: Lay recognition boosted partly by repeated use in The Big Bang Theory; otherwise confined to clinical, legal, and academic contexts.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; used broadly across species in biological and zoological discourse.
records.notes: More generic than coitus — applies to any animal pair, not just human PIV; favored in nature documentary narration.

records.definition: The insertion of a penis, finger, or object into a bodily orifice (vaginal, anal, or oral) for sexual purposes.
records.notes: Appears in legal definitions of rape and sexual assault; slightly elevated crude relative to purely Latin clinical terms due to visceral imagery.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse involving penile insertion into the vagina.
records.notes: Preferred clinical phrase in sex education and medical literature over coitus; explicitly specifies orifice, which matters in legal and health contexts.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse involving penile insertion into the anus.
records.notes: Appears heavily in HIV transmission and public health literature; slightly elevated crude relative to vaginal intercourse reflects persistent cultural taboo around the act in many English-speaking contexts.

records.definition: Sexual activity involving mouth-to-genital or mouth-to-anal contact.
records.notes: Umbrella term covering fellatio, cunnilingus, and anilingus; near-universal recognition due to mainstream media and sex-ed usage; lower technical score because it is also used casually.

records.definition: Oral stimulation of the penis.
records.notes: Entered mass lay awareness largely via the 1998 Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and subsequent media coverage; widely used in legal documents defining sexual acts.

records.definition: Oral stimulation of the vulva and vagina.
records.notes: Slightly lower recognition than fellatio; from Latin cunnus (vulva) + lingere (to lick); used in clinical, legal, and academic registers.

records.definition: Oral stimulation of the anus.
records.notes: Least recognized of the three major oral sex terms; often replaced by slang (rimming, rim job) in non-clinical discourse; elevated crude reflects cultural taboo around anal contact.

records.definition: Self-stimulation of the genitals for sexual pleasure or arousal, typically to orgasm.
records.notes: Near-universal recognition; historical connotation of pathology and moral condemnation (19th-century anti-masturbation movement) has largely dissolved in contemporary clinical and popular usage.

records.definition: Sexual activity in which two or more partners manually stimulate each other's genitals simultaneously.
records.notes: Used primarily in clinical and sex-education contexts; lower recognition than solo masturbation as it lacks a dominant colloquial equivalent.

records.definition: Use of the hand to stimulate a partner's genitals for sexual pleasure.
records.notes: Broad clinical term applicable to any partner and any genital anatomy; overlaps conceptually with mutual masturbation when reciprocal; 'manual' risks ambiguity outside sexual context.

records.definition: Insertion of one or more fingers into the vagina or anus for sexual stimulation.
records.notes: "Digital" derives from Latin digitus (finger), not from digital/electronic technology — a significant source of confusion for lay audiences; appears frequently in legal definitions of sexual assault.

records.definition: Non-penetrative sexual activity involving rubbing genitals against a partner's body.
records.notes: French-derived (frotter = to rub); shares the lexeme with the art technique of making surface rubbings; also a paraphilia term when applied to non-consensual public rubbing (frotteurism); low recognition outside clinical and kink communities.

records.definition: A sexual practice involving vulva-to-vulva genital contact between two people with vulvas, typically involving rhythmic friction.
records.notes: Greek-derived (tribein = to rub); informally called scissoring or tribbing; historically used pejoratively in medical literature; recognized mainly by academics, sexologists, and LGBTQ communities.

records.definition: The expulsion of semen from the penis at orgasm.
records.notes: Also has a non-sexual meaning (to exclaim suddenly); the sexual sense dominates in contemporary usage; default referent is penile unless qualified (see female ejaculation).

records.definition: The expulsion of fluid from the Skene's glands (paraurethral glands) in some people with vulvas during sexual arousal or orgasm.
records.notes: Subject of ongoing scientific debate regarding fluid composition and origin; distinct from coital urinary incontinence; frequently conflated with squirting in popular discourse despite physiological distinctions.

records.definition: The climax of sexual excitement, characterized by intense pleasurable sensations and rhythmic muscular contractions, typically accompanied by ejaculation in people with penises.
records.notes: Near-universal recognition; functions as both noun and verb; used across clinical, popular, and casual registers without register shift.

records.definition: Orgasm; the peak of sexual arousal and pleasure.
records.notes: Semi-clinical; also used in non-sexual narrative contexts (climax of a film or story); lower technical score than orgasm because it crosses into euphemistic and literary registers.

records.definition: A state of physical and psychological sexual excitement, typically involving genital engorgement and increased lubrication or erection.
records.notes: Also used in non-sexual contexts (arousal from sleep, arousal of suspicion); sexual sense requires context but is primary in sex-ed and clinical discourse; very low crude.

records.definition: The engorgement and stiffening of erectile tissue — most commonly the penis, but also the clitoris — due to increased blood flow during sexual arousal.
records.notes: Non-sexual meaning (erection of a building or structure) exists but sexual sense dominates in colloquial usage; heavily reinforced in lay awareness by pharmaceutical advertising (Viagra, Cialis).

records.definition: The production of vaginal fluid during sexual arousal, reducing friction and facilitating penetration.
records.notes: Also used in entirely non-sexual mechanical contexts; sexual sense requires context; conceptually extends to pre-ejaculatory fluid (Cowper's gland) and commercial personal lubricants.

records.definition: The act of inserting the penis into the vagina; the initial penetration phase of penile-vaginal intercourse.
records.notes: Extremely technical; used almost exclusively in sexology, animal behavior research, and some legal contexts; also has a non-sexual meaning in Scots law (unauthorized interference with another's property); very low lay recognition.

records.definition: The introduction of semen into the female reproductive tract, whether through intercourse or artificial means.
records.notes: Primarily associated with artificial insemination (AI) and IVF in lay awareness; the natural-intercourse sense is less commonly invoked; widespread recognition driven by fertility treatment discourse.

records.definition: The fusion of a spermatozoon with an ovum to form a zygote, initiating embryonic development.
records.notes: Near-universal recognition due to school biology curriculum; carries political and legal weight in debates about embryo personhood and abortion policy; also spelled fertilisation in British English.

records.definition: The practice of living together as a sexual or romantic couple outside of legal marriage.
records.notes: Legally and sociologically coded as implying a sexual relationship; appears frequently in family law, tax, and housing contexts. Not purely a sex act but categorized as such in sexual-behavior research.

records.definition: The first act of sexual intercourse following a marriage, historically required to render the marriage legally valid.
records.notes: Still legally relevant in some jurisdictions as grounds for annulment if unconsummated. Register is archaic but not obsolete in legal or religious discourse.

records.definition: The act of first vaginal penetration, historically framed around rupture of the hymen.
records.notes: Carries heavy patriarchal and property-of-body framing; modern gynecology rejects the hymen-centric model. Term has largely been displaced by 'loss of virginity' or 'first penetrative sex' in contemporary usage.

records.definition: A contraceptive method in which the penis is withdrawn from the vagina before ejaculation.
records.notes: Colloquially 'pulling out'. Latin phrase used in clinical and public-health writing. Efficacy as contraception is widely debated due to pre-ejaculate sperm.

records.definition: Sexual arousal and gratification obtained through self-stimulation or self-directed erotic fantasy.
records.notes: Broader than masturbation — encompasses fantasy, body-wide stimulation, and non-genital self-arousal. Term has Freudian clinical lineage; rarely used outside academic or psychoanalytic writing.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; an archaic formal term for coitus.
records.notes: Largely confined to legal briefs, historical texts, and satirical prose today. The word 'congress' (coming together) is the operative metaphor.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; historically the statutory legal phrase used in criminal codes for rape and unlawful sex with a minor.
records.notes: 'Carnal' (from Latin caro, flesh) adds a moral/bodily-sin connotation absent from clinical 'intercourse'. Primarily encountered today in legal history and biblical commentary.

records.definition: A legal and religious term historically encompassing anal intercourse, oral sex, or bestiality, derived from the biblical city of Sodom.
records.notes: U.S. sodomy laws struck down by Lawrence v. Texas (2003). Contemporary colloquial usage has narrowed to anal intercourse. The term carries irreducible moral-religious charge regardless of legal context.

records.definition: Sexual contact or intercourse between a human and a non-human animal.
records.notes: Refers to the act; distinguished from zoophilia (the attraction). Illegal in most jurisdictions. Widely recognized term from legal reporting and taboo-topic discourse.

records.definition: A paraphilia characterized by sexual attraction to non-human animals as the primary or preferred erotic focus.
records.notes: Foregrounds attraction and identity rather than behavior (cf. bestiality). Used in forensic psychiatry and, self-referentially, by zoophile communities online. Very low public recognition of this specific term.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual acts performed with a human corpse.
records.notes: Illegal in most jurisdictions. Clinical literature distinguishes exclusive, preferential, and situational subtypes. Term is broadly recognized from crime reporting, horror fiction, and tabloid media.

records.definition: Any persistent pattern of sexual arousal centered on atypical objects, situations, or individuals, as defined in the DSM-5 classification system.
records.notes: DSM-5 distinguishes paraphilia (atypical but not inherently disordered) from paraphilic disorder (causing distress or harm to self or others). 'Fetish' is the lay equivalent but is narrower. Very low public recognition of the clinical phrase.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse involving penetration of the vagina by the penis; the precise clinical descriptor used in public health and epidemiological research.
records.notes: Abbreviated PVI in research literature. Adoption of this term reflects need to distinguish among sexual act types for STI transmission risk stratification.

records.definition: The act of receiving anal penetration during sexual intercourse; the clinical descriptor for the 'bottom' role.
records.notes: Abbreviated RAI in HIV/STI research. Epidemiologically significant as the highest-risk position for HIV transmission per act. The colloquial equivalent 'bottoming' carries gay male cultural connotations absent from the clinical phrase.

records.definition: The act of penetrating a partner anally during sexual intercourse; the clinical descriptor for the 'top' role.
records.notes: Abbreviated IAI in HIV/STI research. Lower but non-negligible HIV transmission risk compared to RAI. As with RAI, the colloquial 'topping' carries gay male cultural connotations not embedded in the clinical phrase.

records.definition: Sexual stimulation of the perineum, the region of skin and tissue between the genitals and the anus.
records.notes: The perineum is colloquially called the 'taint', 'gooch', 'grundle', or 'chode' (regional variation). Appears in sex therapy and pelvic floor physical therapy literature; extremely low general public recognition of the clinical phrase.

records.definition: Sexual stimulation of the prostate gland, typically via the rectum, for pleasure or therapeutic purposes.
records.notes: Colloquially called 'P-spot' stimulation; also 'milking' in kink contexts. Mainstream awareness has increased through sex-positive media and prostate health campaigns aimed at cis men.

records.definition: Direct or indirect manual, oral, or mechanical stimulation of the clitoris for sexual arousal and pleasure.
records.notes: Central mechanism of orgasm for the majority of vulva-owners; increasingly prominent in mainstream sex education since the 2010s. 'Clitoral' sits near the boundary of clinical and plain English.

records.definition: Stimulation of the anterior wall of the vagina at the presumed location of the G-spot, associated with heightened arousal and sometimes ejaculation.
records.notes: Named after Ernst Gräfenberg (1950). Anatomical existence contested in peer-reviewed literature; widely accepted in popular discourse. Public awareness peaked roughly 2005–2015 with wave of lifestyle-magazine coverage.

records.definition: The intentional restriction of oxygen supply to the brain during sexual activity to intensify arousal or orgasm.
records.notes: Colloquially 'breath play' or 'choking'. Associated with accidental deaths including autoerotic asphyxiation cases (Michael Hutchence 1997, David Carradine 2009), which drove mainstream awareness spikes. 'Choking' as consensual kink has been widely discussed in mainstream media since ~2018.

records.definition: A paraphilia characterized by sexual arousal specifically from oxygen deprivation, whether self-inflicted or partner-inflicted.
records.notes: Subcategory of paraphilia used in forensic psychiatry and sexology literature. Virtually unknown outside clinical audiences; 'erotic asphyxiation' is the public-facing equivalent. Some literature also uses 'hypoxyphilia'.

records.definition: The sexual practice of inserting a fully folded hand, and sometimes part of the forearm, into the vagina or rectum.
records.notes: The term functions as its own clinical-adjacent common name; no more formal alternative is in wide use. Practiced in heterosexual, lesbian, and gay male communities. Requires progressive dilation and lubrication; closely associated with the practice listed as 'stretching'.

records.definition: The gradual dilation of the vaginal or rectal opening using progressively larger objects, practiced in sex therapy or as a kink end in itself.
records.notes: Heavily polysemous — recognition rate is conditional on sexual context being established. Clinical equivalent is 'progressive vaginal/rectal dilation'. In kink communities, also called 'gaping' when referring to the resulting state rather than the process. Recognition figure reflects sexual-context usage only.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse; the most common and most vulgar English verb for the sex act.
records.notes: One of the most versatile words in English — verb, noun, interjection, and intensifier — with many uses fully detached from sexual meaning. Etymology uncertain; attested in English from at least the early 16th century. The crude connotations are irreducible even when used neutrally by speakers; 'have sex' captures the act but loses all register charge.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse; a mildly crude slang verb less transgressive than 'fuck'.
records.notes: Operates on a mechanical metaphor of rotary penetration, shared with 'nail', 'drill', and 'bang'. Also means to cheat or defraud ('screw over'), which somewhat dilutes the sexual salience. Slightly dated as sexual slang; peak usage estimated mid-to-late 20th century.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone.
records.notes: Also used as a noun; very common across US, UK, and Australian English.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone.
records.notes: More prevalent in US than UK; double meaning with the anatomical noun adds crude resonance.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse; describes the physical thrusting motion.
records.notes: Evokes the physical motion of sex; also describes animals mating; sometimes used for humping objects non-sexually.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse (British English, very commonly used).
records.notes: Primarily British English; internationally known partly via Austin Powers films; lower perceived vulgarity than American equivalents; also means a type of tobacco and a carpet texture.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone.
records.notes: Also used as a noun ('an easy lay'); relatively mild register; transitive construction implies sexual access to a partner.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone, implying conquest or dominance.
