records.definition: To have vigorous, aggressive sexual intercourse with someone.
records.notes: Strong aggressive and forceful connotation; emphasizes repeated hard thrusting; higher crude intensity than generic intercourse terms.

records.definition: To have penetrative sexual intercourse with someone aggressively.
records.notes: Tool/machine metaphor emphasizing mechanical penetration; similar crude level to pound but slightly less ubiquitous in everyday spoken slang.

records.definition: To have forceful sexual intercourse with someone; agricultural metaphor for penetration.
records.notes: US spelling; British variant is 'plough'; agricultural metaphor implying force and deep penetration; slightly less common than pound or drill in spoken slang.

records.definition: To have casual sexual intercourse with someone.
records.notes: AAVE-influenced; rose to mainstream via internet culture circa 2012–2018; the phrase 'smash or pass' (would you have sex with or reject this person) drove widespread adoption across demographics.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone.
records.notes: Often appears in the phrase 'I'd tap that'; lighter vulgarity than 'bang' or 'bone'; more common in spoken slang than written.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone, as in 'hit that'.
records.notes: AAVE-influenced; almost always in phrase form ('hit that', 'I'd hit it', 'hit it and quit it'); strongly context-dependent since 'hit' has many non-sexual meanings.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse (idiomatic phrase).
records.notes: Popularized by early 1990s R&B; now dated but still understood by older millennials and Gen X; rarely used in 2026.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone (mild transitive euphemism).
records.notes: Context-dependent; 'I'd do her' / 'I did him'; cross-generational and universal; one of the least vulgar possible expressions for the act.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse ('it' serving as a universal stand-in for sex).
records.notes: One of the most universally understood English sex euphemisms; safe to deploy in most contexts where explicit language is inappropriate; 'just do it' carries an unintentional double meaning.

records.definition: To begin sexual activity; to have sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Popularized by Marvin Gaye's 1973 'Let's Get It On'; enduring cross-generational usage; also used for enthusiastic engagement in non-sexual contexts.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse (passive construction framing sex as received or achieved).
records.notes: Extremely common across all English dialects; passive voice implies sexual access was granted by a partner; heavily used in discussions of sexual frustration or success.

records.definition: To obtain sexual activity; to have casual sex.
records.notes: 'Some' as synecdoche for sexual activity; also used in military context meaning to engage in combat; frames sex as a commodity or resource to be obtained.

records.definition: To have a casual sexual encounter, typically without an ongoing relationship.
records.notes: Deliberately ambiguous; can mean anything from kissing to intercourse depending on context and speaker; the dominant millennial/Gen-Z term for casual sex in 2026; also has a wholly non-sexual meaning (to connect or link up).

records.definition: To succeed in obtaining sexual activity with someone.
records.notes: Frames sex as competitive achievement or athletic success; traditionally male-coded but gender-neutral in usage; also means obtaining drugs in slang.

records.definition: To bring someone to bed for sexual intercourse; to have sex with.
records.notes: Somewhat literary register; more common in written fiction and journalism than spoken slang; 'he bedded her' implies seduction leading to sex.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone (polite euphemism).
records.notes: One of the most universally acceptable English euphemisms; used in news reporting and polite conversation; technically absurd (literal sleep can occur non-sexually) but universally understood.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse (British English, mildly crude).
records.notes: Primarily British; lighter and more playful tone than 'shag'; frequent in 1990s tabloid press; also means to hit someone on the head.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse (Australian English, crude).
records.notes: Almost exclusively Australian English; considered highly vulgar in AU context; largely unrecognized as a sexual term in other English dialects; low global recognition reflects regional restriction.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse with someone (British slang, now largely dated).
records.notes: British English; primarily mid-20th-century usage; largely supplanted by other terms; creates unintentional humor due to conflict with military/aviation communication term meaning 'message received'; also a common given name.

records.definition: To penetrate sexually (verb); also used as a noun referring to the penis.
records.notes: Primary vulgar verb meaning of 'shaft' in everyday use is 'to cheat or swindle'; sexual penetration sense is secondary. 'Shaft' as penis noun is more widespread than the verb usage.

records.definition: To have sex with someone (crude slang).
records.notes: More prevalent in Australian and British English than American; 'had a poke' is a recognizable Australian construction. Multiple non-sexual meanings (prod, bag, poker) coexist.

records.definition: To have sex with someone, often with connotations of dominance or aggression.
records.notes: Primary idiom meaning is 'to punish, defeat, or treat harshly'; sexual meaning is context-dependent and secondary. Directional penetration strongly implied in sexual use.

records.definition: To have sex, typically in a position where one partner straddles the other.
records.notes: Cowgirl and reverse-cowgirl positions strongly implied but usage extends to intercourse generically. 'Give someone a ride' is a common noun form. Extremely widespread recognition.

records.definition: To climb on top of a partner in preparation for or during sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Term is shared with ethology and equestrian contexts, lending a semi-clinical feel despite sexual use. Appears in both formal descriptions of animal reproductive behavior and colloquial human sex.

records.definition: To have sex (comic euphemism; 'uglies' is a self-deprecating euphemism for genitalia).
records.notes: Humor derives from calling genitals 'uglies.' Never used seriously; register is exclusively playful or self-deprecating. American origin; broadly understood across Anglophone cultures.

records.definition: To have sexual intercourse (Shakespearean idiom from Othello, Act 1, Scene 1).
records.notes: Coined or popularized by Shakespeare (Iago's speech to Brabantio). Recognized primarily by educated or culturally literate speakers. Almost never used sincerely; cited as a literary reference or used for comic effect.

records.definition: To have sex; to engage in sexual activity (dated slang, popularized by Will Smith's 1997 single 'Gettin' Jiggy Wit It').
records.notes: 'Jiggy' was semantically ambiguous — cool, excited, or sexual — so the sexual reading was never sole or dominant. Now used mostly ironically. Peak year corresponds to song's chart peak.

records.definition: To have sex, especially energetically or adventurously; can shade into kink territory.
records.notes: African-American Vernacular English origin, now mainstream. 'Freaky' connotes uninhibited or unconventional behavior and can extend to BDSM or kink depending on context.

records.definition: To have sex crudely or uninhibitedly; to engage in explicit sexual behavior.
records.notes: 'Nasty' carries a moral-shame charge that is simultaneously transgressive and approving in certain subcultures, notably hip-hop. Janet Jackson's 'Nasty' (1986) and later rap usage reinforced the approving sense.

records.definition: To engage in penetrative sexual intercourse as the culminating step of a sexual encounter, as opposed to stopping at petting or oral sex.
records.notes: Implies a linear 'bases' model of sexual escalation with penetration as the endpoint. Predominantly heteronormative framing; less naturally applicable to same-sex encounters. Widespread and cross-generational.

records.definition: To engage in casual or non-penetrative sexual activity with someone.
records.notes: Does not typically imply intercourse; covers kissing, petting, oral sex, etc. Dual meaning: 'waste time' or 'be unfaithful.' Among the most widely recognized mild sexual euphemisms in American English.

records.definition: To engage in casual or non-penetrative sexual activity.
records.notes: Near-synonym of 'fool around'; also means 'waste time' or 'tinker with something.' Slightly more prevalent in American English. Long attestation in 20th-century popular music.

records.definition: To engage in casual or non-penetrative sexual activity (British English variant of 'fool around').
records.notes: Predominantly British English; American speakers default almost universally to 'fool around.' For many GB speakers the primary meaning is still 'waste time'; sexual reading requires context.

records.definition: To have vigorous or playful sex.
records.notes: Strongly associated with British tabloid journalism ('bedroom romp,' 'steamy sex romp'). Connotes energy and mutual enjoyment; lower shame register than most synonyms. Also means boisterous non-sexual play.

records.definition: To have sex (archaic British slang, now largely obsolete in this sense).
records.notes: Common in 18th–19th century British English, e.g., Fielding and Smollett. Modern readers may not recognize the sexual meaning without context. 'A tumble in the hay' is a surviving fossil phrase that preserves the sense.

records.definition: To have sex (rustic euphemism evoking pastoral or barn imagery).
records.notes: Folksy register; the hay-barn setting is entirely metaphorical for most contemporary speakers. Used humorously or nostalgically. Widespread in 20th-century American and British film, television, and song.

records.definition: To have sex (euphemism; 'sack' is slang for bed or sleeping bag).
records.notes: Variant of 'roll in the hay' substituting 'sack' (bed) for 'hay.' Less vivid imagery and lower recognition than its counterpart. 'Sack' as bed slang is the connecting link (cf. 'hit the sack = go to sleep').

records.definition: To have sex (rare secondary sexual meaning; primary and dominant meaning is 'to go to sleep').
records.notes: Overwhelmingly understood as 'go to bed to sleep'; sexual meaning is minority usage entirely dependent on explicit context. Recognition figures here reflect the sexual meaning only, not the sleep meaning (which would score ~95).

records.definition: To have sex with someone (euphemism using bed linen as metonym for sexual intimacy).
records.notes: Softer than most synonyms; 'between the sheets' can also connote romance or intimacy without explicit sex. Appears frequently in romance novel titles and pop song lyrics.

records.definition: To have penetrative sex (comic idiom; 'sausage' = penis, referencing the act of insertion).
records.notes: Exclusively humorous register; the children's game metaphor applied to sex is the joke. The penis-as-sausage metaphor is the primary crude element. Rarely if ever used in earnest.

records.definition: To succeed in having sex, especially after a period of social effort or pursuit.
records.notes: Frames sex as a probabilistic win; implies prior effort and an uncertain outcome. Daft Punk's 2013 song reinforced mainstream recognition. Carries mild male-agent framing but used broadly across genders.

records.definition: To have sex as the culminating step of courtship (transactional metaphor borrowed from business).
records.notes: Business-contract metaphor; sex = contract completion after prior 'negotiation.' Slightly more common than 'close the deal' in sexual contexts. Mild male-agent framing implied.

records.definition: To have sex, framed as completing a courtship negotiation (transactional business metaphor).
records.notes: Near-synonym of 'seal the deal'; same transactional register. Primary meaning in most contexts is the literal business sense (completing a sale); sexual meaning is secondary but widely understood.

records.definition: To have sex with someone (mild euphemism; bed is metonym for sexual activity).
records.notes: Among the mildest and most widely understood sexual euphemisms in English. Safe for formal writing, literary prose, and mainstream conversation without causing offense. 'Go to bed' alone carries the same meaning in context.

records.definition: To return home with someone after a social outing with the strongly implied intention of having sex.
records.notes: Contextual euphemism; the sexual meaning is implied by social convention rather than stated explicitly.

records.definition: To seduce someone into a sexual encounter; to bring someone to bed for sex.
records.notes: Slightly dated; foregrounds the initiator's agency and the act of seduction rather than the sex itself.

records.definition: To have sex with someone, with an aggressive or dominant connotation implying the initiator's control over the encounter.
records.notes: Implies dominance or coercion; whether consensual or not depends entirely on context.

records.definition: To have sex with someone, typically implying coercion, dominance, or non-consensual force.
records.notes: Strong coercive or non-consensual connotation in most modern uses; occasionally deployed humorously or ironically.

records.definition: To engage in sexual activity, especially penetrative intercourse; the neutral standard verbal phrase in modern English.
records.notes: The unmarked default term in contemporary English; used across journalism, education, and everyday speech without triggering offense.

records.definition: To engage in sexual intercourse; a clinical-register phrase used in medical, legal, and formal educational contexts.
records.notes: More formal and clinical than 'have sex'; preferred in legal testimony, medical literature, and health curricula.

records.definition: To have sex with a romantic partner; a soft euphemism emphasizing emotional connection over the physical act.
records.notes: Considered earnest or dated by younger speakers; implies a romantic frame absent from 'have sex'. The connotative gap is significant for cross-language comparison.

records.definition: To have sex; a comic euphemism popularized by early-20th-century American vaudeville and popular song.

records.notes: One of several 'man X' compounds for semen; comic rather than erotic in tone.

records.definition: Sexual fluids in general—semen, vaginal lubrication, or both—framed as romantic or playful.
records.notes: Gender-neutral enough to refer to either partner's fluids; more coy than vulgar; common in soft-erotica and euphemistic contexts.

records.definition: Sexual fluids in general, most often vaginal lubrication; mild colloquial slang.
records.notes: Context-dependent; more often implies vaginal lubrication than semen; low crude score reflects its non-offensive, colloquial feel.

records.definition: To ejaculate; also used as a noun for semen; AAVE slang popularized by hip-hop.
records.notes: Peaked around 2003–2005 with Lil Jon & the East Side Boyz track 'Get Low'; primarily a verb but used as noun; AAVE origin that crossed into mainstream youth slang.

records.definition: Semen or vaginal lubrication; also used as a verb meaning to ejaculate or to become highly aroused.
records.notes: The verb 'to cream' (especially 'cream her pants') implies arousal-induced lubrication; very common in pornographic writing and mainstream erotica.

records.definition: Semen ejaculated onto a partner's chest or neck, visually evoking a pearl necklace.
records.notes: The jewelry euphemism softens what is functionally a crude act descriptor; popularized in pornographic and internet culture.

records.definition: The act of ejaculating on a partner's face; also the resulting state.
records.notes: Homonymic collision with the beauty-treatment 'facial'; the sexual meaning is now dominant enough to generate frequent double-entendres; standard category label in pornographic indexing.

records.definition: Genital discharge or secretion; can refer to normal arousal fluid or pathological discharge associated with STIs.
records.notes: Polysemous: 'drip' in 2020s slang also means stylish/cool, making context essential; the STI-discharge connotation gives it a pathological undertone absent from other fluid terms.

records.definition: Vaginal fluid produced by the cervix and vaginal walls; may indicate normal lubrication or infection.
records.notes: Standard medical term; not exclusively sexual—applies to any bodily discharge; clinical register removes most crude associations.

records.definition: Lubrication produced by the vaginal walls and Bartholin's glands during sexual arousal.
records.notes: Clinical two-word compound; among the lowest crude scores in this batch; used in medical, educational, and sexological contexts.

records.definition: Vaginal lubrication during arousal; metonymically, the state of being sexually aroused in women.
records.notes: Metonymic: the property stands for the fluid and the arousal state simultaneously; common in romance fiction and casual speech; low crude score reflects its euphemistic feel.

records.definition: Female ejaculation or the fluid expelled during it; also used as a verb for the act.
records.notes: High recognition driven by prevalence in pornographic categorization; both noun and verb; scientific debate about fluid composition (diluted urine vs. Skene's gland secretion) remains active in sexology.

records.definition: Fluid expelled from the Skene's (paraurethral) glands during sexual arousal or orgasm.
records.notes: Preferred term in sexological and medical literature; 'squirt' is the colloquial equivalent with higher recognition; physiological composition (possible diluted urine admixture) remains debated.

records.definition: Pre-ejaculatory fluid secreted by the Cowper's glands during sexual arousal, before ejaculation.
records.notes: Most common lay term; widely used across demographics and informally in health education.

records.definition: Clinical term for fluid secreted by the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands during sexual arousal prior to ejaculation.
records.notes: Standard medical and public-health usage; debated for its role in sperm transmission and STI risk.

records.definition: Highly specialized anatomical term for pre-ejaculatory fluid, named after the anatomist William Cowper who first described the bulbourethral glands.
records.notes: Appears almost exclusively in academic anatomy and physiology texts; negligible lay recognition.

records.definition: Sebaceous secretion that accumulates beneath the foreskin of the penis or around the clitoral hood; composed of shed skin cells, oils, and moisture.
records.notes: From Greek smēgma ('soap, unguent'). Clinical term but carries strong disgust connotation in lay use; also present in female genital anatomy.

records.definition: Crude slang for smegma, evoking its whitish, cheese-like texture and odor.
records.notes: Used primarily as an insult or to express disgust; the sensory metaphor is deliberately derogatory. Common in locker-room and internet humor.

records.definition: The state of penile tumescence caused by engorgement of erectile tissue with blood in response to sexual arousal or other stimuli.
records.notes: Standard clinical and colloquial term; universal recognition across all English-speaking demographics. Polysemous (architectural 'erection of a building') but sexual meaning dominant in sexual contexts.

records.definition: Slang term for an erect penis or the state of penile erection.
records.notes: One of the oldest and most pervasive English slang terms for erection; used across generations and Anglophone regions.

records.definition: Slang for an erection, referencing the false popular notion of a bone in the penis.
records.notes: Anatomically inaccurate (humans lack a baculum); also had an earlier distinct meaning of 'blunder' or 'mistake' in British English, now largely displaced by the sexual sense in most contexts.

records.definition: British slang for an erection.
records.notes: Predominantly British English; recognized but markedly less common in North American and Australian usage.

records.definition: Slang for an erection, playing on 'wood' as a metaphor for hardness.
records.notes: Gained additional cultural visibility via unintentional double-entendre around the Toy Story character name; widespread across Anglophone regions.

records.definition: Slang for a partial erection, less than fully tumescent.
records.notes: Strongly polysemous; the dominant lay meaning is 'pleasantly plump.' The sexual meaning is primarily North American slang and context-dependent.

records.definition: British slang for a partial or semi-erection; short for 'semi-erection.'
records.notes: Primarily British English for the sexual meaning; in North American English 'semi' predominantly means a large articulated truck, making context essential for disambiguation.

records.definition: Slang for a partial erection, roughly half the tumescence of a full erection.
records.notes: Compound of 'half' and 'chub' (itself slang for partial erection); less common than 'chubby' or 'semi'; more prevalent in internet and younger-generation usage.

records.definition: Slang for penile erection upon waking, caused by REM-sleep autonomic activity rather than sexual arousal.
records.notes: Clinical term is 'nocturnal penile tumescence' (NPT); occurs multiple times nightly but most noticed on waking. The phrase is universal across Anglophone regions and generations.

records.definition: Euphemism for an erection that creates a visible protrusion or bulge through clothing, resembling a tent shape.
records.notes: Used as both noun and verb ('tenting'); the 'visible-through-clothing' specificity distinguishes this concept from erection in general; no single clinical term covers it.

records.definition: Idiomatic phrase meaning to have an erection visible as a protrusion through clothing, from the tent-like shape it creates.
records.notes: Literal camping meaning provides effective cover in polite company; widely understood across Anglophone regions.

records.definition: Clinical adjective for the non-erect, soft, and unengorged state of the penis.
records.notes: Pronunciation disputed: FLAK-sid vs FLAS-id; not exclusively sexual (used in neurology, rhetoric, etc.) but the sexual anatomical sense is primary in medical contexts.

records.definition: Slang for the flaccid state of the penis; also used to describe erectile dysfunction ('went limp', 'stayed limp').
records.notes: Strongly polysemous; the sexual meaning is clear only in context. Sometimes used pejoratively to imply sexual failure or impotence.

records.definition: Euphemism for the flaccid state of the penis, used in direct contrast to 'hard.'
records.notes: Maximally polysemous; sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent. Also used to describe transient erectile difficulty ('I stayed soft') without clinical framing.

records.definition: Slang for the dull testicular ache experienced after prolonged sexual arousal without orgasm or ejaculation.
records.notes: Clinical term is 'epididymal hypertension'; blue discoloration is largely apocryphal. Frequently invoked manipulatively as social pressure to continue sexual activity; the physiological discomfort is real but typically mild and self-resolving.

records.definition: A ring-shaped device worn at the base of the penis, sometimes also encircling the testicles, to restrict venous outflow and prolong or enhance erection.
records.notes: Also written as two words ('cock ring'); clinical equivalent is 'penile constriction ring' or 'vacuum erection device constriction ring.' Sold openly as a sex aid and used medically for erectile dysfunction.

records.definition: Lay term for nocturnal emission: ejaculation occurring during sleep, typically accompanying erotic dreams.
records.notes: Universal recognition; the 'wet' refers to semen. The phenomenon also occurs in people with female anatomy (nocturnal orgasm with vaginal lubrication), though the term is most commonly applied to male physiology.

records.definition: Clinical term for involuntary ejaculation during sleep; the medical counterpart to the lay term 'wet dream.'
records.notes: Standard in medical, educational, and public-health contexts; less familiar to lay audiences than 'wet dream.' Sometimes used in religious or moral discourse around sexuality.

records.definition: Two or more orgasms experienced in rapid succession within a single sexual encounter, without a full intervening refractory period.
records.notes: More physiologically common in people with female anatomy, who typically lack a refractory period; possible but less common in people with male anatomy, often requiring specific training or techniques.

records.definition: An orgasm in which no semen is ejaculated, occurring naturally after repeated orgasms, through deliberate retention techniques, or as a result of medical conditions or surgery.
records.notes: Clinical terms include 'anejaculation' and 'retrograde ejaculation' (distinct mechanisms); also deliberately cultivated in Taoist and tantric sexual practice. Post-prostatectomy patients commonly experience this.

records.definition: The practice of repeatedly bringing oneself or a partner close to orgasm without allowing climax, prolonging arousal.
records.notes: Also categorized under sexual acts; grew in mainstream awareness through sex-positive online communities in the 2010s.

records.definition: A deliberately diminished orgasm achieved by withdrawing stimulation at the moment of climax, used as a dominance or control technique in BDSM.
records.notes: Primarily BDSM/kink subculture terminology; low general population recognition.

records.definition: The peak of sexual excitement; orgasm.
records.notes: Semi-clinical; widely used in literary, mainstream media, and medical contexts.

records.definition: A mild euphemism for orgasm, referring to the apex of sexual arousal.
records.notes: Highly context-dependent; 'peak' has pervasive non-sexual uses, so the sexual meaning requires strong surrounding context to land.

records.definition: To achieve orgasm; also used more broadly to mean deriving sexual pleasure.
records.notes: Applies to all genders. Non-sexual uses (to alight from transport, to escape punishment) are equally common; context disambiguates.

records.definition: To achieve orgasm.
records.notes: Dual spelling convention: 'come' (verb) vs 'cum' (noun for semen, or verb in explicitly sexual writing). One of the most universally recognized sexual terms in English.

records.definition: Euphemism for achieving orgasm, particularly in the context of ejaculation.
records.notes: Very mild; commonly used in mainstream media to avoid explicit language. The softening effect is so strong it can sound clinical or comedic.

records.definition: Crude idiom meaning to ejaculate.
records.notes: Male-specific; 'load' refers to semen. The phrase also has a non-sexual idiomatic meaning (to expend all effort or resources at once), which can cause deliberate or accidental double entendre.

records.definition: Crude verb meaning to ejaculate.
records.notes: Extremely polysemous; sexual meaning recognized in context. Often extended to 'shoot your load' or 'shoot your shot' (the latter now primarily non-sexual).

records.definition: Crude AAVE-originated idiom meaning to ejaculate or achieve orgasm.
records.notes: Originated in AAVE; now widely used across demographics. 'Nut' functions independently as both a noun (semen; orgasm) and verb (to orgasm) in the same register.

records.definition: Sexually aroused or experiencing strong sexual desire.
records.notes: Etymology likely from 'horn' (erection). One of the most common sexual adjectives in English; felt crude in formal contexts but utterly pervasive in casual speech. Applies to all genders.

records.definition: Sexually aroused or having strong sexual desire; primarily British English.
records.notes: Very common in British English; recognition drops sharply in North American contexts where 'Randy' is a common given name, creating persistent confusion and comedy.

records.definition: Sexually aroused or stimulated.
records.notes: One of the most common mild expressions for sexual arousal; broadly used across ages and demographics with little stigma.

records.definition: In a state of sexual excitement; the standard clinical and neutral term for sexual arousal.
records.notes: Also has non-sexual meanings (intellectually stimulated; woken from sleep); in isolation the sexual meaning typically requires context. Default term in medical, psychological, and academic literature.

records.definition: Sexually excited or intensely aroused.
records.notes: Highly polysemous; in modern usage 'hot' primarily means physically attractive. The arousal sense ('I'm so hot for you') is distinct from the attractiveness sense ('she's hot') and requires syntactic context.

records.definition: Mildly sexually flustered or aroused, implying agitation or distraction from desire.
records.notes: Rarely carries sexual meaning when used alone; the sexual sense is almost entirely dependent on the fixed phrase 'hot and bothered'. Standalone sexual recognition is low.

records.definition: In a state of sexual arousal combined with restless agitation or flustered excitement.
records.notes: Fixed idiom; conveys a sense of restless, distracting desire rather than cool arousal. Can also mean simply agitated or overheated without sexual connotation.

records.definition: Intensely sexually aroused; applied to humans by dehumanizing analogy to animals in estrus.
records.notes: Technically refers to estrus in female animals; the transfer to humans is deliberately crude and dehumanizing, though it is sometimes used self-referentially in erotic contexts without pejorative intent.

records.definition: Playfully or mildly sexually aroused; in the mood for sexual play.
records.notes: Light and coy register; commonly used between partners in affectionate contexts. Also means energetically playful in non-sexual contexts (a frisky puppy), which softens its sexual charge.

records.definition: Experiencing or characterized by strong sexual desire.
records.notes: Common in literary and religious contexts; 'lust' is one of the seven deadly sins, which overlays moral condemnation onto desire beyond simple arousal.

records.definition: Having or exhibiting excessive sexual desire; strongly driven by libido.
records.notes: Formal Latinate register; derived from 'libido' as theorized in Freudian psychoanalysis. More common in academic, legal, or literary registers; low general recognition.

records.definition: Having excessive and often predatory sexual desire; inclined to pursue sexual gratification at others' expense.
records.notes: Carries moral condemnation; implies desire directed at unwilling or vulnerable others. Common in Victorian and Shakespearean literature; still in active use as an insult.

records.definition: Feeling or revealing an overt and offensive sexual desire; lewd in manner or expression.
records.notes: Slightly more formal than 'lewd' or 'lecherous'; appears frequently in legal contexts ('lascivious conduct') and literary description. Emphasizes overt display of desire more than internal state.

records.definition: Treating sexual matters in an indecent or gratuitously titillating way; having an undue interest in sexual details.
records.notes: Often applied to content rather than persons (salacious gossip, salacious details). Implies a voyeuristic or prurient interest in others' sexuality rather than one's own desire.

records.definition: Having or stimulating an excessive, unhealthy interest in sexual matters, especially of a voyeuristic kind.
records.notes: Elevated recognition among legal and academic audiences due to its role in U.S. obscenity law (the Miller test requires material to appeal to 'prurient interest'). From Latin 'prurire' (to itch/crave). Low general population recognition.

records.definition: Filled with strong sexual desire; lustful (theological and literary usage).
records.notes: From Latin concupiscere; key term in Augustine's theology of original sin and sexual temptation; rarely encountered outside academic or religious contexts today.

records.definition: Relating to the physical body and its desires, especially sexual appetite, typically contrasted with the spiritual.
records.notes: 'Carnal knowledge' is a legal/archaic term for sexual intercourse; strong religious framing positions carnal desire as morally suspect; from Latin caro (flesh).

records.definition: Sexually uninhibited or promiscuous; lewd and lascivious (archaic/literary adjective or noun for a licentious person).
records.notes: Also means deliberate cruelty unrelated to sex (wanton destruction); gender-neutral historically but often applied to women; found in Shakespeare and Chaucer.

records.definition: Sexually crude, obscene, or explicitly offensive in words, behavior, or appearance.
records.notes: Also a legal term in 'lewd and lascivious conduct'; widely understood and in common use; carries a judgmental tone but is not itself highly vulgar to utter.

records.definition: Sexually or morally unrestrained; disregarding accepted social or moral codes, especially regarding sexuality.
records.notes: From Latin licentia (freedom); implies willful casting off of moral constraint; more formal register than 'promiscuous' or 'slutty'; found in sermons, political rhetoric, and literary criticism.

records.definition: Morally corrupted by overindulgence in sensual pleasures, particularly sex, alcohol, and related excess.
records.notes: Implies broader dissolution beyond sex alone; 'debauched lifestyle' typically connotes multiple vices; from French débaucher (to lure away from duty).

records.definition: Relating to or involving gratification of the physical senses, especially those associated with sexual pleasure.
records.notes: Softer register than 'sexual'; widely used in advertising and romance writing to suggest sexuality with aesthetic distance; positive connotation in most contexts.

records.definition: Tending to arouse sexual desire or excitement; relating to sexual love and pleasure.
records.notes: From Greek Eros (god of love); used freely in literary, artistic, and everyday contexts without embarrassment; 'erotic literature' and 'erotic art' are standard genre labels.

records.definition: Showing or feeling romantic or sexual love; inclined toward love and desire.
records.notes: Blends romantic and sexual desire without cleanly separating them; 'amorous advances' is a common phrase; genteel register; from Latin amor (love).

records.definition: Intensely passionate or enthusiastic; when applied to desire, implies fervent and burning sexual or romantic longing.
records.notes: Not inherently sexual; becomes sexual only in context; equally applied to political passion, religious zeal, etc.; from Latin ardere (to burn).

records.definition: Driven by intense, uncontrolled animal-like sexual urges; behaving like a rutting beast in heat (applied crudely to humans).
records.notes: Primarily a zoological term for the mating season of deer and ungulates; applying it to humans is a deliberate dehumanizing metaphor implying uncontrolled animal lust; 'rutting beast' is the common phrase form.

records.definition: Desperately and urgently wanting to have sex (British crude idiom).
records.notes: Primarily British English; 'gagging' intensifies urgency to near-physical choking desperation; not widely known in North America; gender-neutral in application.

records.definition: Acronym for 'down to fuck': willing or eager to engage in casual sex.
records.notes: Popularized by the reality TV show Jersey Shore (2010–2012) and early dating-app culture; still understood but recognition peaked with that cultural moment.

records.definition: Overtly and desperately seeking sexual attention or romantic validation in a way perceived as needy or unattractive.
records.notes: Pejorative connotation implying the desperation itself is unattractive; extended from general need to specifically sexual/romantic desperation in social media slang; widespread across English-speaking platforms.

records.definition: Lacking sexual responsiveness or desire; sexually cold and unresponsive (most commonly applied pejoratively to women).
records.notes: Strongly gendered: almost always directed at women who decline sex, reflecting mid-20th-century expectation of female sexual availability; clinical psychology replaced it with 'hypoactive sexual desire disorder'; still widely recognized but considered sexist.

records.definition: Experiencing little or no sexual attraction to others; used both as a clinical descriptor and as a sexual identity label.
records.notes: Also a biological term for asexual reproduction; the identity usage was popularized by AVEN (Asexuality Visibility and Education Network) in the 2000s and is now mainstream in LGBTQ+ discourse.

records.definition: A reduced or diminished level of sexual drive or desire.
records.notes: 'Libido' is Freudian terminology absorbed into common medical usage; the compound phrase appears frequently in pharmaceutical advertising for testosterone replacement therapy and hormonal treatments; applies to any gender.

records.definition: Suppressing or holding back sexual feelings, desires, or identity, typically due to cultural, religious, or psychological forces.
records.notes: Psychoanalytic origin (Freud's repression mechanism); widely absorbed into lay speech; often implies the suppressed desire will eventually emerge problematically; 'sexually repressed' is the full common phrase.

records.definition: Excessively modest or easily shocked by sexual content; overly fastidious about propriety in sexual matters.
records.notes: From 'prude' (17th-century French); mildly pejorative suggesting oversensitivity; gender-neutral though historically more applied to women; gentler insult than 'frigid'.

records.definition: Tense, anxious, and unable to relax, especially about sexuality; inhibited and overly conventional.
records.notes: 1960s–70s counterculture slang; sexual inhibition is one application of a broader meaning covering general rigidity and anxiety; still in common use but slightly dated in its specifically sexual connotation.

records.definition: Having very strict moral standards, especially regarding sexuality and social propriety; rigidly conventional.
records.notes: Metaphor from tightly laced corsets constraining the body; also spelled 'straight-laced'; applies to moral conservatism generally, not sex exclusively; formal, older usage.

records.definition: Having an abnormally or compulsively high level of sexual urges, thoughts, or behavior (clinical adjective form).
records.notes: Adjective form; shares concept 'hypersexuality' with the noun form; DSM-5 proposed but did not include 'hypersexual disorder'; sometimes conflated with sex addiction in lay usage.

records.definition: A clinical condition characterized by compulsive and excessive sexual fantasies, urges, or behaviors that cause distress or functional impairment.
records.notes: Noun form; shares concept with 'hypersexual'; proposed as DSM-5 'hypersexual disorder' but excluded; commonly equated with 'sex addiction' in popular discourse despite lacking official diagnostic status.

records.definition: A woman believed to have an insatiable or compulsive need for sex (originally a clinical diagnosis; now typically pejorative or humorous).
records.notes: 19th-century clinical diagnosis; gendered exclusively female (male equivalent 'satyriasis' is barely known); reflects historical double standard; clinically replaced by 'compulsive sexual behavior disorder'; shares concept 'nymphomania' with 'nympho'.

records.definition: Shortened form of nymphomaniac; a woman with an allegedly insatiable sexual appetite (crude and pejorative).
records.notes: More casual and crude than the full form; shares concept 'nymphomania' with 'nymphomaniac'; occasionally reclaimed by some women but predominantly deployed as a derogatory label.

records.definition: A clinical term for abnormally excessive or uncontrollable sexual desire in males.
records.notes: Largely superseded in modern psychiatry by 'compulsive sexual behavior disorder' (ICD-11) or 'hypersexual disorder'; the traditional female equivalent is nymphomania.

records.definition: A lecherous man; derived from the half-human, half-goat creature of Greek mythology associated with sexual excess and drunkenness.
records.notes: Primary recognition is mythological; the sexual characterization sense is secondary and largely literary. Satyriasis derives from this root.

records.definition: A person with compulsive, difficult-to-control sexual thoughts or behaviors that cause distress or functional impairment.
records.notes: Popularized by pop psychology and high-profile celebrity scandals (Tiger Woods, etc.); clinically contested — not an official DSM-5 diagnosis, though ICD-11 includes 'compulsive sexual behaviour disorder'.

records.definition: A psychiatric delusion in which a person believes a higher-status individual is secretly in love with them; historically also used as a synonym for hypersexuality.
records.notes: Dominant modern sense is de Clérambault syndrome (the delusion), not sexual excess; the hypersexuality sense is archaic. The dual meaning causes consistent clinical confusion.

records.definition: A person regarded as having an obsessive or uncontrollable sexual appetite; used pejoratively or humorously.
records.notes: Carries a stronger implication of predatory or deviant behavior than 'sex addict'; somewhat more common in British English. Often used hyperbolically.

records.definition: Currently or regularly engaging in sexual intercourse or other sexual activity.
records.notes: Standard public-health and clinical phrasing, deliberately neutral to avoid stigma. Common in medical history-taking ('are you sexually active?').

records.definition: Having many sexual partners indiscriminately; technically neutral but frequently applied pejoratively, especially to women.
records.notes: The double standard is well-documented: the same behavior in men is often praised as 'virile' while women are shamed as promiscuous. From Latin promiscuus (mixed, indiscriminate).

records.definition: Sexually permissive; not constrained by conventional moral standards regarding sex.
records.notes: Applied almost exclusively to women; considered dated but still understood. May carry a bodily implication (vaginal looseness after many partners), compounding the shame.

records.definition: Readily willing to engage in sex; sexually permissive (in this sense, always pejorative).
records.notes: Heavily polysemous; sexual sense requires context. Applied predominantly to women. Related compounds: 'easy lay', 'easy virtue'. The inversion ('men want someone easy') is culturally notable.

records.definition: Sexually forward or permissive, especially of a woman; morally lax in sexual matters (dated usage).
records.notes: Sexual sense is primarily 19th–mid-20th century; rarely used this way today. Most modern speakers would not parse 'she's fast' as sexual. Peak was pre-living memory.

records.definition: Behaving or appearing like a slut; sexually provocative or permissive, primarily applied to women as a pejorative.
records.notes: Also applied to clothing and appearance ('slutty Halloween costume'). Some reclamation in queer and feminist communities. Adjectival form of 'slut'; slightly softer in crude score due to adjectival distancing.

records.definition: Resembling or characteristic of a whore; sexually promiscuous or overtly provocative in a degrading way.
records.notes: Less common than 'slutty'; carries a stronger implication of transactional or mercenary sexuality than mere promiscuity. Adjectival form of 'whore'.

records.definition: Abstaining from sex outside marriage or from all sexual intercourse; morally pure in a sexual sense.
records.notes: Stronger moral/virtue connotation than 'celibate' or 'abstinent'; implies an internal character quality, not just a behavior. From Latin castus. Usage declining as secularization reduces the moral framework that gives it meaning.

records.definition: Abstaining from marriage and sexual relations, often as a religious vow or deliberate personal commitment.
records.notes: Technically means 'unmarried' (Latin caelibatus) but widely used to mean sexually abstinent. Primarily associated with Catholic clergy. Distinct from 'chaste' (moral purity) and 'abstinent' (behavioral restraint without religious framing).

records.definition: Refraining from sexual activity by deliberate choice, typically for health, moral, or personal reasons.
records.notes: More behavioral and secular in connotation than 'chaste' or 'celibate'; used in both sexual and substance-use contexts ('sexually abstinent', 'alcohol-abstinent'). Associated with abstinence-only education discourse.

records.definition: A woman regarded as sexually promiscuous; one of the most common and loaded misogynistic insults in English.
records.notes: Historical sense: 'slovenly woman' (14th c.), sexual sense developed later. Partial reclamation via SlutWalk movement. Occasionally self-applied by women in sexual contexts as subversion. The anchor term for all slut-shame vocabulary.

records.definition: A woman who has sex for money or is regarded as sexually promiscuous; one of the oldest and most severe sexual pejoratives in English.
records.notes: Spans sex work (transactional sense) and slut-shaming (promiscuity sense). Also used as a generic intensifier ('attention whore', 'pizza whore'). Old English hōre; cognate with German Hure, Dutch hoer. Considered more severe than 'slut' in many registers.

records.definition: A sexually promiscuous woman; AAVE phonetic respelling of 'whore', now widespread in hip-hop and general internet slang.
records.notes: Originated in AAVE; became mainstream via hip-hop from the 1990s onward. The gardening tool homograph creates occasional text ambiguity. Slightly lower crude score than 'whore' due to phonetic distancing and humor register.

records.definition: Variant spelling of 'hoe'; a sexually promiscuous woman (AAVE).
records.notes: Same meaning as 'hoe'; this orthography is common in song lyrics, internet text, and rap. Creates comedic collision with Santa Claus's 'ho ho ho'. Slight recognition drop versus 'hoe' because both spellings compete.

records.definition: Acronym for 'that hoe over there'; a sexually permissive or attention-seeking woman, used pejoratively in AAVE internet culture.
records.notes: Emerged circa 2012 on Twitter and Vine; peaked roughly 2014–2016; declining but still understood. Sometimes pluralized 'thots'. Carries a social-media/performative dimension (seeking attention online) not present in older slut-shame terms.

records.definition: A woman regarded as sexually promiscuous and typically of low social standing or hygiene; a crude pejorative.
records.notes: Uniquely combines sexual shame with class contempt and implied physical uncleanliness — a compound insult. Also a reggae/ska dance move ('skanking'), an entirely unrelated sense.

records.definition: A sexually permissive woman; a mild pejorative implying loose morals.
records.notes: Also means a homeless vagrant (primary meaning in British English). The sexual sense is primarily American. The Disney film 'Lady and the Tramp' uses the vagabond sense, not the sexual one. Considered dated but still understood.

records.definition: A sexually permissive or provocatively dressed woman; a mild British pejorative.
records.notes: Primarily British and Australian; American speakers largely know the pastry sense only. Milder than 'slut' in British usage. Folk etymology connects sweetness/availability to pastry, but origin is uncertain.

records.definition: A disreputable, flirtatious, or sexually loose woman; now used primarily in humorous or ironic contexts.
records.notes: Etymologically a corruption of 'housewife'; meaning degraded over several centuries. Largely archaic; often deployed in mock-scolding ('you little hussy!'). One of the milder slut-shame terms.

records.definition: A sexually promiscuous woman; a crude British pejorative roughly equivalent in force to 'slut'.
records.notes: Primarily British and Australian; largely unknown in American English. Primary metallurgical meaning (waste from smelting) is unrelated. Widely used in British soap operas (EastEnders, Coronation Street). Also used as a general insult for men in British English, though the sexual shame connotation is women-coded.

records.definition: Dated mild pejorative for a woman perceived as sexually promiscuous or cheaply provocative.
records.notes: Softer than 'slut'; connotes tackiness and availability equally; peak use in mid-20th-century American media; now used mostly ironically or humorously.

records.definition: Archaic pejorative for a prostitute or woman regarded as sexually immoral.
records.notes: Strong biblical and literary pedigree (KJV, Shakespeare); archaism softens the sting for modern readers; still deployed in religious rhetoric.

records.definition: A seductive, morally corrupt woman; from the biblical queen; historically weaponized as a racialized stereotype applied disproportionately to Black women.
records.notes: The 'Jezebel stereotype' is a documented racialized trope in American history used to justify sexual exploitation of enslaved and Black women; the racial dimension is analytically significant.

records.definition: Archaic term for a prostitute or sexually immoral woman.
records.notes: Heavy Shakespearean usage; today sounds almost comically theatrical; occasionally repurposed for comic or camp effect.

records.definition: Archaic adjective or noun for a sexually licentious or dissolute woman.
records.notes: Has non-sexual senses (wanton cruelty, wanton destruction) that keep the word in passive recognition; the sexual sense is effectively archaic in everyday speech.

records.definition: Archaic pejorative for a sexually promiscuous or slovenly woman.
records.notes: Connotations blend sexual looseness with general slovenliness; more common in British than American English; has a theatrical, almost pantomime-villain quality today.

records.definition: Dated US slang for a woman easily persuaded into sex, from the image of someone whose heels round off so she tips over backward easily.
records.notes: Effectively dead slang; recognizable mainly to older Americans or slang historians; the physical metaphor (tipping over) makes the submissive posture explicit.

records.definition: In sexual contexts, a person — typically a woman — who can easily be persuaded to have sex; primary meaning is simply 'easily manipulated person.'
records.notes: The sexual sense is strongly secondary to the general meaning; low crude score reflects the dominant non-sexual register; inclusion is contextual rather than inherent.

records.definition: Crude slang for a sexually promiscuous woman in a community, implying she is ridden by everyone.
records.notes: The vehicle metaphor ('everyone gets a ride') is the rhetorical core; 'town pump,' 'town mattress,' and 'community mattress' are structural variants on the same template.

records.definition: Crude slang for a sexually promiscuous woman in a community, implying communal access like a public water pump.
records.notes: Less common variant of 'town bicycle'; the shared-public-resource metaphor carries the same dehumanizing logic; more dated and regional than 'town bicycle.'

records.definition: Crude slang reducing a sexually available woman to a piece of furniture used for sex.
records.notes: Object-reduction metaphor; 'community mattress' is an extended form; the furniture comparison is explicitly dehumanizing; recognition of the sexual sense may be higher among men.

records.definition: Crude slang for a sexually promiscuous woman, from the expression 'everyone gets a turn,' as with a doorknob.
records.notes: Rarer than 'town bicycle'; the 'everybody gets a turn' logic is typically spelled out explicitly when the term is used; sometimes deployed as an explanatory joke.

records.definition: Very crude US pejorative for an extremely promiscuous woman, framing her as a low-value prostitute.
records.notes: The dollar figure signals contempt through cheapness, compounding the shame; 'two-bit whore' is a variant; also used hyperbolically in non-sexual idioms ('spending money like a two-dollar whore').

records.definition: Crude slang that reduces a person, typically a woman, to a sexual object; most common in the compound 'piece of ass.'
records.notes: Overwhelmingly woman-directed in practice; can be applied to men but rarely is; the fragmentation implied by 'piece' (not the whole person) makes the dehumanization structural.

records.definition: Slang for a sexual partner evaluated by performance ('a good lay'), or for the act of sex itself.
records.notes: Dual noun/verb usage; objectifying but mild enough to appear in mainstream fiction without shock; applies to any gender in principle though historically more often woman-directed.

records.definition: A person treated as a prize won through seduction; the act of seducing that person framed as a military or competitive victory.
records.notes: The military metaphor (sex as territorial victory) is so naturalized it is often used without irony; primarily masculine in framing; the partner is cast as passive territory.

records.definition: A sexual partner counted as a tally in a personal history of conquests, as in 'notch on the bedpost.'
records.notes: Metonymic shorthand for the full phrase 'notch on the bedpost'; the counting/scorekeeping frame makes the objectification structurally explicit; primarily masculine usage.

records.definition: A late-night contact made to someone purely for casual sex; also used for the person being contacted in this way.
records.notes: Emerged from 1990s African-American vernacular; fully mainstream by early 2000s; can objectify the person being called or describe the arrangement neutrally depending on context.

records.definition: A man admired for his virility and success in attracting or bedding many women.
records.notes: Derived directly from the male breeding-animal sense; connotation is strongly positive or neutral; the contrast with all-negative female equivalents is a primary data point for gendered shame asymmetry.

records.definition: A man who skillfully pursues and maintains sexual relationships with multiple women, often with tactical self-awareness.
records.notes: Mainstreamed through 1990s hip-hop; 'player' implies calculated skill and 'game' rather than mere promiscuity; frequently self-applied with pride; less morally weighted than 'womanizer.'

records.definition: A seductive, unscrupulous man who pursues women for sexual conquest; from the villain in Nicholas Rowe's 1703 play 'The Fair Penitent.'
records.notes: Literary origin; connotes rakish charm alongside moral callousness; today mainly used in formal writing or with ironic distance; recognition declining as literary literacy falls.

records.definition: A man who is a prolific and skilled seducer of women; eponymous from Giacomo Casanova (1725–1798).
records.notes: Carries connotations of sophistication and romantic talent rather than mere promiscuity; used admiringly at least as often as critically; far less stigmatized than any female counterpart — key data for shame asymmetry.

records.definition: A man who habitually pursues and seduces many women.
records.notes: Mildly pejorative but socially far less damaging than female equivalents like 'slut'; the asymmetry in condemnation between this term and its female-coded counterparts is a core signal for cross-cultural shame measurement.

records.definition: A man so attractive or charming that women find him irresistible; implies great success in seduction.
records.notes: Overwhelmingly positive in connotation; the violence metaphor ('killer') is fully domesticated; emphasizes appearance and charisma more than promiscuity per se; gender-reversed 'mankiller' exists but is rare.

records.definition: A promiscuous man, framed pejoratively by borrowing the female-coded shame term 'whore.'
records.notes: The compound deliberately transfers a feminine shame term to a man; the social damage is measurably lighter than calling a woman a slut, demonstrating that the transfer is imperfect — shame vocabulary is not gender-neutral even when lexically transposed; peak in mid-2000s internet and tabloid usage.

records.definition: A young man who pursues casual sex without emotional commitment, often through manipulation or false romantic signaling.
records.notes: Emerged c. 2014 in internet and hip-hop culture; the 'fuck' prefix marks crudeness; carries social condemnation but is occasionally used aspirationally in certain subcultures.

records.definition: Abbreviated form of 'fuckboy'; a young man who uses women for sexual gratification without emotional commitment.
records.notes: Cleaned-up spelling used on platforms that filter 'fuckboy'; popularized by the HBO Max reality show FBoy Island (2021); primarily Gen Z usage.

records.definition: A male sex worker or paid male companion, especially one financially kept by an older wealthy woman.
records.notes: French loanword; retains a glamorized, Old World connotation absent from female equivalents; covers both paid escort and kept-man meanings simultaneously.

records.definition: A person, typically male, who maintains multiple simultaneous romantic or sexual relationships through charm and deliberate non-commitment.
records.notes: Rooted in African American vernacular English; peaked in 1990s R&B and hip-hop culture; valence is ambivalent—admiring or critical depending on speaker and context.

records.definition: A man who systematically studies and applies psychological and social techniques to seduce women, typically for casual sex.
records.notes: Abbreviated PUA; associated with the seduction community and later red-pill subcultures; popularized by Neil Strauss's The Game (2005) and MTV's The Pickup Artist (2007).

records.definition: A person, typically male, who is persistently or compulsively driven by sexual desire.
records.notes: Compound of 'horny' and 'dog'; the dog component implies animal-like lack of restraint and low social status; primarily American English.

records.definition: A lecherous man; someone who makes persistent unwanted sexual advances or who is indiscreetly and obsessively driven by lust.
records.notes: Clipped from 'lecher' or 'lecherous'; more common in British English; also functions as a verb ('to lech after someone'); alternate spelling 'letch' exists.

records.definition: An older man perceived as inappropriately or predatorily interested in sex, especially toward younger people.
records.notes: The 'dirty' component evokes moral pollution from sexuality; originally framed as a comic archetype, increasingly coded as predatory in post-#MeToo discourse; abbreviated DOM in some online contexts.

records.definition: A pervert; a person whose sexual interests or behaviors are perceived as deviant, predatory, or grossly inappropriate.
records.notes: Clipped form of 'pervert'; applied across a wide spectrum from harmless kink-shaming to serious predation; context-dependent severity; also used as a verb.

records.definition: A person who makes others uncomfortable through unwanted sexual attention, boundary violations, or generally unsettling behavior.
records.notes: Not exclusively sexual—applies to general unsettling behavior—but its dominant use is sexual/romantic; 'creepiness' has been studied academically (McAndrew & Koehnke, 2016); gender-neutral term applied predominantly to men in practice.

records.definition: A person who uses power, manipulation, or coercion to obtain sex from unwilling or unable-to-consent victims.
records.notes: Short for 'sexual predator' in this context; carries legal and clinical weight that distinguishes it from other terms in this section; zero valorizing connotation; no ambivalence.

records.definition: A person sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of the opposite sex or gender.
records.notes: Derived from Greek 'hetero' (other) and Latin 'sexualis'; informal equivalents include 'straight' and 'het'.

records.definition: A person sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of the same sex.
records.notes: Clinical term that can feel cold or medicalizing in community contexts; some LGBT individuals perceive it as pejorative when used by outsiders; preferred alternatives include 'gay' and 'lesbian' in most conversational registers.

records.definition: A person sexually and/or romantically attracted to both men and women, or to people of their own gender and other genders.
records.notes: Abbreviated 'bi'; the prefix 'bi' (two) is debated as potentially excluding non-binary identities, though the practical definition has broadened in community use; remains the most widely recognized clinical and colloquial term.

records.definition: A person sexually and/or romantically attracted to others regardless of their sex or gender identity.
records.notes: Derived from Greek 'pan' (all); distinguishes from bisexual by foregrounding gender-blindness; gained wider visibility alongside increased non-binary awareness from ~2012 onward.

records.definition: A person who experiences little or no sexual attraction to others.
records.notes: Often abbreviated 'ace'; distinct from celibacy (behavioral) and aromanticism (lack of romantic attraction); identity formalized by AVEN (Asexual Visibility and Education Network) from ~2001.

records.definition: A person who experiences sexual attraction only after forming a strong emotional bond with someone.
records.notes: Coined c. 2006 on AVEN forums; considered part of the asexual spectrum ('grey-ace'); relatively low mainstream recognition outside queer and online communities.

records.definition: A person who experiences sexual attraction rarely, weakly, or only under specific circumstances; positioned on the spectrum between asexual and fully sexual.
records.notes: Also spelled 'greysexual'; part of the ace spectrum; abbreviated 'gray-ace'; low mainstream recognition outside asexuality-focused communities.

records.definition: An umbrella term for non-heterosexual and/or non-cisgender identities; reclaimed from its historical use as a slur.
records.notes: Originally meant 'strange/odd'; deployed as a slur against LGBT people; actively reclaimed from ~1990 (Queer Nation); still potentially offensive when used by non-LGBT speakers in some contexts; now standard in academic queer theory.

records.definition: A gender identity that does not fall exclusively within the traditional binary categories of man or woman.
records.notes: Abbreviated NB or 'enby'; umbrella term for genderqueer, genderfluid, agender, and related identities; entered mainstream discourse significantly after ~2014; legal gender marker recognition in several jurisdictions.

records.definition: A person whose gender identity aligns with the sex they were assigned at birth.
records.notes: Derived from Latin 'cis' (on the same side); coined in academic and activist discourse c. 1990s; often abbreviated 'cis'; politically contested in some circles despite functioning as a neutral descriptive complement to 'transgender'.

records.definition: A person whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth.
records.notes: Preferred over the outdated 'transsexual' in most modern contexts; often abbreviated 'trans'; historically a medicalized term, now widely used as a self-identifier; functions as both adjective and noun.

records.definition: A person born with sex characteristics (chromosomes, hormones, gonads, or genitalia) that do not fit typical binary definitions of male or female.
records.notes: Replaced earlier medical term 'hermaphrodite,' now considered offensive; refers to biological variation distinct from gender identity; prevalence estimates range from 0.02% to 1.7% depending on how narrowly the term is defined.

records.definition: A person, especially a man, who is sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of the same sex; also used as a general umbrella for non-heterosexual identity.
records.notes: Originally meant 'happy/lighthearted'; adopted as an LGBT self-identifier from ~1960s; now standard across most English dialects; a secondary pejorative meaning 'lame/stupid' represents distinct semantic drift, more common among younger speakers.

records.definition: A woman who is sexually and/or romantically attracted to other women.
records.notes: Derived from Lesbos, Greek island home of the poet Sappho; functions as both clinical term and self-identifier; abbreviated 'les' or 'lez,' the latter carrying potential derogatory connotation depending on speaker.

records.definition: Colloquial term for a heterosexual person or orientation.
records.notes: Used across clinical and casual registers interchangeably; also has many non-sexual meanings, making contextual disambiguation necessary in corpus work.

records.definition: Informal abbreviation for bisexual, denoting attraction to more than one gender.
records.notes: Fully mainstream abbreviation; used in both identity and descriptive senses with no residual stigma in most English-speaking contexts.

records.definition: Informal abbreviation for pansexual, denoting attraction to people regardless of gender.
records.notes: Common in LGBTQ+ subculture and among younger demographics; the distinction from 'bi' is debated within communities; recognition drops sharply in older cohorts.

records.definition: Informal abbreviation for asexual, denoting little or no sexual attraction to others.
records.notes: The playing-card ace is used as a symbol by asexual communities; recognition is growing but still substantially subculture-bound.

records.definition: Informal abbreviation for aromantic, denoting little or no romantic attraction to others.
records.notes: Less widely known than 'ace'; primarily circulates within ace/aro community spaces; the romantic/sexual distinction it relies on is itself a relatively recent conceptual framework.

records.definition: Experiencing little or no romantic attraction to others, distinct from asexuality which concerns sexual attraction.
records.notes: The romantic/sexual attraction distinction is a conceptual development of the 2000s–2010s; the term is semi-clinical in community use and growing in mainstream awareness.

records.definition: Public health acronym for 'men who have sex with men,' categorizing sexual behavior irrespective of identity.
records.english_term: men who have sex with men
records.notes: Deliberately behavior-based rather than identity-based; developed for HIV/STI epidemiology to capture men who do not identify as gay or bisexual but engage in same-sex behavior; not widely known outside public health or research contexts.

records.definition: Public health acronym for 'women who have sex with women,' categorizing behavior irrespective of identity.
records.english_term: women who have sex with women
records.notes: Appears less frequently in research literature than MSM; same behavior-first framing; recognition is very low outside public health and academic contexts.

records.definition: Term used primarily in religious and conservative contexts for a person who experiences same-sex attraction without adopting a gay or lesbian identity.
records.notes: Preferred in some religious frameworks (e.g. celibate gay Catholic, ex-gay adjacent) to describe experience while resisting identity-label politics; also appears in Australian clinical literature with a more neutral valence; the phrase deliberately separates attraction from identity.

records.definition: Having a gender identity that shifts or varies over time rather than remaining fixed.
records.notes: Term rose to mainstream awareness in the mid-2010s; broadly recognized though acceptance and interpretation vary significantly across political and generational lines.

records.definition: Identifying as having no gender or as existing outside of gender entirely.
records.notes: Distinct from nonbinary (which acknowledges a gender, just not a binary one); recognition is growing but still primarily within LGBTQ+ and online communities.

records.definition: Describing a person who practices or is open to consensual romantic or sexual relationships with multiple partners simultaneously.
records.notes: Adjectival form of polyamory; both terms surged in mainstream recognition in the 2010s–2020s; distinct from swinging in its emphasis on emotional intimacy alongside or instead of recreational sex.

records.definition: The practice of having consensual romantic or sexual relationships with multiple partners simultaneously.
records.notes: Coined circa 1990; Greek/Latin hybrid portmanteau (polys + amor); distinct from polygamy (not marriage-based, gender-neutral); distinct from swinging (emphasis on relationships, not just sex).

records.definition: Maintaining a sexual or romantic relationship with only one partner at a time.
records.notes: The cultural and legal default in most Western societies; used in clinical, legal, and casual registers without distinction; increasing use in contrast with polyamory discourse.

records.definition: Having multiple spouses simultaneously; typically illegal in Western jurisdictions but practiced in some religious and cultural communities.
records.notes: Technically encompasses polygyny (one man, multiple wives) and polyandry (one woman, multiple husbands); in common English usage almost always implies polygyny; carries varying moral weight depending on cultural context.

records.definition: A person who engages in consensual partner-swapping or group sexual activity with other couples.
records.notes: Term became culturally prominent in the 1960s–70s; still active and broadly recognized; distinct from polyamory in its typical emphasis on recreational sex over emotional intimacy; associated with a recognizable subculture with its own venues.

records.definition: The practice of consensual partner-swapping or group sex among couples, typically as a recreational lifestyle.
records.notes: Activity-noun form of swinger; the lifestyle aspect distinguishes it from one-off encounters; still maintains a distinct subculture separate from the newer polyamory community.

records.definition: A romantic partnership in which both parties have agreed that sexual or romantic activity with others outside the relationship is permitted.
records.notes: Broad umbrella term encompassing swinging, polyamory, and don't-ask-don't-tell arrangements; widely understood across generations; less subculture-specific than either 'polyamory' or 'swinging.'

records.definition: A man whose partner has sex with other men; historically a term of humiliation and social shame, now also used for the consensual kink practice involving erotic arousal from the same scenario.
records.notes: Derived from cuckoo bird behavior; the abbreviation 'cuck' had a spike as a political insult circa 2016; kink usage remains active online; the term straddles the honor/shame economy and kink categories depending on era and context.

records.definition: The state or practice of being a cuckold; in modern use, the consensual kink in which a man's erotic arousal derives from his partner's sexual activity with other men.
records.notes: More formal and archaic noun form than 'cuckold' or 'cucking'; appears in historical literature and academic or kink-community writing; the -ry suffix gives it a quasi-clinical or literary register.

records.definition: A married woman who has sex with men other than her husband with his full knowledge and enthusiastic consent, framed as a source of shared erotic pleasure.
records.notes: Distinct from cuckoldry in framing: hotwife arrangements emphasize the wife's desirability and the husband's pride and arousal rather than humiliation; recognized within CNM and kink communities; primarily an internet-era subculture term.

records.definition: In the stag/vixen kink dynamic, the husband or male partner who takes confident pride in facilitating and watching his wife's sexual activity with other men.
records.notes: Used in the 'stag/vixen' pairing as an explicit alternative framing to cuckold; emphasizes confidence and pride rather than humiliation; very niche, primarily found in online kink forums; 'stag' has many common non-sexual meanings that swamp this usage in general corpora.

records.definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from watching others engaged in intimate or sexual behavior.
records.notes: French loanword (voyeur, 'one who sees'); clinical use implies non-consensual watching (DSM voyeuristic disorder); kink use may be fully consensual; the word is broadly understood in general culture and has a neutral-to-titillating register in lay usage.

records.definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from exposing themselves or performing sexually in front of others.
records.notes: Clinical term spanning both DSM exhibitionistic disorder (non-consensual exposure) and consensual kink exhibitionism; also used metaphorically for attention-seeking behavior in non-sexual contexts, which slightly dilutes the sexual signal in general corpora.

records.definition: A person who derives sexual arousal from both inflicting and receiving pain, humiliation, or domination.
records.notes: Portmanteau of sadist (from Marquis de Sade) and masochist (from Leopold von Sacher-Masoch); abbreviated S&M or SM; largely subsumed into the broader BDSM framework in contemporary kink discourse, making 'sadomasochist' feel slightly clinical or dated compared to 'into BDSM.'

records.definition: Highly offensive slur for a gay man, predominantly in American English.
records.notes: Also means cigarette in British English; disambiguation is context-dependent; one of the most commonly deployed anti-gay slurs in North America.

records.definition: Highly offensive slur for a gay man; the full form of 'fag'.
records.notes: Also means a bundle of sticks or a type of British meatball; the slur sense is among the most charged anti-gay insults in American English.

records.definition: Slur for a lesbian woman, often carrying connotations of masculine presentation; significantly reclaimed within lesbian communities.
records.notes: Reclamation well-established — 'Dykes on Bikes' at Pride parades is a prominent example; masculine-presentation connotation makes the mapping to 'lesbian' approximate rather than direct.

records.definition: Diminutive slur for a lesbian woman; partially reclaimed but generally offensive outside the community.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix (-zie) gives it a slightly playful or dismissive tone compared to harder slurs; partially reclaimed in some lesbian subcultures.

records.definition: Shortened slur for a lesbian; partially reclaimed.
records.notes: Truncated form; perceived as slightly less offensive than 'lezzie' in some contexts; used in both derogatory and reclaimed registers.

records.definition: Umbrella term for non-heterosexual and/or non-cisgender identities; historically a slur, now widely reclaimed as a positive self-identifier.
records.notes: Generational divide persists — older LGBTQ+ individuals may still experience it as a slur; Queer Theory in academia further shifted its register toward neutral/positive.

records.definition: A gay man who is flamboyant or effeminate; primarily a community self-identifier, especially in drag culture.
records.notes: Can be an insult in hostile mouths but functions primarily as affirmative within gay male culture; 'drag queen' is the most widely recognized compound form.

records.definition: Dated slur for an effeminate gay man.
records.notes: Peak usage mid-20th century; still recognizable but rarely deployed as a fresh insult today; typically appears in period fiction or historical reference.

records.definition: Dated slur for an effeminate or cowardly man, with strong implied homosexuality.
records.notes: Named after the flower; broader than strictly gay — can mean any perceived weakling; the gay connotation dominates in most uses.

records.definition: British slur for a gay man.
records.notes: Primarily British English; considered a strong slur in the UK; less familiar in North America.

records.definition: British and Australian emphatic slur for a gay man; extended form of 'poof'.
records.notes: Common in Australia as well as Britain; globally known via British and Australian media exports.

records.definition: Derogatory abbreviation of 'homosexual', used as a slur primarily for gay men.
records.notes: Clipped form strips the clinical neutrality of 'homosexual'; slightly elevated technical score due to clinical root; used broadly for LGBTQ+ people in hostile contexts.

records.definition: Religious and legal-historical term for a man who practices anal sex; used primarily to condemn gay men; derived from the biblical city of Sodom.
records.notes: Appears in historical sodomy laws; carries theological weight absent from secular slurs; technically refers to the act rather than gay identity, making the mapping approximate.

records.definition: Dated British slur for an effeminate or cowardly man, with implied homosexuality.
records.notes: A feminine given name repurposed as insult; also used adjectivally ('nancy ways'); largely dated but still in passive use.

records.definition: British compound slur for an effeminate or cowardly man.
records.notes: Compound of 'nancy' + 'boy'; the 'boy' suffix emphasizes perceived childlike emasculation; dated but still recognizable.

records.definition: Slur for an effeminate or weak man or boy; implies failure to conform to masculine norms; frequently directed at gay men.
records.notes: Derived from 'sister'; broader than exclusively gay — applied to any insufficiently masculine male; has a secondary kink meaning in BDSM (feminization/sissy play).

records.definition: Dated American slur for a gay man.
records.notes: Often appears in compound 'old fruit'; 'fruitcake' carries similar meaning; largely dated in mainstream use but still widely recognizable.

records.definition: British crude slur for a gay man who takes the receptive role in anal sex, evoking the image of biting a pillow during penetration.
records.notes: More positionally specific than generic gay slurs — implies the receptive sexual role; slightly elevated technical score due to explicit sexual-act imagery.

records.definition: British crude slur for a gay man, evoking lifting clothing for anal sex.
records.notes: Primarily British; largely unknown in North America; the euphemistic clothing metaphor is characteristic of mid-20th-century British slang style.

records.definition: British slur for a gay man; likely derived from 'bending over' for anal sex.
records.notes: Well-known in the UK; the Futurama character Bender's name is an intentional British double entendre; etymology disputed.

records.definition: British crude slur for a gay man, with explicit reference to anal sex.
