records.notes: 'Bum' is British English for buttocks; less common in American English where 'bum' has different primary salience; the compound makes the anal reference explicit.

records.definition: Crude American slur for a gay man, using piracy imagery as a metaphor for anal sex.
records.notes: The maritime/piracy framing creates a mock-heroic comic register; somewhat less charged than 'fag/faggot' due to its comedic quality; widely known in North American English.

records.definition: Crude slur for a gay man, using scatological theft imagery as a metaphor for anal sex.
records.notes: Scatological reference elevates crude score; parallels the mock-criminal structure of 'butt pirate'; maximally offensive in intent due to fecal association.

records.definition: Crude term for a woman who performs cunnilingus on another woman; used as a slur for lesbians.
records.notes: 'Muff' refers to pubic hair or vulva; can technically describe any person who performs cunnilingus, so the lesbian identity mapping is approximate; slightly elevated technical score due to the anatomical reference.

records.definition: Crude slur for a lesbian, using an eating metaphor for cunnilingus.
records.notes: 'Carpet' is slang for pubic hair; parallel structure to 'muff diver' but 'munching' imagery is considered slightly more offensive; both terms define the identity through the sex act rather than orientation.

records.definition: Derogatory slang for a lesbian, referencing cunnilingus.
records.notes: Offensive slur; rarely if ever reclaimed by the community.

records.definition: Derogatory term for a heavily masculine-presenting lesbian; 'bull' intensifies the masculinity implication.
records.notes: Some partial reclamation among older lesbians; considerably more offensive than 'dyke' alone.

records.definition: Masculine-presenting lesbian or queer person; an affirming identity term inside LGBTQ+ communities, sometimes pejorative when used by outsiders.
records.notes: Insider use is neutral to positive; outsider use can be contemptuous; also applied to masculine gay men.

records.definition: Feminine-presenting lesbian or queer person; a positive identity term in LGBTQ+ communities.
records.notes: Borrowed from French 'femme' (woman); essentially never used as a slur; carries connotations of intentional, politicized femininity.

records.definition: Highly offensive slur for a transgender person.
records.notes: Recognition has risen with cultural debate; some older trans people use it self-referentially, but this is increasingly rare and contested.

records.definition: Offensive slang for a transgender woman, especially one with a penis; entrenched in pornographic taxonomy.
records.notes: Considered deeply offensive outside adult entertainment; porn industry continues using it as a search/genre tag despite widespread objection.

records.definition: Term for a transgender or gender-nonconforming person, especially in Southeast Asian (primarily Thai) context; offensiveness is context-dependent.
records.notes: Less offensive in Thai cultural context where 'kathoey' is the local parallel; Western use tends toward fetishization; not considered an equivalent of 'tranny'.

records.definition: Derogatory compound pronoun used to deny or mock a transgender person's gender identity.
records.notes: Highlights perceived gender contradiction as a form of insult; feels more dated than 'tranny' but still recognized; no community reclamation.

records.definition: Use of the neuter pronoun 'it' applied to a transgender or non-binary person to dehumanize them as a non-person.
records.notes: The word itself is universal English; this entry captures the specific slur usage. Recognition score reflects awareness of the slur application, not the pronoun itself.

records.definition: Internet slur for a transgender woman or feminine-presenting man, implying they 'trap' straight men into homosexual contact.
records.notes: Originated in anime/4chan culture ~2010s; implies deception as core insult; peak usage roughly 2014–2018; still active in anti-trans online spaces.

records.definition: Internet slur for a transgender person, coined and circulated in anti-trans online communities.
records.notes: Primarily found on 4chan, Reddit, and Twitter/X anti-trans communities; niche but virulent; low mainstream recognition as of 2026.

records.definition: Crude and community-used term for the penis of a transgender woman, affirming her gender identity while naming her anatomy.
records.notes: Used affirmingly within trans and queer communities; used as a slur by outsiders; no neutral clinical equivalent exists for this specific framing.

records.definition: Portmanteau slang (boy + pussy) for the anus of a male or transgender person when used in a sexual context.
records.notes: Originated in AAVE and gay male communities; spread to mainstream internet culture; used affirmingly in queer contexts; carries no analog in clinical language.

records.definition: Extremely offensive general-purpose insult derived from fellatio; among the strongest insults in American English.
records.notes: Primarily American; less severe in some British registers; used as both noun insult and exclamation; literal sexual meaning largely absent in insult use.

records.definition: Extremely offensive general insult and intensifier derived from incest imagery; one of the harshest expletives in English.
records.notes: In AAVE can function as an intensifier of admiration ('that motherfucker can play'); literal incest meaning entirely absent in modern use.

records.definition: General-purpose insult for a contemptible person; derived from 'fuck'.
records.notes: Can be used affectionately or neutrally in British English and AAVE ('the poor fucker'); severity is highly context-dependent.

records.definition: Very common insult for a selfish, unpleasant, or contemptible person; derived from the anatomical anus.
records.notes: American spelling; British 'arsehole' is functionally identical but registers as slightly less crude to American ears. One of the most commonly uttered insults in American English.

records.definition: Insult for a stupid or contemptible person; compound of 'dick' (penis slang) and 'head'.
records.notes: Common in both American and British English; somewhat less severe than 'cocksucker' or 'cunt'.

records.definition: Insult for an unpleasant, self-important, or contemptible person; derived from slang for penis.
records.notes: More prevalent as an insult in British English than American; also functions as a standalone slang term for penis.

records.definition: In American English, the most severely offensive common insult; in British and Australian English considerably less severe and used more casually between peers.
records.notes: Stark regional severity split: US treats this as near-untouchable; UK/AUS use casually as general intensifier or even term of address. Also denotes the anatomical vagina.

records.definition: Insult for a stupid or contemptible person; derived from slang for vagina; predominantly British in usage.
records.notes: Far more common in UK than US; many Americans are unaware of the vagina meaning; British severity is relatively mild compared to 'cunt'.

records.definition: Insult meaning coward or weak person; derived from slang for vagina; implies femininity as synonymous with weakness.
records.notes: This entry covers the coward sense specifically, distinct from the vagina and cat meanings; the insult is primarily directed at men, encoding a misogynist logic.

records.definition: Very common insult for a contemptible or unpleasant person, especially a woman; also used in AAVE as an intensifier, term of address, or even affectionate label.
records.notes: Literally female dog; range of severity is enormous: gendered slur in one context, affectionate in-group address in another; partially reclaimed in feminist discourse.

records.definition: Insult for a contemptible person; originally a legal term for an illegitimate child; severity has decreased substantially over time.
records.notes: The illegitimacy etymology is the origin but rarely the intended meaning today; can be affectionate in British and Australian English ('you old bastard'); relatively mild by modern standards.

records.definition: Strong general-purpose insult and exclamation; literally 'son of a female dog'; one of the oldest and most widely used American expletives.
records.notes: Abbreviated 'SOB'; can express admiration or surprise as well as contempt depending on context; the gendered insult to the mother is the etymological core but functionally absent in modern use.

records.definition: An obnoxious, arrogant, or contemptible person, derived from the name of a vaginal hygiene irrigation device.
records.notes: Sexual origin largely opaque to modern users who treat it as a generic insult; the hygiene-product etymology is known but rarely foregrounded.

records.definition: Abbreviated form of douchebag; a contemptible or obnoxious person; retains a literal medical meaning (vaginal irrigation) alongside the insult use.
records.notes: Slightly lower crude score than 'douchebag' because the standalone word also circulates in clinical/medical contexts; insult use otherwise identical.

records.definition: A stupid or contemptible person; etymology uncertain but likely combines 'dip' (dialectal fool or chewing-tobacco user) with 'shit' as an intensifier, with possible sexual overtones in some dialect chains.
records.notes: Sexual derivation is partial and disputed; included here because 'shit' anchors it to the scatological-sexual expletive cluster; used freely across genders.

records.definition: A versatile expletive referring primarily to feces; deployed in sexual contexts as an intensifier, exclamation of displeasure, or crude descriptor of situations and people.
records.notes: Primarily scatological rather than sexual; included in this section because it seeds compound sexual insults (dipshit, shit-for-brains) and functions as a general-purpose crude intensifier in sexual situations.

records.definition: A person—typically a woman or a demanding authority figure—perceived as destroying a man's confidence, ease, or sexual dominance through relentless demands or criticism.
records.notes: Can extend to any exhausting situation ('that job is a real ballbuster'); primary insult targets emasculating behavior; 'balls' = testicles = male potency in metaphor.

records.definition: A person who emasculates others or who is exceptionally demanding and difficult; hyphenated variant of ballbuster with identical meaning and usage.
records.notes: Interchangeable with 'ballbuster'; hyphen is the only distinction; both forms appear in print; neither form has clear dominance by region.

records.definition: Pejorative for a cowardly or ineffectual person, equating the literal or figurative absence of a penis with lack of courage or competence.
records.notes: Explicitly male-coded; can target men (implying they lack masculine grit) or occasionally women (as crude negation of authority); logic mirrors 'spineless' but anchors to genital anatomy.

records.definition: Pejorative for a cowardly person, invoking the absence of testicles as a metaphor for lacking courage or resolve.
records.notes: Often deployed as a direct taunt ('you've got no balls'); the 'balls = bravery' metaphor is so entrenched it appears in sports commentary without conscious sexual reference.

records.definition: Variant of 'no-balls'; pejorative for a spineless or cowardly person, equating absence of testicles with lack of resolve.
records.notes: Rare in print; the compounded suffix '-less' applied to 'ball' is grammatically productive but phonetically awkward compared to 'no-balls'; same concept, lower frequency.

records.definition: A contemptible, cowardly, or ineffectual person; evokes erectile dysfunction as a metaphor for weakness, failure, or lack of resolve.
records.notes: More sexually explicit than 'dickless' because it references erectile dysfunction specifically rather than absence; functions as both noun ('he's a limp-dick') and adjective ('a limp-dick policy').

records.definition: An internet-era phrase describing insecure, overcompensating, or bullying behavior metaphorically attributed to anxiety about having a small penis.
records.notes: Emerged as the inversion of 'big dick energy' (BDE), which itself was popularized in 2018; used across genders to describe behavioral patterns rather than literal anatomy; notably more acceptable in mainstream media than most phallic insults.

records.definition: A sycophant or uncritical fanboy who idolizes someone; also deployed as a homophobic slur implying the target performs oral or anal sex on the person they admire.
records.notes: Dual register: in hip-hop slang it primarily means sycophant (circa 1990s onward); in homophobic contexts it literalizes the sexual imagery; recognition concentrated in younger urban US demographics.

records.definition: Shortened form of 'cuckold'; an internet and far-right slur for a man perceived as weak, emasculated, or politically submissive, especially one who tolerates humiliation from women or political opponents.
records.notes: Derived from cuckold fetish communities (where men eroticize their partner having sex with others) and weaponized as a political insult c. 2015–2016; peak use in alt-right rhetoric around the 2016 US election; now general internet shorthand for any perceived submissive male.

records.definition: A man who is excessively attentive, deferential, or servile toward a woman in the hope of gaining sexual access or romantic approval.
records.notes: Originally 1990s hip-hop slang ('sucker idolizing mediocre pussy'); revived by incel and manosphere communities c. 2018 and exploded mainstream via TikTok in 2019–2020; now broadly recognized across age groups.

records.definition: 'Involuntary celibate'; a man who attributes his inability to have sex to women's choices and society's structural unfairness rather than his own behavior, typically with expressed resentment or misogyny.
records.notes: Coined 1997 by a Canadian woman as a neutral self-description; hijacked by misogynistic online forums c. 2014; entered mainstream after violence attributed to incel ideology (2018 Toronto van attack); now functions simultaneously as self-identification, community label, and slur.

records.definition: 'Virgin' repurposed as a pejorative implying the target is naive, socially incompetent, or pitiful, with their sexual inexperience standing as evidence of broader social failure.
records.notes: The literal word predates internet culture by centuries; its use as a pure social insult (divorced from literal sexual status) peaked in meme culture c. 2016–2018, especially the 'Virgin vs. Chad' meme format; the insult relies on treating virginity as shameful rather than virtuous.

records.definition: In manosphere discourse, a man who is submissive, non-dominant, or romantically unattractive; the opposite of 'alpha'; used as an insult for perceived weakness, social passivity, or failure to attract women.
records.notes: Borrowed from debunked wolf-pack dominance research; foundational to incel, red-pill, and pick-up artist ideology; widely used mockingly by mainstream culture to satirize that same ideology.

records.definition: In manosphere discourse, a sexually dominant, confident, high-status man who attracts women without visible effort; valorized within the subculture but widely mocked outside it as a self-flattering fantasy.
records.notes: Used sincerely in pick-up artist and red-pill communities; used ironically by mainstream and feminist commentary; the term's double life (sincere/ironic) makes crude/register scores context-dependent; no single peak year because it remains actively in use.

records.definition: In manosphere discourse, the lowest-status male, below even the 'beta'; considered sexually invisible, socially irrelevant, and without realistic hope of female attention.
records.notes: Less widely recognized than 'alpha' or 'beta'; primarily circulates within incel and red-pill communities; the Greek-letter hierarchy (alpha > beta > delta > gamma > omega) has multiple variants across different manosphere factions.

records.definition: A man so controlled or dominated by his romantic or sexual partner that he abandons his own preferences, friendships, or dignity to please her.
records.notes: Shortening of 'pussy-whipped'; the crude origin is largely forgotten in everyday use; mild enough to appear in mainstream TV and film; widely understood across age groups and genders.

records.definition: A man nagged, dominated, and controlled by his wife; a mid-20th-century domestic term evoking a hen (female chicken) pecking a subordinate rooster.
records.notes: Largely displaced by 'whipped' in contemporary usage; survives in passive recognition and period fiction; the agricultural metaphor dates to at least the 17th century; peak recognition predates living memory so peak_year is set null.

records.definition: A man so driven by desire for his partner's sexual approval that he submits entirely to her will; the vulgar root form of 'whipped,' making the genital reference explicit.
records.notes: 'Pussy' refers to female genitalia; the metaphor implies sexual desire as a leash; considered significantly cruder than plain 'whipped' due to the explicit anatomical reference; still in active use despite the softer 'whipped' being more socially acceptable.

records.definition: Having been stripped of male power, authority, or sexuality; rendered weak, ineffectual, or feminized, either literally (castration) or—far more commonly—figuratively.
records.notes: Distinctly more formal/literary than other terms in this section; common in political commentary, psychology, and sociology; the literal meaning (surgical castration) is almost never invoked; the figurative use dominates entirely in modern English.

records.definition: An attractive but unintelligent man; the male counterpart to 'bimbo,' often used affectionately for a good-natured, sexually appealing man without intellectual depth.
records.notes: Blend of 'him' + 'bimbo'; unlike 'bimbo,' which is frequently cruel and derogatory, 'himbo' is often celebratory or affectionate, especially in queer and feminist online spaces; peaked in mainstream visibility c. 2019–2021 as a cultural archetype.

records.definition: A compound insult attacking a woman's intelligence and sexual morality simultaneously; 'dumb' functions as an amplifier for 'slut,' framing the target as both promiscuous and too stupid to recognize her own degradation.
records.notes: 'Slut' carries most of the semantic weight; 'dumb' intensifies by adding contempt for the target's cognition; the pairing is common enough to function as a stock phrase rather than a novel coinage; directed almost exclusively at women.

records.definition: Compound insult attacking both intelligence and sexual character; 'whore' functions as a general pejorative amplifier rather than a literal accusation of sex work.
records.notes: 'Whore' here operates as a general intensifier; the compound is a generic all-purpose put-down, not specifically targeted at sex workers.

records.definition: The practice of stigmatizing a person, typically a woman, for real or perceived sexual promiscuity or nonconformity to sexual norms.
records.notes: Entered mainstream discourse ~2011; used both descriptively in academic/activist contexts and colloquially; 'slut' retains crude charge even in compound.

records.definition: Clipped form of 'pervert'; a person perceived as having deviant, intrusive, or unwanted sexual interests or behavior.
records.notes: Can be deployed humorously between friends or seriously as an accusation; context determines severity.

records.definition: Person who provokes discomfort through socially violating behavior; in sexual contexts, specifically one who pursues or fixates on others in unwanted ways.
records.notes: Not exclusively sexual — any boundary-violating behavior qualifies — but sexual harassment is the dominant modern use case.

records.definition: Older man regarded as lecherous, especially one who makes inappropriate sexual advances toward younger people.
records.notes: 'Dirty' carries a moral/sexual connotation, not hygienic; often abbreviated 'DOM' in online contexts.

records.definition: Variant spelling of 'lech'; a person, typically an older man, who behaves in a lecherous or lasciviously opportunistic way toward others.
records.notes: 'Lech' is more standard spelling; both derive from 'lecherous.' Slightly more common in British usage.

records.definition: Person considered strange or socially aberrant; in sexual contexts implies deviant or unsolicited sexual fixation.
records.notes: Sexual coding is contextual and secondary; the word primarily signals general social aberrance and acquires sexual meaning from context.

records.definition: Person who persistently and unwantedly harasses others sexually; a chronic sexual nuisance.
records.notes: Predominantly British; a tabloid staple in the UK. American speakers generally understand it but would not naturally produce it.

records.definition: Person who gropes — touches the body sexually — without the other person's consent.
records.notes: Usage increased substantially during and after #MeToo (2017–2018); more specific than 'harasser' in naming a physical act.

records.definition: Person who exposes their genitals in public to unwilling strangers for gratification.
records.notes: Derived from 'to flash'; the clinical equivalent is 'exhibitionist.' The act is a criminal offense in most jurisdictions.

records.definition: Adjective for someone or something that provokes sexual or moral disgust and a desire to recoil.
records.notes: Possibly from Italian 'schifo' (disgust) via Italian-American dialect; primarily American slang. Overlaps with 'sleazy' and 'creepy.'

records.definition: General insult for a despicable, contemptible person; originally referred to a used condom.
records.notes: Etymology (used condom) is unknown to most current speakers; now functions as a generic pejorative with the original sexual meaning entirely bleached out.

records.definition: Person regarded as morally squalid, sexually disreputable, or persistently lecherous.
records.notes: Intensified form of 'sleaze'; '-bag' suffix adds contempt. Interchangeable with 'sleazeball' in most contexts.

records.definition: Person of low moral or sexual character, especially one who pursues others in a predatory or disreputable way; also refers to the quality of such behavior or environments.
records.notes: Functions as noun (the person), mass noun (the quality), and adjective root ('sleazy'); versatile across registers.

records.definition: Person, typically male, who is persistently and single-mindedly focused on sexual gratification to an annoying or disreputable degree.
records.notes: From 'horny' + 'dog'; can be used as playful teasing or as a genuine accusation; predominantly American.

records.definition: Clinical term for compulsive or excessive sexual desire in women; widely repurposed as a pejorative to stigmatize sexually active women.
records.notes: No longer a recognized DSM diagnosis; superseded by 'hypersexual disorder.' Survives mainly as insult and pornographic category label; applied exclusively to women, which itself encodes a gendered double standard.

records.definition: Older woman, typically 40+, who pursues sexual or romantic relationships with significantly younger men.
records.notes: Peaked in mainstream use ~2009–2012, amplified by the TV series 'Cougar Town'; connotation ranges from admiring to condescending depending on speaker and context.

records.definition: Acronym for 'mother I'd like to fuck'; objectifying label for an attractive woman who is a mother, regardless of her consent to the categorization.
records.notes: Popularized by the 1999 film 'American Pie'; now also a major pornographic genre category. Recognition has remained high rather than declining, so peak_year left null.

records.definition: Acronym for 'dad I'd like to fuck'; objectifying label for an attractive father, derived by analogy from MILF.
records.notes: Coined later than MILF and never achieved the same cultural saturation; more common among younger speakers and LGBTQ+ communities.

records.definition: Older person who pursues or dates someone significantly younger, with the implication of predatory or inappropriate intent.
records.notes: British equivalent is 'cradle snatcher.' The robbery metaphor frames the younger party as passive victim; applies to any gender.

records.definition: Older, typically wealthy man who provides money, gifts, or lifestyle support to a younger partner in exchange for companionship or sexual access.
records.notes: Not always pejorative; both parties may embrace the label. The term carries implications of transactional sex without formally naming it as such.

records.definition: Person financially maintained by a romantic or sexual partner, typically in exchange for sexual availability or companionship.
records.notes: Slightly dated formulation; 'kept woman' has older historical use as a near-synonym for mistress. Euphemistic in tone — the sexual transaction is implied rather than stated.

records.definition: Person who engages in sexual acts in exchange for payment.
records.notes: Remains the standard legal and clinical term but is increasingly considered stigmatizing by sex worker advocacy groups, who prefer 'sex worker.' From Latin 'prostituere' (to expose publicly).

records.definition: The practice or trade of engaging in sexual activity in exchange for payment.
records.notes: Dominant term in law, policy, and journalism; advocacy discourse increasingly favors 'sex work' or 'sex trade' to reduce stigma and shift framing toward labor rights.

records.definition: Crude slang for a prostitute or sex worker.
records.notes: Etymology disputed: commonly attributed to Corlear's Hook in Manhattan or to the verb 'to hook' (snag clients); neither is definitively proven. More derogatory in tone than 'prostitute' but far less clinical.

records.definition: A crude pejorative for a female prostitute; also used as a general insult implying sexual promiscuity.
records.notes: Dual use as occupational descriptor and sexual slur makes it heavily stigmatizing; one of the oldest recorded sex-work terms in English.

records.definition: A euphemism for a sex worker, framing the service as paid companionship to provide legal and social cover.
records.notes: Preferred in advertising and classified listings; plausible deniability makes prosecution harder in many jurisdictions.

records.definition: A female sex worker who arranges appointments by telephone, typically operating at a higher price tier than street-based workers.
records.notes: The 'call' referred to telephone contact; predates mobile phones and now sounds dated; class connotations imply higher-end indoor work.

records.definition: A sex worker who solicits clients on public streets rather than through agencies or indoor venues.
records.notes: Implies lower-tier, higher-risk sex work; strong class connotations compared to 'escort' or 'call girl'.

records.definition: The practice of soliciting clients for sex work in public spaces, particularly on streets.
records.notes: Gerund/activity noun form of 'streetwalker'; appears in legal and policy contexts as well as colloquial usage.

records.definition: North American slang for a male client who pays for sex work services.
records.notes: The generic placeholder name implies client anonymity and interchangeability; primarily US usage; known but less natural in British English.

records.definition: A sex work client; also used as a verb meaning to perform a single sex work transaction.
records.notes: Polysemous: 'he was a trick' (client) vs. 'she turned tricks' (performed sex work); meaning is context-dependent.

records.definition: To complete a single sex work transaction in exchange for payment.
records.notes: Phrasal idiom emphasizing the discrete transactional unit; widely recognized from film and TV depictions of sex work even among those with no direct experience.

records.definition: The neutral clinical term for a person who purchases sex work services.
records.notes: Preferred in public health, harm reduction, and policy advocacy; deliberately avoids moral framing; shares its primary non-sex-work meaning (business client), which also aids plausible deniability.

records.definition: British slang for a sex work client.
records.notes: In general British slang 'punter' means any customer or gambler; the sex-work sense is context-dependent; low recognition outside the UK and Ireland.

records.definition: A person who manages sex workers and takes a share of their earnings, typically through control and sometimes coercion.
records.notes: Also adopted as slang for 'to customize or improve' (pimp my ride), which diluted but did not erase the criminal connotation; pervasive in hip-hop culture.

records.definition: The practice of managing and profiting from sex workers, often through control, exploitation, or coercion.
records.notes: Legal term in many jurisdictions ('pimping and pandering'); early-2000s pop-culture peak (Pimp My Ride, 2003) temporarily softened public perception before criminal framing reasserted.

records.definition: A woman who owns or manages a brothel, overseeing its sex workers and business operations.
records.notes: Strongly gender-coded feminine; implies authority and business acumen; common in period fiction and historical accounts; still widely understood but sounds dated.

records.definition: More broadly, any person who manages sex workers and coordinates bookings, not necessarily tied to a fixed premises.
records.notes: Extended sense beyond brothel management; feminine gender framing persists even in broader usage; the two 'madam' entries are near-synonymous with differing scope.

records.definition: A person who obtains sex workers or sexual partners for others, often in an exploitative or criminal capacity.
records.notes: Primarily legal and criminological register; 'procuring' is the formal charge in many jurisdictions for what 'pimping' describes colloquially; low recognition outside legal and academic contexts.

records.definition: An establishment where customers pay to have sex with sex workers on the premises.
records.notes: Standard term across legal, journalistic, and historical contexts; not fully clinical but not maximally crude; understood globally.

records.definition: A brothel, especially one presented with a sense of exoticism, luxury, or historical distance; an Italian loanword.
records.notes: Italian origin lends aesthetic distance; favored in fiction, travel writing, and historical narrative; softer connotation than 'brothel' or 'whorehouse'.

records.definition: A crude, blunt compound term for a brothel.
records.notes: Compound of 'whore' + 'house'; maximally direct; common in American regional speech and period westerns; imports the full stigma of its 'whore' component.

records.definition: Dated American slang for a brothel.
records.notes: 'Cat' as slang for a woman or sex worker is now largely obsolete; term is mostly encountered in mid-20th-century American fiction and film; low current recognition especially outside the US.

records.definition: A business nominally offering massage services that operates wholly or in part as a front for sex work.
records.notes: Euphemistic framing allows grey-area legal operation; legitimate massage therapists face significant stigma from the association; widespread in North America and Southeast Asia.

records.definition: A euphemism for manual sexual stimulation to orgasm offered at the conclusion of a massage, typically for an additional fee.
records.notes: Culturally pervasive enough to function as a comedy trope; the euphemism successfully displaces crudeness, keeping the crude score moderate despite describing an explicit act.

records.definition: An urban neighborhood known for the concentration of sex work, strip clubs, adult entertainment venues, and related businesses.
records.notes: Term derives from red lanterns historically used to mark brothels; now a global concept adopted across many languages; applies to both legal and illegal sex work zones.

records.definition: The act of offering sexual services for payment in a public place; a criminal charge in many jurisdictions.
records.notes: 'Solicitation' is the formal charge form; the word also applies to non-sexual contexts (fundraising, sales), making the sex-work sense context-dependent.

records.definition: The recruitment, transportation, or harboring of persons through force, fraud, or coercion for the purpose of sexual exploitation.
records.notes: Serious human-rights and criminal-law term; explicitly distinct from consensual sex work; high recognition driven by sustained media coverage, NGO campaigns, and law enforcement publicity since the early 2000s.

records.definition: A person held against their will and forced to perform sexual acts, typically for the financial benefit of captors or traffickers.
records.notes: Used in serious human-rights, journalistic, and legal contexts; also claimed as a consensual identity within BDSM communities, creating semantic tension between coercion and roleplay contexts.

records.definition: Travel to another location, often internationally, primarily to engage with sex workers, typically exploiting economic disparities between the traveler's and destination country.
The umbrella term for exchanging sexual services, performances, or content for money or goods; preferred in advocacy, academic, and clinical contexts over 'prostitution'.
records.notes: Deliberately de-stigmatizing framing; implies labor-rights perspective on the practice.

records.definition: A younger person who receives money, gifts, or lifestyle benefits from a wealthier older partner in exchange for companionship and typically sexual access.
records.notes: Gendered usage skews female but applies to any gender; the 'baby' framing softens the transactional element.

records.definition: An arrangement in which a wealthier older partner provides financial support or gifts to a younger partner in exchange for companionship and typically sexual access, framed as a dating rather than commercial transaction.
records.notes: The 'dating' framing is central to how participants distance it from sex work; platforms like Seeking Arrangement popularized the term post-2010.

records.definition: A woman financially maintained by a man, typically outside of marriage, in exchange for sexual availability and exclusive companionship.
records.notes: Term declined with second-wave feminism; 'sugar baby' is the functional modern successor. Implies a degree of social shame not present in newer terminology.

records.definition: A woman who has an ongoing sexual relationship with a married man outside of his marriage, often with financial or social dependency.
records.notes: No male equivalent carries comparable connotations; historically implies kept status alongside the affair. The word's primary historical meaning (woman in authority) has been largely displaced by the sexual sense.

records.definition: A woman who cohabits with a man and is sexually available to him but holds lower legal and social status than a wife; historically common in polygynous societies across many cultures.
records.notes: Primarily used in historical, biblical, or anthropological contexts in modern English; retains literary/archaic quality; concept spans many cultures (Chinese, Roman, Islamic, biblical).

records.definition: A high-status woman who provided sexual and social companionship to wealthy or powerful men in exchange for money, gifts, and patronage, often wielding significant social influence herself.
records.notes: Carries romantic or literary connotations that flatly distinguish it from 'prostitute'; extensively used in historical fiction. From Old French 'courtisan', originally meaning a court attendant.

records.definition: A woman of the 19th-century demimonde: the Parisian fringe of kept women, courtesans, and women of ambiguous social respectability living on patronage rather than marriage.
records.notes: French loanword; near-extinct in modern English. 'Demimonde' (the collective social stratum) has slightly wider recognition. The concept is highly specific to 19th-century French bourgeois social structure.

records.definition: In English usage, typically an exotic shorthand for a high-class Japanese female companion or sex worker; in reality, a geisha is a traditional Japanese entertainer trained in music, dance, and conversation whose role is not inherently sexual.
records.notes: Canonical example of cross-cultural misconception: the actual geisha role (skilled traditional artist) has no English equivalent, but English speakers apply the word with courtesan-level sexual connotation. The misconception was amplified by Western wartime occupation and media like 'Memoirs of a Geisha'.

records.definition: A sanitizing euphemism for women, primarily Korean and Chinese, who were forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II.
records.notes: English translation of the Japanese euphemism 'ianfu' (慰安婦); the term itself is part of the historical cover-up. Reality was systematic abduction, rape, and enslavement. Ongoing diplomatic flashpoint between Japan and South Korea.

records.definition: A woman who performs sexual or erotic acts live on webcam in exchange for payment, tips, or subscriptions.
records.notes: Emerged with widespread broadband adoption circa 2000–2005; became mainstream term by 2010s.

records.definition: A man who performs sexual or erotic acts live on webcam in exchange for payment, tips, or subscriptions.
records.notes: Far lower recognition than 'cam girl' reflecting the market asymmetry; male camming grew significantly in the OnlyFans era.

records.definition: A subscription-based content platform widely used for explicit sexual content; in common usage, a generic shorthand for online sex work or explicit content creation.
records.notes: Proper noun used as a common noun and sometimes verb ('she has an OnlyFans'); recognition spiked during COVID-19 lockdowns (2020–2021) when many people turned to it for income. Platform hosts non-sexual content too but sexual connotation dominates popular usage.

records.definition: A secondary pseudonymous Instagram account, hidden from one's main social network; sometimes used by sex workers or explicit content creators to advertise or post without exposure to family, employers, or main followers.
records.notes: Portmanteau of 'fake' + 'Instagram'; primary use is private sharing among close friends, not exclusively sex work. Declining as Instagram itself cedes ground to TikTok.

records.definition: In sex-work contexts, a neutral or euphemistic self-descriptor for a person who produces and sells explicit sexual content online, typically via subscription platforms.
records.notes: Identical term is also used for non-sexual YouTubers, bloggers, etc.; context disambiguates. Adopted by sex workers as a stigma-reducing alternative to 'pornographer' or 'sex worker'.

records.definition: The sending of sexually explicit messages, photographs, or video via mobile phone or digital messaging.
records.notes: Portmanteau of 'sex' + 'texting'; coined circa 2005, mainstream by 2009. Remains fully current. Legal liability around minors sexting drove significant policy attention 2009–2015.

records.definition: A photograph of a person without clothing, typically in a sexual or erotic context (noun form, colloquial).
records.notes: Noun usage ('send me a nude') is colloquially distinct from the adjective ('nude model') and the art-historical sense ('a classical nude'); the sexual noun connotation is dominant in everyday digital-era speech.

records.definition: Nude photographs of a sexual or erotic nature; the standard colloquial plural noun for such images.
records.notes: 'Send nudes' became a prominent internet meme phrase circa 2015–2016, cementing the plural as the primary colloquial form. Also appeared in the context of non-consensual image sharing ('revenge porn').

records.definition: Printed, visual, or digital material depicting sexual acts or nudity intended primarily to cause sexual arousal.
records.notes: From Greek 'pornographos' (writing about prostitutes). The standard legal and regulatory term; crude score reflects subject matter rather than the word's clinical register.

records.definition: Colloquial abbreviation of 'pornography'; sexually explicit material.
records.notes: So dominant in casual usage that 'pornography' now sounds formal or legalistic by contrast. Also used productively in compound slang (food porn, architecture porn) to indicate intensely gratifying imagery.

records.definition: Of, relating to, or constituting pornography; sexually explicit in a manner intended to arouse.
records.notes: Adjectival form; frequent in legal, regulatory, and journalistic language ('pornographic material', 'pornographic content'). The Latinate suffix lends clinical distance despite the subject.

records.definition: Pornographic or obscene material, especially writing or imagery; implies contempt, moral disapproval, or a sense of dirtiness.
records.notes: Carries a moralizing or dismissive tone not present in 'pornography'; favored by critics of explicit content and in conservative discourse. Also used affectionately within fan-fiction communities for explicit fan content.

records.definition: Literary or artistic material designed to cause sexual arousal, typically distinguished from pornography by aesthetic or artistic framing.
records.notes: The erotica/pornography distinction is socially constructed and contested; 'erotica' typically implies higher-brow, literary, or female-oriented framing. The distinction is often described as 'erotica is what I like; pornography is what you like.'

records.definition: Sexually explicit or pornographic material framed as appropriate only for adults; the standard neutral euphemism in platform policy, content moderation, and regulatory language.
records.notes: Deliberately vague; preferred by platforms and payment processors seeking policy-neutral language that avoids triggering legal classification. 'Adult content' also technically covers non-pornographic age-restricted material (gambling, alcohol), giving it additional euphemistic utility.

records.definition: A euphemistic umbrella term for the pornographic media and performance industry.
records.notes: Used in business, legal, and mainstream media contexts to sanitize references to the porn industry.

records.definition: Denoting sexually explicit content, derived from the MPAA film rating system's X classification.
records.notes: The MPAA replaced X with NC-17 in 1990, but X-rated persists colloquially to mean any sexually explicit material.

records.definition: An informal intensified marker of extremely explicit sexual content, tripling the X rating symbol.
records.notes: Triple-X has no official rating basis; used by the porn industry as a marketing intensifier and adopted broadly as shorthand for pornographic.

records.definition: A dated informal term for a pornographic film.
records.notes: Etymology of 'blue' meaning indecent is disputed; most current mid-20th century, now recognized but not actively used.

records.definition: A mild colloquial term for a sexually explicit or pornographic film.
records.notes: Less dated than 'blue movie' or 'stag film'; still in colloquial use, particularly in casual or ironic speech.

records.definition: A dated American slang term for a pornographic or sexually explicit film.
records.notes: Common in American English through the 1970s; rarely produced in speech today but still widely understood.

records.definition: A dated mild term for a film featuring nudity or soft-core sexual content.
records.notes: Often refers specifically to the 'nudie cutie' subgenre of early-1960s American soft-core films; softer connotation than 'stag film'.

records.definition: A coin-operated booth or pay-per-view venue where patrons view sexual performances or pornographic films through a small aperture or screen.
records.notes: Physical institutions declined sharply with internet pornography; the term remains widely understood and is also used figuratively.

records.definition: A dated term for early privately circulated pornographic films, originally screened at all-male 'stag' gatherings.
records.notes: Historically significant; stag films circulated underground from the 1920s through 1960s before commercial porn distribution existed.

records.definition: The scene in a pornographic film depicting visible external male ejaculation, regarded as the climactic and commercially required shot.
records.notes: Also used in mainstream film and advertising for any single high-value shot; the sexual and general meanings coexist with minimal collision.

records.definition: A crude pornographic term for a scene or image depicting external male ejaculation.
records.notes: Synonymous with 'money shot' but cruder and more explicit; used primarily within porn industry and consumer communities rather than mainstream press.

records.definition: A pornographic act and category term for ejaculation on a partner's face.
records.notes: Form-identical to the cosmetic treatment noun, producing genuine ambiguity in everyday speech; context almost always disambiguates.

records.definition: A pornographic category depicting internal ejaculation followed by visible display of semen from the vagina or anus.
records.notes: Euphemistic food-noun form obscures an explicitly sexual act; widely recognized among porn consumers, less so in general population.

records.definition: Sexual activity in which one person is penetrated or serviced by multiple partners in succession or simultaneously.
records.notes: Also written 'gangbang'; has historical overlap with violent connotation (mob attack) which the consensual pornographic genre meaning has largely displaced in contemporary use.

records.definition: Simultaneous penetration of two orifices of one person by two partners, a common pornographic category.
records.notes: Semi-clinical phrasing despite explicit content; abbreviated DP in industry and consumer usage.

records.definition: Acronym for bondage, discipline, dominance, submission, sadism, and masochism; an umbrella term for consensual power-exchange and pain-play sexual practices.
records.notes: Mainstream recognition spiked after '50 Shades of Grey' (2011); the acronym is a deliberate community coinage from 1990s internet newsgroups.

records.definition: Slang for conventional, non-kinky sexual activity, used within BDSM and kink communities to describe mainstream sex.
records.notes: Originally BDSM subculture jargon; now broadly understood outside the community, often used self-deprecatingly or with irony.

records.definition: A style of pornographic production shot from a first-person or handheld perspective without a narrative script, emphasizing rawness and viewer immersion.
records.notes: Term borrowed from gonzo journalism (Hunter S. Thompson); style pioneered in the 1990s by directors like John 'Buttman' Stagliano; now the dominant mode of online amateur and professional porn.

records.definition: Pornographic content produced by non-professional individuals, often self-filmed and self-distributed via online platforms.
records.notes: Category lines blurred when studios began producing faux-amateur content; user-generated platforms (OnlyFans, PornHub) further complicated the distinction between amateur and professional.

records.definition: The practice of performing sexual acts or striptease live via webcam in exchange for payment or virtual tips.
records.notes: Grew rapidly with platforms like Chaturbate and OnlyFans; COVID-19 lockdowns (2020) caused a notable surge in both supply and mainstream awareness.

records.definition: The act of performing an erotic dance involving the progressive removal of clothing for an audience, typically for payment.
records.notes: The sexual sense dominates in American English; the word also has non-sexual senses (stripping wire, paint) that rarely cause confusion in context.

records.definition: A person who performs striptease dances for an audience, typically in a club setting, in exchange for payment.
records.notes: The dominant colloquial term; considered blunt but not especially vulgar; some workers prefer it to the euphemism 'exotic dancer' as more direct.

records.definition: An erotic dance performed by a stripper directly on or facing a seated client's lap, often involving simulated sexual contact.
records.notes: Became widespread in American strip clubs in the late 1980s and early 1990s; now a near-universal feature of the industry across Western markets.

records.definition: British slang for a striptease performer or stripper.
records.notes: Common in British English through the 1970s–80s; largely displaced by 'stripper'. Polysemous: 'peeler' also means police officer in Irish/British slang (from Sir Robert Peel), causing occasional ambiguity.

records.definition: A euphemistic occupational title for a striptease dancer, preferred in legal, licensing, and formal employment contexts.
records.notes: Used in business registration, liquor licenses, and journalism; workers themselves are divided on whether they prefer it or find it evasive about the nature of the work.

records.definition: A sheath-shaped barrier contraceptive worn on the penis during sex to prevent pregnancy and reduce STI transmission.
records.notes: Standard clinical and everyday term; appears in sex-ed curricula globally; low crude score despite being fully sexual because it is the neutral default.

records.definition: Informal North American term for a condom, derived from the material historically used in manufacture.
records.notes: In British English 'rubber' primarily means eraser; the condom sense is predominantly North American and can cause transatlantic confusion.

records.definition: AAVE slang for a condom, widely circulated through hip-hop culture in the 1990s–2000s.
records.notes: Recognition is high within US urban and hip-hop communities; noticeably lower outside that register and globally; peak tied to late-90s hip-hop saturation.

records.definition: Playful euphemism for a condom, likening it to waterproof outerwear that keeps things dry.
records.notes: Transparent metaphor; mostly appears in humor or mild innuendo rather than functional conversation; less common than 'rubber' or 'condom'.

records.definition: Euphemism for a condom, best known from the safe-sex slogan 'no glove, no love.'
records.notes: Mostly encountered embedded in slogans rather than standalone natural speech; the rhyming phrase dramatically boosted recognition.

records.definition: British slang for a condom.
records.notes: Predominantly British English; largely displaced by 'condom' in everyday usage but still widely understood in the UK among over-40s.

records.definition: Clinical or formal term for a condom or any disease-preventing contraceptive device.
records.notes: Semantically broader than 'condom' (any preventive measure), but in sexual contexts almost always means condom; formal register sounds dated in everyday speech now.

records.definition: Any device, drug, or method used to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: Umbrella clinical term covering all methods; sexually relevant but low charge; functions as both noun and adjective.

records.definition: Colloquial term for a daily oral hormonal contraceptive taken to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: The definite article 'the' is semantically load-bearing — it marks this pill as the culturally dominant one requiring no further specification; so ubiquitous it needs no disambiguation.

records.definition: The practice or methods of preventing unwanted pregnancy; used interchangeably with 'contraception' in everyday speech.
records.notes: Term popularized by Margaret Sanger in the early 20th century; dominant everyday phrase in American English; slightly less clinical-feeling than 'contraception'.

records.definition: Colloquial name for emergency contraceptive pills taken after unprotected sex to reduce the risk of pregnancy.
records.notes: The name implies next-morning use but it is effective up to 72–120 hours; the slight inaccuracy is baked into the common name and resists correction.

records.definition: US brand name for a levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive, widely used generically to refer to any morning-after pill.
records.notes: Classic brand-as-generic shift; primarily US; the double meaning with 'plan B' (backup plan) adds an involuntary euphemistic layer that eased mainstream acceptance of the term.

records.definition: Intrauterine device: a small T-shaped contraceptive device implanted in the uterus by a clinician to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: Clinical abbreviation that has entered everyday speech; many users say 'IUD' without knowing the expansion; recognition has grown significantly with increased media coverage since ~2010.

records.definition: The withdrawal method of contraception, in which the penis is removed from the vagina before ejaculation.
records.notes: Vernacular phrase that avoids clinical language while remaining fully explicit; common in casual discussion of contraceptive risk and failure rates.

records.definition: Having sex without a condom, emphasizing unmediated physical contact.
records.notes: Carries connotations of deliberate risk-taking or heightened intensity; more charged than 'bareback' in straight contexts; prevalent in hip-hop, urban slang, and internet usage.

records.definition: Engaging in anal (or vaginal) sex without a condom; originated in gay male usage during the AIDS era, now broader.
records.notes: Borrowed from equestrian terminology ('riding bareback'); entered sexual vocabulary through the gay community as HIV risk language; now used across orientations but retains strongest association with MSM sex.

records.definition: Sexually transmitted disease: any infection or illness passed primarily through sexual contact.
records.notes: Being phased out in clinical settings in favor of 'STI' to reduce stigma, but still dominant in lay speech; the two terms are functionally interchangeable in most conversations.

records.definition: Sexually transmitted infection: the current preferred clinical term for infections passed through sexual contact.
records.notes: Preferred over 'STD' in medical and public-health contexts since ~2000 because not all infections develop into diagnosable diseases; still less widely recognized than STD among lay audiences.

records.definition: Slang for gonorrhea.
records.notes: Etymology disputed; possibly from Old French 'clapoir' (brothel sore); attested in English since the 16th century; still widely understood though usage has declined relative to clinical terms.

records.definition: Venereal disease: a dated abbreviation for sexually transmitted diseases, dominant in medical and public discourse from the 1940s through the 1970s.
records.notes: 'Venereal' derives from Venus; the term carries faint moral stigma that STD/STI framing deliberately moved away from; still recognized but rarely used by adults under 40.

records.definition: A fictitious sexually transmitted disease — purportedly causing the vulva to turn blue and become severely infected — invented as an internet shock hoax circa 2008–2010.
records.notes: No medical basis whatsoever; originated on shock-image forums; spread via chain messages and gross-out culture; notoriously referenced in a 2013 New Jersey legislative hearing after a state assemblywoman was misled by constituents, demonstrating the real-world reach of internet sex hoaxes.

records.definition: Acronym for bondage and discipline, dominance and submission, sadism and masochism; umbrella term for consensual power-exchange and pain-play sexual practices.
records.notes: Entered mainstream vocabulary substantially after 'Fifty Shades of Grey' (2011–2012); carries subculture-specific consent ethics (SSC — safe, sane, consensual; and RACK — risk-aware consensual kink).

records.definition: The practice of physically restraining a partner with rope, cuffs, or other materials for sexual arousal or power-exchange purposes.
records.notes: Non-sexual meaning (servitude, captivity) predates and coexists with the sexual meaning; context almost always disambiguates; represents the first B in BDSM.

records.definition: In BDSM contexts, punishment-based sexual practice — typically spanking, impact play, or structured correction — used as a dynamic of behavioral control between consenting partners.
records.notes: Heavily polysemous; the sexual sense is only reliably activated in BDSM framing; represents the D in BD (bondage and discipline) within the BDSM acronym.

records.definition: The role of holding authority, control, or power in a BDSM dynamic; the active counterpart to submission.
records.notes: Highly polysemous; sexual meaning is context-dependent; represents the first D in DS (dominance and submission) within the BDSM acronym; often shortened to 'dom' in subculture usage.

records.definition: The act or role of yielding power, control, or autonomy to a dominant partner within a BDSM dynamic.
records.notes: Non-sexual senses (political, social, religious) are far more common; sexual sense is widely understood in BDSM contexts.

records.definition: Sexual gratification derived from inflicting pain, humiliation, or suffering on another person.
records.notes: Named after the Marquis de Sade; has a secondary non-sexual sense (enjoyment of cruelty generally) that is also widely used.

records.definition: Sexual gratification derived from experiencing pain, humiliation, or subjugation.
records.notes: Named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch; also used metaphorically in lay speech for self-destructive or self-defeating behavior.

records.definition: A sexual practice or orientation combining both sadistic and masochistic elements, commonly abbreviated S&M.
records.notes: Often used interchangeably with BDSM in lay speech, though BDSM is the broader umbrella term encompassing bondage, discipline, dominance, and submission as well.

records.definition: Sexual arousal triggered by a specific object, body part, or material not typically considered inherently sexual.
records.notes: The lay form 'fetish' is far more commonly used; the -ism nominalization is primarily clinical or academic. Also has unrelated anthropological/religious senses.

records.definition: A clinical term for any intense or persistent sexual interest in atypical objects, situations, or individuals.
records.notes: DSM-5 distinguishes a paraphilia (unusual interest) from a paraphilic disorder (interest causing distress or harm); recognition is largely limited to psychology students and clinicians.

records.definition: Sexual arousal derived from secretly watching others undress or engage in sexual activity without their knowledge or consent.
records.notes: Loanword from French; widely recognized via cultural references. DSM-5 diagnostic label is voyeuristic disorder. Lay synonym is 'peeping tom.'

records.definition: Sexual arousal from exposing one's genitals to an unsuspecting or non-consenting person.
records.notes: Has a widely-used non-sexual sense (attention-seeking behavior) which may inflate recognition estimates; lay sexual synonym is 'flashing.'

records.definition: Sexual arousal derived from rubbing against or touching a non-consenting person, typically in a crowded space.
records.notes: From French 'frotter' (to rub); used almost exclusively in clinical and forensic psychiatric contexts; lay speakers would say 'groping' or 'grinding.'

records.definition: The practice of wearing clothing associated with the opposite sex, particularly when used as a source of sexual arousal.
records.notes: Now considered dated and potentially pejorative; largely replaced by 'cross-dressing' in contemporary clinical and lay usage. Not synonymous with transgender identity. Peak use was DSM-III era (1980s–1990s).

records.definition: The practice of wearing clothing conventionally associated with a gender other than one's own, for any reason including performance, gender expression, or sexual arousal.
records.notes: Preferred neutral term over 'transvestism'; not inherently sexual and explicitly not synonymous with being transgender or nonbinary.

records.definition: The deliberate restriction of oxygen to the brain during sexual activity to heighten arousal or intensify orgasm.
records.notes: Associated with accidental deaths, including high-profile celebrity cases that boosted public recognition. BDSM community preferred term is 'breath play'; 'autoerotic asphyxiation' refers to the solo variant.

records.definition: A paraphilia characterized by sexual arousal from oxygen deprivation, choking, or suffocation.
records.notes: Used almost exclusively in clinical and forensic literature; lay speakers use 'erotic asphyxiation' or 'breath play.' Coined in academic sexology and rarely appears outside it.

records.definition: Sexual arousal or gratification associated with feces or defecation.
records.notes: Colloquially called 'scat' in sexual contexts; the clinical term is rarely encountered outside sexology literature. High crude score reflects the strong disgust response the subject matter elicits even in clinical framing.

records.definition: Sexual arousal or gratification associated with urine or urination.
records.notes: Colloquially called 'water sports' or 'golden shower'; the clinical term is rarely used outside sexology. The 2017 Steele dossier briefly elevated public awareness of the practice.

records.definition: A clinical variant term for sexual arousal from urine or the act of urination, used interchangeably with urophilia.
records.notes: Less common clinical synonym for urophilia; the '-lagnia' suffix (from Greek for lust/coitus) recurs across several paraphilia names (e.g., osmolagnia, dacrylagnia).

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual contact with corpses.
records.notes: Illegal in most jurisdictions; recognition is relatively high due to frequent references in crime fiction, horror media, and true-crime coverage. High crude score despite clinical register because the subject matter is near-universally perceived as deeply transgressive.

records.definition: A clinical term for primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children.
records.notes: British English spelling is 'paedophilia.' High recognition due to saturation in news media and public discourse. High crude score reflects extreme moral condemnation; the word is often used as an accusation rather than a clinical descriptor in lay usage.

records.definition: A clinical term for primary or preferential sexual attraction to mid-to-late adolescents, typically defined as ages 15–19.
records.notes: Distinct from pedophilia (prepubescent) and hebephilia (early pubescent); the term is sometimes deployed online to minimise or rationalise attraction to minors, which has given it a secondary polemical valence.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual contact with animals.
records.notes: 'Zoophilia' foregrounds psychological attraction; 'bestiality' foregrounds the act. Illegal in most jurisdictions. The community-preferred self-identifier is 'zoo.'

records.definition: Sexual or romantic attraction to inanimate objects, often including emotional attachment or a sense of relationship with the object.
records.notes: Distinct from fetishism in that objectophiles typically describe deep emotional bonds with a specific object; cases involving the Eiffel Tower and the Berlin Wall received wide media coverage and boosted lay awareness.

records.definition: Sexual arousal from being on stage, being the center of public attention, or being photographed or filmed in a sexual context.
records.notes: Coined by sexologist John Money; almost exclusively confined to clinical sexology literature; one of the lowest-recognition terms in the paraphilia lexicon.

records.definition: Sexual arousal derived from receiving or administering enemas.
records.notes: From Greek 'klysma' (enema); used almost exclusively in clinical sexology; the lay term in kink communities is 'enema play.' Occasionally spelled 'klysmaphilia.'

records.definition: Sexual arousal from filth, dirt, or objects considered unclean or contaminated.
records.notes: From Greek 'mysos' (filth, pollution); broader than coprophilia or urophilia, covering any perceived uncleanliness; almost exclusively clinical usage.

records.definition: Sexual arousal from hair, typically human head hair, whether through touching, smelling, or viewing it.
records.notes: From Greek 'trichos' (hair); one of the more benign and relatively common paraphilias; lay speakers invariably say 'hair fetish.' Clinical term is rarely encountered outside sexology literature.

records.definition: A paraphilia characterized by sexual arousal from feet or footwear.
records.notes: Greek-derived clinical term; the lay phrase 'foot fetish' is far more widely recognized at ~70% vs ~25% for the clinical term.

records.definition: A paraphilia in which sexual arousal is derived from contact with or fantasy about amputees.
records.notes: Distinguished from apotemnophilia (desire to be an amputee); both terms are rare outside clinical sexology literature.

records.definition: A paraphilia in which a person is sexually aroused by the fantasy or reality of being an amputee themselves.
records.english_term: erotic desire to be an amputee
records.notes: Overlaps with body integrity identity disorder (BIID); the erotic component distinguishes it from the broader identity condition. No concise lay English term exists.

records.definition: A BDSM practice in which participants adopt personas of different ages, typically involving a caregiver and a younger role.
records.notes: Can be non-sexual (caregiver/little headspace as self-regulation) or explicitly sexual; the distinction is important to community members and legally significant.

records.definition: A paraphilia in which an adult derives sexual arousal from adopting the role, dress, or behavior of an infant or young child.
records.notes: Also called paraphilic infantilism; 'infantilism' has a separate non-sexual psychological meaning (developmental regression), which complicates recognition counts.

records.definition: A BDSM relationship structure in which one partner takes a nurturing dominant role ('Daddy') and the other takes a childlike submissive role ('girl' or 'little').
records.notes: The slash notation signals the paired roles as a unit; variants include Mommy/boy and gender-flipped versions. The 'girl' role is not age-specific in meaning.

records.definition: The dominant partner in a DD/lg BDSM dynamic, who exercises authority through nurturing, protection, and structure rather than strict discipline.
records.notes: Capitalization (Daddy Dom vs daddy dom) conventionally signals it as a formal role title. Abbreviated DD. Emotional caretaking distinguishes the style from harsher domination archetypes.

records.definition: The activity of a submissive partner entering and performing a childlike persona and behaviors within a DD/lg or ageplay BDSM context.
records.notes: Names the submissive's activity specifically rather than the overall dynamic; 'little space' is the associated headspace term. Less common than 'ageplay' even within the community.

records.definition: A genre of animated or illustrated erotica, originating in Japanese hentai, depicting sexual acts involving tentacled creatures.
records.notes: Iconographic roots in Hokusai's 'The Dream of the Fisherman's Wife' (c. 1814); became a global internet meme archetype. Legal in most jurisdictions as fictional content.

records.definition: Japanese animated or illustrated pornography; in English usage refers broadly to sexually explicit anime or manga.
records.notes: In Japanese, 変態 (hentai) means 'pervert' or 'perversion' generally; English speakers narrowed it to mean specifically explicit anime. Recognition boosted by internet meme culture in 2010s.

records.definition: A person with a strong interest in anthropomorphic animal characters, which may or may not include a sexual component.
records.notes: The sexual connotation is culturally prominent but not universal; Furscience surveys suggest roughly 25% of self-identified furries report sexual motivation as primary. Conflating all furries with sexual interest is considered reductive within the community.

records.definition: The organized community of people who share an interest in anthropomorphic animal characters, encompassing art, conventions, costumes, and social identity.
records.notes: Distinct from the individual identity term 'furry'; emphasizes the collective and social dimension. Major conventions (FurFest, Anthrocon) draw tens of thousands of attendees annually.

records.definition: Sexual or erotic play involving diapers, often practiced as a component of infantilism or the adult baby/diaper lover (ABDL) community.
records.notes: ABDL is the broader community umbrella term; 'diaper play' specifically names the activity rather than the identity. Not all ABDL participants combine diapers with sexual arousal.

records.definition: A person who takes the dominant role in BDSM activity, exercising control, authority, or discipline over a submissive partner.
records.notes: Clipped from 'dominant'; gender-neutral. Capitalization (Dom vs dom) sometimes signals a formal title within a committed power-exchange relationship.

records.definition: A woman who takes the dominant role in BDSM activity.
records.notes: Feminine form of 'dom' coined to distinguish from the gender-neutral default. 'Dominatrix' is a more mainstream synonym but carries a stronger professional/commercial connotation than the community term 'domme'.

records.definition: A person who takes the submissive role in BDSM activity, yielding control or power to a dominant partner.
records.notes: Clipped from 'submissive'; gender-neutral. Also used as adjective ('a sub headspace') and in compounds ('sub drop' — the emotional crash after a scene).

records.definition: A person in BDSM who comfortably takes both dominant and submissive roles, either across different relationships or within the same session.
records.notes: Everyday word repurposed to mean 'one who flips roles'; BDSM-specific sense of 'switch' is distinct from the gay male community's 'verse', though both denote role flexibility.

records.definition: The partner who takes the insertive or dominant role during sexual activity, particularly in gay male or BDSM contexts.
records.notes: Originated in gay male community to describe the penetrating role; adopted more broadly in BDSM and queer contexts to indicate control. High recognition due to mainstream cultural spillover.

records.definition: The partner who takes the receptive or submissive role during sexual activity, particularly in gay male or BDSM contexts.
records.notes: Complementary to 'top'; widely used in queer and kink communities. In mainstream culture sometimes used humorously or without sexual connotation; context disambiguates.

records.definition: Short for 'versatile'; a person who comfortably takes both top and bottom roles in sexual activity.
records.notes: Primarily gay male community terminology for sexual role flexibility; clipped from 'versatile'. Distinct from BDSM 'switch' in that it emphasizes physical role rather than dominance/submission orientation.

records.definition: The consensual, negotiated transfer of authority or control from a submissive to a dominant partner, considered the core dynamic of BDSM relationships.
records.notes: Framing as 'exchange' emphasizes mutuality and active consent of both parties; the term is used rhetorically to distinguish ethical BDSM from coercive control.

records.definition: A pre-agreed word or signal used during BDSM activity to immediately halt or slow the scene when a participant needs to stop.
records.notes: Has entered mainstream cultural awareness via film, TV, and comedy. The traffic-light system (red/yellow/green) is a common implementation. High recognition does not imply understanding of BDSM practice broadly.

records.definition: Acronym for 'safe, sane, and consensual,' the foundational BDSM ethics framework emphasizing risk avoidance and mutual informed consent.
records.notes: Coined by David Stein in 1983 for the Gay Male S/M Activists organization. Later critiqued by RACK proponents as too subjective — 'sane' and 'safe' are not objectively determinable. Still the most commonly cited entry-level ethical standard.

records.definition: Acronym for 'risk-aware consensual kink,' an alternative BDSM ethics framework that acknowledges inherent risk rather than demanding total safety.
records.notes: Developed in response to SSC's perceived naivety about safety; preferred in communities practicing high-risk activities such as edge play and breath control. Less known outside active BDSM communities than SSC.

records.definition: A discrete BDSM activity session with a defined start, end, and negotiated scope, conducted between consenting participants.
records.notes: Also used as a collective noun for the BDSM community broadly ('the scene'), analogous to how any subculture may refer to itself. Context disambiguates. 'Aftercare' is the recovery period following a scene.

records.definition: In BDSM contexts, any consensual kinky, sexual, or power-exchange activity between participants.
records.notes: Highly context-dependent; the word carries no inherent sexual meaning outside BDSM subculture, making it invisible to outsiders in conversation.

records.definition: A dedicated space equipped for BDSM activities, typically containing restraint furniture, impact implements, and other kink equipment.
records.notes: Borrowed from medieval architecture; the sexual meaning only activates in BDSM context. Public kink dungeons exist at many leather/kink events.

records.definition: A multi-tailed whip-like implement used in BDSM impact play to strike the body for sensation, discipline, or erotic stimulation.
records.notes: Derived from 'flog'; comes in many materials (leather, suede, rubber) producing different sensations; considered a gateway impact toy in BDSM.

records.definition: A short riding crop used in BDSM impact play to deliver sharp, stinging strokes, often associated with dominant/submissive and pony-play dynamics.
records.notes: Short for 'riding crop'; the equestrian origin is part of its dominant-aesthetic appeal; BDSM meaning is secondary but recognizable.

records.definition: A flat, rigid or semi-rigid implement used in BDSM to spank the buttocks, producing a broad thuddy impact.
records.notes: Shares referent with fraternity hazing and historical school corporal punishment; BDSM use is one of several common meanings, which inflates recognition_pct.

records.definition: In BDSM, a collar worn by a submissive partner as a symbol of ownership, commitment, or active D/s relationship status.
records.notes: 'Collaring' is a formal ceremony in some BDSM relationships, analogous to engagement or marriage; the object itself is unremarkable without context.

records.definition: A leash attached to a BDSM collar, used in pet play or control-based power exchange to guide, restrain, or display ownership of a submissive.
records.notes: Non-sexual meaning (dog leash) is dominant in general usage; the BDSM sense requires collar + power-exchange context to be understood.

records.definition: A BDSM roleplay style in which one or more participants embody an animal persona, often combined with D/s power dynamics and associated gear.
records.notes: Umbrella term encompassing puppy play, kitten play, pony play, and other animal personas; the erotic component varies — some participants find it non-sexual.

records.definition: A form of pet play in which a participant acts as a horse, often involving tack, bit gags, harnesses, tail plugs, and being ridden or driven by a handler.
records.notes: Has its own dedicated competitive community with formalized 'pony shows'; one of the more elaborate pet-play subgenres due to equestrian equipment aesthetics.

records.definition: A form of pet play in which a participant embodies a dog persona, typically wearing a hood, mitts, kneepads, and tail plug, and behaving as a dog.
records.notes: The most mainstream of the pet-play subgenres; has significant visibility in queer male communities and has received sympathetic mainstream media coverage.

records.definition: A form of pet play in which a participant embodies a cat persona, combined with D/s dynamics and accessories such as cat ears, collar, and tail.
records.notes: Particularly associated with female-presenting participants; has aesthetic crossover with cosplay and Tumblr/internet subculture, and sometimes with age play.

records.definition: In kink contexts, a man who derives erotic pleasure from his partner having sex with other men, typically with his knowledge and consent.
records.notes: Historically a term of shame for men with unfaithful wives (Shakespeare-era); modern kink usage reframes it as a consensual erotic identity with a humiliation or compersion component.

records.definition: Shortened form of cuckold used both as a kink self-identifier and as a political/social insult implying weakness, submission, or willingness to be humiliated.
records.notes: Achieved mainstream political currency circa 2015–2016 as an alt-right insult ('cuckservative'); this dual-register explosion makes recognition_pct unusually high for a kink-origin term.

records.definition: In cuckolding dynamics, the man who has sex with the cuckold's partner, typically selected for sexual dominance or physical prowess.
records.notes: Term implies virility analogous to a stud bull; the non-kink meaning (male bovine) dominates general use. Recognized only within cuckolding subculture.

records.definition: A married woman who, with her husband's knowledge and approval, has sex with other men as part of a consensual non-monogamy or cuckolding arrangement.
records.notes: Framing emphasizes the wife's desirability and agency rather than the husband's humiliation, distinguishing it from cuckold framing; has its own distinct community and porn genre.

records.definition: In consensual non-monogamy, a husband who proudly and without humiliation shares his wife (the 'vixen') with other men, explicitly contrasted with the shame-based cuckold dynamic.
records.notes: Part of the 'stag/vixen' paired terminology; the distinction from cuckold is ideological — compersion and pride rather than humiliation. Extremely low mainstream recognition.

records.definition: A BDSM practice in which a dominant partner controls when or whether the submissive is permitted to orgasm, used as an ongoing form of power exchange.
records.notes: Umbrella term covering denial, edging, and forced orgasm; the clinical compound-noun construction makes it sound more technical than its crude content warrants.

records.definition: A BDSM practice in which a dominant partner withholds orgasm from the submissive, either indefinitely or until explicit permission is granted, as an instrument of control.
records.notes: Closely related to edging (bringing to the brink without completion); longer-duration denial is frequently combined with chastity devices for physical enforcement.
