records.definition: Rioplatense slang for the anus or buttocks; literally 'bass drum'; primarily Argentine colloquial usage.

records.definition: Mild childlike euphemism for the buttocks; a gentle infantile-register term for the posterior frequently used with young children.

records.definition: Euphemistic slang for the clitoris, derived from 'little bell', evoking its pendant shape when the hood is retracted.

records.definition: The standard informal-to-neutral Spanish word for buttocks; used freely in everyday speech, sexual contexts, and public health materials.

records.definition: Mexican and Central American slang for the buttocks; informal and widely used within its regional range.

records.definition: Clinical term for coitus, specifically penile-vaginal sexual intercourse; the standard medical term for heterosexual penetrative sex.

records.definition: The universally understood neutral phrase for sexual intercourse or sexual activity in Spanish; the default in sex education, public health, and journalism.

records.definition: Clinical term for masturbation; self-stimulation of the genitals for sexual pleasure or orgasm.

records.definition: Clinical phrase for anal intercourse; the medical and legal standard for penetrative anal sex.

records.definition: To fuck; the dominant crude verb for sexual intercourse in Castilian Spanish.

records.definition: To fuck; the dominant crude verb for sexual intercourse across most of Latin America.

records.definition: To fuck, with strong connotations of aggression, domination, or violation; also the most charged all-purpose Mexican expletive.

records.definition: To fuck; literally 'to throw/pull'; crude slang for sexual intercourse especially dominant in Argentina and the Southern Cone.

records.definition: To fuck; derived from 'culo' (ass); crude verb for sexual intercourse common in Colombia, Venezuela, and parts of Central America.

records.definition: To fuck; also a general-purpose Spanish expletive analogous to English 'fuck' in its multi-functional vulgarity.

records.definition: To fuck; literally 'to tread/step on'; crude slang for sexual intercourse implying domination, primarily Argentine.

records.definition: To fuck; literally 'to nail/to drive in'; crude slang for penetrative sex widely used across the Spanish-speaking world.

records.definition: To fuck; the most distinctively Argentine crude verb for sexual intercourse.

records.definition: To fuck; literally 'to temper/tune'; crude verb for sexual intercourse used primarily in Costa Rica and parts of the Caribbean.

records.definition: To fuck; literally 'to buzz/hum'; crude slang for sexual intercourse used primarily in Cuba.

records.definition: To fuck; derived from 'culo' (ass); crude verb for sexual intercourse dominant in Chile and common in the Andean region.

records.definition: To fuck; a variant form of 'singar'; crude verb for sexual intercourse in the Dominican Republic and some Caribbean contexts.

records.definition: To fuck ('singar'); the most charged and primary crude verb for sexual intercourse in Cuban Spanish, here typeset with asterisks due to its extreme vulgarity.

records.definition: To fuck; a variant of 'cachar'; crude verb for sexual intercourse used in Chile and parts of the Andean region.

records.definition: To fuck; crude verb for sexual intercourse primarily used in Peru and parts of the Andean region.

records.definition: To fuck; literally 'to wet/dip'; crude slang for penetrative sex widely understood across the Spanish-speaking world.

records.notes: Standard Spanish word meaning 'to descend'; sexual meaning is widely inferred in context, especially among younger and bilingual speakers. Used with indirect object: 'bajarle' = to go down on him/her.

records.definition: To eat pussy; River Plate crude phrase for cunnilingus using concha, the dominant vulgar term for vagina in Argentina and Uruguay.
records.notes: 'Concha' (shell) is a neutral word in Spain but the primary extreme vulgarity for vagina in Argentina, Uruguay, and Chile; the phrase reaches maximum offensiveness in River Plate dialect.

records.definition: Literally 'to give oneself a straw'; the most widespread Spanish-language phrase for masturbation, overwhelmingly used for penile self-stimulation.
records.notes: 'Paja' (straw) as masturbation metaphor is etymologically opaque but lexically fixed across all Spanish dialects. Technically gender-neutral but in practice nearly always implies penile masturbation.

records.definition: To masturbate; verb derived from paja, primarily used for male masturbation but grammatically applicable to any gender.
records.notes: Simpler verb form of 'hacerse una paja'; transitive form 'pajear a alguien' means to masturbate someone else; reflexive 'pajearse' means to masturbate oneself.

records.definition: Reflexive form of pajear; to masturbate oneself, applicable in principle to any gender but overwhelmingly used for penile self-stimulation.
records.notes: The reflexive -se construction explicitly marks self-stimulation and distinguishes the act from stimulating a partner. Near-synonymous with 'hacerse una paja' but slightly more colloquial in register.

records.definition: Literally 'to give oneself a Manuela'; Spain slang for male masturbation in which manuela is a feminized diminutive of mano (hand) given a woman's proper name.
records.notes: The personification of the hand as 'Manuela' (a female given name) follows a common euphemistic convention in Iberian Spanish. Primarily Spain usage; less recognized in Latin America.

records.definition: Literally 'to pull it'; crude Latin American, especially Mexican, slang for male masturbation.
records.notes: 'Jalar' (to pull) is the Latin American equivalent of Iberian 'tirar'; the -la clitic is feminine, agreeing with an implicit noun (polla, pija, verga). Not commonly used in Spain.

records.definition: Literally 'to crack it' or 'to break it'; crude slang for male masturbation used across Spain and Latin America.
records.notes: 'Cascarse' literally means to crack or break; the violence-of-impact metaphor for masturbation recurs across multiple languages. The -la clitic implies a feminine noun (polla, verga, etc.).

records.definition: To masturbate; derived from puñeta, a Spain expletive whose historical core meaning is the act of masturbation.
records.notes: Standard orthography is 'puñetearse' (with ñ); input form may reflect a transcription variant without the tilde. 'Puñeta' in modern Iberian Spanish functions mainly as a frustration exclamation with the sexual meaning largely bleached out; 'puñetearse' retains the explicit masturbation sense.

records.definition: Vulgar slang for male masturbation; literally 'to peel it,' referencing manual retraction of the foreskin during self-stimulation.
records.notes: Pan-Hispanic but rooted in uncircumcised male anatomy. Overwhelmingly male-coded; some female speakers use it loosely but the foreskin reference marks it as male.

records.definition: To rub oneself; a mild euphemistic verb for masturbation or self-genital stimulation applicable to any gender; secondarily evokes non-penetrative rubbing against a partner.
records.notes: Ambiguous: can mean solo masturbation or mutual frottage depending on context. In the masturbation register the reflexive solo reading predominates.

records.definition: To touch oneself; the most broadly understood Spanish euphemism for masturbation, applicable to all genders and recognized across every Spanish-speaking region.
records.notes: Children are routinely told not to 'tocarse en público,' embedding the sexual reading from an early age and extending its recognition to essentially all adult speakers.

records.definition: To manipulate oneself; a semi-clinical or formal euphemism for masturbation typical in sex-education, therapy, or medical discourse.
records.notes: More clinical-feeling than tocarse; functions near the neutral medical register rather than slang. The reflexive form is virtually always used in this sense.

records.definition: To masturbate; an idiomatic phrase meaning literally 'to do the solitary one,' widely understood across the Hispanic world as a colloquial term for self-stimulation.
records.notes: Gender-inflected: 'el solitario' masculine, 'la solitaria' feminine. The solitude metaphor makes it relatively polite for its referent; not particularly taboo in casual speech.

records.definition: To masturbate; an internet slang verb formed by applying the Spanish '-ear' suffix to the English onomatopoeia 'fap,' associated with chan culture and gaming communities.
records.notes: Peaked with global chan/Reddit culture circa 2012–2016. Almost exclusively used by young male internet users; rarely encountered outside Spanish-language online forums and gaming spaces.

records.definition: To penetrate; the standard clinical Spanish verb for inserting the penis, finger, or object into a body orifice during sexual activity.
records.notes: Used across clinical, legal, and everyday registers. Crude score rises sharply in crude descriptive contexts but the isolated verb is register-neutral. Also used non-sexually (markets, walls, defences).

records.definition: Regional crude slang for sexual penetration; likely a variant or corruption of 'empalar' (to impale), suggesting forceful or deep insertion.
records.notes: Poorly attested in standard references; appears in regional Latin American vernacular. Exact etymology and geographic distribution uncertain — may be localized to specific countries or subcultures rather than broadly pan-LATAM.

records.definition: To skewer or impale sexually; a crude metaphorical verb for penetration drawn from the literal sense of threading beads onto a string or skewering food on a spit.
records.notes: Widely understood across Spanish-speaking regions. The food-craft metaphor is vivid and deliberately crude. Used almost exclusively for penile penetration.

records.definition: To perform fisting; a Spanglish verb formed by applying the '-ear' suffix to English 'fist,' used in LGBTQ+ and BDSM communities to refer to inserting the entire hand into a partner's orifice.
records.notes: Created by standard Spanish loanword verbalization. Used alongside the English noun 'fisting' interchangeably. Essentially unrecognized outside LGBTQ+ and BDSM communities.

records.definition: Fisting; the English loanword used directly in Spanish for the sexual practice of inserting the entire hand into a partner's vagina or anus.
records.notes: Functions as both noun and gerund in Spanish usage. Preferred over 'fistear' in LGBTQ+ health writing due to the English term's international recognizability. Higher recognition than 'fistear' due to pornographic and internet exposure.

records.definition: To tie or bind; a general Spanish verb applied in sexual contexts to physically restraining a partner with rope, cuffs, or other materials as part of erotic bondage play.
records.notes: Completely neutral in everyday Spanish; sexual BDSM meaning is entirely context-dependent. BDSM practitioners often use it alongside the loanword 'bondage' or the noun 'atadura.'

records.definition: To whip, lash, or spank; used in sexual contexts for impact play — striking a partner with a hand, strap, flogger, or implement for erotic arousal or BDSM discipline.
records.english_term: to whip / to spank / to flog
records.notes: Common in non-sexual contexts ('el viento azotaba las ventanas'); sexual application is context-dependent. Crude score reflects sexual use rather than the neutral verb itself.

records.definition: To humiliate; in sexual contexts refers to consensual verbal or physical degradation of a partner as a form of BDSM erotic play.
records.notes: Strongly negative in everyday usage; the consensual BDSM application is a contextual inversion. Recognition score reflects the common general-purpose verb, not specifically its kink application.

records.definition: To dominate; to take the controlling, authoritative role during sexual or BDSM activity, directing the pace, acts, and conduct of the encounter.
records.notes: One of the most common Spanish verbs across many non-sexual registers; the sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent. Low crude score reflects the verb's everyday neutrality.

records.definition: To submit or subdue; to place someone or oneself in a subordinate role, yielding control to a dominant partner in a sexual or BDSM dynamic.
records.notes: Used transitively ('someter a la sumisa') and reflexively ('someterse'). The reflexive form skews toward the submissive's voluntary surrender; transitive toward the dominant's assertion of control.

records.definition: To discipline; in BDSM contexts refers to punitive sexual practices such as spanking, structured correction, or behavioral control between consenting partners.
records.notes: The word's institutional and pedagogical register (disciplining students or employees) makes it a natural euphemism for consensual BDSM punishment dynamics.

records.definition: Semen; the clinical Spanish term for the seminal fluid ejaculated from the penis at orgasm, composed of spermatozoa and secretions from the prostate and seminal vesicles.
records.notes: Identical in form and meaning to the English clinical term; a direct Latin borrowing. Recognized without stigma across all Spanish-speaking regions and registers.

records.definition: Sperm or semen; colloquially used for the entire seminal ejaculate rather than strictly the gamete cells, occupying a middle ground between clinical and everyday registers.
records.notes: Technically refers to sperm cells (see espermatozoides) but in common usage often means the whole ejaculate interchangeably with 'semen.' Less crude than slang alternatives such as 'leche' or 'lefa.'

records.definition: Spermatozoa; the clinical plural noun for the male gamete cells produced in the testes, present in semen, and capable of fertilizing an ovum.
records.notes: Purely clinical; introduced through biology education across the Hispanic world. No slang applications. Recognition reflects school curriculum exposure rather than everyday conversational use.

records.definition: Vaginal discharge; the clinical compound noun for fluid secreted by the cervix and vaginal walls, which may represent normal arousal lubrication or indicate pathological conditions.
records.notes: Standard gynecological and lay health term; understood by most adult speakers from healthcare or sex-education contexts. Mild crude score reflects intimate subject matter rather than the term's register.

records.definition: Lubrication; refers to natural vaginal fluid produced during sexual arousal, or more broadly to any lubricant applied to reduce friction during sexual activity.
records.notes: Entirely clinical in register; applies equally to physiological and artificial lubricants. No slang connotation. Understood pan-Hispanically.

records.definition: Iberian crude slang for semen; literally 'milk,' one of the most versatile and prevalent vulgar terms in Peninsular Spanish, functioning also as a general expletive and intensifier.
records.notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish. In most of Latin America 'leche' retains only its dairy meaning and the semen sense reads as bizarre. In Spain it operates across multiple vulgar registers beyond the semen sense ('¡Me cago en la leche!', 'qué mala leche').

records.definition: Highly vulgar Iberian slang for semen or ejaculate; among the crudest and most explicit terms for seminal fluid in Peninsular Spanish, with essentially no non-vulgar contexts of use.
records.notes: Virtually unknown in Latin America. Etymology is debated. Carries a stronger transgressive charge than 'leche' and appears almost exclusively in pornographic, crudely humorous, or shock-value contexts.

records.definition: Iberian slang for an ejaculation, orgasm, or cumshot; derived from the reflexive verb 'correrse' (to come/orgasm); also the standard Spanish word for a bullfight.
records.notes: The dual meaning (bullfight vs. ejaculation) generates bawdy wordplay in Spain. In Latin America 'corrida' means a run or bullfight with no ejaculation sense; the productive base verb 'correrse' is pan-Hispanic but the nominalized sexual 'corrida' is Iberian-specific.

records.definition: Pre-ejaculatory fluid secreted before ejaculation; the standard Spanish clinical term.
The clinical and standard Spanish term for penile erection.
Spain Spanish colloquial noun for an erection; literally means a splice or junction.
records.notes: Derived from 'empalmar' (to splice or connect); predominantly Spain Spanish; in Latin America 'empalme' retains only its literal junction meaning.

records.definition: Spain Spanish reflexive verb meaning to get an erection; the verbal form of empalme.
records.english_term: to get a boner / to get hard
records.notes: Reflexive construction; primarily Spain Spanish.

records.definition: Crude idiom meaning to have an erection; literally 'to have it standing/stopped,' with the direct object pronoun implicitly referring to the penis.
records.notes: Elliptical construction; 'la' omits explicit naming of the penis; widely understood across all Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: Phrasal expression meaning to get an erection; literally 'to become hard,' with the feminine adjective implicitly agreeing with a colloquial feminine noun for penis.
records.notes: The feminine form 'dura' reflects implicit agreement with 'polla' (Spain slang for penis, feminine noun) rather than 'pene' (masculine); widely understood across regions.

records.definition: Euphemism for vaginal lubrication during sexual arousal; literally 'moisture' or 'humidity.'
records.notes: General word for moisture; sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent; relatively mild and widely used.

records.definition: Reflexive verb meaning to become sexually aroused and produce vaginal lubrication; literally 'to get wet.'
records.notes: Polysemous; context always disambiguates the sexual from the literal sense; universal across Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: Predicative phrase meaning to be sexually aroused and lubricating; literally 'to be wet,' with feminine agreement specifying a female subject.
records.notes: The feminine adjective 'húmeda' specifies the subject as female; contextually understood as referring to vaginal lubrication rather than any literal moisture.

records.definition: The state of sexual arousal or excitation; used in both clinical and everyday speech.
records.notes: Also used for non-sexual excitement; context disambiguates; recognized universally across all Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: Colloquial noun meaning sexual horniness or arousal; literally 'heat' or 'fever.'
records.notes: Primary literal meaning is fever or heat illness; the sexual sense of persistent horniness is colloquial and widespread; context-dependent.

records.definition: Crude reflexive verb meaning to reach orgasm or ejaculate; literally 'to run oneself'; the dominant vulgarity for orgasm in Spain Spanish.
records.notes: Predominantly Spain Spanish for this sexual sense; understood in Latin America but 'venirse' and 'acabar' are strongly preferred there.

records.definition: Reflexive verb meaning to reach orgasm; the most widespread pan-Hispanic equivalent of 'to come.'
records.notes: More common than 'correrse' in Latin America; universally understood across all Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: Colloquial verb meaning to reach orgasm or ejaculate; literally 'to finish' or 'to end.'
records.notes: Lower crude score than 'correrse' because the primary meaning is simply 'to finish'; the euphemistic quality is entirely context-dependent; used across all Spanish regions.

records.definition: English loanword used as both noun and verb in Spanish to refer to female ejaculation or the fluid expelled during it.
records.notes: Recognition concentrated among younger generations and those exposed to English-language pornography; functions as both noun and verb in colloquial Spanish.

records.definition: Nativized Spanish verb meaning to ejaculate (female); formed by adding the productive Spanish infinitive suffix '-ear' to the English 'squirt.'
records.notes: The '-ear' suffix is a standard Spanish pattern for nativizing English loanword verbs (e.g., googlear, tuitear); informal and internet-influenced.

records.definition: Adjective meaning sexually aroused or horny; literally 'hot'; applies to both men and women.
records.notes: Polysemous — primary meaning is hot (temperature); the sexual meaning is context-dependent; universal across Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: Adjective meaning sexually aroused or randy in Spain Spanish; in several Latin American varieties primarily means funny or amusing instead.
records.notes: Significant semantic bifurcation by region: Spain = horny; Mexico and many Latin American countries = funny/amusing. Cross-regional misunderstandings are common and documented.

records.definition: Crude adjective meaning sexually aroused or horny; widely used in Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Central America, and other Latin American regions.
records.notes: Not used in Spain; in some Andean varieties can secondarily mean brave or determined, but the sexual meaning dominates in colloquial speech.

records.definition: Spain Spanish adjective meaning sexually aroused or in a state of persistent horniness; literally 'gone out' or 'protruding,' derived from 'salir.'
records.notes: Primarily Spain Spanish for this sexual sense; in Latin America 'salido' retains only its literal spatial meaning.

records.definition: Adjective meaning sexually aroused; the past-participial adjective from 'excitar'; spans colloquial and semi-clinical registers.
records.notes: Also means generally excited or enthusiastic; context disambiguates; recognized universally across all Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: Adjective meaning lustful or lecherous; driven by excessive sexual desire; derived from 'lujuria' (lust).
records.notes: More common in written and literary Spanish than in everyday speech; carries a moralistic or condemnatory tone; recognized passively even by speakers who would not use it actively.

records.definition: Adjective meaning libidinous or excessively driven by sexual desire; directly derived from Latin 'libido.'
records.notes: More clinical and literary than colloquial; relatively low frequency in everyday speech; cognate with English 'libidinous' and recognizable to educated speakers.

records.definition: Archaic adjective meaning lascivious, lustful, or in a state of sexual excitement; now rarely used in everyday speech.

records.definition: Adjective meaning lascivious or wantonly sexual; implying shameless, indecent sexual desire or behavior.
records.notes: More common in written and literary Spanish than in spoken registers; carries a moralistic or condemnatory tone; direct cognate with English 'lascivious' aiding educated recognition.

records.definition: Relating to or providing pleasure through the physical senses, especially in a sexually suggestive or pleasurable way; implies slow, touch-oriented eroticism rather than crude explicitness.
Relating to or tending to arouse sexual desire or excitement; erotic in content, tone, or imagery.
Fiery and sexually passionate; describes someone with intense burning sexual energy or vigor, especially as a lover.

records.definition: Burning, ardent; describes intensely passionate romantic or sexual desire, most often in literary or poetic contexts.
records.notes: More literary and less colloquial than fogoso; frequently appears in romantic literature and song lyrics rather than everyday speech.

records.definition: Slang for someone persistently or annoyingly sexually aroused; a randy or horny person.
records.notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; informal diminutive-augmentative of caliente (hot); mildly derogatory; also spelled calentorra for feminine.

records.definition: Having a prurient or morbidly fascinated interest in something transgressive, forbidden, or sexual; titillating in an unhealthy way.
records.notes: In Spanish, el morbo is a noun for the specific frisson of transgressive titillation; morboso describes the person or stimulus producing it; the English 'prurient' captures only part of the meaning.

records.definition: A sexually dirty or filthy person; someone with crude, depraved, or gratuitously vulgar sexual behavior or tastes.
records.notes: Intensified diminutive of guarro/a (pig, dirty); predominantly Iberian Spanish; refers specifically to sexual filthiness rather than general uncleanliness.

records.definition: Pig; used as a sexual insult for someone lecherous, sexually depraved, or behaving in a crude and dirty manner.
records.notes: Primary meaning is the animal; in sexual contexts implies someone who behaves with crude carnal depravity or makes unwanted advances.

records.definition: Dirty or risqué in a sexual sense; used to describe sexually suggestive jokes, humor, or content, as in chiste verde (dirty joke).

records.definition: A person given to vice or sexual excess; someone with strong, possibly deviant sexual appetites who pursues pleasure without moral restraint.

records.definition: A pervert; a person with deviant, socially unacceptable, or transgressive sexual interests or behavior.
Frigid; lacking sexual responsiveness or desire; applied most often pejoratively to women perceived as unresponsive to sexual advances.

records.definition: Literally extinguished or switched off; colloquially used of someone with very low sexual energy, passion, or libido.

records.definition: Impotent; unable to achieve or sustain an erection; also used figuratively for someone helpless or without power.

records.definition: Anorgasmic; clinically unable to achieve orgasm despite normal or adequate sexual stimulation.
records.notes: Strictly clinical; no dedicated anorgasmic slug in the registry; mapped to sexual_frigidity as nearest available — the conditions are clinically distinct (absent orgasm vs. absent desire).

records.definition: Without libido; having no sexual drive or desire; a clinical phrase used colloquially to describe absent or very low sexual appetite.

records.definition: A person sexually and romantically attracted to people of the same sex; the clinical Spanish term corresponding to English homosexual.

records.definition: A person sexually attracted primarily to people of a different sex; the clinical term for straight orientation.
A person sexually or romantically attracted to both men and women, or to more than one gender.
A person who experiences little or no sexual attraction to others; used both as a clinical descriptor and as a self-identity label.

records.definition: A person sexually and romantically attracted to others regardless of their sex or gender identity.
records.notes: Loanword from English; recognition rising among younger and urban Spanish speakers but still limited among older demographics.

records.definition: A woman sexually and romantically attracted to other women; the standard Spanish term for lesbian, used both clinically and colloquially.
records.notes: Can be deployed as a slur in hostile contexts but functions primarily as the standard neutral term; widely reclaimed within the community.

records.definition: Gay; a person, especially a man, sexually attracted to people of the same sex; the dominant everyday term across all Spanish-speaking regions.
records.notes: Loanword from English; has largely displaced homosexual in conversational use across Spain and Latin America.

records.definition: A person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth, especially one who has pursued or undergone hormonal or surgical transition; the older Spanish clinical term.
records.notes: Note single 's' in Spanish spelling; increasingly considered dated or overly clinical by activists and medical bodies, being replaced by transgénero in formal contexts.

records.definition: Transgender; a person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth; the contemporary preferred term in Spanish medical, legal, and activist discourse.
records.notes: Loanword/calque from English; increasingly preferred over transexual in formal and activist contexts; recognition still lower than transexual among older generations.

records.definition: Clinical and advocacy term for a person born with sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary definitions of male or female.
records.notes: Direct calque of English 'intersex(ual)'; standard in medical and LGBTQ+ advocacy discourse across all Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: English loanword adopted as an umbrella term for non-heterosexual and non-cisgender identities in Spanish-language LGBTQ+ and academic discourse.
records.notes: Pronunciation follows English; usage concentrated in urban, educated, and activist circles; more prevalent in Latin America than Spain; does not carry the historical sting of the English slur in Spanish contexts.

records.definition: A gender identity that does not fall exclusively within the traditional binary categories of man or woman.
records.notes: Direct calque of English 'non-binary'; adjective agreement varies by speaker — 'no binarie' is used as a gender-neutral form in some activist communities.

records.definition: A person who experiences sexual attraction only after forming a significant emotional bond with someone.
records.notes: Direct English loanword; recognition largely confined to online asexuality-spectrum and LGBTQ+ communities; negligible outside those circles.

records.definition: A gender identity characterized by fluidity, shifting between or among gender expressions rather than remaining fixed at one point on the spectrum.
records.notes: Direct translation of English 'gender fluid'; also appears as the untranslated loanword 'genderfluid'; primarily activist and academic usage; low recognition among older Spanish speakers.

records.definition: Highly offensive slur for a gay man; also deployed as a general-purpose insult for any weak, cowardly, or contemptible man regardless of sexuality.
records.notes: The single most universally recognized gay slur in the Spanish-speaking world; augmentative of 'marica'; used as a standalone expletive, general insult, and targeted homophobic attack; partially reclaimed in some Latin American gay communities.

records.definition: A slur for an effeminate or gay man; softer than 'maricón' and partially reclaimed as a neutral or affectionate term of address within some Latin American gay communities.
records.notes: Base form from which 'maricón' and 'mariquita' derive; in Colombia and parts of South America, widely reclaimed as a casual in-group address between gay men with reduced stigma.

records.definition: Slur for a gay man or male sex worker; also functions as a powerful all-purpose intensifier and insult across Spanish.

records.definition: Mexican and Central American slur for a gay or effeminate man; one of the primary anti-gay insults in Mexico.
records.notes: Predominantly Mexican and Central American; rarely used in Spain or South America; etymology disputed — possible link to Tagalog 'hoto' or to the letter J in Spanish; partially reclaimed in Mexican gay culture.

records.definition: Mexican slur derived from 'culo' (ass), meaning a man who has anal sex; used as a gay slur and as a general insult for a contemptible or cowardly person.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'marica'; a moderately offensive slur for an effeminate or gay man, somewhat gentler than 'maricón' but still pejorative.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'marica'; a strong slur for a gay or extremely effeminate man, the intensifying '-ón' suffix amplifying the insult.
records.notes: The augmentative form implies greater degree than 'marica'; widely used across Spain and Latin America; recognized pan-regionally though more common in Spain and the Southern Cone.

records.definition: An effeminate man; a man displaying stereotypically feminine mannerisms or behavior; implicitly codes as homosexual in everyday usage though not definitionally so.

records.definition: Archaic term for a homosexual person derived from 19th-century sexology's theory of 'sexual inversion' as a pathological reversal of normal gender roles and desires.
records.notes: Borrowed directly from Krafft-Ebing and Havelock Ellis's 'sexual inversion' framework; appeared in Spanish legal, medical, and literary texts through the mid-20th century; now obsolete except in historical quotation.

records.definition: Religious and legal term for a person who practices sodomy; historically used primarily to condemn and prosecute gay men; derived from the biblical city of Sodom.
records.notes: Maintained in conservative Catholic and evangelical discourse; was an operative legal category in Spanish colonial and Inquisitorial law; peak usage spans the colonial period; still deployed in some religious contexts today.

records.definition: Offensive slur for a lesbian woman; literally 'female tortilla maker,' a metaphor invoking the grinding and rubbing motion of tribadism.
records.notes: Widely used throughout Spain and recognized across Latin America; the culinary metaphor (tortilla-pressing as genital rubbing) is transparent to most speakers; partially reclaimed by Spanish lesbian activists and communities.

records.definition: A masculine-presenting or tomboy woman; a slur implying that a woman is excessively masculine, often carrying implied lesbianism though not exclusively.

records.definition: Spanish slur for a butch or heavily masculine-presenting lesbian woman; literally 'female truck driver,' invoking the cultural stereotype of truckers as hyper-masculine.

records.definition: Highly offensive Castilian Spanish slur for a lesbian woman; one of the two primary anti-lesbian insults in Spain alongside 'tortillera.'

records.definition: Offensive Latin American slur for a transgender woman, shortening of 'travestida' or 'travesti.'

records.definition: Argentine and Uruguayan slur for a gay or effeminate man; also used loosely as a general insult for a foolish or contemptible person.
records.notes: Primarily Argentine and Uruguayan; etymology uncertain; partially reclaimed in Buenos Aires gay culture where it can be used as an in-group term with reduced hostility; less widely recognized outside the Southern Cone.

records.definition: Spanish slur for an effeminate or camp gay man, implying theatrical, flamboyant, or over-the-top feminine behavior.
records.notes: Primarily Castilian Spanish; etymology disputed — possibly from 'sarasa' (printed cotton chintz fabric, connoting something gaudy and floral) or from a proper name; targets visible campness and gender nonconformity specifically.

records.definition: Literally 'madwoman'; used across Latin American gay communities for a flamboyant or effeminate gay man; simultaneously a pejorative slur and a widely embraced in-group identity term.
records.notes: One of the most culturally rich terms in this set; functions on a spectrum from slur to celebration depending on who uses it; central to Latin American camp and drag culture; the word's feminine gender is part of its subversive force.

records.definition: Literally 'old madwoman'; Latin American slang for an older flamboyant or effeminate gay man; tone ranges from affectionate irreverence to dismissive ageism depending on the speaker's relationship to the target.
records.notes: Compounds 'vieja' (old woman) with 'loca' (queen/madwoman); the age marker adds a layer absent from 'loca' alone — can signal either fond familiarity toward an elder of the community or dismissal of someone past their sexual prime.

records.definition: Euphemism for a gay person, literally 'one who understands' or 'someone in the know'; used as a discreet coded signal of homosexual identity, especially during the Franco dictatorship in Spain.
records.notes: Classic coded euphemism of Franco-era Spain, when open gay identity was criminally dangerous; semantically similar to English 'friend of Dorothy' or 'family'; declining since the Transition but still recognized by older speakers; the feminine 'entendida' was used for lesbians.

records.definition: Euphemism for homosexual, literally 'from the other side'; avoids naming homosexuality by marking gay people as categorically other.
records.notes: Common in Mexico and broader Latin America; 'estar del otro lado' = to be gay. Preferred by older or conservative speakers who want to acknowledge homosexuality without invoking the word directly.

records.definition: Euphemism for gay or homosexual, literally 'of the others'; marks gay identity as belonging to a separate, unnamed category.
records.notes: Used across Spain and Latin America; 'ser de los otros' = to be gay. The 'others' framing othersizes without labeling. More commonly found in older or conservative registers.

records.definition: A man who takes the active (penetrating) role in sex with other men while publicly maintaining a heterosexual identity; does not consider himself gay.
records.notes: Primarily Caribbean Spanish (Dominican Republic, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Venezuela) but understood broadly in Latin America. The bugarrón preserves masculine identity through role exclusivity; the passive partner is the one marked as gay. This role-based rather than partner-gender-based identity structure is discussed in Latin American queer studies. English 'trade' in gay slang is the closest equivalent but lacks the specific cultural framing.

records.definition: Literally 'one who masturbates' (from paja, masturbation); used as a general insult meaning wanker, jerk, or worthless person.
records.notes: Derived from 'paja' (masturbation, literally straw). The Mitsubishi Pajero SUV was rebranded 'Montero' for Spanish-speaking markets for this reason. Universal across Spain and Latin America; can be used with mild affection between male friends similarly to British 'wanker'.

records.definition: Literally 'little girl' or 'baby girl'; used as a slur to feminize and demean an effeminate or gay man.
records.notes: The word itself is a common term of endearment entirely free of vulgarity; its use as a slur is purely contextual, working by gender imposition on men perceived as failing masculine norms. Mild crude score because the insult comes from gendering, not explicit sexual vocabulary. Similar dynamic to English 'princess' or 'little girl' directed at men.

records.definition: Literally 'son of a whore'; the most prevalent severe Spanish insult, equivalent to 'son of a bitch' at minimum and 'motherfucker' at full intensity.
records.notes: Universal across all Spanish-speaking regions; often abbreviated HDP. Severity varies: in Spain it can be used casually between friends; in Mexico and much of Latin America it carries near-maximum weight. Heavier than English 'son of a bitch' because 'puta' (whore) is a starker referent than 'bitch' (female dog).

records.definition: Literally 'big male goat'; originally denoted a cuckold; now functions as a versatile insult for a bastard, asshole, or contemptible person; in Spain can be affectionate between close friends.
records.notes: One of the most common and flexible Spanish insults. In Spain, 'cabrón' between male friends often signals affection comparable to British 'you bastard'; in Latin America it retains stronger negativity. Cuckold etymology survives in 'poner los cuernos' (to cuckold someone, literally to put horns on them). Female form 'cabrona' is common and equally flexible.

records.definition: Literally 'horned one'; a cuckold — a person (prototypically a husband) whose partner has been sexually unfaithful; the horns symbolize the deceived spouse across pan-Mediterranean folk tradition.
records.notes: More specifically tied to marital infidelity than the generalized 'cabrón'; less used as a free-floating insult. The horned symbolism is shared across Mediterranean cultures (Italian 'cornuto', Greek 'keratas'). 'Poner los cuernos' is the standard Spanish phrase for committing adultery. Female form 'cornuda' exists but is used less often, reflecting the asymmetric shame distribution in honor-culture framing.

records.definition: Literally 'one who sucks' (from mamar, to nurse/suck); insult for an annoying, contemptible, or submissive person, with implied fellatio or homosexual receptivity connotations.
records.notes: Derives from 'mamar' (to suckle/nurse). In Spain and parts of Latin America it primarily means 'annoying idiot' or 'sycophant'; in Mexico and Colombia it carries a stronger implication of homosexual receptivity. Also used in football contexts for players who embellish fouls. Female form 'mamona' is less common.

records.definition: A dickhead, idiot, or contemptible fool; one of the most common general-purpose insults in Castilian Spanish.
records.notes: Distinctly Castilian Spanish; rarely used in Latin America. Etymology disputed: likely combines an archaic term for simpleton with 'pollas' (dicks). Grammatically invariable — same form for singular/plural, masculine/feminine. Despite the crude score, so normalized in Spanish media and everyday speech that many Spanish speakers are startled by foreigners' reactions to it.

records.definition: Literally 'pubic hair'; used across Latin America as an insult for a stupid, cowardly, or contemptible person; exact meaning varies by country.
records.notes: Extremely common in Latin America but rare in Spain. Regional meaning shifts: in Mexico primarily coward or fool; in Argentina idiot or jerk; in Colombia and Venezuela leans toward dumbass. The pubic hair etymology suggests smallness and uselessness, though this is not felt by most current speakers. Widely used by US Hispanic communities and borrowed into some English registers.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'puta' (whore); an extremely promiscuous woman; an intensified version of the puta insult.
records.notes: The '-ón'/'-ona' augmentative amplifies the insult. 'Putón verbenero' is a fixed phrase for a trashy, sexually available woman seeking hookups at popular summer festivals ('verbenas'). Applied to men, 'putón' implies homosexual promiscuity in some regional registers. Universal across Spain and Latin America.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'zorra' (female fox/slut); a little slut; the diminutive '-ita' can soften, ironize, or infantilize the insult depending on context.
records.notes: The diminutive creates ambiguity: in youth and internet slang it can be ironic or mildly affectionate ('eres una zorrita'); in direct insult use it patronizes and infantilizes. Widely used in online sexual content. Less severe than bare 'zorra' in most registers.

records.definition: Literally 'female fox (vixen)'; a very common slur for a promiscuous woman or slut.
records.notes: One of the most widely used Spanish slurs for a sexually promiscuous woman; the vixen/fox metaphor (cunning, sexually available female) appears across Romance languages. Extremely high frequency in Spain; universally understood in Latin America though competing with local alternatives. 'Zorra' retains its literal animal meaning in formal usage, enabling double entendres.

records.definition: Literally 'female pig' (from guarro, filthy/sow); a dirty, trashy, or sexually promiscuous woman combining physical uncleanliness with sexual looseness.
records.notes: Primarily Spain; significantly less common in Latin America. 'Guarro/guarra' as adjective means dirty or disgusting; applied to women as a noun it adds heavy sexual shaming to the filth connotation. The pig association centers on degradation and uncleanliness rather than promiscuity per se, differentiating it from 'zorra'. The masculine 'guarro' applied to men connotes filth without the sexual promiscuity implication.

records.definition: Literally 'so-and-so' (the female generic placeholder name, equivalent to Jane Doe); used to call a woman a prostitute or woman of loose morals through dismissive indirection.
records.notes: Primary meaning is simply an unnamed woman ('una fulana de tal' = some woman); the sexual insult meaning is entirely contextual. The dated/euphemistic register makes it gentler than 'puta' or 'zorra' — more a dismissive label than a direct slur. Part of the Fulano/Fulana/Mengano/Mengana series (Spanish John/Jane Doe equivalents).

records.definition: Literally 'anyone' or 'whatever'; used as a slur to describe a woman sexually available to all comers — 'una cualquiera' implies she will sleep with anyone who asks.
records.notes: The insult operates through the indefinite pronoun's logic: a 'cualquiera' belongs to no one specifically and therefore to anyone. Sharply gendered: 'ser una cualquiera' is a sexual insult applied almost exclusively to women, while 'ser un cualquiera' (masculine) simply means being a nobody or insignificant person with no sexual connotation. Milder than 'puta' or 'zorra' — functions as euphemistic insinuation.

records.definition: Literally 'whore mother'; both a standalone exclamation of rage or pain and a severe personal insult; paradoxically, 'de puta madre' functions as the highest superlative of excellence.
records.notes: Unique semantic inversion documented in Spanish pragmatics: as interjection or insult it is purely derogatory, but 'de puta madre' ('it was de puta madre') means something was fucking excellent. This polarity has no English parallel in 'motherfucker'. Universal across all Spanish-speaking regions; among the highest-frequency severe expletives in everyday speech.

records.definition: Literally 'fuck your mother'; the most severe Mexican Spanish expletive, a direct provocation equivalent to the hardest uses of 'motherfucker' or 'fuck you'.
records.notes: The nuclear option in Mexican Spanish insults; uttering this in the wrong context can precipitate physical violence. The verb 'chingar' (to fuck/screw over) is analyzed by Octavio Paz in 'El laberinto de la soledad' (1950) as central to Mexican cultural identity and power dynamics. Understood broadly in Latin America but especially charged in Mexico. Often abbreviated CTM.

records.definition: Literally 'your mother's cunt'; a severe maternal insult combining explicit genital vocabulary with the universal attack on the mother.
records.notes: Characteristic of Caribbean Spanish (Cuba, Puerto Rico, Venezuela, Dominican Republic) where 'coño' is a pervasive expletive used with far greater frequency and lower shock value than elsewhere. 'Coño' alone in Spain is roughly 'fuck' or 'damn'; in the Caribbean it approaches the default expletive filler. The combination with 'tu madre' escalates it to a direct severe insult.

records.term: me cago en tu puta madre
records.definition: Literally 'I shit on your fucking whore mother'; one of the most extreme Spanish insults, combining coprophilic imagery with maternal and sexual attack simultaneously.
records.english_term: I shit on your fucking mother
records.notes: Distinctly Castilian in flavor; the 'me cago en...' (I shit on...) template is a Spanish insult construction with many variants ('me cago en dios', 'me cago en la leche'). This extended form targeting 'tu puta madre' is near the apex of severity. Cross-linguistically remarkable for fusing fecal, sexual, and maternal imagery in one utterance; has no structural equivalent in English.

records.definition: Literally 'go take it up the ass'; the canonical Castilian Spanish equivalent of 'go fuck yourself.'
records.notes: The standard dismissive expletive in Spain; 'tomar por culo' is the idiomatic phrase for anal penetration. So normalized in Spain it appears routinely in mainstream media. Less common in Latin America where 'vete a la chingada' (Mexico) or 'vete al carajo' (broadly Latin American) dominate. 'A tomar por culo' can stand alone as an exclamation of dismissal or disgust.

records.definition: Literally 'may a fish fuck you'; a colorful absurdist curse wishing sexual humiliation by a fish upon the target.
records.notes: Distinctly Castilian; the absurdist specificity of the fish elevates this beyond standard dismissive curses into humorous creative vulgarity. Popularized through Spanish internet culture in the 2000s–2010s. Functions similarly to 'vete a tomar por culo' but with surrealist flair that makes it memorable and repeatable online. No direct English equivalent for this specific phrasing.

records.definition: Literally 'dick in vinegar'; used as a dismissive exclamation or sarcastic retort meaning 'like hell!', 'yeah right!', or 'my ass!'
records.notes: Used in Spain as a contemptuous dismissal: '¡y una polla en vinagre!' = 'yeah, right!' / 'like hell!'. The vinegar adds the sense of something disagreeable and acidic — possibly the pickled, useless penis as the vehicle of contempt. Functions as a sexually-grounded expression of disbelief rather than a direct insult at a specific person. Primarily Castilian.

records.definition: Literally a blowjob (from mamar, to suck); also widely used in Mexico and Latin America as an exclamation meaning 'bullshit', 'nonsense', or an annoying situation.
records.notes: Primary meaning is fellatio across all Spanish-speaking regions. In Mexico and Central/South America the word has extended to mean 'bullshit' or 'what a pain' ('¡qué mamada!' = what bullshit!), paralleling how English 'bullshit' extends from a literal referent to a general term for falsehood or nuisance. The sexual act sense remains the base meaning from which the expletive sense derives.

records.definition: To mistreat, harass, or make life difficult for someone; derived from 'puta' (whore), with semantic drift from sex-slur verb to general abuse verb; also means to work as a prostitute in some dialects.
records.notes: Polysemous: (1) to give someone a hard time/mistreat them [most common, pan-Hispanic], (2) to hurl whore-slurs at someone, (3) to engage in sex work [regional, less common]. The mistreatment sense has fully decoupled from its sexual origin in everyday use.

records.definition: Fucked; screwed; ruined; also used as an intensifying adjective meaning 'damned' or 'bloody'; derived from 'joder' (to fuck).
records.notes: Extremely common pan-Hispanic expletive adjective. 'Estoy jodido' = I'm screwed. 'El jodido coche' = the damned car. Crude rating is lower than English 'fucked' because high frequency of use has partially neutralized its shock value across Spain and Latin America.

records.definition: Shameless person; a scoundrel or brazenly immoral individual who acts without sexual or social restraint; literally 'without shame' (sin = without, vergüenza = shame).
records.notes: In honor-shame cultures, 'vergüenza' carries strong sexual-moral coding, especially for women; calling a woman 'sinvergüenza' implies sexual and moral abandonment simultaneously. For men it more often implies general roguishness. Gender-neutral noun but gendered in its connotations.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'cabrón' (etymologically: cuckold; literally: male goat); used as a mild insult or sometimes affectionate address for a minor rogue or scoundrel; reduces the severity of 'cabrón'.
records.notes: Diminutive suffix '-ete' softens the insult; can be used affectionately between close friends. Etymologically from 'cabra' (goat) → 'cabrón' (big goat / man whose wife sleeps around). More characteristic of Spain than Latin America, where 'cabrón' itself is used more.

records.definition: Literally gonorrhea (the STI); repurposed in Colombian and Venezuelan slang as a strong pejorative meaning bastard, asshole, or contemptible person; one of the strongest everyday insults in Colombian Spanish.
records.notes: Classic disease-name-as-insult pattern. In Colombia 'gonorrea' as an insult is highly context-dependent: between close friends it can be warmly provocative; directed at a stranger it is a serious threat. Literal STI meaning would score crude≈10, technical≈80; the insult meaning is scored here.

records.definition: Abbreviation of 'hijo de puta' (son of a whore); a very strong general-purpose insult and exclamation, considered harsher than its English equivalent 'son of a bitch' because 'puta' is sexually explicit rather than canine.
records.notes: Written abbreviation used especially in digital communication to soften the visual impact while preserving the referent. 'Hijo de puta' is one of the most fundamental Spanish curses; the 'whore-mother' framing makes it more sexually charged than the English parallel.

records.definition: Coward; literally 'shit-ass' (culo = ass, cagado = shit-soiled/scared stiff); someone so frightened they have defecated in their pants; also a general pejorative for a weak or contemptible person.
records.notes: Compound of 'culo' (ass) and 'cagado' (covered in shit / scared); primarily Colombian slang. The 'scared-into-shitting' etymology is transparent and drives the cowardice meaning. Closely related to 'cagado de miedo' (shit-scared) used across Spanish.

records.definition: Chilean all-purpose crude insult and intensifier derived from 'culear' (to have anal sex); the single most characteristic Chilean expletive, equivalent to 'fucker' or 'motherfucker' depending on context.
records.notes: Past participle of 'culear'; literally 'the one who was anally fucked.' In Chile, used constantly as an intensifier between friends with low offense in-group, or as a harsh insult toward strangers. Spelling variant of 'culiado.' Virtually synonymous with 'huevón' in casual Chilean speech.

records.definition: Literally 'big-balled person'; used either as a friendly term of address meaning 'dude/bro' (especially in Chile) or as an insult meaning idiot/dumbass, from the folk notion that oversized testicles impede rational thought.
records.notes: One of the most context-dependent words in Spanish: in Chile 'huevón' between friends is warm and unmarked (like 'dude'), but directed at a stranger it is a strong insult. 'Weón' is the informal orthographic variant. Understood across Latin America; most characteristic of Chile and Colombia. Crude score reflects the mid-range between affectionate and insulting uses.

records.definition: Literally 'your mother's cunt/vagina'; a very strong compound expletive invoking the mother's genitalia as the ultimate insult; the strongest common Andean Spanish expletive, analogous in force to English 'motherfucker'.
records.notes: 'Concha' = vagina in Chilean/Rioplatense slang (elsewhere 'concha' = seashell, causing unintended comedy in pan-Hispanic contexts). Considered more taboo than 'hijo de puta' in Chilean Spanish due to the direct anatomical genital reference. Also used in Argentina and other Andean countries.

records.definition: Prostitute; the standard formal and clinical Spanish term for a woman who provides sexual services for payment.
records.notes: Default formal register term in legal, journalistic, and medical contexts. Not a slur but carries social stigma. Masculine form 'prostituto' exists but is rarely used. Preferred by institutions over more colloquial or stigmatizing alternatives.

records.definition: Prostitution; the practice or trade of engaging in sexual activity in exchange for payment; the standard institutional term for the sex work industry.
records.notes: Near-cognate to English 'prostitution.' Used in law, journalism, policy, and academia. Carries moral and legal associations but is not itself crude. Favored in conservative and institutional discourse over the rights-based 'trabajo sexual'.

records.definition: Prostitute; an archaic and literary term for a woman who sells sexual services, derived directly from Latin 'meretrix'; used in elevated prose, historical writing, and ecclesiastical texts.
records.notes: From Latin 'meretrix' (prostitute, from 'merere' = to earn/deserve). Appears in Spanish Golden Age literature and colonial religious texts. Rarely used in contemporary speech; recognized mainly by educated speakers. The elevated register strips it of visceral crudeness despite its referent.

records.definition: Prostitute; an archaic Spanish term derived from 'rama' (branch), referencing the practice of hanging a branch at the entrance of a brothel as a commercial sign in medieval Spain.
records.notes: Historical etymology: medieval Spanish brothels and prostitutes displayed a 'rama' (branch) as a trade sign. Largely displaced by 'prostituta' and 'puta' in modern speech; recognized by most Spanish speakers but actively used only in historical, literary, or humorous contexts. More informal and pejorative in register than 'meretriz'.

records.definition: Slang for a prostitute or sexually promiscuous woman; a pejorative slur used primarily in Spain that straddles actual sex work and general sexual shaming of women perceived as loose.
records.notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; less common in Latin America. Can denote a literal sex worker or any woman deemed sexually promiscuous. Etymology uncertain; possibly from Italian 'forca' or a Germanic source. Has declined somewhat since the 1980s–90s peak but still in active use.

records.definition: Whore; prostitute; also the foundational Spanish expletive and all-purpose insult for women; the source root of virtually every Spanish sexual slur in this section.
records.notes: Functions as: (1) noun for a sex worker, (2) sexual insult directed at any woman, (3) standalone expletive ('¡Puta!' = Fuck!), (4) intensifying modifier ('de puta madre' = fucking great). The single most generative word in Spanish sexual vocabulary; nearly every insult in the preceding section derives from it.

records.definition: Sex work; the modern rights-affirming term for the provision of sexual services for payment; direct calque of the English advocacy term.
records.notes: Reflects a rights-based framework adopted by advocacy organizations and progressive media since the 1990s. Less common among older speakers and absent from conservative institutional discourse, which prefers 'prostitución'. Recognition lower among older speakers; higher among urban and educated demographics.

records.definition: Sex worker (feminine); the modern, rights-affirming Spanish term for a woman who engages in sex work professionally; direct calque of the English advocacy term.
records.notes: Preferred by sex worker organizations (e.g. AMMAR in Argentina, OTRAS in Spain) and in progressive journalism. Masculine form 'trabajador sexual' exists but is less commonly used. Framing sex work as labor ('trabajo') is itself a political stance contested in conservative and abolitionist discourse.

records.definition: Hostess or bar girl who works in a Spanish club encouraging male customers to buy drinks, typically in a context that is a legal cover for sex work; the standard Spanish euphemism for a woman working in the 'alterne' sex industry.
records.notes: 'Alterne' refers to the practice of a woman circulating among male bar customers to boost drink sales, with sex work implied or explicit but legally deniable. Characteristic of Spanish 'clubs de alterne' which operate as brothels while nominally being entertainment venues. Declined since its 1980s–90s peak as the industry shifted online.

records.definition: Companion lady; a polished euphemism for an upscale escort or high-end sex worker, foregrounding social companionship while leaving the sexual transaction unstated.
records.notes: Classic euphemistic register: the sexual element is linguistically erased, replaced by 'companionship' ('compañía'). Widely used in newspaper classifieds and escort directories. Parallels English 'escort' or 'companion' in its coded meaning; implies higher social status and discretion than 'prostituta'.

records.definition: Escort; a high-end sex worker or paid companion, borrowed directly from English; connotes greater discretion and higher social register than 'prostituta'.
records.notes: English loanword used across the Spanish-speaking world; the English word's connotation of upscale, discreet sex work has transferred intact into Spanish. Standard in online classified advertising and escort directories. More neutral in affect than any native Spanish equivalent.

records.definition: Argentine Rioplatense slang for a street prostitute; from 'girar' (to walk around / to turn), evoking a woman who walks the streets soliciting clients.
records.notes: Classic lunfardo (Buenos Aires criminal argot) vocabulary, now dated. The related verb 'yirar' (to walk the streets as a sex worker) also exists. Immortalized in Enrique Santos Discépolo's 1929 tango 'Yira, yira.' Recognition mostly confined to older Rioplatense speakers and tango culture enthusiasts today.

records.definition: Brothel; the standard colloquial Spanish word for an establishment where clients pay for sex; slightly informal compared to 'prostíbulo' but the more common everyday term.
records.notes: Derived from French 'bordel.' The default word for brothel in colloquial speech, journalism, and literature across the Spanish-speaking world. Neither highly clinical nor aggressively crude; occupies the mid-register between formal 'prostíbulo' and more colorful slang equivalents.

records.definition: Brothel; the formal and clinical Spanish term for an establishment providing paid sexual services; preferred in legal statutes, police reports, and official journalism over the colloquial 'burdel'.
records.notes: Derived from Latin 'prostibulum' (place of prostitution, from 'prostare' = to stand in front of / to prostitute oneself). More formal in register than 'burdel'; standard in legal and institutional Spanish. Both terms are well understood across Latin America and Spain; 'prostíbulo' skews more formal and written.

records.definition: Brothel; a rare archaic and literary Spanish term derived from Latin 'lupanar' (brothel, from 'lupa' = she-wolf, Roman slang for a prostitute who howled to attract clients).
records.notes: From Latin 'lupa' (she-wolf), used as Roman slang for a prostitute. 'Lupanar' is the classical Latin form; 'lupanario' is the Spanish nominal adaptation. Appears in scholarly translations of Roman texts, Golden Age literature, and historical writing. Not used in contemporary spoken Spanish; recognized mainly by classically educated speakers.

records.definition: A euphemistic term for a brothel or house of prostitution, literally 'house of appointments.'
records.notes: The euphemistic framing ('citas' = appointments/dates) distances it from cruder 'burdel'; widely used in historical and journalistic contexts across the Spanish-speaking world.

records.definition: An urban neighborhood or area known for concentrated sex work and adult entertainment, the Spanish calque of 'red-light district.'
records.notes: 'Roja' (red) may also evoke danger or prohibition beyond the color-of-lights etymology; used across Latin America and Spain in journalism and urban contexts.

records.definition: The formal, legal, and journalistic Spanish term for a person who manages sex workers and profits from their earnings; procurer or pimp in legal usage.
records.notes: Used in criminal statutes, court reporting, and journalism; carries grave legal weight; less emotionally charged in casual speech than street-slang equivalents; from Latin 'proxeneta' (broker).

records.definition: In Spain, a pimp or man who lives off a sex worker's earnings; in broader pan-Hispanic usage also means attractive, flashy, or arrogant.
records.notes: Highly polysemous: the pimp sense is dominant in Spain ('chulo de putas'); in Latin America 'chulo' predominantly means 'cute' or 'cool' with the pimp connotation absent or weak; context is essential.

records.definition: Chilean and Argentine slang for a pimp, a man who controls and profits from sex workers' earnings.
records.notes: Primarily Chilean; also circulates in Argentina; etymology uncertain, possibly from lunfardo or criminal argot; carries strong contempt and association with exploitation.

records.definition: Argentine lunfardo slang for a pimp or man who lives off the proceeds of sex work.
records.notes: Lunfardo term from the Río de la Plata region; likely derives from Italian immigrant slang in Buenos Aires; somewhat dated but still understood; the accent distinguishes it from 'macro' (large/big).

records.definition: Mexican slang for a pimp, a man who controls and profits from sex workers' earnings.
records.notes: Predominantly Mexican; literally augmentative of 'padre' (father), implying a controlling dominant male; widely used in journalism on trafficking; carries heavy negative stigma.

records.definition: A procurer, go-between, or facilitator of sexual arrangements; also used broadly for anyone who covers up or enables another's misdeeds.
records.notes: From Arabic 'al-qawwad'; historically denotes a sexual intermediary rather than a controlling pimp; the feminine form 'alcahueta' is equally common; modern usage extends to any enabler or snitch, diluting the sexual specificity.

records.definition: Argentine lunfardo slang for a pimp.
records.notes: Niche lunfardo term specific to the Río de la Plata criminal argot; likely derives from Italian 'figlio' (son) via Buenos Aires underworld slang; recognized mainly by older Argentines or lunfardo enthusiasts.

records.definition: The standard formal Spanish term for pornography; sexually explicit printed, visual, or digital material intended primarily to cause sexual arousal.
records.notes: Used in legal, medical, and journalistic registers; feels less charged in casual discourse than its English cognate; the formal baseline against which all colloquial variants are measured.

records.definition: Colloquial abbreviation of 'pornografía'; used in everyday speech as both noun and attributive adjective.
records.notes: Universal across all Spanish-speaking regions and age groups; functions as both noun ('ver porno') and adjective ('película porno', 'actor porno'); no meaningful regional variation.

records.definition: An X-rated or pornographic film; a euphemistic term borrowed from the X-rating classification system.
records.notes: The 'X' framing functions as a distancing euphemism allowing use in print media and retail contexts; widely recognized though slightly more common in Spain and among older speakers than 'porno' alone.

records.definition: A female pornographic film performer; a woman who acts in pornographic productions.
records.notes: Compound of 'actriz' (actress) and 'porno'; neutral-to-descriptive register used in journalism, crime reporting, and casual speech; carries more stigma in socially conservative regions.

records.definition: A male pornographic film performer; a man who acts in pornographic productions.
records.notes: Male counterpart to 'actriz porno'; slightly less socially stigmatized than the female form in many Spanish-speaking cultural contexts due to persistent double standards around male vs. female sexuality.

records.definition: In sex-work contexts, shorthand for webcam-based erotic performance or sex work for a live paying online audience; also the device itself.
records.notes: English loanword; in general use simply means the camera device; the sex-work meaning is activated by phrasing like 'hacer webcam' or 'trabajar de webcam'; widely recognized but context-dependent.

records.definition: A woman who performs sexually or erotically on live webcam streams for a paying online audience.
records.notes: English loanword adopted without phonetic or orthographic adaptation; recognition skews toward younger, internet-connected speakers; associated with platforms like Chaturbate, OnlyFans, and similar services.

records.definition: A man who performs sexually or erotically on live webcam streams for a paying online audience; male counterpart to 'camgirl.'
records.notes: English loanword; less common in usage than 'camgirl' reflecting the market demographics of webcam sex work; recognized primarily by younger, internet-connected Spanish speakers.

records.definition: An erotic dance involving the progressive removal of clothing performed for an audience; English loanword used in Spanish without adaptation.
records.notes: Universally adopted across Spanish-speaking world; also written 'strip-tease' or 'strip tease'; verb form 'hacer un striptease' standard; no Spanish native equivalent has displaced it.

records.definition: A nightclub offering erotic entertainment; in Latin American usage typically implies a venue where sex workers operate alongside the entertainment, functioning as a de facto brothel.
records.notes: In Spain, closer to a legitimate performance venue; in Mexico and much of Latin America 'cabaret' strongly implies sex work is available alongside entertainment, making 'brothel' the closer English equivalent in those contexts; French loanword.

records.definition: A euphemism for sexually explicit or pornographic material; 'adult content.'
records.notes: Direct calque of English 'adult content'; used in platform terms of service, parental controls, and media contexts where 'pornografía' is considered too blunt; prevalence has increased sharply with global internet platform policies.

records.definition: The subscription content platform widely used for explicit sexual material; in Spanish vernacular often used generically for subscription-based sex work or explicit content creation.
records.notes: Brand name functioning as a generic term; used in phrases like 'tener un OnlyFans' or 'hacer OnlyFans'; recognition skews under-35; peak recognition around 2020–2022 when mainstream media coverage was highest.

records.definition: Pornographic content produced by non-professional individuals rather than commercial studios.
records.notes: 'Amateur' is a French loanword standard in Spanish; describes production style (DIY, non-professional) rather than content type; widely used in internet search queries and platform taxonomy.

records.definition: Homemade pornographic content produced domestically by private individuals, emphasizing the intimate domestic setting.

records.definition: The standard everyday Spanish word for a condom; a sheath-shaped barrier contraceptive worn on the penis to prevent pregnancy and reduce STI transmission.

records.definition: The standard Spanish clinical and everyday term for a condom; a sheath-shaped barrier contraceptive worn on the penis during sex.

records.definition: Argentine and River Plate slang for a condom; the word literally means 'lining' or 'sheath' in standard Spanish.

records.definition: Latin American colloquial slang for a condom, derived from 'goma' meaning rubber, eraser, or gum.

records.definition: Slang for a condom comparing it to a balloon (globo = balloon in Spanish); more common in Spain than Latin America.

records.definition: Lit. 'reverse gear'; the universal pan-Spanish colloquial term for coitus interruptus, the withdrawal method of contraception.

records.definition: The standard Spanish clinical term for a contraceptive or contraception; used as both noun and adjective.

records.definition: Lit. 'pill'; shorthand for la píldora anticonceptiva, the daily oral hormonal contraceptive pill, equivalent to English 'the pill'.

records.definition: Acronym for Dispositivo Intrauterino; the Spanish clinical equivalent of IUD, a T-shaped contraceptive device implanted in the uterus by a clinician.

records.definition: The clinical Spanish term for the hymen, a thin mucous membrane partially occluding the vaginal opening; carries heavy cultural weight as a presumed virginity indicator.

records.definition: Virginity; the state of never having had sexual intercourse; carries strong moral, cultural, and religious significance across Spanish-speaking societies.

records.definition: To deflower; to take someone's virginity through first vaginal penetration; carries archaic literary and moralistic overtones common in the Spanish literary tradition.

records.definition: Lit. 'the first time'; the universal Spanish euphemism for a person's first sexual experience or loss of virginity.

records.definition: Submission; in sexual contexts, the role of yielding control, autonomy, or power to a dominant partner within a BDSM dynamic.

records.definition: Sadomasochism; the clinical and colloquial Spanish term for sexual arousal derived from both inflicting and receiving pain, humiliation, or domination.

records.definition: Sadism; sexual or psychological gratification derived from inflicting pain, humiliation, or suffering on another person.

records.definition: Masochism; sexual or psychological gratification derived from experiencing pain, humiliation, or subjugation.

records.definition: Flagellation; the act of whipping or flogging, practiced both as Catholic penitential self-mortification and as a BDSM impact play technique.

records.definition: Fetish; in sexual contexts, an object, body part, or material that triggers sexual arousal, or more broadly any strong non-conventional sexual interest or preference.
records.notes: Also used in anthropological contexts (fetiche = ritual object of power); the sexual sense is now dominant in everyday Spanish usage; 'tener un fetiche con X' is standard phrasing.

records.definition: Sexual arousal triggered by a specific object, body part, or material not typically considered inherently sexual; the Spanish clinical and popular term for fetishism.
records.notes: Loanword from French 'fétichisme'; used both clinically and in mainstream media. The sexual sense dominates in practice; everyday meaning of 'fetish' (obsessive interest) is secondary.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual contact with animals; the Spanish clinical equivalent of zoophilia, used in legal and sexological discourse.

records.definition: Primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children; the standard Spanish clinical and journalistic term.

records.definition: Sexual arousal or gratification associated with feces or defecation; the Spanish clinical term for coprophilia.

records.definition: The clinical and sexological term for sexual arousal or gratification associated with urine or urination; used in Spanish medical literature.

records.definition: Literally 'golden rain/shower'; the standard Spanish slang phrase for the sexual act in which one person urinates on another for erotic purposes.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual acts performed with a human corpse; the Spanish clinical and popular term for necrophilia.
records.notes: Recognition driven by horror media, crime reporting, and true-crime coverage rather than direct familiarity with the paraphilia; extremely high crude score reflects one of the most universally taboo sexual subjects.

records.definition: English loanword used in Spanish for erotic scenarios in which participants adopt fictional personas, costumes, or power dynamics during sexual activity.

records.definition: Literally 'role game'; the native Spanish phrase for sexual role-playing in which partners adopt fictional personas or power hierarchies during erotic activity.
records.notes: Functionally equivalent to the English loanword 'roleplay', which also circulates freely in Spanish; 'juego de roles' tends to read as slightly more explanatory and is preferred in educational or descriptive contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'power game'; the Spanish phrase for consensual BDSM power exchange, in which one partner cedes authority or control to another for erotic purposes.
records.notes: Primarily recognized within Spanish-language kink and BDSM communities; less widely known in mainstream culture. 'Intercambio de poder' is an alternative but equally niche phrasing.

records.definition: In Spanish BDSM subculture, the collar worn by a submissive partner as a symbol of ownership, D/s commitment, or active power-exchange relationship status.
records.notes: 'Collar' is an ordinary Spanish word meaning 'necklace/collar'; the BDSM meaning is a semantic extension imported from English BDSM discourse and only recognizable in kink context. Low recognition reflects the specialist subculture audience.

records.definition: Literally 'master/owner' (masculine amo, feminine ama); used in Spanish BDSM to denote the dominant partner in a D/s or master-slave dynamic.

records.definition: Literally 'slave' (masculine esclavo, feminine esclava); used in BDSM to denote a submissive partner in total power exchange or master-slave dynamics.

records.definition: Feminine form of 'sumiso'; a woman who takes the submissive role in BDSM dynamics, yielding control to a dominant partner.

records.definition: Clinical term for compulsive or excessive sexual desire in women; widely repurposed in popular use as a pejorative for sexually active women.
records.notes: Retains a surface clinical register but is predominantly encountered as a stigmatizing popular label; the DSM has moved toward 'hypersexual disorder', but 'ninfomanía' remains the dominant everyday and media term in Spanish.

records.definition: The clinical term for compulsive or excessive sexual desire in men; the male equivalent of ninfomanía, derived from the Greek satyrs symbolizing uncontrolled lust.
records.notes: Very low recognition outside medical and sexological literature; vastly less used than 'ninfomanía' because male hypersexuality has historically been less pathologized in Spanish-speaking cultures. Essentially a specialist term.

records.definition: English loanword used in Spanish for a person who engages in consensual partner-swapping or group sexual activity with other couples.

records.definition: Literally 'partner exchange'; the native Spanish descriptive phrase for swinging — consensual sexual activity between couples who share or swap partners.

records.definition: Consensual romantic or sexual relationships with multiple partners simultaneously, with full knowledge and consent of all involved; the Spanish adaptation of 'polyamory'.

records.definition: A sexual gathering involving multiple participants engaging freely and simultaneously; also used loosely for any wild, hedonistic party.

records.definition: A sexual encounter involving exactly three participants; the standard and universal Spanish term for a threesome.
records.notes: The word 'trío' carries no inherent crude charge in its primary musical meaning; context fully disambiguates the sexual sense. One of the most universally recognized terms on this list; used across all Spanish-speaking regions without regional variation.

records.definition: Literally 'group sex'; a neutral descriptive phrase for sexual activity involving multiple participants simultaneously.
records.notes: More clinical and journalistic in tone than 'orgía', which carries stronger transgressive or hedonistic connotations; 'sexo en grupo' is preferred in public health communication, news reporting, and app interfaces.

records.definition: French loanword used in Spanish for a sexual or romantic arrangement involving three people, often implying an ongoing or domestic arrangement rather than a one-off encounter.

records.definition: Simultaneous penetration of two orifices of the same person by two penises, fingers, or objects; the standard Spanish phrase for double penetration.

records.definition: Literally 'black kiss'; a Spanish slang phrase for anilingus — oral stimulation of a partner's anus.

records.definition: Euphemism 'to do it'; refers obliquely to sexual intercourse without naming the act.

records.definition: Literally 'to make love'; emphasizes emotional intimacy and romantic framing over the physical act.

records.definition: Literally 'to be with someone'; a circumlocution implying sexual activity by referencing shared presence rather than naming the act.

records.definition: Literally 'to lie down with someone'; a widely understood euphemism for having sexual intercourse.
