records.definition: Colloquial noun for an undefined casual romantic or sexual 'thing' or fling with someone, without commitment or labels.

records.definition: Verb meaning to pick someone up romantically or sexually; to flirt successfully to the point of arranging a sexual or romantic encounter.

records.definition: Slang noun meaning a fuck or a shag; literally 'dust/powder,' applied to sexual intercourse.

records.definition: Phrasal verb meaning to have a fuck; the canonical crude Iberian Spanish expression for having sex.

records.definition: Reflexive verb meaning 'to shake/move oneself'; in sexual context refers to masturbation, especially male self-stimulation.

records.definition: Literally 'to be feeling like it / in the mood'; a mild euphemism for experiencing sexual desire or arousal.

records.definition: Idiom literally 'to warm up the engines'; refers to foreplay or building sexual arousal in preparation for intercourse.

records.definition: Literally 'the thing'; a generic euphemism for the genitals or for sex itself without further specification.

records.definition: Literary phrase meaning 'pleasures of the flesh'; refers broadly to sexual and sensual gratification.
records.notes: Used in religious, philosophical, and literary registers; evokes the theological tension between spiritual life and physical desire. Pan-Hispanic.

records.definition: Idiom literally 'between the sheets'; refers to sexual activity or one's conduct and prowess in bed.

records.definition: Idiom literally 'to get to the grain / to get to the point'; in sexual context means to skip foreplay and move directly to penetrative sex.

records.definition: Verb meaning to make out; to kiss passionately and at length, typically involving tongues and often in a semi-public setting.
records.notes: Derived from 'morro' (snout/lips in colloquial Castilian). Primarily Iberian; equivalent to 'comerse a besos' or 'besuquearse' in Latin America.

records.notes: Noun derived directly from 'morrear'; same etymology, register, and geographic distribution. Iberian Spanish only.

records.definition: Idiom literally 'to throw oneself into the envelope/bag'; primarily means to go to bed or nap, but used euphemistically to imply sexual activity in bed.

records.definition: Slang verb meaning to pull or score; to successfully attract and have sex with someone, framed as catching or snagging a conquest.

records.definition: Idiom meaning to have a secret romantic or sexual affair; 'lío' literally means 'mess' or 'tangle,' euphemistically implying an entangled romantic or sexual involvement.

records.definition: Colloquial peninsular-Spanish noun for a sexual romp or fuck, etymologically derived from 'follar'; primary meaning is 'mess' or 'commotion,' and the sexual sense is secondary but well-established in Spain.

records.definition: Euphemistic phrase meaning 'bedroom matter' or 'bedroom affair,' used to refer obliquely to sexual activity or an ongoing sexual relationship between two people.
records.notes: Deliberately vague construction; can describe a one-time encounter or a sustained clandestine relationship depending on context. Tactful enough for use in mixed or formal company.

records.definition: Archaic legal and ecclesiastical term meaning 'carnal union' or 'carnal joining,' denoting sexual intercourse especially in the context of marriage law and annulment proceedings.

records.definition: Archaic clinical and legal phrase for 'carnal copulation,' used in ecclesiastical, juridical, and medical texts to denote sexual intercourse with full anatomical detachment.
records.notes: Frequent in Inquisition trial records, canon law, and 19th-century medical and forensic treatises. The Latin root 'copula' keeps the register clinical; 'carnal' specifies the physical, non-spiritual dimension.

records.definition: Clinical and legal term for living together as a sexual or romantic couple outside of formal marriage.
records.notes: Feels bureaucratic or legalistic to most speakers; everyday Spanish prefers 'vivir juntos' or 'pareja de hecho.' Appears in census forms, legal codes, and notarial documents rather than casual speech.

records.definition: One of the seven deadly sins in Catholic moral theology; intense and unrestrained sexual desire or appetite.
records.notes: Highly recognizable across all Spanish-speaking cultures due to biblical and catechetical transmission. Carries heavy Catholic moral freight; 'lujurioso/a' is the adjectival form. Used in literary and moral contexts more than in crude slang.

records.definition: Wanton sexual desire or lascivious conduct; the quality of being sexually immodest, licentious, or given to overt sensual indulgence.
records.notes: Semantically adjacent to 'lujuria' but emphasizes external behavior and display over interior desire. Common in moral treatises, Inquisition proceedings, and Golden Age drama. Adjectival form: 'lascivo/a.'

records.definition: Archaic noun denoting sexual immodesty, unchastity, or shameless behavior; the absence of sexual modesty or 'pudor,' especially in conduct.
records.notes: Directly from Latin 'impudicitia.' Common in patristic texts, moral theology, and Spanish treatises through the 18th century; largely extinct in modern usage. Distinct from 'lujuria' (desire) and 'lascivia' (display) in stressing the absence of shame.

records.definition: The social and moral dishonor accruing to a woman and her family through sexual transgression — rape, seduction, premarital sex, or adultery — within the Iberian honor-shame system.
records.notes: Central concept of Golden Age drama (the 'dramas de honor' of Calderón, Lope de Vega). English 'dishonor' lacks the gendered, familial, and sexually specific dimension; 'ruined woman' is approximate but individual rather than systemic. The concept encodes a collective family shame triggered by one woman's sexual status, with no tidy English equivalent.

records.definition: A woman who cohabits with and is sexually available to a man of higher status without being his legal wife; a concubine.
records.notes: Widely recognized from biblical transmission and historical literature. Modern usage is almost exclusively historical, literary, or journalistic (historical reportage). The institution was legally regulated in medieval Iberian law.

records.definition: Archaic term for a mistress, kept woman, or lower-status concubine; a woman maintained by a man outside of marriage for sexual purposes.
records.notes: 'Mancebo/manceba' originally meant simply 'young man/woman' (from Arabic 'mancab'); the female form acquired sexual connotations of availability. Appears in medieval legal codes and Golden Age literature including Cervantes. Largely extinct; modern readers may not parse the sexual meaning without context.

records.definition: A woman who lived with a man in 'barraganía,' a semi-legal informal union recognized in medieval Castilian and Aragonese law that granted her certain protections without the full legal status of wife.
records.notes: Distinct from generic concubinage: 'barraganía' was a legally codified Iberian institution with specific rights (inheritance claims in some fueros). Etymologically from Arabic 'barragan.' Specialists-only term today; virtually no recognition outside medieval history contexts.

records.definition: To fornicate; to engage in sexual intercourse outside of marriage, framed through a lens of religious and moral condemnation.
records.notes: Widely recognized from biblical and ecclesiastical transmission; occasionally deployed humorously in modern speech precisely because of its portentous register. The noun form is 'fornicación'; the agent noun 'fornicador/a' is also current.

records.definition: Carnal sin; in Catholic moral theology, any sexual act considered sinful — primarily fornication, adultery, sodomy, or onanism — framed as an offense against God and nature.
records.notes: Broader than 'fornication' alone: encompasses all sexual sins in Catholic taxonomy. Appeared ubiquitously in confessional manuals, penitentials, and homiletical literature throughout the Spanish-speaking world. Still recognized in cultures with strong Catholic formation.

records.definition: Carnal act; an archaic legal, medical, and ecclesiastical euphemism for sexual intercourse, emphasizing the physical dimension over the emotional or moral.
records.notes: Standard phrasing in Inquisition records, colonial penal codes, and 19th-century forensic medicine. Still surfaces in some Latin American legal contexts. More distancing and clinical than emotionally charged.

records.definition: Defloration; the act of taking a woman's virginity through first penetrative intercourse, framed around rupture of the hymen.
records.notes: Botanical metaphor (stripping petals from a flower). Variant form 'desfloración' also circulates. Found in Golden Age literature, colonial legal codes, and 19th-century medical texts. Carries heavy honor-economy weight: defloration without marriage constituted 'deshonra.'

records.definition: From Hymen, Greek god of marriage; in Spanish literary usage, refers to the wedding, the marital union, and by extension the sexual consummation of marriage.
records.notes: Primarily a poetic synecdoche: the god's name stands for the rite and its consummation. Used by Lope de Vega, Góngora, and other Golden Age poets. In modern Spanish, 'himeneo' is essentially unrecognizable outside classical-education contexts; the anatomical cognate 'himen' (hymen) is far more current.

records.definition: Archaic Spanish term for the hymen or, by extension, the physical state of virginity; primarily an anatomical reference to the membranous structure at the vaginal opening.
records.notes: From Latin 'virgo' (virgin maiden). Used in older medical texts and Golden Age literature where the hymen was treated as proof of chastity. Modern speakers recognize 'virgo' chiefly as a zodiac sign; the anatomical meaning requires context. Current medical term is 'himen.'

records.definition: Archaic collective euphemism for women as a sex, emphasizing their beauty and erotic appeal; the Spanish equivalent of the English 'the fair sex.'
records.notes: Patronizing 18th–19th century idiom treating all women as a unified class defined by attractiveness and desirability. Appeared widely in Enlightenment-era Spanish literature, journalism, and conduct manuals. Now considered sexist and archaic; occasionally deployed ironically in modern usage.

records.definition: The marriage bed or bridal chamber; a poetic and literary metonym for the conjugal bed where a married couple consummmates their union.
records.notes: From Greek 'thalamos' (inner chamber). Common in Golden Age poetry and drama as a metonym for marital sexual union. In modern Spanish, 'tálamo' primarily denotes the neurological thalamus (part of the brain); the nuptial meaning is effectively dead outside literary contexts.

records.definition: Concupiscence; in Catholic theology, the inherited disordered inclination of human nature toward sin, especially the irrational drive toward sensual and sexual pleasure.
records.notes: Key term in Augustinian and Thomistic moral theology; the Spanish form mirrors the Latin exactly. Recognition is concentrated among those with formal religious or theological education; general-population recognition has declined with secularization.

records.definition: Intense sexual desire or libido; a Latinate literary term for lustful appetite, closely related to 'lujuria' but with a more visceral, sensory connotation.
records.notes: Directly from Latin 'libido.' Less common than 'lujuria' in Spanish; restricted to highly literary or scholarly registers. Some speakers conflate it with 'líbido' (the psychoanalytic term). Stress falls on the second syllable: li-BÍ-di-ne. Very low modern recognition outside classical literature contexts.

records.definition: To lust; to act on or be consumed by carnal desire; the verbal form of 'lujuria,' meaning to engage in or be driven by lustful behavior.
records.notes: Rarely encountered in modern Spanish; 'lujurioso/a' (adjective) and 'lujuria' (noun) survive in active use while the verb has retreated almost entirely to archaic literary texts. Conjugates as a regular -ar verb but practically unused in speech or contemporary writing.

records.definition: Literally 'weak flesh'; a religious idiom for the human body's inherent vulnerability to sexual temptation, drawn from Catholic doctrine on the frailty of physical human nature.
records.english_term: the weakness of the flesh, the flesh is weak
records.notes: Derives from the biblical phrase 'el espíritu está dispuesto, pero la carne es débil' (Matthew 26:41, Vulgate: 'caro autem infirma'). Used rhetorically to excuse or contextualize sexual sin by attributing it to bodily frailty rather than willful vice. Still widely understood in Catholic-formation cultures; occasionally ironic in modern usage.

records.definition: Historical Spanish legal term for statutory rape or the coercive or deceptive defloration of a minor or virgin; distinct from forcible rape ('violación'), covering seduction-based first sexual contact without constituting forcible assault.
records.notes: Persists in several Latin American criminal codes as a specific charge between seduction and forcible rape; in modern Spain largely subsumed by broader sexual offense statutes.

records.definition: Archaic medical term for sexually transmitted infections, derived from Venus, goddess of love; the dominant clinical phrase until replaced by 'enfermedad de transmisión sexual (ETS)' and later 'infección de transmisión sexual (ITS)' in the 1990s–2000s.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'venereal disease'; both fell from clinical use simultaneously across Western medical communities; still understood but marked as dated.

records.definition: More archaic variant of 'enfermedad venérea,' literally 'venereal evil' or 'venereal sickness'; encountered primarily in 19th- and early 20th-century Spanish medical writing and literature.
records.notes: Even more dated than 'enfermedad venérea'; the noun 'mal' (evil/illness) marks it as pre-modern medical register; rarely encountered outside historical texts.

records.definition: Archaic Greco-Latin term for a woman who has sex with other women, particularly through genital rubbing; the historical medical and moralizing label for what is now called a lesbian.
records.notes: Derived from Greek 'tribein' (to rub); used in Inquisition-era and early modern medical texts; almost entirely replaced by 'lesbiana' in contemporary usage; occasionally reclaimed in academic or queer historical contexts.

records.definition: Archaic literary and early sexological term for female homosexuality or lesbianism, named after the Greek lyric poet Sappho of Lesbos; used predominantly in 19th- and early 20th-century Spanish letters and sexology.
records.notes: Near-perfect cognate of English 'sapphism'; found in modernista and Generation of '98 literary criticism; virtually absent from contemporary Spanish except in historical analysis.

records.definition: Adjective meaning 'sapphic': relating to female homosexuality or to the poetic style of Sappho; used in literary and archaic contexts to describe love between women.
records.notes: Seeing selective revival in contemporary LGBTQ+ literary and academic spaces as a gentler or more aestheticized alternative to 'lesbiana'; still predominantly archaic in everyday register.

records.definition: Historical Spanish term for a licensed or municipally tolerated brothel, especially the institutionalized sex establishments of medieval and Golden Age Spain; etymologically related to 'mancebo' (young man).
records.notes: Refers specifically to the regulated prostitution system of early modern Spain; carries significant historiographical weight in scholarship on gender and sexuality in the Siglo de Oro; not a direct synonym for modern 'burdel'.

records.definition: Literally 'female' (the biological/zoological term); when applied to human women it is either archaic/crude objectification reducing a woman to her sex, or in contemporary reggaeton and urban slang, an admiring term for an attractive woman.
records.notes: The word itself is current and clinical when referring to animals; its application to human women ranges from crude objectification (archaic lit) to affectionate slang (Latin American urban); context determines register completely.

records.definition: Direct loanword from English: the practice of sending sexually explicit messages, images, or videos via mobile device or messaging app.
records.notes: Adopted without modification into Spanish across all regions; used in journalism, law, and everyday speech; appears in child-protection legislation across several Spanish-speaking countries.

records.definition: Spanish internet slang (from English 'pack') for a collection or archive of someone's explicit or nude photos and videos, typically compiled and circulated without the subject's consent.
records.notes: Non-consensual distribution is implicit in most uses; 'pack' of a minor constitutes CSAM production or distribution under most jurisdictions; distinct from 'nudes' (individual images) by the sense of compiled collection.

records.definition: Direct loanword from English: nude or sexually explicit photographs shared digitally; used identically to the English term across Spanish-speaking internet culture.
records.notes: Used as an untranslated anglicism; native equivalents 'fotos desnudas' or 'fotos íntimas' exist but 'nudes' dominates in informal digital registers among younger speakers.

records.definition: Spanish internet phrasal verb meaning 'to ask someone for their pack': to request that another person send their nude or explicit photos, typically unsolicited and frequently directed at minors or strangers online.
records.notes: The predatory and minor-targeting dimension is statistically frequent; constitutes grooming when directed at minors; widely discussed in Spanish digital safety campaigns aimed at teenagers.

records.definition: Spanish internet phrase meaning 'to make or compile a pack': to gather someone's explicit images from multiple sources and aggregate them into a collection, typically for distribution without the subject's consent.
records.notes: Often involves scraping images from social media, messaging apps, or third-party leaks; constitutes non-consensual pornography under laws in most Spanish-speaking jurisdictions.

records.definition: Spanish verb derived from English 'to leak': to non-consensually distribute someone's private or explicit images or videos online; to publish intimate content without the subject's consent.
records.notes: Follows standard Spanish -ar verb conjugation: 'leakeó', 'leakearon'; also used in non-sexual tech contexts for data or document leaks; the sexual sense is now the primary association among younger speakers.

records.definition: Loanword from English: the deliberate process by which an adult cultivates trust and emotional dependency with a child or teenager online in order to facilitate sexual abuse or exploitation.
records.notes: Adopted into Spanish legal and journalistic discourse without translation; 'cibergrooming' specifies the online variant; increasingly codified in child protection legislation across Spanish-speaking countries; distinct from 'acoso' (harassment) by emphasizing the slow trust-building process.

records.definition: Loanword from English: a deliberately sexualized photo or video posted on social media to attract desire, attention, and validation from viewers.
records.notes: Used in Spanish primarily in its English form; concentration among younger bilingual urban speakers and influencer culture; 'trampa del deseo' exists as a calque but is rarely used.

records.definition: English acronym 'Friends With Benefits' used directly in Spanish dating and internet discourse: a sexual arrangement between friends with no romantic commitment or exclusivity.
records.notes: Recognition concentrated among younger Spanish speakers with Anglophone internet exposure; native equivalents 'amigos con derechos' (Mexico/LA) or 'amigos con beneficios' exist and are more common in spoken Spanish.

records.definition: Loanword from English: a casual sexual encounter between people with no expectation of an ongoing relationship; also refers broadly to the dating-app culture enabling such encounters.
records.notes: Fully integrated into Spanish-language dating app culture and youth vernacular; also used as a verb 'hookupear' or 'hacer un hookup' in some communities; Grindr and Tinder have accelerated adoption.

records.definition: Loanword from English: an undefined romantic or sexual relationship that functions like a committed partnership but lacks explicit labels, mutual agreement, or formal commitment.
records.notes: Among the most recent anglicisms adopted into Spanish youth relationship vocabulary; used without translation in Spanish-language social media; recognition still climbing as of 2026.

records.definition: Loanword from English: a man who is excessively attentive, deferential, or servile toward a woman in hopes of gaining sexual or romantic approval, used mockingly as an insult.
records.notes: Fully adopted into Spanish internet culture; also used as a verb 'simpear' and noun 'simpeada'; peak viral use was approximately 2020–2022; recognition remains high but the term is slightly past peak freshness.

records.definition: Loanword from English: an 'involuntary celibate' — a man who is unable to find a sexual partner and attributes this to women's choices and systemic injustice, typically with expressed resentment or misogyny.
records.notes: Adopted directly from English; Spanish-language incel communities exist on Reddit, Discord, and dedicated forums; pluralized as 'incels'; discussed extensively in Spanish media in the context of gender-based violence and radicalization.

records.definition: Spanish adaptation of 'alpha male': in manosphere discourse, a dominant, confident, sexually successful man who commands high social status and attracts women without visible effort; valorized earnestly within the subculture and mocked outside it.
records.notes: Direct calque of 'alpha male'; used both earnestly by manosphere adherents and ironically by critics; widely disseminated across Spanish-speaking regions via YouTube, TikTok, and podcasts centered on 'masculinidad' discourse.

records.definition: Loanword from English internet slang: to masturbate; an onomatopoeic term originating in Anglophone chan and forum culture, primarily coding male masturbation.
records.notes: Used as a verb ('fapear') and exclamation in Spanish internet communities; associated with chan culture and Reddit; the 'NoFap' movement and its discourse have been adopted wholesale into Spanish under the same name.

records.definition: English acronym 'Not Safe For Work' used directly in Spanish-language internet spaces as a content warning for sexually explicit, violent, or otherwise inappropriate material.
records.notes: Used without translation across Spanish-speaking internet communities; understood primarily by internet-literate users; the native paraphrase 'no apto para el trabajo' or 'no apto para menores' exists but NSFW dominates in digital contexts.

records.definition: Euphemism for sexually explicit material — pornography, nude images, or graphic sexual content — widely used on digital platforms, in legal frameworks, app store ratings, and content warnings as a platform-safe alternative to 'pornografía'.
records.notes: The standard compliance-friendly euphemism across Spanish-language digital spaces; appears in platform terms of service, parental guidance labels, and child-protection legislation; directly mirrors English 'explicit content' as a regulatory category.

records.definition: Phrase meaning 'for adults only,' used as a content warning for sexually explicit or age-restricted material online and in broadcast media.
records.notes: Standard Spanish equivalent of NSFW or the 18+ label; used on websites, apps, and television alike. Non-transgressive in tone; purely regulatory.

records.definition: Sexual activity conducted via internet-based channels — live video calls, text chat, or audio — where participants engage sexually in real time without physical contact.
records.notes: Broader than 'sexting,' which the registry maps to text/image exchange; sexo virtual encompasses live webcam sex, erotic video calls, and sexual roleplay chat. 'Sexting' is the closest registry concept but does not capture live interactive virtual sex.

records.definition: To obsessively monitor someone's social media presence and activity, typically in a romantic or sexual context, often without the target's knowledge.
records.notes: Direct borrowing of English 'stalk' with the Spanish productive -ear infinitive suffix. Broader than post_rejection_orbiting: stalkear can precede any romantic contact and implies active surveillance rather than passive engagement after rejection. Well-understood across all age-connected demographics.

records.definition: The act of abruptly cutting off all communication with a romantic or sexual partner without explanation; borrowed directly from English.
records.notes: Used without phonological or morphological adaptation across all Spanish-speaking regions. Recognized even by speakers who do not use it actively.

records.definition: A mutual match on a dating app — primarily Tinder — where both parties signal explicitly sexual rather than romantic intent; also the person so matched.
records.notes: Blends the English loanword 'match' (from app-dating culture) with 'sexual' to distinguish a hookup-oriented pairing from a romantic one. The concept precedes the encounter itself but presupposes it.

records.definition: An older, typically wealthy man who provides money, gifts, or lifestyle support to a younger partner in exchange for companionship and sexual access; borrowed directly from English.
records.notes: Used without modification in Spanish. Circulates primarily in digital and social media contexts; well-understood across Spanish-speaking regions.

records.definition: An older, typically wealthy woman who provides money or gifts to a younger partner in exchange for companionship and sexual access; the gender-inverted equivalent of 'sugar daddy.'
records.notes: Registry contains only the male-coded 'sugar_daddy' concept; this entry is its gender-inverted counterpart. Slightly less common in Spanish than 'sugar daddy.' Also encountered as 'sugar mama' in some regions.

records.definition: A distinctly Castilian concept denoting the erotic thrill of transgression: the dark, morbidly exciting arousal that arises from what is forbidden, taboo, or culturally off-limits, combining sexual excitement with a frisson of wrongness.
records.notes: No English concept captures the specific fusion of morbid fascination with erotic excitement. 'Titillation,' 'prurience,' and 'forbidden desire' each cover partial aspects but miss the keynote of pleasurable wrongness. Most strongly associated with Iberian Spanish; present but less culturally central in Latin American varieties. The word shares etymology with 'morbid' (Latin morbus, disease).

records.definition: Predicative phrase meaning 'to be a source of transgressive erotic excitement,' applied to a person, situation, or object that produces the characteristic morbo thrill.
records.notes: 'Ese tío es un morbo' = 'That guy is such a turn-on in a transgressive way.' Lexically, morbo is used here as a countable noun; the phrase foregrounds the quality as residing in the stimulus rather than the experiencer.

records.definition: Verbal phrase meaning 'to possess the quality of transgressive erotic appeal,' used of a person or situation that inherently carries morbo.
records.notes: 'Esa chica tiene mucho morbo' = 'That girl has a lot of transgressive erotic charge.' The possession framing emphasizes morbo as a stable attribute of the stimulus rather than a fleeting reaction.

records.definition: Verbal phrase meaning 'to provoke or cause transgressive erotic excitement in another person,' emphasizing the directional transfer of the morbo sensation from stimulus to experiencer.
records.notes: 'Me da morbo' = 'It/he/she gives me that transgressive erotic thrill.' The dar (give) construction is the most common of the morbo verbal collocations and the primary way the concept is expressed in conversation.

records.definition: Augmentative intensification of morbo; an overwhelming, intense jolt of transgressive erotic excitement, used when the sensation is especially strong or surprising.
records.notes: The Spanish -azo augmentative suffix intensifies morbo to convey a sudden or exceptionally powerful surge of transgressive arousal. Less frequent than the base form; mainly used for emphatic effect in speech. 'Menudo morbazo' = 'What an intense burst of that dark erotic charge.'

records.definition: A woman's sexual honor or reputation for chastity; in classical and early modern Spanish culture, the social standing of a woman (or her male guardian) derived from her sexual purity and strict conformity to female modesty codes.
records.notes: English 'honor' or 'chastity' are partial translations; neither captures the specifically social, gendered, and transactable nature of honra as a commodity that can be lost, defended, or violently restored. Central to Golden Age Spanish drama (Calderón, Lope de Vega). Understood but largely archaic in modern Spanish; survives in fixed phrases and historical registers.

records.definition: Sexual dishonor; the irreversible stain on a woman's or family's social standing resulting from premarital or extramarital sexual activity, framed as a public and permanent loss.
records.notes: English 'dishonor' lacks the same specific sexual and gendered charge; deshonra in traditional Spanish and Latin American societies was effectively a social death sentence, and its narrative restoration through marriage or violence drove entire dramatic genres. More archaic than honra but still culturally legible.

records.definition: To dishonor a woman sexually; to take her virginity or engage in illicit sexual relations that destroy her social reputation, whether through seduction, consent outside marriage, or force.
records.notes: Maps approximately to 'defloration' but the emphasis is on the social consequence (loss of honor) rather than the physical act alone. Uniquely, the transgression is framed as the man's violation of social norms — rape, seduction, and consensual premarital sex are linguistically equivalent under this framework.

records.definition: Shame or embarrassment related to sexual matters; in the honor/shame economy, the internalized social emotion that enforces sexual propriety by making transgression feel disgraceful and publicly visible.
records.notes: General word for shame/embarrassment; in sexual contexts it is the psychological enforcement mechanism of the honor economy. English 'shame' is approximate; it lacks the specifically social and family-honor dimension of vergüenza in traditional contexts, where one's sexual shame is also the family's.

records.definition: Sexual modesty, decency, and shame; the sense of bodily and moral propriety that leads one to conceal or avoid explicit discussion of sexual matters, often framed as a virtue in traditional and religious contexts.
records.notes: More positive and classical in tone than English 'prudishness,' which implies excessive inhibition; pudor can describe either virtuous modesty or dysfunctional inhibition depending on context. From Latin pudor (shame, modesty); used in formal, legal, and literary registers. Atentado al pudor = indecent assault (legal).

records.definition: Circumspection, modesty, and sexual reserve as a social and moral virtue, particularly expected of women; the quality of keeping sexual matters private and behaving with proper restraint.
records.notes: Recato is traditionally framed as praiseworthy, not repressive, distinguishing it from English 'prudishness.' Primarily describes female behavior; a woman described as 'de recato' is virtuous in the traditional frame, not inhibited. More archaic in everyday usage; survives in fixed phrases and religious discourse.

records.definition: Feminine adjective describing a woman as modest, sexually reserved, and circumspect; a woman who adheres to traditional codes of female sexual propriety.
records.notes: Adjectival form of recato applied specifically to women. In traditional Spanish culture an unambiguous compliment; in contemporary usage it can carry ironic or condescending overtones when wielded by younger speakers to describe conservative female behavior.

records.definition: Indecent; sexually offensive, improper, or violating norms of public decency, applied to behavior, language, or material.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'indecent'; used in both legal registers (acto indecente, propuesta indecente) and colloquial condemnation. Functions across the full spectrum from mild prudishness to serious legal sanction.

records.definition: Indecency; the quality of being sexually improper or offensive, or a specific act that violates standards of sexual propriety.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'indecency'; functions in colloquial, journalistic, and legal contexts. Often used in exclamation: '¡Qué indecencia!' expressing moral outrage at sexual impropriety.

records.definition: Obscene; sexually explicit, offensive, or grossly indecent in a manner that violates community standards of public decency.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'obscene'; the /a ending indicates the feminine adjectival form. Used in legal contexts (publicación obscena), moral condemnation, and colloquial speech. Slightly stronger register than 'indecente.'

records.definition: Obscenity; sexually explicit or grossly offensive material or behavior that violates standards of public decency, or a specific instance thereof.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'obscenity'; operates in legal definitions (obscenidad pública) and colloquial moral outrage alike. Countable ('una obscenidad') or uncountable ('la obscenidad').

records.definition: Sexual looseness or moral frivolity; the quality of being lax, permissive, or irresponsible in sexual matters, implying a dangerous absence of moral gravity.
records.notes: From liviano (light, insubstantial); the metaphor frames sexual morality as having weight — liviandad is the failure to take it seriously. More alive in Latin American Spanish than Iberian; somewhat archaic overall. Less severe than libertinaje; the slight softness of the term makes it useful for coded condemnation.

records.definition: A sexually loose woman; a woman considered to have light morals or to be sexually promiscuous, applied pejoratively within the honor/shame framework.
records.english_term: loose woman / woman of easy virtue
records.notes: Substantivized or predicate-adjective use of the feminine form of liviano: 'es una liviana' or 'mujer liviana.' Functions as a mild-to-moderate pejorative in Latin American Spanish; less severe than 'puta' but occupying the same honor/shame vocabulary. Primarily LATAM; Iberian speakers would more likely use 'fresca' or 'ligera de cascos' for similar meaning.

records.definition: A 'fallen woman'; a woman who has lost her sexual honor or moral standing through premarital sex, adultery, or other sexual transgression against the norms of the honor/shame economy.
records.notes: Implies permanent social stigma and exclusion from respectable society; the 'fall' metaphor positions sexual transgression as a moral descent with no easy recovery.

records.definition: Literally 'public woman'; a euphemism for a prostitute, framing sex work as availability to the general public rather than naming the commercial transaction directly.
records.notes: Now dated; historically used in legal and journalistic registers to avoid 'prostituta'; the 'public' framing contrasts with the 'private' woman (wife, mother) of the domestic sphere.

records.definition: The social reputation of sexual virtue and chastity, especially applied to unmarried women; the positive pole of the female honor/shame reputation axis that communities actively managed and policed.
records.notes: No English equivalent concept: English lacks a single term for a woman's standing on the female sexual-honor continuum. The positive counterpart to mala_fama; central to marriage-market value, family alliances, and the social regulation of female sexuality across the Spanish-speaking world.

records.definition: Bad sexual reputation; the social stigma attached to a woman known or believed to be sexually promiscuous or unchaste, resulting in diminished marriage prospects and community exclusion.
records.notes: English 'bad reputation' lacks the sexual-honor-economy specificity; mala_fama indexes female sexual transgression as a collective social verdict with concrete social consequences rather than merely a personal moral failing.

records.definition: Literally 'easy'; applied to a person, overwhelmingly a woman, to mean sexually available or quickly persuaded to have sex with minimal resistance or courtship.
records.notes: Mirrors English 'easy' exactly in meaning and register; applying it to a man carries far weaker pejorative force, reflecting the double standard embedded in the honor/shame economy.

records.definition: Literally 'loose' or 'unbound'; applied to a woman to imply sexual looseness, lack of restraint, and willingness to engage in casual sex outside appropriate relational structures.
records.notes: Semantic structure mirrors English 'loose woman' exactly; the metaphor of constraint vs. freedom maps directly onto the honor/shame economy's expectation that women's sexuality must be bound by marriage and family control.

records.definition: Literally 'light'; applied to a woman to describe sexual frivolity or looseness, implying she gives herself with little moral weight or seriousness attached to the act.
records.notes: Softer than 'suelta'; frequently appears in the fuller phrase 'ligera de cascos' (literally 'light-hoofed', meaning frivolous); the lightness metaphor implies sexual frivolity rather than the full weight of moral violation.

records.definition: The collective dishonor brought upon an entire family by a member's — typically a daughter's or wife's — sexual transgression outside marriage, understood as a shared social wound affecting all members' standing.
records.notes: No precise English equivalent: honor-based collective family shame for individual sexual conduct is not a named concept in Anglophone sexual vocabulary. Central to honor-killing discourse and to the social mechanisms that enforce female sexual control across the Spanish-speaking and broader Mediterranean world.

records.definition: The collective sexual honor of a family, understood as a shared social asset upheld primarily through the sexual purity and chastity of female members and the virility and cuckold-resistance of male members.
records.notes: English 'family honor' exists but lacks the specific mechanism linking a daughter's virginity or a wife's fidelity to the entire family's social standing. This positive pole is managed through chaperonage, arranged marriage, and punishment of sexual transgression.

records.definition: Literally 'fucking shame'; a crude intensified exclamation of social disgrace in which 'puta' functions as a vulgar intensifier (equivalent to 'fucking') rather than literally meaning 'whore.'
records.notes: 'Puta' as intensifier is a grammaticalized function distinct from its literal sex-work meaning (compare 'puta madre' as intensifier); the phrase expresses communal condemnation of sexual or moral transgression and is the oral weapon of honor enforcement.

records.definition: Literally 'shameless woman'; a woman who openly flouts sexual and social norms without displaying the expected modesty or remorse, placing the absence of shame itself as the primary offense.
records.notes: The feminine grammatical form (-a) targets women specifically; in honor culture, shamelessness is a graver condemnation than the transgression itself because it forecloses the possibility of redemption through remorse and reform.

records.definition: Literally 'woman of happy life'; a genteel euphemism for a prostitute or sexually permissive woman, softening moral condemnation with an ironic positive gloss.
records.notes: Sardonic undertone: 'alegre' (merry/happy) inverts the social reality of stigma; structurally parallel to French 'fille de joie' and English 'woman of easy virtue'; more literary in register than 'mujer pública.'

records.definition: Literally 'woman of the street'; a sex worker who solicits clients in public spaces, specifically implying street-based rather than indoor or agency-mediated sex work.
records.notes: Parallel to English 'streetwalker' and Italian 'donna di strada'; the 'street' framing also carries secondary moral homelessness — a woman expelled from the domestic sphere of respectability into the unprotected public world.

records.definition: A man who embodies dominant aggressive masculine virtues: physical toughness, sexual prowess, emotional stoicism, and the authority to protect and control his family's honor.
records.notes: Borrowed directly into English with the same core meaning; in Spanish, can be used straightforwardly admiringly by traditionalists; in English often carries a pejorative or ironic register that is less consistently present in Spanish usage.

records.definition: The cultural ideology and practice of male dominance, sexual conquest valorization, emotional hardness, and expected female subordination embedded in traditional Spanish-speaking societies.
records.notes: Borrowed into English as a loanword with essentially the same meaning; maps imperfectly to any single registry concept — male_virility is the closest anchor, but machismo is properly an ideological system governing both sexual and non-sexual masculine behavior.

records.definition: A person, typically a man, who enacts or endorses machismo: male chauvinism, the sexual double standard, and the expectation of female sexual submission and domestic subservience.
records.notes: Functions as both noun and adjective; 'mujer machista' (machista woman who enforces gender hierarchy on other women) exists; English 'male chauvinist' is approximate but lacks the specifically sexual-honor dimension of the Spanish concept.

records.definition: Manliness; the aggregate of masculine virtues including courage, sexual potency, decisiveness, and the capacity to defend and uphold one's own and one's family's honor against all challenges.
records.notes: Carries stronger cultural freight than English 'manliness'; specifically includes not being cuckolded and fulfilling sexual expectations of dominance; loss of hombría is a social catastrophe in honor-culture contexts.

records.definition: Virility; the quality of being sexually potent, physically vigorous, and capable of fulfilling the reproductive and social expectations of dominant masculinity.
records.notes: Direct cognate with English 'virility'; slightly more clinical in register than 'hombría' and more narrowly focused on sexual-reproductive potency rather than the full honor-culture masculine package.

records.definition: Literally 'to be very much a man'; an idiomatic affirmation that someone fully embodies masculine virtues, especially sexual confidence, courage, and honor-protective authority.
records.notes: Used admiringly by traditionalists and sarcastically by critics of machismo; curiously, 'ser muy hombre' can also be applied to a woman to compliment exceptional courage, importing masculine virtue into female bravery.

records.definition: Literally 'big underpants/trousers'; a man completely dominated by his wife or partner, who yields all domestic and sexual authority despite nominally being the one who wears the trousers.
records.notes: Augmentative of 'calzón' (underpants/trousers); the garment metaphor ironically inverts the 'who wears the trousers' idiom — he has oversized pants but no real authority in them; implies failure to maintain the masculine sexual and social dominance that hombría requires.

records.definition: From 'mandil' (apron); a man dominated or controlled by his wife, evoking the feminizing image of a man wearing a kitchen apron instead of exercising masculine authority outside the domestic sphere.
records.notes: Most common in Mexican and Central American Spanish; the apron metaphor specifically feminizes the man by placing him in the domestic sphere assigned to women; carries stronger feminization implication than 'calzonazos' and a sharper insult to his hombría.

records.definition: Literally 'one who consents or permits'; a man who knowingly tolerates his partner's infidelity rather than defending his masculine honor through confrontation, punishment, or departure.
records.notes: Subtler and more damning than 'cornudo' in some readings — cornudo may be deceived, but consentidor knows and allows it; in honor-economy terms, active toleration of infidelity is the greater loss of hombría because it cannot be explained by ignorance.

records.definition: Literally 'horned one'; the standard Spanish term for a man whose partner is sexually unfaithful to him, derived from the pan-Mediterranean folklore of the deceived husband growing horns as a mark of his shame.
records.notes: Horn symbolism for cuckoldry is pan-Mediterranean and pan-European (cf. Italian 'cornuto', French 'cocu'); the 'cuernos' (horns) hand gesture directed at a man is a public act of humiliation; loss of cornudo status requires honor-restoring action in traditional communities.

records.definition: Literally 'he-goat'; etymologically a cuckold, now the most common all-purpose Spanish expletive (bastard, fucker, asshole), having expanded far beyond its sexual origin while retaining the cuckold sense in explicitly sexual contexts.
records.notes: Semantic evolution mirrors English 'bastard' (literal legal meaning → general insult); retains the specific cuckold meaning in contexts where infidelity is the subject; also widely used as warm address between male friends in the same register as British English 'bastard' — context determines whether it's an insult, a descriptor, or an endearment.

records.definition: Literally 'viper'; a treacherous, manipulative, or venomous woman, especially one who dominates or emasculates her male partner through cunning and malice rather than open confrontation.
records.notes: 'Viper' exists in English but lacks the specifically gendered sexual-emasculation connotation; in Spanish honor-culture context 'víbora' specifically invokes the machismo fear of female cunning undermining male authority from within the domestic space; also applied to treacherous people of any gender in general usage.

records.definition: A woman who seduces men, typically implying cunning allure and manipulative intent; feminine form of seductor.
records.notes: Carries both admiring and condemning connotations depending on speaker and context; common in telenovela and literary register.

records.definition: A dangerously alluring woman who seduces men and leads them to ruin; French loanword embedded in Spanish via literary and cinematic tradition.
records.notes: Used identically to the English/French term; strongly associated with noir film archetypes and literary villainess figures; the French phrase is borrowed wholesale.

records.definition: Coded term for the LGBTQ+ community or gay social scene; literally means 'atmosphere' or 'environment' but used within and around queer communities to refer to that world.
records.notes: Used in phrases like 'es de ambiente' (he's gay); a discreet in-group euphemism recognizable to LGBTQ+ communities and their allies across the Spanish-speaking world; the metaphor frames queerness as a social climate one inhabits.

records.definition: 'The scene' — definite-article form referring specifically to the collective LGBTQ+ social world; treated as a proper-noun-like concept within queer communities.
records.notes: The definite article elevates ambiente from a generic descriptive to a specific social referent; compare English 'the scene' or 'the life'; slightly higher recognition than bare ambiente because the phrasing is more distinctive.

records.definition: Verb phrase meaning 'to be gay' or 'to belong to the LGBTQ+ community'; a discreet, non-explicit formulation that avoids naming sexuality directly.
records.english_term: to be gay / to be in the life
records.notes: Used in third person ('es de ambiente' = he's gay) as often as first person; avoids explicit naming while signaling queer identity clearly to initiates; the phrase functions as a shibboleth.

records.definition: Literally 'feather'; refers to visible effeminacy or camp mannerisms in a gay man; 'tener pluma' means to present visibly as gay through feminine behavior, speech, or gesture.
records.notes: Not inherently pejorative — can be a neutral descriptor or source of pride; 'sin pluma' (without pluma) describes a gay man who passes as straight in presentation; valence determined entirely by speaker intent and context.

records.definition: Diminutive of pluma; a gay man with moderate or subtle visible effeminacy; the diminutive implies 'a little camp' and can carry a teasing or slightly dismissive tone.
records.notes: Less widely used than pluma; primarily Spain; the diminutive suffix adds a sense of 'not fully pluma' which can read as affectionate minimization or mild mockery.

records.definition: Literally 'butterfly'; pejorative slang for a gay man, especially one considered effeminate; offensiveness varies by country and context.
records.notes: Used across the Spanish-speaking world; in some communities partially reclaimed or used playfully within in-groups; the butterfly metaphor codes gay men as flitting, delicate, and not-serious; still functions as a clear slur when deployed with hostility.

records.definition: Collective noun for lesbians or the lesbian community; derived from 'bollo' (Spanish lesbian slang); literally 'pastry shop'; pejorative from outsiders, sometimes reclaimed within lesbian communities.
records.notes: Spain-specific; 'bollo' (bun/bread roll) as lesbian slang is the base term; food-item coding is common in Spanish LGBTQ+ slang; outsider use is generally pejorative while insider use can be affectionate or political.

records.definition: Lesbianism; the sexual orientation, identity, or practice of women attracted to women; the standard Spanish noun for female homosexuality as a concept.
records.notes: Broadly understood and largely neutral in register; slightly more clinical than simply 'ser lesbiana'; used in academic, journalistic, and everyday speech without strong stigma in most current contexts.

records.definition: A male performer who dresses as a woman for theatrical, nightclub, or entertainment purposes; not necessarily transgender-identified; the traditional Latin American term for drag performance before 'drag queen' became dominant.
records.notes: Predates the English loanword 'drag queen' in Spanish-speaking contexts; emphasis is on theatrical performance rather than gender identity; less common among younger LGBTQ+ generations who default to 'drag queen'; still in active use in older entertainment contexts.

records.definition: A performer, typically a gay man, who adopts exaggerated feminine costume, makeup, and persona for entertainment; English loanword used unchanged in Spanish, dramatically boosted by global exposure to RuPaul's Drag Race.
records.notes: Fully lexicalized English loanword that has largely supplanted 'transformista' among younger speakers; the Spanish Drag Race franchise accelerated saturation; treated as an invariant compound noun in Spanish grammar.

records.definition: A performer, typically a woman or non-binary person, who adopts exaggerated masculine costume and presentation for artistic or entertainment purposes; English loanword used unchanged in Spanish.
records.notes: Significantly lower recognition than 'drag queen' due to lesser media exposure in Spanish-speaking markets; concept understood in LGBTQ+ circles but the performance tradition is far less mainstream; borrowed entirely from English without translation.

records.definition: The practice of wearing clothing associated with another gender; the Spanish equivalent of 'transvestism'; clinical or semi-clinical in register, may or may not include sexual arousal as a component.
records.notes: Has receded as more specific identity vocabulary (transgender, travesti, cross-dresser) has emerged; still used in psychological, legal, and older journalistic contexts; the term carries less stigma than 'travesti' which is more loaded with class and sex-work associations.

records.definition: In Latin American contexts, a distinct self-defined gender and social identity for people assigned male at birth who adopt feminine presentation and may pursue body modification, but who do not necessarily identify as women in the Western transgender sense.
records.notes: Genuinely distinct from both 'transvestite' (cross-dresser for whom it is theatrical performance) and 'transgender woman' (who identifies fully as a woman); theorized as its own category by Argentine and Brazilian scholars including Lohana Berkins; carries strong class and sex-work associations in Latin America while also being a reclaimed political identity; in Spain the word tracks more closely to European 'transvestite' without the distinct identity politics.

records.definition: The receptive partner in anal intercourse between men; the 'bottom'; in Latin American machismo culture this role carries heavier social stigma than its English equivalent, often coding the pasivo as subordinate or feminized regardless of broader identity.
records.notes: In many Latin American cultural frameworks stigma attaches to the pasivo but not the activo; a man who penetrates another man may be considered masculine while the one penetrated is coded as gay; this asymmetry is sharper and more socially consequential than in Anglophone gay culture.

records.definition: The insertive partner in anal intercourse between men; the 'top'; in Latin American machismo culture this role is sometimes framed as compatible with heterosexual masculine identity.
records.notes: The activo/pasivo binary is more culturally loaded in Latin America than the top/bottom binary in Anglophone gay culture; penetrating is coded as masculine dominance so the activo escapes some of the stigma that same-sex activity normally carries.

records.definition: A vigorous or extended fuck session; the act or prolonged experience of fucking; derives from 'singar,' the Cuban vulgar verb for sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Highly regional — almost exclusively Cuban Spanish and diaspora; 'singar' and its derivatives are among the most characteristic crude terms in Cuban Spanish; minimal recognition outside Cuba and Cuban diaspora communities.

records.definition: Cuban and Caribbean crude slang for penis; one of the most iconic and widely recognized Caribbean Spanish vulgar terms, used throughout the Cuban diaspora and recognizable to many other Spanish speakers.

records.definition: Literally 'bug' or 'creature'; Puerto Rican crude slang for penis; in most other Spanish regions the word means insect or small animal with no sexual connotation.

records.definition: Literally 'man with big eggs (testicles)'; used across Latin America as a general-purpose address term, intensifier, or insult; meaning ranges from 'dude/man' to 'idiot/moron' depending entirely on tone and country.
records.notes: In Chile so thoroughly neutralized it is the default second-person address among friends; in other countries retains more insulting or crude edge; 'huevo' = egg = testicle in Latin American slang; severity wildly variable by country, tone, and relationship; represents one of the most polysemous terms in Latin American colloquial speech.

records.definition: Chilean orthographic variant of 'huevón'; identical in meaning and usage, reflecting vowel-reduction patterns of Chilean colloquial speech.
records.notes: The 'we-' spelling is immediately identifiable as Chilean and signals national identity in itself; functionally interchangeable with 'huevón' but the spelling dominates in Chilean digital communication (texting, social media); outsiders find the orthography confusing precisely because the vowel reduction is so strong.

records.definition: Caribbean slang for a young woman, girlfriend, or attractive girl; diminutive of 'jeva' (girl/girlfriend in Caribbean slang), whose origin may be from 'Eva' or African-derived vocabulary.

records.definition: Sexually aroused; horny; in Venezuela and Colombia almost always sexual in meaning; in Central America can additionally mean angry or intensely agitated.

records.definition: Originally a slur for a gay man; in Caribbean Spanish, especially Venezuelan, substantially neutralized and widely used as a general address term or expletive among friends regardless of sexual orientation.

records.definition: Literally 'his/her mother's cunt'; an extreme Chilean expletive of rage or contempt, functionally equivalent to 'motherfucker.'

The third-person possessive distinguishes it from 'conchetumadre' (second-person direct address). Severity is culturally calibrated: at maximum fury it is maximally offensive, but between male peers at the right register it can signal intense solidarity.

records.definition: Chilean crude slang for a contemptible or stupid person, derived from 'culiar' (to fuck via the ass); also functions as a general intensifier.

Can express pure contempt ('ese culiao nos estafó' = 'that fucker scammed us') or rough affectionate familiarity between male peers depending on tone and context. records.definition: Mexican classist slur for a person regarded as vulgar, tasteless, and culturally inferior, with implicit racial coding and—for women specifically—strong sexual-shame connotations.

The female form 'naca' carries heavier sexual shame implications than the male 'naco.' Etymology contested: possible derivation from 'Totonaco' (indigenous group name) or from reduced 'ignorante.' records.definition: Colombian and Venezuelan slang for a prostitute or sexually promiscuous woman; a highly offensive pejorative for women deemed sexually loose.
