records.notes: The famous Pompeii brothel excavated in the 1st century CE is called the Lupanare; encountered mainly in classical studies, archaeology, and literary contexts; very low general recognition.

records.definition: The standard Italian word for pornography; printed, visual, or digital material depicting sexual acts intended to cause arousal.
Italian compound noun for a pornographic film.
records.notes: Typically written as one word or hyphenated; widely used in journalistic and colloquial contexts.

records.definition: Italian compound for a male pornographic film star; a man who performs in pornography as a named and recognized performer.
records.notes: Compound of porno and divo (idol or male star); the divo component implies celebrity status within the adult industry, distinguishing a recognized performer from an anonymous one.

records.definition: Italian compound for a female pornographic film star; a woman who performs in pornography as a named and recognized performer.
records.notes: Compound of porno and diva (goddess or female star); the diva component carries connotations of glamour and celebrity; slightly more widely recognized than pornodivo, likely due to broader press coverage of female performers.

records.definition: Italian compound for a male actor who performs in pornographic films.
records.notes: More neutral than pornodivo; attore (actor) frames the role as a professional performance occupation rather than stardom; preferred in legal and journalistic contexts.

records.definition: Italian compound for a female actress who performs in pornographic films.
records.notes: More neutral and more frequently encountered than pornodiva in journalism and legal texts; attrice (actress) normalizes the role as a professional occupation.

records.definition: Italian word for an orgy; a sexual gathering involving multiple participants engaging with each other simultaneously.
records.notes: Retains the secondary historical sense of ritual excess in ancient Greco-Roman religious rites (from Greek orgia); the modern sexual sense is overwhelmingly dominant in contemporary usage.

records.definition: Italian term for the lifestyle practice of consensual partner-swapping or swinging among couples.
records.notes: Derived from scambiare (to exchange or swap); the standard Italian term for the swinger lifestyle; used in community self-identification and in sociological and journalistic coverage of the practice.

records.definition: Archaic and literary Italian word for the prostitution trade as an institution or industry.
records.notes: From Latin meretrix (prostitute); appears in legal and historical texts, particularly in debate over the Legge Merlin; rarely encountered in everyday speech; the related verb meretriciare is virtually extinct.

records.definition: Italian phrase for sex tourism; travel undertaken primarily to engage with sex workers, typically exploiting economic disparities.
records.notes: Standard journalistic and legal terminology; appears in Italian criminal code provisions addressing international sexual exploitation and child sex tourism; two-word noun phrase, never contracted to a single compound.

records.definition: The standard everyday Italian word for a condom; a latex sheath worn on the penis during sex to prevent pregnancy and STI transmission.
records.notes: Cognate with French préservatif and Spanish preservativo; the default term in public health campaigns, pharmacy contexts, and everyday speech; neither crude nor strongly clinical.

records.definition: The clinical and formal Italian term for a condom, derived from profilassi (prophylaxis) and emphasizing the disease-prevention function.
records.notes: Preferred in medical literature, pharmacological labeling, and institutional public health communication; the English cognate prophylactic occupies the same register; less common in casual speech than preservativo.

records.definition: Slang for condom, literally 'glove'; refers to the sheath covering the penis during intercourse.
records.notes: Mild euphemism; 'mettere il guanto' (to put on the glove) is a common safer-sex expression; less prevalent than 'preservativo' or 'gomma'.

records.definition: Slang for condom, literally 'hood' or 'cap'; evokes the sheath covering the glans penis.
records.notes: Creates ambiguity with the anatomical sense of 'cappuccio del pene' (foreskin/prepuce); less widely used as condom slang than 'gomma' or 'preservativo'.

records.definition: Diminutive slang for condom, literally 'little hat' or 'little cap'; a gentle, playful euphemism.
records.notes: Less common than 'gomma' or 'preservativo'; the diminutive suffix softens any crude connotation; often used humorously or to avoid bluntness.

records.definition: Common slang for condom, literally 'rubber'; one of the most widespread informal terms for a condom in Italian.
records.notes: Direct parallel to British English 'rubber'; primary everyday meanings are eraser and rubber material, but in a sexual context universally understood as condom.

records.definition: Clinical term for any contraceptive agent or method; used as both noun and adjective in medical and pharmaceutical contexts.
records.notes: Standard medical and pharmaceutical vocabulary; appears on drug packaging, in clinical guidelines, and in sex-education curricula.

records.definition: Standard Italian term for an intrauterine device (IUD); literally 'coil' or 'spiral', describing the device's approximate shape.
records.notes: The dominant lay and clinical term for IUD in Italian; analogous to British English 'coil'; used by gynecologists and patients alike without technical awkwardness.

records.definition: The oral contraceptive pill; 'la pillola' with the definite article is universally understood to mean hormonal birth control.
records.notes: 'Prendere la pillola' (to take the pill) is the standard idiom for being on hormonal contraception; context disambiguates from other pill types.

records.definition: Unprotected sex; sexual intercourse conducted without barrier contraception, especially without a condom.
records.notes: Standard public health and sex-education phrase; literal calque of English 'unprotected sex'; used in STI prevention campaigns and clinical consultations.

records.definition: Surgical sterilization as a permanent contraceptive method; encompasses tubal ligation in women and vasectomy in men.
records.notes: No exact concept slug in registry; mapped to 'contraception' as closest match. Purely clinical term; used in gynecological and urological contexts with no slang or crude dimension.

records.definition: Vasectomy; surgical male sterilization involving severing or occluding the vas deferens to prevent sperm from being present in ejaculate.
records.notes: No exact concept slug in registry; mapped to 'contraception' as closest match. Cognate with English 'vasectomy'; purely clinical and urological in register.

records.definition: Unwanted or unintended pregnancy; a pregnancy that was not planned or desired by the person carrying it.
records.notes: No exact concept slug in registry; mapped to 'contraception' as closest contextual category. Standard clinical and public health phrase appearing in reproductive counseling and policy documents.

records.definition: Acronym for bondage/discipline, dominance/submission, sadism/masochism; used in Italian kink communities identically to its English usage.
records.notes: English acronym adopted wholesale into Italian; pronounced letter by letter; used in Italian media, academic sexology, and online kink communities without modification.

records.definition: The sexual practice of physically restraining a partner with rope, cuffs, or other materials; used in Italian identically to English.
records.notes: Direct English loanword; native Italian alternatives ('legatura erotica', 'imbragatura') exist but are rarely used in kink contexts; the English term dominates in Italian BDSM communities.

records.definition: Sexual or BDSM domination; the dominant role in a power-exchange dynamic, implying control over a submissive partner.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'domination'; polysemous across political, military, and psychological contexts; recognition_pct reflects the proportion who associate it with the sexual/BDSM sense.

records.definition: Submission in a BDSM context; the act of yielding power and control to a dominant partner within a power-exchange dynamic.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'submission'; covers general submission in non-sexual contexts as well; recognition_pct reflects proportion understanding the BDSM-specific sense.

records.definition: Sadomasochism; sexual arousal from both inflicting and receiving pain, humiliation, or subjugation.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'sadomasochism'; well established in Italian clinical sexology (DSM/ICD translations) and popular culture; often abbreviated 'SM' in Italian discourse.

records.definition: Sadism; sexual or psychological gratification derived from inflicting pain, humiliation, or suffering on another person.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'sadism'; derived from the Marquis de Sade; used in clinical psychology, criminology, and popular discourse; high recognition due to broad cultural familiarity.

records.definition: Masochism; sexual gratification derived from experiencing pain, humiliation, or subjugation.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'masochism'; derived from Leopold von Sacher-Masoch; used colloquially beyond sexual contexts ('sei un masochista!' = 'you're a glutton for punishment!').

records.definition: Fetishism; sexual arousal triggered by a specific object, body part, or material not typically considered inherently sexual.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'fetishism'; polysemous — covers religious fetishism (animism) and commodity fetishism (Marxist economics) as well; context disambiguates the sexual sense.

records.definition: Voyeurism; sexual gratification derived from secretly observing others engaged in intimate or sexual behavior.
records.notes: Loanword from French via English; used clinically in Italian DSM/ICD translations and in popular culture, including non-sexual usage for fascination with others' private lives.

records.definition: Exhibitionism; the paraphilia of deriving sexual gratification from exposing one's body or genitals to unwitting strangers; also used loosely for ostentatious attention-seeking behavior.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'exhibitionism'; Italian usage extends metaphorically to any showy public display (e.g., 'esibizionismo politico') well beyond the clinical sexual-psychiatric sense.

records.definition: An exhibitionist; a person who derives sexual pleasure from exposing themselves to others, or more broadly any attention-seeking show-off.
records.notes: The non-sexual usage (show-off, attention-seeker) is more frequent in everyday Italian than the paraphilia sense; context determines which interpretation applies.

records.definition: A female dominatrix; a woman who takes the dominant role in BDSM activity, often professionally, exercising control over a submissive partner.
records.notes: Italian feminine formation (dominatore → dominatrice); the Latin 'dominatrix' is also used directly in Italian BDSM communities; both forms co-exist comfortably.

records.definition: A submissive person in a BDSM dynamic who yields control to a dominant partner; also the standard Italian adjective for 'meek' or 'compliant' in non-sexual contexts.
records.notes: Dual meaning: ordinary adjective (quiet, compliant) and BDSM-specific noun for the submissive role; recognition_pct reflects those who associate it with the kink sense.

records.definition: A riding crop or small whip used in BDSM impact play; literally 'little whip' or 'riding switch', primarily an equestrian term repurposed in kink contexts.
records.notes: Primary meaning is equestrian (horse-riding crop); in BDSM discourse it specifically denotes the short implement used for striking in dominant/submissive play; context determines sense.

records.definition: Japanese rope bondage art practiced in Western BDSM communities for erotic and aesthetic purposes.
records.notes: Loanword from Japanese; 'kinbaku' is the stricter Japanese term for erotic rope bondage; shibari is the broader Western BDSM usage. Recognized mainly in Italian kink subculture.

records.definition: The sexual practice of inserting an entire hand or fist into a partner's vagina or anus.
records.notes: English loanword fully absorbed into Italian sexual vocabulary; no competing native Italian term exists.

records.definition: A sexual act in which one person urinates on another for erotic purposes.
records.notes: English loanword preferred over the Italian calque 'doccia d'oro'; better known in Italian slang contexts than the clinical 'urofilia'.

records.definition: Sexual activity involving exactly three participants; the Italian term for a threesome.
records.notes: Derived from 'trio'; sounds more clinical or formal than English 'threesome'; 'menage à trois' (French loanword) also common in Italian. 'Triolismo' is also used non-sexually in music (a musical trio).

records.definition: Clinical term for any persistent pattern of sexual arousal centered on atypical objects, situations, or individuals.
records.notes: Direct Italian cognate of the Greek-derived clinical term; plural 'parafilie' equally common; recognized mainly by clinicians, students, and kink-community members.

records.definition: Clinical term for primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children.
records.notes: Ubiquitous in Italian legal and media discourse; very high recognition driven by high-profile criminal cases and public-awareness campaigns. Italian law criminalizes acts under art. 600-bis et seq. of the Codice Penale.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or sexual acts performed with a human corpse.
records.notes: Recognized primarily from criminal cases, horror media, and psychology curricula; the clinical register dominates because the act itself is so extreme that slang has not developed around it.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to animals, distinct from the behavioral term 'bestialità'.
records.notes: Italian criminal law (art. 544-ter Codice Penale) references 'atti sessuali con animali', giving 'zoofilia' a legal as well as clinical standing. Italian usage tends to prefer 'zoofilia' over 'bestialità' for the paraphilia as an orientation.

records.definition: Sexual contact or intercourse between a human and a non-human animal; the behavioral act, distinct from the attraction-oriented 'zoofilia'.
records.notes: Carries archaic moral overtones (general brutishness) beyond its sexual meaning; the sexual meaning is primary in modern usage; has partial religious/legal framing from historical canon law.

records.definition: Sexual arousal or gratification associated with feces or defecation.
records.notes: Recognized mainly through clinical psychology literature and internet subculture; rarely surfaces in mainstream Italian media; the crude act is more culturally taboo than the clinical label.

records.definition: Sexual arousal or gratification associated with urine or urination; the clinical term contrasting with the slang 'golden shower'.
records.notes: The English slang 'golden shower' is more widely recognized in Italian than the native clinical term 'urofilia'; niche recognition outside medical and kink communities.

records.definition: The kink in which a person derives erotic arousal from their partner having sex with others; English gerund used as-is in Italian BDSM and online discourse.
records.notes: The English gerund form is preferred in Italian kink discourse over native constructions ('far portare le corna'); reflects internet-culture importation of Anglophone kink vocabulary into Italian usage.

records.definition: A consenting cuckold; a man who knowingly allows or encourages his partner to have sex with others for mutual erotic pleasure.
records.notes: 'Cornuto' (lit. 'horned') is the classic Italian insult for a cuckolded man; adding 'consenziente' (consenting) reclaims and reframes the insult as a kink self-identifier. The two-word phrase is the standard Italian way to distinguish the kink from the insult.

records.definition: A person who performs striptease dances for an audience, typically in a club setting, in exchange for payment.
records.notes: Gender-neutral in form (same ending for male and female performers); derived from 'spogliarello' (strip act) + '-ista' (agent suffix); slightly more neutral in register than English 'stripper'; peak recognition is modestly higher reflecting mid-20th-century cabaret culture when the term was more prominent.

records.definition: The act of performing an erotic dance involving the progressive removal of clothing for an audience.
records.notes: English-French loanword fully naturalized in Italian; 'spogliarello' exists as a native synonym but 'striptease' dominates in contemporary usage; universally recognized.

records.definition: An erotic dance performed by a performer directly on or facing a seated client's lap, often involving simulated sexual contact.
records.notes: English loanword used unchanged in Italian; no native Italian equivalent has emerged; 'ballo erotico' is used in formal or legal contexts but 'lap dance' dominates in practice.

records.definition: A vibrating device used for sexual stimulation, typically of the clitoris or other erogenous zones.
records.notes: Standard Italian translation of 'vibrator'; broadly recognized and not considered highly taboo; younger Italian speakers also use the anglicism 'vibe' colloquially.

records.definition: A penis-shaped object designed for sexual penetration or stimulation, not intended to be worn.
records.notes: No widely-used native Italian equivalent; 'fallo' (phallus) exists as an archaic/literary alternative but is rarely used for the sex toy; 'dildo' has been borrowed wholesale.

records.definition: A dildo mounted in a wearable harness enabling the wearer to perform penetrative sex; used in lesbian sex, pegging, and BDSM contexts.
records.notes: English loanword used as-is in Italian BDSM and lesbian communities; clinical Italian uses 'imbragatura con dildo' or 'imbragatura fallica'; 'pegging' is increasingly used in Italian for the act of a woman penetrating a male partner with one.

records.definition: A paraphilia characterized by sexual arousal from feet or footwear.
records.notes: Literal Italian calque of 'foot fetish'; widely understood; Italy has a historically documented association with this fetish in early sexological literature (Binet, Freud), giving it cultural salience.

records.definition: Sexual arousal triggered by clothing or garments as objects; clothing fetishism as a specific subtype of object fetishism.
records.notes: 'Abiti' means clothing/garments; broader than lingerie fetishism ('feticismo della biancheria intima'); encompasses uniforms, leather, latex, and fabric generally; niche recognition outside kink and psychology communities.

records.definition: A ring-shaped device worn at the base of the penis to restrict venous outflow and prolong or enhance erection.
records.notes: Literal Italian translation; the anglicism 'cockring' (single word) is common in Italian kink retail and online contexts; 'anello fallico' appears in some clinical product descriptions.

records.definition: To make love; the canonical Italian romantic euphemism for sexual intercourse, emphasizing emotional intimacy.
records.notes: Universal Italian phrase; borrowed from French 'faire l'amour'; entirely positive and affectionate in connotation; the most socially acceptable way to refer to sex in mixed or formal company.

records.definition: To go to bed together; Italian circumlocution implying sexual activity by referencing a shared bed rather than naming the act.
records.english_term: to sleep together / to go to bed together
records.notes: Very common Italian euphemism; 'insieme' (together) emphasizes mutuality and consent; slightly more explicit in implication than 'fare l'amore' but still firmly non-explicit; universally understood.

records.definition: To be in a relationship; Italian phrase for being a romantic couple, which implies but does not name sexual activity.
records.english_term: to be together / to be an item
records.notes: Primarily a relationship-status declaration rather than a sexual act descriptor; sexual implication is secondary and contextually inferred; 'approximate' translation quality because English 'to be together' is slightly less definitive than Italian 'stare insieme', which implies an established, named couple status.

records.definition: To be in an ongoing romantic or sexual relationship; frequently implies a secret or extramarital liaison, though context determines whether the relationship is licit or illicit.
records.notes: Ambiguity is intrinsic: can describe a legitimate dating relationship or an extramarital one. The vagueness is part of its appeal as a euphemism.

records.definition: To have a romantic or sexual fling; more clearly implies a brief, often extramarital liaison than 'avere una storia', with the framing of an exciting adventure.
records.notes: 'Avventura' (adventure) casts infidelity as thrilling and temporary, softening its moral weight. Stronger implication of extramarital context than 'avere una storia'.

records.definition: To have a flirtation; a light, playful, non-committed romantic or sexual exchange stopping well short of intercourse.
records.notes: 'Flirt' is a loanword (from French via English); implies predominantly verbal and social teasing with minimal physical contact. Less serious than 'avventura'.

records.definition: To be sexually unfaithful to a romantic partner; the standard Italian verb for infidelity, literally meaning 'to betray'.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'to betray' in any context; in romantic discourse the sexual reading dominates so strongly that non-sexual uses require explicit clarification.

records.definition: To cuckold one's partner; the active Italian idiom for cheating on a partner, from the pan-Mediterranean tradition of placing symbolic cuckold's horns on the betrayed person.
records.notes: Refers to the cheater's act, not the victim's state; distinguished from 'portare le corna'. The corna gesture (index and pinky extended) is the most widely used Italian insult gesture, mocking the cuckolded party.

records.definition: To be cheated on by one's partner; the Italian idiom for being cuckolded, evoking the image of the betrayed party wearing symbolic horns.
records.notes: The passive counterpart to 'mettere le corna'. Does not carry the modern English kink connotation of 'cuckolding'; in Italian it is purely about non-consensual betrayal and public humiliation.

records.definition: To consummate the marriage; the first act of sexual intercourse following a wedding, historically required for the marriage to be legally and canonically valid under both civil and Catholic canon law.
records.notes: Retains strong religious-legal framing; Catholic canon law (Can. 1061) still formally recognizes non-consummation as grounds for a declaration of nullity. Still in active legal and formal use.

records.definition: To satisfy a sexual craving; literally 'to remove the urge', used as a colloquial euphemism for having sex specifically to relieve built-up sexual tension.
records.notes: Frames sex instrumentally as tension-relief rather than intimacy. 'Voglia' implies urgency and appetite. Can describe non-sexual cravings (food, etc.) but the sexual reading is strongly implied in appropriate context.

records.definition: To satisfy (sexual) desire; a more formal or literary euphemism for engaging in sexual activity to fulfill longing.
records.notes: More elevated register than 'togliersi la voglia'; appears in literary and romantic contexts. 'Desiderio' alone frequently implies sexual longing in Italian without further specification.

records.definition: To tease or titillate sexually; to provoke arousal through playful, suggestive behavior, suggestive remarks, or light physical contact.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'to poke, prod, or tease' (also used for food and conversation); the sexual sense is a natural extension and heavily context-dependent. Not exclusively sexual.

records.definition: Euphemism for sexual intercourse; literally 'to do things', functioning as a vague placeholder for any explicitly sexual act.
records.notes: Extremely broad avoidance phrase; universally understood in context. Common across age groups in spoken Italian. The plural 'cose' (things) adds further deliberate vagueness.

records.definition: To have sex; the single most common Italian euphemism for sexual intercourse, literally 'to do it'.
records.notes: The clitic 'lo' (it) refers to the contextually understood act. Direct equivalent of English 'to do it'. Completely transparent to Italian speakers across all registers.

records.definition: Euphemism for the sex act or, secondarily, for genitalia; literally 'the thing', used to avoid naming either the act or the anatomy.
records.notes: Deeply ambiguous: 'la cosa' can denote the sex act itself or female genitalia depending on context. The most minimal avoidance term in Italian sexual discourse.

records.definition: For a man to show off or preen in order to attract sexual or romantic attention; to deliberately present himself as attractive to prospective partners.
records.notes: Reflexive construction ('darsi' = to give oneself); male form. Often carries a mildly ironic or deprecatory tone implying vanity. Paired with the female form 'darsi bella'. The self-presentation is deliberate, unlike the effortless quality implied by English 'charisma'.

records.definition: For a woman to show off or preen in order to attract sexual or romantic attention; to deliberately present herself as attractive to prospective partners.
records.notes: Female form of 'darsi bello'; same reflexive construction. Slightly more frequent in usage than the male form, reflecting cultural expectations around female self-presentation for romantic purposes.

records.definition: To enjoy sexual activity; to have a good time sexually; literally 'to enjoy it' with a reflexive intensifier emphasizing personal pleasure.
records.notes: The reflexive particle 'se' combined with object 'la' marks this as personally felt enjoyment. Not exclusively sexual but in suggestive contexts the sexual reading dominates. Implies active, willing participation.

records.definition: To have fun; used as a very mild and deniable euphemism for sexual activity, especially casual or non-committal sex.
records.notes: Primary meaning is simply 'to have fun' in any sense; the sexual reading is entirely context-dependent and deniable. Often deployed in past tense ('ci siamo divertiti') as a winking reference. Minimal commitment to sexual content.

records.definition: To engage in sexual play or activity; literally 'to play the games', used as a euphemism for foreplay, sex games, or full intercourse depending on context.
records.notes: 'Giochi' (games) frames sex as ludic and recreational. Less universally recognized than 'farlo'; more common in certain regional or generational registers. Implies playfulness and mutual willingness.

records.definition: Sexual inclinations or tendencies; used historically in Italian medical, journalistic, and official discourse as a polite euphemism primarily for homosexuality.
records.notes: Typically appeared as 'inclinazioni sessuali' or alone with understood sexual meaning. Peak usage 1950s–1970s in Italian newspapers and medical writing. Now archaic as a homosexuality euphemism; younger speakers would only recognize the general Italian meaning of 'inclinations'.

records.definition: Masturbation; literally 'solitary vice', the traditional Italian Catholic-inflected euphemism for self-pleasuring.
records.notes: A classic moralistic framing that encodes masturbation as both sinful ('vizio') and shamefully private ('solitario'). Peaked in pre-sexual-revolution Catholic discourse. Still widely recognized but sounds archaic or comical to younger speakers today.

records.definition: The third sex; a historical Italian term for homosexuals, derived from 19th-century German sexology (das dritte Geschlecht), applied loosely to gay men, lesbians, and intersex individuals.
records.notes: Borrowing from Karl Heinrich Ulrichs' and Magnus Hirschfeld's framework. Used in Italian popular and medical writing through the mid-20th century. Now archaic; occasionally extended to intersex or gender-nonconforming persons. Not offensive in the way of a slur but reads as clinically outdated.

records.definition: To have sex; literally 'to change the sheets', implying the sheets became soiled or disheveled as a result of sexual activity.
records.notes: Humor derives from the mundane domestic act standing in for vigorous sex. A moderately dated expression; more common in older generations. No direct English equivalent idiom with the same implied structure.

records.definition: To have sex; literally 'to remake the bed', implying the bed was left in disarray after sexual activity and now requires tidying.
records.notes: Similar mechanism to 'cambiare le lenzuola': implication of sex through subsequent domestic act. Slightly rarer and more dated than its companion idiom. No direct English equivalent idiom.

records.definition: Fornication; sexual intercourse between two people not married to each other, a term freighted with explicit Catholic moral condemnation.
records.notes: Derived from Latin 'fornicatio'. Primarily encountered in Catholic theology, historical legal texts, and literary Italian. Rarely in casual speech; its use immediately signals a religious or archaic register. The Italian Church's dominance historically made this term far more charged than its English counterpart.

records.definition: To fornicate; to engage in sexual intercourse outside of marriage, with the same inherent religious and moral condemnation as the noun form.
records.notes: Verb form of 'fornicazione'; identical register and usage profile. Appears in Catholic theology, historical legal contexts, and literary Italian. Occasionally used with ironic or comedic intent in modern speech precisely because of its archaism.

records.definition: The practice of living without moral or sexual restraint; libertinism or habitual sexual licentiousness as a deliberate lifestyle.
records.notes: Derives from 'libertino' (libertine); implies systematic philosophical rejection of moral constraints, not merely occasional excess; used in both religious-moral polemics and secular literary contexts from the 17th century onward.

records.definition: A woman who cohabits with a man without being his legal wife, holding subordinate social and legal status; a concubine.
records.notes: Recognized from biblical and classical Latin contexts; still used in historical and theological discussions; the institution was legally recognized in pre-unification Italian states and debated in canon law; the male equivalent 'concubino' exists but is rarely attested.

records.definition: The institutionalized practice or legal condition of a man living with a concubine; concubinage as a social and legal arrangement distinct from both marriage and prostitution.
records.notes: More abstract and institutional than 'concubina'; found in historical legal texts, canon law discussions, and civil law treatises; rarely used in everyday modern Italian; the Italian Civil Code of 1942 did not recognize concubinage, pushing the term into historical register.

records.definition: Sexual attraction to or activity with adolescent males; in 19th-century Italian medical-legal usage, also the standard clinical term for male homosexuality in general regardless of partner age.
records.notes: In 19th-century Italian sexology and criminology (Lombroso, Tamassia), 'pederasta' was the clinical label for a gay man with no age-specific restriction; the term progressively narrowed to the adult-minor sense across the 20th century; in modern Italian 'pederastia' is understood as sexual abuse of boys, distinct from 'omosessualità'; a significant semantic narrowing over 150 years obscures the word's historical breadth.

records.definition: Clinical and archaic term for vulva-to-vulva genital friction between two women; the historical medical term for what is now called tribbing or scissoring.
records.notes: Used in 19th-century Italian sexological literature; largely replaced in modern slang by 'tribbing' and in everyday speech by 'sesso lesbico'; retained in academic and historical contexts; the practitioner was historically called 'tribade'; derived from Greek 'tribein' (to rub); Lombroso discussed 'tribadismo' as a form of 'inversione sessuale' among women.

records.definition: Sexual inversion; the 19th-century Italian sexological term for homosexuality, framing same-sex attraction as a reversal of the normal heterosexual instinct.
records.notes: Andrea Tamassia's 1878 article 'Sull'inversione dell'istinto sessuale' introduced the term to Italian medical literature, paralleling Krafft-Ebing's German framing; the model implied that a homosexual man possessed a female psyche in a male body (congenital neurological anomaly rather than vice); replaced by 'omosessualità' across the 20th century; closely associated with Lombrosian criminal anthropology.

records.definition: Sexual perversion; any sexual impulse, desire, or practice deviating from heterosexual procreative norms, framed in moral, religious, or historical clinical terms.
records.notes: Common word in modern Italian but its specifically sexual-pathological register is archaic or literary; 'perversione sessuale' was the standard Italian translation of Krafft-Ebing's clinical categories; replaced in clinical usage by 'parafilia'; in contemporary colloquial Italian 'perversione' often functions as ironic mild praise ('che perversione!' = 'how kinky!'), marking a register shift from condemnation to humor.

records.definition: Venereal pleasures; an archaic literary phrase for the pleasures of sexual activity, derived from Venus, the Roman goddess of love.
records.notes: Multi-word phrase typical of 16th–18th-century Italian prose and poetry; 'venerico' (from Latin venereus, relating to Venus) was the standard adjective for anything pertaining to sexual pleasure; 'malattia venerea' (venereal disease) survives as a set phrase in formal Italian; the phrase sounds archaic-ornate to modern ears and is unlikely to be used sincerely outside historical quotation.

records.definition: Crime against decency; the Italian Penal Code category covering sexual offenses against public morality, including exhibitionism, obscene acts, and related violations of 'pudore' (modesty).
records.notes: Title IX of Book II of the Codice Rocco (1930) was headed 'Dei delitti contro la moralità pubblica e il buon costume'; 'delitti contro il pudore' formed a specific subcategory protecting 'pudore' as the legal value; Law 66/1996 reclassified sexual offenses as crimes against the person rather than against public morality, effectively retiring this framing and replacing 'pudore' with 'libertà sessuale' as the protected interest.

records.definition: Obscenity; sexually explicit or morally offensive material, speech, or behavior that violates standards of public decency.
records.notes: Common Italian word still in everyday use; both a live legal term (Arts. 528–529 Codice Penale define 'atti osceni' and 'scritti osceni') and a colloquial intensifier ('ha detto delle oscenità' = he said filthy things); the specifically sexual-legal register feels archaic but the word itself is not dated; no recognition drop expected.

records.definition: In Catholic moral theology, any sinful sexual emission; specifically nocturnal emission (polluzione notturna) but extended to masturbation and any non-procreative ejaculation outside the conjugal act.
records.notes: From Latin 'pollutio' (ritual defilement); the sexual-theological sense was primary for centuries; in modern Italian 'inquinamento' has displaced it in the environmental sense, so younger speakers encountering 'polluzione' in historical texts may misread it as environmental; 'polluzione notturna' (wet dream) survives as a technical phrase in medical and theological Italian; the moral gravity in Catholic tradition ranked it among the gravest sins against the sixth commandment.

records.definition: Softness, moral laxness, and effeminate weakness; in Italian classical and humanist writing, the sexual and moral degeneracy associated with luxury, ease, and unmartial character.
records.notes: Classical Italian moral concept linking sexual passivity and effeminacy to broader political and civic decline; Machiavelli uses 'mollezza' as a vice of decadent rulers contrasted with 'virtù'; the sexual component is always implied — penetrability and passive submission are the physical correlates — but 'mollezza' is never exclusively sexual; implies that luxury saps the masculine energy required for political and military greatness.

records.definition: Effeminacy; the quality of a man displaying feminine mannerisms, appearance, or character, historically carrying implications of sexual passivity, moral weakness, and homosexuality.
records.notes: Standard Italian noun for effeminacy; not a slur per se (unlike 'frocio' or 'checca') but functions as an insult in contexts framing effeminacy as sexually or morally shameful; in classical Italian moral thought 'effeminatezza' was simultaneously a sexual failing (the passive role) and a political one (compromising civic and martial virtue); the concept is now partially reclaimed in Italian LGBTQ+ culture.

records.definition: Softening, moral weakening, or emasculation; the process by which a man becomes effeminate, sexually passive, and morally inert through excess comfort or corrupting influences.
records.notes: Literally 'softening' (from 'rammollire,' to soften); in archaic Italian moral-political discourse implied both sexual passivity and civic-military degeneration; 'rammollimento cerebrale' (cerebral softening, i.e., late-stage syphilis or dementia) is now more familiar than the moral-sexual sense; the word sounds clinical or unintentionally comic to modern speakers when used in a sexual-moral register.

records.definition: Immodesty, unchastity, and sexual licentiousness; the quality of being sexually immodest or morally unrestrained; violation of the virtue of pudicizia (chastity).
records.notes: From Latin 'impudicitia'; a standard term in Catholic moral theology for sexual immorality short of the gravest offenses; specifically the vice opposed to the cardinal feminine virtue of 'pudicizia'; used in confessional manuals, moral theology textbooks, and ecclesiastical legal proceedings; rarely heard in secular modern Italian outside historical or theological contexts.

records.definition: Immodest, unchaste, and sexually licentious; as noun, a person who violates sexual and moral decency norms; lewd and shameless in conduct.
records.notes: Adjective and noun from Latin 'impudicus'; closer to 'unchaste' or 'immodest' than to the cruder English 'lewd'; describes a character trait rather than a specific act; notably in Roman usage 'impudicus' specifically meant the passive partner in male-male sex, carrying particular shame; this anatomical specificity was lost as the word generalized across centuries of Italian usage.

records.definition: Moral corruption; in sexual contexts, the seduction or debasement of a person's morals through sexual vice; also a specific Penal Code offense involving the sexual corruption of minors.
records.notes: 'Corruzione di minorenne' (corruption of a minor) remains a specific offense under Italian law; the primary modern meaning is bribery (Arts. 318–319 Codice Penale), making the sexual-moral sense a secondary archaic register; in literary usage implies active debasement of another's character through sexual influence rather than one's own self-indulgence, hence the distinction from 'libertinaggio.'

records.definition: Seduction; the act of persuading or enticing someone to engage in sexual activity, especially outside marriage; historically a criminal offense when targeting a young person with false promises of marriage.
records.notes: 'Seduzione con promessa di matrimonio' (seduction with promise of marriage) was a crime under Art. 526 of the Codice Rocco, repealed 1981; very common word still active across romantic, advertising, and culinary contexts ('seduzione gastronomica'); the sexual-legal sense is archaic but the word is not; mapped to the 'debaucher' concept because seduction is precisely the act of leading another into licentiousness, even though 'seduzione' is an act noun rather than an agent noun.

records.definition: Brothel; an establishment where sexual services are sold; an archaic and literary synonym for 'bordello' or 'casa di tolleranza.'
records.notes: From Latin 'prostibulum'; used in literary, historical, and journalistic contexts; more elevated register than 'bordello' (common) or 'casino' (crude slang); the Merlin Law (Law 75/1958) closed Italy's state-licensed brothels ('case chiuse'), after which 'postribolo' became entirely historical in application; the word still appears in literary and political rhetoric as a metaphor for moral corruption.

records.definition: A man financially kept by a wealthier woman, typically an older one, in exchange for companionship and sexual access; a male escort or sex worker who services female clients.
records.notes: Direct French loanword (from 'gigolette,' a female dancehall girl); fully naturalized in Italian; invariable in the plural (i gigolò); carries connotations of elegant parasitism and studied charm rather than street-level prostitution; the female counterpart in Italian is 'mantenuta' (kept woman), though the asymmetric social judgment between the two terms is considerable.

records.definition: A gallant encounter; an archaic euphemism for a romantic or sexual assignation, implying elegance and discretion around an illicit or prearranged amorous meeting.
records.notes: 'Galante' in 18th-century Italian usage implied refined courtship and amorous pursuit; 'avventura galante,' 'conversazione galante,' and 'incontro galante' were synonymous circumlocutions for affairs or sexual meetings in aristocratic culture; the word set is now heavily dated and reads as comic if used sincerely in modern Italian; 'galante' itself has narrowed to mean merely 'chivalrous' in contemporary usage, losing most of its erotic charge.

records.definition: Carnal diversion; an archaic euphemistic phrase for sexual activity framed as a bodily recreation or pastime of the flesh.
records.notes: 'Svago' (diversion, recreation, hobby) paired with 'carnale' (of the flesh) produces a distancing euphemism that frames sex as a trivial bodily amusement; typical of 18th-century and early 19th-century prose registers; sounds comic or deliberately ironic to modern Italian speakers; very low current recognition among speakers under 50, primarily encountered in historical fiction or period drama subtitles.

records.definition: A prearranged romantic or sexual meeting, especially a clandestine one; French loanword used in Italian to imply discretion and sophistication around an amorous appointment.
records.notes: French loanword used identically in Italian and English; always written with hyphen in formal Italian; French pronunciation preserved; implies secrecy and elegance absent from the plain Italian 'appuntamento'; sexual implication is contextual rather than inherent; increasingly displaced by 'appuntamento' or the English loanword 'date' in modern Italian, especially among younger speakers.

records.definition: In 18th-century Italian aristocratic society, a married woman's publicly acknowledged male companion and escort — not a secret lover but an institutionalized courtly attendant who accompanied her socially and typically had an implied or openly tolerated sexual relationship with her, with the husband's tacit or explicit approval.
records.notes: Uniquely Italian 18th-century institution with no direct English equivalent; the cicisbeo (also called 'cavalier servente') was socially normalized in Piedmontese, Venetian, and Neapolitan aristocratic culture; crucially distinguished from a secret lover or gigolo by being publicly acknowledged and institutionally sanctioned, often with the husband's formal consent documented in marriage contracts; etymology disputed (possibly from 'cici,' trinket, or onomatopoeia for whispering flirtation); declined with Napoleonic reforms and the Risorgimento's bourgeois moral reconfiguration.

records.definition: A kept woman; a woman financially maintained by a wealthy man, typically outside of marriage, in exchange for sexual availability and exclusive companionship.
records.notes: Feminine past participle of 'mantenere' (to maintain/support) used as a standalone noun; distinguished from a prostitute by exclusivity and ongoing financial arrangement rather than per-act payment; the male equivalent 'mantenuto' (kept man) carries substantially stronger social stigma; the word still circulates in contemporary Italian journalism and tabloid culture; its female counterpart for the male role is 'gigolò,' itself a French loanword.

records.definition: Italian verbification of 'sexting'; to exchange sexually explicit messages or images via digital device.
records.notes: Formed by appending Italian infinitive suffix -are to English 'sext'; typical of Italian internet morphology. Less common than the noun 'sexting'.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian for the practice of exchanging sexually explicit messages or images via mobile device or messaging application.
records.notes: More widely recognized than the verbified form 'sextare'; appears in Italian law and mainstream media coverage; fully naturalized in Italian press spelling.

records.definition: English loanword for nude or sexually explicit self-photographs shared digitally; broadly understood across Italian internet culture.
records.notes: Dominates over native alternatives such as 'foto nude'; frequently appears in Italian headlines about revenge porn and sextortion cases.

records.definition: Italian phrase meaning 'to send nudes'; the act of digitally transmitting nude or sexually explicit photographs to a recipient.
records.notes: Native Italian construction; preferred in journalistic and legal contexts where the English loanword 'nudes' is considered too informal.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian for the non-consensual distribution of intimate or sexually explicit images, typically by a former partner as retaliation.
records.notes: Codified in Italian criminal law (art. 612-ter c.p.) under the formal label 'diffusione illecita di immagini o video sessualmente espliciti'; 'revenge porn' nonetheless dominates public and journalistic usage.

records.definition: AI-generated pornographic content that superimposes a real person's likeness onto sexually explicit footage without their consent.
records.notes: 'Deepfake' is an English loanword; 'erotico' is the Italian adjective. Conceptually distinct from revenge porn in that imagery is synthetically generated rather than originally captured; no registry entry exists for this technology-specific category.

records.definition: Abbreviation of 'webcam'; in Italian internet subculture denotes the practice of live sexual or erotic performance via webcam for a paying audience.
records.notes: Used as noun ('fare la cam' = to do cam work) and attributively; less role-specific than 'camgirl' or 'camboy'.

records.definition: English loanword for a woman who performs sexual or erotic acts live via webcam for a paying online audience.
records.notes: Fully integrated into Italian internet vocabulary; also spelled 'cam girl' (two words); the female-coded counterpart of 'camboy'.

records.definition: English loanword for a man who performs sexual or erotic acts live via webcam for a paying online audience.
records.notes: Less recognized than 'camgirl', reflecting the smaller but growing male webcam performer market; also spelled 'cam boy'. The registry entry cam_performer specifies female, so webcam_sex_work used as the gender-neutral fit.

records.definition: The subscription-based content platform widely associated in Italian discourse with sexual content creation and digital sex work.
records.notes: Used as both proper noun and common noun in Italian; in popular usage almost universally implies adult content regardless of the creator's actual category.

records.definition: Italian internet slang phrase meaning 'to work as an OnlyFans adult-content creator'; 'OFer' blends the abbreviation OF with the English agent suffix -er.
records.notes: Neologism circulating primarily in Italian social media discourse; lower recognition than 'OnlyFans' itself; the construction implies sexual content specifically.

records.definition: English loanword for a man who is excessively deferential or servile toward a woman in hope of sexual or romantic approval.
records.notes: Peak usage around 2020 driven by TikTok and Twitch culture; still in circulation but declining as the meme ages; used identically to its English source.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian far-right and manosphere communities for an emasculated or politically submissive man.
records.notes: Primarily a political insult in Italian internet discourse; the kink sense is secondary. Peak around 2016 aligned with its spread through anglophone alt-right communities into Italian equivalents.

records.definition: English loanword for an involuntary celibate: a man who attributes his inability to find sexual or romantic partners to women's choices and systemic unfairness rather than his own behavior.
records.notes: Widely covered in Italian media during 2018–2020 following high-profile attacks linked to incel ideology; peak recognition coincided with that media cycle.

records.definition: Italian compound for a professional performer in pornographic films; direct equivalent of English 'pornstar'.
records.notes: Also written 'porno star'; gendered forms 'pornoattrice' (female) and 'pornoattore' (male) exist but 'pornostar' is the dominant unisex form. No dedicated registry entry for pornographic performer; pornography_industry is the closest available slug.

records.definition: English acronym ('Mother I'd Like to Fuck') used in Italian as an objectifying label for a sexually attractive woman who is a mother.
records.notes: Established as a pornographic content-category label in Italian; popularized internationally by the 1999 film American Pie; used colloquially and in adult content tagging.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian gay communities for a young, slender, smooth-skinned gay man projecting a boyish aesthetic.
records.notes: No native Italian equivalent; used directly in Italian LGBTQ+ discourse and pornographic taxonomy. Part of the anglophone gay male body-type taxonomy (bear, otter, cub, wolf) imported wholesale into Italian subculture. No registry entry exists.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian gay communities for a large, stocky, heavily hairy or bearded gay man projecting a traditionally masculine persona.
records.notes: No native Italian equivalent; borrowed directly from anglophone gay subculture. Companion terms twink, otter, cub, and wolf are also used in Italian without translation. No registry entry exists.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian internet culture for a sexually attractive, dominant, and typically older man; in BDSM contexts specifically the caretaker-dominant role in a DD/lg dynamic.
records.notes: The broader colloquial sense (attractive older man) predominates in Italian social media; the narrower BDSM sense is understood within kink communities. Italian 'papà' carries no sexual connotation.

records.definition: English loanword for a stylish, sexually attractive, and typically financially successful older man who projects effortless confidence and swagger.
records.notes: Primarily recognized among younger English-literate Italians through US social media; considerably less established than 'daddy' in Italian usage; adoption driven by pop-culture imports.

records.definition: Abbreviation of Japanese 'netorare' (寝取られ); in Italian anime and hentai communities, the genre depicting one's romantic partner being seduced or taken by another person, experienced from the betrayed partner's perspective.
records.notes: Cited in this project's instructions as a canonical example of a culturally-specific novel concept; restricted to Italian communities consuming Japanese anime, manga, and hentai. 'Cuckold' is a rough gloss but lacks the specific voyeuristic subjective framing intrinsic to NTR.

records.definition: Japanese loanword for the exaggerated orgasm facial expression — rolled-back eyes, flushed cheeks, protruding tongue — depicted in erotic manga and hentai as a marker of overwhelming pleasure.
records.notes: Briefly crossed into mainstream Italian internet awareness in 2019 via the 'ahegao hoodie' meme; known primarily among Italian anime fandom. No native-language equivalent exists; the English 'ahegao' is itself a Japanese loanword.

records.definition: Japanese loanword used in Italian for sexually explicit animated or illustrated content in Japanese style; the primary Italian term for this category of pornography.
records.notes: In Japanese, 変態 (hentai) means 'pervert' or 'abnormality'; in both Italian and English usage the meaning is restricted entirely to the pornographic animation/illustration sense.

records.definition: English loanword used in Italian for female ejaculation — the expulsion of fluid from the Skene's glands or urethra during intense sexual arousal or orgasm.
records.notes: Preferred over native 'eiaculazione femminile' in pornographic and internet contexts; its ban from certain UK and Australian streaming platforms generated news coverage that raised Italian public recognition.

records.definition: English loanword for the act of ejaculating inside a partner's vagina or anus without a condom, or the visible result of semen leaking out afterward.
records.notes: Primarily encountered in pornographic content taxonomy in Italian; native alternatives 'interno' or 'sborrata interna' exist but 'creampie' dominates in search and tagging contexts.

records.definition: English loanword for the visible external male ejaculation shot in pornographic video, adopted unchanged in Italian online and pornographic subculture.
records.notes: Unmodified English borrowing; recognized primarily by internet-active adults; largely absent from mainstream Italian media.

records.definition: English loanword for the act of ejaculating onto a partner's face, used unchanged in Italian pornographic and online sexual discussion.
records.notes: Shares form with the Italian adjective 'faciale' but in sexual contexts the English borrowing 'facial' is used without modification; context always disambiguates.

records.definition: English loanword for vulva-to-vulva genital friction between two people with vulvas, widely circulated in Italian LGBTQ+ and internet sexual subculture.
records.notes: The scissors-blade leg metaphor is visually transparent, which likely facilitated adoption over native Italian alternatives such as 'fregamento'.

records.definition: English loanword for tribadism; less common in Italian than 'scissoring' and confined to niche LGBTQ+ and pornographic online communities.
records.notes: Derived etymologically from 'tribade' (a classical term for a woman who has sex with women); carries slightly more technical connotations than scissoring in Italian online use.

records.definition: English loanword for the practice of repeatedly approaching orgasm and withdrawing stimulation to prolong arousal and intensify eventual climax; used in Italian kink and online sex communities.
records.notes: The Italian phrase 'controllo dell'orgasmo' exists but is rarely used; 'edging' dominates in Italian online sexual discussion and BDSM subculture.

records.definition: English loanword for extended pornography-assisted edging sessions that produce a dissociative, trance-like state of arousal; very niche in Italian online spaces.
records.notes: Virtually unknown outside Italian-language corners of communities that closely follow English-language hypno-porn or NoFap subcultures; no native Italian equivalent exists.

records.definition: English loanword for a sexual act in which one person is engaged simultaneously or in sequence by multiple partners; widely used in Italian online and pornographic contexts.
records.notes: Among the most thoroughly absorbed English sexual loanwords in Italian; appears in mainstream Italian journalism discussing pornography and internet sexual culture.

records.definition: English loanword for a casual sexual encounter without romantic commitment; dominant in Italian dating-app culture and urban youth discourse.
records.notes: Has largely displaced native Italian expressions such as 'avventura' or 'scopata' in urban youth and social-media contexts; also deployed as a verb ('fare un hookup').

records.definition: Italian phrase for a mobile application used to meet potential sexual or romantic partners, encompassing both dating-oriented apps and explicitly hookup-focused apps.
records.notes: Literal translation is 'meeting app'; mapped to hookup because in Italian popular discourse the sexual and casual-encounter use case dominates the term's connotations; 'app di appuntamenti' is a rarer alternative phrasing.

records.definition: English loanword for a woman who practices financial domination as a BDSM or fetish service, receiving monetary tributes and exercising control over a submissive's finances.
records.notes: Compound of 'fin(ancial)' and 'domme'; used without modification in Italian BDSM online communities; the practice itself is referred to as 'findom' (also borrowed unchanged).

records.definition: A man whose wife or partner is sexually unfaithful; etymologically from Latin for 'horned,' invoking the metaphor of shame-horns placed on the deceived partner.
records.notes: Dual use: literal sexual meaning and a general-purpose insult (analogous to English 'bastard') fully detached from its sexual origin; among the most culturally loaded sexual terms in Italian; the associated hand gesture extends the metaphor into gesture culture.

records.definition: Italian idiom meaning to be sexually unfaithful to one's partner; literally 'to put horns on someone,' naming the act from the cheater's active perspective.
records.notes: Framed from the cheater's side; forms a semantic triplet with 'portare le corna' (victim's state) and 'fare le corna' (the mocking gesture); the horn metaphor derives from cuckoo bird behavior and Roman-era folklore.

records.definition: Italian idiom meaning to be the victim of a partner's infidelity; literally 'to carry the horns,' naming the cuckolded person's shameful condition.
records.notes: Passive/victim perspective counterpart to 'mettere le corna'; the metaphor of carrying an unwanted burden (horns) maps cleanly onto the English passive construction 'to wear the horns.'

records.definition: To perform the hand gesture with index and pinky fingers extended toward someone, either to mock them as a cornuto or—in a completely unrelated use—to ward off the evil eye (malocchio).
records.notes: The sexual-shaming and apotropaic meanings coexist so thoroughly that ambiguity is pervasive; directed at a person it typically means cuckold-shaming, directed outward it means evil-eye protection; the overlap is culturally specific and has no clean English parallel.

records.definition: Sexual honor; specifically, a woman's (and by extension her family's) reputation for sexual purity, functioning as a jealously guarded form of social capital in Mediterranean honor-shame culture.
records.notes: The ordinary Italian word for 'honor' carries a highly specific sexual valence in the honor-shame framework that the English gloss understates; a woman's onore is simultaneously her own and her family's to protect or destroy, with material social consequences.

records.definition: Sexual dishonor; the state of having violated or lost sexual honor, whether through premarital sex, rape, adultery, or perceived sexual looseness, with attendant social ostracism.
records.notes: Historically triggered concrete consequences—family violence, forced marriage, exile—far beyond what the English gloss implies; crucially, a woman could acquire disonore through rape with no agency on her part.

records.definition: Sexual shame; the acute social and emotional distress experienced when one has violated or is perceived to have violated the norms of sexual propriety in an honor-shame culture.
records.notes: The everyday Italian word for 'shame'; in the honor-shame framework it is the internal counterpart to the external sanctions of slut-shaming; 'far vergogna' (to bring shame) is a common construction applied to women's sexual behavior.

records.definition: A shameless person who behaves without regard for sexual propriety; one who has lost or deliberately abandoned vergogna, especially in a sexual context.
records.notes: Adjective or noun; feminine form 'svergognata' carries heavier sexual connotation when applied to women due to the asymmetric honor-shame framework; roughly equivalent to archaic English 'brazen hussy' when used of a woman.

records.definition: A dishonored woman; a female who has lost her sexual honor through premarital sex, rape, adultery, or perceived sexual looseness and is consequently treated as a social outcast.
records.notes: Crucially, a woman could be 'disonorata' through rape with no volitional sexual act on her part, exposing the victim-blaming core of the concept; historically used to justify family violence ('lavare l'onore col sangue').

records.definition: A stain on one's honor; the permanent, indelible mark of sexual disgrace left on an individual and their family by any perceived sexual transgression.
records.notes: The stain metaphor implies irreversibility: unlike a temporary failure, a macchia sull'onore cannot be washed away, only revenged; this framing historically justified honour killings as acts of 'cleansing.'

records.definition: An archaic and literary Italian word for deep shame, infamy, or dishonor, especially of a sexual nature; more severe and formal in register than vergogna.
records.notes: Etymologically related to Latin 'ignominia'; retained today in elevated or deliberately archaizing register; functions as an intensified and publicly visible vergogna implying irremediable social infamy rather than private shame.

records.definition: Sexual jealousy; the possessive emotional response to a partner's real or suspected infidelity, which in the Italian honor-shame framework functions simultaneously as an emotion and as a social obligation for men.
records.notes: The ordinary Italian word for jealousy; in honor-shame culture a man who fails to exhibit gelosia is suspected of being complicit in his own cuckolding; this social obligation of jealousy is the emotional engine of the cornuto complex.

records.definition: Sexual betrayal or infidelity within a committed relationship; encompasses both the act of infidelity and the moral violation of the trust and honor it represents.
records.notes: The ordinary Italian word for 'betrayal'; in sexual discourse it specifically denotes partner infidelity; carries heavier moral weight than English 'cheating' because it explicitly frames infidelity as a breach of honor-code obligation, not merely a personal failing.

records.definition: Adultery; extramarital sexual intercourse committed by a married person, historically a criminal offense in Italy until 1969 and still carrying strong moral weight in honor-shame culture.
records.notes: More specific than fornication (requires at least one party to be married); a criminal offense in Italy until 1969 under a gender-asymmetric law that punished wives but not husbands equally, reflecting the honor-shame framework's legal institutionalization.

records.definition: An adulteress; a woman who commits adultery, typically carrying severe moral condemnation and social consequences within the Italian honor-shame framework.
records.notes: Feminine form of 'adultero'; the asymmetric application of shame means 'adultera' historically triggered far more severe social and legal consequences for women than the masculine form did for men under the same legal code.

records.definition: An adulterer; a married person who has sexual relations outside of marriage, violating the conjugal bond.
records.notes: Registry lacks a dedicated adulterer concept; extramarital_lover is closest available. Adultero denotes the married party who commits the betrayal, not the outside lover.

records.definition: Fidelity; the virtue of sexual and romantic faithfulness to one's partner, especially within marriage, carrying strong moral and religious weight in Italian culture.
records.notes: Mapped to monogamy as closest registry concept; fedeltà names the virtue of faithfulness rather than the structural fact of having one partner. Central to the honor-shame system as the feminine counterpart to male sexual freedom.

records.definition: Infidelity; the state or act of being sexually unfaithful to one's partner, especially within marriage.
records.notes: No dedicated infidelity concept in registry; love_affair is closest available. Infedeltà can describe a single act or a pattern without necessarily implying an ongoing romantic liaison.

records.definition: Bastard; used as a general insult for a contemptible person, or literally to denote a child born outside of marriage.
records.notes: Retains its original literal meaning (illegitimate birth) more strongly in Italian than in English, where it has largely shifted to pure insult; in Italian both senses remain fully active.

records.definition: Illegitimate child; the formal or legal term for a child born outside of marriage, carrying heavy social stigma in the traditional Italian honor-shame framework.
records.notes: Registry has no dedicated illegitimate-birth-status concept; bastard_insult is closest available. Now dated in everyday speech since Italian law abolished the legal distinction in 1975.

records.definition: 'Child of nobody'; a poetic or euphemistic expression for an illegitimate child, emphasizing social abandonment and the absence of a recognized father.
records.notes: Captures the social shame dimension more vividly than the legal term; the 'nobody' framing evokes paternal denial and community exclusion rather than mere legal status.

records.definition: A womanizer; a man who habitually pursues and seduces many women, often described with a tone of grudging admiration rather than pure condemnation.
records.notes: Can be used admiringly in Italian male culture; the double standard encoded here — male promiscuity as prowess, female promiscuity as shame — is central to the honor-shame system.

records.definition: A theatrical admirer who makes exaggerated, dramatically lovestruck displays of romantic interest; literally 'fallen dead', evoking collapsing at the sight of a beautiful person.
records.notes: The theatrical-performative element — publicly dying of desire — is specifically Italian/Mediterranean and has no precise English equivalent. Can be mocking or affectionate. Mapped to suitor as closest registry concept.

records.definition: 'Family wrecker'; a woman who seduces married men and thereby destroys their family units.
records.notes: Always applied to women in traditional usage; encodes the honor-shame expectation that women are responsible for protecting family sanctity. The married man is rarely blamed equivalently. Debaucher is closest registry concept.

records.definition: Lover; a person with whom one is having a romantic or sexual relationship, typically implying an ongoing and often illicit or extramarital liaison.
records.notes: Italian amante is more commonly used and less literary-sounding than English 'lover'; its surface neutrality masks strong honor-shame implications when the relationship is extramarital.

records.definition: A kept woman; a woman financially supported by a man outside of marriage in exchange for sexual availability and companionship.
records.notes: Always feminine in Italian; carries social stigma in the honor-shame framework while simultaneously implying a pragmatic arrangement. Slightly dated as a term but still widely recognized.

records.definition: 'Woman of easy habits/customs'; a classic Italian euphemism for a sexually permissive woman, imputing moral looseness through behavioral indirection rather than direct accusation.
records.notes: The circumlocution signals shame through indirection — naming the social behavior ('easy customs') rather than the body or act. Common across generations; somewhat more formal than ragazza facile.

records.definition: 'Light woman'; a dated euphemism for a sexually permissive or promiscuous woman, using lightness as a metaphor for moral looseness.
records.notes: 'Leggerezza' (lightness) has a long literary history in Italian as a metaphor for moral unreliability, especially in women. Slightly more dated than donna di facili costumi.

records.definition: 'Easy girl'; a common Italian expression for a young woman perceived as sexually permissive or easily persuaded into sex.
records.notes: More direct than donna leggera; primarily applied to younger women. The Italian 'facile' parallels English 'easy' almost exactly in usage and connotation in this context.

records.definition: 'She goes with everyone'; a verbal idiom describing a woman as sexually promiscuous, stating she has sex with any willing man.
records.notes: Phrase rather than single lexeme; highly transparent in meaning. The 'tutti' (everyone) signals indiscriminate sexuality, which is the core of the shame implication. Almost always applied to women.

records.definition: 'She goes around / she rotates'; crude shorthand verb implying a woman is sexually promiscuous.
records.notes: Context-dependent: gira alone simply means 'she turns/goes around', but in the relevant register it functions as a shorthand accusation of promiscuity. More common in spoken than written Italian; lower recognition reflects its colloquial rather than literary status.

records.definition: Diminutive of puttana (whore); 'little slut' or 'little whore' — used harshly as an insult or sometimes with mock-affectionate irony.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix -ella softens relative to puttana but the word remains strongly pejorative. In some regional uses it carries a cruel ironic tenderness, e.g. as a teasing address between women who know each other well.

records.definition: 'Of dubious morality'; a euphemistic adjective phrase used to impute sexual promiscuity or moral looseness without naming the behavior explicitly.
records.notes: The most indirect and formally polite way to impute sexual impropriety in Italian; favored in official, journalistic, or older-generation speech. Slightly higher technical score because the formal register borrows from legal/ethical discourse.

records.definition: A person assigned male at birth who lives in a feminine role within traditional Neapolitan society, occupying a recognized third-gender position with specific cultural and ritual functions.
records.notes: Not equivalent to Western transgender identity; femminielli traditionally hold auspicious roles in Neapolitan popular religion and folk ritual — presence at a birth is considered to bring luck. The category is specific to Campania's cultural context and predates modern LGBTQ frameworks by centuries. Crude score low because within Naples the role commands respect.

records.definition: Feminine grammatical variant of femminiello; refers to the same Neapolitan third-gender social role, sometimes treated as interchangeable with femminiello and sometimes as a slightly more distanced external descriptor.
records.notes: Some Neapolitan community members prefer femminiello as the self-referential form; femminiella can feel more like an outsider's label. Recognition outside Naples is lower than for the base form. The -a ending imposes a binary feminine grammatical gender that arguably sits uneasily with the concept's third-gender status.

records.definition: Sicilian dialect for penis; an extremely common expletive across Sicily and southern Italy that functions as an all-purpose intensifier analogous to English 'fuck' or 'damn'.
records.notes: Though rooted in Sicilian dialect, minchia is now near-universally recognized throughout Italy via television and internal migration. As an exclamation it expresses surprise, admiration, or dismay without necessarily invoking its anatomical meaning. One of the most versatile expletives in the Italian dialect spectrum.

records.definition: Venetian dialect for the vulva or vagina; also used as a general insult meaning fool or idiot.
records.notes: In Veneto, mona is so entrenched in everyday speech that it loses much shock value in regional context — comparable to how 'cunt' is less severe in parts of the UK than in the US. The dual use (genitalia + idiot) parallels English 'cunt' and 'twat' structurally.
