records.notes: Used in legal, journalistic, and everyday discourse; no more vulgar than the English word 'pornography.'

records.definition: Informal colloquial abbreviation for 'pornografia'; porn.
records.notes: Universal across age groups; can function as noun or adjective (e.g., 'film porno').

records.definition: A euphemism for a pornographic film; literally 'film for adults.'
records.notes: Standard broadcast and retail euphemism; mirrors the English 'adult film' exactly in form and function.

records.definition: An adult cinema that screens pornographic films; literally 'cinema for adults.'
records.notes: Mapped to peep_show as the closest registry concept for a paid venue to view explicit content; distinct in being a full cinema rather than a coin-operated booth. Largely a pre-internet concept; recognition is declining as physical venues disappear.

records.definition: An erotic literary work, poem, or softcore film; material designed to arouse with an artistic or literary framing.
records.notes: Classically refers to an erotic poem; colloquially extended to softcore erotic films. Less explicit in connotation than 'pornografia'; carries an artsy legitimizing register.

records.definition: Striptease; an erotic performance involving the progressive removal of clothing.
records.notes: Polish phonetic adaptation of English 'striptease'; fully nativized into Polish vocabulary and morphology.

records.definition: A female striptease performer; a stripper.
records.notes: Derived from 'striptiz' with Polish feminine agent suffix '-erka'; the standard term for a female strip performer.

records.definition: A male striptease performer; a male stripper.
records.notes: Masculine counterpart of 'striptizerka'; less commonly encountered than the feminine form, reflecting the gender distribution in the profession.

records.definition: A coin-operated or pay-per-view booth where patrons view sexual performances or explicit films.
records.notes: Direct English loanword used without phonetic adaptation in Polish. Recognition remains relatively high but the concept is declining as physical venues disappear with internet proliferation.

records.definition: A retail shop selling sex toys, adult films, lingerie, and related adult products.
records.notes: Direct English compound loanword; mapped to pornography_industry as the nearest registry concept, though the actual referent is specifically a retail store; the registry lacks a dedicated 'sex shop' entry.

records.definition: A sex worker who accompanies clients to social events or private meetings in exchange for payment.
records.notes: Direct English loanword; in Polish usage consistently implies sex work rather than mere companionship; perceived as a classier-sounding alternative to 'prostytutka.'

records.definition: In Polish slang, a wealthy older man who provides money, gifts, or lifestyle support to a younger woman in exchange for companionship and sexual access; a sugar daddy.
records.notes: Euphemistic semantic shift of the standard word 'sponsor'; the sexual connotation is inferred from context and contrasts with its innocent business meaning. Peaked in Polish youth slang during the 2000s–2010s.

records.definition: The practice of a young woman accepting financial support from a wealthy older man in exchange for companionship and sexual access; sugar dating as a gerundive noun.
records.notes: Gerund/nominalization of 'sponsorować' in its slang sexual sense; describes the arrangement as an activity; carries the same euphemistic softening as 'sponsor.'

records.definition: A woman financially maintained by a man, typically outside of marriage, in exchange for sexual availability and companionship; a kept woman.
records.notes: Derived from 'utrzymywać' (to maintain/support); the feminine form; somewhat archaic in tone but still understood and used; implies total financial dependency on the benefactor.

records.definition: A man financially maintained by a woman or wealthy partner in exchange for companionship and sexual access; a male kept partner.
records.notes: Masculine counterpart of 'utrzymanka'; rare in usage; carries an emasculating connotation because the gender role reversal is culturally stigmatized in Poland.

records.definition: Condom; the dominant standard Polish clinical and everyday term for a barrier contraceptive worn on the penis.
records.notes: Loanword from French 'préservatif' (itself from Latin); used in sex education, pharmacy, and everyday speech; not considered vulgar.

records.definition: Condom; an alternative loanword for a barrier contraceptive used interchangeably with 'prezerwatywa.'
records.notes: Loanword from German 'Kondom'; slightly more informal-sounding than 'prezerwatywa' but equally non-vulgar; both forms are in common standard use.

records.definition: Colloquial slang for a condom; literally 'rubber' or 'eraser,' exploiting the material properties of latex.
records.notes: Parallel semantic shift to English 'rubber'; primarily used among younger speakers and in casual speech; understood by virtually all adult speakers.

records.definition: A playful or coy euphemism for a condom; literally 'little hood' or 'little cap.'
records.notes: Diminutive of 'kaptur' (hood/cap); mildly humorous and somewhat dated. Shares the root with fairy-tale character 'Czerwony Kapturek' (Little Red Riding Hood), giving it an inadvertently whimsical quality.

records.definition: A contraceptive agent or method; literally 'contraceptive means'; the standard clinical Polish phrase for any form of contraception.
records.notes: A noun phrase rather than a single word; used in medical, legal, and educational contexts; entirely clinical in register with no vulgar connotation.

records.definition: The oral contraceptive pill; literally 'contraceptive pill.'
records.notes: Full clinical noun phrase; 'pigułka' is the standard Polish word for a pill or tablet; used in pharmacy, medicine, and general discourse without stigma.

records.definition: Colloquial shorthand for the oral contraceptive pill; literally 'tablet' or 'pill,' with the contraceptive meaning inferred entirely from context.
records.notes: Context-dependent metonym; in everyday conversation between women, 'tabletka' or 'tabletki' (plural) is understood to mean oral contraceptives; mirrors the English idiom 'the pill.'

records.definition: Colloquial and semi-clinical term for an intrauterine device (IUD); literally 'spiral' or 'coil,' referencing the shape of the device.
records.notes: Mirrors the British English colloquialism 'coil' for IUD; used by patients and clinicians alike; not vulgar; the shape-based metaphor is immediately transparent to Polish speakers.

records.definition: Clinical Polish term for an intrauterine device (IUD); a small T-shaped contraceptive inserted into the uterus by a clinician to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: Wkładka = insert; domaciczna = intrauterine. Standard gynecological term; entirely non-vulgar. This is the generic copper-IUD sense; cf. wkładka hormonalna for the hormonal variant.

records.definition: Polish clinical term for coitus interruptus; the withdrawal method in which the penis is removed from the vagina before ejaculation to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: Stosunek = intercourse; przerywany = interrupted. Standard term in gynecological consultations and sex-education materials; mild crude score because it names intercourse but in a clinical framing.

records.definition: Colloquial shorthand for the withdrawal method; literally 'break' or 'pause' in Polish, used as an abbreviated euphemism for coitus interruptus in informal speech.
records.notes: Highly ambiguous standalone term — primary meaning is simply 'break/recess/pause' (school recess, commercial break). In contraceptive contexts may also refer to the pill-free interval or periodic abstinence. Crude score is near zero because the word itself is entirely non-sexual; the contraceptive meaning must be inferred from context.

records.definition: Polish public-health phrase for 'safe sex'; denotes sexual activity conducted with precautions — primarily condom use — to prevent STIs and unintended pregnancy.
records.notes: Direct calque of the English public health term (bezpieczny = safe; seks = sex). Broader than 'condom' alone but condom use is its primary practical referent in Polish health campaigns. Concept mapped to condom as the central tool implied.

records.definition: Clinical Polish term for a hormonal intrauterine device such as Mirena or Kyleena, which releases progestin locally to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: Hormonalna = hormonal; distinguishes this from the copper wkładka domaciczna. Increasingly common as hormonal IUDs gain market share in Poland; frequently discussed in women's health magazines and gynecological consultations.

records.definition: English-origin acronym used unchanged in Polish; umbrella term for bondage and discipline, dominance and submission, sadism and masochism — consensual kink and power-exchange practices.

records.notes: Classic confessional euphemism: generations of Polish Catholics were asked 'Czy popełniłeś grzech nieczysty?' (Did you commit the impure sin?) as the standard confessional question about masturbation. Also covers other sexual acts but masturbation is the primary and most culturally resonant referent.

records.definition: Prostitution or sexual debauchery; in modern Polish legal and formal usage specifically denotes prostitution; historically meant sexual immorality or licentiousness more broadly.
records.notes: 'Dom nierządu' (house of nierząd) = brothel. Etymologically from nie- (un-) + rząd (order/rule) — 'disorder/lawlessness' applied metaphorically to sexual behavior. Appears in the Polish Penal Code. Sounds formal and legalistic rather than viscerally crude; the weight is moral-legal.

records.definition: Not Safe For Work; an English-origin internet acronym used unchanged in Polish online communities to tag sexually explicit, violent, or otherwise inappropriate content.
records.notes: Used identically to English usage in Polish internet spaces — no Polish equivalent has emerged. Pronounced letter by letter ('en es ef wu') by Polish speakers. Primarily understood by internet-active Poles under 45; older demographics may not recognize it.

records.definition: Nude photographs of a sexual or intimate nature; borrowed directly from English into Polish internet slang, typically referring to self-taken photographs shared via messaging apps or social media.
records.notes: Used unchanged from English in Polish internet slang. Treated as an indeclinable noun in Polish ('wysłać nudes' = to send nudes). More common among under-30 speakers. 'Nagie zdjęcia' is the native Polish equivalent but sounds formal by comparison.

records.definition: Sexts; a Polish adaptation of the English word 'sexts', referring to sexually explicit text messages, images, or videos sent via mobile devices or messaging applications.
records.notes: Polish plural form adapted from English 'sext'. The verb 'sekstować' (to sext) also exists in Polish internet slang. Recognition highest among under-40 Polish speakers. Formal native alternative 'wiadomości seksualne' is used in journalistic and older-speaker contexts.

records.definition: The act of sending sexually explicit messages or images via mobile device or internet; used as a direct English loanword in Polish.
records.notes: Recognized across age groups in Poland; practiced primarily by younger adults. Sometimes polonized in verb form as 'sextować'.

records.definition: An unsolicited or solicited photograph of a penis sent via digital messaging; used as an English loanword in Polish internet vernacular.
records.notes: Also written 'dickpic' in Polish usage. Widely discussed in Polish media in contexts of online harassment and dating app behavior.

records.definition: The climax of sexual excitement characterized by intense pleasurable sensations and rhythmic muscular contractions; the standard Polish word for orgasm.
records.notes: The primary, unremarkable Polish word for orgasm, adapted from French/Latin via scientific channels. Neither crude nor coldly clinical in everyday Polish perception — it is simply the normal term.

records.definition: Japanese animated or illustrated pornography; borrowed directly from Japanese into Polish internet slang to denote sexually explicit anime or manga content.
records.notes: Used identically to English usage. Primarily known among younger, internet-connected Poles and anime fan communities.

records.definition: The exaggerated orgasmic facial expression depicted in hentai, characterized by rolled-back eyes, protruding tongue, and flushed cheeks; used in Polish as a direct loanword from Japanese via internet culture.
records.notes: Recognized primarily among anime and hentai consumers. Crossed into broader Polish internet awareness through memes and controversial clothing merchandise circa 2018–2020.

records.definition: In anime and manga internet subculture, a young-appearing or explicitly underage female character archetype depicted in sexualized contexts; also the genre of hentai featuring such characters, which is illegal in many jurisdictions.
records.notes: Flagged as controversial in source. Content depicting such characters is illegal in Poland under child pornography statutes even when fictional. The term itself circulates in Polish anime spaces to denote the archetype or genre.

records.definition: A genre of Japanese manga, anime, and illustrated fiction depicting romantic or sexual relationships between male characters, primarily created for and consumed by female audiences.
records.notes: Also referred to as BL (boys' love) in contemporary usage. Ranges from non-explicit romance to pornographic content. Popular in Polish female anime fan communities.

records.definition: A genre of Japanese manga, anime, and illustrated fiction depicting romantic or sexual relationships between female characters.
records.notes: Sometimes called GL (girls' love) in contemporary usage. Ranges from mild romance to explicit content. Less widely recognized in Poland than yaoi.

records.definition: A subcategory of Japanese anime and manga featuring sexually suggestive but non-explicit content, characterized by fanservice, innuendo, and partial nudity; lighter than hentai.
records.notes: Derived from the Japanese pronunciation of the letter H, itself an abbreviation of hentai in casual Japanese usage. In Polish anime fandom, used to describe softcore or fanservice-heavy anime that stops short of explicit pornography.

records.definition: The internet adage stating that pornographic content exists for any conceivable subject, character, or object; used identically in Polish internet culture as an English loanword.
records.notes: Always used in English numeral form in Polish. Widely circulated in Polish internet communities, especially on forums and social media.

records.definition: Acronym for 'Mother I'd Like to Fuck'; an objectifying label for an attractive woman who is a mother; used as a pornographic category and colloquial expression in Polish internet slang.
records.notes: Widely recognized across Polish demographics due to internet and mainstream media exposure. Used both seriously as a pornographic category tag and humorously in everyday speech.

records.definition: Acronym for 'Dad I'd Like to Fuck'; an objectifying label for an attractive father; used in Polish internet slang modeled on MILF.
records.notes: Less widely known than MILF in Poland; primarily recognized among younger, internet-savvy demographics and in pornographic content categorization.

records.definition: Acronym for 'Grandparent I'd Like to Fuck'; an objectifying label for a sexually attractive elderly person; used in Polish internet slang as a direct English borrowing.
records.notes: Niche even within Polish internet communities; significantly less recognized than MILF or DILF. Primarily encountered in pornographic category labeling.

records.definition: In gay subculture, a young, slim, smooth-bodied, typically hairless gay man, usually in his late teens to mid-twenties; used in Polish as a direct English loanword in LGBTQ+ and internet communities.
records.notes: Part of the body-type taxonomy in gay male culture alongside bear, otter, cub, etc. Used in Polish gay dating apps and LGBTQ+ online spaces without modification.

records.definition: A genre of Japanese manga and illustrated art featuring muscular, masculine gay men, typically created by and for gay men; used in Polish anime and LGBTQ+ internet communities.
records.notes: Very niche in Poland; primarily known among dedicated anime fans with interest in gay content. Derived from Japanese word for rose, historically used as a gay euphemism in Japan. Contrasts with yaoi, which targets female audiences.

records.definition: Short for 'involuntary celibate'; a man who attributes his inability to find sexual or romantic partners to women's choices and societal unfairness, typically with expressed resentment or misogyny; used in Polish internet discourse.
records.notes: Used in Polish primarily in media, social commentary, and online forum contexts. Polish-language incel communities exist on domestic forum sites. Recognized widely but practiced as an identity by a smaller subset.

records.definition: A man who is excessively attentive or servile toward a woman in hopes of gaining sexual or romantic approval; used as a direct English loanword and light insult in Polish internet slang.
records.notes: Peak virality around 2020 aligned with global spread. Still in active use but slightly past peak. Used by younger Polish internet users both as an insult and self-deprecating label.

records.definition: Abbreviation for 'one night stand'; a casual sexual encounter between two people with no intention of meeting again; used in Polish internet and dating app contexts.
records.notes: Used primarily in written internet communication and dating app profiles. The full English phrase 'one night stand' is also used in Polish and may be more recognizable to some speakers than the abbreviation.

records.definition: Abbreviation for 'friends with benefits'; a relationship between friends who engage in sexual activity without romantic commitment; used in Polish dating and internet contexts.
records.notes: More common in written dating platform profiles than in spoken Polish. Younger Poles also use the full English phrase or occasionally the Polish calque 'przyjaciele z przywilejem'.

records.definition: A casual sexual encounter typically without ongoing relationship expectations; used as a direct English loanword in Polish internet and dating discourse.
records.notes: Also used as a verb, sometimes polonized as 'hookupować'. Widely recognized among younger Polish adults, especially dating app users. One of the more successfully integrated English loanwords in this domain.

records.definition: A late-night contact made to someone purely for casual sex; used as a direct English loanword in Polish internet slang.
records.notes: Slightly dated in global internet culture; still recognized in Poland among users with exposure to English-language media. Less frequently used in contemporary Polish speech than hookup or ONS.

records.definition: An ongoing casual sex partner with no romantic commitment; a regular sexual arrangement between two people who are not romantically involved; used as a direct English loanword in Polish.
records.notes: Cruder than FWB; implies sex is the explicit and primary purpose, without the friendship framing. The presence of 'fuck' raises crude score substantially. Widely understood among internet-active younger Polish adults.

records.definition: The practice of creating a false online identity to deceive someone into a romantic or sexual relationship; used as a gerund loanword in Polish internet discourse.
records.notes: Popularized by the 2010 documentary and subsequent MTV reality show. Recognized in Poland primarily as an online safety and digital literacy concept. Sometimes inflected with Polish verb endings.

records.definition: A person who creates a false online identity to deceive others romantically or sexually; the noun form of catfishing as used in Polish internet vernacular.
records.notes: Used as both noun (the deceiver) and verb in Polish internet speech. Slightly less recognized than the gerund form in Polish usage due to the false-friend collision with the Polish word for catfish the fish (sum).

records.definition: A woman who performs sexual or erotic acts live on webcam in exchange for payment or tips; used as a direct English loanword in Polish internet and media contexts.
records.notes: Widely recognized in Poland due to mainstream media coverage of OnlyFans and similar platforms. The gender-neutral or male equivalent 'camboy' is also used but less common. Sometimes used without sexual connotation to refer to any female streamer.

records.definition: A male performer who streams sexual or erotic content live via webcam for a paying online audience.
records.notes: English loanword used in Polish internet culture; male counterpart to camgirl; recognized primarily by younger, internet-active demographics; used without morphological adaptation in Polish.

records.definition: Subscription content platform used generically in Polish to mean online explicit content creation and digital sex work.
records.notes: Used generically in Polish — 'założyć OnlyFans' (to start an OnlyFans) has become a general idiom for entering the online sex content industry regardless of platform; morphologically invariant in Polish.

records.definition: Polish phrase for 'adult content creator'; a neutral-to-euphemistic self-descriptor for a person who produces and sells explicit sexual content online.
records.notes: Direct calque of the English 'adult content creator'; preferred on social media and in professional self-presentation to avoid platform content moderation bans; 'treści dla dorosłych' literally means 'content for adults'.

records.definition: Brand name used generically in Polish to mean online pornography or pornographic streaming sites broadly.
records.notes: Metonymic generalization in Polish internet usage; 'oglądać PornHub' simply means to watch online pornography regardless of platform; reflects near-universal name recognition; used as a generic noun and verb base in informal register.

records.definition: Sexual trolling; the act of making deliberately offensive, sexually provocative, or harassing comments online for shock value, amusement, or to distress others.
records.notes: Polish calque of English 'trolling' + the adjective 'seksualny'; covers both edgelord shock humor and targeted sexual harassment in online spaces; the concept maps imperfectly to edgelord as it can involve targeted victims rather than general provocation.

records.definition: Non-consensual distribution of intimate or sexually explicit images of a person, typically by a former partner as retaliation.
records.notes: English phrase used unchanged in Polish discourse; criminalized in Poland under Article 191a of the Criminal Code since 2017 (up to 3 years imprisonment); the Polish equivalent 'pornografia zemsty' exists but 'revenge porn' dominates everyday usage.

records.definition: AI-synthesized pornographic video or image depicting a real person without their consent, created using deep learning face-swap technology.
records.notes: Hybrid term: 'deepfake' borrowed intact from English, 'porno' is the Polish colloquial form; technically distinct from revenge porn (synthetic vs real footage) but legally and ethically overlapping; Polish criminal law coverage is still developing as of 2026.

records.definition: Polish internet slang for sex or a sexual encounter, used analogously to 'przelecieć kogoś' (to bang/screw someone) with a similar conquest framing.
records.notes: Niche internet slang; the associated term 'przelecieć' (literally 'to fly over') is well-established Polish crude slang for having sex with conquest framing; 'neta' appears to be a coded or shortened derivative used in specific online communities; very low mainstream penetration.

records.definition: Sin; the primary Polish Catholic term for moral transgression, widely used in sexual contexts to mean sexual sin or violation of chastity norms.
records.notes: The generic Polish word for sin; in Catholic sexual discourse it functions as a meta-category encompassing all sexual transgressions; mapping to 'fornication' is approximate — fornication is one paradigmatic referent among many; near-universal recognition in Poland's majority-Catholic culture; the phrase 'to grzech' (that is a sin) is a commonplace moral judgment.

records.definition: Impure sin; the standard Polish Catholic catechetical term for sexual sins specifically, including fornication, masturbation, homosexual acts, and other violations of chastity.
records.notes: Direct phrase from Polish Catholic catechesis; 'nieczysty' means impure/unclean; covers a broader range of sexual sins than fornication alone; routinely taught in Polish religious education (lekcje religii) and used in confessional contexts; recognition lower among younger secular Poles.

records.definition: Carnal sin or sin of the flesh; a Catholic theological term for sins arising from bodily desire, specifically sexual sins framed as the corruption of the body.
records.notes: Theologically frames sexual sin as rooted in the carnal (cielesny = bodily) nature; contrasted with sins of the spirit; slightly more literary and theological in register than 'grzech nieczysty'; maps to 'concupiscence' as both concepts locate the sinful tendency in the inherited carnal appetite.

records.definition: Impurity; the Catholic moral concept of sexual uncleanness, denoting the state of having committed or being disposed toward sexual sin.
records.notes: 'Nieczysty' literally means unclean; central to Polish Catholic sexual shame discourse; appears in catechism, confessional language, and moral theology; also has non-sexual meanings (physical uncleanliness, ritual impurity) making the sexual sense context-dependent; the abstract noun form used to describe a condition of moral-sexual corruption.

records.definition: Archaic Polish term for lewdness, wantonness, or sexual licentiousness; a moralistic condemnation of uninhibited or promiscuous sexual behavior.
records.notes: Now largely obsolete; found in 19th-century Polish religious and literary texts and in older Bible translations (particularly Protestant); 'wszetecznica' (a lewd woman) was a common derived form; recognized mainly by older, educated, or religiously informed Poles; effectively replaced by 'rozwiązłość' and 'lubieżność' in contemporary usage.

records.definition: Promiscuity, dissoluteness, or sexual licentiousness; a Polish moral condemnation of having many sexual partners or living a sexually unrestrained life.
records.notes: 'Rozwiązły' (the adjective) means dissolute or licentious; commonly used in Catholic moral discourse and conservative journalism; retains a clearly disapproving tone even in secular contexts; slightly more formal than everyday speech; often applied to women with heightened social force.

records.definition: Shamelessness; the absence of sexual or moral shame, specifically behaving in ways that violate Catholic norms of decency without remorse or inhibition.
records.notes: 'Bez' (without) + 'wstyd' (shame); the adjective 'bezwstydny' (shameless) is the more common form; used both in Catholic moral discourse and in everyday condemnation; the framing of public decency violation as rooted in lacking shame is characteristic of honor-shame culture; slightly more emotional and condemnatory in tone than 'nieczystość'.

records.definition: Sexual abstinence or continence; the deliberate restraint from sexual activity, presented as a virtue in Catholic moral theology and natural family planning discourse.
records.notes: Formal theological register; also used in non-sexual contexts (e.g., abstinence from alcohol); in sexual discourse refers specifically to the virtue of continence; prominent in Polish Catholic catechesis, NFP (natural family planning) advocacy, and pre-marital preparation courses.

records.definition: Purity or chastity; the Catholic virtue of sexual purity, encompassing abstinence before marriage, fidelity in marriage, and freedom from sexual sin.
records.notes: The primary Polish word for both physical cleanliness and moral purity; in sexual contexts denotes chastity specifically; 'czystość serca' (purity of heart) is a major Polish Catholic spiritual concept; maps approximately to 'sexual_abstinence' though czystość is a broader virtue covering thought and intention as well as act; near-universal recognition as a common word with a heightened theological register in Catholic discourse.

records.definition: Virginity; the state of not having had sexual intercourse, treated as a moral, social, and religious value in Polish Catholic culture.
records.notes: Near-universal recognition; concept maps approximately to 'defloration' since no registry entry names the virgin state itself, only its loss; 'zachować dziewictwo' (to preserve one's virginity) was a dominant norm in Polish Catholic upbringing for generations; carries both physical and spiritual dimensions in Catholic discourse.

records.definition: Virgin; a woman who has not had sexual intercourse; also the title of the Virgin Mary ('Najświętsza Dziewica'), giving the word profound religious resonance in Polish culture.
records.notes: Extremely common; carries simultaneously secular and deeply religious weight due to Marian devotion ('Dziewica Maryja'); the male form 'dziewiczak' exists but is far less culturally charged; maps approximately to 'defloration' as the registry lacks a concept entry for the virgin state itself.

records.definition: Virtue; in Polish usage most commonly connotes sexual virtue or chastity specifically, making 'stracić cnotę' (to lose one's virtue) the standard Polish euphemism for losing virginity.
records.notes: The general word for virtue but in everyday Polish usage it is most commonly understood to mean chastity or virginity specifically; 'cnotliwy' (virtuous) in sexual contexts means chaste; the narrowing of virtue to sexual virtue reflects the centrality of chastity in Polish Catholic moral culture.

records.definition: Loss of virtue; the standard Polish Catholic euphemism for losing one's virginity, framing the event as an irreversible moral diminishment.
records.notes: Nominal phrase; 'utrata' means loss (irreversible); frames virginity as a virtue that, once lost, cannot be recovered; carries strong moral weight in Catholic contexts; used across generations in both formal discourse and everyday speech; the euphemistic framing avoids naming the sexual act directly.

records.definition: To lose one's virtue; the standard Polish verbal euphemism for losing one's virginity, carrying the same Catholic moral framing as 'utrata cnoty'.
records.notes: Verbal phrase equivalent of 'utrata cnoty'; 'stracić' means to lose irreversibly; used across generations and registers; the moral-religious framing is implicit but widely understood even in secular contexts; the most common way to express first intercourse in a non-crude register in Polish.

records.definition: Modesty; the Catholic virtue of sexual and behavioral restraint, including modest dress, language, and deportment, presented as an ideal especially for women.
records.notes: Very common Polish word with both general and specifically sexual-moral usage; in Catholic sexual discourse 'skromność' is a central feminine virtue covering dress, conduct, and sexual restraint; maps approximately to 'sexual_conservatism' though skromność is a positive ideal rather than a conservative political stance.

records.definition: A modest woman; the Polish Catholic archetype of a woman who embodies sexual restraint, modest dress, and chastity norms.
records.notes: A phrase rather than a single lexical item; 'skromna kobieta' functions as a culturally loaded social archetype contrasting with 'rozwiązła kobieta' (licentious woman); used approvingly in conservative and Catholic contexts and sometimes ironically by more secular speakers; the gendering is significant — 'skromny mężczyzna' (modest man) carries far less moral weight.

records.definition: Public decency or sexual morality; the Polish legal and moral standard of acceptable sexual conduct, also a formal legal term in obscenity and indecency offenses.
records.notes: 'Obraza obyczajności publicznej' (offense against public morality) is a formal charge under Polish administrative and criminal law; 'obyczajność' names the positive standard that indecency violates; formal register recognized primarily by educated speakers and those familiar with legal or Catholic moral discourse; recognition has declined among younger secular demographics.

records.definition: A fallen woman; an archaic phrase for a woman who has lost her sexual virtue and social standing through pre-marital sex, seduction, or prostitution.
records.notes: Direct calque of Victorian English 'fallen woman'; widely used in 19th–20th century Polish literature and Catholic pastoral texts; parallels French 'femme déchue' and Russian 'padshaya zhenshchina'; the 'fall' metaphor implies irreversible moral descent; still understood today but used mainly in archaic or ironic registers.

records.definition: Infamous or notorious (feminine form); used as an adjective or noun for a woman of ill repute, particularly one known for sexual immorality or moral looseness.
records.notes: Feminine form of 'niesławny' (inglorious/infamous); in sexual contexts implies public notoriety for sexual misconduct; more literary than spoken; focuses on reputation rather than any specific act; used as a substantivized adjective ('ta niesławna' = that infamous woman).

records.definition: Whore; the primary and most loaded Polish slur for a sexually promiscuous woman or prostitute, functioning as both a literal reference to sex work and a general misogynistic insult.
records.notes: 'Kurwa' (originally also a whore-slur) has largely shifted to a general expletive, leaving 'dziwka' as the more specifically sexual insult; covers both literal prostitution and general promiscuity; context determines which reading applies; among the most severe misogynistic slurs in Polish.

records.definition: A slut or sexually promiscuous woman; a crude insult for a woman perceived as sexually loose, with connotations of aimless wandering and disreputable character.
records.notes: Etymology related to 'szlajać się' (to wander/roam aimlessly); implies the woman drifts from partner to partner without purpose or fidelity; somewhat regional; slightly less extreme than 'dziwka' but still strongly pejorative; also applied to women considered generally low-class or slovenly.

records.definition: To sleep around; a crude reflexive verb meaning to drift promiscuously from partner to partner, with connotations of aimlessness, moral looseness, and disrepute.
records.notes: Primary literal meaning is 'to wander/loiter aimlessly'; the sexual meaning frames promiscuity as purposeless drifting — sexual loyalty is figured as rootedness, promiscuity as homelessness; applied to both sexes but carries far greater stigma when used of women.

records.definition: To put out; a common colloquial phrase meaning to be sexually permissive or easy, used pejoratively for a woman who has sex readily or with multiple partners.
records.notes: Literally 'to release or let go of oneself'; the idiom applies the sense of releasing physical restraint to releasing sexual restraint; almost always applied to women; a man who 'puszcza się' faces negligible stigma by comparison; nominal derivative 'puszczalska' is its pejorative agent noun.

records.definition: A woman who puts out easily; a pejorative noun for a sexually permissive woman derived from 'puszczać się,' labeling her as sexually available and of low moral standards.
records.notes: Suffix '-alska' creates a feminine agent noun denoting habitual action; more specifically targets sexual availability than 'dziwka,' less overtly linked to prostitution; widely recognized across all age groups; commonly used among teenagers and young adults.

records.definition: Literally 'small rag or cloth'; a crude insult for a woman of sexual looseness or low moral character, dehumanizing her by comparing her to a used, disposable cleaning rag.
records.notes: Object metaphor implies the woman has been used by multiple men and is now soiled and discarded; diminutive '-ka' softens the sound slightly without reducing the sting; also applied to women simply regarded as low-class or slovenly regardless of sexual behavior.

records.definition: A slovenly and sexually immoral woman; an older insult combining connotations of physical untidiness and sexual looseness, suggesting a woman who is neither clean in appearance nor morally restrained.
records.notes: The fusion of physical slovenliness with sexual looseness distinguishes 'flejtucha' from pure slut-shaming vocabulary; closest English equivalent is archaic 'slattern'; declining in use among younger speakers; more rural and regional in distribution.

records.definition: A crude slang term for a sexually promiscuous woman; a coarse insult labeling a woman as sexually available and of low moral character.
records.notes: One of the less common Polish slut-shame terms; etymology uncertain, possibly related to 'pryskać' (to spray/squirt) with sexual innuendo; recognition and usage vary significantly by region and generation; more common in colloquial speech than in media or print.

records.definition: The normative category 'decent/respectable woman' invoked as the virtuous pole of the Madonna/whore binary; naming it implicitly shames any woman who deviates from its standard.
records.notes: The parenthetical 'jako odwrotność' (as the opposite) signals that research interest is in the phrase's function, not its surface meaning: 'porządna kobieta' operates as a shaming baseline against which sexually active women are measured and found wanting. The phrase is itself unmarked; the shame work is done entirely by contrast.

records.definition: Feminine adjective meaning immodest or unchaste; applied to women who violate norms of sexual restraint, modesty of dress, or decorous behavior.
records.notes: Standard Polish adjective carrying strong moral-religious undertones; in the Catholic Polish context 'skromność' (modesty) is a cardinal female virtue, so its negation is a mild but institutionally loaded accusation. Less crude than direct sexual slurs; its power comes from moral framing rather than vulgarity.

records.definition: Silesian dialect crude term for the vagina, borrowed from South/Central German dialectal Fut or Fud; used both anatomically and as a general insult for a stupid or contemptible person.
records.notes: Etymology: South/Central German dialect Fut/Fud (vagina), imported via centuries of German linguistic influence in Upper Silesia. Largely opaque to non-Silesian Polish speakers. The insult use parallels English 'cunt' deployed as a generic contempt term rather than an anatomical reference.

records.definition: Silesian dialect insult for a promiscuous, slovenly, or disreputable woman; derived or feminized from fjut, functioning analogously to 'slut' or 'tramp' in standard Polish.
records.notes: Gendered feminine; confined to Upper Silesian dialect and largely unintelligible to non-Silesians. Carries connotations of both sexual looseness and general low character. The -a suffix feminizes the base form fjut.

records.definition: Silesian dialect slur for a promiscuous, disreputable, or slovenly woman, with connotations of both sexual looseness and personal degradation.
records.notes: Likely borrowed from German dialect; possible relation to German Schlampe (slob/slut) or a similar etymon. Almost exclusively Silesian; opaque to outside speakers. The -unga suffix is a distinctively regional morphological pattern with no standard Polish equivalent.

records.definition: A contemptible, spineless, or morally degraded person; masculine noun derived from szmata (rag), implying someone with no self-respect or backbone.
records.notes: In standard Polish, 'szmata' as an insult skews toward promiscuous women (rag/slut); the -iak suffix masculinizes the concept. In prison and military slang, specifically implies a man who has lost status through submission, betrayal, or failure to resist sexual coercion in the hierarchy.

records.definition: Silesian exclamation of surprise or annoyance, literally 'pale ass'; used as a mid-level expletive and sometimes as a noun insult for a worthless or ineffectual person.
records.notes: The modifier 'blada' (pale) softens the crude base 'dupa' (ass), creating a characteristically Silesian euphemistic buffer. Has migrated into broader Polish colloquial speech. Can also stand alone as a noun insult meaning an ineffectual, useless fool, distinct from its exclamatory use.

records.definition: Silesian compound noun literally meaning 'hen-catcher'; used pejoratively for a man who obsessively and indiscriminately pursues women.
records.notes: Plays on 'kura' (hen; colloquially a woman) + 'łapać' (to catch/grab). The chicken-theft literal meaning gives the word a comic, rustic register alongside its sexual sense. Mostly opaque outside Silesia. Less severe than standard Polish 'kobieciarz'; the rural-animal framing adds ridicule.

records.definition: Prison slang for a man who has been sexually subordinated through rape or coercion and occupies the lowest, permanently degraded caste in prison hierarchy; in civilian use, an extreme insult implying homosexuality, cowardice, and complete worthlessness.
records.notes: One of the harshest insults in Polish. Within grypsera, the cwel is ritually untouchable — food, utensils, and clothing cannot be shared with him. The status is permanent and irrevocable once assigned. Fully crossed into civilian speech as a general extreme insult. 'Prison bitch' captures degradation and sexual coercion but not the rigid caste permanence of the Polish concept.

records.definition: The secret cant or argot of the dominant prisoner class in Polish prisons, encoding a strict caste hierarchy that governs sexual status, rituals of degradation, and social taboos.
records.notes: From 'gryps' (a secret note passed in prison, itself from German Grips = wit). Grypsera is not a single term but a complete linguistic register; its sexual vocabulary is the mechanism by which the dominant class ('grypsmen' or 'gitowcy') classifies and controls subordinated prisoners ('cwelowie'). Included here as the source system generating Polish prison sexual slang, not as a sexual term itself.

records.definition: Phrasal verb meaning to rape someone; literally 'to take by force'; in prison slang specifically refers to coercive sexual assault used to subordinate a victim and assign cwel status.
records.notes: Mapped to 'ravishment' as closest registry concept, though ravishment is archaic and sometimes euphemistic; 'brać na gwałt' is unambiguously contemporary and non-consensual. 'Gwałt' alone is the standard Polish legal and clinical term for rape; the phrasal form adds the predatory 'taking' framing dominant in prison usage.

records.definition: Crude phrasal verb meaning to penetrate someone anally from behind; in prison slang specifically refers to the dominant sexual act through which cwel status is assigned to the victim.
records.notes: Literally 'to take from behind.' Context disambiguates: in civilian use it can cover doggy-style vaginal penetration; in prison and military slang the anal and coercive reading dominates. The phrasing emphasizes the active subject's dominance rather than naming the anatomical act.

records.definition: Contemptuous augmentative of cipka (vagina); used as a crude insult for a weak, cowardly, or sexually submissive man, directly parallel to English 'pussy' used as a cowardice insult.
records.notes: The -uch suffix marks contemptuous augmentation rather than affection (cf. diminutive cipeczka). In prison slang, applied to men who fail to resist sexual subordination in the hierarchy. The genital-to-cowardice mapping mirrors standard Polish 'ciota' and broad cross-linguistic patterns of feminized anatomy as cowardice insult.

records.definition: Literally 'ass to the wall'; a prison idiom for keeping one's back against the wall to prevent being grabbed and raped from behind; used broadly as an expression of extreme vulnerability requiring constant defensive vigilance.
records.notes: Encodes the sexual threat environment of Polish prisons in a single spatial image. Has migrated into civilian speech as a general idiom for being cornered with no allies or escape route. No English phrase captures both the specific prison-rape referent and the embodied spatial survival posture simultaneously.

records.definition: Archaic Polish verb meaning to commit adultery; to engage in sexual intercourse with someone outside marriage while one or both parties are married.
records.notes: Specifically denotes marital infidelity (adultery), narrower than registry concept 'fornication' (all extramarital sex); mapped there as the closest moral-religious condemnation frame. Standard in Catholic theology and historical Polish law. The noun form 'cudzołóstwo' (adultery) remains current in legal Polish.

records.definition: Archaic Polish masculine noun for an adulterer; a man who commits adultery or has sex with a married woman.

records.definition: Polish literary noun for lasciviousness or lechery; the quality of being driven by excessive, shameless sexual desire openly expressed.

records.definition: Archaic Polish noun for raw carnal lust or sexual appetite; one of the oldest native Slavic words for sexual desire in the language.

records.definition: Polish literary phrase for carnal desires; identical in meaning to 'cielesne żądze' with inverted word order producing a slightly more emphatic or poetic register.

records.definition: Polish noun for debauchery, moral dissipation, or sexual licentiousness; excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures framed as moral degradation.

records.definition: Polish noun for licentiousness or sexual promiscuity; the quality of being sexually and morally uninhibited beyond accepted social norms.

records.definition: Archaic Polish noun for a person of low moral character; a scoundrel or villain, with implied sexual licentiousness in period usage.
records.notes: Literally 'non-virtue/non-honor'; sexual connotation is secondary and context-dependent. In modern Polish used humorously or affectionately for a mischievous person, largely desexualized. records.definition: Polish literary phrase for sensual pleasures; the delights of the physical senses, especially sexual ones, framed in elevated aesthetic or philosophical discourse.

records.definition: Polish literary phrase for carnal or bodily pleasure; the pleasure derived from physical or sexual experience, explicitly contrasted with spiritual fulfillment.

records.definition: Polish noun for obscenity, lewdness, or smuttiness; sexually offensive or indecent content or behavior that violates public decency standards.

records.definition: Polish phrase for 'sin of the flesh'; any sexual transgression conceived as a sin against divine law, including fornication, adultery, lust, and masturbation.

records.definition: Polish noun meaning womb, lap, or bosom; in archaic and literary sexual contexts also used broadly for the female genital area.

records.definition: Archaic Polish plural noun for 'loins'; the pelvic or lumbar region associated with procreation and sexual vitality in biblical and literary usage.

records.definition: Polish noun for virginity; the state of not having had sexual intercourse, especially in a woman, carrying strong cultural and religious value.

records.definition: Polish noun meaning virtue or chastity; in archaic and literary Polish specifically denotes sexual purity and female chastity as a positive moral virtue.

records.definition: Archaic Polish phrase literally meaning 'shameful organ'; a historical euphemism for the genitals, especially female genitalia, expressing shame-based avoidance of direct anatomical naming.

records.definition: Polish feminine noun for a shameless or immodest woman; applied to a woman who violates sexual modesty norms without remorse or embarrassment.

records.definition: Polish masculine noun for a lecher or lascivious man; a man consumed by excessive sexual desire who pursues gratification without moral restraint.

Recognition boosted by American TV export ('Cougar Town', celebrity tabloid culture) in the 2009–2013 period.

records.definition: Catholic moral category for sins of sexual impurity, encompassing masturbation, fornication, and any sexual act outside of marriage and its procreative purpose; literally 'impure sin'.
records.notes: The canonical Polish Catholic confessional phrase for sexual transgression. In everyday confessional practice most often refers specifically to masturbation, though theologically broader. Mapped to 'fornication' as the closest registry concept carrying explicit religious condemnation framing; no registry concept covers 'sexual sin as a categorical class'.

records.definition: Catholic term for sins rooted in bodily desire, specifically sexual sins; literally 'sin of the flesh'.
records.notes: 'Ciało' (flesh/body) connects to the Pauline theological opposition of flesh (sarx) vs. spirit (pneuma). Near-synonym of 'grzech nieczysty' and 'grzech cielesny'; emphasizes the bodily origin of sin rather than its moral impurity. All three variants appear interchangeably in homiletic and catechetical literature.

records.definition: Carnal sin; a Catholic moral term for sexual transgression understood as bodily appetite overcoming spiritual will; literally 'carnal sin'.
records.notes: 'Cielesny' is the adjectival form of 'ciało' (body/flesh), giving a slightly more literary register than the genitive 'grzech ciała'. The adjectival construction is more common in theological prose and philosophical writing; the three 'grzech' compounds are effectively synonymous in popular usage.

records.definition: Carnal temptation; in Catholic moral theology, the enticement of bodily desire toward sexual sin, theologically distinct from the sin itself.
records.notes: Theologically distinct from the 'grzech' (sin) compounds: 'pokusa' is temptation, not transgression. In Catholic doctrine, yielding to 'pokusa cielesna' with full consent of the will produces 'grzech nieczysty'. Connects to the Augustinian concept of concupiscence as the inherited human tendency toward disordered desire.

records.definition: Moral fall or downfall; in Catholic and conservative secular usage, a decline into sexual or broader moral corruption; literally 'moral fall'.
records.notes: 'Upadek' (fall) carries theological resonance echoing the Fall of Man in Polish Catholic culture. In practice the phrase often implies sexual transgression but is not exclusively sexual — it encompasses any serious moral failure. Less specific than the 'grzech' compounds; common in conservative media rhetoric about cultural decline.

records.definition: Moral corruption or depravity; describes a state of having been degraded by habitual sexual or moral transgression; literally 'moral rottenness/spoilage'.
records.notes: 'Zepsucie' derives from 'psuć się' (to spoil/rot), evoking irreversible organic decay. Emphasizes the end-state of moral degradation rather than specific acts. Prominent in Polish right-wing Catholic rhetoric about societal decline attributed to secularization, Western influence, or LGBTQ+ visibility.

records.definition: Impure thoughts; the Catholic moral category for sexually sinful mental content, including deliberate fantasy, lustful desire for forbidden persons, and willful entertainment of erotic imagery.
records.notes: Key phrase in Polish Catholic confessional practice: penitents are asked whether they 'harbored impure thoughts'. Theologically, voluntary consent to the thought constitutes the sin; involuntary intrusive thoughts do not. Captures the interiority of sexual sin — the only grzech-cluster term that operates at the level of cognition rather than act.

records.definition: Sexual licentiousness or promiscuity; the state of being sexually and morally unrestrained; literally 'unboundness'.
records.notes: Derived from 'rozwiązać' (to unbind/untie): moral constraint experienced as a binding that the licentious person has shed. Used in religious condemnation and elevated secular literary criticism. Register is literary/archaic — not typical of everyday speech; common in 19th-century Polish novels and Catholic homiletics.

records.definition: Archaic Polish word for wantonness, lewdness, or sexual debauchery, carrying strong connotations of moral condemnation.
records.notes: Old Polish / Church Slavonic-influenced term found primarily in 16th–19th century religious texts, sermons, and belles-lettres. Virtually never used in contemporary speech except for deliberate archaizing effect. The feminine form 'wszetecznica' historically denoted a prostitute or sexually loose woman. Related to Old Slavic roots meaning 'shameless/immodest'. Peak_year not set: the term predates living memory and was never slang.

records.definition: Premarital chastity; the Catholic norm of abstaining from all sexual activity until marriage; literally 'premarital purity'.
records.notes: 'Czystość' means both physical purity and chastity in Polish. Recognition peaked in the 1990s following the reintroduction of Catholic religious education in Polish public schools. Taught systematically in pre-marriage preparation courses ('kursy przedmałżeńskie') mandated by the Church for couples seeking Catholic marriage.

records.definition: Celibacy; the permanent commitment to abstention from marriage and sexual activity, obligatory for Catholic priests in the Latin Rite.
records.notes: Latin loanword (caelibatus). Exceptionally high recognition in Poland due to the cultural centrality of Catholicism and recurring public debate about mandatory priestly celibacy. Narrower than 'sexual_abstinence': implies a permanent religious vow, not temporary restraint. Term is stable and shows no recognition decline.

records.definition: Abstinence or continence; in sexual contexts, the deliberate restraint of sexual desire and activity as a moral virtue; applicable broadly to any appetitive restraint but prominent in Catholic sexual moral discourse.
records.notes: Derived from 'wstrzymywać się' (to hold back, refrain). Not sex-specific — the same term governs food, drink, and speech — but heavily deployed in sexual moral contexts as 'cnota wstrzemięźliwości' (the virtue of continence). More elevated and archaic than the everyday synonym 'powściągliwość'. Recognition declining with secularization of Polish society.

records.definition: A carnal sinner; a person who has committed sins of the flesh in the Catholic moral framework, covering any mortal sexual transgression including fornication, adultery, or masturbation.
records.notes: Broader than the English 'fornicator,' which implies only pre-marital sex; grzesznik cielesny covers all sexual mortal sins in Catholic theology. Recognition declining with falling church attendance among youth.

records.definition: Immoral behavior; conduct that violates moral or religious standards of decency, most commonly invoked in sexual contexts by clergy, conservative media, and Catholic public discourse.
records.notes: Generic phrase — context determines whether immorality is sexual or otherwise. Very high recognition as an everyday compound. Used both in religious homiletics and secular moral condemnation. Not inherently sexual without context.

records.definition: Immorality; the state or quality of being morally unrestrained, especially in sexual matters, as judged by religious or traditional Catholic standards.
records.notes: Abstract noun form. In Polish Catholic public discourse predominantly refers to sexual immorality. Carries moral condemnation but no intrinsic vulgarity — found in broadsheet journalism, Church documents, and political rhetoric equally.

records.definition: Sin of impurity; the Catholic sacramental umbrella term for all mortal sins of a sexual nature, including fornication, masturbation, adultery, and sodomy, as used in confession and catechism.
records.notes: Specifically confessional-Catholic vocabulary; penitents use it as a catch-all when confessing sexual sins without naming the specific act. Broader than English 'fornication' which covers only pre-marital intercourse. Recognition declining with declining sacramental practice.

records.definition: Carnal sin; sin of the flesh; the Catholic moral label for any sexual transgression, foregrounding the bodily/fleshly nature of the sin against spiritual purity.
records.notes: Synonymous with grzech nieczystości but carries a slightly more literary and theological flavor through the adjective 'cielesny' (bodily/carnal). Word-order variant 'grzech cielesny' also exists. Evokes the Pauline body-spirit dualism central to Catholic sexual ethics.

records.definition: Moral filth; a rhetorical phrase in Polish Catholic and conservative discourse for sexual immorality, framing it as spiritual and moral contamination through the pollution metaphor.
records.notes: Strongly metaphorical — uses brud (dirt, filth, grime) as a purity metaphor for spiritual corruption. Common in sermons targeting pornography, homosexuality, or premarital sex. Not a clinical or legal term. Rhetorical rather than descriptive register.

records.definition: Sinful desires; the yearning for carnal or sexual pleasure identified in Catholic theology as the inherited inclination toward sin, equivalent to the theological concept of concupiscence in pastoral Polish language.
records.notes: Near-direct pastoral equivalent of theological concupiscence. The formal theological term is 'pożądliwość'; 'grzeszne pragnienia' is the more accessible homiletic version used in sermons and catechism. Direct conceptual match in the Catholic moral framework.

records.definition: Living in sin; cohabitation of a sexually active unmarried couple, framed through Catholic moral condemnation of domestic arrangements outside the sacrament of marriage.
records.notes: Direct structural and semantic calque of the English phrase 'living in sin.' Both phrases carry identical moralizing Catholic register. Used by clergy, devout Catholics, and older generations to describe unmarried cohabitation. Younger secular Poles use it neutrally or ironically.

records.definition: Concubinage; the formal legal and ecclesiastical term for cohabitation as an unmarried sexual couple, used in Church documents, Polish civil law discussions, and conservative media.
records.notes: Loanword from Latin concubinatus. More formal and legalistic than życie w grzechu; carries overtones of the historical institution of the concubine rather than just modern cohabitation. In modern secular Polish usage increasingly neutral, simply denoting an unofficial domestic partnership.

records.definition: Adultery; sexual intercourse in which at least one partner is married to someone else, constituting a major mortal sin in Catholic doctrine and historically a legal offense under Polish law.
records.notes: Canonical Polish term enshrined in the Sixth Commandment ('Nie cudzołóż'). Distinct from fornication (sex between unmarried people) — cudzołóstwo specifically requires at least one married party. Extremely high recognition due to biblical ubiquity. Proposed novel concept slug 'adultery' as the registry lacks this distinct concept.

records.definition: Adulterer; a man who commits adultery, i.e., who engages in sexual relations outside his marriage or with a married person.
records.notes: Masculine agent noun derived from cudzołóstwo. Feminine equivalent is cudzołożnica. Found in biblical translations, Catholic homiletics, and historical legal texts. Carries strong moral condemnation in Catholic Poland. References the novel concept 'adultery' introduced in the preceding record.

records.definition: Sexual dishonoring; the act or state of bringing irreversible shame and social disgrace upon a person — typically a woman — through a sexual transgression such as premarital sex, rape, or adultery, within a patriarchal honor economy.
records.notes: English 'slut-shaming' captures the social shaming mechanism but not the gravity or permanence; zhańbienie implies a lasting stain on honor with real social consequences (reduced marriage prospects, family ostracism). 'Ravishment' in its archaic sense covers only the assault dimension. Culturally specific to Catholic Polish honor culture — proposed novel concept 'sexual_dishonoring.'

records.definition: Family shame; the collective dishonor brought upon an entire family unit by a member's — typically a daughter's — sexual transgression, including premarital pregnancy, scandal, or assault, within the Polish Catholic honor economy.
records.notes: The shame is explicitly collective: the entire family, not just the individual, is dishonored and loses social standing in the community. No English equivalent encapsulates this collective honor-economy concept with its specific sexual valence. Still invoked in traditionalist rural and conservative Catholic communities. Proposed novel concept 'family_sexual_shame.'

records.definition: To bring dishonor upon oneself; the reflexive act of forfeiting one's sexual honor through a transgression that causes shame to oneself and one's family in a patriarchal honor economy.
records.notes: Reflexive perfective verb form of zhańbić (to dishonor). Approximate match to slut_shaming: the honor-shame mechanism is the same but the agency is self-directed rather than externally imposed. A woman 'zhańbi się' by her own act; slut_shaming describes others' reaction. Less recognized than the noun zhańbienie.

records.definition: Loss of honor; in traditional Polish Catholic culture, the irreversible forfeiture of a woman's social and moral standing resulting from any sexual act that violates the community's honor code — premarital sex, assault, adultery, or public scandal.
records.notes: Broader than 'defloration' (which targets only virginity loss) and broader than 'slut-shaming' (which targets social practice). Historically had concrete economic consequences: reduced bride price, broken engagements, family ostracism. Still invoked in conservative Catholic and rural communities. Proposed novel concept 'sexual_honor_loss.'

records.definition: Sexual shame; the internalized feeling of guilt, embarrassment, or humiliation regarding one's own sexual desires, behavior, or body, typically rooted in Catholic upbringing or patriarchal norms.
records.notes: More of a psychological/emotional state than a moral label. Increasingly common in contemporary Polish sex therapy discourse and feminist writing. Approximate match to sexual_repression — wstyd seksualny describes the felt shame itself; repression describes the behavioral suppression that typically results from it. The concepts are related but distinct.

records.definition: An 'easy' or sexually permissive woman; a derogatory slur for a woman perceived as willing to have sex indiscriminately or without selectivity or emotional commitment.
records.notes: Derived from the verb puścić się (to let oneself go, to be easy sexually). Less raw in register than zdzira or dziwka — implies looseness and lack of standards rather than prostitution per se. One of the most common everyday Polish insults directed at women. Approximate rather than direct because 'slut' carries heavier connotations of pure vulgarity; puszczalska is more about the concept of being 'easy.'

records.definition: Rag; when applied to a woman, a derogatory slur comparing her to a filthy, used-up piece of cloth to denote sexual promiscuity and low social worth.
records.notes: Literal meaning is dishcloth or rag — the sexual insult operates through the pollution/used-up metaphor. Also used as a gender-neutral insult meaning spineless pushover (for men: 'he's a szmata') making the sexual sense context-dependent. Closest English equivalent is British 'slag' which similarly implies cheapness/used-up quality.

records.definition: One of the most offensive Polish slurs for a sexually promiscuous woman; broadly equivalent in force and deployment to English 'slut' or 'whore,' used in heated arguments, street insults, and as an intensified misogynistic attack.
records.notes: Among the harshest single-word insults in Polish when directed at a woman. Etymology unclear — possibly related to zdzierać (to scrape, wear out), reinforcing the 'used up' metaphor. Ubiquitous across generations and social classes. Public use against a named individual is prosecutable under Polish civil law as an insult (zniesławienie).

records.definition: A floozy; a dated derogatory term for a sexually loose or promiscuous woman with a somewhat theatrical, grandmotherly contempt — implying moral looseness, gaudy appearance, and low social standing.
records.notes: Archaic in active use — primarily vocabulary of older generations and period drama. Carries a slightly comic or theatrical tone that has blunted its offensiveness; more likely to provoke amusement than outrage from younger speakers. Possibly derived from German or Yiddish. Recognition declining with generational turnover.

records.definition: Flounder (the fish); when applied to a woman, a crude slur denoting sexual promiscuity — the flat-lying fish evokes a woman supine and sexually available to anyone.
records.notes: Literal meaning is the flatfish species (Platichthys flesus). The sexual insult is zoomorphic — the fish's flat prone posture evokes a woman lying on her back. Also used regionally for a lazy or slovenly woman regardless of sexual connotation. Less severe than zdzira; the zoological origin lends it a slightly cartoonish quality.

records.definition: Whore; the most ubiquitous and offensive Polish slur for a woman, used both literally for sex workers and as a maximally intensified general insult against any woman whose behavior the speaker condemns.
records.notes: Etymology uncertain — possibly from dziwna (strange creature) or dialectal dziwa. Saturation-level recognition and use across all generations, social classes, and regions; appears in football stadium chants, political invective, domestic arguments, and cinema. Public directed use against a named person is civilly actionable. The single most socially loaded word in Polish directed at women.

records.definition: Harlot; an archaic Polish term for a sexually loose woman or prostitute, primarily preserved in biblical translations, 19th-century literature, and historical texts.
records.notes: Appears in the Polish Bible (e.g., Rahab the ladacznica in Joshua). Has effectively zero offensive charge in modern colloquial speech due to total archaism — reads as literary or historical rather than insulting. High recognition among educated speakers and churchgoers; low among youth. Etymological origin disputed — possibly from lada (shelf, trifle) or a Slavic root for 'slattern.'

records.definition: A crude slur for a sexually promiscuous or loose woman; also used more broadly for a contemptible, slovenly, or morally degraded person of either sex.
records.notes: Possibly related to wywłóczyć (to drag out, to haul around), with the implication of a woman who 'gets dragged around' between men. Less universally recognized than zdzira or dziwka; more regional variation in usage. When applied to men it functions as general contempt without sexual connotation.

records.definition: Dissolute woman; the feminine form of the adjective rozwiązły, denoting a woman who is sexually or morally unrestrained, licentious, and heedless of sexual propriety.
records.notes: Feminine adjectival form of rozwiązły (dissolute, licentious); functions as both adjective ('kobieta rozwiązła' = a dissolute woman) and substantivized noun ('ta rozwiązła' = that loose woman). More literary and elevated in register than zdzira or puszczalska; found in journalism, moral essays, and literary fiction. Lower crude score reflects the formal register — the word shames through elevated language rather than street invective.

records.definition: Feminine adjective meaning 'immoral,' applied to a woman deemed sexually or morally transgressive, implying she has violated social or religious norms of female propriety.
records.notes: Feminine form of 'niemoralny' (immoral); in Polish culture heavily weighted toward sexual transgression rather than general ethical failing when applied to women. Rarely applied to men with the same sexual connotation.

records.definition: The loss of a woman's virginity framed through honor and virtue rather than anatomy; 'cnota' carries both 'virtue' and 'chastity' simultaneously, making the loss a social and moral catastrophe rather than merely a physical event.
records.english_term: loss of virtue, loss of chastity
records.notes: More honor-coded than the English 'defloration' — 'cnota' in Polish simultaneously means virtue, chastity, and moral worth; losing it is framed as irreversible. Contemporary younger Poles find the phrase archaic; survives primarily in Catholic moral discourse and older literature.

records.definition: To take a woman's virginity, framed as robbing her of virtue and social standing; the verb 'pozbawić' means 'to deprive or strip of,' making the act an explicit theft of both physical and moral integrity.
records.english_term: to deflower, to deprive of virtue
records.notes: Unlike the softer English 'deflower,' 'pozbawić' is inherently accusatory — it frames the act as a form of theft from both the woman and her family. The agent (typically male) is implicitly a predator; this phrasing appears in legal and ecclesiastical historical texts.

records.definition: To sexually disgrace a woman — whether through rape, seduction, public exposure, or coerced sex — thereby destroying her social standing, marriageability, and familial honor in an honor-based community.
records.notes: No single English concept captures this: 'zhańbić' (to bring shame or dishonor) focuses on the social consequence rather than the physical act. The disgrace may result from rape, seduction, or even rumor. The woman's honor belongs partly to her family, so zhańbienie kobiety damages a kinship unit, not merely an individual.

records.definition: Euphemistic participial phrase meaning 'poorly conducting herself,' used to describe a woman of loose morals or sexual promiscuity while avoiding explicit sexual language.
records.notes: The participial construction ('she who conducts herself badly') emphasizes ongoing behavior rather than fixed identity, though it functions as a social label. Preferred by older generations who find direct vocabulary too crude; younger Poles tend toward more direct terms. Avoids naming the sexual acts while communicating the condemnation fully.

records.definition: Feminine adjective meaning 'light,' used euphemistically for a sexually available or promiscuous woman; functions as a one-word social verdict equivalent to English 'easy.'
records.notes: Shorthand for 'lekkich obyczajów' (of light morals); can stand alone as a compact condemnation. The 'light' metaphor implies she offers little resistance. Distinguished from 'łatwa' (easy) by register: 'lekka' retains a slight poetic quality while 'łatwa' is more blunt.

records.definition: Feminine adjective meaning 'easy,' used colloquially for a sexually permissive or readily available woman; slightly cruder and more direct in register than the near-synonym 'lekka.'
records.notes: Compared to 'lekka,' 'łatwa' uses the mundane everyday word for 'easy' with no softening metaphor — 'easy task,' 'easy woman,' same word. The lack of poeticism makes it marginally more contemptuous. Both terms are widely understood across generations.

records.definition: Euphemism for a prostitute or woman of extreme promiscuity; a calque of 'woman of the streets,' invoking public sexual availability without naming sex work explicitly.
records.notes: Less common than the direct 'prostytutka'; used as a polite or distancing alternative, often by speakers who find 'prostytutka' too blunt. The street imagery simultaneously invokes public availability and low social class. Can also be applied more loosely to highly promiscuous women who are not sex workers.

records.definition: Participial phrase meaning 'one who goes with everyone,' implying a woman who has sex with any man without discrimination; exploits the Polish euphemism 'chodzić z kimś' (to go with someone = to date or sleep with).
records.notes: The sexual meaning is implied through the euphemism 'chodzić z kimś'; the participial feminine construction (chodząca) makes this a label applied to an absent woman rather than an address or accusation. Common in gossip register. The universalizer 'każdym' (everyone, any man) is the primary carrier of contempt.

records.definition: Participial phrase meaning 'one who goes with just anyone,' implying a woman with no sexual standards or discrimination; 'byle kim' specifically connotes contemptibly random or worthless partners.
records.notes: The addition of 'byle' (mere, just any old, beneath consideration) layers contempt not present in 'chodząca z każdym' — it implies not only quantity but absence of standards. 'Byle kim' describes the partners as interchangeable refuse, amplifying the degradation of both the woman and her partners.

records.definition: Crude past-tense statement meaning 'she gave herself to everyone,' using the euphemistic verb 'dać' (to give) to imply a woman has had sex with all comers; delivered as a social verdict about an absent woman.
records.english_term: she put out for everyone, she slept with everyone
records.notes: 'Dać' (to give) as a sex euphemism frames the woman as giving away something — chastity, honor — that cannot be recovered. The past tense and third-person framing makes this a statement of social fact or gossip delivered by a narrator; it is almost never addressed directly to the woman. Among the more cutting formulations because it implies the act is already irrevocably completed.

records.definition: Formal phrase describing a woman whose sexual reputation has been publicly exposed or ruined; 'skompromitowana' (compromised/disgraced) centers the social exposure of the transgression rather than the sexual act itself.
records.notes: Has a bureaucratic or journalistic register compared to other honor-shame vocabulary; often appears in reporting or legal discussion when describing a situation rather than naming a woman directly. The term locates the damage in the public sphere (exposure, reputation collapse) rather than in the woman's behavior, making it slightly more neutral than alternatives.

records.definition: Literary phrase for a 'fallen woman' — one who has lost her virtue through sexual transgression; 'upadła' (fallen, past participle of 'upaść') echoes the religious concept of the Fall and implies irreversible moral collapse.
records.notes: A near-calque of the Victorian English 'fallen woman' concept, common in Polish 19th-century literature and Catholic moral discourse. Rarely used in contemporary speech; survives primarily in literary, historical, or religious rhetoric. 'Seksualnie' is often implicit rather than stated — 'upadła kobieta' (fallen woman) carries the same charge without the adverb.

records.definition: The complete and irreversible destruction of a woman's moral and social standing due to sexual transgression or exposure; frames sexual dishonor not merely as shame but as total social annihilation.
records.notes: The 'ruina' (ruin, rubble) metaphor implies an irreversibility and totality that English 'disgrace' or 'shame' do not capture. In Polish Catholic culture, moralna ruina following sexual transgression could effectively end a woman's social existence — no marriage prospects, no community standing. No single English concept maps this totality of honor destruction as a terminal social condition.

records.definition: The standard Polish legal and clinical term for rape; non-consensual sexual penetration by force, coercion, or incapacitation.
records.notes: The registry concept 'ravishment' is archaic in English while 'gwałt' is the living standard clinical and legal term. 'Gwałt' historically meant 'violence or force' broadly (cf. 'gwałtowny' = violent, sudden), with the sexual meaning becoming dominant. Both senses survive in compound forms: 'gwałt na naturze' (violation of nature) remains a non-sexual idiom.

records.definition: The standard Polish legal and clinical agent noun for a rapist, formed from 'gwałcić' (to rape or violate) with the standard Polish agentive suffix '-ciel.'
records.notes: More specific than 'sexual_predator' — 'gwałciciel' refers exclusively to a rapist, not to sexual predators in general. The '-ciel' suffix marks the perpetrator of an action (cf. 'nauczyciel' = teacher, from 'nauczyć' = to teach); no ambiguity about the role. No single Polish agent noun covers the broader English 'sexual predator' concept without additional specification.

records.definition: The standard Polish legal term for sexual assault, encompassing non-consensual sexual acts that may not meet the legal threshold for rape, including groping, coerced sexual contact, and assault short of penetration.
records.notes: Broader than 'gwałt' (rape) — 'napaść seksualna' covers the full spectrum of non-consensual sexual acts. 'Napaść' (assault or attack) implies physical aggression. The registry's 'indecent_act' is the closest available but frames a misdemeanor-level violation, whereas 'napaść seksualna' is a serious criminal charge. Standard in legal documents and journalism.

records.definition: Gerund or verbal noun for molestation or harassment; can refer to sexual harassment, child sexual abuse, or any repeated unwanted sexual behavior; borrowed into Polish from international legal terminology.
records.notes: The term spans from workplace sexual harassment to child sexual abuse depending on context; standalone 'molestowanie' in Polish public discourse often implies the latter. Latin loanword that entered Polish through legal and clinical channels. The full form 'molestowanie seksualne' is used when disambiguation from non-sexual harassment is needed.

records.definition: The standard Polish formal two-word term for sexual harassment or sexual molestation, specifying the sexual nature of the unwanted conduct; used in legal, journalistic, and institutional contexts.
records.notes: Usage expanded significantly during the Polish #MeToo discourse (2017–2018), entering mainstream public vocabulary. Covers both workplace sexual harassment and physical molestation of minors; context disambiguates. Carries more institutional weight than the shorter 'molestowanie' alone.

records.definition: A formal synonym for sexual harassment with a stronger aggressive connotation; 'napastować' (to harass, pester, or assail) derives from 'napaść' (to attack), lending this term more explicit hostility than 'molestowanie.'
records.notes: Less common in everyday usage than 'molestowanie seksualne'; the 'napaść' (attack) root makes it read as more aggressive and predatory.
