Polish legal statutes use both terms in different statutory contexts, creating a two-tier system where 'napastowanie' can imply active pursuit while 'molestowanie' implies unwanted conduct more broadly.

records.definition: Descriptive clinical-legal phrase for non-consensual sexual touching; literally 'touching without consent,' used in legal discourse, sex education, and activist contexts to define the boundary between permitted and criminal contact.
records.notes: A descriptive phrase rather than a single lexical item; became prominent in Polish consent education following #MeToo. 'Zgoda' (consent) entered Polish sexual-legal discourse as a technical term; 'bez zgody' (without consent) is now a standard legal qualifier. The registry concept 'frotteurism' is the closest available but is a psychopathological framing, whereas 'dotykanie bez zgody' is a victim-centered legal description.

records.definition: The act of groping — sexually handling someone's body with the hands; covers both aggressive non-consensual fondling and, less commonly, consensual heavy petting, with context determining the charge.
records.notes: Verbal noun from imperfective 'obmacywać'; the prefix 'ob-' implies covering or surrounding (cf. 'obierać' = to peel all around), giving the word a sense of thorough, all-over handling rather than a single touch. While frotteurism in the registry is specifically non-consensual, 'obmacywanie' can appear in consensual foreplay contexts but leans heavily non-consensual in public discourse.

records.definition: Perfective verb meaning 'to have groped' or 'to grope as a completed act'; the perfective aspect implies the violation was carried through to completion, adding finality to the accusation.
records.notes: Perfective counterpart to imperfective 'obmacywać'; aspectual distinction matters in Polish — 'obmacywać' suggests ongoing or habitual groping while 'obmacać' implies a single completed episode. The perfective 'obmacać' dominates accusatory contexts ('obmacał ją' = 'he groped her'), making it the more legally charged form between the two.

records.definition: Base imperfective verb meaning 'to feel, touch, or grope'; semantically broader than 'obmacywać,' it ranges from non-sexual (feeling in the dark for a switch) to sexual handling, with the sexual meaning activated by context.
records.english_term: to feel, to grope, to fondle
records.notes: The most general verb in this lexical family; 'macanie w ciemności' (groping in the dark) is entirely non-sexual. In sexual contexts 'macać kogoś' implies manual handling of a partner's body. Unlike 'obmacywać/obmacać,' the non-consensual framing is not baked in — context and object determine whether it reads as assault or foreplay. Mapped to 'manual_stimulation' rather than frotteurism to reflect this neutrality.

records.definition: The standard Polish clinical and legal umbrella term for sexual abuse or exploitation, encompassing any non-consensual sexual use of a person — from child sexual abuse to adult coercion — with emphasis on power differential and the instrumentalization of the victim.
records.notes: The noun 'wykorzystanie' derives from 'wykorzystać' (to use, exploit, or take advantage of), placing instrumentalization at the semantic core. Broader than 'gwałt' (rape) or 'napaść seksualna' (assault) — it is the clinical umbrella encompassing all forms of sexual victimization. No single registry concept covers this breadth: 'ravishment' is too narrow (rape only), 'sex_trafficking' is too specific, 'sexual_predator' names the perpetrator rather than the act.

records.definition: Sexual exploitation or abuse; the act of using another person for sexual purposes without free and informed consent, typically involving a power imbalance.
records.notes: Standalone 'wykorzystanie' means 'use' or 'exploitation' generically; sexual meaning requires context or the full compound 'wykorzystanie seksualne'.

records.definition: Sexual consent; the voluntary, informed, and ongoing agreement to participate in sexual activity.
records.notes: Adoption of this compound has grown significantly in Polish public discourse post-MeToo (~2017); before then the concept was rarely named as an explicit term.

records.definition: Without consent; used in legal, clinical, and journalistic contexts to describe sexual acts performed without the other party's agreement.
records.notes: 'Bez zgody' is a general Polish phrase ('without permission/agreement') repurposed in sexual-rights and legal discourse; not a fixed technical term but universally understood in context.

records.definition: Sexual coercion; the use of pressure, manipulation, or threats to compel another person into sexual activity.
records.notes: Legally distinct from 'gwałt' (rape); covers non-physical pressure and manipulation short of physical force; appears mainly in legal texts and NGO materials.

records.definition: Sexual intimidation; the use of threatening behavior or language to frighten or coerce another person in a sexual context.
records.notes: Less common than 'molestowanie seksualne' or 'przemoc seksualna'; appears primarily in legal and academic texts rather than everyday speech.

records.definition: Sexual violence; any act of a sexual nature committed against a person without consent, including rape, assault, and coercion.
records.notes: Standard umbrella legal and journalistic term; widely used by NGOs and in media coverage of rape and sexual assault cases in Poland.

records.definition: Sexual abuse; the act of subjecting another person to unwanted sexual acts, especially within a relationship of trust, authority, or dependency.
records.notes: Carries connotation of ongoing or systemic abuse rather than a single incident; frequently used in contexts of clergy abuse, domestic violence, and child protection.

records.definition: Perfective crude slang verb meaning to fuck someone; to have sex with someone, framed as conquest or a completed act.
records.notes: Perfective aspect of 'ruchać'; 'wyruchał ją' = 'he fucked her.' 'Ruchać' is among the most common Polish crude sex verbs, comparable in frequency to 'pierdolić'.

records.definition: Youth slang verb for having sex; to fuck someone, with a crude or aggressive connotation.
records.notes: Primarily identified in teen/youth registers ca. 2010–2018; now declining. The base verb 'zaciukać' also means to stab/kill in some dialects, which may intensify the aggressive connotation in sex usage.

records.definition: Regional youth slang perfective verb for having sex; to have a fuck, often implying a casual or quick encounter.
records.english_term: to shag, to have a quickie
records.notes: Primarily southern Polish regional usage; 'fiknąć' literally means to flip or somersault, repurposed as sex slang. Not spreading nationally; stable within its regional register.

records.definition: Crude reciprocal imperfective verb meaning to fuck each other; vigorous or sustained mutual sexual intercourse.
records.notes: From 'pierdolić' with na- intensifier prefix and reflexive -się marking mutual action; one of many Polish crude sex verbs in the 'pierdolić' family. The na- prefix adds intensity.

records.definition: Regional vulgar imperfective verb meaning to fuck; to have sex with someone with crude and often aggressive connotation.
records.notes: Less universal than 'ruchać' or 'pierdolić'; weighted toward rural and working-class registers; known nationally but used actively mainly in regional speech communities.

records.definition: Perfective form of rypać; to fuck once, to have sex with someone on a single completed occasion.
records.notes: Perfective aspect implies a completed single act; 'rypnął ją' = 'he fucked her.' Used interchangeably with rypać where perfective aspect is required.

records.definition: Verbal noun from rypać; the act of fucking; crude regional slang for sexual intercourse as an ongoing activity.
records.notes: Nominalized form; 'ostre rypanie' = 'hard fucking.' Less widespread than 'ruchanie' (from ruchać) or 'pierdolenie' (from pierdolić), which dominate nationally.

records.definition: Literally 'to let oneself be fucked'; passive construction implying willing sexual submission, used pejoratively about someone regarded as sexually available or loose.
records.notes: The 'dać się' (to allow oneself) construction frames the subject as passive and consenting; typically slut-shaming when said about a woman, but can be neutral in first-person use.

records.definition: Very crude slang verb meaning to fuck in the ass; to perform anal intercourse, emphasizing penetrative insertion into the anus.
records.notes: Compound from 'w' (into) + 'dup-' (ass, from 'dupa') + verbal suffix -czyć; the anal meaning is fully transparent to Polish speakers from the morphology.

records.definition: Perfective regional crude slang verb meaning to fuck someone; to have sex with someone.
records.notes: Rare; primarily eastern Poland; perfective counterpart to 'bzdyczyć.' Etymology unclear — possibly onomatopoeic or from eastern dialect roots. Largely unknown outside its origin region.

records.definition: Imperfective regional crude slang verb meaning to fuck; habitual or ongoing sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Rarer than its perfective counterpart 'nabzdyczyć'; both terms are confined to eastern Polish regional speech and virtually unknown to younger urban speakers nationally.

records.definition: Literally 'to let oneself be fucked'; passive construction implying sexual willingness or submission; used pejoratively about someone regarded as sexually permissive.
records.notes: From 'pierdolić', one of the most vulgar Polish sex verbs; the 'dać się' construction is the key marker of passivity and willing submission; standard in slut-shaming register.

records.definition: Literally 'to beg for sex'; describes someone so sexually desperate that they make their need humiliatingly explicit.
records.notes: Not a fixed idiom but a transparent compositional phrase; used to mock or pity someone whose sexual desperation has become socially visible. Implied subject is usually male.

records.definition: Literally 'hungry for it' (feminine grammatical form); idiom expressing intense female sexual craving or horniness.
records.notes: The feminine adjective 'głodna' grammatically marks the subject as female; the male counterpart is 'głodny tego.' 'Tego' (genitive of 'to') is a vague deictic standing in for sex.

records.definition: Literally 'hungry for it' (masculine grammatical form); idiom expressing intense male sexual craving or horniness.
records.notes: The masculine adjective 'głodny' grammatically marks the subject as male; the female counterpart is 'głodna tego.' Both forms use 'tego' as a vague genitive deictic for sex.

records.definition: Literally 'to fly toward someone'; very common Polish colloquial idiom meaning to fancy, be attracted to, or have a crush on someone.
records.english_term: to fancy someone, to be into someone
records.notes: 'Leci na nią' = 'he's into her.' Not inherently sexual — covers romantic attraction and celebrity infatuation as well as sexual desire. One of the most widely used attraction idioms in Polish.

records.definition: Literally 'to have an appetite for someone'; Polish idiom expressing strong desire or lust directed at a specific person.
records.english_term: to have the hots for someone, to lust after someone
records.notes: More intense than 'lecieć na kogoś'; 'chrapka' implies hungry appetite. The phrase is also used for non-sexual coveting (wanting someone's job or possession), but in sexual contexts maps to lust.

records.definition: Noun meaning strong appetite or craving; in sexual contexts, lust or desire for a specific person.
records.notes: Rarely appears standalone; almost always in the fixed phrase 'mieć chrapkę na kogoś/coś.' Not exclusively sexual: covers ambition, greed, and covetousness generally.

records.definition: Sexual fantasies; erotic mental imagery or imaginative scenarios used for arousal or pleasure.
records.notes: Straightforward compound noun, neither clinical nor crude; listed under age/gender slang because younger speakers use it more freely in casual conversation; the registry lacks a dedicated sexual_fantasy concept, so eroticism is the closest available slug.

records.definition: In Polish prison slang, a male prisoner forced into sexual submission and used by other inmates; extended broadly as a street insult for any weak, contemptible, or debased man.
records.notes: One of the harshest words in Polish vernacular; carries extreme honor-shame economy weight in prison culture; has migrated to general street speech as a severe insult for cowardice or submissiveness, somewhat diluting the original sexual meaning.

records.definition: Prison slang verb meaning to sexually subjugate another male prisoner, typically through anal rape, thereby reducing him to cwel status and establishing dominance.
records.notes: Primarily prison-specific; carries connotations of coerced sexual domination rather than consensual sex; also used loosely outside prison to mean 'to humiliate or overpower'; derives directly from the noun cwel.

records.definition: Prison slang verb meaning to alter a prisoner's cwel status through a sexual act: either to restore a former cwel's standing by making him perform a dominant sex act on another, or conversely to complete the process of making someone a cwel for the first time.
records.notes: Highly ambiguous due to the Polish 'od-' prefix, which can denote either reversal or completion of an action; the specific meaning depends on context; no English concept captures this honor-economy ritual of using forced sex to grant or strip prison status; genuinely novel concept.

records.definition: Crude slang verb meaning to penetrate sexually, drawn from the literal meaning 'to plant' (as in planting a tree or seedling); applied to decisive penile insertion.
records.notes: Agricultural metaphor for penetration; the 'za-' prefix adds purposive/completive aspect suggesting deliberate, committed penetration; common in both prison and general street crude speech.

records.definition: Crude phrasal verb meaning to have sex with someone, literally 'to do someone'; in prison context emphasizes domination and instrumental use of the other person.
records.notes: Precise structural and connotative parallel to English 'to do someone'; widely recognized outside prison as general crude sexual slang; in prison context the dominance and objectification reading is foregrounded.

records.definition: Crude phrase meaning to anally penetrate someone, literally 'to take from behind'; used in prison slang for rape and in general crude speech for consensual anal sex.
records.notes: Literal translation maps cleanly to English 'to take from behind'; in prison context strongly implies non-consensual anal penetration establishing dominance; in civilian use simply denotes anal or doggy-style sex.

records.definition: Prison and street slang verb meaning to penetrate sexually with aggression, derived from the literal meaning 'to cut into' or 'to score'; implies forceful, predatory intercourse.
records.notes: Knife/blade metaphor implies aggressive or potentially non-consensual penetration; the primary civilian meaning is 'to carve' or 'to swindle someone,' so the sexual reading is context-dependent; 'na-' prefix adds downward or onto-target directionality.

records.definition: Crude slang verb meaning to mount and have sex with someone, from the literal meaning 'to cover' (as one animal mounts another); in prison slang used for forced intercourse from above.
records.notes: Animal-mounting metaphor exploiting the 'covering from above' imagery; the dominant civilian meaning of 'nakryć' is to catch someone red-handed, so the sexual sense is heavily context-dependent and less recognized outside prison slang.

records.definition: Common sexual euphemism meaning to penetrate, literally 'to enter'; used for penile insertion in vaginal or anal sex across civilian and prison registers.
records.notes: One of the most widely used Polish sexual euphemisms; crude score is moderate because it is also normalized in non-prison sexual discourse and lacks the aggressive valence of most prison-slang verbs on this list; parallels English 'to go in' or 'to enter.'

records.definition: Crude verb meaning to impale or skewer sexually, derived from the literal meaning 'to thread onto a spit or spike'; describes aggressive anal or vaginal penetration with a strong violent image.
records.notes: Among the more graphically violent sexual metaphors in Polish slang; the literal meaning involves threading meat onto a spit, making the image of brutal penetration explicit; used in both prison and general crude speech.

records.definition: Prison and military crude slang verb meaning to ejaculate, derived from 'prztykać' (to snap or flick with a finger); the 'wy-' prefix signals outward expulsion, evoking shooting or flicking semen out.
records.notes: Low recognition outside prison and military subcultures; the base verb 'prztykać' means to flick/snap, making this a kinetic metaphor for the expulsive force of ejaculation; relatively rare in mainstream Polish crude slang.

records.definition: Military term for bayonets repurposed as a phallic double entendre in prison and military slang; the long rigid pointed weapon serves as a coded metaphor for erect penises or acts of penetration.
records.notes: Used in contexts where overt sexual language is suppressed; 'skrzyżować bagnety' (to cross bayonets) can imply mutual sexual contact; double entendre relies on the bayonet's phallic shape and its penetrative military function; recognition has declined as military culture becomes less dominant in Polish society.

records.definition: Term for a small-caliber sporting or hunting rifle repurposed as a phallic double entendre in military and prison slang; the long barrel functions as a euphemism for the penis.
records.notes: Less widely recognized as a sexual term than 'bagnety'; requires explicit context to be read sexually; 'sztucer' is a borrowing from German 'Stutzen' (a short-barreled rifle); the double entendre operates purely on phallic shape without an obvious action metaphor.

records.definition: Polish prison slang phrase literally meaning 'to drag someone into the bedding/blanket'; denotes the specific act of forcibly pulling another prisoner into one's bunk to sexually assault them and initiate them into cwel status.
records.notes: 'Materiał' (literally fabric/material) is prison slang for a prisoner's bedding or sleeping area; the phrase encodes the specific physical choreography of Polish prison sexual coercion — the dragging to a private bunk — as a culturally codified ritual act with no single English-language concept equivalent; genuinely novel concept.

records.definition: Crude slang verb meaning to penetrate deeply and forcefully during sex, from the literal meaning 'to bury' or 'to dig in'; implies sustained, aggressive deep thrusting.
records.notes: Burial metaphor for deep penetration; the 'za-' prefix conveys completion (fully buried to the hilt); used in both prison and general crude slang; parallels English 'to bury it in her/him.'

records.definition: Very common crude slang verb meaning to have sex with someone, derived from the literal meaning 'to hit, strike, or whack'; one of the most versatile and widely recognized Polish vulgar terms for sex.
records.notes: Precise English parallel is 'to bang' — identical percussive/striking metaphor, same crude register, same broad versatility; also used non-sexually to mean to hit something hard; extremely common in Polish crude speech well beyond the prison context.

records.definition: Crude slang verb meaning to thrust into sexually with sharp force, from the literal meaning 'to drive in' or 'to hammer in' as one would drive a nail; implies a single decisive, forceful act of penetration.
records.english_term: to drive it in / to hammer in
records.notes: Construction metaphor (hammering a nail) for forceful penetration; 'w-' prefix encodes inward motion and the perfective aspect signals a single completed act rather than ongoing thrusting; common in both prison and general crude Polish vocabulary.

records.definition: Crude reflexive slang verb meaning to force one's way into someone sexually, from the literal meaning 'to break in' or 'to invade'; used for forcible penetration with strong connotations of violation and conquest.
records.english_term: to force one's way in / to break into
records.notes: The reflexive 'się' particle combined with the violent root 'wedrzeć' (to break in, as a burglar breaks into a building) makes this one of the most explicitly coercive sexual verbs in Polish slang; carries very strong connotations of non-consent or at minimum extreme aggressive dominance.

records.definition: The standard clinical and anatomical term for the external male reproductive and urinary organ.
Literary and symbolic term for the penis or phallus, from Greek via Latin; used in psychoanalytic, art-historical, and academic contexts.
records.notes: Common in Lacanian psychoanalysis, anthropology, and discussions of phallic iconography; not used in everyday speech or clinical consultations.

records.definition: Euphemistic phrase meaning 'virile member,' used as a polite or literary circumlocution for the penis in journalism, legal documents, and older fiction.
records.notes: Typical of written registers where anatomical precision is needed but direct terms feel inappropriate; found in Brazilian court rulings and news reporting on sexual offenses.

records.definition: The rounded distal tip of the penis; the glans penis.
records.notes: The same term applies to the glans clitoridis in female anatomy; context determines which organ is referenced. Encountered mainly in medical and sex-education settings.

records.definition: The retractable fold of skin covering the glans penis in uncircumcised males; the foreskin or prepuce.
records.notes: Also applies anatomically to the clitoral hood (prepúcio do clitóris); primarily encountered in urology, neonatology, and religious-circumcision discourse.

records.definition: Transparent descriptive phrase meaning 'male sexual organ,' used when naming the penis directly feels too explicit or clinical.
records.notes: Common in sex-education curricula for minors, official public-health materials, and formal journalism; transparency of meaning ensures near-universal recognition despite the circumlocution.

records.definition: Either of the paired columns of erectile tissue in the penis that engorge with blood to produce an erection; corpus cavernosum.
records.notes: Encountered almost exclusively in urology, sexual medicine, and anatomy education; essentially unknown outside those specialist fields.

records.definition: The segment of the urethra running through the penis, serving as the common channel for urine and semen.
records.notes: 'Uretra' alone is moderately known by the general public; 'peniana' is the anatomical adjective specifying the penile segment; the combined term is specialist medical usage only.

records.definition: Extremely widespread crude slang for the penis, literally meaning 'stick' or 'wood'; the single most frequently used vulgar penis term in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Also the most productive morphological base for derived forms: pauzão (large), pauinho (small/diminutive), pau-duro (erect, literally 'hard stick'). Context strongly affects offense level — common in male banter but offensive in mixed or formal settings.

records.definition: Very crude slang for the penis; considered more vulgar than 'pau' and strongly avoided in polite or mixed company.
records.notes: Etymology uncertain, possibly onomatopoetic or from Tupi. Ranks among the most offensive standard penis terms in Brazilian Portuguese alongside 'caralho' and 'rola'; heavy presence in funk carioca and baile funk lyrics.

records.definition: Crude slang for the penis, possibly related to the verb 'rolar' (to roll) or the noun for a turtledove.
records.notes: Shares its spelling with 'rola' (Eurasian collared dove), occasionally generating double meanings in bird-watching or ornithology contexts. Heavily used in hip-hop, funk carioca, and internet slang.

records.definition: One of the most offensive crude slang terms for the penis in Brazilian Portuguese, and simultaneously the language's most versatile general expletive, functioning like 'fuck' as an interjection, intensifier, or exclamation.
records.notes: Far more commonly encountered as a general expletive than as a literal anatomical reference: 'Vai pro caralho!' (fuck off!), 'Que caralho?' (what the fuck?), 'Pra caralho' (a shitload of). Etymology possibly from Latin 'carallus' or the nautical crow's-nest 'carel'.

records.definition: Crude slang for the penis, literally meaning 'club, bludgeon, or truncheon'; also functions as a strong expletive expressing frustration or emphasis.
records.notes: Dual register as anatomical slang and general expletive ('Que cacete é esse?' = 'What the fuck is this?'). Somewhat more characteristic of São Paulo usage than Rio; slightly less common as a pure expletive than 'caralho'.

records.definition: Common informal slang for the penis, milder than most alternatives; also used in children's speech and family contexts with reduced offense.
records.notes: Literally means 'painted' (past participle) or 'young bird/chick.' Its overlap with children's language makes it unique among Brazilian Portuguese penis terms — it can appear in parenting, pediatric, and family contexts where most slang would be entirely inappropriate.

records.definition: Crude slang for the penis, from 'picar' (to sting, peck, or bite); very common in informal speech, song lyrics, and internet content.
records.notes: Shares spelling with the medical term 'pica' (eating disorder involving non-food substances), creating inadvertent ambiguity in clinical texts. The anatomical slang meaning is the dominant connotation in colloquial speech.

records.definition: Crude slang for the penis, literally meaning 'rod, pole, or long stick'; evokes rigidity and length.
records.notes: 'Vara de pescar' (fishing rod) is the primary everyday meaning, generating frequent double-entendre. Somewhat more common in older generations and rural registers than among urban youth.

records.definition: Slang for the penis, literally meaning 'turnip'; often carries an implication of a thick, short, or unimpressive organ and can be used dismissively.
records.notes: Unlike cucumber or sausage metaphors, the turnip shape does not imply length, lending 'nabo' a subtly pejorative connotation. High lexical ambiguity since 'nabo' is also simply the vegetable in everyday supermarket speech.

records.definition: Euphemistic slang for the penis, literally meaning 'tool'; implies the organ as a functional implement and often carries a boastful or humorous tone.
records.notes: The functional connotation can frame the penis as skilled or capable, giving 'ferramenta' a mildly flattering register compared with neutral anatomical slang. Parallel to English 'tool' in both meaning and register.

records.definition: Augmentative form of 'pau' (stick/dick) formed with the '-ão' suffix, meaning a large or impressively sized penis.
records.notes: The augmentative '-ão' suffix is morphologically regular and immediately parsed by any speaker of Brazilian Portuguese; 'pauzão' is among the most transparent derived forms. Often used admiringly, boastfully, or in pornographic taxonomy.

records.definition: Euphemistic or mock-solemn term for the penis, literally meaning 'instrument'; implies the organ as a formal implement and is typically used with ironic or comedic intent.
records.notes: Noticeably more literary and ironic than 'ferramenta'; often appears in self-deprecating humor or in written comedy ('meu humilde instrumento' — 'my humble instrument'). Less naturalistic in ordinary speech.

records.definition: Slang for the penis, literally meaning 'earthworm'; typically implies a small, thin, or limp penis and is therefore used mockingly or dismissively.
records.notes: The earthworm metaphor emphasizes thinness, smallness, or flaccidity rather than length or girth; rarely deployed as a neutral descriptor. Semantically unrelated to the idiom 'ter uma minhoca na cabeça' (to have a worm in one's head = to have an obsessive idea).

records.definition: Slang for the penis, literally meaning 'hot-dog sausage'; a food-based metaphor emphasizing the phallic shape of the frankfurter.
records.notes: Implies a rounder, shorter shape relative to linguiça; the food-metaphor register keeps the term in the humorous rather than offensive range. High everyday recognition because 'salsicha' is an extremely common food word.

records.definition: Slang for the penis, literally meaning 'pork sausage / chouriço'; the food metaphor implies greater length than 'salsicha' due to the sausage type's elongated form.
records.notes: Linguiça is a longer, thinner sausage than salsicha, so the implied penile shape differs subtly. Both are well-established food metaphors in Brazilian popular culture; linguiça appears frequently in Carnaval double-entendre songs and humor.

records.definition: Slang for the penis, literally meaning 'cucumber'; a food metaphor that implies both length and girth.
records.notes: Shared metaphor with English, where 'cucumber' serves the same function. In Brazilian Portuguese 'pepino' also colloquially means 'a problem or difficult situation' ('que pepino!' = 'what a mess!'), adding significant lexical ambiguity that requires context to disambiguate.

records.definition: Slang for the penis, literally meaning 'trumpet'; an object metaphor referencing the instrument's elongated, flared shape, which evokes the glans.
records.notes: Less common than food-based or rod-based metaphors and therefore less immediately parsed as penis slang; requires stronger contextual cues. 'Trombeta' also colloquially describes a loud, pompous person ('ele é um trombeta' = 'he's a windbag'), so penis usage must be made clear by context.

records.definition: Slang for penis derived from the everyday word for 'paintbrush,' evoking the organ's elongated shape.
records.notes: Playful, mild register; the double meaning is widely understood but less common than coarser alternatives.

records.definition: General Brazilian slang for 'thing' or 'stuff,' repurposed as a casual euphemism for the penis in sexual contexts.
records.notes: Polysemous; primary meaning is 'thing/object'; sexual meaning is context-dependent and not universal; common in funk carioca registers.

records.definition: Slang for penis based on 'bisnaga,' a squeeze tube or elongated bread roll, emphasizing the organ's cylindrical shape.
records.notes: Humor relies on the mundane double meaning; more common in informal spoken registers than in written erotica.

records.definition: Augmentative slang for a large penis, from 'mangueira' (hose or pipe); the -ão suffix marks exceptional size.
records.notes: 'Mangueira' can mean a garden hose or fire hose; augmentative suffix implies the organ is impressively large rather than naming it neutrally.

records.definition: Slang for a short, stubby penis, from 'toco' meaning a tree stump or cut-off stub; implies inadequate length.
records.notes: Mildly derogatory due to implied inadequacy; not the most frequent term but widely understood across Brazil.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'pau' (wood/dick), meaning 'little stick'; implies a small penis, inheriting crudeness from the base form.
records.notes: 'Pau' alone is the dominant crude slang for penis in Brazil; the -inho diminutive explicitly encodes small size and carries a mildly derogatory edge.

records.definition: Slang for an impressively large or powerful penis, from 'estouro' ('explosion' or 'bang'), emphasizing dramatic impact or exceptional size.
records.notes: Broadly means something outstanding; sexual meaning is context-dependent and less lexically fixed than other penis slang terms; can also describe an impressive sex act.

records.definition: Crude slang for the penis, originally a nautical term for a ship's yard or spar, now widely used as a direct vulgar term for the organ.
records.notes: Also appears in the idiom 'não vale uma verga' (not worth a damn), where it functions as a dismissive intensifier; usage spans Brazil and Portugal.

records.definition: Euphemism for the penis from the anatomical sense of 'member' (body part or limb); polite and indirect, used when speakers avoid crude or clinical terms.
records.notes: Parallel to English 'member'; common in written erotica and soft-register sexual discourse; neither clinical enough to be technical nor crude enough to offend.

records.definition: General Brazilian slang for 'thing' or 'object,' used as a vague deictic euphemism for the penis.
records.notes: Non-specific; sexual meaning depends entirely on context; lower intrinsic crudeness than explicit slang; more common in São Paulo and southern Brazil than in the Northeast.

records.definition: Standard anatomical term for the internal muscular canal in females extending from the cervix to the vulva.
Clinical term for the external female genitalia, comprising the labia, clitoris, mons pubis, and vaginal opening.
records.notes: Frequently conflated with 'vagina' in lay usage; lower recognition than 'vagina' despite being the more anatomically precise term for external structures.

records.definition: Clinical and common term for the small erectile organ at the anterior junction of the labia minora; the primary locus of female sexual pleasure.
Clinical term for the two outer folds of skin forming the outer boundary of the vulva (labia majora).
records.notes: Primarily encountered in medical, educational, and public health contexts; rarely used in casual speech.

records.definition: Clinical term for the two inner folds of skin within the labia majora surrounding the vaginal opening and urethral meatus (labia minora).
records.notes: Even less commonly known than 'lábios maiores' among lay speakers; primarily encountered in medical or health education settings.

records.definition: Clinical term for the rounded mound of fatty tissue overlying the pubic symphysis in females (mons pubis).
records.notes: Encountered mainly in medical, anatomical, and health education contexts; effectively synonymous with 'monte de Vênus' in lay use where both are known.

records.definition: Literary and historical anatomical term for the mons pubis, 'Mount of Venus,' named after the Roman goddess of love.
records.notes: Older term with a romantic or poetic register; parallels the classical Latin 'mons veneris'; still circulates in literary erotica and popular anatomy references more than the purely clinical 'monte pubiano'.

records.definition: Clinical term for the thin mucous membrane partially covering the vaginal opening; highly variable in form and medically irrelevant as a virginity indicator.
records.notes: Above-average lay recognition driven by Brazil's strong cultural emphasis on female virginity; the term carries significant moral and social weight beyond its anatomical meaning.

records.definition: Highly technical clinical term for the vaginal introitus, the entrance to the vaginal canal at the vaginal opening.
records.notes: Used primarily by medical professionals and in clinical documentation; rarely encountered outside gynecological or anatomical contexts.

records.definition: Clinical descriptive term for the vaginal canal, emphasizing the tubular internal anatomy from cervix to vaginal opening.
records.notes: More specific than 'vagina' alone; used to clarify anatomical location in medical and sex education contexts.

records.definition: Clinical term for the muscular and mucosal walls of the vaginal canal, referenced in anatomy, gynecology, and sex education.
records.notes: Encountered primarily in medical documentation and clinical contexts; essentially absent from lay or erotic discourse.

records.definition: The most prevalent and most vulgar Brazilian Portuguese slang term for the vagina; a primary sexual expletive.
records.notes: The dominant crude term for vagina in Brazil; socially significantly less catastrophic than English 'cunt' in most Brazilian registers but still highly offensive in formal contexts; ubiquitous in erotica, insults, and casual crude speech.

records.definition: Crude Brazilian slang for the vagina, widely recognized and used, generally perceived as slightly less intense than 'buceta' in typical social contexts.
records.notes: Often used interchangeably with 'buceta' and 'xoxota'; the register distinction between the three is subtle and speaker-dependent rather than categorical.

records.definition: Crude Brazilian slang for the vagina; a reduplicated variant of 'xota' that can carry a slightly more familiar or diminutive tone without meaningfully lowering crudeness.
records.notes: Reduplication of 'xota'; sometimes perceived as marginally warmer or more intimate than the base form; equally offensive in formal contexts; common across all regions of Brazil.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina; the dominant term in European Portuguese, recognized in Brazil largely through internet and media exposure but rarely the default choice for Brazilian speakers.
records.notes: Primarily a European Portuguese term; Brazilian recognition has grown with internet connectivity and streaming consumption of Portuguese content; in-group usage frequency in Brazil is substantially lower than 'buceta' or 'xoxota'.

records.definition: Crude Brazilian Portuguese slang for the vagina or vulva, widely understood across Brazil.
records.notes: Moderate-to-high vulgarity; less charged than 'buceta' but clearly crude; broad national recognition.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina derived from 'racha' meaning split or crack, referencing the labial cleft.
records.notes: Polysemous: primary meaning is 'crack' or 'split'; the sexual meaning is unambiguous in context; also used for the buttock cleft.

records.definition: Crude Brazilian slang for the vagina; phonetically distinct from 'buceta' but similarly vulgar in register.
records.notes: Etymology uncertain; may be a phonetic euphemistic distortion; less universal than 'buceta' but broadly recognized.

records.definition: Crude Brazilian slang for the vagina, widely used and broadly understood across age groups.
records.notes: Occasionally used in child-directed speech as a mild euphemism, which slightly lowers perceived vulgarity compared to 'buceta'.

records.definition: The most heavily crude and common Brazilian slang for the vagina; variant spelling of 'buceta'.
records.notes: Among the strongest profanities in Brazilian Portuguese; the 'buceta' spelling is more standard, but 'boceta' appears in some regional and written contexts; recognition near-universal among adult speakers.

records.definition: Childish or euphemistic Brazilian Portuguese term for the vagina, used in child-directed speech and playful adult registers.
records.notes: Not to be confused with the English 'xoxo' (hugs and kisses); in Brazilian Portuguese the 'x' represents the 'sh' phoneme, linking it phonetically to 'xota' and related slang.

records.definition: Euphemism for the vagina, literally 'small female parakeet'; used in playful or child-directed speech.
records.notes: Animal-name euphemism common in Portuguese-speaking cultures; the feminine diminutive form reinforces the genital mapping.

records.definition: Baby-talk term for the vagina used in child-directed speech and among adults in an intentionally cute register.
records.notes: Very low vulgarity; deliberately non-threatening; 'totó' is also a colloquial name for a small dog in some contexts, adding to its soft connotation.

records.definition: Regional crude slang for the vagina; 'fuça' primarily means snout or muzzle in standard Portuguese.
records.notes: Polysemous; sexual meaning is secondary and requires context; less universally known than core vagina slang; possible link to 'focinho' (animal snout) by analogy.

records.definition: Crude Brazilian slang for the vagina, carrying a strong connotation of unpleasant genital odor.
records.notes: Derogatory implication of odor is intrinsic rather than contextual; used as an insult more than a neutral anatomical descriptor; regional distribution skews toward Northeast and Southeast Brazil.

records.definition: Euphemism for the vagina, literally 'little bird', used in child-directed speech and playful adult contexts.
records.notes: Animal-name euphemism parallel to 'periquita'; primary meaning is simply a small bird; sexual meaning recognized contextually by most adult speakers.

records.definition: Metaphorical slang for the vagina, literally 'grotto' or 'cave', referencing the concave internal anatomy.
records.notes: More humorous or poetic than aggressively vulgar; understood by most adults in the sexual sense in context; occasionally appears in erotic fiction.

records.definition: Hyperbolic slang for the vagina, literally 'abyss', implying an exceptionally wide or gaping vaginal opening; typically deployed as an insult.
records.notes: Carries an implicit insult about vaginal laxity or size; more of a creative epithet than standard slang; low frequency but broadly understood when encountered.

records.definition: Regional crude slang for the vagina, primarily attested in Northeastern Brazil, with limited national distribution.
records.notes: Etymology unclear; low national recognition; confidence in regional attribution is moderate; may be hyperlocal to specific cities or communities.

records.definition: Playful euphemism for the vagina; diminutive of 'mexerica', a type of mandarin orange, evoking a small, rounded fruit.
records.notes: Fruit-based genital metaphor; the double diminutive suffix '-inha' adds an affectionate or childlike tone; relatively niche and context-dependent.

records.definition: Slang for the vagina, literally 'little mouse' or 'little rat', likely referencing pubic hair and the hidden anatomy of the vulva.
records.notes: Animal metaphor; the '-inha' diminutive softens vulgarity somewhat; pubic-hair association is the primary motivating image for the metaphor.

records.definition: Rare baby-talk euphemism for the vagina in some regional or family dialects; 'papai' ordinarily means 'daddy'.
records.notes: Extremely low recognition in this sexual sense; the primary meaning (father/daddy) dominates; use as vagina slang is hyperlocal or idiolectal; data confidence is low.

records.definition: Slang for the vagina, literally 'slit' or 'fissure', referencing the visible labial cleft.
records.notes: 'Fenda' in standard Portuguese refers to any narrow linear opening or crack; the genital metaphor is anatomically transparent and recognized by most adult speakers in context.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina derived from 'racha' meaning split or crack, referencing the labial cleft.
records.notes: Duplicate of entry 2; included as listed in source word list. Polysemous: primary meaning is 'crack' or 'split'; the sexual meaning is unambiguous in context.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian Portuguese slang term for the clitoris; 'grelo' literally means a germinated plant sprout or shoot.
records.notes: Primary sexual meaning is firmly established; the botanical source metaphor evokes the small protrusion of a sprout emerging from its base; widely used across all ages and registers.

records.definition: Informal slang for the clitoris, literally 'button', evoking its small rounded shape and tactile quality.
records.notes: 'Button' is used as clitoris slang in English as well, making this a cross-linguistic parallel metaphor; low vulgarity, broadly usable in mixed company.

records.definition: Slang for the exposed clitoral glans, literally 'little head', referencing the rounded tip of the clitoris.
records.notes: Anatomically more precise than most clitoris slang, targeting specifically the glans rather than the entire structure; the diminutive '-inha' adds an affectionate tone; occasionally used for the glans penis, requiring context.

records.definition: Rare euphemism for the clitoris, literally 'little lamb', used in affectionate or playful contexts.
records.notes: Low national recognition in this sexual sense; animal-name euphemism with soft, tender connotations; may be hyperlocal or idiolectal; likely motivated by the soft, rounded feel of the mons pubis rather than the clitoris specifically.

records.definition: The clinical anatomical term for the anus; the external orifice of the gastrointestinal tract at the terminal end of the rectum.
records.notes: Standard medical and formal register term borrowed from Latin; used in health education, clinical settings, and formal written Portuguese; carries no vulgarity in itself.

records.definition: Clinical term for the rectum, the terminal segment of the large intestine extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal.
records.notes: 'Reto' also means 'straight' or 'direct' as a common adjective in Portuguese; the anatomical meaning is the full form 'intestino reto' (straight intestine); the abbreviated 'reto' is unambiguous only in medical context.

records.definition: The ring-shaped muscular valve that controls the opening and closing of the anal orifice, used exclusively in clinical and anatomical contexts.
The short terminal segment of the large intestine between the rectum and the anal opening, used exclusively in medical and anatomical contexts.
The clinical term for the skin and soft tissue immediately surrounding the anal opening.
records.notes: Mapped to 'anus' concept as the closest registry entry; the perianal region is technically distinct from the anal canal and sphincter but no registry concept covers it precisely.

records.definition: The most common and foundational crude term for the anus in Brazilian Portuguese, ubiquitous in colloquial speech, sexual slang, and general insults.
records.notes: Appears in dozens of compound expressions (e.g., 'olho do cu', 'dar o cu', 'de cu'); doubles as a general-purpose insult comparable to 'asshole' in severity.

records.definition: Literally 'hole'; used as crude slang for the anus, emphasizing its function as a penetrable orifice.
records.notes: Primary meaning is a generic hole or pit; anatomical meaning is inferred entirely from context; occasionally applied to the vagina as well.

records.definition: Literally the seat or crotch panel of trousers; used euphemistically to refer to the anus or general rear area.
records.notes: Primary meaning is a tailoring term for the seat of pants; anatomical use is indirect and euphemistic, relying on metonymic association between the garment zone and the body underneath.

records.definition: Humorous slang framing the anus as a 'portal' or gateway, used playfully in online and informal speech.
records.notes: Ironic, internet-influenced coinage; the English 'back door' carries an analogous playful-euphemistic framing.

records.definition: In-group slang for the anus circulating primarily in Brazilian LGBTQ+ and gay male communities.
records.notes: Low general-population recognition; likely Caló-influenced or originating in gay community lexicon; usage concentrated in major urban LGBTQ+ scenes (São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro).

records.definition: Literally 'eye of the ass'; extremely common crude compound slang for the anus, evoking the circular appearance of the sphincter.
records.notes: The eye-sphincter visual metaphor is shared across Romance languages (cf. Spanish 'ojo del culo', French 'l'oeil de bronze'); widely used in sexual speech and as a general insult.

records.definition: Literally 'tail'; in explicit sexual contexts specifically denotes the anus as the posterior orifice targeted for penetration.
records.notes: Same lexeme is used for buttocks in general slang; in explicitly sexual speech 'rabo' narrows to mean the anus specifically rather than the buttocks broadly.

records.definition: Crude and relatively rare slang for the anus; etymology uncertain, possibly a blend of 'buraco' (hole) with a pejorative augmentative suffix.
records.notes: Low-frequency term; may be regional or limited to specific social groups; etymology and geographic distribution are not well-documented.

records.definition: Literally 'groove' or 'slot'; crude slang for the anus, emphasizing the slit-like contour of the anal cleft.
records.notes: Primary meaning is a mechanical groove or notch; occasionally applied to the vagina as well; anatomical use is context-dependent.

records.definition: The dominant everyday Brazilian Portuguese word for the buttocks, used across all social registers and only mildly crude.
records.notes: Of African origin (Kimbundu 'bunda'); significantly less crude than 'cu'; celebrated in Brazilian popular culture, music, and advertising as a cultural symbol.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'bunda'; a large, prominent pair of buttocks, applied admiringly or descriptively to a person with notable gluteal mass.
records.notes: Positive or neutral in Brazilian cultural context given widespread valorization of the large female posterior; tone can shift to pejorative depending on delivery.

records.definition: Literally 'tail'; common crude slang for the buttocks in general everyday usage.
records.notes: Same lexeme is used to mean the anus more specifically in explicitly sexual speech; in non-sexual slang 'rabo' defaults to the buttocks broadly.

records.definition: Literally 'rear' or 'back'; the standard polite euphemism for the buttocks in Brazilian Portuguese, safe for formal and broadcast contexts.
records.notes: Analogous to 'posterior' or 'backside' in English register; widely used in journalism, television, and professional speech.

records.definition: The formal anatomical term for the gluteal muscles and overlying tissue constituting the buttocks.
records.notes: Used in medical, legal, and formal educational contexts; sounds clinical and slightly stilted in everyday speech compared to 'bunda' or 'traseiro'.

records.definition: Childlike reduplicated slang for the buttocks, used in child-directed speech and affectionately among adults.
records.notes: Tone is infantile and affectionate; widely used by adults in non-sexual contexts and has crossed into advertising and popular-culture usage.

records.definition: Baby-talk euphemism for the buttocks, used primarily in speech directed at young children.
records.notes: Strongly associated with parental and caregiver registers; adult use is ironic or deliberately infantilizing.

records.definition: A woman with very large, prominent buttocks; derived from 'cu' with augmentative suffix, placing it in a cruder register than 'bunduda'.
records.notes: Feminine-gendered form; can be appreciative in Brazilian sexual culture or pejorative depending on speaker intent; derived from 'cu' (anus/ass) rather than 'bunda', which accounts for its higher crude score.

records.definition: Literally 'rear quarters'; a humorous or arch literary euphemism for the buttocks borrowed from equine anatomy terminology.
records.notes: Borrowing livestock anatomical vocabulary to describe human anatomy creates a comic or distancing effect; used in written humor, journalism, or ironic speech rather than everyday slang.

records.definition: The standard clinical and lay term for the female breasts in Brazilian Portuguese, spanning medical texts, public health communication, and everyday speech.
records.notes: The official clinical term used in medicine and education; also common in lay speech, making it less purely technical than 'glândulas mamárias'.

records.definition: The most common everyday Brazilian Portuguese word for the female breasts, spanning colloquial, literary, and journalistic registers.
records.notes: Originally meaning 'bosom' or 'chest cavity'; has fully shifted to denote the breasts; slightly more literary or romantic in connotation than 'mamas'.

records.definition: The strictly anatomical term for the mammary glands, emphasizing the breast as a glandular biological structure rather than a sexual or aesthetic object.
records.notes: Sounds heavily clinical in lay conversation; recognition below 'mamas' or 'seios' because most speakers default to shorter terms in everyday speech.

records.definition: The standard Brazilian Portuguese term for the nipple, the erectile protrusion at the apex of the breast.
records.notes: Used in clinical, educational, and everyday contexts; not considered particularly crude despite referring to an anatomically specific erogenous structure.

records.definition: The pigmented circular area of skin surrounding the nipple of the breast.
records.notes: Standard clinical and educational term; universally understood in medical contexts.

records.definition: The glandular and fatty tissue comprising the breast, used in clinical and oncological contexts.
records.notes: Primarily encountered in medical literature, oncology, and anatomy education; rarely used in everyday speech.

records.definition: The most common everyday Brazilian Portuguese word for female breasts; neutral-to-mild in register.
records.notes: Literal meaning is chests; universally understood; mild enough for casual conversation without strong stigma.

records.definition: Crude slang for female breasts, emphasizing their sexual rather than anatomical function.
records.notes: Considered vulgar; cognate with Spanish tetas, making it cross-linguistically familiar; more offensive than peitos.

records.definition: Augmentative of peito; refers to a notably large pair of breasts, used with a tone of admiration or objectification.
records.notes: The -ão augmentative suffix emphasizes large size; often used in a sexualized, admiring context; can also refer to a single large breast.

records.definition: A semi-informal term for the breast, used in both medical discourse and everyday speech.
records.notes: Sits between clinical and informal registers; entrenched in public health campaigns (câncer de mama); also means mother colloquially, creating no meaningful ambiguity in context.

records.definition: Slang for nipple, literally meaning beak or tip; the most common informal term for the nipple in Brazil.
records.notes: Also has many non-sexual meanings (beak, spout, casual job); context disambiguates easily; carries no particular stigma in breast-feeding discussions.

records.definition: Diminutive of mama; a playful or affectionate term for a small breast or, in some usages, the nipple.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix -inha softens and infantilizes the term; also a popular cut of beef in Brazil (rump tip), creating potential for wordplay.

records.definition: Literally melons; a euphemistic metaphor for large, round breasts.
records.notes: Cross-linguistically parallel to English melons; implies large size; used humorously or admiringly; requires no disambiguation in sexual context.

records.definition: Literally globes; a euphemistic term for breasts emphasizing their round, spherical shape.
records.notes: Somewhat literary or humorous register; less common than melões or peitos; can also refer to the TV network Globo in unrelated contexts.

records.definition: Literally eggplants; used as a slang metaphor for large, pendulous breasts in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Culturally notable: in English the eggplant emoji is a penis metaphor; in Brazil it is applied to large drooping breasts — a cross-cultural divergence in food-organ mapping.

records.definition: Literally spheres; a mildly euphemistic geometric descriptor for breasts.
records.notes: More neutral and abstract than other metaphors; sometimes used humorously in a pseudo-scientific register; low crude score reflects its clinical-sounding framing.

records.definition: Literally big flat expanse; derogatory slang for a flat-chested woman or nearly nonexistent breasts.
records.notes: The augmentative -ão applied to chapa (flat surface/slab) creates a mocking term for flatness; used as a body-shaming insult targeting women with small breasts.

records.definition: Augmentative of mamilo (nipple); refers to a notably large or prominent nipple, often in an objectifying or humorous context.
records.notes: Mamilo is the clinical term for nipple; the -ão augmentative sexualizes and amplifies it; used both as description and as mild body-shaming.

records.definition: Regional slang term for breasts, primarily attested in the Northeast of Brazil.
records.notes: Low national recognition; etymology uncertain; limited to Northeastern regional dialect; may derive from topo (top/peak) referencing the breast's protrusion.

records.definition: Regional slang from southern Brazil for breasts, derived from butiá, a small round palm fruit native to Rio Grande do Sul.
records.notes: Highly regional; the butiá fruit is round and palm-sized, making it a natural anatomical metaphor; largely unknown outside the South; is_novel_concept false because the breast mapping exists in English euphemism too.

records.definition: The clinical anatomical term for the testicles, the paired male reproductive glands.
records.notes: Standard medical and educational term; widely known due to health campaigns around testicular cancer; occasionally used in formal or mock-formal insults.

records.definition: The clinical term for the scrotum; also widely used as a general insult for a contemptible or disgusting person.
records.notes: Uniquely in Brazilian Portuguese, escroto functions as a common insult meaning disgusting or contemptible person, parallel to English asshole — the insult use is arguably more frequent than the anatomical one in daily speech.

records.definition: Clinical compound noun for the scrotal sac; more explicitly anatomical than escroto alone.
records.notes: Primarily encountered in medical contexts; the redundancy of saco + escrotal (both meaning sac/scrotal) is intentional clinical precision, not error.

records.definition: The coiled duct behind each testis in which sperm matures and is stored before ejaculation.
records.notes: Extremely low public recognition; no slang or euphemistic uses; encountered almost exclusively in medical or biology education; Portuguese speakers will not recognize it without scientific training.

records.definition: Literally balls; the most common everyday slang for testicles in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Also metaphorically means courage or nerve, identical to English balls; universally understood across all demographics and age groups.

records.definition: Literally sack; crude slang for the scrotum and testicles collectively.
records.notes: Also central to common expressions: que saco! (what a drag) and encher o saco (to annoy someone, literally to fill one's sack); the anatomical and idiomatic uses coexist without confusion.

records.definition: Very crude slang for testicles; also used idiomatically to mean audacity, guts, or courage.
records.notes: One of the most emphatic testicle terms in Brazilian Portuguese; ter colhões (to have balls) means to be courageous; considered strongly vulgar; may derive from colher (to harvest/pick), evoking hanging fruit.

records.definition: Crude slang for testicles; derived from bago, denoting grains, seeds, or grape berries, evoking small round objects.
records.notes: More emphatic and crude than bolas; the seed or berry etymology evokes testicular shape and texture; used in profane expressions of frustration or bravado.

records.definition: Literally eggs; a common slang metaphor for testicles, analogous to English slang eggs.
records.notes: The egg metaphor for testicles exists across multiple Romance languages; appears in common dismissive phrases such as mandar tomar no cu (sending someone to fuck off, with ovos implied or explicit).

records.definition: Crude Brazilian Portuguese slang for the testicles; from the word for a small round fruit or berry, the round shape supplying the metaphor.
records.notes: Less prevalent than 'bolas' or 'saco'; the botanical meaning (grape berry) makes the sexual use mildly humorous; used across Brazil but not dominant in any single region.

records.definition: Humorous slang for the testicles or male genitals collectively; literally 'dangling trinkets' or 'hanging baubles', from 'pendurar' (to hang).
records.notes: Primarily comedic or self-deprecating in tone; the plural noun emphasizes multiple hanging objects; rarely deployed as a genuine insult.

records.definition: Slang for the testicles or male genitalia collectively, using the past-participial adjective 'hanging' as a euphemistic noun.
records.notes: Passive-participle form ('the thing that hangs') supplies mild euphemistic distance; less direct than 'bolas' or 'saco'; usage is scattered and not regionally dominant.

records.definition: Clinical and medical term for sexual intercourse, borrowed directly from Latin 'coitus'; standard in medical education and legal documentation.
records.notes: Recognized by most Brazilian adults through sex-education curricula; carries no vulgarity but is immediately identified as a sex term; appears in forensic reports and court documents.

records.definition: The most formally clinical Portuguese term for copulation, from Latin 'copula'; used in medical, zoological, and legal texts.
records.notes: In Brazilian Portuguese grammar, 'cópula' also denotes a linking verb (e.g., 'ser', 'estar'), which keeps this usage firmly academic; lay speakers virtually never use it for sex.

records.definition: The universally recognized neutral phrase for sexual intercourse in Brazilian Portuguese; literally 'sexual relation'.
records.notes: Dominant term in journalism, public health campaigns, and polite conversation; no register restriction whatsoever; the default educated-neutral choice.

records.definition: Clinical-neutral phrase meaning 'sexual act'; semantically broader than intercourse alone but routinely used as a euphemism for penetrative sex in legal and journalistic prose.
records.notes: Preferred in legal texts and news reporting when the specific act need not be named; broader scope than 'coito' allows it to cover non-penetrative acts as well.

records.definition: Clinical term for sexual penetration; the insertion of the penis, finger, or object into a vaginal, anal, or oral orifice.
records.notes: Standard in forensic medicine, court documents, and public health materials; slight clinical framing lowers the crude score but the term is not innocent in lay speech.

records.definition: Highly clinical compound specifying penile-vaginal intercourse; used in medical, forensic, and reproductive health contexts.
records.notes: Rarely encountered outside medical or legal texts; lay speakers use 'sexo vaginal' or simply 'relação sexual'.

records.definition: Clinical compound specifying anal intercourse; standard in forensic medicine, STI-prevention literature, and legal proceedings.
records.notes: Appears in medical reports and court documents requiring technical precision; lay usage strongly prefers 'sexo anal' or crude equivalents.

records.definition: Highly specialized clinical term for the insertion of the penis into the vagina or anus; the penile-intromission phase of coitus as defined in forensic sexology.
records.notes: Extremely narrow register; found in forensic pathology and classical sexology texts; not recognized by the majority of lay Brazilian Portuguese speakers.

records.definition: Maximally clinical compound specifying copulation with the penis inside the vagina; encountered in forensic pathology and reproductive medicine literature.
records.notes: The most technically specialized formulation in this set; encountered almost exclusively in forensic medicine and academic sexology; unrecognized by most lay speakers.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse between unmarried persons; carries inherent moral condemnation in Catholic and evangelical Protestant traditions dominant in Brazil.
records.notes: Widely used in Brazilian evangelical and Catholic sermons and broadcasting; the religious framing is inseparable from the word — a secular speaker would say 'relação sexual' instead.

records.definition: Archaic literary term for sexual intercourse, from Latin 'concubitus' (lying together); found in 19th and early 20th-century Portuguese literature and ecclesiastical texts.
records.notes: Virtually obsolete in contemporary Brazilian Portuguese; the stress pattern preserves the Latin form; encountered today only in literary classics or ecclesiastical scholarship; peak was pre-20th century.

records.definition: Clinical phrase for oral copulation; refers to any form of oral-genital contact including fellatio or cunnilingus.
records.notes: Used in forensic and medical contexts where clinical precision is required; lay speakers almost exclusively use 'sexo oral', 'boquete', or 'chupeta'.

records.definition: The primary Brazilian Portuguese crude verb for sexual intercourse; the functional and emotional equivalent of English 'fuck' in both sexual and expletive uses.
records.notes: Also a versatile general-purpose expletive and intensifier mirroring the full semantic range of 'fuck'; among the most commonly heard vulgarities in Brazil across all demographics.

records.definition: Very common crude slang verb for sexual intercourse; literally 'to climb/mount', evoking the physical act.
records.notes: Slightly less intense than 'foder'; the transparent 'climbing' metaphor contributes expressiveness; used across all age groups in informal speech without strong taboo avoidance.

records.definition: The most common colloquial verb for having sex in Brazilian Portuguese; relatively neutral in register compared to 'foder' or 'trepar'.
records.english_term: to have sex / to sleep with
records.notes: Can also mean 'to deal', 'to hang out', or 'to be involved in something' depending on context; when sexual intent is clear it is widely used without strong vulgarity; the safe midpoint between clinical and crude.

records.definition: Crude slang for sexual penetration in the active role; literally 'to insert/put in', foregrounding the physical act of insertion.
records.english_term: to stick it in / to nail
records.notes: Grammatically positions the penetrating partner as the agent; 'ele meteu nela' frames the act as the man inserting himself into the woman; the directional/inserting semantics make the active role structurally obligatory.

records.definition: Crude slang for having sex in the dominant/penetrating role; literally 'to eat', metaphorically framing sex as masculine consumption or conquest of the passive partner.
records.english_term: to bang / to nail / to have
records.notes: Culturally loaded with dominance and conquest; the partner who 'eats' is always the active agent; direct counterpart to 'dar'; central to Brazilian honor-shame sexual dynamics where penetrating is an act of power and being penetrated is submission.

records.definition: Crude slang for taking the receptive/passive role in penetrative sex; literally 'to give', framing the passive partner as yielding their body; most strongly associated with anal receptivity.
records.english_term: to give it up / to bottom
records.notes: The antonym of 'comer'; 'ela dá' implies she takes the receptive role. In discussions of male homosexuality 'dar' specifically implies anal receptivity. Central to the Brazilian honor-shame matrix where any act of being penetrated, regardless of gender, connotes submission.

records.definition: Crude slang for receiving penetration during sex; literally 'to take/receive'; most unambiguous in the phrase 'tomar no cu' (to be anally penetrated).
records.english_term: to take it / to get it
records.notes: Semantically ambiguous in isolation — active-voice 'tomar' can mean to take/conquer someone (penetrating), while 'tomar no cu' is unambiguously receptive. The receptive/passive sense dominates in sexual slang contexts.

records.definition: Crude slang for vigorous sexual intercourse; literally 'to pump/bomb', emphasizing forceful rhythmic thrusting.
records.notes: Narrower than 'foder' in that it specifically connotes high-intensity energetic intercourse; also used for other vigorous physical activities (working out, dancing at a club), so context typically disambiguates the sexual meaning.

records.definition: Slang verb for oral stimulation of a partner using lips and tongue; from 'bico' (beak/tip), evoking the pecking motion; also used for passionate kissing or, in some regions, intercourse.
records.english_term: to go down on / to eat out
records.notes: The beak/pecking etymology gives a lighter, more playful register than direct equivalents; regional variation determines whether it refers to oral sex specifically or to intercourse more broadly; the intercourse reading is reinforced when 'bico' is understood as the penile glans.

records.definition: Slang verb meaning to successfully have sex with someone; related to 'safado' (licentious, shameless), implying obtaining sexual gratification through boldness or cunning.
records.notes: Derived from 'safado' (lewd/impudent person); the verb implies succeeding at a licentious act rather than simply describing sex; more dated than 'transar'; recognition appears to be declining among younger speakers.

records.definition: The primary crude verb for 'to fuck' in Brazilian Portuguese; applies to any form of penetrative sex with implications of dominance or vigor.
records.notes: Variant spelling of the more standard 'foder'; both forms are widely recognized; functions as an all-purpose sexual expletive and general intensifier beyond strictly sexual contexts.

records.definition: Crude verb meaning to sodomize or perform anal sex on someone; derived from 'rabo' (tail/buttocks).
records.notes: 'Rabo' is ubiquitous Brazilian slang for the buttocks; the prefix 'en-' marks the causative entry; the word specifically implies the active/insertive role in anal sex rather than the receptive.

records.definition: Literally 'to insert or shove in'; used in sexual contexts as a crude-neutral verb for penile penetration.
records.notes: Primary non-sexual meaning is 'to thread or insert' (e.g., a needle through fabric); sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent; the word itself is not inherently obscene.

records.definition: Literally 'to put or place'; used as crude-neutral slang for having sex, emphasizing the act of penile insertion.
records.notes: More prevalent in Northeastern Brazil, where 'botar' is the standard variant of 'pôr'; primary meaning is 'to place/put'; in sexual use implies the penetrating role; also means 'to lay' eggs in agricultural contexts, which adds a productive/insertion connotation.

records.definition: Mexican Spanish-origin crude verb for fucking; encountered in Brazilian Portuguese through internet culture and cross-border media but not a native Brazilian term.
records.notes: Not a native Brazilian Portuguese term; primarily a Mexican Spanish expletive with different semantic range ('chingar' in Mexican Spanish covers a much broader range of meanings than just sex); recognized by some Brazilians through social media and Mexican film/TV but rarely used in Brazilian speech.

records.definition: To engage in sexual naughtiness or mischief with someone; derived from 'sacana' (scoundrel, dirty-minded person); implies sexual shenanigans or messing around rather than intercourse specifically.
records.notes: The primary non-sexual meaning is 'to trick, cheat, or mess with someone'; the sexual sense is a secondary connotation via the adjective 'sacana' (lewd/roguish); the noun 'sacanagem' covers both trickery and sexual naughtiness, making this term semantically broader than any single English equivalent.

records.definition: Literal translation of 'to have sex'; the neutral, clinical-register phrase for sexual intercourse used in education, journalism, and polite discourse.
records.notes: The standard phrase in institutional and polite contexts; completely non-taboo; preferred in Brazilian sex education curricula, public health messaging, and news reporting.

records.definition: Informal noun and verb for sex or a sexual encounter; mild slang equivalent of 'a lay' or 'a roll in the hay.'
records.notes: The verb form is 'transar' (to have sex); also means a shady deal or dubious scheme in non-sexual contexts — the overlap between sex and a dodgy transaction is semantically interesting; one of the most versatile and widely used mild sex terms in Brazilian Portuguese.

records.definition: Noun for a sexual encounter; from 'trepar' (to climb, to have sex); somewhat dated informal slang for a fuck.
records.notes: The verb 'trepar' remains more common than the noun 'trepa'; the term has faded relative to 'transa' and 'foda' among younger speakers; peak usage was in the 1980s–90s; 'trepar' literally means to climb, giving the word a physical/athletic connotation.

records.definition: Gerund of 'ferrar' (to brand with iron, to screw over); used crudely to mean 'fucking,' with connotations of vigorous or forceful sex.
records.notes: 'Ferrar' has primary meanings of 'to shoe a horse' and 'to brand with iron'; the sexual meaning derives from notions of hard, forceful contact; less universal than 'fodendo' (gerund of foder); may be perceived as more aggressive or violent in connotation.

records.definition: Idiomatic phrase meaning 'acting as / doing the role of [sexual partner]'; functions as a circumlocution implying sexual intercourse, often with undertones of the receptive role.
records.notes: Incomplete phrase requiring context; 'dar' in Brazilian sexual slang specifically means to be the receptive partner in sex (giving one's body); 'dando uma de' can therefore imply performing the receptive role; deeply context-dependent and not a fixed sexual term on its own.

records.definition: Literally 'to do that thing'; a polite euphemism for sexual intercourse, avoiding direct naming of the act through deictic reference.
records.notes: 'Aquilo' (that thing) functions as a placeholder for the unspoken sexual act; universally understood in context; used when speakers wish to imply sex without stating it, often in front of children or in mixed-formality settings; the same deictic strategy appears across most world languages.

records.definition: Literally 'to put the stick in'; crude phrasal verb for penile penetration and sexual intercourse, equivalent to 'to stick it in.'
records.notes: 'Pau' (stick/wood) is one of the most common Brazilian slang terms for penis; the phrase explicitly foregrounds penetration as the defining act; applicable to vaginal or anal penetration depending on context; 'meter' (to put in/insert) carries a stronger sense of thrusting than 'enfiar'.

records.definition: Literally 'to give a fuck'; crude phrase for having a casual sexual encounter; the diminutive 'fodida' maintains crudeness while slightly softening the register.
records.notes: 'Foda' is the noun form of 'foder' (to fuck); 'fodida' is a diminutive/casual variant suggesting a casual or opportunistic encounter; does not specifically imply brevity the way 'rapidinha' does — the diminutive here signals informality rather than speed.

records.definition: Literally 'a quick one'; the standard Brazilian Portuguese idiom for a quickie — a brief, hasty sexual encounter.
records.notes: 'Rapidinha' is a feminine diminutive of 'rápida' (quick, fast); very widely used across all regions and demographics; relatively mild and euphemistic despite its unambiguous sexual meaning; the diminutive suffix softens the crudeness while also suggesting something furtive or stolen.

records.definition: Clinical Brazilian Portuguese term for fellatio; oral stimulation of the penis.
records.notes: The standard medical and legal designation; used in court documents, medical literature, and sex education curricula; rarely appears in casual conversation where 'boquete' overwhelmingly dominates; the lower recognition reflects limited exposure to clinical vocabulary among the general public.

records.definition: Unmutated Latin term for oral stimulation of the penis; encountered in Brazilian legal, medical, and academic texts alongside the Portuguese adaptation 'felação.'
records.notes: Used interchangeably with 'felação' in some formal and academic Brazilian contexts; international medical literature read by Brazilian professionals often retains the Latin form; lower recognition than 'felação' because the Portuguesized spelling is more commonly taught.

records.definition: Clinical Brazilian Portuguese term for cunnilingus; oral stimulation of the vulva.
records.notes: The standard medical and legal designation for this act in Brazilian Portuguese; much lower recognition than crude equivalents; appears primarily in clinical texts, legal documents, and sex education materials; the lower recognition compared to 'felação' likely reflects historical under-discussion of female pleasure in public health contexts.

records.definition: Unmutated Latin term for oral stimulation of the vulva; used in Brazilian medical, legal, and academic texts alongside the Portuguese adaptation 'cunilíngua.'
records.notes: Sometimes used interchangeably with 'cunilíngua' in formal Brazilian texts; Brazilian recognition is lower than in English-speaking countries because English-language sex education and media have made the Latin form familiar to English speakers in a way that Portuguese has not replicated.

records.definition: Literally 'oral stimulation'; a clinical descriptor for any oral-to-genital sexual contact, encompassing both fellatio and cunnilingus.
records.notes: Preferred in medical and public-health contexts for its gender-neutral and act-neutral framing; appears in Brazilian HIV-prevention literature and sexual health guidelines; the act-neutral quality makes it useful when the specific genital involved need not be specified.

records.definition: The standard everyday Brazilian Portuguese term for oral sex; neutral in register and suitable for journalism, conversation, and sex education alike.
records.notes: Universally recognized; not perceived as vulgar; the dominant term across all contexts where precision is needed but clinical register is unnecessary; coverage in mainstream Brazilian media and public-health campaigns has made it fully mainstream.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian Portuguese slang for a blowjob; oral stimulation of the penis performed on a partner.
records.notes: Derived from 'boca' (mouth); the default slang term throughout Brazil across all age groups and regions; considered crude but not extreme; also spelled 'boquête' in some orthographic conventions; the near-total recognition rate reflects how thoroughly it has displaced clinical alternatives in everyday speech.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'boquete'; denotes an enthusiastic, thorough, or extended blowjob; implies notably greater depth, duration, or skill than a standard 'boquete.'
records.notes: The augmentative suffix '-ão' intensifies along multiple dimensions simultaneously (size, thoroughness, quality); some speakers use it specifically to imply deep-throat technique; others use it hyperbolically for any particularly satisfying or prolonged blowjob; no single English term captures the augmentative nuance precisely.

records.definition: Literally 'to suck'; the most common verb for performing oral sex on any partner; applies to both fellatio and cunnilingus depending on context.
