records.notes: Primary meaning is simply 'to suck' (candy, through a straw, etc.); sexual meaning is context-dependent and universally understood; one of the most versatile oral-sex verbs in Brazilian Portuguese precisely because it does not specify the genital involved.

records.definition: Literally 'to breastfeed or suckle'; used as crude slang for performing oral sex, most commonly fellatio.
records.notes: Primary meaning is infant nursing; the sexual connotation derives from the intimate oral-suckling motion; more commonly implies fellatio than cunnilingus though technically applicable to both; the transfer from nursing to sex gives the word a distinctive taboo charge absent in 'chupar'; the word also appears in the phrase 'mamar gostoso' (to suck deliciously) as explicit praise.

records.definition: Brazilian slang verb meaning to perform cunnilingus; derived from 'xoxo,' a regional crude term for the vulva.
records.notes: Derives from 'xoxo' (vulva in some Brazilian dialects); more geographically distributed in the Southeast and South.

records.definition: Literally 'to lick'; in sexual contexts, a verb for oral stimulation of genitals or anus, with the specific act determined by context.
records.notes: Primary meaning is entirely non-sexual; sexual meaning is derived purely from context; serves all three oral sex subcategories.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian Portuguese phrase for performing fellatio; 'boquete' (from 'boca,' mouth) is the unmarked crude noun for blowjob.
records.notes: 'Dar' (to give) is the standard verb frame; 'boquete' is the dominant noun form and can stand alone.

records.definition: Explicit phrase meaning to suck the penis; 'chupar' (to suck) combined with 'pau,' the default crude term for penis in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: 'Pau' (stick/wood) is the most frequent crude lexeme for penis in pt-BR; this phrase is maximally explicit and unambiguous.

records.definition: Literally 'Greek kiss'; the standard Brazilian Portuguese term for anilingus, paralleling the pan-Romance convention of assigning anal practices to ancient Greece.
records.notes: The 'Greek' framing is shared across Spanish, French, Italian, and Portuguese; widely understood without sounding maximally crude.

records.definition: Explicit phrase meaning to lick the anus; 'lamber' (to lick) combined with 'cu,' the dominant crude term for the anus in pt-BR.
records.notes: 'Cu' is maximally offensive in non-sexual contexts; the full phrase is among the cruder anilingus expressions in Brazilian Portuguese.

records.definition: Literally 'to eat with the mouth'; euphemistic phrase for performing oral sex, exploiting 'comer' which is simultaneously 'to eat' and crude slang for penetrative sex.
records.notes: The parenthetical 'com a boca' (with the mouth) distinguishes oral from penetrative 'eating'; the double entendre of 'comer' is the engine of the euphemism.

records.definition: Colloquial phrase meaning to perform oral sex; shortened from 'sexo oral'; the most neutral, everyday expression covering fellatio, cunnilingus, and anilingus.
records.notes: Gender-neutral and act-neutral; the safest register for everyday speech short of full clinical terminology.

records.definition: Primarily 'to urinate' (childish register); in very niche Brazilian slang, repurposed as a playful euphemism for oral-genital contact, particularly cunnilingus.
records.notes: Primary meaning is urination; use as an oral-sex euphemism is rare, highly context-dependent, and possibly regional; the childish register creates ironic distance when deployed sexually.

records.definition: Compound slang literally meaning 'suck-dick'; functions as both a noun for one who performs fellatio and as an insult; built from 'mamar' (to suckle) and 'pau' (dick).
records.notes: Primarily used as an insult rather than a neutral act descriptor; the insult sense dominates in everyday speech.

records.definition: The standard clinical Portuguese term for masturbation; self-stimulation of the genitals for sexual pleasure or arousal, typically to orgasm.
'Onanism'; masturbation framed as a moral or theological transgression, derived from the biblical Onan who spilled his seed rather than impregnate his dead brother's wife.
records.notes: Recognition has declined as religious condemnation of masturbation weakened in Brazilian culture; persists in formal, theological, and literary registers.

records.definition: 'Autoeroticism'; the clinical and psychosexual term for self-directed erotic stimulation; broader than masturbation in that it encompasses fantasy and non-contact arousal as well.
records.notes: Slightly broader than 'masturbação' in clinical usage; associated with sexology and psychology rather than everyday speech.

records.definition: 'Manual stimulation'; clinical phrase for genital stimulation with the hand, encompassing both self-directed masturbation and partner-directed handjobs.
records.notes: Act-neutral and partner-neutral; context specifies whether self-directed or partner-directed.

records.definition: The dominant crude Brazilian Portuguese noun for male masturbation; the default lexical item when Brazilians reach for a vulgar term for jerking off.
records.notes: Probably from 'punho' (fist); the unmarked crude baseline against which all other masturbation slang is measured in pt-BR.

records.definition: A single act or session of male masturbation; the event-noun form of 'punheta,' produced by the Portuguese '-ada' suffix that nominalizes a completed action.
records.notes: The '-ada' suffix emphasizes the singularity or completeness of the event; semantically distinguishes a discrete instance from the general state-noun 'punheta.'

records.definition: The most common verbal phrase for male masturbation in Brazilian Portuguese; 'bater' (to beat/hit) plus 'punheta,' paralleling English 'beat off.'
records.notes: The 'bater' (beat) frame mirrors English 'beat off' and Spanish 'hacerse una paja'; the colloquially unmarked verbal choice.

records.definition: Reflexive verb meaning to masturbate oneself; formed by verbalizing the noun 'punheta' and adding the reflexive clitic 'se.'
records.notes: Less frequent than 'bater punheta'; the verbalized form ('punhetar') is informal and primarily oral; accepted but slightly marked.

records.definition: To masturbate; primarily a European Portuguese (pt-PT) slang term with limited penetration into Brazilian Portuguese, mainly via internet exposure.
records.notes: Strongly associated with Portugal; Brazilian speakers may passively recognize it from online content but rarely produce it natively; included here as a recognized loanword within pt-BR digital registers.

records.definition: Literally 'to knead dough'; repurposed as slang for male masturbation, evoking the rhythmic kneading or squeezing motion of penile stimulation.
records.notes: Primary meaning is culinary; the sexual metaphor transfers the tactile motion of kneading dough to stroking the penis.

records.definition: Literally 'to touch oneself'; the most widely used gender-neutral euphemism for masturbation in Brazilian Portuguese, frequently applied to female masturbation in particular.
records.notes: Gender-neutral in form but in practice often connotes female masturbation, as the peripheral vocabulary for female self-stimulation is less developed than for male.

records.definition: Literally 'to give a little hand'; euphemistic phrase for providing manual genital stimulation to a partner; the diminutive 'mãozinha' softens the crudeness.
records.notes: Primarily non-sexual in everyday use ('to lend a hand'); the sexual meaning is activated by context; the diminutive creates deliberate ambiguity and deniability.

records.definition: Literally 'to rub' or 'to create friction'; in sexual contexts, to masturbate or engage in manual genital stimulation; primarily found in clinical and educational registers.
records.notes: Rarely used as a standalone sexual term outside clinical writing; more likely to appear in sex-therapy literature than everyday speech.

records.definition: Literally 'to maneuver' or 'to operate'; slang for masturbation derived from the mechanical handling implied by penile manipulation.
records.notes: Not a primary or high-frequency term; understood when context is clear but Brazilians would typically reach for 'bater punheta' or 'se tocar' first.

records.definition: Literally 'to grab one's own [genitals]'; crude slang phrase for masturbation implying direct self-handling of the genitals.
records.notes: 'Própria' is feminine form, which may reflect speaker gender or function as a colloquial unmarked form; contextually unambiguous as masturbation regardless of morphological gender.

records.definition: To finger someone; to digitally stimulate a partner's genitals, or for a woman to digitally stimulate her own genitalia.
records.notes: Literally 'to do it with the finger'; applies to both self and partner stimulation depending on context; placed in the masturbation section by convention but frequently transitive.

records.definition: To touch or move oneself; a highly context-dependent euphemistic verb for masturbation.
records.notes: Literally 'to move oneself'; the sexual meaning requires heavy contextual support; the dominant everyday use means 'to hurry up' or 'to get moving.'

records.definition: To rub oneself; slang for masturbation, particularly associated with female self-stimulation through friction.
records.notes: Literally 'to rub oneself'; friction-based framing makes it more commonly associated with vulvar/clitoral rubbing than penetrative self-stimulation; non-sexual uses (towel-drying, chafing) coexist.

records.definition: Anal sex; the standard Brazilian Portuguese term for any sexual act involving penetration of the anus.
Anal; shorthand for anal sex, widely used in casual speech, internet contexts, and pornographic taxonomy.
To put it in the ass; crude expression for performing insertive anal sex.
records.english_term: to put it up the ass
records.notes: 'Cu' is the dominant crude Brazilian Portuguese word for anus; 'colocar' (to place/put) is milder than 'meter' but the phrase overall is unambiguously crude.

records.definition: To stick it in the ass; crude slang for insertive anal penetration.
records.english_term: to stick it up the ass
records.notes: 'Meter' is a high-frequency crude verb for penetration in Brazilian Portuguese; slightly more aggressive in tone than 'colocar no cu.'

records.definition: To give up one's ass; crude expression specifying the receptive role in anal sex.
records.english_term: to take it up the ass
records.notes: Literally 'to give the ass'; the 'giving' framing specifies passivity; heavily used as an insult implying weakness, submission, or defeat far beyond sexual contexts.

records.definition: To take it in the ass; crude expression for the receptive role in anal sex.
records.english_term: to take it up the ass
records.notes: Also used figuratively to mean suffering a serious setback or being badly cheated ('tomei no cu nessa negociação' = 'I got royally screwed in that deal').

records.definition: To sodomize; to anally penetrate someone; a verb derived from 'rabo' (tail/buttocks).
records.notes: Derived from 'rabo' (ass/tail); implies insertive anal penetration; somewhat more dated or regional than phrases built on 'cu'; also appears as a metaphor for cheating someone.

records.definition: To shove it in the hole; crude expression for anal penetration, occasionally ambiguous with vaginal penetration.
records.english_term: to shove it in the hole
records.notes: 'Buraco' (hole) defaults to the anus in sexual context; some regional usage extends 'buraco' to the vagina, creating occasional ambiguity.

records.definition: To do it through the back end; a crude-euphemistic expression for anal sex using 'fundilho' (trouser seat/crotch seam) as a metonym for the anus.
records.english_term: to do it through the back door
records.notes: 'Fundilho' refers to the seat/crotch seam of pants; lower recognition among younger speakers for whom 'fundilho' itself is unfamiliar vocabulary.

records.definition: To break open; to forcefully and roughly penetrate anally, implying tearing or extreme dilation.
records.notes: Literally 'to break down a door'; in sexual use implies violent or rough anal penetration to the point of injury; also an all-purpose Brazilian expletive and metaphor for defeating someone decisively.

records.definition: Sperm or semen; the standard semi-clinical term used in everyday speech and sex education in Brazil.
records.notes: In Brazilian Portuguese, 'esperma' is used interchangeably for both individual spermatozoa and bulk semen fluid, collapsing the English distinction; appears in health curricula and mainstream media without censorship.

records.definition: Semen; the strictly clinical anatomical term for the fluid ejaculated at orgasm.
records.notes: The circumflex accent (sêmen) was orthographically required pre-2009 Acordo Ortográfico; post-reform the accent was dropped in Brazil, so both spellings appear in texts; more formal than 'esperma.'

records.definition: Ejaculate; the fluid expelled at orgasm; a nominalized past participle of 'ejacular.'
records.notes: Less commonly used as a standalone noun than 'esperma' or 'sêmen'; more natural in clinical writing than in speech; the verb form 'ejaculou' (he/she ejaculated) is more frequently encountered.

records.definition: Cum; semen; and simultaneously the most ubiquitous Brazilian Portuguese expletive, roughly equivalent to 'fuck' or 'damn.'
records.notes: Historically denoted semen; now functions primarily as an all-purpose expletive with near-universal recognition across all age groups and socioeconomic strata; the semen meaning is retained only in explicitly sexual contexts.

records.definition: Little milk; an affectionate or playful diminutive euphemism for semen.
records.notes: Diminutive of 'leite' (milk); the '-inho' suffix adds cuteness or intimacy, making it noticeably less crude than 'porra'; common in flirtatious texting and softcore pornographic contexts.

records.definition: Milk; a euphemism for semen exploiting the visual and textural resemblance to cow's milk.
records.notes: Primary meaning (dairy milk) vastly dominates in neutral contexts; sexual meaning is activated only by surrounding context; common in pornographic dialogue and internet sexual slang.

records.definition: Orgasm; climax; the noun form of 'gozar,' the standard colloquial verb for reaching orgasm in Brazil.
records.notes: 'Gozar' and 'gozo' are culturally more neutral in Brazil than 'cum' is in English — used freely in song lyrics and mainstream media; the word can secondarily refer to the ejaculate itself.

records.definition: A load; a cumshot; an event noun denoting the act of orgasming or the ejaculate expelled.
records.notes: Feminine noun derived from 'gozar'; can denote the orgasmic event or the ejaculate as a product; more graphic and event-focused than 'gozo'; widely used in pornographic description.

records.definition: Vaginal secretion; the clinical term for any fluid produced by the vagina, whether arousal-related or pathological.
Lubrication; the clinical term for vaginal wetness produced during sexual arousal.
Wet; colloquial adjective describing a woman as sexually aroused and producing vaginal lubrication.
records.notes: Adjective with feminine gender agreement; sexual meaning requires context — base word is generic; 'estar molhada' = to be wet/aroused.

records.definition: To get wet; the inchoative colloquial phrase for a woman becoming sexually aroused and producing vaginal lubrication.
records.notes: The stative-change verb 'ficar' (to become/to get) combines with 'molhada' to mark the onset of arousal rather than a static state; used in first-person self-report and third-person description alike.

records.definition: Idiom for becoming vaginally lubricated during sexual arousal; literally 'to wet one's panties.'
records.notes: Playful and widely used; emphasizes the physical outcome of arousal rather than the psychological state.

records.definition: Clinical adjective describing pre-ejaculatory fluid secreted during arousal before orgasm; the Portuguese equivalent of 'pre-ejaculatory.'
records.notes: Primarily appears in health-education and medical contexts; lay speakers more commonly say 'líquido de excitação' or 'líquido de pré-ejaculação.'

records.definition: Clinical term for seminal fluid; the medically precise designation for the fluid ejaculated from the penis.
records.notes: More technical than the colloquial 'sêmen'; preferred in academic and medical writing.

records.definition: The standard Portuguese noun for penile erection; fully clinical but universally recognized across all registers.
Very common crude slang for an erect penis; literally 'hard stick/cock.'
records.notes: 'Pau' is itself primary crude slang for penis in Brazilian Portuguese, making the compound doubly crude.

records.definition: Colloquial adjective meaning sexually aroused or having an erection; literally 'stiff' or 'rigid.'
records.notes: Applies to both the physical state (erection) and the general psychological state of arousal; usable for any gender, though most commonly male-coded.

records.definition: The most ubiquitous Brazilian Portuguese noun for sexual desire or the state of arousal; also used for the person or thing causing arousal.
records.notes: Extremely versatile: 'estou com tesão' (I'm horny), 'ela é um tesão' (she's a turn-on). Straddles fluids/states and desire/arousal domains equally.

records.definition: Phrasal verb meaning to get an erection or to become sexually aroused; literally 'to become stiff.'
records.english_term: to get hard / to get turned on
records.notes: Most commonly associated with male arousal and erection specifically, though 'teso' can apply broadly.

records.definition: Adjective describing someone habitually or intensely sexually aroused; one who is full of tesão.
records.notes: Derived from 'tesão'; implies a dispositional or habitual state of arousal rather than a momentary one. Less universal than 'tesão' itself.

records.definition: English loanword for a penile erection, widely understood in Brazil through internet culture, memes, and dubbed media.
records.notes: Adoption accelerated with social media; predominant among younger Brazilians; used in meme contexts and informal digital speech.

records.definition: The standard Portuguese clinical verb for ejaculation; to expel semen from the penis at orgasm.
records.notes: Spans registers comfortably from medical to casual discussion; less crude than 'gozar' but fully understood.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian slang verb for reaching orgasm or ejaculating; applicable to all genders.
records.notes: Literally 'to enjoy/to have pleasure' in standard Portuguese; the sexual sense is so dominant in Brazilian colloquial speech that the neutral sense often requires context to disambiguate.

records.definition: Colloquial euphemism for reaching orgasm; literally 'to come,' parallel to the English usage.
records.notes: The sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent; the word is standard Portuguese for 'to come/arrive' in all other uses.

records.definition: Mild euphemism for reaching orgasm; literally 'to arrive' or 'to reach,' used in the sense of reaching climax.
records.notes: The mildest of the orgasm euphemisms in this set; extremely context-dependent; also used in expressions like 'você chegou?' (did you finish?).

records.definition: The standard Portuguese term for orgasm; clinical in origin but universally known and used across all registers.
A slightly more formal or literary synonym for orgasm; literally 'climax,' borrowed from the narrative sense.
records.notes: Also used in its original narrative/dramatic sense (story climax); the sexual sense is clear in context; carries less crudeness than 'orgasmo' due to literary register.

records.definition: Euphemism for ejaculation or orgasmic release; literally 'discharge' or 'unloading.'
records.notes: Used in both clinical contexts (e.g., 'descarga elétrica' = electric shock) and as a sexual euphemism; the sexual sense requires contextual inference.

records.definition: The most ubiquitous Brazilian Portuguese noun for sexual desire or lust; the quintessential word for horniness in Brazilian culture.
records.notes: Appears in both fluids/states and desire/arousal sections because it spans both domains. Can function as a noun ('tenho tesão por ela') or qualify a person ('ela é um tesão').

records.definition: Slang noun/adjective for a person with an obsessive or uncontrollable sexual appetite; can be affectionately teasing or genuinely pejorative depending on context.
records.notes: Feminine form 'tarada' is equally common. The word spans a wide affective range: 'você é tarado!' between friends is playful; from a stranger it reads as accusatory.

records.definition: Crude slang for a person, typically male, who is persistently driven by sexual desire and always pursuing sex; literally connotes dog-like sexual aggression.
records.notes: Likely derived from 'cachorro' (dog) connoting animalistic sexual drive; less universal than 'tarado' and carries slightly more pejorative weight; feminine form 'cacheira' exists but is rarer.

records.definition: Slang adjective/noun for a naughty, dirty-minded, or sexually shameless person; ranges from affectionate to insulting depending on tone and context.
records.notes: One of the most versatile words in Brazilian sexual slang; 'safado' between close friends is often playful praise; applied to a stranger it becomes an accusation of moral looseness. Feminine form 'safada' is equally common and carries heavier misogynistic loading when used pejoratively.

records.definition: Adjective describing a sexually passionate or fiery person; one who is intensely and enthusiastically sexual or romantic; literally 'fiery/full of fire.'
records.notes: Derived from 'fogo' (fire); implies a positive, energetic sexual passion rather than a compulsive or excessive one; commonly used in admiring descriptions of sexual partners.

records.definition: Adjective meaning sexually aroused; the most neutral and widely applicable term for the state of sexual excitement.
records.notes: Straddles clinical and colloquial registers; low enough crude score to be usable in health contexts while still carrying a clear sexual meaning in everyday speech.

records.definition: Adjective meaning libidinous or lecherous; describing a person driven by excessive or predatory sexual desire.
records.notes: More clinical and Latinate than most Brazilian sexual vocabulary; often used by educated speakers or in journalism to describe sexual predators or the excessively lustful without using crude terms.

records.definition: Literary/formal adjective meaning lascivious; expressing or suggesting overt sexual desire in a lewd or wanton manner.
records.notes: Among the most formal and literary terms in this dataset; more common in written texts, legal discourse, and literary criticism than in speech; the average Brazilian speaker recognizes it but would not spontaneously produce it in conversation.

records.definition: Adjectival use of 'puteiro' (brothel): describes a person, event, or atmosphere as exhibiting the sexual excess, moral looseness, and general debauchery of a whorehouse.
records.notes: Primary form is the noun 'puteiro' (brothel, from 'puta' = whore); the adjectival use — 'festa puteira', 'ambiente puteiro' — describes something as raunchy, sexually chaotic, or morally depraved in a brothel-like way.

records.definition: Lustful, lascivious; describing a person or behavior as driven by strong carnal desire, typically with a moral charge.
records.notes: False cognate trap: English 'luxurious' means opulent; Brazilian Portuguese 'luxurioso' retains the Latin meaning of excessive sexual appetite. Predominantly literary register; rarely used in casual speech.

records.definition: Sexually attractive, hot; describes a person as physically desirable and pleasurable to look at or be with.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'tasty/delicious'; sexual sense ('hot/sexy') is a natural food metonymy and is arguably the most ubiquitous Brazilian Portuguese compliment for physical attractiveness. Extremely high-frequency in everyday speech across all age groups.

records.definition: Augmentative of gostoso/gostosa; an intensified term for someone who is extremely sexually attractive or physically irresistible.
records.notes: The augmentative suffix '-ão/-ona' intensifies 'gostoso' to mean 'super sexy'; '-ona' for women can carry connotations of voluptuous physical largeness that are still framed positively in Brazilian culture.

records.definition: Sensual; describing a person, movement, or experience as relating to or gratifying the physical senses, especially in a sexually arousing way.
records.notes: Direct cognate from Latin via Portuguese; essentially identical in meaning and register to English 'sensual'. Used across all registers from advertising copy to literary prose.

records.definition: Literally 'spiced/peppered'; describes content, situations, or people as sexually risqué, titillating, or erotically charged.
records.notes: Food metaphor euphemism for sexual heat; 'uma conversa apimentada' (a spicy conversation), 'cena apimentada' (a steamy scene). Positive or neutral in connotation; not pejorative.

records.definition: Literally 'hot'; used to describe a person as sexually attractive or a situation/content as arousing and sexually charged.
records.notes: Universal temperature-to-sexuality metaphor; 'estar quente' means 'to be turned on'; used freely for both people ('ela é quente') and situations ('cena quente'). Overlaps with 'gostoso' but 'quente' emphasizes active arousal and heat over aesthetic appeal.

records.definition: Sexual naughtiness, crudeness, or shameless lewdness; also a specific crude or raunchy act.
records.notes: Noun derived from 'safado/safada' (crude, naughty, shameless); denotes either the abstract quality of sexual shamelessness or a concrete naughty act ('que safadeza!' = 'what a filthy thing to do!'). Broadly celebrated rather than condemned in Brazilian popular culture.

records.definition: The state of intense sexual arousal or horniness; also the quality of being highly sexually exciting or attractive.
records.notes: Derived from 'tesão' (crude slang for sexual arousal/horniness); 'tesudeza' is the noun of quality — either the state of being turned on ('que tesudeza que eu tô') or describing a person or situation as intensely arousing.

records.definition: Sexually suggestive, naughtily knowing, or dirty-minded; describes a manner, look, or remark that implies sexual intent beneath a surface innocence.
records.notes: In a sexual context specifically describes the quality of sly, knowing sexual innuendo — 'olhar malicioso' (a suggestive look), 'sorriso malicioso' (a knowing smile). Less about explicit content and more about implying sexual intent.

records.definition: Frigid; lacking sexual desire or responsiveness; applied predominantly to women in clinical and popular discourse.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'frigid'; historically over-applied to women as a catch-all diagnosis; now considered dated and sexist. Peak usage in mid-20th-century Brazilian psychoanalytic discourse; fading from everyday speech.

records.definition: Literally 'cold'; used metaphorically to describe a person as sexually unresponsive or lacking warmth and desire during intimacy.
records.notes: Secondary sexual sense relying on the universal cold/heat responsiveness metaphor; 'ela é fria na cama' (she's cold in bed). Less clinical than 'frígido'; often simply means sexually disengaged rather than diagnosing a clinical condition.

records.definition: Sexually inhibited; tense and unable to relax or freely express sexuality due to psychological or social constraints.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'inhibited'; used across clinical psychology and everyday speech without vulgarity; commonly contrasted with 'desinibido/desinibida' (uninhibited).

records.definition: Sexually repressed; one whose sexual desires are suppressed or denied expression, typically due to cultural, religious, or psychological forces.
records.notes: Derived from the Freudian 'recalque' (repression); widely popularized in Brazilian popular speech through psychoanalytic culture; stronger and more pathologizing than 'inibido'; often used semi-humorously ('você é um recalcado!').

records.definition: Sexually square or uptight; a person or attitude that is conventionally conservative, unwilling to sexually experiment, or easily shocked by sexual content.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'grimace' or colloquially 'a boring/straight-laced person'; in sexual contexts means prudish or adventurously avoidant; also used in drug culture for someone who doesn't use drugs — the sexual meaning is not its only sense.

records.definition: Literally 'locked'; describes a person as completely sexually blocked, unable to let go or express themselves sexually due to deep inhibition.
records.notes: The locked-door metaphor extended to sexual personality; implies total inability to express sexuality rather than mere reluctance; stronger than 'inibido'; 'ela é trancada sexualmente' = 'she's totally locked up sexually'.

records.definition: Modest, chaste, or prudish; excessively protective of sexual propriety or easily offended by sexual content.
records.notes: Formal/literary register; cognate of Latin 'pudicus' (modest, chaste); rarely used in contemporary everyday Brazilian Portuguese; understood by educated speakers but largely displaced by colloquial alternatives like 'careta' or 'moralista'.

records.definition: Sexless or de-sexualized; lacking sexual characteristics, sexual desire, or sexual identity; applied to persons and to things.
records.notes: Distinct from 'assexual' (asexual as an identity label); 'assexuado' means descriptively 'without sexuality' and can modify anything lacking a sexual dimension. The identity term in Brazilian Portuguese is 'assexual'; 'assexuado' is descriptive rather than a claimed identity.

records.definition: Metaphorically castrated; describing a person as stripped of sexual desire, vitality, or masculine power — rendered sexually or socially neutered.
records.notes: Literal meaning is 'castrated (animal or person)'; the metaphorical sexual use means emasculated, without libido, or lacking sexual courage or drive; used hyperbolically in Brazilian popular speech ('você é um castrado' = 'you have no balls/drive'). Parenthetical '(metaphorically)' in the source list signals this non-literal sense.

records.definition: Literally 'soft cock'; describes a man as impotent or sexually incapable of achieving an erection; also used more broadly for cowardice or weakness.
records.notes: 'Pau' is standard crude slang for penis in Brazilian Portuguese; 'mole' means soft/limp; the compound is one of the most common crude terms for male impotence. Extended metaphorically to general spinelessness ('não seja pau-mole' = 'don't be spineless').

records.definition: Softness, limpness; in sexual context refers to penile flaccidity, inability to sustain erection, or broad sexual passivity and laziness.
records.notes: Primary meaning is general 'softness, flabbiness, laziness'; the sexual meaning exploits the same literal quality applied to the penis; can also describe overall sexual passivity in either sex ('ela/ele é uma moleza na cama' = she/he is limp/lazy in bed). Distinct from 'pau-mole' in that 'moleza' can be gender-neutral.

records.definition: Literally 'loose/slack'; in sexual contexts means sexually weak, unenthusiastic, or lacking libido; also implies sexual cowardice or unwillingness to engage.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'loose, slack, cowardly'; in sexual contexts implies low energy, low drive, or lack of passion; overlaps with 'moleza' but 'frouxo' foregrounds weakness/cowardice while 'moleza' foregrounds softness/laziness.

records.definition: Literally 'dry'; used to describe sexual unresponsiveness, especially lack of vaginal lubrication in women; also used colloquially to mean 'not getting any sexual action'.
records.notes: Exploits the dryness/wetness antonym for arousal ('molhada' = wet = aroused; 'seca' = dry = unresponsive); dual meaning: physically unlubricated AND more broadly sexually inactive or frustrated ('tô seco/a' = I'm not getting any). Context disambiguates.

records.definition: Homosexual; a person sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of the same sex.
records.notes: Direct cognate; the clinical/formal term in Brazilian Portuguese; in everyday speech largely displaced by 'gay' (men) and 'lésbica' (women); 'homossexual' reads as institutional and can feel distancing or pathologizing in community contexts.

records.definition: Heterosexual; a person sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of a different sex.
records.notes: Direct cognate; the formal clinical term; informally often shortened to 'hétero' in casual Brazilian Portuguese speech; the full form is most common in academic, medical, or institutional settings.

records.definition: A person sexually and/or romantically attracted to more than one gender; the standard clinical and self-identifier term in Brazilian Portuguese.
A person who experiences little or no sexual attraction to others; the standard clinical and community self-identifier in Brazilian Portuguese.
A person attracted to others regardless of sex or gender identity; loanword from English widely used in Brazilian LGBTQ+ communities and media.
records.notes: Retains English form unchanged; recognized primarily by younger, urban, and LGBTQ+-adjacent populations.

records.definition: A woman sexually and/or romantically attracted to other women; the standard clinical and identity term in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Universally understood across generations and regions; carries mild clinical register but is used freely in everyday speech.

records.definition: Fully assimilated English loanword for a gay man or non-heterosexual identity more broadly; the most common neutral term across all demographics in Brazil.
records.notes: Pronounced /gɛj/ or /gaj/ depending on region; universally understood by all ages; has largely displaced older clinical terms like 'homossexual' in everyday use.

records.definition: A person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth; the standard clinical and activist term in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Growing recognition in line with media coverage; coexists with the more culturally embedded 'travesti' as a distinct identity category in Brazilian discourse.

records.definition: A specifically Brazilian and Latin American gender identity for people assigned male at birth who adopt feminine gender expression (often including hormones and breast implants) but who may explicitly reject the Western 'transgender woman' label as a distinct cultural and political identity.
records.notes: Critically distinct from English 'transvestite' (a cross-dresser, not a gender identity) and not simply synonymous with 'transgender woman' — many travestis reject the latter label. Has a strong historical association with street sex work but is also a proud political identity in Brazilian activism and law. Recognized as a distinct gender category in Brazilian legal and health policy contexts.

records.definition: A person born with sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary definitions of male or female; the standard clinical and activist term in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Relatively low recognition outside medical and activist contexts; older populations may be unfamiliar with the term entirely.

records.definition: English loanword used as an umbrella identity term for non-heterosexual and/or non-cisgender Brazilians; known primarily among younger, urban, and educated LGBTQ+-adjacent populations.
records.notes: Retains English pronunciation; carries academic and activist register; significantly less integrated than 'gay'; older Brazilians may not recognize it as an identity term at all.

records.definition: A person whose gender identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth; standard clinical and activist descriptor in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Often abbreviated 'cis'; recognition is strongly correlated with LGBTQ+ exposure, education level, and urban residence; unfamiliar to much of the general population.

records.definition: A person whose gender identity does not fall exclusively within the traditional binary categories of man or woman; direct calque translation of English 'non-binary'.
records.notes: Also written 'não binário' without hyphen; recognition growing rapidly among younger generations; in Brazilian Portuguese, speakers using this identity sometimes adopt gender-neutral language endings (e.g., '-e' suffix).

records.definition: A person who experiences sexual attraction only after forming a significant emotional bond with someone; loanword from English 'demisexual'.
records.notes: Known almost exclusively within LGBTQ+/asexuality-spectrum online communities; extremely low recognition among the general Brazilian public.

records.definition: A person attracted to multiple but not necessarily all genders; distinct from pansexual in that specific genders may fall outside the person's attraction.
records.notes: Mapped to 'pansexual' as nearest registry entry; polysexual and pansexual are meaningfully distinct (polysexual = multiple genders, not all; pansexual = all genders regardless). Extremely low recognition even within activist spaces; the pansexual/polysexual distinction is rarely observed in casual Brazilian usage.

records.definition: A person combining or embodying both masculine and feminine characteristics in appearance or gender identity; can denote aesthetic presentation or a gender identity distinct from the binary.
records.notes: Mapped to non_binary as closest registry entry; in Brazilian Portuguese usage 'andrógino' frequently describes aesthetic androgyny (a visual quality, not necessarily a gender identity) — context determines whether it is a descriptor or an identity claim.

records.definition: Shorthand for 'gênero fluido'; a person whose gender identity shifts or varies over time rather than remaining fixed.
records.notes: Used both as the standalone identity marker 'fluido/a' and in the full phrase 'gênero fluido'; recognition growing with younger generations and LGBTQ+ media coverage.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian Portuguese slur for a gay man, especially an effeminate one; phonetically reduced spoken variant of 'veado'.
records.notes: More common in informal speech than the full form 'veado'; one of the most frequently used anti-gay slurs in Brazil; partially reclaimed within gay communities, especially in northeastern Brazil and in carnival and drag culture. Severity is strongly context-dependent.

records.definition: Primary written-form slur for a gay man in Brazilian Portuguese; literally means 'deer' (male cervid), with the homosexual meaning derived from the passive/submissive position the animal is imagined to occupy.
records.notes: The deer etymology is the standard explanation though debated; 'viado' is the more common phonetic reduction in speech. Both forms are among the most loaded anti-gay slurs in the Brazilian lexicon; widely reclaimed in queer communities.

records.definition: A deeply embedded Brazilian slur for a gay man, especially an effeminate one; also means 'worm', 'bug', or 'creature' in other registers; extensively reclaimed within gay and queer culture.
records.notes: One of the most culturally complex LGBTQ+ words in Brazilian Portuguese: simultaneously a violent slur and a fully reclaimed community identity marker (e.g., 'bicha má', 'bichice', carnival self-identification). Reclamation is widespread but incomplete — remains offensive from out-group mouths. Also standard in northeastern Brazil as an almost affectionate peer term among gay men.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'bicha'; denotes an exaggeratedly effeminate gay man; used as an intensified slur from outsiders or as exaggerated camp self-identification within the community.
records.notes: The augmentative suffix -ona amplifies the effeminacy implication and intensifies both the insult potential and the camp self-affirmation potential. Common in both hostile and celebratory contexts depending on speaker identity.

records.definition: Alternate orthography of 'bichona' using 'x' for 'ch'; same meaning and register; especially common in informal digital and social media writing.
records.notes: The 'x' spelling reflects a widespread Brazilian internet orthographic convention where 'x' represents the /ʃ/ phoneme of 'ch'; functionally identical to 'bichona' semantically; recognition slightly lower than bichona among older generations unfamiliar with digital spelling conventions.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian Portuguese slur and partially-reclaimed identity term for a lesbian, especially a masculine-presenting one; literally the augmentative of 'sapato' (shoe), evoking the stereotype of lesbians wearing large or men's footwear.
records.notes: Widely reclaimed within Brazilian lesbian communities as a proud political and cultural marker; the shoe etymology encodes older stereotypes about masculine gender presentation. Severity is strongly context-dependent: celebratory within the community, offensive from hostile outsiders. The augmentative -ão also implies bigness/strength, which the community has embraced.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'sapata'/'sapatão'; a softer or affectionate term for a lesbian, literally 'ballet slipper' or 'little shoe'; sometimes implies a more femme or recently out lesbian relative to the more butch connotations of sapatão.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix -ilha substantially softens the slur into something approaching gentle teasing or affectionate in-group use; far less widely known than sapatão; sometimes used to contrast a more feminine or younger lesbian against the more butch/older sapatão image.

records.definition: Slur for a lesbian in Brazilian Portuguese, especially a masculine-presenting one; the base form of the shoe-family lexical set from which 'sapatão' (augmentative) and 'sapatilha' (diminutive) derive.
records.notes: Less frequent in contemporary speech than sapatão; the plain form without augmentative suffix carries less intensity. The shoe etymology — sapato (shoe) → sapata → sapatão — is the most productive lesbian-slur word family in Brazilian Portuguese.

records.definition: A highly offensive Brazilian slur for an effeminate or gay man, explicitly conflating homosexuality with cowardice and lack of masculine resolve; etymology is disputed, possibly from 'boi' (ox) or a phonetic variant of 'bicha'.
records.notes: Carries a stronger implication of cowardice and weakness than 'viado' or 'bicha'; frequently used as a general masculinity attack even against men whose sexual orientation is not in question; common across generations and social classes; less reclaimed by gay communities than 'bicha'.

records.definition: A slur for a gay man derived from 'panela' (cooking pot/pan), invoking stereotypes of domestic femininity; used equivalently to 'bicha' or 'viado'.
records.notes: The kitchen-utensil etymology encodes the stereotype of gay men performing 'women's work'; also widely used in European Portuguese (Portugal), where it may be even more prevalent than in Brazil; less universally known in Brazil than viado/bicha but still very broadly recognized.

records.definition: Derogatory slang for a gay or effeminate man; literally 'chicken,' invoking cowardice and unmanliness.
records.notes: Less severe than 'viado'; primarily targets effeminacy or perceived cowardice rather than gay identity per se; the ordinary word for chicken creates contextual ambiguity.

records.definition: Slur for a gay man; literally 'fruit,' a direct semantic parallel to the English gay slur 'fruit' or 'fruitcake.'
records.notes: Less common than 'viado' or 'baitola'; the parallel to English 'fruit' is exact and likely intentional; slightly dated but still recognized.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'fruto'; a slightly softer slur for an effeminate or young gay man; literally 'little fruit.'
records.notes: The diminutive -inha softens the slur and can imply youth or small build; sometimes used mock-affectionately within gay communities; functions as a gentler register of 'fruto.'

records.definition: Highly offensive Brazilian slur for a gay man, particularly one perceived as passive or effeminate; etymology disputed, possibly northeastern dialectal in origin.
records.notes: Severity roughly equivalent to 'viado'; strongly associated with northeastern Brazil but understood nationwide; not reclaimed to any meaningful degree.

records.definition: Highly offensive pejorative for a travesti or transgender woman; derived from 'travesti' with the contemptuous augmentative suffix -eco.
records.notes: 'Travesti' is the neutral or community-reclaimed term; 'traveco' is unambiguously pejorative. Travestis are a culturally distinct gender category in Brazil, not simply equivalent to Western transgender women; the -eco suffix signals contempt.

records.definition: A man whose homosexuality is highly visible and unmistakable; from 'pinta' (mark, sign), meaning one who shows obvious signs of being gay.
records.notes: Emphasizes visibility of gay identity rather than effeminacy per se; 'pintoso' (m.) also used; can be pejorative or community-affirmative depending on speaker; derived from the idiom 'ter pinta de' (to look like, to give off signs of).

records.definition: In gay community slang, a descriptor for a man — typically a bottom — defined by having a large, prominent buttocks; from 'bunda' (butt) + augmentative -udo.
records.notes: In straight usage simply means 'large-butted' (neutral or complimentary); in gay community the term carries the additional implication of receptive sexual role; the big butt becomes the identity marker for the bottom role.

records.definition: Brazilian gay community pejorative for a promiscuous or sexually very available gay bottom; the augmentative -ona implies excess or disparagingly large scale.
records.notes: Used primarily within gay communities; etymology uncertain — possibly from a root meaning 'hole' or availability; the -ona augmentative intensifies and feminizes, adding a contemptuous valence; not widely known outside LGBTQ+ communities.

records.definition: Traditionally, a masculine man who has sex with gay or feminized men while assuming the active role and not identifying as gay; more recently reclaimed to mean simply a masculine or handsome gay man.
records.notes: Reflects the Latin American sexual system in which active/passive role — not partner gender — historically defined gay identity; the 'bofe' was categorically not gay in older usage despite male-male sex. The closest English subculture term is 'trade.' Now somewhat dated as Brazil's sexual identity framework has westernized.

records.definition: Dated coded euphemism for a gay or LGBTQ+ person; literally 'one who understands,' used as an in-group shibboleth when open gay identity was dangerous or stigmatized.
records.notes: Functioned as a secret signal in Brazil from roughly the 1950s through the 1980s; 'entendida' applied to lesbians; now almost entirely replaced by 'gay,' 'lésbica,' 'bicha,' etc.; the low crude score reflects its deliberate innocuousness as a coded term. Primarily known by LGBTQ+ people of the older generation and historians of Brazilian gay culture.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'gay'; a very or flamboyantly gay man; the -zão suffix implies exaggerated, visible, or over-the-top gayness.
records.notes: Tone is highly context-dependent — affirmative within community, dismissive or mocking from outsiders; the augmentative does not imply critique in all uses; common in humor, social media, and casual conversation.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'fresco'; a man who is mildly effeminate or slightly gay-seeming; literally 'a little fresh/cool'; softer register of the slur 'fresco.'
records.notes: The diminutive -inho substantially reduces the offense and is often used teasingly or ironically; implies low-level effeminacy rather than a full accusation of homosexuality; sometimes used quasi-affectionately within male friend groups.

records.definition: Slur for an effeminate or cowardly man who fails to conform to masculine norms; frequently applied to gay men; derived from the female name Maria.
records.notes: Shared with European Portuguese; the -icas suffix is an Iberian morpheme unusual in Brazilian Portuguese, giving it a slightly old-fashioned or foreign quality; still widely understood and actively used; emphasizes gender nonconformity over sexual orientation.

records.definition: Common and widely used slang for an effeminate, prissy, or gay man; literally 'fresh/cool' but pejoratively implies fussiness, effeminacy, or homosexuality.
records.notes: One of the most widely used Brazilian terms for effeminate men; less severe than 'viado'; 'fazer fresco' (to make fresco) = to be unnecessarily fussy or demanding; used both for actual gay men and for straight men perceived as insufficiently masculine.

records.definition: Standard adjective meaning effeminate; applied to men whose behavior, appearance, or mannerisms are perceived as feminine; functions as description or slur depending on context and speaker.
records.notes: The most clinical of the terms in this cluster; used in journalism, medical, and legal discourse without necessarily being pejorative; higher technical score reflects this semi-clinical register; pejorative force is entirely context-dependent.

records.definition: In Brazilian drag queen and travesti culture, the state of being fully assembled in femme presentation — hair, makeup, costume, and persona all complete; from 'montar' (to assemble, to mount).
records.notes: A positive insider term; the antonym is 'desmontada' (out of drag, undone). Not a slur; primarily used within drag and travesti communities and adjacent audiences. The 'mounting' metaphor implies constructing or building an alter-persona, distinct from simply wearing women's clothing.

records.definition: A masculine-presenting woman or butch lesbian; compound of the female name Maria and 'macho' (male), marking the incongruity between gender presentation and expected femininity.
records.notes: Shared with Spanish; can be pejorative, neutral, or even self-affirming depending on context; less severe than 'sapatão' or equivalent hardcore slurs; widely understood across all age groups and regions of Brazil.

records.definition: Literally 'female truck driver'; used as a slur or stereotype for a butch or masculine-presenting lesbian, invoking blue-collar masculine occupation as a mark of gender deviance.
records.notes: The truck driver archetype for butch women is cross-cultural; 'caminhoneiro' carries strong masculine blue-collar associations in Brazil; the feminine grammatical suffix -eira signals the incongruity that generates the stereotype. Can be used humorously within the community.

records.definition: 'Son of a whore'; the primary all-purpose strong expletive in Brazilian Portuguese, used both as a targeted insult and as a non-directed exclamation of frustration, pain, or surprise.
records.notes: The single most common severe expletive in Brazilian Portuguese; 'puta' (whore) is the vulgar element; the literal meaning (calling someone the son of a sex worker) is largely semantically bleached in most uses; functions across nearly all emotional registers when intensification is needed.

records.definition: Feminine form of 'filho da puta'; literally 'daughter of a whore'; directed at women or used gender-neutrally; identical force and function to the masculine form.
records.notes: Less frequent than the masculine default 'filho da puta' but universally understood; the feminine grammatical marking can carry the additional sting of calling the target herself the offspring of a sex worker; also used as a non-directed exclamation.

records.definition: Initialism for 'filho da puta'; used in text, social media, journalism, and any context where the full form is too explicit; decoded instantly by virtually all Brazilian adults.
records.notes: The abbreviation reduces surface vulgarity without diminishing communicative force; common in WhatsApp, Twitter/X, and Brazilian political commentary; bypasses automated profanity filters while remaining fully understood; the periods are often dropped: 'fdp.'

records.definition: 'Go fuck yourself'; a direct and emphatic dismissal using the formal subjunctive imperative 'vá' (go) + reflexive 'se foder' (to fuck oneself).
records.notes: The formal subjunctive 'vá' (rather than colloquial 'vai') adds rhetorical weight; 'foder' is the standard vulgar verb for sexual intercourse; one of the harshest dismissal insults in Brazilian Portuguese; the colloquial variant 'vai se foder' / 'vai se fuder' is more common in everyday speech.

records.definition: Literally 'go take it in the ass'; an extremely common dismissal expletive with anal sex imagery, roughly equivalent to 'go fuck yourself' but specifically evoking anal penetration of the target.
records.notes: Among the most frequently heard strong curses in Brazilian Portuguese; the anal sex framing implies the target is submissive or weak; often shortened in speech to 'tomar no cu' or even just 'no cu'; the concept maps imperfectly to any single English phrase because the anal framing is load-bearing in ways that 'go fuck yourself' is not.

records.definition: Colloquial spelling and pronunciation variant of 'vá se foder'; 'go fuck yourself'; uses the indicative 'vai' and the variant spelling 'fuder,' reflecting everyday spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Functionally identical to 'vá se foder'; the 'vai' indicative form is more colloquial and dominant in informal speech and writing; 'fuder' vs 'foder' reflects a common vowel reduction in fast speech; the two forms are interchangeable in all registers.

records.definition: Literally 'wooden ass'; an insult for a stingy, ungenerous, or obstinately unyielding person, whose orifice is metaphorically too rigid to give anything.
records.notes: The 'wood' metaphor implies an anus so tight as to be impenetrable — hence miserly or unyielding; primarily means cheap or stubbornly obstinate rather than being a simple anatomical insult; 'cu' (ass/anus) is also used as a standalone insult or exclamation, but 'cu de pau' is a fixed idiomatic compound with its own distinct meaning.

records.definition: Exclamatory expletive of shock or extreme frustration; literally 'cum that birthed you'; one of Brazil's strongest interjections, functionally equivalent to 'holy fuck' or 'what the fucking hell.'
records.notes: Often used interchangeably with 'puta que pariu'; 'porra' (semen) rather than 'puta' (whore) gives this variant a slightly different register but near-identical pragmatic function; never directed at a specific person, only hurled as a freestanding exclamation.

records.definition: The most common Brazilian Portuguese exclamatory expletive of shock, pain, or frustration; literally 'whore that birthed you'; structural and functional equivalent of English 'son of a bitch' or 'what the fuck.'
records.notes: Ubiquitous across all social classes; the birth-insult structure parallels the English 'son of a bitch' but is used exclusively as a standalone interjection, never as a directed personal insult at a specific individual.

records.definition: A person who masturbates; used as a contemptuous general-purpose insult implying worthlessness, unreliability, or being a time-wasting loser; the Brazilian Portuguese equivalent of the British 'wanker.'
records.notes: From 'punheta' (a masturbatory session); the feminine form 'punheteira' is applied to women despite the act's anatomical specificity to the penis; in practice the insult has largely shed its sexual meaning and functions as a generic pejorative for a contemptible person.

records.definition: Slur for a promiscuous, morally loose woman; derived from 'vagabundo' (vagrant/bum) with the added implication of sexual wandering from man to man; a Brazilian Portuguese equivalent of 'slut' or 'tramp.'
records.notes: Carries a dual meaning of sexual promiscuity and itinerant moral worthlessness ('she wanders around men like a vagrant'); somewhat less severe than 'puta' as it implies promiscuity without necessarily implying commercial sex work.

records.definition: Slur for a promiscuous or morally loose woman; from 'vadio/a' (idle, vagrant); used interchangeably with 'vagabunda' as the Brazilian Portuguese equivalent of 'slut' or 'whore.'
records.notes: In some northeastern Brazilian regions 'vadia' can also mean 'girlfriend' in a neutral sense, creating cross-regional confusion; in the south and southeast the insult reading is dominant and unambiguous.

records.definition: The primary Brazilian Portuguese word for a prostitute or sexually promiscuous woman used as a loaded gendered insult; also functions as an intensifying prefix in compound terms and as a standalone intensifier.
records.notes: Extreme versatility: standalone insult ('puta!'), intensifier ('puta que raiva' = what fucking anger), prefix in compounds ('putaria', 'puteiro', 'putinha'); as a directed insult at a woman it carries maximum misogynistic charge; when used in exclamations it functions as a general intensifier without gendered targeting.

records.definition: Slur for an aggressively promiscuous or sexually predatory woman who exploits men; invokes the piranha's voracious feeding frenzy to imply a woman who hunts men for sex and resources.
records.notes: The predatory angle distinguishes 'piranha' from passive slut-shame terms; implies the woman actively seeks out and 'consumes' men rather than merely being available; also carries gold-digging connotations beyond pure promiscuity.

records.definition: Slur for a promiscuous woman; literally 'hen/chicken'; implies a woman sexually available to any man, as a hen is available to any rooster in the yard.
records.notes: One of the milder entries in this cluster; the hen metaphor emphasizes passive availability rather than active predation; 'galinha' can sometimes be used affectionately or self-referentially within female friend groups with reduced sting.

records.definition: Insult for a contemptible or unpleasant woman, occasionally also implying promiscuity; literally 'cow'; functions as an equivalent of 'bitch' or British English 'cow' with the bovine metaphor adding connotations of stupidity and passive sexual availability.
records.notes: Primarily targets women perceived as bitchy or unpleasant rather than specifically promiscuous; the promiscuity reading is present but secondary; most closely parallels British English 'cow' as an insult for an unpleasant woman.

records.definition: Insult for a contemptible or promiscuous woman; literally 'female dog'; the direct Brazilian Portuguese mechanical equivalent of the English 'bitch,' carrying both hostility and promiscuity connotations.
records.notes: The most structurally direct equivalent of 'bitch' in Brazilian Portuguese — female dog applied as a woman-insult — including the same animal-origin slur mechanics; can also be used with ironic affection between close female friends, mirroring English 'bitch' reclamation dynamics.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'puta' (whore); used as a slur for a promiscuous young woman, or paradoxically as an affectionate erotic diminutive between consenting partners; the diminutive suffix softens or eroticizes the base insult depending entirely on relational context.
records.notes: One of few Brazilian sexual insults that functions bidirectionally as both insult and intimate endearment; in couples 'sua putinha' can be a term of erotic possession and affection; the same phrase from a stranger is a severe insult.

records.definition: In Brazilian Portuguese, a strong slur for a promiscuous woman or low-status prostitute; a false friend: in European Portuguese the same word neutrally means 'girl' or 'young woman.'
records.notes: A textbook cross-dialect false friend; Brazilian listeners hearing European Portuguese speakers use 'rapariga' in a neutral context may react with shock; the divergence reflects independent semantic drift and is not fully understood by speakers of either variant without cross-dialect exposure.

records.definition: Adjective or noun for a sexually uninhibited, shameless, or naughty person; used as an insult implying lack of moral restraint, but routinely flipped into a playful or affectionate compliment within couples and friend groups.
records.notes: Gender-inflected: safada (f), safado (m); unusual in that it is simultaneously one of the most common sexual insults and one of the most common playful sexual compliments in Brazilian Portuguese; context and intonation are entirely determinative of meaning.

records.definition: Insult for a shameless or brazenly immoral person; literally 'without shame'; in sexual contexts applied to someone who acts with complete disregard for sexual propriety or social norms.
records.notes: Not exclusively sexual — equally applied to dishonesty, brazenness, or general moral failings; in the sexual register it implies someone who openly flaunts behavior that should, by social convention, be kept private or restrained.

records.definition: Insult for a brazenly shameless or impudent person; from 'cara' (face), implying someone who lacks the face to feel embarrassed; in sexual contexts applied to someone who acts with no modesty or sexual propriety.
records.notes: The etymological image of losing one's face (shame) parallels East Asian face-honor discourse; less specifically sexual than most terms in this section; the sexual reading is contextual and secondary to the general brazenness meaning.

records.definition: Insult implying vulgarity, low social character, and moral baseness; in sexual contexts applied to a person whose sexual behavior is considered crude and unrestrained in a way that marks them as lower class.
records.notes: Carries strong class-shaming undertones alongside the sexual insult; calling someone 'ordinária' implies both sexual looseness and social inferiority — the misconduct is attributed to lack of breeding rather than mere immorality; parallels British English 'common' as a class-tinged insult.

records.definition: Extremely crude general-purpose insult derived from 'arrombar' (to break or force open a lock or door); for women implies repeated rough vaginal penetration having broken the opening; for men implies anal penetration; functions as a versatile 'fucker,' 'asshole,' or 'cunt' equivalent.
records.notes: The forced-penetration etymology — the orifice broken/widened through repeated violent use — is transparent to native speakers, adding a dimension of sexual degradation absent from English equivalents like 'asshole'; one of the most severe and versatile Brazilian general-purpose insults.

records.definition: A cuckold, or the act of cuckolding someone; from the horn imagery of cuckoldry tradition; also used loosely for any act of deception or betrayal where someone is metaphorically given horns.
records.notes: Less common than 'corno' as a noun for the cuckolded person; more frequently used as a verb ('dar uma corneta' = to cuckold or to deceive) or to describe the act itself; the deception meaning has partly generalized beyond strictly sexual betrayal.

records.definition: The canonical Brazilian Portuguese term for a cuckold; a man whose romantic partner has been sexually unfaithful to him; from the pan-Romance tradition of metaphorically placing horns on the betrayed husband's head.
records.notes: Carries enormous weight in the Brazilian honor-shame economy; historically among the worst social stigmas a man could bear; the horned-cuckold image is pan-Romance (Italian 'cornuto', Spanish 'cornudo') and predates modern usage; calling a man 'corno' is a serious provocation historically capable of triggering violence.

records.definition: A 'tame' or 'docile' cuckold; a man who is cheated on and either doesn't know, doesn't care, or accepts it without protest; the 'manso' qualifier implies cowardly acceptance or willful ignorance, considered more contemptible than ordinary cuckoldry.
records.notes: No direct English equivalent for the passive-acceptance distinction; in the Brazilian honor economy the 'corno manso' is considered more pitiable and contemptible than a regular 'corno' who at least reacts with appropriate outrage; implies either naivety or emasculating cowardice.

records.definition: The feminine form of 'corno'; a woman whose romantic partner has been sexually unfaithful to her; carries considerably less social stigma than the male equivalent due to asymmetric gender expectations in the Brazilian honor-shame economy.
records.notes: 'Cuckquean' is an extremely rare English term unknown to most speakers; a betrayed wife in English has no common single-word label; the 'corna' typically receives sympathy rather than ridicule — in sharp contrast to the 'corno' who faces shame — reflecting the gendered double standard of the honor economy.

records.definition: A cuckold; from 'chifre' (horn/antler) with the augmentative suffix '-udo,' implying conspicuously large and obvious horns; synonymous with 'corno' but used in a more emphatically mocking or contemptuous register.
records.notes: The augmentative '-udo' implies the horns are large, visible, and impossible to miss, adding a dimension of public humiliation; the 'chifre' derivation rather than 'corno' is a stylistic variant — both draw from the same pan-Romance horn-of-cuckoldry imagery.

records.definition: Feminine augmentative of 'cuzão' (big asshole), itself derived from 'cú' (anus); a contemptuous insult for a woman regarded as a complete or extreme asshole.
records.notes: The '-zona' augmentative (feminine of '-zão') intensifies the base insult; less frequently encountered than 'cuzão' since the anus-derived general insult is more commonly applied to men; the female form preserves gender agreement when the target is a woman.

records.definition: Dismissive slur for a cheap, worthless, or low-grade prostitute or promiscuous woman; 'de meia' implies being half-assed or of the lowest tier; used to demean a woman as not worth even a full price.
records.notes: 'Meia' can mean either 'half' or 'sock/stocking'; either reading implies cheapness — a woman worth only socks as payment or commanding only half a real prostitute's price; the phrase targets social worth and status as much as sexual behavior.

records.definition: Insult for a clumsy, stupid, useless, or burdensome person; originally a heavy block tied to an animal's leg to impede movement; also used crudely to refer to a large, ungainly penis regarded as more of a burden than a pleasure.
records.notes: Unusual in this list because its primary etymology is non-sexual (an impediment device for livestock); its inclusion in sexual vocabulary is secondary — 'trambolho' can dismissively denote a large, awkward, unpleasant penis ('aquele trambolho' = 'that thing'); the worthless-person insult use dominates in practice.

records.definition: Compound insult meaning 'useless limp-dick,' attacking a man as simultaneously incompetent and sexually impotent.
records.notes: Combines 'inútil' (useless/worthless) with 'pau mole' (limp penis); attacks general competence and sexual potency in a single phrase; 'pau' (stick/wood) is the standard Brazilian crude term for penis.

records.definition: Slur for a cowardly, effeminate, or sexually timid man; implies failure to perform masculine norms of bravado and sexual assertiveness.
records.notes: Literally 'slack' or 'loose'; applied to men who fail expectations of masculine aggression or sexual prowess; also used for inanimate things that are limp or without tension; frequently directed at gay men.

records.definition: Slang for a woman perceived as ostentatiously provocative and sexually available, with strong class-based contempt implying lower-class origins and flashy presentation.
records.notes: Carries a socioeconomic dimension absent from most English equivalents; implies gaudy, sexually aggressive presentation from a working-class milieu; peaked in mainstream Brazilian media discourse around 2008–2012.

records.definition: Intensified compound insult for a promiscuous woman of the lowest social stratum; 'piranha' denotes predatory sexual voraciousness and 'do lixo' marks extreme class contempt.
records.notes: 'Do lixo' (of the garbage/trash) places the target at the absolute bottom of the social hierarchy; combines sexual and class-based degradation in a single phrase; typically deployed as a final, annihilating insult.

records.definition: General insult meaning 'trash' or 'garbage,' applied to a person deemed utterly worthless or morally depraved; not inherently sexual but frequently paired with sexual slurs to amplify contempt.
records.notes: Primary meaning is literal garbage; the insult use is contextual; in sexual insult strings it functions as a status-annihilating amplifier rather than a standalone sexual term; universal recognition as an everyday word.

records.definition: Phrase meaning 'street-corner prostitute,' used both as a literal descriptor and as an intensified insult placing the target at the lowest rung of sex-work hierarchy.
records.notes: 'De esquina' (of the corner) specifies outdoor solicitation, the most exposed and stigmatized form of sex work; used as an insult to invoke maximum social degradation regardless of the target's actual profession.

records.definition: Dismissive expletive command roughly equivalent to 'go fuck yourself' or 'go to hell,' used to reject or dismiss someone with contemptuous finality.
records.notes: 'Lascar-se' implies going to ruin or being wrecked rather than literally fucking; less sexually explicit than 'vai se foder' and therefore more deployable across social contexts; functions from heated arguments to casual banter.

records.definition: Compound homophobic slur literally meaning 'ass-eater,' used to degrade a man by implying he performs anilingus or takes the receptive role in anal sex.
records.notes: Derived from 'comer' (Brazilian vulgar for sexual penetration/fucking) + 'cu' (anus); the anatomical literalism makes this particularly aggressive; also deployed as a general contempt insult irrespective of the target's actual sexual orientation.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'buceta' (vagina), used as an insult for a weak or cowardly person, directly analogous to 'pussy' in American English.
records.notes: The augmentative suffix '-ão' intensifies both the anatomical reference and the contempt; equates femininity with weakness; can also refer literally to a large vagina, though the cowardice-insult sense dominates in this register.

records.definition: Standard Portuguese term for a prostitute or sex worker; the default word used in legal, medical, and journalistic contexts.
records.notes: Less charged than 'puta' but still carries social stigma; the statutory term in Brazilian legal codes; used across registers from clinical to accusatory.

records.definition: Neutral euphemistic phrase for a sex worker, emphasizing the professional labor framing over moral judgment.
records.notes: Preferred by sex worker rights organizations and public health bodies in Brazil; avoids the stigma of 'prostituta' or 'puta'; common in NGO materials, harm-reduction programs, and progressive journalism.

records.definition: Clinical and politically neutral term for a female sex worker, equivalent to 'sex worker' in English rights-based and public-health discourse.
records.notes: Gendered female form ('trabalhadora'); the male form is 'trabalhador sexual'; primarily found in academic, advocacy, and public-health contexts; rarely used in everyday speech outside those registers.

records.definition: Archaic literary term for a prostitute, derived from Latin 'meretrix'; appears in 19th- and 20th-century literature, legal codes, and formal journalism.
records.notes: Still embedded in some Brazilian legal texts and criminal-law scholarship; virtually absent from everyday speech; recognizable to educated adults primarily through literature or legal study.

records.definition: The most common vulgar Brazilian Portuguese term for a prostitute or whore; also functions as a powerful general-purpose intensifier in profanity.
records.notes: Extraordinarily versatile: noun (sex worker, insult), adjective intensifier ('puta merda'), and exclamation ('puta que pariu!'); the intensifier use is nearly universal and not perceived as sexual in isolation by most speakers.

records.definition: Diminutive of 'puta' (whore), meaning 'little whore'; used as an insult, a degrading label, or an erotic term of address in sexual contexts.
records.notes: The diminutive '-inha' paradoxically can soften or intensify depending on context; widely used in Brazilian pornography as a submissive erotic form of address and as a contempt insult in everyday arguments.

records.definition: Slang for a sexually predatory or promiscuous woman; the piranha fish metaphor implies voracious, aggressive sexual appetite and willingness to exploit men.
records.notes: Implies active sexual predation rather than passive promiscuity; can denote a sex worker or a non-professional promiscuous woman; the fish metaphor is fully opaque in everyday use; also appears as the first element in compound insults like 'piranha do lixo.'

records.definition: Brazilian slang for a male sex worker, especially one who has sex with men for pay while often publicly identifying as heterosexual.
records.notes: Predominantly used in the MSM sex-work context; 'michê' frequently maintains a heterosexual self-identity while accepting pay for sex with men, a culturally specific positioning that distinguishes him from 'garoto de programa' who may serve any gender client.

records.definition: Euphemistic Brazilian term for a female sex worker or escort; literally 'program girl,' where 'programa' is the coded term for a paid sexual appointment.
records.notes: The most common neutral-to-euphemistic designation in Brazilian journalism and everyday speech; 'programa' as a coded term for a paid sexual encounter is understood universally by Brazilian adults.

records.definition: Euphemistic term for a male sex worker or escort; the masculine counterpart of 'garota de programa,' potentially serving clients of any gender.
records.notes: Less stigmatized in everyday language than 'michê' due to the neutral 'programa' framing; used in journalism and harm-reduction contexts; does not carry the same heterosexual-performance connotation as 'michê.'

records.definition: The standard Brazilian Portuguese coded term for a paid sexual appointment or sex-work transaction; literally 'program,' 'schedule,' or 'show.'
records.notes: Entirely opaque as a euphemism since 'programa' has abundant innocent meanings; the sex-work sense is understood universally by Brazilian adults; can refer to the transaction itself, a single booking, or the session with a client.

records.definition: The standard Brazilian Portuguese term for a male pimp; a man who manages sex workers and appropriates part of their earnings through control or coercion.
records.notes: Etymology uncertain; possibly from French 'cafeté' or independent Brazilian coinage; the feminine form 'cafetina' denotes a female pimp or madam; universally recognized across all social strata.

records.definition: A female pimp or madam who manages sex workers, controls their appointments, and takes a share of their earnings; sometimes also manages a fixed brothel premises.
records.notes: Feminine form of 'cafetão'; 'madam' in English specifically implies brothel management whereas 'cafetina' can refer more broadly to any woman who controls or profits from sex workers' labor in any setting.

records.definition: A male sex worker or kept man financially supported by a wealthier woman, typically older, in exchange for companionship and sexual access.
records.notes: Direct loanword from French/English 'gigolo'; Brazilian usage emphasizes financial dependence on a female patron more than active solicitation; culturally distinguished from 'michê' who primarily serves male clients.

records.definition: A brothel; an establishment where sex workers receive paying clients on the premises.
records.notes: Loanword from French 'bordel'; carries a slightly elevated or literary register compared to the cruder 'puteiro'; used in journalism, historical writing, and formal contexts alongside the vernacular alternative.

records.definition: Crude slang for a brothel or whorehouse, derived from 'puta' (whore) and the productive Portuguese place-forming suffix '-eiro.'
records.notes: The '-eiro' suffix productively forms place-nouns in Portuguese (padaria=bakery, puteiro=place of whores); more vulgar than 'bordel'; also used metaphorically for any chaotic, sexually charged, or morally anarchic environment.

records.definition: An area of a city designated or known for prostitution and sex work; the Brazilian equivalent of a red-light district.
records.notes: Polysemous: primary meaning is simply 'zone/area,' but in isolation or with context it denotes a prostitution district; very common in Brazilian Portuguese.

records.definition: House of tolerance; a historical Brazilian euphemism for a licensed brothel, reflecting the official policy of regulated toleration of prostitution.
records.notes: Reflects a specific Brazilian legal-historical framework of tolerância (official toleration rather than prohibition); still encountered in journalism and historical writing.

records.definition: A nightclub or entertainment venue that in Brazilian usage often doubles as a venue for sex work, derived from the French cabaret.
records.notes: Carries much stronger sex-work connotations in Brazil than the European artistic cabaret tradition; commonly found in smaller cities and truck-stop corridors.

records.definition: Nightclub; in Brazilian Portuguese frequently a euphemism for a venue where sex work takes place, particularly upscale or semi-disguised establishments.
records.notes: From French 'boîte'; primarily means nightclub/discotheque but in many contexts — especially smaller cities and highway towns — functions as a euphemism for a brothel.

records.definition: Brothel; the standard formal Portuguese term for an establishment where sex workers receive paying clients on the premises.
records.notes: Used in legal documents, journalism, and academic writing; more formal and clinical than 'zona' or 'casa de tolerância.'

records.definition: Pornography; the formal clinical term for sexually explicit material designed to arouse, used in legal, academic, and journalistic contexts.
records.notes: Standard term across all registers when precision is needed; less commonly used in casual conversation than the abbreviation 'pornô.'

records.definition: Porn; the ubiquitous colloquial abbreviation of 'pornografia,' functioning as both noun and attributive adjective.
records.notes: Functionally universal in informal speech; used attributively in compounds such as 'atriz pornô' and 'site pornô.'

records.definition: Male pornographic actor; a man who performs in pornographic films for payment.
