records.notes: Grammatically masculine; the gender-marked pair to 'atriz pornô.' No registry concept specifically covers pornographic performers; 'sex_worker' used as the closest individual-level match.

records.definition: Female pornographic actress; a woman who performs in pornographic films for payment.
records.notes: Grammatically feminine counterpart to 'ator pornô'; discussed more frequently in Brazilian media due to the industry's gender dynamics.

records.definition: Stripper; a direct English loanword for a person who performs erotic dances involving the progressive removal of clothing for a paying audience.
records.notes: Widely used English loanword that has largely displaced native alternatives in everyday speech; gender-neutral in use, applied to both male and female performers.

records.definition: Erotic dancer; a euphemistic phrase for a striptease performer, used in employment advertising and media coverage to soften the nature of the occupation.
records.notes: More formal and distancing register than 'stripper'; commonly seen in classified ads and journalistic contexts; grammatically feminine by default.

records.definition: Companion or escort; the dominant Brazilian Portuguese euphemism for an upscale sex worker, used widely in online ads and personal profiles.
records.notes: The most socially accepted self-descriptor among Brazilian sex workers in the middle-to-high price tier; avoids the stigma of 'prostituta'; conversational context almost always disambiguates from non-sexual companionship.

records.definition: Escort; an English loanword used in the Brazilian sex industry for a high-end or discreet sex worker, slightly more international and premium in connotation than 'acompanhante.'
records.notes: Often used interchangeably with 'acompanhante' in online advertising; the English loanword lends a cosmopolitan framing and distances the term from overt prostitution stigma.

records.definition: Adult content; a platform-neutral euphemism for pornographic or sexually explicit material, widely used on digital platforms, subscription services, and content warnings.
records.notes: Avoids the stigma of 'pornografia'; standard terminology on Brazilian social media, OnlyFans-equivalent platforms, and digital streaming services.

records.definition: Paid sex; a straightforward compound phrase for a sex work transaction, more blunt than euphemisms but less crude than slang alternatives.
records.notes: Journalistic and matter-of-fact in tone; used in public health, news reporting, and social policy discussions about sex work regulation.

records.definition: Sexual service; a clinical or bureaucratic phrase for sex work services, maintaining formal distance and used predominantly in legal, policy, and public health contexts.
records.notes: Common in Brazilian public health literature, human rights reports, and legislative discussions around sex work regulation.

records.definition: Sexual livelihood; an informal compound phrase framing sex work as an occupational means of income, literally 'sexual bread-winner.'
records.english_term: sexual livelihood / sex as a living
records.notes: 'Ganha-pão' alone (livelihood / bread-winner) is very common; the sexual compound is less standardized and context-dependent; encountered primarily in advocacy journalism and labor-rights writing.

records.definition: Paid lewdness; a crude colloquial phrase for a paid sex act, combining 'sacanagem' (sexual misbehavior / lewdness / dirty tricks) with 'paga' (paid).
records.notes: 'Sacanagem' is one of the most versatile crude-register words in Brazilian Portuguese, covering sexual misconduct, lewd behavior, and unfair trickery; the compound is blunt and carries a pejorative or dismissive tone toward the transaction.

records.definition: Condom; the dominant everyday Brazilian Portuguese word for a condom, literally 'little shirt,' reflecting the sheathing function of the device.
records.notes: Overwhelmingly preferred over 'preservativo' in informal speech; heavily promoted in Brazilian public health campaigns (particularly HIV/AIDS prevention); functionally universal across age groups.

records.definition: Condom; the formal clinical Portuguese term for a condom, used on product packaging, pharmaceutical literature, and official health communications.
records.notes: Rarely used in casual conversation; found on product packaging, medical prescriptions, and formal public health materials; shared pan-Portuguese usage across Brazil and Portugal.

records.definition: Rubber; an informal slang term for condom derived from the material it is made of, analogous to English 'rubber.'
records.notes: Less common than 'camisinha'; polysemous — 'borracha' primarily means rubber material or pencil eraser, requiring context for the condom meaning; perception of the term as a condom synonym may be stronger among older speakers.

records.definition: Overcoat; a colloquial slang term for condom evoking the metaphor of a coat or covering placed over the penis, literally 'overcoat' or 'large cape.'
records.notes: One of several garment-metaphor slang terms for condom in Brazilian Portuguese; less universal than 'camisinha'; may show regional or generational variation in frequency.

records.definition: Cover or cape; a colloquial slang term for condom emphasizing the covering or sheathing function, literally 'cover,' 'cape,' or 'jacket.'
records.notes: Less standardized than 'camisinha' or 'capote'; highly context-dependent; 'capa' alone carries many non-sexual primary meanings (book cover, raincoat, superhero cape).

records.definition: Hat or cap; an informal slang term for condom metaphorically evoking a fitted cap placed over the glans penis, literally 'woolen hat' or 'beanie.'
records.notes: Less widely recognized than 'camisinha'; the visual metaphor of a fitted hat over the penis head is intuitive; possibly shows stronger regional variation than other clothing-metaphor condom slang.

records.definition: Contraceptive; the standard Brazilian Portuguese term for any contraceptive method or device, though in everyday speech it most commonly defaults to meaning the oral contraceptive pill.
records.notes: Functions as both noun and adjective; in informal speech often implies the pill specifically ('tomar o anticoncepcional' = to take the pill); used universally across medical, pharmaceutical, and public health registers.

records.definition: Colloquial shorthand for the oral contraceptive pill.
records.notes: Short for 'pílula anticoncepcional'; universally understood by Brazilian adults; the default word in everyday speech for hormonal birth control.

records.definition: Euphemistic phrase meaning to take the morning-after pill first thing in the morning after unprotected sex.
records.notes: Phrase literally means 'early in the morning'; used as a veiled instruction or reference to emergency contraception rather than a fixed lexical term; recognition as a euphemism is low and context-dependent.

records.definition: The morning-after pill; an emergency oral contraceptive taken within 72 hours of unprotected sex to prevent pregnancy.
records.notes: The standard Brazilian Portuguese term for emergency contraception; literally 'pill of the next day'; sold over the counter and widely advertised in pharmacies.

records.definition: Vasectomy; a surgical procedure for permanent male sterilization in which the vas deferens is cut or sealed to prevent sperm from entering semen.
records.notes: Clinical loanword from medical Latin/Greek; widely recognized; subject to cultural resistance in Brazil due to masculinity norms and historical access barriers in the public health system.

records.definition: Tubal ligation; a surgical procedure for permanent female sterilization in which the fallopian tubes are cut, tied, or blocked.
records.notes: Short for 'laqueadura de trompas'; the dominant vernacular term for female surgical sterilization in Brazil; historically one of the most common forms of contraception in Brazil, especially in lower-income populations.

records.definition: Abortion; the termination of a pregnancy, whether spontaneous (miscarriage) or induced; in Brazilian law, induced abortion is criminalized except in cases of rape, risk to the mother's life, or anencephalic fetus.
records.notes: Covers both induced abortion ('aborto induzido/provocado') and spontaneous miscarriage ('aborto espontâneo'); politically and religiously charged in Brazil; proposed slug: abortion.

records.definition: To abort; to terminate a pregnancy, whether through induced abortion or spontaneous miscarriage.
records.notes: Verbal form of 'aborto'; used clinically and in everyday speech; also used metaphorically in non-reproductive contexts (e.g., abortar uma missão); proposed slug: abortion.

records.definition: Unwanted or unintended pregnancy, typically resulting from contraceptive failure, non-use, or sexual violence.
records.notes: Standard public health phrase; appears extensively in Brazilian reproductive health policy and sex education materials; proposed slug: unwanted_pregnancy.

records.definition: Acronym for bondage and discipline, dominance and submission, sadism and masochism; umbrella term for consensual power-exchange and pain-play sexual practices.
records.notes: English acronym used unchanged in Brazilian Portuguese; recognition spiked after the Brazilian release of Fifty Shades of Grey (2015); actively practiced and discussed in Brazilian kink communities and mainstream media.

records.definition: The erotic practice of physically restraining a partner with rope, cuffs, or other materials for sexual arousal or power exchange.
records.notes: English loanword used directly; native alternatives such as 'amarração' or 'restrição' exist but are uncommon in kink contexts; increasingly recognized outside subculture due to mainstream media coverage.

records.definition: Domination; in BDSM, the exercise of authority, control, or power over a submissive partner within a consensual power-exchange dynamic.
records.notes: Has broad general meanings (political, military) in addition to its BDSM-specific use; context disambiguates; the BDSM meaning is now widely understood by non-practitioners.

records.definition: Submission; in BDSM, the consensual yielding of power, control, or autonomy to a dominant partner within a power-exchange dynamic.
records.notes: General meaning (religious submission, surrender) is primary for most speakers; BDSM meaning requires context; often used together with 'dominação' in BDSM discourse.

records.definition: Dominant; in BDSM, the partner who exercises control, authority, or discipline over the submissive partner.
records.notes: Functions as both adjective and noun; the sexual BDSM sense is secondary to the general meaning; used in BDSM communities as a role identifier and personal identity label.

records.definition: Submissive; in BDSM, the partner who yields power and control to the dominant, often within a negotiated and consensual dynamic.
records.notes: Gender-inflected: submisso (masculine), submissa (feminine); used as both adjective and noun in BDSM contexts; general meaning (meek, compliant) is more widely recognized than the BDSM-specific use.

records.definition: Short for 'dominant'; in BDSM, the partner who takes the controlling, authoritative role in a power-exchange dynamic.
records.notes: English loanword used in Brazilian BDSM communities; creates potential confusion with the honorific 'Dom' (a Portuguese title for clergy or nobility); recognition limited to kink-aware audiences.

records.definition: Short for 'submissive'; in BDSM, the partner who yields control and authority to the dominant.
records.notes: English loanword; the BDSM meaning requires kink-community context to be understood; 'sub' is also a common Portuguese prefix and abbreviation in non-sexual contexts.

records.definition: Sadomasochism; sexual gratification derived from both inflicting and receiving pain, humiliation, or domination.
records.notes: Clinical-origin compound of sadismo and masoquismo; widely known through psychology, media, and cultural discourse; often abbreviated as S&M in Brazilian popular usage.

records.definition: A woman who takes the dominant role in BDSM, often as a professional, exercising control over submissive clients or partners.
records.notes: Latin/English loanword used unchanged in Brazilian Portuguese; widely recognized through films, television, and internet culture; professional dominatrices ('dominatrixes') operate openly in major Brazilian cities.

records.definition: Voyeurism; the paraphilia or practice of deriving sexual pleasure from watching others in intimate or sexual situations without their knowledge or consent.
records.notes: Adapted from French via English clinical psychology; recognized both as a paraphilia in clinical contexts and as a general cultural concept in Brazilian media discourse.

records.definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from watching others in intimate or sexual situations without their knowledge.
records.notes: French loanword used directly in both English and Brazilian Portuguese; widely understood without kink-community background; also used loosely to mean any curious observer.

records.definition: Exhibitionism; the paraphilia or practice of deriving sexual pleasure from exposing one's genitals or body to others, typically strangers.
records.notes: Clinical-origin term; also widely used non-sexually to mean flamboyant attention-seeking behavior, which can dilute the sexual connotation in casual speech.

records.definition: An exhibitionist; a person who derives sexual pleasure from publicly exposing their genitals or performing sexual acts in front of others.
records.notes: Used as both noun and adjective; the non-sexual meaning (show-off, attention-seeker) is primary for most Brazilians; the sexual meaning requires context; both uses are fully recognized.

records.definition: Fetishism; a paraphilia in which sexual arousal is derived from a specific atypical object, body part, or material.
records.notes: Clinical psychology term borrowed into Portuguese; also has an anthropological sense (religious object worship) that predates the sexual meaning; the sexual meaning is now the primary connotation in everyday discourse.

records.definition: A fetish; a specific object, body part, or scenario that a person finds sexually arousing, often to an intense or compulsive degree.
records.notes: From French 'fétiche' via Portuguese colonial-era anthropology; now broadly used in sexual and non-sexual senses ('tenho um fetiche por sapatos'; 'ele tem um fetiche por organização'); the sexual meaning is widely understood.

records.definition: Masochism; sexual gratification derived from experiencing pain, humiliation, or subjugation inflicted by another person.
records.notes: Named for Leopold von Sacher-Masoch; entered Portuguese through clinical psychology; also widely used metaphorically for non-sexual self-punishing behavior ('trabalhar assim é masoquismo puro').

records.definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from receiving pain, humiliation, or subjugation.
records.notes: Used both in clinical psychology and casual Brazilian conversation; the scientific-sounding suffix gives it a moderately technical register despite widespread lay use.

records.definition: Sexual gratification derived from inflicting pain, humiliation, or suffering on another person.
records.notes: More clinical-sounding than most kink vocabulary; used by psychologists, kink communities, and educated laypeople alike. Named after the Marquis de Sade.

records.definition: A person who derives pleasure from inflicting pain or humiliation; also used adjectivally for any cruel or punishing behavior, sexual or otherwise.
records.notes: Gender-inflected: sádico (masculine), sádica (feminine). Frequently used outside sexual contexts to describe general cruelty, which dilutes the kink-specific signal.

records.definition: The sexual practice of inserting an entire hand or fist into a partner's vagina or anus, used as a direct English loanword.
records.notes: No common native Portuguese equivalent in circulation; the English loanword dominates. Recognition skews toward sexually experienced adults and LGBTQ+ communities; lower among conservative or older demographics.

records.definition: Erotic spanking of a partner for sexual arousal, used as a direct English loanword in Brazilian BDSM communities.
records.notes: Native equivalents include 'surra' and 'palmada'; the English loanword is preferred in kink-community and pornographic contexts. Recognition higher among younger and internet-connected Brazilians.

records.definition: In BDSM contexts, an erotic beating or impact-play session; in general Brazilian Portuguese, any severe physical thrashing or defeat.
records.notes: Primary meaning is non-sexual (sports, fights, punishment); the BDSM meaning is a register shift via context. The word is never inherently sexual — only context disambiguates. Highly recognizable universally.

records.definition: A whip used in BDSM impact play to strike a partner's body for erotic stimulation or discipline; also the standard Brazilian Portuguese word for any whip.
records.notes: Technically denotes a single-tail whip, not a multi-tailed flogger; mapped to bdsm_flogger as the nearest registry concept covering whip-type BDSM implements. In everyday language refers to any whipping instrument (horsewhip, riding crop, etc.).

records.definition: Handcuffs used in erotic restraint or bondage play; also the standard Brazilian Portuguese word for police or restraint handcuffs.
records.notes: Universally recognized as the word for handcuffs; the BDSM meaning is a direct transfer of the primary denotation into an erotic context. No inherent sexual meaning — fully context-dependent.

records.definition: A gag device used in BDSM to silence or restrain a partner's ability to speak; also the standard Brazilian Portuguese word for any gag or muzzle.
records.notes: No gag-specific concept in the canonical registry; mapped to bondage as the nearest category. Covers all gag types (ball gag, bit gag, tape). The word is also used in political speech to mean censorship or silencing.

records.definition: Rope used in sexual bondage to physically restrain a partner for erotic purposes; also the standard everyday Brazilian Portuguese word for any rope or cord.
records.notes: One of the most common words in Portuguese repurposed for BDSM; in kink contexts often implies shibari-style aesthetics. The English compound 'bondage rope' captures the full concept; 'corda' alone only signals the tool.

records.definition: Sexual activity in which participants adopt fictional personas, characters, or scenarios to enact erotic fantasies; used as a direct English loanword in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: No sexual_roleplay slug in canonical registry; mapped to bdsm_play as nearest structured consensual play concept. Role play is broader than BDSM but overlaps heavily in Brazilian kink communities. The native equivalent 'jogo de papéis' is less common.

records.definition: In sexual contexts, an erotic fantasy or imaginative scenario used for arousal; in general use, the everyday Portuguese word for fantasy or imagination.
records.notes: Not inherently sexual; meaning is fully determined by context. Mapped to eroticism as nearest registry concept — no sexual_fantasy slug exists in the registry. Low crude score because the word itself is completely neutral; it is the context that sexualizes it.

records.definition: A sexual fantasy; an erotic imaginative scenario deliberately constructed for arousal, often shared with a partner or enacted in role play.
records.notes: The 'sexual' modifier removes all ambiguity. More deliberate and plannable in connotation than 'fantasia' alone — implies a scenario that could potentially be enacted. Mapped to eroticism as nearest registry concept.

records.definition: Literally 'game of roles'; the native Brazilian Portuguese phrase for sexual role play, in which participants adopt fictional personas or scenarios for erotic purposes.
records.notes: Less common than the English loanword 'role play' in Brazilian kink communities; sounds slightly more formal or pedagogical. Mapped to bdsm_play as nearest registry concept. Recognition lower because Brazilians typically use the English loanword in kink contexts.

records.definition: Group sex; sexual activity involving three or more participants simultaneously or in overlapping encounters.
records.notes: Neutral descriptive compound; less charged than 'orgia' or 'gangbang'. Functions as the default everyday Brazilian Portuguese descriptor for multi-partner sex when a neutral register is intended.

records.definition: A sexual act in which one person is simultaneously or sequentially engaged sexually by multiple partners; used as a direct English loanword.
records.notes: Among the cruder English loanwords in Brazilian sexual vocabulary; used in pornographic taxonomy and crude casual speech. No widely-used native Portuguese equivalent exists. Recognition highest among young adults and regular pornography consumers.

records.definition: An orgy; a sexual gathering involving multiple participants freely engaging with each other in an unstructured or celebratory atmosphere.
records.notes: Derives from Latin/Greek 'orgia' (secret Bacchic rites); carries historical connotations of excess, debauchery, and transgression beyond mere group sex. More evocative and colorful than 'sexo em grupo'.

records.definition: Literally 'couple exchange'; the standard Brazilian Portuguese euphemism for swinging, in which couples consensually swap sexual partners.
records.notes: Preferred in-community term among Brazilian swingers; sounds considerably less sexually explicit than 'swing' or 'orgia' in casual conversation, functioning as an effective euphemism. 'Clubes de troca de casais' are a well-documented institution in Brazil.

records.definition: The swinging lifestyle; consensual sexual partner-swapping between couples, used as an English loanword in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Used as noun ('entrar no swing', 'mundo do swing') and attributively ('clube de swing'). Coexists with 'troca de casais'; 'swing' is the loanword form while 'troca de casais' is the native phrasing. Brazil has a particularly active swinger community.

records.definition: A person who participates in the swinging lifestyle, engaging in consensual sexual partner-swapping with other couples.
records.notes: Used unchanged from English; forms the identity noun for practitioners of 'swing'. Recognized primarily among those familiar with the lifestyle, adult entertainment media, or tabloid journalism.

records.definition: A man who derives erotic pleasure from his partner having sex with other men; used as an English loanword in Brazilian kink and pornographic communities.
records.notes: The English loanword coexists with the native term 'corno'; 'cuckold' is used specifically in kink-community and pornographic contexts with the fetish-positive connotation, while 'corno' carries the primary meaning of a shamed, deceived husband.

records.definition: In fetish contexts, a man whose partner has sex with other men with his knowledge and erotic pleasure; in general Brazilian Portuguese, a highly offensive slur for a man being cheated on.
records.notes: Literally 'horn' (referencing the cuckold's horns of European tradition). The same word functions as both a severe insult (cheated-on husband who doesn't know or is helpless) and a kink identity term — the fetish register is a deliberate reappropriation. Near-universal recognition. Crude score reflects the insult register, which is primary.

records.definition: A married woman who has sex with men other than her husband with his full knowledge and enthusiastic consent, framed as shared erotic pleasure for both spouses.
records.notes: More niche than 'cuckold' or 'swing'; primarily recognized in Brazilian swinger, cuckold, and online pornography communities. Conceptually distinct from 'troca de casais' in that only the wife has additional partners while the husband watches or otherwise participates vicariously.

records.definition: A sexual encounter involving exactly three participants; a French loanword used in Brazilian Portuguese as a sophisticated or euphemistic alternative to 'sexo a três'.
records.notes: French for 'household of three'; used across many languages as an elegant or ironic euphemism for a threesome. In Brazilian Portuguese carries a slightly refined or humorous register relative to the blunter native alternative. Often written without the grave accent on 'à' in Brazilian usage.

records.definition: Literally 'sex at/with three'; the standard colloquial Brazilian Portuguese phrase for a sexual encounter involving exactly three participants.
records.notes: The everyday Brazilian Portuguese descriptor for a threesome; more direct and less euphemistic than 'ménage a três'. The preposition 'a' (at/with) is the standard construction; 'sexo a três' functions as the default neutral phrasing across all demographics familiar with the concept.

records.definition: Female ejaculation or the fluid expelled during intense sexual arousal; English loanword used in Brazilian Portuguese informal and pornographic contexts.
records.notes: Borrowed from English; widely circulated via pornography and internet culture in Brazil; used both as noun and verb.

records.definition: The act of female ejaculation; English gerund adopted into Brazilian Portuguese sexual discourse, used interchangeably with 'squirt'.
records.notes: Used identically to the English gerund; the Brazilian native equivalent 'gozar' or 'ejaculação feminina' is less common in pornographic slang registers.

records.definition: Erotic play involving urine; English loanword used in Brazilian Portuguese kink communities as a euphemistic label for urophilia activities.
records.notes: Preferred in online kink spaces over 'chuva dourada' by some communities; the English form softens the crude impact slightly through foreignness.

records.definition: French loanword meaning 'golden shower'; a sexual act in which one person urinates on another for erotic purposes.
records.notes: French borrowing, rarer than 'chuva dourada' or 'pee play'; the French framing imparts a slightly more euphemistic register; encountered mainly in written erotica and cosmopolitan kink circles.

records.definition: Clinical term for any persistent pattern of sexual arousal centered on atypical objects, situations, or individuals; the Portuguese adaptation of 'paraphilia'.
records.notes: Direct Portuguese cognate of the DSM-5 clinical term; used in psychology, psychiatry, and academic sexology; largely unfamiliar outside educated or therapeutic contexts.

records.definition: English loanword for a person with a strong interest in anthropomorphic animal characters; adopted into Brazilian internet subculture, with or without a sexual component.
records.notes: Used identically to the English term; Brazil has one of the largest furry fandoms outside English-speaking countries; stigma in mainstream culture, acceptance within the community.

records.definition: 'Heavy BDSM'; refers to intense or extreme BDSM practices involving significant pain, strict restraint, or deeply immersive power exchange beyond beginner-level play.
records.notes: 'Pesado' (heavy/intense) functions as a severity qualifier; the contrasting term 'BDSM leve' (light BDSM) marks the softer end; recognized in Brazilian kink communities but not mainstream.

records.definition: 'Sexual slavery'; in BDSM contexts, a consensual total power exchange dynamic in which the submissive adopts a slave role, surrendering broad autonomy to the dominant partner.
records.notes: Inherently ambiguous between the consensual BDSM slave dynamic and literal non-consensual trafficking; context disambiguates; within kink communities the consensual sense is assumed; maps imperfectly to any single registry concept.

records.definition: 'Servitude'; in BDSM contexts, the lifestyle state of ongoing service and submission to a dominant partner, emphasizing the service dimension of total power exchange.
records.notes: More formal and literary than 'submissão'; implies a 24/7 lifestyle dynamic rather than a discrete scene; used in TPE (total power exchange) relationship discourse.

records.definition: English loanword for the fetish practice of being walked on or stepped on by another person for erotic arousal, often combined with foot fetishism or dominance dynamics.
records.notes: No established Portuguese equivalent; the English term is used as-is in Brazilian kink communities; closely associated with foot fetish and body worship; 'sensation_play' is the closest broad registry concept.

records.definition: 'Feet'; used as shorthand in Brazilian Portuguese for foot fetishism, the sexual arousal from feet or footwear, one of the most commonly reported paraphilias.
records.notes: 'Pés' literally means 'feet'; the sexual reading is metonymic; commonly appears in compounds like 'fetiche de pés' or 'fetichismo de pés'; the parenthetical in source material confirms the fetish reading.

records.definition: 'Latex'; in kink contexts, refers to the fetish for wearing or seeing latex garments, associated with skin-tight enclosure, shiny texture, and sensory restriction.
records.notes: Covers both the material and the subculture aesthetic; latex garments are common in Brazilian BDSM and fetish communities, particularly in São Paulo club scenes.

records.definition: 'Leather'; in kink contexts, refers to the leather fetish and leather subculture, encompassing sexual arousal from leather garments and the associated hypermasculine or dominant aesthetic.
records.notes: 'Couro' also means 'hide' or 'skin'; has strong associations with the gay leather subculture and BDSM communities in Brazil; São Paulo's Pride events feature visible leather community presence.

records.definition: 'Uniform'; refers to the uniform fetish, sexual arousal from wearing or seeing authority-figure uniforms such as police, military, nurse, or schoolgirl outfits.
records.notes: Broad category covering many uniform types; frequently combined with dominant/submissive roleplay dynamics; the parenthetical in the source material confirms the fetish rather than literal reading.

records.definition: 'Teacher/student'; a sexual roleplay scenario in which participants adopt teacher and student personas, exploiting the authority differential and discipline connotations of the academic relationship.
records.notes: One of the most commonly cited heterosexual roleplay scenarios in Brazilian contexts; the slash notation signals the two complementary roles; frequently combined with uniform fetish elements.

records.definition: 'Make love'; a romantic euphemism for sexual intercourse, foregrounding emotional connection and mutual desire over the physical act.
records.notes: The most universally recognized romantic euphemism for sex in Brazilian Portuguese; appropriate across all registers and audiences; direct calque of the English idiom.

records.definition: 'Do that thing'; a maximally vague demonstrative euphemism for sexual activity, relying entirely on shared context and implication to communicate the referent.
records.notes: Typical of embarrassed, bashful, or euphemistic speech about sex; the referent is disambiguated entirely by pragmatic context; used across all age groups in Brazil.

records.definition: 'The thing / the business'; a colloquial euphemism for sexual intercourse, substituting a generic masculine noun to avoid explicit naming.
records.notes: 'O negócio' has many non-sexual meanings; the sexual reading depends entirely on pragmatic context; often deployed humorously; regional variation in frequency across Brazil.

records.definition: 'That certain thing'; a vague coy euphemism for sexual activity, with 'tal' adding a knowing, conspiratorial quality to the circumlocution.
records.notes: The 'tal' (such / that certain) adds a sense of shared understanding between speaker and listener; slightly more coy than 'o negócio'; used in nervous or humorous registers.

records.definition: 'Intimacy'; a broad euphemism ranging from emotional closeness to sexual activity; context and collocation determine whether the physical or emotional dimension is foregrounded.
records.notes: One of the most socially acceptable euphemisms; used in journalism, therapy, and polite conversation; does not exclusively denote sex but frequently implies it in appropriate contexts.

records.definition: 'Intimate relation'; a formal euphemism for sexual intercourse widely used in journalism, legal proceedings, and medical contexts to name sex without explicit language.
records.notes: Standard journalistic register for sexual intercourse in Brazilian news coverage of rape cases, affairs, and sexual health; can non-sexually denote a close personal relationship, but the sexual reading is strongly entrenched.

records.definition: 'Go to bed (with someone)'; a euphemistic idiom implying sexual intercourse by referencing movement to the bedroom rather than naming the act.
records.notes: Requires a complement ('ir para a cama com alguém') to carry the sexual meaning; the sexual reading is strong but not exclusive; understood universally across Brazilian age groups.

records.definition: 'Sleep together'; a euphemism for sexual intercourse implying a shared bed without explicitly naming the sexual activity.
records.notes: Direct parallel to English 'sleep together'; sexual meaning is inferred from the togetherness rather than the sleeping; universally understood in context; can occasionally be literal.

records.definition: 'They stayed/hooked up together'; indicates that two people had a casual romantic or sexual encounter, at minimum kissing but often implying further physical activity.
records.notes: 'Ficar' is distinctly Brazilian Portuguese usage for casual hookup (making out or more); 'ficaram juntos' is the past-tense form most used in third-party reports; the degree of sexual activity implied is deliberately ambiguous and varies by speaker age.

records.definition: 'To roll / to happen'; colloquial Brazilian Portuguese verb used as a vague euphemism for sexual activity occurring, with 'rolou' (past third-person) being the canonical form.
records.notes: 'Rolou' (it happened / something went down) is the most common conjugation in this sexual sense; can refer to anything from kissing to full intercourse; the deliberate ambiguity is central to its euphemistic function; also used for non-sexual events.

records.definition: The practice or culture of casual romantic and sexual encounters, typically kissing and light physical intimacy with strangers or acquaintances, especially at parties.
records.notes: Derives from the verb 'pegar' (to catch/grab someone romantically). In Brazil, pegação typically implies kissing and light intimacy but not necessarily intercourse; it describes the activity pattern rather than a single encounter. Foundational concept in Brazilian dating culture.

records.definition: To hook up with or make out with someone in a casual, non-committal way, typically implying kissing and light physical intimacy but not necessarily intercourse.
records.notes: 'Ficar' (to stay/remain) implies a brief, non-exclusive interaction explicitly distinguished from 'namorar' (to date seriously). This ficar/namorar distinction is culturally fundamental in Brazil. The phrase can encompass a range from kissing to sex depending on context and generation.

records.definition: To do that sexual thing; a deliberately vague idiom implying sexual activity without naming the act, requiring contextual inference.
records.notes: Elliptical phrase playing on 'dar,' which in Brazilian slang also means to be the receptive partner in sex. The vagueness is intentional; what 'aquela' (that thing) refers to is understood from context. Less fixed than other idioms in this set.

records.definition: A quickie; a brief, hastily conducted sexual encounter.
records.notes: Diminutive of 'rápida' (quick, feminine form), softening the crudeness through affectionate diminutive suffix. Extremely common and widely understood across all demographics and age groups.

records.definition: A sex work session; a commercial sexual encounter using the diminutive to soften or euphemize the transaction.
records.notes: 'Programa' is the standard Brazilian term for a sex work session ('fazer programa' = to turn a trick). The diminutive '-inha' makes it sound more innocent or casual. Primarily denotes commercial sex, though sometimes used loosely for any casual encounter.

records.definition: The wedding night; the first night of a married couple together, implying consummation of the marriage through sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Formal and literary in register; references the historical and religious requirement that marriage be consummated sexually. 'Núpcias' is a Latinate plural noun for nuptials, elevating the register of the phrase.

records.definition: Honeymoon; the period immediately following marriage associated with romantic and sexual intimacy between newlyweds.
records.notes: Literal calque of 'honeymoon.' Mapped to consummation as closest registry concept for post-marriage sexual context; the term is broader than consummation alone, encompassing the full honeymoon period. Universally known and carries no vulgarity whatsoever.

records.definition: To give oneself sexually; a reflexive euphemism for consenting to and engaging in sexual intercourse, typically framing the act from the receptive partner's perspective.
records.notes: Reflexive construction of 'dar' (to give). In Brazilian slang, 'dar' also means to be the receptive partner in sex, so 'dar-se' carries a gendered or receptive-role implication. The framing is culturally loaded regarding female sexual agency and surrender.

records.definition: She or he surrendered herself/himself sexually; a euphemism for yielding to sexual intercourse, often implying the first sexual experience or a morally significant act of capitulation.
records.notes: Past tense of 'entregar-se' (to surrender/hand oneself over). Appears frequently in mid-20th-century Brazilian literature and telenovelas to describe a woman's first sexual experience or moral 'fall.' The surrender framing places moral weight on the moment of sexual initiation.

records.definition: Got involved with someone; a neutral euphemism for entering into a sexual or romantic relationship.
records.notes: So mild it barely registers as a euphemism; the sexual implication is entirely contextual. No inherent vulgarity. Comparable to 'they became involved' in English. Usable in virtually any social context without offense.

records.definition: They got to know each other better; a playfully indirect way of saying two people had sex.
records.english_term: they got to know each other better
records.notes: Classic winking euphemism, fully transparent to any adult listener. No sexual vocabulary is used, making it functional in polite or mixed-audience contexts. The humor depends on the shared understanding that the phrase obviously means sex.

records.definition: They did dirty things; a euphemism for sexual activity that invokes the idea of sex as messy, transgressive, or naughty.
records.notes: Literal meaning is 'they made filth/dirt.' The framing of sex as 'sujeira' (filth) reflects a Catholic-adjacent cultural ambivalence about sexual pleasure. Slightly dated in urban usage; more common in older generations or rural and conservative speech communities.

records.definition: Sexual suggestiveness, naughtiness, or knowing wink; the quality of being playfully and sensually aware of sexual double meanings or innuendo.
records.notes: Unlike its English cognate, Brazilian 'malícia' is frequently a positive quality: the knowing, flirtatious sensuality associated with samba and capoeira. 'Ter malícia' (to have malícia) implies sophisticated erotic awareness. The word resists full English translation; 'naughtiness' loses the positive, culturally valorized dimension.

records.definition: Naughtiness or mischief; used euphemistically to refer to sexual play or transgressive behavior between adults, framing sex as playful rule-breaking.
records.notes: Primary meaning is childlike mischief or pranks; the sexual usage is a soft euphemism that frames adult sex as innocent playfulness. The childhood-vocabulary register makes it suitable for advertising, comedy, and affectionate teasing contexts.

records.definition: Adult play or adult games; a euphemism for sexual activity that frames sex as a form of play appropriate only for grown-ups.
records.notes: Compositional phrase rather than a fixed lexical item. 'Brincadeira' (play/game) is a childhood word applied to adult sex, creating a coy distancing effect. Widely understood; often deployed humorously. Can range from mild intimacy to explicit sex depending on context.

records.definition: Special affection or special tenderness; a euphemism for intimate physical attention that implies more than ordinary care or affection.
records.notes: 'Carinho' normally means gentle affection or a soft touch; adding 'especial' signals that what is being described exceeds ordinary caring. Extremely mild register. Often used in contexts where directness would be socially inappropriate, such as around children or in professional settings.

records.definition: To give that thing that one likes; a vague idiomatic phrase for providing sexual pleasure or engaging in a desired sexual act.
records.notes: Combines 'dar' (to give; also slang for receptive sex) with 'gostar' (to like/enjoy), creating a deliberately opaque pleasure-reference. Context-dependent and not a fixed idiom; recognition and interpretation vary by generation and region.

records.definition: To jump the fence; an idiomatic expression for committing adultery or cheating on a romantic partner.
records.notes: The fence metaphor frames fidelity as a physical boundary between permitted and forbidden territory. Functionally equivalent to 'trair' but far less direct; often used humorously or to soften the charge of infidelity. Widely understood across Brazil.

records.definition: To put horns on someone; the standard Brazilian idiom for cheating on a romantic partner, symbolically making them a cuckold.
records.notes: The horn-cuckold imagery is widespread across Romance and Mediterranean cultures. 'Botar' is a northeastern and informal Brazilian colloquial variant of 'pôr' (to put/place). The cheated partner becomes a 'cornudo' (horned one). Universally understood in Brazil; used colloquially without particular stigma around the speaker.

records.definition: To place horns on someone; synonymous with 'botar chifre,' meaning to betray a romantic partner through sexual infidelity.
records.notes: Same horn metaphor as 'botar chifre' with the more standard verb 'colocar' (to place). 'Colocar' is more prevalent in southern Brazil and more formal registers; 'botar' is more northeastern and colloquial. The two phrases are semantically interchangeable.

records.definition: To betray; the direct, unmarked Portuguese verb for cheating on a romantic or sexual partner.
records.notes: Standard Portuguese vocabulary, not slang. Unlike 'botar chifre,' 'trair' is the neutral, direct term for infidelity and appears freely in formal, legal, and literary contexts. Mapped to sexual_misbehavior as closest available concept; no registry slug covers romantic betrayal specifically.

records.definition: The act or pattern of betrayal and cheating in a relationship; a Brazilian internet-era noun derived from 'trair.'
records.notes: Neologism formed by adding the action/augmentative suffix '-agem' to the verb stem 'trair.' Emerged prominently in Brazilian social media and internet culture circa 2015–2019. Implies a habitual or dramatic pattern of betrayal rather than a single incident. Peak usage around 2017–2018; somewhat dated now but still understood.

records.definition: An affair; a secret or illicit romantic and sexual relationship conducted outside a primary commitment.
records.notes: 'Caso' literally means 'case' or 'matter.' In romantic/sexual context, 'ter um caso' (to have an affair) is the standard Brazilian euphemism for an extramarital or illicit relationship. The word's primary neutrality in other contexts makes it useful for discreet reference.

records.definition: An adventure; a casual or brief sexual encounter or fling, typically one-off and without expectation of ongoing commitment.
records.notes: Frames casual sex as exciting and exploratory rather than transgressive or shameful. Less loaded than 'caso' (affair), which implies ongoing betrayal; 'aventura' typically refers to a single exciting encounter. Can describe extramarital sex without implying the sustained emotional entanglement of 'caso.'

records.definition: To fornicate; to engage in sexual intercourse outside of marriage, carrying inherent moral-religious condemnation.
records.notes: Direct cognate of Latin 'fornicari' and equivalent to English 'fornicate.' Primarily used in religious preaching, theological texts, biblical translations, and literary or ironic contexts. Sounds pompous or deliberately archaic in everyday speech. Recognition remains fairly broad due to its appearance in Biblical Portuguese translations and Catholic discourse.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse between two people not married to each other; carries inherent religious and moral condemnation rooted in Catholic tradition.
records.notes: Direct cognate; predominantly used in religious and legal-moral discourse in Brazil given the country's Catholic heritage.

records.definition: Lewd, lascivious, or morally dissolute; the word simultaneously means physically slippery, a quality shared with the Latin root lubricus.
records.notes: Shares etymology with English 'lubricious' and 'lubricity'; the sexual and literal senses coexist in both languages; feminine form lúbrica.

records.definition: Lewdness or lasciviousness; the abstract quality of being lúbrico — sexually dissolute or morally slippery.
records.notes: Noun form of lúbrico; cognate with English 'lubricity'; uncommon in contemporary speech; found primarily in 19th-century literary and moralistic texts.

records.definition: A woman who cohabits with a man in a long-term intimate relationship outside legal marriage, holding lower social and legal status than a wife.
records.notes: Still recognized due to biblical and historical references; rarely deployed in contemporary social contexts outside religious or historical discourse.

records.definition: A woman living with a man outside of legal marriage; a common-law wife or kept woman; historically used in Brazilian legal and social contexts for the female partner in a consensual non-marital domestic union.
records.notes: More neutral than concubina in Brazilian usage; specifically implies cohabitation and a stable domestic arrangement outside wedlock rather than mere financial dependency or commercial sex; appeared in civil law contexts well into the 20th century.

records.definition: An archaic term for a kept woman, concubine, or mistress; a woman maintained by a man outside of marriage for sexual companionship.
records.notes: Feminine counterpart to mancebo; both terms were common in classical and early modern Portuguese literature; now almost exclusively encountered in historical texts.

records.definition: A young man; in archaic and literary contexts, specifically a young male lover, suitor, or rustic admirer; the masculine counterpart to manceba.
records.notes: In archaic usage can refer simply to any youth or to a male kept in a sexual arrangement; the feminine form manceba carries stronger sexual connotations than the masculine; found in pastoral and courtly literary traditions.

records.definition: Gross moral corruption and excessive indulgence in sexual licentiousness and dissolute behavior; the abstract noun form of devasso.
records.notes: The adjective devasso/devassa remains moderately current in Brazilian Portuguese; the abstract noun devassidão is more literary. Caution: devassa also means 'investigation' in legal contexts, creating a false-friend risk.

records.definition: The practice of libertinism; sexual and moral licentiousness; the condition of living outside moral restraint, especially in sexual matters.
records.notes: Corresponds to the abstract noun form of libertino; appears in literary, journalistic, and moral discourse; more current than its English cognate and still encountered in everyday Brazilian journalism.

records.definition: A person who freely pursues sexual pleasure without moral restraint; one who lives outside accepted moral codes, especially regarding sex.
records.notes: Direct cognate; used as both noun and adjective; feminine form libertina; still appears in literary criticism, journalism, and cultural commentary without being fully archaic.

records.definition: Dissolute; given over to sexual immorality and debauchery; morally unrestrained in sexual conduct.
records.notes: Direct cognate; feminine form dissoluta; used as adjective and occasionally noun; found in literary, religious, and journalistic registers; rare in casual contemporary speech.

records.definition: Relating to the physical body and its sexual appetites, especially as opposed to the spiritual; used in theological and literary contexts to designate sinful bodily desire.
records.notes: Direct cognate; in Brazilian Portuguese carnal also carries an everyday meaning of 'full sibling' (irmão carnal), requiring context to disambiguate the sexual from the kinship sense.

records.definition: Sexual licentiousness driven by libidinous impulses; the state of being governed by unrestrained sexual desire; archaic noun form related to libidinoso.
records.notes: Rare archaic noun; less common than related forms such as libidinoso (adj.) or lubricidade; primarily found in 19th-century literary texts; the adjective libidinoso remains marginally current.

records.definition: Vulva-to-vulva genital contact between two women, typically involving rhythmic friction; the formal clinical and historical term for the practice colloquially called tesoura (scissors) in Brazil.
records.notes: The everyday Brazilian slang tesoura has almost entirely displaced tribadismo in popular usage; the formal term persists in academic sexology and historical literature.

records.definition: In Brazilian archaic legal and moral usage, anal intercourse between men; historically used in the Penal Code to denote sexual acts committed against male minors; in classical usage, the Greek erotic tradition of adult male–adolescent relationships.
records.notes: The Brazilian Penal Code included 'pederastia qualificada' as a crime until the 1988 constitutional reform. In pejorative colloquial use the term was applied loosely against gay men. Semantic overlap between classical pederasty, sodomy, and child abuse creates substantial ambiguity across registers.

records.definition: Religious, legal, and historical term for anal intercourse or other non-procreative sexual acts condemned by the Catholic Church and encoded in early Brazilian colonial law.
records.notes: Direct cognate; attested extensively in Brazilian Inquisition records and colonial legislation; still used in conservative religious discourse and historical literature.

records.definition: A person who practices sodomy; historically used to condemn gay men; a term from religious and Inquisitional legal discourse derived from the biblical city of Sodom.
records.notes: Appears extensively in Brazilian Inquisition trial records; still deployed in conservative religious contexts as a condemnation of homosexuality.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; coitus; a Latinate archaic term for the sexual union between two persons.
records.notes: Extremely rare in contemporary Brazilian Portuguese; found in 18th–19th-century literary and legal texts; most educated Brazilians today would not recognize it without contextual support.

records.definition: Dated Brazilian slur for an effeminate gay man; implies excessive delicacy, fussiness, and gender non-conformity in addition to homosexuality.
records.notes: Fresco also means 'fresh' or 'cool' in standard Portuguese, a polysemy that allows it to pass under the radar in speech. Peak usage circa mid-20th century; still broadly understood but somewhat dated relative to current slurs.

records.definition: The abominable vice; a euphemistic phrase used in Portuguese Inquisitional and colonial legal texts to denote sodomy without naming the act directly.
records.notes: A formulaic Inquisitional euphemism; nefando means unspeakable or abominable; the phrase systematically avoided direct naming of the act. Found extensively in Brazilian Inquisition trial records from the 16th–18th centuries.

records.definition: The abominable act; a companion phrase to vício nefando, denoting a specific instance of sodomy in Inquisitional and colonial legal language, emphasizing the discrete act rather than the habitual vice.
records.notes: Like vício nefando, this is an Inquisitional euphemism for sodomy; the distinction between ato (act) and vício (vice) tracks whether a specific occurrence or a recurring behavioral pattern is being condemned. Both phrases recur in Brazilian Inquisition documentation.

records.definition: Archaic term for the institution of concubinage, the collective state of kept women, or a brothel; derived from the same root as mancebo and manceba.
records.notes: Polysemous: can mean (1) the social institution of keeping concubines, (2) the condition of being a manceba, or (3) a brothel. The brothel meaning was common in medieval and early modern Portuguese texts; the institutional meaning dominates in later literary usage.

records.definition: Mischievously naughty or slyly risqué in a playful, winking way; describes a person or behavior that is suggestively improper without being overtly vulgar.
records.notes: Carries a distinctively Brazilian quality of good-humored sexual teasing rooted in the malícia carioca tradition — a culturally admired knowing wit associated with Rio de Janeiro. Does not map cleanly to 'bawdy' since it implies charm and cleverness rather than crudeness; feminine form brejeira.

records.definition: A gallant; a man who courts or flatters women with charm and attentiveness; a romantic suitor or admirer who pursues women with gracious manners.
records.notes: Cognate with English 'gallant' and French 'galant'; in sharper contexts can shade toward philanderer; still used today in somewhat ironic or literary registers rather than being fully extinct.

records.definition: A courtesan; a high-status woman who provided sexual and social companionship to wealthy or powerful men in exchange for money, gifts, and patronage in historical contexts.
records.notes: Cognate with French courtisane; still recognized from historical fiction and literary contexts; not used for contemporary sex workers, for whom the register has shifted to sex workers or garotas de programa.

records.definition: Archaic literary term for a courtesan or prostitute, literally 'worldly woman,' evoking a woman immersed in secular, sensual life.
records.notes: From Latin mundanus (worldly); used in 19th–early 20th century Brazilian fiction and journalism as a genteel circumlocution for sex worker; the sexual meaning is now largely opaque to younger speakers.

records.definition: Archaic Portuguese term for a prostitute or sexually promiscuous woman, cognate with Spanish ramera.
records.notes: Folk etymology links it to ramo (branch), supposedly because women advertised brothels with branches at the door; used in classical Portuguese literature including Camões; largely unintelligible to modern Brazilians outside literary contexts.

records.definition: Primarily a fado singer or devotee; historically carried a secondary connotation of a bohemian woman of loose morals living at the margins of respectable society.
records.notes: The sexual implication derives from the disreputable associations of 19th-century Lisbon fado culture; in Brazil the term arrived through literature and carries almost no active sexual meaning today—recognition in a sexual sense is very low.

records.definition: Euphemistic phrase meaning 'woman of the life/streets,' used to refer to a prostitute or sex worker without naming the profession directly.
records.notes: Still widely understood across generations in Brazil; declining in active use as sex worker discourse shifts to 'profissional do sexo'; the phrase frames the profession as an entire life trajectory rather than a single act.

records.definition: Literally 'lost woman'; an archaic moral judgment applied to a woman who has had sex outside marriage or engaged in sex work, implying she is irreversibly ruined.
records.notes: Rooted in Brazilian Catholic honor-shame culture; the 'loss' is of virtue, not location—once applied, the label was considered permanent and social rehabilitation nearly impossible; more about shame than commercial sex work specifically.

records.definition: Archaic pejorative phrase meaning 'woman of bad life,' designating a prostitute or a woman of disreputable sexual morals.
records.notes: Stronger moral condemnation than 'mulher da vida'; common in 19th–20th century Brazilian police reports, court documents, and Catholic moral discourse; differs from 'mulher perdida' by emphasizing ongoing conduct rather than a singular fall.

records.definition: Nude or sexually explicit photographs of oneself, typically shared or requested digitally; direct English loanword fully assimilated into Brazilian internet Portuguese.
records.notes: Plural form used as a mass noun in pt-BR ('mandar nudes' = to send nudes); universal recognition across all demographics with internet access; appears in journalism, court cases, and sex education materials.

records.definition: A bundled collection of intimate, nude, or explicit photos and videos of one person, typically sold, traded, or leaked in Brazilian internet communities.
records.notes: Culturally specific usage: in pt-BR internet culture, 'pack' implies a curated set of content attributable to a single person, often sold via Telegram or distributed non-consensually; distinct from 'nudes' (individual images) by its bundled, commodified nature.

records.definition: To leak someone's intimate or nude images without their consent, typically as revenge or for social humiliation.
records.notes: 'Vazar' (to leak) applies broadly in Brazilian Portuguese; the phrase maps closely to the legal concept of 'exposição pornográfica não consensual' enshrined in Brazilian Law 13.718/2018; 'revenge porn' is the nearest English term but vazar nudes is neutral on motive.

records.definition: Sending sexually explicit text messages, images, or videos via mobile device; English loanword used unchanged in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Entered pt-BR circa 2010 with smartphone proliferation; used in journalism, sex education campaigns, and legal contexts; fully assimilated with no Portuguese phonological adaptation.

records.definition: A screenshot of an intimate, sexual, or personal conversation, photo, or video message, often shared without the subject's consent.
records.notes: 'Print' = screenshot (from 'print screen'); 'íntimo' = intimate; the phrase is itself neutral but appears most frequently in non-consensual sharing contexts; distinct from 'nudes' in being a screenshot rather than an original image.

records.definition: Euphemistic label for sexually explicit material; the Brazilian Portuguese equivalent of 'adult content,' used by platforms, creators, and media to avoid explicit terminology.
records.notes: Corporate and journalistic register; functions as a polite shield word covering everything from mild nudity to hardcore pornography; universally understood as a euphemism.

records.definition: Brazilian shorthand for OnlyFans; used as a noun for the platform or metonymically for online sexual content creation as a profession.
records.notes: 'Tem um Only' (has an Only) or 'faz Only' (does Only) signals that a person creates and sells explicit content online; the abbreviation is so common that 'Only' alone is understood in context without the full brand name.

records.definition: Literally 'creates content'; Brazilian internet euphemism for producing and selling explicit sexual material online, typically via subscription platforms.
records.notes: Functions as a socially legible euphemism understood by all internet users; the phrase is grammatically a third-person singular verb phrase used attributively ('ela cria conteúdo' = she does sex work online); plausible deniability in polite contexts.

records.definition: Live streaming session; in sexual contexts, a real-time webcam performance for a paying or subscribing audience.
records.notes: 'Live' in pt-BR can refer to any live stream (gaming, music, talk), not inherently sexual; the sexual meaning is context-dependent ('fazer uma live' on an adult platform); one of the most widely used English loanwords in Brazilian internet Portuguese.

records.definition: The device or the profession; in Brazilian internet slang, refers to the practice of performing sexually for pay via live video stream.
records.notes: Dual meaning as both the physical device and the sex work practice; 'trabalhar de webcam' (to work via webcam) or 'modelo de webcam' are common formations; predates OnlyFans-era vocabulary and now coexists with newer terms.

records.definition: Shortened form of webcam; refers to webcam sex work or the performer engaged in it.
records.notes: More subculture-internal than 'webcam'; used in compounds ('camgirl,' 'camboy,' 'fazer cam'); largely understood by Brazilian internet users but less transparent to older or offline demographics.

records.definition: Older, typically wealthy man who provides financial support or gifts to a younger partner in exchange for companionship and sexual access; English loanword used unchanged.
records.notes: Widely recognized across Brazilian social media; pronounced with Portuguese phonetics by many speakers; associated specifically with apps such as SeekingArrangement (known in Brazil as 'aplicativo de sugar').

records.definition: A younger person who receives money, gifts, or lifestyle support from a wealthier older partner in exchange for companionship and typically sexual access.
records.notes: Female-coded in most Brazilian discourse but applies to any gender; heavily covered in Brazilian lifestyle journalism and true-crime content about exploitation within sugar relationships.

records.definition: Shorthand for the sugar dating lifestyle or arrangement, in which financial support is exchanged for companionship and sexual access.
records.notes: Used both as a noun ('entrar no sugar') and modifier ('mundo sugar,' 'relacionamento sugar'); functions as an umbrella covering both the daddy and baby roles and the culture itself; more abstract than 'sugar daddy' or 'sugar baby.'

records.definition: An illicit or secret romantic and/or sexual relationship, especially extramarital; English loanword used unchanged in Brazilian Portuguese.
records.notes: Used as a more sophisticated or cosmopolitan alternative to native 'caso'; implies mutual romantic entanglement rather than pure sexual opportunism; common in Brazilian social media discourse about infidelity.

records.definition: A lover, especially a secret or extramarital one; a person with whom one has a clandestine romantic or sexual relationship outside a primary partnership.
records.notes: Native Portuguese word, fully active in modern Brazilian usage; gender-neutral grammatically but socially marks both male and female lovers equally; placed in internet_subculture section due to high-volume infidelity discourse on social media, though the word itself predates the internet by centuries.

records.definition: Augmentative of 'amigo' (friend); in internet slang, a male friend who is also a casual sexual partner, i.e., a friend with benefits.
records.notes: The augmentative -ão softens and slightly ironizes the implication of sexual involvement; the term implies ongoing casualness rather than a single encounter; the female equivalent in context is typically 'amiga' or 'amigona'; recognition in this specific sexual sense is lower than recognition of the word amigão in general.

records.definition: A secret or illicit ongoing romantic and/or sexual relationship; the quintessential Brazilian Portuguese word for an affair, especially extramarital.
records.notes: Literally 'case' or 'situation'; 'ter um caso' (to have a case/affair) is the standard colloquial construction; implies duration and emotional investment beyond a one-night encounter; older and more native-feeling than 'affair' or 'fling'; universally understood by all Brazilian Portuguese speakers.

records.definition: A brief, casual romantic and/or sexual relationship without commitment; English loanword used in Brazilian Portuguese social media and dating app contexts.
records.notes: Less widespread than 'caso' or 'affair'; used mainly by younger Brazilians with strong English exposure; implies short duration and lightness rather than secrecy; coexists with native alternatives like 'ficada' (hookup) and 'rolo' (short fling).

records.definition: Diminutive of 'gostosa'; a cute or sexy woman, used flirtatiously or as mild objectification.
records.notes: Diminutive suffix '-inha' softens the term relative to 'gostosa', layering cuteness onto sexual attractiveness; can be affectionate or objectifying depending on context.

records.definition: A strikingly beautiful and desirable woman treated as an idealized object of collective admiration and desire, often a celebrity or influencer.
records.notes: Literary origin ('muse') repurposed in Brazilian internet culture to denote an admired female figure with implicit sexual desirability; applied to models, influencers, and fitness personalities.

records.definition: Colloquial term for a physically attractive person; 'gata' (female) and 'gato' (male) are both widely used.
records.notes: Literally 'cat'; one of the most universally understood attractiveness terms in Brazilian Portuguese across all ages and regions.

records.definition: An exceptionally attractive and desirable person, typically a woman, likened to a sweet bonbon candy.
records.notes: Playful food metaphor; slightly more dated compared to 'gata' in current internet slang but still in active circulation.

records.definition: Colloquial term for an older person — man or woman — who is sexually attractive or romantically involved with someone younger.
records.notes: Literally 'crown'; gender-neutral in Portuguese, unlike English 'cougar' which is female-only. Can refer to an attractive older man (equivalent to 'silver fox') or older woman.

records.definition: Mature, older person regarded as sexually attractive; used both colloquially and as a pornographic category label equivalent to English 'mature.'
records.notes: 'Madura' maps roughly to MILF; 'maduro' to DILF. Widely used as pornographic content category labels in Brazilian adult media, borrowed directly from the English 'mature' category.

records.definition: Collective noun for sexually lewd acts, sexual debauchery, or a sexually charged environment; derived from 'puta' (whore).
records.notes: Can carry positive connotations in Brazilian internet culture where sexual openness is celebrated; simultaneously deployed as criticism of moral laxity. Extremely high frequency on Brazilian social media.

records.definition: Lewdness, naughtiness, or sexually inappropriate behavior; derived from 'safado' (dirty or naughty person).
records.notes: Unlike English 'lewdness', can be used approvingly in flirtatious contexts. The root 'safado/safada' is frequently used as a term of affectionate endearment between partners.

records.definition: Sexual misbehavior, naughty sexual acts, or illicit sexual activity; also used broadly for any dirty trick or unfair behavior.
records.notes: One of the most semantically versatile Brazilian slang terms; spans from mild mischief to explicit sexual acts depending on context, matching the registry definition precisely.

records.definition: Content rating label indicating material suitable only for adults aged 18 and over, typically signaling sexually explicit or otherwise inappropriate content.
records.notes: Used identically to English '18+' across Brazilian social media, streaming platforms, and online communities; universally understood.

records.definition: Sexually explicit; used to label or describe content depicting sexual acts without censorship or euphemism.
records.notes: Cognate from Latin via Portuguese; used in both clinical and internet content-classification contexts. In online use, often paired with 'conteúdo explícito' (explicit content).

records.definition: English loanword for hardcore sexually explicit content showing penetrative sex and genitalia without censorship, contrasted with 'soft.'
records.notes: Part of a binary 'hard/soft' taxonomy borrowed from English adult content categorization; used among Brazilian internet and adult content communities to label content intensity.

records.definition: English loanword for softcore sexual content: sexually suggestive or partially nude material that stops short of explicit penetrative depiction.
records.notes: Paired with 'hard' as a binary content-level taxonomy borrowed from English; used in Brazilian social media content labeling and OnlyFans-adjacent discourse.

records.definition: Japanese animated or illustrated pornography, used in Brazil identically to English internet usage.
records.notes: Japanese loanword adopted via English internet culture; widely recognized among Brazilian youth with heavy internet use, especially in anime and gaming communities.

records.definition: Abbreviation of Rule 34: the internet adage that pornographic content exists for any conceivable subject, character, or object.
records.notes: Used identically to English internet subculture; recognition concentrated among gaming, anime, and imageboard communities in Brazil. Often appears as a hashtag or comment.

records.definition: Acronym for 'Not Safe For Work'; content warning tag indicating sexually explicit or otherwise inappropriate material.
records.notes: Used untranslated in Brazilian internet communities; recognition skews toward younger, internet-native demographics with English exposure.

records.definition: Mixed-language phrase referring to the act of sending or receiving nude photographs via direct message.
records.notes: Code-switched phrase mixing English 'DM' (direct message) and 'nudes'; functions as both noun phrase and verb phrase in Brazilian internet discourse.

records.definition: Brazilian Portuguese phrase meaning 'asks for nudes'; the act of requesting nude photographs from someone via digital messaging.
records.notes: Mixes Portuguese 'pede' (asks/requests) with English 'nudes'; frequently appears in discussions of digital sexual solicitation, harassment, and boundary violations.

records.definition: Mixed-language imperative phrase meaning 'send nudes'; a request or command to transmit nude photographs via digital messaging.
records.notes: Peaked as a widespread internet meme around 2016–2017 alongside the English original; still in active use but has receded from peak meme saturation.

records.definition: Brazilian Portuguese phrase meaning 'slide into my DMs'; an invitation to send a private message, typically with romantic or sexual intent.
records.notes: Mixes Portuguese 'coloca' (put/place) with English acronym 'DM'; romantic or sexual intent is conveyed contextually rather than explicitly stated.

records.definition: A person one has a strong romantic or sexual attraction toward, or the feeling of that attraction itself; used identically to English.
records.notes: Direct English loanword fully integrated into Brazilian Portuguese youth vernacular; understood across virtually all demographics with internet access.

records.definition: A romantic or sexual relationship conducted primarily through digital channels, typically outside one's primary partnership.
records.notes: Calque mixing English 'affair' (used untranslated) with Portuguese 'digital'; the modifier specifies the online-mediated nature of the infidelity, distinguishing it from a traditional in-person affair.

records.definition: An undefined or ambiguous romantic and/or sexual involvement with someone; neither purely friendship nor a formal relationship.
records.notes: Literally 'involvement'; widely used in Brazilian social media to describe undefined romantic entanglements without labels. Broader and vaguer than the English 'situationship'.

records.definition: Acronym for 'filho da puta' (son of a whore); a strong general-purpose Brazilian expletive and insult for a contemptible person.
records.notes: The acronym form allows the phrase to circulate in censored or semi-public contexts. 'Puta' (whore) makes it nominally harsher than English 'son of a bitch'; one of the most universally recognized Brazilian Portuguese insults.

records.definition: Slang for a disappointing or unsatisfying sexual experience, or more broadly anything lame, boring, or a waste of time.
records.notes: Literally 'straw'; metaphorically extended to mean anything dull or worthless. In sexual context specifically denotes anticlimactic or skill-less sex. Also used outside sexual contexts for general disappointment with no direct English single-word equivalent.

records.definition: To act like a horndog or sexually forward person; to perform a flirtatiously lewd, naughty persona in social interaction.
records.english_term: to act like a perv / to play the horndog
records.notes: 'Safado' means sexually naughty, shameless, or dirty-minded; 'dar uma de' means to put on the persona of. Used playfully or self-deprecatingly, rarely purely pejorative.

records.definition: Sexual catfishing; creating or using a false online identity to deceive someone into a romantic or sexual relationship.
records.notes: 'Catfish' is borrowed directly from English internet slang; the compound 'catfish sexual' adds the explicit sexual motivation to distinguish it from non-romantic identity fraud.

records.definition: Digital sexual harassment; a pattern of unwanted sexual attention, messages, explicit images, or coercive advances conducted via online platforms or messaging apps.
records.notes: 'Assédio' means harassment; the registry concept is person-focused while this term names the act or pattern of behavior. Usage has risen sharply alongside #MeToo-adjacent discourse in Brazil since 2017.

records.definition: To hook up with someone in a non-committed encounter, typically involving kissing and making out and sometimes more; the foundational verb of Brazilian casual-dating culture.
records.english_term: to hook up / to make out
records.notes: Literally 'to stay/remain' but the sexual usage is ubiquitous. The defining feature is absence of romantic commitment, not the specific physical act, which can range from a kiss to full sex depending on context.

records.definition: A hookup session; a single instance of ficando — a non-committed romantic-sexual encounter typically spanning kissing to light sexual activity.
records.notes: Noun form of 'ficar.' 'Tivemos uma ficada' = 'we hooked up once.' Carries no implication of a continuing relationship. Less crude in feel than the English 'hookup.'

records.definition: A non-committed hookup partner; someone one makes out with or hooks up with regularly but without romantic commitment or exclusivity.
records.notes: Not necessarily a friend first, unlike the FWB connotation. The relationship is defined by mutual ficadas with no strings. More explicitly non-committal than most FWB framings in English.

records.definition: A hookup partner with explicitly negotiated zero commitment; a ficante arrangement where both parties have verbally confirmed the no-strings-attached terms.
records.notes: 'Sem compromisso' = 'without commitment,' a phrase that recurs across many Brazilian social contexts. The redundancy over plain 'ficante' signals that at least one party wanted to formally foreclose expectations.

records.definition: Past-tense idiom meaning someone hooked up with another person; the standard way to report a completed ficar encounter.
records.notes: 'Ela ficou com o João na festa' = 'She hooked up with João at the party.' The phrase is so ubiquitous it functions almost as a grammatical construction rather than slang.

records.definition: Succeeded in finding a romantic or sexual partner for the night; 'got with someone' at a social event.
records.notes: Literally 'arranged/found someone.' Very mild in register; emphasizes the social outcome of finding a partner over any physical act. Context determines whether this implies a kiss, a full hookup, or just someone's phone number.

records.definition: The act, practice, or ambient culture of casual hookups and making out; the general pursuit of non-committed physical encounters at parties or social events.
records.notes: Nominalization of 'pegar.' 'Muita pegação nessa festa' = 'lots of hooking up at this party.' Can name one event's atmosphere or the broader Brazilian social phenomenon. Slightly more physically charged in connotation than the ficar family.

records.definition: To hook up with someone; to make out with or have sexual contact with a person, typically in a casual, non-committed encounter.
records.english_term: to hook up with / to pull
records.notes: Literally 'to catch/grab.' More assertive in physical connotation than 'ficar'; can cover a kiss through full sex depending on context. 'Consegui pegar ela' = 'I managed to hook up with her.' One of the most versatile sexual slang verbs in Brazilian Portuguese.

records.definition: To fail to hook up at a party or social event; to strike out and go home without a partner after attempting pegação.
records.english_term: to strike out / to go home empty-handed
records.notes: Literally 'to spin/rotate,' evoking the image of circling the venue all night without success. Opposite of 'pegar' in outcome. No registry concept covers this failure-to-hookup meaning specifically; concept slug denotes the same domain with the negative outcome flagged here.

records.definition: To successfully pull or attract someone into a hookup; to 'drag' a target into a romantic-sexual encounter, emphasizing the active triumph of the seduction.
records.english_term: to pull / to score / to drag someone home
records.notes: Literally 'to drag/pull.' Implies the pursuer's effort and the target being drawn along. More emphatic about conquest than 'pegar'; the metaphor foregrounds the pursuer's agency.

records.definition: To hook someone romantically or sexually; to attract and land a partner through charm or calculated seduction, invoking the fishing metaphor of setting a hook.
records.notes: Literally 'to hook' (as in fishing). Frames the target as a fish and the pursuer as an angler. More playful and strategic in connotation than 'arrastar'; implies patient technique over brute persistence.

records.definition: To hit on someone; to make direct romantic or sexual advances toward a person in a persistent or obvious manner.
records.english_term: to hit on / to come on to
