records.notes: Literally 'to give on top of.' The single most standard Brazilian expression for making advances. Universally understood across all generations, regions, and registers.

records.definition: A pickup line or flirtatious verbal approach; a charm offensive directed at someone to signal romantic or sexual interest.
records.notes: From 'cantar' (to sing), historically evoking a troubadour's serenade. A cantada can be a single witty opener or a sustained conversational approach. Not inherently crude; tone ranges from sweet to sleazy depending on content.

records.definition: A heavy, forceful, or sexually overt pickup advance; a come-on that escalates beyond playful flirting into direct or pressuring sexual solicitation.
records.notes: 'Pesada' = heavy/intense. Frames the advance as more pressuring and sexual than a standard cantada; can border on harassment depending on context and delivery. The compound is descriptive rather than pejorative per se.

records.definition: A dirty or sexually explicit pickup line; a come-on whose content is overtly vulgar, licentious, or lewd rather than merely forward.
records.notes: 'Safada' (fem. of safado) = dirty/naughty/perverted. Characterizes both the moral register of the approach and implicitly the character of its deliverer. More about explicit content than forcefulness — contrasts with cantada pesada which is about intensity.

records.definition: Seduction talk; the verbal game or smooth conversational approach deployed to attract and seduce a potential partner.
records.notes: 'Papo' = chat/talk; 'sedução' = seduction. Foregrounds the verbal and performative dimension of seduction rather than physical escalation. Sometimes used admiringly to describe someone with unusually effective social charisma.

records.definition: Flirting; playful, light romantic-sexual banter and mutual attention exchanged between two people who are attracted to each other, without overt pressure.
records.notes: One of the most culturally central terms in Brazilian romantic vocabulary. Lighter and more reciprocal than a cantada; paquera implies mutual enjoyment rather than one-sided pressure. Also used as a noun for the flirting stage of a courtship.

records.definition: Actively flirting; present-participle form indicating someone is currently in the middle of a paquera exchange with another person.
records.english_term: flirting with / hitting it off with
records.notes: Progressive form of 'paquerar.' 'Ele está paquerando a colega' = 'He's flirting with his colleague.' Slightly more dynamic and ongoing than the noun 'paquera'; the gerund marks the act as actively in progress.

records.definition: Flirting; a romantic-sexual verbal or behavioral exchange signaling attraction, borrowed directly from English.
records.notes: Direct loanword from English 'flirt/flirtation.' Slightly more deliberate or adult in register than 'paquera' and more common in print journalism and social media commentary on romantic dynamics. The loanword status gives it a mildly cosmopolitan or modern feel.

records.definition: Sexually worked up, frisky, or in a state of restless flirtatious arousal; describes someone who is visibly amorous, agitated, and eager for romantic or sexual attention.
records.notes: Gendered adjective (masc./fem. forms given). Literally relates to being ruffled or agitated, applied to humans and animals alike. The behavioral restlessness is as central as the arousal; it implies the person is acting on or displaying their excitement, not merely feeling it internally.

records.definition: To make a move on someone; to approach a person with romantic or sexual intent, typically implying boldness or cooperative social effort.
records.english_term: to make a move / to step to someone
records.notes: Literally 'to come alongside/together.' Used both for an individual making a solo move and, in youth slang influenced by AAVE, for friends coordinating to help one of them hook up. Less aggressive in connotation than 'dar em cima'; implies smooth confidence rather than overt pressure.

records.definition: To use a subtle, indirect, or flattering approach to seduce someone; to ease in romantically 'under the radar' through ingratiation rather than direct advance.
records.english_term: to play it cool / to ease in / to butter someone up
records.notes: Literally 'to come from below.' Contrasts strategically with a direct cantada: the pursuer uses compliments, small favors, and gradual escalation to lower the target's guard. Carries a mildly manipulative connotation — the indirectness is calculated, not shy.

records.definition: The act of first vaginal penetration of a woman, historically central to Brazilian honor culture and codified as a criminal offense in the 1940 Penal Code.
records.notes: Artigo 218 of the 1940 Código Penal criminalized defloramento; the term framed virginity as patrilineal property whose loss constituted harm to the family; the offense was removed from the code in 2005 but the cultural concept persists in religious and conservative discourse.

records.definition: To deflower a woman; to have first penetrative sex with a virgin, framed as an act of dispossession within the Brazilian honor economy.
records.notes: Verb form of defloração; carries the same legal and honor-economy freight; now archaic in everyday usage but still appears in literary, religious, and conservative legal contexts.

records.definition: Latin-derived clinical and forensic term for defloration, used in historical Brazilian medical jurisprudence and colonial-era legal texts.
records.notes: The Latin orthographic form appearing in 19th- and early 20th-century Brazilian forensic medicine and legal scholarship that cited French and Latin sources verbatim; less common than the Portuguese form defloração in everyday or modern legal usage.

records.definition: The emblematic Brazilian archetype of a charming, street-smart man who lives by his wits, avoids honest labor, and seduces women, celebrated in samba and working-class Rio culture.
records.notes: No English concept captures the full malandro: seduction is inseparable from cunning, glamorized idleness, and class position; theorized by anthropologist Roberto DaMatta as structurally central to Brazilian social navigation; the malandro moves between official society and the street through charm rather than compliance.

records.definition: The ethos, lifestyle, and skill set of the malandro: seductive charm, social cunning, flexible ethics, and the use of sexual conquest as social currency.
records.notes: Abstract noun of malandro; encompasses a worldview where seduction and cunning replace honest labor as survival strategies; DaMatta and others have analyzed it as a macro-level feature of Brazilian social relations, not merely a personal trait.

records.definition: A man who courts women through flowery compliments, flattery, and gallant gestures; a charmer relying on verbal courtship rather than crude pursuit.
records.notes: From galante (gallant); softer and more genteel than other terms in this section; associated with old-fashioned verbal courtship rather than sexual conquest; increasingly dated but still understood by older speakers.

records.definition: A man who sexually conquers many women, framing seduction as military conquest; a serial womanizer with a dominant, predatory self-image.
records.notes: Deliberately evokes the colonial-era conquistadors; the conquest metaphor is central — sex as territorial domination; slightly more aggressive and martial in connotation than sedutor; can be self-applied with pride within male peer culture.

records.definition: A seducer; a man who attracts and draws in women through charm, magnetism, or manipulation.
records.notes: The most neutral and widely applicable term in this cluster; functions as noun or adjective (olhar sedutor = seductive gaze); can carry mild admiration or mild condemnation depending on context.

records.definition: A man who successfully picks up women for casual sex; the quintessential Brazilian pickup artist, admired within male peer culture for sexual skill and social desirability.
records.notes: From pegar (to catch/get), which also functions as sexual slang for hooking up; ubiquitous in Brazilian youth slang; overwhelmingly positive within male peer groups, implying skill rather than moral condemnation.

records.definition: A man who habitually pursues and chases women; a womanizer defined by compulsive, ingrained interest in female sexual conquest.
records.notes: The -engo suffix implies habitual, entrenched behavior; slightly dated but widely understood; can be mildly pejorative or humorously affectionate depending on context.

records.definition: A man who obsessively pursues many women sexually; a more emphatic and crude synonym for mulherengo implying near-professional dedication to female pursuit.
records.notes: The -eiro suffix implies a person defined by an activity at professional or obsessive-level engagement; slightly cruder and more emphatic than mulherengo; the two terms are near-synonyms but mulhereiro carries a stronger edge of excess.

records.definition: A serial seducer modeled on the literary archetype; a man who habitually pursues and abandons women after conquest.
records.notes: Borrowed from the Spanish/Portuguese literary tradition via Tirso de Molina; the hyphenated form is standard in Brazilian Portuguese; implies a pattern of seduction followed by abandonment more explicitly than other terms in this cluster.

records.definition: A wealthy, idle, fashionable young man who pursues sexual pleasure; in Brazil specifically connotes upper-class privilege combined with sexual promiscuity and contemptuous ease.
records.notes: The Brazilian usage adds a strong class dimension absent in the English original — a Brazilian playboy is not just sexually active but specifically privileged and idle; this class-based connotation is a locally distinctive feature not carried by the English term or the Playboy brand.

records.definition: A person who is sexually shameless, morally unrestrained, and lasciviously forward; depending on tone and relationship, either an insult or a playful term of sexual admiration.
records.notes: One of the most versatile sexual insult/compliments in Brazilian Portuguese; 'que safado!' from a romantic partner typically signals approving arousal, while the same phrase from a stranger is a moral accusation; the dual valence (admiration vs. condemnation) is culturally encoded and entirely context-dependent; etymologically from safar (to wear out the bottom).

records.definition: A person who is boldly, recklessly sexual and morally unrestrained; typically used admiringly to imply sexual daring and prowess rather than moral condemnation.
records.notes: Literally 'damned one'; softer and more playful than safado; in sexual contexts typically implies desirable boldness rather than predatory behavior; widely used in expressions like 'esse cara é danado' to admire someone's sexual confidence and daring.

records.definition: Adjective describing Don Juan-like behavior or personal style: charming, manipulative, dedicated to the seduction and ultimate abandonment of women.
records.notes: Primarily literary register; rarely used in casual speech; found in journalism and literary criticism to characterize a behavioral type rather than as a direct personal label; lower recognition reflects its restricted register.

records.definition: A crude, boorish, and stupid person who makes sexually offensive or clumsy advances; the antithesis of the smooth malandro.
records.notes: General insult for uncouthness and stupidity; placed in this section as the negative counterpart to malandro archetypes — the boçal pursues women in an offensive, unsubtle, and unappealing manner that signals social failure and the absence of malandro-style charm.

records.definition: In a state of restless, agitated sexual excitement; overly frisky, flirtatious, or sexually worked up to the point of pushy or distracted pursuit.
records.notes: From assanhar (to provoke, stir up); applies to men or women; implies a sexually charged restlessness that manifests as flirtatious behavior, fidgeting, or inappropriate pursuit; can be self-referential and humorous ('tô assanhada hoje' = I'm feeling frisky today).

records.definition: A sexually dominant man who fucks many women; 'one who inserts,' valorized within male peer culture for sexual frequency and conquest.
records.notes: From meter (to put in/insert), a common Brazilian slang verb for penetrative sex from the male-dominant perspective; more mechanically crude and action-focused than pegador; implies high volume of sexual activity rather than seductive finesse.

records.definition: A serial pickup artist; a man who systematically and repeatedly picks up women for casual sex as a persistent, pattern-based behavioral mode.
records.notes: Modern compound borrowing 'serial' (English loanword) applied to pegador; emphasizes the systematic and compulsive repetition of casual sexual acquisition; more prevalent in online discourse than in speech.

records.definition: A man who fucks many women; 'one who eats,' valorizing aggressive, high-volume sexual conquest through the Brazilian slang verb comer.
records.notes: From comer (to eat), the most widespread Brazilian slang verb for male-dominant penetrative sex; comer implies the man as sexual agent consuming the woman as object, encoding an explicitly asymmetric power dynamic; comedor is its agentive nominalization, more action-crude than metedor.

records.definition: The sexually licentious debauchery of Brazilian Carnival; the temporally bounded, culturally sanctioned, and collectively celebrated suspension of ordinary sexual norms during Carnival season.
records.notes: Putaria (from puta = whore) means sexual chaos or licentiousness; the compound de carnaval frames it as ritually bounded and socially authorized — unlike 'debauchery' in English, putaria de carnaval is not morally condemned but anticipated, organized, and celebrated as an annual institution, making it conceptually distinct from ordinary excess.

records.definition: Wild Carnival revelry encompassing music, dance, costumes, and sexual liberality; the festive chaos in which normal social and sexual constraints are suspended.
records.notes: From Portuguese/Spanish folia (folly, madness); entrar na folia means to join the festivity and release inhibitions; while not exclusively sexual, folia is culturally understood to encompass sexual liberation; the mapping to 'debauchery' is approximate — debauchery implies moral failure whereas folia implies celebratory communal freedom.

records.definition: A sexually energetic, flirtatious young woman who embodies the free-spirited and physically uninhibited essence of frevo, the acrobatic Carnival dance of Pernambuco.
records.notes: Diminutive of frevo, the syncopated Carnival dance-music of Recife and Olinda; frevinha as a sexual archetype is primarily a northeastern Brazil cultural reference; the concept of a regionally specific Carnival dancer embodying sexual freedom and playfulness has no English equivalent; recognition is limited largely to northeastern Brazil and Carnival enthusiasts.

records.definition: The publicly displayed nude body during Carnival; the erotic exhibition of nakedness as a culturally celebrated act of sexual liberation and collective spectacle.
records.notes: Literally 'naked body'; in the Carnival context public nudity is a site of erotic display and liberation rather than moral offense; the phrase appears in both celebratory Carnival discourse and in older legal and censorship debates about public nudity; maps approximately to exhibitionism as the concept of erotic public bodily display, though the consensual and celebratory framing differs from clinical exhibitionism.

records.definition: A person who has sexually or morally deviated from accepted norms; the dominant Catholic-influenced term used to condemn non-normative sexuality, especially homosexuality.
records.notes: Core term of mid-20th-century Catholic and state-medical discourse condemning homosexuality in Brazil; persists in conservative religious and family contexts; 'desviado do caminho de Deus' (deviated from God's path) is a common phrasing.

records.definition: A morally corrupt or sexually deviant person; implies near-satanic corruption of divinely ordained natural order in Catholic theological framing.
records.notes: Functions as both adjective and noun; the theological sense of corruption of natural law is more salient in Brazilian use than in secular English; commonly applied to paedophiles, gay men, and kink practitioners in conservative discourse.

records.definition: Morally transgressive, especially in sexual conduct; used in Catholic-influenced Brazilian discourse to condemn any sexuality outside marriage or Church teaching.
records.notes: Applied broadly in conservative Brazilian contexts to homosexuality, premarital sex, divorce, and contraception; near-universal recognition across generations; frequently deployed in political speech against LGBTQ+ rights.

records.definition: Sexually or socially offensive behavior that violates public decency norms; used in both religious and legal registers in Brazil.
records.notes: Appears in Brazilian Penal Code provisions on obscenity and indecency (art. 233); also ubiquitous in everyday Catholic-influenced moral speech about dress, language, or public conduct.

records.definition: Sexually explicit or grossly offensive material or behavior lacking redeeming value; used in both legal and moral-religious discourse.
records.notes: Standard orthography is 'obsceno'; 'obceno' is a common popular variant reflecting phonological simplification. Used in Brazilian criminal law (Código Penal art. 234) and everyday moral condemnation alike.

records.definition: Lacking decorum and sexual or social propriety; a more formal and elevated synonym of indecente, typically applied to public conduct or dress that shocks bourgeois sensibility.
records.notes: Higher register than indecente; more common in written or institutional contexts; recognition has declined somewhat among younger speakers who prefer more colloquial terms; carries class inflection beyond purely religious condemnation.

records.definition: Treating the sacred with irreverence; in sexual contexts, engaging in carnal acts that desecrate the God-given body or violate religious sanctity.
records.notes: In Brazilian Catholic framing, sexuality outside marriage is profano because it desecrates the body as temple of the Holy Spirit; the sacred/secular binary carries more active doctrinal weight in Brazilian use than in secular English; the English 'profane' has weakened considerably in everyday usage.

records.definition: A distinct Brazilian gender identity of feminine-presenting individuals assigned male at birth who typically maintain their male genitalia and self-identify within a culturally specific category separate from the Western transgender woman concept.
records.notes: Not equivalent to transvestite (cross-dresser) or transgender woman; travesti is a recognized sui generis category in Brazilian sociology and trans activism with its own political organizations and community history predating Western transgender discourse in Brazil; the identity carries specific class and racialized dimensions tied to street sex work and carnaval culture.

records.definition: The practice or clinical condition of cross-dressing; in Brazilian psychiatric and legal usage also loosely applied to the travesti lifestyle and identity.
records.notes: Clinical borrowing from European psychiatry; largely superseded in community discourse by identity-affirming language; still appears in Brazilian legal and psychiatric documents; conflation with travesti identity is contested and considered reductive by travesti activists.

records.definition: Highly offensive derogatory slur for a travesti or trans woman; the pejorative augmentative-disparaging suffix -eco intensifies contempt and dehumanization.
records.notes: The -eco suffix in Brazilian Portuguese commonly marks ugliness, contempt, or poor quality (livreco = bad book); strongly rejected by travesti and trans communities; widely used in hostile street speech, police violence contexts, and hate crimes targeting travestis.

records.definition: In Brazilian travesti and drag culture, the state of being fully assembled in feminine presentation — makeup, wig, clothing, and accessories all in place; from montar (to assemble or mount).
records.notes: No direct English equivalent; in drag contexts approximates 'in full drag' or 'serving full beat,' but montada in travesti discourse also describes everyday feminine identity presentation rather than theatrical performance exclusively; the antonym is desmontada (disassembled, out of femme presentation).

records.definition: A performer who transforms between gender presentations on stage; a broadly neutral term for drag and gender-transformation artists that predates drag queen as the dominant label in Brazil.
records.notes: Older and more neutral than drag queen; covers theatrical transformistas who may or may not identify as trans or gay; usage has declined among younger audiences in favor of the English loanword drag queen; historically tied to boate (nightclub) culture in Brazilian cities.

records.definition: English loanword fully integrated into Brazilian Portuguese; a person who performs exaggerated femininity through elaborate makeup, wigs, costumes, and live entertainment.
records.notes: Used without phonological modification in Brazilian speech; popularized through RuPaul's Drag Race (widely watched with Portuguese subtitles) and homegrown Brazilian drag competitions; near-universal recognition across age groups post-2015.

records.definition: English loanword; a person, typically a woman or non-binary person, who performs exaggerated masculinity through costume, prosthetic facial hair, and performance art.
records.notes: Significantly less well-known in Brazil than drag queen; recognition concentrated among LGBTQ+-adjacent audiences; gaining visibility through queer festivals and feminist spaces but not yet mainstream.

records.definition: An older clinical and community term for a person whose gender identity differs from their assigned sex at birth, especially one who has undergone or seeks medical transition.
records.notes: Gradually replaced in community discourse by trans or transgênero; carries medicalization and surgery-oriented implications absent from the broader term trans; still common in Brazilian legal documents, SUS (public health system) protocols, and older journalism.

records.definition: Short and widely preferred community self-identifier for transgender and gender-nonconforming people; used as both adjective and noun.
records.notes: The dominant neutral term in Brazilian trans activist communities; used across all registers from casual speech to academic discourse; preferred over transsexual by most community members under 40.

records.definition: Gender transition; the social, medical, and legal process by which a trans or travesti person aligns their presentation and body with their gender identity.
records.notes: Maps to the process rather than the identity; closest registry concept (transgender) denotes identity rather than transition process; typically phrased as transição de gênero for precision; used in SUS protocols and trans rights legislation.

records.definition: To gender-transition; the verbal form, encompassing hormone therapy, social transition, name and pronoun change, and surgical procedures.
records.notes: Community neologism modeled on English 'to transition'; more common in online forums and activist discourse than in formal writing; maps to the process not the identity; often paired with de gênero.

records.definition: To undergo hormone replacement therapy as part of gender transition; a Brazilian Portuguese coinage from hormônio (hormone) plus the verb-forming suffix -izar.
records.english_term: to go on hormones / to start HRT
records.notes: No English single-word verb equivalent exists; hormonizar condenses a multi-word English phrase into a productive neologism widely used in trans community forums, Tumblr, and Twitter discourse; recognition concentrated in trans and LGBTQ+-adjacent communities.

records.definition: A trans woman or travesti who has undergone gender confirmation surgery; the feminine past participle of operar used as a community identity marker for surgical status.
records.notes: Operada vs não-operada is a key social distinction in Brazilian travesti communities; some individuals use operada as a proud identity marker; the term implicitly marks the speaker/referent as feminine through grammatical gender agreement.

records.definition: A trans woman or travesti who has not undergone gender confirmation surgery; the negated form of operada, used as a stable identity marker rather than necessarily a transitional state.
records.notes: In Brazilian travesti culture, não-operada is often a permanent identity choice rather than a pre-surgical waiting state; this differs from the Western pre-op framing which implies future surgery is planned; the distinction matters politically for travesti identity advocacy.

records.definition: The capacity or degree to which a trans person is perceived as their gender identity without being read as transgender; the Brazilian noun form of the concept of passing.
records.notes: English uses the phrase passing privilege or ability to pass; passabilidade is a single-word Brazilian nominalization common in trans activist and academic discourse that has no direct English noun counterpart; carries strong political valence around safety and social access.

records.definition: In trans contexts, to be perceived as one's gender identity without being identified as transgender; the Brazilian Portuguese verb for passing as one's gender.
records.notes: Passar has numerous general meanings (to pass, to go through, to iron clothes); in trans contexts it carries the specific English sense of passing as one's gender and requires disambiguation; typically phrased as passar por mulher or passar por homem.

records.definition: In LGBTQ+ contexts, to come to recognize and understand one's own sexual orientation or gender identity; the reflexive internal process of sexual and gender self-discovery.
records.english_term: to come out to oneself / to realize one is queer
records.notes: Literally to discover oneself; in LGBTQ+ discourse specifically denotes the private internal recognition of queer identity before any disclosure to others, in contrast to assumir-se (the external coming-out act); often used with a temporal marker: se descobriu aos 18 anos.

records.definition: To come out; to publicly acknowledge or declare one's sexual orientation or gender identity to others; the standard Brazilian Portuguese equivalent of coming out of the closet.
records.notes: Literally to assume oneself or to own oneself; the dominant phrase in Brazilian LGBTQ+ discourse for disclosing queer identity to family, peers, or publicly; collocates freely: assumir-se gay, assumir-se trans, assumir-se bissexual; near-universal recognition among younger Brazilians.

records.definition: Reflexive verb meaning to come out as gay, trans, or another non-heteronormative identity; to publicly own and declare one's sexual or gender identity; heavily used in travesti and trans communities.
records.notes: Carries stronger connotations of internal self-acceptance than the English 'coming out.' In travesti communities, 'se assumir' often precedes legal recognition and may refer to public social presentation before any medical or bureaucratic process. Not crude — entirely neutral-to-positive in register.

records.definition: In prison context, the male prisoner who takes the passive sexual role and loses masculine status; more broadly a highly offensive slur for an effeminate gay man.
records.notes: Polysemous in Brazilian Portuguese: also means 'queue' (line of people) and is partially reclaimed in urban LGBTQ+ communities as a self-identifier. The prison usage is derogatory and role-based rather than identity-based — it marks status loss, not gayness per se. Crudeness rated for the slur and prison usage.

records.definition: The receptive or penetrated partner in anal sex; used as a neutral role descriptor in gay male culture and as a status marker in prison honor hierarchies.
records.notes: In Brazilian gay culture, standard and relatively neutral on hookup apps. In prison and traditional masculine culture, passivo carries heavy honor-shame weight: only the passivo is considered to have compromised masculine identity; the ativo does not.

records.definition: The insertive or penetrating partner in anal sex; used as a neutral role descriptor in gay male culture and as a marker of retained masculine identity in prison honor culture.
records.notes: In Brazilian prison and traditional masculine honor culture, the ativo retains full heterosexual masculine status even during same-sex acts — penetrating another man does not make one gay within this schema. Only the passivo loses masculine identity. This asymmetry is less emphasized in Anglophone gay culture.

records.definition: Crude phrasal verb meaning to submit the anus for penetration; literally 'to give the ass'; to take the receptive role in anal sex.
records.notes: One of the most ubiquitous crude phrases in Brazilian Portuguese. Has a widely used figurative sense: 'dar o cu' without sexual context means to surrender humiliatingly or to get screwed over, making it a versatile general expletive beyond the literal sexual meaning.

records.definition: Extremely crude phrasal verb meaning to receive anal penetration; literally 'to take it in the ass'; more emphatic and degrading in connotation than 'dar o cu.'
records.english_term: to take it up the ass
records.notes: Used both literally for the sexual act and as a general expletive equivalent to 'fuck you' or 'go to hell.' The verb 'tomar' (to receive/endure) frames the act as something undergone passively rather than offered. Base form of the insult 'vai tomar no cu' (go fuck yourself), one of the most common Brazilian curses.

records.definition: Prison slang for a male prisoner coerced into or occupying the passive sexual role; literally 'chicken'; connotes weakness, cowardice, and sexual submissiveness.
records.notes: Outside prison, 'frango' also means coward in general Brazilian slang and a goalkeeper's error in football. The prison sexual meaning directly overlaps with the cowardice meaning — both invoke failure of masculine performance. Not exclusively prison-specific; used broadly for an effeminate or weak man.

records.definition: Compound insult for a man who takes or was forced into the passive sexual role in prison; literally 'prison faggot'; 'boiola' is itself a highly offensive standalone slur for a gay man.
records.notes: 'Boiola' alone is among the harshest gay slurs in Brazilian Portuguese. Adding 'de cadeia' (from prison / of jail) further degrades by marking the person as having acquired their sexual submissiveness through prison victimization, implying they were coerced or broken. Lower recognition than 'bicha' because the compound is more niche and prison-specific.

records.definition: In prison and criminal subculture, to surrender masculine status by submitting to the passive sexual role; literally 'to lose oneself'; implies irreversible fall within the prison honor hierarchy.
records.notes: Unlike English 'to get turned out' (which describes external coercion by another), 'se perder' frames the loss as internally experienced and self-referential — the man loses himself. No English concept combines passive-role submission with this specific self-dissolution honor-loss framing. The irreversibility and identity-collapse aspect is specific to Brazilian and broader Latin American masculine honor culture.

records.definition: Literally 'man'; in Brazilian prison and traditional masculine honor culture, specifically designates the insertive/active partner in male-male sex who retains full masculine identity and heterosexual status through his role.
records.notes: The word itself is the standard everyday word for 'man' — the sexual-role meaning is entirely contextual. The underlying cultural concept, that only the passive partner is considered gay or feminized while the active partner remains 'homem,' is deeply embedded in Brazilian and broader Latin American masculine honor culture. 'Ativo' and 'homem' function as synonyms in this framework.

records.definition: Crude phrasal expression meaning to submit sexually to the active partner; literally 'to give to the active one'; explicitly frames the passive-to-active direction of sexual service.
records.notes: More explicitly relational than 'dar o cu' — names both the act and the recipient (the ativo). Most common in prison and criminal subculture discourse where the ativo/passivo hierarchy is explicit and status-bearing. 'Pro' is a contraction of 'para o' (for the).

records.definition: In prison context, to sexually coerce or rape another prisoner, typically by forcing anal penetration to establish dominance; the standard verb 'to force' applied to sexual assault.
records.notes: 'Forçar' is the standard Portuguese verb meaning 'to force' in any context, giving it a quasi-clinical veneer even in the prison-rape context. Crudeness score reflects the sexual coercion usage rather than the word's general neutral register. Distinguished from 'estuprar' (to rape — the more explicit legal/medical term).

records.definition: To sexually force a specific person; the transitive form of 'forçar' that makes the victim explicit; in prison context means to rape or sexually coerce another prisoner into the passive role.
records.notes: The addition of 'alguém' (someone/a person) highlights the victim and transitive nature of the act. Entirely standard Portuguese syntactically; the prison-rape meaning is contextually derived. Marginally higher crudeness than bare 'forçar' because explicit victim-naming makes the violation more concrete.

records.definition: Prison slang for a man who was tricked or naively allowed himself to be coerced into the passive sexual role; literally 'fell like a duck'; implies naive victimization and permanent status loss in the prison hierarchy.
records.notes: 'Pato' (duck) in Brazilian slang means a naive sucker or easy victim. The phrase captures the concept of someone whose masculine naivety or social incompetence caused their own downfall into the passive role — distinct from being forcibly raped ('forçar alguém') in that the victim's own weakness is implicated in their fall. No English equivalent exists for this specific honor-shame framing of naive masculine failure leading to permanent sexual subordination.

records.definition: Prison slang for an older male prisoner who is forced into or occupies the passive sexual role; literally 'male goat'; emphasizes age combined with subordinate sexual status.
records.notes: 'Bode' (male goat) in general Brazilian slang also means scapegoat or an ugly/unpleasant person ('bode expiatório' = scapegoat). In prison, the term specifically marks older inmates who are sexually coerced, where age does not confer protection but vulnerability. Distinct from 'frango' in emphasizing the older age of the forced passive partner.

records.definition: A young, typically new and sexually inexperienced male; in prison targeted as sexual prey by older inmates; in gay culture broadly a positive or neutral descriptor for a young effeminate gay man, equivalent to 'twink.'
records.notes: Diminutive of 'novo' (new/young) with affectionate suffix '-inho.' Outside prison, extremely common in Brazilian gay hookup apps and pornography as a desirable category. In prison the same word marks a new young inmate as a target. The term straddles desirability in gay culture and prey-marking in prison culture simultaneously — a dual valence that highlights the word's role in Brazil's specific sexual honor economy.

records.definition: In prison, to attach oneself to a stronger prisoner for protection with the implicit understanding that sexual favors are exchanged; literally 'to glue to / to stick with someone.'
records.notes: Outside prison, 'colar com' is casual dating slang meaning 'to hook up with' or 'to start seeing someone.' In prison the same phrase describes a survival arrangement where the weaker prisoner initiates the attachment to avoid random predation. Unlike the civilian 'kept partner' (financial dependency, voluntary), the prison version operates under physical threat and survival pressure. The sexual implication is fully contextual and unstated in the phrase itself.

records.definition: Standard Russian clinical term for the penis; lit. 'sexual member', used in medical education, legal documents, and official contexts.

records.definition: From Greek phallos; refers to the penis or its symbolic/ritual representation, used in literary, psychoanalytic, and anthropological discourse.

records.definition: Literally 'small genital lips'; the standard clinical Russian term for the labia minora, the two inner folds of skin within the labia majora surrounding the vaginal opening.

records.definition: The central Russian mat word for the vagina/vulva; equivalent in vulgarity to English 'cunt'; also used extensively as a general expletive, intensifier, and insult.

records.definition: Literally 'slit,' 'slot,' or 'narrow crack'; a crude slang term for the vagina/vulva, referencing the visible external cleft of the genitalia.

records.definition: Childish or playful euphemism for the vagina, from a dialectal word for 'doll' or 'toy'; used especially when speaking to or about young children.
records.notes: More common in southern Russian and Ukrainian-influenced speech; low crudeness but clearly sexual in context; often used by parents with small children.

records.definition: Crude slang for pubic lice, formed from манда (vulgar word for vulva/vagina) plus вошки (lice); grouped in vaginal vocabulary because of its morphological root.
records.notes: The word itself means 'pubic lice,' not 'vagina'; its high crudeness rating derives from the root манда, itself a mat-adjacent obscenity for the vulva; proposed new slug: pubic_lice.

records.definition: Diminutive form of пизда used as crude slang for the vagina; the diminutive suffix slightly reduces force but keeps it firmly in the mat register.
records.notes: Diminutive of пизда; the -ёнка suffix suggests smallness or youth; sometimes carries a condescending or sexualizing diminutive tone rather than simple size reference.

records.definition: The primary and harshest Russian obscenity for the vagina; a mat-level obscenity comparable in severity to 'cunt' in American English, though even more culturally taboo in most Russian contexts.
records.notes: One of the four canonical Russian mat words (alongside хуй, ебать, блядь); used as a general intensifier and in many fixed expressions beyond its anatomical meaning; cognate with Ukrainian піzда and other Slavic forms.

records.definition: The standard clinical and everyday Russian term for the clitoris, a direct loanword from Greek/Latin via European medical terminology.
records.notes: Used in both medical contexts and ordinary speech; no inherent vulgar connotation though the subject matter may cause social embarrassment in conservative settings.

records.definition: Clinical anatomical term for the clitoris, literally 'genital tubercle' or 'sexual bump'; used primarily in medical and embryological contexts.
records.notes: Половой = sexual/genital (from пол = sex/gender); бугорок = small mound or tubercle; most common in embryological and developmental anatomy contexts where the homology with the glans penis is being described.

records.definition: Slang for the clitoris, literally 'button,' a cross-linguistic metaphor based on its small size and the way it is stimulated.
records.notes: The button metaphor for the clitoris appears in many languages; playful rather than crude; кнопка is also the ordinary Russian word for a button or thumbtack, so context disambiguates.

records.definition: Mild slang for the clitoris, literally 'little mound' or 'small bump'; descriptive rather than crude, functioning as a non-offensive circumlocution.
records.notes: Shares the root of the clinical term половой бугорок but used in casual rather than strictly medical speech; understood primarily by adults familiar with the anatomy.

records.definition: Affectionate diminutive slang for the clitoris, literally 'tiny button'; the diminutive suffix adds endearment, typically used in intimate or playful contexts.
records.notes: Diminutive of кнопка; the -очка suffix marks it as affectionate or tender; lower crudeness than кнопка because the diminutive frames it as something precious rather than merely colloquial.

records.definition: The standard neutral Russian word for breast or chest; the default everyday term for the female breast used in speech, literature, and semi-clinical contexts.
records.notes: Грудь means both 'chest' (anatomical region) and 'breast' (mammary organ); context disambiguates; not crude and used freely in polite company; applies to both male and female anatomy.

records.definition: The standard clinical Russian term for mammary glands, literally 'milk glands'; used in medical, scientific, and educational contexts.
records.notes: Plural; молочные = milky/milk (from молоко); железы = glands; purely clinical, rarely used outside medical or health education contexts; recognized by most educated adults.

records.definition: Clinical anatomical term for a single mammary gland, literally 'chest gland'; less common than the plural молочные железы but appears in medical texts.
records.notes: Singular form; грудная = of the chest/breast (from грудь); железа = gland; slightly less common in practice than молочные железы; both terms appear in medical literature.

records.definition: The standard Russian term for nipple, used in both clinical and everyday speech; derived from the verb сосать (to suck), referencing the breastfeeding function.
records.notes: From сосать = to suck; mild crudeness arises from the erogenous nature of the organ rather than the word itself; universally known and used freely in medical and everyday speech.

records.definition: Clinical term for the areola, the pigmented ring surrounding the nipple; a direct loanword from Latin areola via European medical terminology.
records.notes: Direct cognate with English 'areola'; purely clinical and rarely encountered outside medical or detailed anatomical contexts; recognition is growing through online health education.

records.definition: The most widespread crude slang for female breasts in Russian; extremely common in informal speech, humor, internet culture, and vulgar contexts.
records.notes: One of the most ubiquitous vulgar body-part terms in Russian; used across all adult age groups in informal settings; appears in countless memes, songs, and jokes; the root сися may relate to dialectal terms for breast or to the sucking action.

records.definition: Crude slang for female breasts derived from the verb доить (to milk a cow), directly likening a woman's breasts to a cow's udder.
records.notes: From доить = to milk livestock; the cow-milking metaphor is dehumanizing but the term is widely used humorously; similar register and connotation to English 'milkers' or 'udders' in crude speech.

records.definition: Slang for female breasts, literally 'buffers' (as in train bumpers or mechanical shock absorbers), playing on the protrusion and cushioning of large breasts.
records.notes: Буфер = buffer/bumper (mechanical/railway); the plural буфера evokes locomotive front buffers; humorous in tone rather than purely derogatory; comparable to English 'knockers' or 'bumpers.'

records.definition: Crude slang for female breasts; phonetically similar to сиськи but phonologically distinct; common in southern Russian dialects, Ukrainian-influenced speech, and informal internet usage.
records.notes: Possibly derived from or reinforced by Ukrainian цицьки; in contemporary Russian internet culture often used interchangeably with сиськи; the phonetic form suggests dialectal or cross-Slavic origin.

records.definition: Humorous slang for large female breasts, literally 'watermelons'; emphasizes size and roundness rather than being derogatory.
records.notes: Used specifically to imply large breasts; the watermelon metaphor parallels English 'melons'; tone is more admiring or humorous than degrading; арбуз is also simply the everyday Russian word for watermelon.

records.definition: Slang for female breasts meaning 'balls' or 'spheres'; less reliable in this sense than other breast terms because шары more commonly refers to eyes or testicles in standard Russian slang.
records.notes: Шары primarily means 'eyes' in criminal argot and 'testicles' in general crude slang; its use for 'breasts' is contextually dependent and less universal than сиськи or дойки; may cause ambiguity without clear context.

records.definition: Childish or playful euphemism for female breasts; softer than сиськи; used when talking to young children, in affectionate contexts, or when playfully avoiding more explicit terms.
records.notes: Likely a reduplication or softened form related to the сиська root; the infantilizing form substantially lowers crudeness; used by adults in tender or playful registers as well as with children.

records.definition: Humorous slang for female breasts, literally 'zucchinis' or 'courgettes'; implies an elongated or somewhat pendulous shape rather than round fullness.
records.notes: Кабачок = zucchini/courgette; the vegetable metaphor implies a specific elongated shape and is less flattering than арбузы; used mostly in humorous or self-deprecating contexts; awareness as a breast term is lower than арбузы or сиськи.

records.definition: Playful slang for nipples or very small breasts, literally 'little buttons,' evoking their small round shape.
records.notes: More naturally refers to nipples than to the whole breast despite section classification; tone is playful or affectionate rather than crude; implies smallness.

records.definition: Crude slang for protruding or erect nipples, literally 'things that stick out,' from торчать (to protrude).
records.notes: Emphasizes protrusion or erectness, often visible through clothing; can loosely extend to perky breasts as a whole.

records.definition: Affectionate diminutive slang for breasts, literally 'little titties'; diminutive of сиськи.
records.notes: Conveys smallness or cuteness; tone ranges from affectionate to mildly crude depending on context; softer than сиськи.

records.definition: Standard Russian word for breasts (plural of грудь), used in clinical and everyday speech without vulgarity.
records.notes: Грудь also means 'chest' broadly; in anatomical or sexual context груди unambiguously means breasts; the neutral unmarked term.

records.definition: Standard clinical and everyday Russian term for testicles, literally 'little eggs,' reflecting their oval shape.
records.notes: The primary non-vulgar Russian term for testicles; used in medical contexts and ordinary conversation; яйцо means 'egg.'

records.definition: Strictly clinical Russian term for the testes as glands, literally 'seed-holders'; equivalent to Latin testes.
records.notes: Biological/anatomical register; rarely used outside textbooks or clinical settings; семя means 'seed/semen.'

records.definition: Standard clinical Russian term for the scrotum, the skin pouch enclosing the testicles.
records.notes: Not vulgar; used in medical and general speech without strong crude connotation.

records.definition: Clinical Russian phrase for the sex glands or gonads (testes or ovaries), literally 'sexual glands.'
records.notes: Strictly anatomical; rarely heard outside medical education; applies to both male and female gonads; most adults recognize it but few use it spontaneously.

records.definition: Very common crude Russian slang for testicles, literally 'eggs'; also used metaphorically for courage or audacity.
records.notes: Direct functional equivalent of English 'balls'; the most frequently used crude term for testicles; яйца also means 'eggs' literally, which motivates the euphemism.

records.definition: Mildly crude diminutive slang for testicles; a softer, slightly playful form of яйца.
records.notes: Diminutive of яйца; less crude and more affectionate or playful in tone; used when яйца would feel too harsh for the register.

records.definition: Slang for testicles, literally 'nuts'; a direct parallel to English 'nuts.'
records.notes: Cross-linguistic metaphor matching English 'nuts'; widely understood; less crude than яйца but still informal.

records.definition: Humorous or euphemistic collective noun for male genitalia, roughly equivalent to 'the family jewels' or 'the whole package.'
records.notes: Refers collectively to penis and testicles; slightly comical tone; etymology obscure, possibly Ukrainian in origin; used to sidestep naming specific anatomy.

records.definition: Soft euphemism for male genitalia, literally 'household' or 'property,' implying the genitals as one's personal domain or estate.
records.notes: Хозяйство normally means farm/household/estate; applying it to genitals is a wry joke about ownership; very common understated euphemism.

records.definition: Crude collective slang for male genitalia, literally 'innards' or 'offal,' treating the genitals dismissively as visceral body matter.
records.notes: Primarily means animal entrails/offal; applying it to genitals is humorous or contemptuous; can sometimes extend to female genitalia; the offal connotation adds a deliberately dehumanizing edge.

records.definition: Highly vulgar slang for testicles, sharing the obscene Slavic root 'муд-' that underlies the major insult мудак (asshole).
records.notes: One of the oldest obscene Slavic roots; мудя specifically denotes the testicles; shares etymology with мудак; not classified as full мат but rated near-мат in social vulgarity.

records.definition: Crude slang for testicles, literally 'spheres' or 'balls.'
records.notes: Direct structural equivalent of English 'balls'; шар means 'sphere'; also means 'eyes' in Russian thieves' argot (феня), occasionally producing humorous ambiguity.

records.definition: Clinical Russian term for the anus, a Latin loanword used in medical and educational contexts.
records.notes: Standard medical loanword; not vulgar; used in clinical, educational, and formal contexts.

records.definition: Clinical Russian term for the rectum, literally 'straight intestine.'
records.notes: Standard anatomical term; the literal translation reflects the organ's relatively straight path compared to the rest of the colon.

records.definition: Clinical Russian phrase for the anal opening or anus, literally 'anal aperture.'
records.notes: Multi-word clinical descriptor emphasizing the orifice specifically; used in medical documentation, sex education, and legal contexts.

records.definition: Clinical Russian term for the perineum, the region of tissue between the genitals and anus.
records.notes: Standard anatomical term; derived from промежуток (gap/interval); rarely used in casual speech; recognized primarily by medical professionals and educated adults.

records.definition: Very common crude Russian slang for the buttocks; also used idiomatically to mean a bad situation, mess, or disaster.
records.notes: One of the most frequently used crude words in Russian everyday speech; not full мат but borderline; appears in numerous fixed expressions (e.g., жопа случилась = shit happened).

records.definition: Mildly crude Russian colloquial term for the buttocks, somewhat softer than жопа.
records.notes: Derived from зад (back/rear); more polite register than жопа but still informal; used in situations where жопа would be too harsh.

records.definition: Childish or playful Russian term for the buttocks, equivalent to English 'bottom' or 'bum.'
records.notes: The mildest Russian term for buttocks; used freely with children and in affectionate adult contexts; not vulgar; used across all age groups.

records.definition: Crude Russian slang specifically for the anus or anal sphincter, literally 'little eye' or 'pip,' referring to the circular aperture.
records.notes: Literally means 'little eye,' a card-game pip, or a score point; as genitalia slang it refers specifically to the anal orifice rather than the buttocks broadly; also names a Russian blackjack-like card game and a toilet bowl — all from the 'round opening' meaning.

records.definition: Highly vulgar Russian slang for the buttocks, cruder than жопа and carrying a scatological undertone from the root срать (to defecate).
records.notes: Shares the root with срать (to shit), intensifying its vulgarity beyond жопа; the scatological connotation makes it more offensive; used in aggressively crude or emphatic contexts.

records.definition: Slang for the buttocks, literally 'bread rolls'; used humorously or affectionately to refer to the butt cheeks.
records.notes: Derives from the visual resemblance of rounded bread rolls to buttock cheeks; widely used and not strongly offensive.

records.definition: Euphemism for the buttocks, literally 'fifth point'; a polite and humorous way to refer to the rear end without vulgarity.
records.notes: The 'fifth point' refers to the fifth contact point when sitting or landing after a fall — the buttocks. Very widely recognized across all registers including children's speech.

records.definition: The rear or backside; a common, mildly informal term for the buttocks.
records.notes: From the root meaning 'back/behind'; extremely common and only mildly marked; used freely in everyday speech.

records.definition: Diminutive of зад; affectionate or playful slang for the buttocks, often used in a flirtatious or fond register.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix -ок softens and sexualizes; commonly used in complimentary or teasing contexts about an attractive posterior.

records.definition: Anal sex; a loanword used as a noun or modifier to denote anal intercourse.
records.notes: Though source-categorized under 'anus (slang/crude)', in Russian usage 'анал' primarily denotes the sex act, not the anatomical structure (which is 'анус'). Borrowed from English/French.

records.definition: Humorous slang for the buttocks, literally the 'stern' of a ship; implies a large or prominent rear end.
records.notes: Nautical metaphor applied to the human rear; used humorously rather than crudely, often implying appreciable size.

records.definition: The pubic mound or mons pubis; a semi-clinical term also used colloquially to refer to the pubic region and pubic hair.
records.notes: Used in medical texts as a near-clinical term and colloquially by the general public; also extends metonymically to pubic hair (лобковые волосы).

records.definition: Pubic hair; the standard clinical and neutral Russian compound noun for hair in the pubic region.
records.notes: Fully neutral anatomical phrase; the clinical default for any medical, educational, or public health context.

records.definition: The perineum; the anatomical region of tissue between the genitals and the anus; standard clinical term.
records.notes: Primarily recognized by medical professionals and educated laypeople; rarely used outside clinical or anatomical discourse.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; a formal legal and medical compound term for penetrative sex.
records.notes: The standard phrasing in Russian criminal law (e.g. rape statutes) and medical documentation; not used in everyday conversation.

records.definition: Coitus; a Latin-derived clinical term for sexual intercourse used in medical, sexological, and academic writing.
records.notes: International medical loanword from Latin; recognized mainly by educated or medically literate speakers; essentially never used colloquially.

records.definition: Copulation or sexual union; a formal and literary Russian term for sexual intercourse derived from 'to join together'.
records.notes: Used in literature, medical texts, and legal documents; sounds archaic or overly formal in everyday speech; more native-feeling than коитус.

records.definition: Sexual contact; a clinical and legal phrase denoting any form of sexual activity, broader than penetrative intercourse alone.
records.notes: Commonly appears in legal codes, medical consent forms, and public health materials; deliberately broad in scope.

records.definition: Sexual act or intercourse; the most commonly used formal-register phrase for sexual intercourse in Russian.
records.notes: The default euphemistic-clinical term that most Russian speakers reach for in public or semi-formal speech; appears universally in journalism, legal contexts, and polite conversation.

records.definition: Intimate closeness; a polite euphemism for sexual intercourse that foregrounds emotional and physical intimacy over the mechanical act.
records.notes: Common in media, counseling, and everyday polite speech; implies emotional connection as well as sex; the preferred phrasing when speakers wish to avoid both clinical and crude registers.

records.definition: Copulation; a highly technical Latin-derived term for sexual intercourse, used primarily in biology, zoology, and sexology.
records.notes: More technical and narrower in register than совокупление; appears in scientific literature describing both human and animal reproduction; vanishingly rare in everyday speech.

records.definition: To fuck; the primary mat-system verb for sexual intercourse in Russian, imperfective aspect, denoting ongoing or habitual action.
records.notes: One of the core roots of Russian mat (obscene profanity system); generates hundreds of derivatives and compound expletives; among the most taboo words in Russian; imperfective aspect implies repeated or continuous action.

records.definition: To fuck or screw; the most widely used non-mat crude verb for sexual intercourse, imperfective aspect.
records.notes: Does not belong to the formal mat system and is thus slightly less taboo than ёбать, but still considered crude; ubiquitous in colloquial speech. Primary etymology unclear — possibly from трах (crash/bang).

records.definition: To fuck or nail; slang verb for sexual intercourse derived from шпилька (hairpin/spike), evoking the image of penetration.
records.notes: Less widespread than трахать; the root implies a sharp pinning action; used in a mildly humorous or crude register, often in male-coded boastful speech.

records.definition: To fuck (perfective); the perfective aspect form of трахать, denoting a single completed act of sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Perfective aspect marks completion; used in past-tense narration or to denote a discrete, one-time sexual encounter as opposed to an ongoing activity.

records.definition: Fucking; a mat-system noun derived from ёбать, referring to sexual intercourse as an activity or the act itself.
records.notes: Part of the core Russian mat vocabulary; used both as a noun naming the sex act and as a general expletive amplifier; among the strongest obscenities in Russian.

records.definition: To have sex for a while; reflexive perfective of трахать, implying a mutually participatory and somewhat casual or extended sexual encounter.
records.notes: The по- prefix adds a sense of casual duration ('a bit'); the -ся reflexive emphasizes mutuality; slightly less crude in feel than the base form трахать due to the diminutive-casual tone of по-.

records.definition: To fuck aggressively; literally 'to tear off'; implies vigorous or forceful sexual intercourse with a dominant, conquest-oriented connotation.
records.notes: Derived from драть (to tear/flog/thrash); the от- prefix implies thoroughness and completion; strongly implies the active partner dominating the passive; can shade toward forceful or predatory framing.

records.definition: To fuck vigorously; literally 'to fry up thoroughly'; crude slang for intense sexual intercourse emphasizing heat, energy, and force.
records.notes: From жарить (to fry/grill/roast); the на- prefix implies thorough completion; evokes the heat and vigor of aggressive sex; less common than трахать or отодрать. Input romanization 'nazhirit'' appears to be a typo; correct form is 'nazharit''.

records.definition: To fuck; an imperfective variant of шпилить used interchangeably in crude slang for sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Variant form alongside шпилить; the -ять ending is a common imperfective aspect alternant; slightly less widespread than шпилить; both derive from шпилька (spike/pin).

records.definition: To put out; to consent to sex — used almost exclusively of the receptive (typically female) partner 'giving' sex to the pursuer.
records.notes: Structurally asymmetric: the partner who pursues 'takes' (взять), the partner who consents 'gives' (дать); the asymmetry encodes a transactional view of female sexuality.

records.definition: Literally 'to sleep across/through'; the standard everyday Russian euphemism for having sex, implying an overnight stay.
records.notes: The dominant non-vulgar verb for the sex act in modern Russian; used across all registers except clinical writing.

records.definition: Onomatopoeic crude verb for having sex, evoking the wet slapping sound of thrusting.
records.notes: The onomatopoeia gives it a faintly comic or juvenile tone compared to harder terms like ёбать; sometimes used ironically.

records.definition: Literally 'to fry/roast'; crude slang for vigorous, heat-intensive sex, strongly connoting the active-dominant role.
records.notes: The thermal metaphor (frying, heat) implies energetic or aggressive intercourse; nearly always framed from the penetrating partner's perspective.

records.definition: Literally 'to wind/reel/swing'; crude slang for sex emphasizing the rhythmic gyrating motion of intercourse.
records.notes: Less frequent in sexual use than жарить or долбить; the winding/reeling metaphor focuses on the mechanical rhythm rather than force or heat.

records.definition: Literally 'to chisel/hammer'; crude slang for forceful, repetitive penetrative sex connoting aggressive pounding.
records.notes: The chiseling metaphor strongly implies hard, repeated thrusting; frequently used in descriptions of anal sex as well as vaginal; also a general verb for relentless repetition (e.g., 'hammering a question').

records.definition: Literally 'to beat/knock rapidly'; crude slang for vigorous thrusting sex, slightly less common than долбить in sexual contexts.
records.notes: Primary meaning is physical beating; sexual meaning is a secondary but well-understood extension; less specifically sexual than долбить and therefore slightly less crude in practice.

records.definition: Literally 'to blow into'; crude perfective verb for penetrative sex framed from the insertive partner's perspective.
records.notes: The 'blow into' metaphor treats the vagina or anus as a cavity being filled with air; perfective aspect frames the act as a completed event; used almost exclusively of the penetrating role.

records.definition: Literally 'to insert/put in'; crude perfective slang focusing on the act of initial penetration, used as a synecdoche for the entire sex act.
records.notes: The relatively anatomical framing (insertion) gives it slightly higher technical score than pure affect-based slang; also widely used in internet memes and humorous sexual contexts.

records.definition: Perfective of ёбать ('to fuck'); 'to fuck (once, suddenly, or hard)'; also used non-sexually to mean 'to hit hard' or as a generalized expletive.
records.notes: Belongs to the mat (мат) register — the formal Russian category of the most taboo obscenities; the perfective aspect adds suddenness or completion; dual sexual/violent meaning is common across mat verb roots.

records.definition: Perfective of иметь, literally 'to have/acquire'; crude slang for having sex framed as conquest or possession of the other person.
records.notes: The по- prefix shifts иметь from ongoing possession to achieved acquisition, strongly connoting dominance and conquest; frequently implies the partner was an unwilling or hard-won target.

records.definition: Literally 'to have'; used across registers from mildly euphemistic to crude for sexual possession of a partner.
records.notes: Imperfective; the milder, more literary counterpart to ёбать; retains the ownership/possession framing inherent in поиметь but with less aggressive force; found in everything from 19th-century literature to contemporary crude speech.

records.definition: Literally 'to engage in sex'; the default neutral everyday Russian phrase for having sex, equivalent to English 'to have sex'.
records.notes: The loanword секс entered mainstream Russian usage in the late Soviet glasnost era; before that, the topic lacked a polite everyday verb entirely; now this phrase is the standard non-clinical, non-vulgar option.

records.definition: Crude mat noun derived from ёбать; 'fucking' as a noun, referring either to the sex act or (more commonly) to any chaotic, disorderly, or frustrating situation.
records.notes: In contemporary usage the non-sexual sense ('what a shitshow/clusterfuck') is more frequent than the literal sexual sense; one of several -ня abstract nouns in the mat register.

records.definition: Extended variant of ёбня; crude noun for the sex act or, more often, prolonged chaotic nonsense and frustrating activity.
records.notes: The -отня suffix implies ongoing, drawn-out activity more strongly than -ня; in practice used more for 'endless bullshit' than for sexual intercourse; slightly less common than ёбня.

records.definition: The clinical Russian term for fellatio; direct transliteration of Latin fellatio, used in medical and sexological literature.
records.notes: Rarely used outside academic, medical, or legal contexts; most Russian speakers would understand it but would never use it in conversation.

records.definition: 'Oral sex'; the standard neutral-register Russian phrase covering both fellatio and cunnilingus.
records.notes: Fully calqued from English; the most socially acceptable everyday term when the speaker wants to be understood without being vulgar or overly clinical.

records.definition: The dominant Russian colloquial word for a blowjob; understood by virtually all adult speakers.
records.notes: Borrowed from French 'minette' (originally meaning cunnilingus) but in Russian shifted to refer exclusively to fellatio; the semantic inversion is complete and universal in modern Russian usage.

records.definition: Perfective verb meaning 'to suck off'; to perform fellatio to completion.
records.notes: The от- prefix indicates completion of the sucking action; also used as a standalone vulgar insult ('go suck a dick') and widely understood as such independently of sexual context.

records.definition: Literally 'to suck'; in sexual context, to perform oral sex, primarily fellatio; also functions as a general pejorative ('it sucks') identical to English usage.

records.definition: Noun form of отсосать; a blowjob or the act of performing fellatio; also a stand-alone crude insult for a contemptible person.
