records.definition: Literally 'deep throat'; Russian calque for the practice of taking the full length of a penis into the throat during fellatio, suppressing the gag reflex.
records.notes: Direct semantic calque of English 'deep throat'; the Watergate informant meaning is also known but less salient in everyday Russian usage; sometimes shortened colloquially.

records.definition: Literally 'to do a blowjob'; the most common Russian phrasal construction for performing fellatio.
records.notes: The canonical everyday phrasing; делать (to do/give) functions identically to English 'give' in 'give a blowjob'; the phrase is neutral enough to appear in mainstream media reporting on sex education.

records.definition: Agent/instrument noun from сосать; 'sucker' — a person who performs fellatio or, by extension, a servile or contemptible person.
records.notes: The -алка suffix creates ambiguity between agent (the person sucking) and instrument (the mouth or act itself); primarily used as an insult rather than a neutral descriptor of the act; less common than отсос in pure sexual contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'to take into the mouth'; crude phrasal verb for performing fellatio, focusing on the act of oral reception of the penis.
records.notes: Syntactically ambiguous about who performs the action — the subject can be the one fellating or the one receiving — but typically framed from the perspective of the person performing oral sex; the most anatomically explicit of the common non-mat phrases.

records.definition: Clinical transliteration of the Latin term for oral stimulation of the female genitalia.
records.notes: Direct loanword from Latin via international clinical vocabulary; encountered mainly in medical and educational texts.

records.definition: Colloquial abbreviation for cunnilingus; the default everyday Russian slang term for the act.
records.notes: Most widely used non-clinical term; neutral-to-mild register among younger speakers; no strong taboo connotation in casual speech.

records.definition: Literally 'to lick'; used as crude slang for cunnilingus or oral sex on a woman.
records.notes: Primary meaning is the generic verb 'to lick'; sexual meaning is wholly context-dependent; universally understood.

records.definition: Perfective aspect of лизать ('to lick'); denotes a single completed act of oral sex on a woman.
records.notes: Perfectivity implies a completed act rather than ongoing action; slightly more explicitly sexual in context than the imperfective лизать.

records.definition: Phrasal construction meaning 'to perform cunnilingus'; literally 'to do kuni.'
records.notes: Standard verbal construction using the slang noun куни with the light verb делать; widely used and understood across generations.

records.definition: Instrumental case of 'tongue' (язык), used elliptically as a metonymic euphemism for oral sex, predominantly cunnilingus.
records.notes: The word itself is not vulgar; sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent; often appears alone or in phrases like ласкать языком.

records.definition: Clinical loanword from Latin masturbatio; the standard medical and educational term for self-stimulation of the genitals.
records.notes: Direct cognate with English 'masturbation'; used in medical, educational, and journalistic contexts without taboo.

records.definition: Masturbation; derived from the biblical figure Onan; used in Soviet-era medical literature and formal religious speech.
records.notes: Carries a slightly moralistic or Soviet-medical flavor compared to мастурбация; still encountered in formal texts and Orthodox discourse.

records.definition: Literally 'self-satisfaction'; a formal euphemism for masturbation used to avoid clinical or crude terminology.
records.notes: Compound of само- (self) and удовлетворение (satisfaction); polite or occasionally ironic register; rarely used in casual speech.

records.definition: The primary Russian crude verb for masturbating; also used figuratively to mean wasting time or engaging in futile effort.
records.notes: Most common crude term for masturbation; origin uncertain, possibly related to дрожать (to tremble); figurative usage denoting pointless effort is widespread in informal speech.

records.definition: Noun derived from дрочить; the act of masturbation; also used figuratively for pointless, obsessive, or futile activity.
records.notes: Productive nominal form; figurative extension to 'empty busy-work' is widespread; appears as the base in the compound суходрочка.

records.definition: Verb form of мастурбация; to masturbate; used in clinical, journalistic, and formal contexts.
records.notes: Verb counterpart to the clinical noun мастурбация; slightly more formal-sounding than everyday use; fully understood across registers.

records.definition: To masturbate; verb derived from онанизм; primarily found in Soviet-era medical literature.
records.notes: Increasingly dated; mostly encountered in older medical texts or in intentionally stilted usage; peak recognition coincides with height of Soviet medical literature production.

records.definition: Archaic Church Slavonic compound meaning 'hand-fornication'; used in pre-revolutionary religious and moral texts to condemn masturbation.
records.notes: Рука (hand) + блудие (fornication/lechery); primarily encountered in religious texts, historical documents, or deployed as a deliberate archaic flourish.

records.definition: Internet slang verb for masturbating, borrowed from English 'fap'; popularized via Russian imageboards and chan culture.
records.notes: Direct transliteration of English onomatopoeic chan-culture term 'fap'; peaked with Russian imageboard culture ca. 2010–2015; declining slightly among non-internet-native populations.

records.definition: Pejorative noun for a person who masturbates compulsively; also a general insult for a contemptible or worthless person.
records.notes: Derived from дрочить; functions both literally (habitual masturbator) and as a general insult analogous to English 'wanker'; widely understood.

records.definition: Literally 'to fidget with, to pick at, to tug'; used as a mild euphemism for masturbation, particularly female self-stimulation.
records.notes: Primary meaning is non-sexual (tugging at fabric, picking at something); sexual meaning is inferred from context; often heard as теребить себя.

records.definition: Literally 'to pull, jerk, or tug'; used crudely for male masturbation by analogy with the stroking motion.
records.notes: Primary meaning is generic (to yank or tug at something); sexual meaning relies on context; typically appears in дёргать себя or дёргать член.

records.definition: Literally 'dry wank'; masturbation without lubrication; metaphorically, any futile, pointless, or purely theoretical exercise.
records.notes: Сухо (dry) + дрочка (wank); the metaphorical usage — denoting empty intellectual effort or circular debate — is extremely common in Russian internet discourse.

records.definition: Clinical phrase for anal intercourse; the standard medical and journalistic term.
records.notes: Direct calque of English 'anal sex'; widely used in health education materials, journalism, and legal contexts without strong taboo.

records.definition: Sodomy; derived from the biblical city of Sodom; a legal and religious term historically encompassing anal sex and other non-procreative acts.
records.notes: Used in the Russian Orthodox tradition and pre-Soviet legal codes; has seen renewed deployment in anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric since the 2010s.

records.definition: Formal clinical phrase meaning 'anal coitus'; сношение is a dated medical term for sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Сношение is a Soviet-era medical term for intercourse; анальное сношение is found mainly in legal and forensic-medical texts; lower everyday recognition than анальный секс.

records.definition: Etymologically pederasty, but widely used in crude Russian speech as a catch-all for male homosexual anal sex and as a homophobic insult.
records.notes: Substantial semantic drift in popular usage: denotes any male-male anal sex rather than specifically adult-minor relations; also functions freely as a general homophobic insult.

records.definition: Extremely crude phrase meaning 'fucking in the ass'; ёбля is a vulgar noun for sexual intercourse, жопа is the crude term for buttocks/anus.
records.notes: Both components are maximally taboo mat vocabulary; ёбля derives from ебать (to fuck); among the crudest possible phrasings for anal sex in Russian.

records.definition: Prepositional phrase meaning 'in the back/rear'; used as a crude shorthand for anal sex.
records.english_term: in the ass / up the rear
records.notes: Зад literally means 'back' or 'rear'; milder than жопу variants because зад is less taboo than жопа; used alone or in constructions like трахать в зад.

records.definition: Prepositional phrase meaning 'in the butt/ass'; used colloquially to describe receiving anal intercourse.
records.notes: Uses 'попа', the infantilized/colloquial word for buttocks, producing a crude-casual tone rather than maximum obscenity; lower register intensity than the parallel phrase 'в жопу'.

records.definition: Verb phrase meaning 'to take it in the rear'; crude colloquial expression for receiving anal intercourse.
records.english_term: to take it up the ass
records.notes: 'Зад' (rear/backside) is slightly more euphemistic than 'жопа'; perfective infinitive form implies completion of the act.

records.definition: Instrumental case of 'рак' (crayfish/crawfish) used adverbially to mean 'like a crayfish / on all fours'; the standard Russian crude term for rear-entry sexual position.
records.notes: Position-agnostic despite being listed under anal-sex slang — applies equally to vaginal or anal rear entry; the crayfish metaphor refers to the crawling posture; 'рак' also means cancer (the disease) but the sexual meaning is unambiguously crayfish-derived.

records.definition: Russian loanword from Latin/English 'anilingus'; oral stimulation of a partner's anus.
records.notes: Clinical register; recognition is limited outside educated or sexually-informed circles; the act itself carries significant social stigma in mainstream Russian culture.

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'fisting'; sexual insertion of the entire hand into the vaginal or anal canal.
records.notes: Entered Russian via internet pornography and Western sex-education imports; primarily recognized among younger, internet-exposed speakers.

records.definition: Clinical loanword meaning 'stimulation'; in sexual contexts denotes manual, oral, or mechanical excitation of erogenous zones; requires qualification to specify type.
records.notes: Rarely used standalone in sexual discourse; typically appears in compounds: клиторальная стимуляция (clitoral stimulation), анальная стимуляция (anal stimulation).

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'petting'; mutual sexual caressing and touching of erogenous zones stopping short of intercourse.
records.notes: Entered Russian with Western sexuality literature during perestroika and peaked in 1990s sex-education discourse; somewhat dated among younger speakers today who use descriptive circumlocutions.

records.definition: Clinical compound meaning 'mutual masturbation'; reciprocal manual genital stimulation between partners.
records.notes: Formal, clinical phrasing; rarely used in casual speech; speakers more often describe the act or use more graphic colloquialisms.

records.definition: Clinical loanword from Greek/Latin 'tribadism'; vulva-to-vulva genital contact and friction between two people with vulvas.
records.notes: Very low mainstream recognition; known primarily in clinical, academic, and LGBTQ+ discourse; vernacular speakers default to 'лесбийский секс' or more graphic colloquialisms.

records.definition: Verb meaning 'to sniff/smell'; in sexual contexts refers to olfactory genital stimulation — sniffing a partner's genitals or body as a component of sexual arousal or fetishistic behavior.
records.notes: Primary meaning is entirely non-sexual (to smell anything); mapped to 'fetishism' as nearest registry concept since no olfactophilia entry exists; in crude sexual discourse can also function as a euphemism for cunnilingus.

records.definition: Food-metaphor loanword 'sandwich'; denotes a sexual act in which one person is simultaneously penetrated vaginally or anally and orally by two partners.
records.notes: Shares the sandwich metaphor with English sexual slang; direct cultural import via internet pornography; can loosely refer to any threesome configuration with one person between two others.

records.definition: Clinical compound meaning 'double penetration'; simultaneous penetration of two bodily orifices of the same person.
records.notes: Direct calque of the English pornographic term; primarily encountered in adult content and sex-education contexts.

records.definition: Clinical loanword from Latin/Greek; in Russian covers both 'sperm' (the gamete cells) and 'semen' (the ejaculatory fluid) — a semantic distinction that English maintains but Russian collapses into one term.
records.notes: Russian does not routinely distinguish sperm cells from seminal fluid at the everyday level; 'сперматозоид' is available for the individual gamete but 'сперма' serves both meanings in ordinary use.

records.definition: Clinical compound meaning 'seminal fluid'; the formal medical designation for semen in Russian.
records.notes: Strictly medical register; rarely used outside clinical or formal educational contexts; the common-language equivalent is 'сперма'.

records.definition: Clinical noun for ejaculate; the semen expelled at male orgasm, emphasizing the substance rather than the physiological process.
records.notes: Lower recognition than its process-noun counterpart 'эякуляция'; appears mainly in medical literature, andrology, and fertility-treatment contexts.

records.definition: Clinical loanword meaning 'ejaculation'; the physiological process of semen expulsion at orgasm.
records.notes: Standard clinical and sex-education term; widely understood, but the slang pair 'кончить/кончать' is strongly dominant in informal speech.

records.definition: Perfective aspect of 'кончать'; crude slang verb meaning 'to come' — to achieve orgasm, emphasizing completion of the climax.
records.notes: The perfective aspect signals a completed, bounded event: 'он кончил' = 'he came'; applies to all genders; the dominant colloquial verb for orgasm in Russian and effectively universal among adult speakers.

records.definition: Imperfective aspect of 'кончить'; crude slang verb meaning 'to be coming' — to be in the process of orgasming, expressing ongoing action or habitual behavior.
records.notes: Imperfective aspect foregrounds the ongoing process: 'я кончаю' = 'I'm coming'; aspectual verbal pair with perfective 'кончить'; both forms are near-universal in adult Russian sexual vocabulary.

records.definition: Perfective verb meaning 'to flood/fill/pour into'; in sexual contexts, to ejaculate on or inside a partner.
records.notes: More general than English 'creampie': 'залить лицо' = facial ejaculation; 'залить внутрь' = internal ejaculation (creampie); the bare verb is act-agnostic without a qualifier; mapped to 'creampie' as closest registry entry.

records.definition: Primary meaning is mechanical lubricant or grease; in sexual contexts refers to vaginal lubrication or artificial sexual lubricant.
records.notes: The non-sexual meaning (grease, machine oil) is the dominant sense; the sexual meaning is secondary but universally understood; functions as the Russian equivalent of English 'lube'.

records.definition: Clinical plural noun meaning 'secretions/discharge'; in sexual and medical contexts refers to any genital secretions, including normal arousal fluid and pathological discharge.
records.notes: Contextually ambiguous without a modifier: вагинальные выделения (vaginal secretions), патологические выделения (pathological discharge); commonly encountered in gynecological and sexual-health contexts.

records.definition: Everyday word for 'juice'; used as a colloquial or playful euphemism for vaginal lubrication or sexual fluids.
records.notes: Shares the food-fluid metaphor with English slang 'juice'; most commonly applied to vaginal lubrication but can denote any sexual fluid in context; the euphemistic use is understood by essentially all adult speakers.

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'squirt'; female ejaculatory fluid expelled during intense sexual arousal or orgasm.
records.notes: Entered Russian via internet pornography; noun form referring to the fluid itself; paired with verbal noun 'сквиртинг' for the act.

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'squirting'; the act of female ejaculation — forceful expulsion of fluid from the urethra or vaginal area during sexual arousal or orgasm.
records.notes: Verbal noun/gerund form corresponding to the noun 'сквирт'; source romanization 'skvicting' in the input list is a transcription error; correct romanization is 'skvirting'.

records.definition: Clinical loanword meaning 'erection'; the state of penile tumescence caused by vascular engorgement during sexual arousal or other stimuli.
Colloquial verb meaning to have an erection; literally 'to stand,' used in phrases such as 'у него стоит' (he's hard).
records.notes: Imperfective aspect denotes ongoing erect state. Transparent body-position metaphor. Paired with perfective встать for the onset of erection.

records.definition: Colloquial perfective verb meaning to get an erection; literally 'to stand up/rise,' as in 'у него встал' (he got hard).
records.notes: Perfective aspect marks the transition to erection rather than the sustained state. Aspectual pair of стоять. Equally common and equally non-stigmatized in informal speech.

records.definition: Colloquial verb meaning to stick out or protrude; in sexual context describes an erect or visibly prominent penis.
records.notes: Broad polysemy beyond sex: also means to jut out, to be high on drugs (slang). In sexual use it foregrounds protrusion/visibility. Slightly more crude than стоять because the visual image is more explicit.

records.definition: Sexual arousal or excitement; the physical and psychological state of being turned on; used both clinically and in everyday speech.
records.notes: Polysemous: equally standard for non-sexual excitement (crowd agitation, nervous energy). Clinical texts and popular discourse use the same word without register shift.

records.definition: Orgasm; the climax of sexual excitement; direct loanword from Greek/Latin via European languages, fully naturalized in Russian.
records.notes: Entered Russian in the 20th century. Used without stigma across medical, popular-science, and colloquial registers. No strong crude valence; primarily a technical loanword repurposed colloquially.

records.definition: Euphemism for sexual release or orgasm; literally 'discharge' or 'tension release'; polysemous with the political term for Cold War détente.
records.notes: The détente meaning (разрядка напряжённости) is equally well-known. Sexual usage exploits the identical mechanics of tension-discharge. Low crude score reflects the euphemistic distance from explicit vocabulary.

records.definition: Noun form of the crude slang verb кончать/кончить (to cum); refers to orgasm or ejaculation, predominantly in male contexts.
records.notes: The underlying verb кончать (to finish) is one of the most common Russian sexual slang verbs. The noun кончание is less frequent than the verb itself but fully understood. Also carries the non-sexual meaning of 'ending/finishing.'

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'cumshot'; the pornographic depiction of visible external male ejaculation.
records.notes: Opaque to older and porn-naive speakers. Recognized primarily among younger demographics and online pornography consumers. Spelling varies (камшот / кам-шот).

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'creampie'; ejaculation inside a partner's vagina or anus without a condom, or the visible result.
records.notes: Narrow reach: mainly used in online pornography forums and communities. Not recognized by a general adult audience. Transliteration reflects approximate Russian phonology of the English source.

records.definition: Clinical/technical loanword for vaginal lubrication; the secretion of moisture by the vaginal walls during sexual arousal.
records.notes: Primarily clinical and educational register. General population more likely to use descriptive phrases. Also used for mechanical lubrication (engines, machinery), which shares the same Russian word.

records.definition: Adjective meaning sexually aroused or excited; adjectival form of возбуждение; equally valid in non-sexual contexts for general excitement.
records.notes: Same polysemy as the noun: 'возбуждённая толпа' = excited crowd, not a sexual crowd. The ё (yo) vowel is often written as е in informal text, producing 'возбужденный.'

records.definition: Adjective meaning lustful or lascivious; describing a person driven by excessive or overt sexual desire; carries a pejorative and judgmental tone.
records.notes: Derived from похоть (lust). Typically applied to others as a condemnation rather than self-applied. More elevated and literary than colloquial equivalents; frequency declining in everyday speech.

records.definition: Adjective meaning dissolute, licentious, or sexually immoral; implying chronic promiscuity and moral laxity.
records.notes: Etymological root of the historical figure's nickname Rasputin (Распутин). Implies not just occasional transgression but habitual moral looseness. Somewhat dated in everyday speech but widely recognized.

records.definition: Adjective meaning depraved, debauched, or morally corrupt; implies active sexual corruption slightly stronger than распутный.
records.notes: From развращать (to corrupt/deprave). Carries an implication of having been corrupted or of corrupting others, not merely of personal indulgence. Stronger moral weight than распутный.

records.definition: Archaic adjective meaning wanton, lecherous, or given to fornication; derived from блуд (fornication), carrying strong religious-moral overtones.
records.notes: From Old Church Slavonic блудъ (fornication; also wandering/straying from righteousness). Still appears in historical and religious texts. General recognition is lower among speakers under 40. Note: блудливая кошка = a cat that strays; the animal idiom kept some currency.

records.definition: Colloquial adjective literally meaning 'preoccupied' or 'worried,' but so thoroughly adopted as slang for sex-obsessed that the sexual sense dominates in informal speech.
records.notes: Classic Russian semantic shift: the formal word for 'concerned/preoccupied' became slang for someone preoccupied specifically with sex. Context usually disambiguates but in informal speech the sexual reading is the default assumption.

records.definition: Adjective meaning passionate or ardent; in romantic and sexual contexts describes intense, fervent desire or physical expression.
records.notes: Positive connotation; страстный поцелуй = passionate kiss. Applies equally to non-sexual contexts (a passionate speaker, a passionate love of music). Not inherently condemning; low crude score reflects cultural neutrality.

records.definition: Noun meaning lust or carnal desire; intense sexual appetite used in both secular literary and Orthodox religious-moral contexts.
records.notes: In Orthodox theology, похоть is one of the passions (страсти) to be overcome. The moral-condemnatory register is therefore always latent even in secular literary use. Root shared with похотливый.

records.definition: Noun meaning intense longing or sexual craving; more poetic and elevated than похоть, with emphasis on yearning rather than moral condemnation.
records.notes: High-register literary term used by Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and other canonical authors. The yearning quality distinguishes it from the more condemnatory похоть. Active use declining in contemporary speech; primarily recognized through literary exposure.

records.definition: Noun meaning voluptuousness or sensuality; literally 'sweet passion'; describes abandoned, pleasurable indulgence in carnal sensation.
records.notes: Compound of сладкий (sweet) + страсть (passion). Classic 19th-century literary register; sharply less common in contemporary speech. English 'voluptuousness' and 'sensuality' are only approximate — the Russian retains a heady, almost intoxicated quality the English lacks.

records.definition: Adjective meaning voluptuous, sensuous, or pleasure-seeking; the adjectival form of сладострастие, used to describe a sensuous gaze, voluptuous form, or lascivious manner.
records.notes: Adjectival counterpart of сладострастие. Marked decline in active use compared to 19th-century literature; recognized mainly by readers of classical Russian texts or educated speakers.

records.definition: Noun meaning passion; intense consuming emotion including romantic desire, sexual appetite, or zealous drive; a foundational term in Russian romantic discourse.
records.notes: One of the most versatile high-frequency emotional nouns in Russian. In sexual contexts страсть implies consuming, uncontrollable desire. Not inherently vulgar — the low crude score reflects its use across registers without stigma.

records.definition: Noun meaning desire or wish; in sexual contexts the standard neutral term for wanting or desiring another person.
records.notes: Fully neutral: equally valid for 'I desire you' and 'I want a new car.' No moral loading. Sexual reading is entirely context-dependent; the word itself carries no sexual valence.

records.definition: Verb meaning to want; the phrase 'я хочу тебя' (I want you) is the most common everyday Russian expression of sexual desire.
records.notes: The standard 'to want' verb with no inherent sexual meaning; sexual reading entirely dependent on object ('тебя' = you). Slightly blunter register than желать in sexual contexts due to everyday directness. Very slightly higher crude score than желать for this reason.

records.definition: Verb meaning to desire or wish for; in sexual contexts a more literary and intense-sounding form of хотеть; 'я желаю тебя' = I desire you.
records.notes: More elevated register than хотеть; желать sounds more deliberate, poetic, or formal in a sexual context. Both verbs take the genitive of the person desired ('тебя'), but желать is more marked stylistically and less colloquial.

records.definition: Russian colloquial noun for sexual obsessiveness or preoccupation; used pejoratively to label someone—especially a man—whose thoughts and behavior are dominated by sex to a creepy or pathetic degree.
records.notes: Base adjective озабоченный (sexually preoccupied) is extremely common; the nominalized form names the quality or condition. Distinct from clinical hypersexuality—more of a lay moral judgment.

records.definition: Clinical and colloquial Russian adjective meaning sexually frigid; applied almost exclusively to women who lack sexual responsiveness or desire.
records.notes: Borrowed from Latin frigidus via medical terminology; carries a pejorative undertone despite clinical framing; the gendering of the term mirrors its English usage.

records.definition: Clinical Russian noun for sexual frigidity; the condition of lacking sexual responsiveness, desire, or arousal, applied predominantly to women.
records.notes: Standard nominalized form of фригидный; appeared extensively in Soviet-era popular-science and medical literature; now largely replaced by clinical descriptors of hypoactive sexual desire disorder.

records.definition: Freudian loanword for libido; the psychological energy or drive associated with sexual instinct, as defined in psychoanalytic theory and contemporary sexology.
records.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian; entered via Freudian translations. Mapped to 'lust' as nearest registry concept, but libido is specifically the neutral psychoanalytic drive-energy—not raw craving.

records.definition: Russian clinical and everyday noun for sexual potency; the capacity for sexual performance, especially a man's ability to achieve and sustain an erection.
records.notes: Recognition is high partly due to saturation of erectile-dysfunction advertising in Russian-language media. Carries strong cultural weight: male identity is closely tied to потенция.

records.definition: Clinical Russian adjective meaning impotent; unable to achieve or sustain an erection; also used figuratively as an emasculating insult meaning powerless or ineffectual.
records.notes: The figurative insult usage ('politically impotent,' 'он импотент в жизни') is very common in Russian and amplifies the shame attached to the literal sexual sense.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning dissolute, sexually unrestrained, or morally undisciplined; applied to a person who indulges in licentiousness without self-control or shame.
records.notes: Literally 'let loose' or 'undone'; conveys both general moral laxity and specifically sexual promiscuity depending on context; used of either sex but carries harsher stigma when applied to women.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning insatiable; in sexual contexts, describing a person with an unquenchable or excessive sexual appetite.
records.notes: A general-purpose word for 'insatiable' applied to sex by context; not exclusively sexual. Can be complimentary or pejorative depending on tone.

records.definition: Russian noun for a lecherous man; a male driven by uncontrollable lust who obsessively and inappropriately pursues sexual gratification.
records.notes: Derived from похоть (lust, concupiscence); masculine agentive suffix -ник. Implies not only desire but shameless or predatory pursuit of it. Feminine counterpart is похотница.

records.definition: Russian pejorative noun for an excessively lustful or lecherous woman; the feminine counterpart of похотник, labeling a woman perceived as driven by shameless, uncontrolled sexual desire.
records.notes: Less common than its masculine counterpart; reflects the double standard in Russian culture: female lust is more harshly stigmatized. Not clinical—purely a social insult.

records.definition: Russian noun for a libertine or debauchee; a person, typically male, who pursues sexual pleasure without moral restraint and who actively corrupts others.
records.notes: Derived from развращать (to corrupt or deprave); carries stronger moral condemnation than the English 'libertine,' which can be used admiringly. Feminine form развратница exists but is less common than распутница.

records.definition: Russian pejorative noun for a sexually promiscuous or morally dissolute woman; a common and contemptuous slur for a woman of perceived loose morals.
records.notes: Shares the etymological root with the surname Rasputin (Распутин), from распутный (unchaste, dissipate); implies not just sexual promiscuity but comprehensive moral degradation.

records.definition: Russian literary noun for lasciviousness or wantonness; the quality of being habitually and shamelessly lustful, sexually forward, or lecherous.
records.notes: From блуд (fornication, lust), a term with deep Old Church Slavonic roots; блудливый (the adjective) survives in colloquial use more robustly than this nominalized form, which is largely literary.

records.definition: Russian literary noun for a sweet, languid erotic or amorous yearning; a pleasantly aching desire tinged with melancholy, distinct from urgent lust.
records.notes: No single English equivalent captures the full blend of desire, yearning, and bittersweet physical suffering; highly characteristic of 19th-century Russian literary eroticism (Pushkin, Turgenev, Fet). The sexual sense is implied by context.

records.definition: Russian literary phrase meaning 'the call of the flesh'; refers to carnal desire or the bodily sexual impulse, typically contrasted with spiritual or rational self-control.
records.notes: Stock phrase in Russian literary and religious discourse; плоть (flesh) carries Old Church Slavonic connotations of the sinful body distinct from тело (body in a neutral sense). Appears in theological as well as secular literary contexts.

records.definition: Russian clinical and everyday noun for attraction or drive; in Freudian-influenced Russian psychology, the direct equivalent of Trieb (drive/instinct); in everyday use, any compelling pull toward a person or object.
records.notes: Polysemous: sexual sense must be inferred from context. The Freudian mapping to 'drive' makes it more clinical than the English 'attraction'; commonly appears in phrases like влечение к женщинам (attraction to women).

records.definition: Standard Russian clinical compound phrase for sexual attraction or sexual drive; the most neutral and unambiguous formal term for libido in contemporary usage.
records.notes: Preferred in psychology, sexology, and medical contexts. Less emotionally loaded than colloquial synonyms; the registry concept 'lust' is an imprecise match—this phrase is closer in register to 'sexual drive' or 'libido.'

records.definition: Slightly dated Russian clinical phrase for sexual drive or libido using половой (of or pertaining to sex/genitalia) rather than the more modern сексуальный.
records.notes: Soviet-era clinical usage; половой sounds more anatomical and dated than сексуальный and has been gradually displaced in post-Soviet medical writing. Still encountered in translated Freud and pre-1990 Soviet sexology texts.

records.definition: Russian clinical adjective meaning homosexual; describing a person sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of the same sex.
records.notes: Neutral in register but carries heavy social stigma in the Russian context, amplified by the 2013 and 2023 'gay propaganda' legislation that made public use of this word in affirming contexts legally fraught.

records.definition: Russian clinical and journalistic noun for homosexuality as an orientation, practice, or social phenomenon; associated with Soviet-era pathologizing of same-sex attraction.
records.notes: The -изм suffix carries a pathologizing or ideological flavor absent from the English -ity suffix; гомосексуальность is increasingly preferred in affirming or academically neutral contexts; гомосексуализм is retained in conservative and official state discourse.

records.definition: Russian clinical adjective meaning heterosexual; describing a person sexually attracted exclusively to people of a different sex.
records.notes: Rarely appears in everyday Russian speech; speakers default to leaving heterosexuality unmarked. Mainly used in clinical, sociological, or comparative contexts where orientation must be specified explicitly.

records.definition: Russian clinical adjective meaning bisexual; describing a person sexually and/or romantically attracted to people of more than one gender.
records.notes: Recognition is rising with global media; colloquially shortened to бисекс. Bisexuality has lower political visibility in Russia than homosexuality because the 'propaganda' legislation focuses primarily on same-sex relationships.

records.definition: Standard Russian noun for a lesbian; a woman who is sexually and/or romantically attracted to other women.
records.notes: Derived from the Greek island Lesbos, as in English; dictionary-neutral in register but frequently deployed derogatorily in Russian colloquial speech; subject to 'gay propaganda' law restrictions in affirming public discourse since 2013.

records.definition: Russian loanword from English 'gay'; refers primarily to a homosexual man, though sometimes used as a broader LGBTQ+ umbrella term.
records.notes: Post-Soviet loanword that largely displaced педераст in neutral and self-identifying usage. In Russian political and legal discourse it carries intense stigma amplified by the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling classifying the 'international LGBT movement' as extremist.

records.definition: Russian loanword for transgender; a person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth.
records.notes: Partially declinable in Russian (трансгендера, трансгендеру, etc.). Russia's 2023 legislation banning legal gender reassignment and recognition has made this term highly politically charged; official discourse tends to avoid or erase it entirely.

records.definition: Clinical Russian loanword for a transsexual person; one whose gender identity differs from their birth sex, historically implying desire for or completion of medical and surgical transition.
records.notes: Increasingly supplanted in clinical and activist Russian by 'трансгендер'; 'транссексуал' retains the older surgery-focused connotation and is still the more widely recognized of the two forms.

records.definition: Russian loanword for 'asexual'; a person who experiences little or no sexual attraction to others.
records.notes: Recognition concentrated among younger urban Russians and online communities; widely misunderstood as synonymous with celibacy by general audiences.

records.definition: Russian transliteration of 'queer'; umbrella term for non-heterosexual and/or non-cisgender identities, used primarily by LGBTQ+ activists and community members inside Russia.
records.notes: Carries the reclaimed activist valence of English 'queer' but penetration outside urban LGBTQ+ circles is minimal; largely opaque to older Russians and those outside major cities.

records.definition: Russian clinical loanword for 'intersex'; a person born with sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary male or female definitions.
records.notes: Rarely encountered outside clinical or activist contexts; general Russian public awareness of the term is very low.

records.definition: Russian loanword for 'pansexual'; a person sexually and/or romantically attracted to others regardless of sex or gender identity.
records.notes: Very low recognition outside urban LGBTQ+ communities and Russian-language internet spaces; often conflated with bisexuality even among those who know the word.

records.definition: Russian calque of 'non-binary'; identifying as having a gender identity that does not fall exclusively within male or female categories.
records.notes: Essentially confined to urban activist and online LGBTQ+ discourse; generates strong negative reactions in mainstream Russian media and politics, particularly post-2023 legislative environment.

records.definition: Russian colloquial label for a heterosexual person, literally 'a natural one'; widely used in contrast to gay or bisexual identity, with an implicit claim that heterosexuality is the natural default state.
records.notes: The normativity embedded in the term makes it ideologically loaded even when used without hostile intent; common in everyday Russian speech across age groups.

records.definition: Clipped Russian loanword for 'hetero(sexual)'; a neutral, everyday abbreviation for a heterosexual person or orientation.
records.notes: More clinical-sounding than 'натурал' and entirely neutral in connotation; common in both casual conversation and online identity discourse.

records.definition: Russian abbreviation for 'bisexual'; a person attracted to more than one gender; widely recognized and generally used without strong vulgarity in isolation.
records.notes: High recognition across age groups due to widespread use in media and internet discourse; no particular vulgarity attaches to the abbreviation itself regardless of attitudes toward bisexuality.

records.definition: Russian abbreviation for 'trans(gender)' or 'trans(sexual)'; broadly used shorthand identity label that is affirming within LGBTQ+ community contexts but often dismissive or contemptuous in mainstream Russian usage.
records.notes: Register is sharply context-dependent; particularly charged given Russia's anti-LGBTQ+ legislative environment post-2023; crude score elevated above English 'trans' because it more frequently appears in hostile framing in Russian public discourse.

records.definition: Russian loanword for 'drag queen'; a person, typically a gay man, who performs exaggerated femininity through elaborate costume, makeup, and theatrical presentation.
records.notes: Recognition boosted significantly by RuPaul's Drag Race and its local derivatives; gay_queen is the closest registry concept but does not fully capture the performance-art specificity of drag; the practice faces increasing legal hostility in Russia.

records.definition: Russian loanword for 'drag king'; a person, typically a woman or non-binary individual, who performs exaggerated masculinity through costume, prosthetics, and theatrical performance.
records.notes: Significantly less recognized than 'дрэг-квин' even within LGBTQ+ communities; cross_dressing is the closest registry concept but does not capture the staged performance-art specificity of drag king practice.

records.definition: Russian loanword for 'crossdresser'; a person who habitually wears clothing typically associated with a gender other than their own, for any motivation including performance, gender expression, or sexual arousal.
records.notes: Mostly confined to LGBTQ+ community usage and online spaces; the average Russian adult may have encountered the term passively but is unlikely to use it spontaneously in conversation.

records.definition: The most common and most severe Russian slur for a gay man, derived from 'педераст'; deployed both as an extreme homophobic insult and as a general-purpose expletive equivalent to 'motherfucker' or 'asshole.'
records.notes: One of the most culturally taboo words in Russian; severity is comparable to the n-word in American English; despite that severity it appears far more frequently in ordinary Russian speech than equivalents do in English, reflecting lower baseline social censure in Russian public culture.

records.definition: Intensified and phonetically extended form of 'пидор'; the added syllable '-ас' amplifies contempt; used as both a homophobic slur and an extreme general-purpose insult.
records.notes: Considered slightly more emphatic and deliberate than 'пидор'; the form typically chosen when the speaker wants to project maximum contempt rather than casual swearing; both forms traverse all social registers in Russian speech.

records.definition: Regional and phonetic variant of 'пидор' with a shifted vowel; carries identical homophobic and expletive force but is less universally standard across Russian-speaking regions.
records.notes: More prevalent in certain regional dialects; fully interchangeable with 'пидор' in most contexts but less frequent in standard Moscow-register colloquial Russian.

records.definition: Diminutive-inflected colloquial slur for a gay man derived from 'гомо-' (homo-); less explosively offensive than 'пидор' but clearly derogatory, with a mocking rather than furious tone.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix '-ик' gives the word a sneering or condescending quality rather than raw aggression; widely understood across all age groups; sits at the milder end of the Russian gay-slur spectrum.

records.definition: Literally 'light blue'; a Soviet-era and post-Soviet coded euphemism for a gay man, exploiting an entrenched Russian cultural association between the color light blue and male homosexuality.
records.notes: The color association is so deep that Russian speakers sometimes avoid the innocent sense of 'light blue' to prevent ambiguity; analogous in mechanism to English 'gay' displacing its older meaning of 'happy.' The origin of the color coding is debated but predates the Soviet period.

records.definition: Clipped derogatory abbreviation of 'гомосексуалист' (homosexual); used as a slur for gay men with explicit etymological connection to the clinical term, giving it a sneering pseudo-clinical quality.
records.notes: Sits in severity between 'гомик' and 'пидор'; the truncation of '-сексуалист' to '-сек' carries contempt without the raw force of the most taboo forms; common in anti-LGBTQ+ discourse in mainstream Russian media and online spaces.

records.definition: Diminutive-derived slur for a gay man, clipped from 'педераст'; moderately severe, carrying both homophobic force and general-purpose contempt.
records.notes: Despite derivation from 'педераст' (etymologically: adult-child sexual contact), in contemporary Russian usage 'педик' functions purely as a gay slur with no necessary implication of pedophilia; few speakers are conscious of the etymological link.

records.definition: In Russian colloquial usage, a severe slur for a gay man; though etymologically and clinically referring to adult sexual contact with male minors, in everyday Russian speech it functions as a general homophobic insult with that clinical meaning effectively lost.
records.notes: Critical disambiguation: the Russian colloquial meaning (gay man) diverges sharply from the clinical English meaning (pederasty); the technical score is elevated because the word's form retains a quasi-clinical legibility, but the crude use dominates overwhelmingly in practice.

records.definition: Russian borrowing of the English slur 'faggot'; used as a homophobic insult for gay men, particularly among younger speakers exposed to English-language internet and media culture.
records.notes: Secondary homonym conflict: 'фагот' is also the standard Russian word for the bassoon (woodwind instrument), creating occasional unintentional ambiguity in written text; the slur usage is unambiguously an English loanword.

records.definition: Colloquial and mildly derogatory Russian term for a lesbian; shorter and cruder than the clinical 'лесбиянка' but considerably less severe than 'лесбуха'; partially reclaimed within Russian lesbian communities.
records.notes: Occupies an ambiguous register: clearly informal and often pejorative when used by outsiders, but sometimes neutral or self-referential within lesbian communities; its dual-use dynamics parallel English 'dyke' in its reclaimed-vs-slur tension.

records.definition: Pejorative Russian term for a lesbian; the augmentative-derogatory suffix '-уха' adds contempt compared to 'лесба,' making this the more openly hostile of the common lesbian slur forms.
records.notes: The '-уха' suffix in Russian typically signals augmentation with contempt or dismissal; less amenable to reclamation than 'лесба' due to its overtly derogatory morphological marking.

records.definition: Playful or mildly mocking Russian term for a lesbian, derived from the Greek island of Lesbos (the etymological namesake of lesbianism); used humorously, derogatorily, or sometimes neutrally depending on context.
records.notes: The Lesbos reference gives the word a more literary or ironic register than 'лесбуха'; less aggressive in tone, occasionally used without strong pejorative intent in humorous contexts; lower recognition than 'лесба' or 'лесбуха.'

records.definition: Offensive Russian slur for a transgender person, clipped from 'транс' (trans); used to mock or dehumanize trans individuals.
records.notes: Functional parallel to English 'tranny'; uniformly offensive, not reclaimed; usage growing as trans visibility and anti-trans discourse both intensify in Russia.

records.definition: A pervert or sexual deviant; a person with socially condemned or atypical sexual interests or behavior.
records.notes: The standard Russian word for 'pervert'; straddles colloquial and mildly formal register; applied broadly to any sexual nonconformist, not only those with clinical paraphilias.

records.definition: In Russian prison slang (феня), the lowest-status caste: men who have been forcibly sexually degraded and are permanently stigmatized as receptive; widely used outside prison as an extreme insult implying total irreversible social degradation.
records.notes: Literal meaning 'rooster'; the феня caste-system concept has no direct English equivalent — American prison slang 'punk' is roughly analogous but lacks the same elaborate permanent-social-death framing and ritual enforcement; being labeled петух is considered irreversible within criminal subculture hierarchy.

records.definition: Literally 'hole'; used crudely for the vagina or anus, and pejoratively for a person — especially a woman or gay man — reduced to their sexual orifice, denying personhood.
records.notes: As a body-part reference it is contextually crude; as a person-insult it fully dehumanizes by reducing the target to a mere receptacle; closer in register to 'she's just a hole' than to 'cunt,' which carries more active hostility.

records.definition: Literally 'lowered/put down'; in Russian prison slang, a person who has been ritually or forcibly relegated to the петух caste through sexual humiliation; outside prison, an extreme insult for someone utterly and permanently socially degraded.
records.notes: The verb 'опустить' (to degrade someone into the петух caste) and this past-participle form name a concept pair with no English analogue: the idea of a permanent, ritually enacted sexual demotion that defines social status for life is specific to Russian/Soviet criminal subculture.

records.definition: A degenerate; a person considered morally or sexually depraved and beneath normal human behavioral standards.
records.notes: Loanword from German/Latin via early-20th-century scientific-racial discourse; retains pseudo-clinical flavor making it sound slightly more formal than 'извращенец'; widely deployed by Russian conservatives and Orthodox commentators as a catch-all condemnation of LGBTQ+ people.

records.definition: Sodomite; a biblical and legal-historical term for a man who practices anal sex, especially with another man; carries inherent religious condemnation derived from Genesis 18–19.
records.notes: Direct cognate of English 'sodomite'; used in Russian Orthodox and conservative political discourse; carries heavier implied theological condemnation than the more neutral clinical term 'гомосексуалист'.

records.definition: Literally 'one who lies with men'; an archaic ecclesiastical-legal term for a man who engages in male-male anal intercourse; the specific term used in Soviet Criminal Code Article 121 (in force until 1993).
records.notes: Article 121 of the Soviet Criminal Code used this term; decriminalisation in 1993 generated its recognition peak in public discourse; now archaic except in Orthodox Church texts; heavier legalistic-ecclesiastical register than 'содомит'; the compound муже- (man) + лож- (lie/lay) is Church Slavonic in character.

records.definition: Literally 'fucked your mother'; one of the most powerful Russian mat curses, expressing extreme anger, contempt, or shock.
records.notes: Structurally a past-tense declarative ('I fucked your mother') rather than the English nominal form 'motherfucker'; abbreviated in writing as ЁТМ; the maternal violation is a culturally salient axis of Russian obscenity that may carry greater symbolic weight than the English equivalent.

records.definition: Literally 'go to the cock'; the canonical Russian directive meaning 'fuck off' or 'go fuck yourself.'
records.notes: Directional preposition 'на' + 'хуй' (cock/dick); parallel constructions: 'иди на хер,' 'иди в жопу'; among the most common dismissal phrases in Russian mat; deployed in anger, contempt, or exasperated dismissal.

records.definition: Literally 'to the cock'; standalone expletive meaning 'fuck off,' 'to hell with it,' 'no way,' or used as a general crude intensifier of negation and dismissal.
records.notes: Shorter standalone form of 'иди нахуй'; extremely versatile — intensifies refusals ('да нахуй!'), expresses disbelief, dismisses proposals, or punctuates contempt; one of the highest-frequency mat words in everyday spoken Russian.

records.definition: Derived from 'пизда' (cunt); used as a noun or interjection meaning 'it's all fucked,' 'total disaster,' 'we're doomed,' or 'the end'; the ultimate word for a complete and irredeemable catastrophe.
records.notes: Functions as a catastrophe noun ('это был пиздец' = 'it was a total disaster') and as a one-word doom verdict ('пиздец' = 'we're completely fucked'); closest English approximations are 'clusterfuck' or 'FUBAR,' though пиздец also functions as a standalone interjection of finality.

records.definition: Derived from 'хуй' (cock/dick); a predicative adverb or short-form adjective meaning 'shittily,' 'terribly,' or 'it's bad/awful.'
records.notes: 'Мне хуёво' = 'I feel like shit / I feel terrible'; 'всё хуёво' = 'everything sucks'; mirrors the grammatical slot of 'хорошо' (good/well) but is emphatically crude; one of several хуй-derived quality-descriptors covering negative states.

records.definition: Derived from 'хуй' (cock/dick); a noun meaning 'bullshit,' 'nonsense,' 'crap,' or 'a worthless thing'; extremely versatile as a dismissive term for arguments, objects, or situations.
records.notes: One of the most common mat nouns in everyday speech; grammatically feminine; dismisses arguments ('это полная хуйня' = 'this is total bullshit'), refers to broken or worthless objects, or expresses contempt for a situation; less specifically tied to deception than 'пиздёж'.

records.definition: Derived from 'пизда' (cunt); a noun specifically meaning 'blatant lies,' 'bullshitting,' or 'a pack of nonsense'; the verbal form 'пиздеть' means to lie or to talk obvious nonsense.
records.notes: More semantically specific than 'хуйня' — пиздёж primarily connotes falsehood rather than general worthlessness; 'это пиздёж' = 'this is bullshit/lies'; the counterpart verb 'пиздеть' means specifically to bullshit or lie, distinguishing it functionally from other mat nouns.

records.definition: Derived from archaic 'муда' (testicles); an asshole, jerk, or thoroughly contemptible person; one of the most common Russian insults for someone who is selfish, stupid, or unpleasant.
records.notes: Among the most widely used mat insults in everyday Russian; gender-neutral in application despite the masculine-anatomical etymology; the root 'муда' survives only in derivatives such as мудак and мудила.

records.definition: An emphatic variant of 'мудак'; a contemptible, stupid, or offensive person, with added contempt or colorfulness relative to the base form.
records.notes: The suffix '-ила' adds intensity or pejorative emphasis; perceived as slightly more archaic or regional than мудак; the two forms are often interchangeable but мудила carries a heavier or more exasperated register.

records.definition: Past passive participle of 'ёбать' (to fuck); used as an intensifying adjective meaning 'fucking,' as in 'ёбаный идиот' (fucking idiot), expressing disgust, exasperation, or emphasis.
records.notes: Functions grammatically as an attributive adjective and applies freely to non-human targets ('ёбаная машина' = 'fucking car'); the exclamation 'ёбаный в рот!' is an extreme interjection of shock or irritation; one of the most productive mat modifiers in Russian.

records.definition: One of the five canonical Russian mat words; primary meaning 'whore' or 'slut'; secondary use as a general expletive equivalent to 'fuck!' or 'damn!' when deployed as a standalone interjection.
records.notes: Church Slavonic root meaning 'fornication/harlotry'; alongside хуй, пизда, ёбать, and пиздец forms the core of Russian mat; its standalone interjection function ('блядь!' expressing shock or pain) is as frequent as its person-insult function; both misogynistic target-insult and all-purpose expletive.

records.definition: An emphatic augmentative of 'блядь'; 'a total whore' — a more contemptuous form of the same insult, typically directed at a woman regarded as particularly promiscuous or contemptible.
records.notes: The suffix '-ина' creates an augmentative-pejorative; used primarily as a direct person-insult rather than a standalone expletive, distinguishing it from 'блядь' which freely serves both functions.

records.definition: A minced oath substitute for 'блядь'; literally 'badge' or 'metal plate,' repurposed as a mild expletive for contexts where the full mat word is socially unacceptable.
records.notes: The extended form 'бляха-муха' (literally 'badge-fly') is also common; phonetic proximity to 'блядь' carries the emotional resonance while avoiding the taboo; crude score is low because the word itself navigates around the transgression; widely used in media, at work, and around children.

records.definition: Derived from 'ёбать' (to fuck); means 'crazy,' 'nuts,' or 'fucked in the head'; describes a person whose behavior is wildly irrational or beyond all reason.
records.notes: Not primarily a sexual insult despite its etymology; functions semantically like 'batshit crazy' or 'fucking nuts'; can be used with affectionate exasperation ('ты ёбанутый?' = 'are you crazy?') as well as genuine contempt; cf. ёбаный, which acts as an intensifier adjective rather than a descriptor of mental state.

records.definition: Slut or whore; one of the most common Russian insults for a woman regarded as sexually promiscuous; also used as a general-purpose strong insult.
records.notes: Slightly less crude in register than 'блядь' (the canonical mat word for the same concept) but unambiguously offensive; derivation possibly from German 'Schlucht' or a Slavic root meaning to drag/trail; the standard non-mat equivalent of 'блядь' in the slut-shame register; the two words are largely interchangeable in practice.

records.definition: A dated Russian slur for a sexually promiscuous woman; 'tramp,' 'tart,' or 'trollop'; connotes a woman who chases after men or is sexually available, with an archaic flavor relative to 'шлюха'.
records.notes: From the verb 'тащить' (to drag/pull); the image is of a woman trailing after men; less vulgar than 'шлюха' and more archaic; more common in literature and older speech; recognition has declined among speakers under 35.

records.definition: Literally 'female dog'; used as a general-purpose insult for a contemptible, unpleasant, or treacherous person, especially a woman; also carries the specific meaning of 'traitor' or 'snitch' in prison and criminal slang.
records.notes: The criminal-subculture secondary meaning (сука = informer/traitor) is an additional semantic layer absent from English 'bitch'; in everyday use closely parallels English 'bitch' in full range — woman insult, person-insult, intensifier, and occasionally a term of address between friends.

records.definition: Diminutive of сука (female dog); used as a contemptuous insult for a promiscuous or treacherous woman, or as a general intensified pejorative.
records.notes: The diminutive suffix -ка creates a tone simultaneously more intimate and more snide than the base word сука; occasionally affectionate when addressing pets or women one is fond of, but harshly insulting in most contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'dry masturbation'; used figuratively for a frustratingly futile activity that consumes effort and yields nothing.
records.notes: The primary contemporary meaning is fully desexualized — 'это суходрочка' = 'this is a pointless waste of effort.' The dry (сухой) component implies joyless futility; you exhaust yourself and get nothing. Sexual etymology is transparent to speakers and adds contemptuous coloring.

records.definition: Perfective verb derived from ёбать (to fuck); to exhaust, pester, or annoy someone to the absolute limit of endurance.
records.notes: Completely desexualized in primary use: 'он меня заёбал' = 'he has exhausted my patience completely / driven me absolutely crazy.' The за- prefix marks completive or excessive action. Among the most common ёб- derivatives in everyday speech.

records.definition: Literally 'fucked in the mouth'; a stand-alone exclamatory expletive expressing extreme frustration or shock, not a description of an act.
records.notes: Phrasal expletive rather than a single word. 'Ёбаный в рот!' functions as a pure exclamation equivalent to 'fucking hell!' or 'Jesus Christ!' The oral sex imagery is completely idiomatized; no sexual meaning survives in use.

records.definition: Anatomically, the glans penis or the fold of foreskin that retracts; used as a strong insult for a stupid, contemptible person.
records.notes: The anatomical meaning is immediately legible to speakers, reinforcing the vulgarity. As an insult it functions like 'dickhead' but is considered somewhat stronger; the specific anatomical referent (glans or foreskin fold) adds a crudeness that the English compound lacks.

records.definition: Literally 'a dick in a coat'; an idiomatic dismissive phrase used as a sarcastic non-answer meaning 'nothing,' 'not a chance,' or as a stand-in for something utterly worthless.
records.notes: Functions as a deadpan response to 'what did you get?' — the answer is хуй в пальто = absolutely nothing. The 'в пальто' (in a coat) component is purely idiomatic with no independent semantic contribution. Less widely known than core single-word mat.

records.definition: Adjective derived from пизда (cunt/vagina); meaning 'excellent, great, fucking awesome' — a strongly positive evaluation despite the maximally crude root.
records.notes: Canonical semantic reversal: the most vulgar Russian word for vagina becomes a positive superlative adjective. 'Пиздатая машина' = 'an awesome car.' Still firmly in the crude register — not usable in polite company — but the meaning is unambiguously positive.

records.definition: Reflexive verb derived from пизда; to go crazy, lose one's mind, or do something utterly unhinged or reckless.
records.english_term: to lose one's fucking mind / to go nuts
records.notes: Also carries a literal physical sense of 'to slam/crash into something' (пиздануться об стену = to slam into a wall), but the mental-state meaning dominates in casual insult usage.

records.definition: Imperfective verb derived from пизда with three fully desexualized meanings: 1) to beat or thrash someone; 2) to steal or pilfer; 3) to lie or talk nonsense continuously.
records.english_term: to beat (sense 1) / to steal (sense 2) / to bullshit (sense 3)
records.notes: Rare triple polysemy from a single crude anatomical root. Context always disambiguates among assault, theft, and deception. All three senses are fully desexualized and extremely common in colloquial Russian.

records.definition: Person noun derived from пизда; a chronically irresponsible, slovenly, and unreliable individual who can never be counted on to do anything properly.
records.english_term: fuckup (noun for an unreliable, slovenly person)
records.notes: Implies habitual irresponsibility and carelessness rather than malice; closer to 'fuckup' or 'screw-up' than 'asshole.' 'Он полный распиздяй' = 'He's a total fuckup / completely unreliable.'

records.definition: Agent noun from ёбать (to fuck); one who fucks around a lot; a sexually voracious individual; also used loosely as a general insult for an annoying or troublesome person.
records.notes: The sexual meaning (someone with many partners) can carry grudging admiration or contempt depending on context; the generalized insult meaning ('some fucker') is fully desexualized. Less commonly known than other ёб- derivatives.

records.definition: Compound of муде (archaic/dialectal for testicles) + звонить (to ring/call); an idiot, windbag, or nuisance who constantly pesters others with idiotic chatter.
records.notes: The 'ringing' element implies someone who calls/makes noise constantly but says nothing of value. The archaic testicle root (муде, not the common яйца) gives the word a slightly literary flavor while remaining crude. Implies more blowhard-nuisance than malice.

records.definition: Compound of хуй (cock) + сосать (to suck); literally 'cocksucker'; one of the most severe general insults in Russian mat, equivalent in force to 'cocksucker' in American English.
records.notes: Near-direct structural calque of the English 'cocksucker.' Used almost exclusively as a pure insult for a contemptible, servile, or despised person rather than as a literal description of sexual behavior.

records.definition: Compound adjective meaning 'cunt-eyed'; applied to a person with a dull, vacant, or stupidly oblivious expression.
records.notes: Less widely known than core mat vocabulary; the compound structure (пизда + глаз) feels productively derived and somewhat improvised or creative. No structural English equivalent — 'cunt-eyed' does not exist as a compound insult in English.

records.definition: Reflexive verb derived from ёбать; to show off, put on airs, or act in an ostentatiously superior or pretentious manner; to be insufferably full of oneself.
records.english_term: to show off / to be a prick about it
records.notes: Completely desexualized. 'Не выёбывайся!' = 'Stop showing off!' or 'Cut the crap!' The crude root adds contemptuous coloring to the showing-off behavior. Common in everyday speech across age groups.

records.definition: Imperfective verb derived from ёбать; to deceive, swindle, cheat, or trick someone; to fuck someone over.
records.notes: 'Он меня наёбывает' = 'He's conning me / fucking me over.' The perfective наебать is extremely common. Fully desexualized — no erotic connotation survives in usage. One of the core mat verbs for deception.

records.definition: Noun derived from ёбать; something of extremely poor quality, worthless junk, or meaningless nonsense.
records.notes: 'Это полная поёбень' = 'This is complete garbage/rubbish.' Less widely used than other ёб- derivatives; somewhat more colloquially marked or regional in feel. The abstract quality-noun derivation is productive in Russian mat morphology.

records.definition: Augmentative form of блядь (whore); an intensified insult for a woman considered sexually promiscuous or morally contemptible; also used as a strong general insult regardless of sex.
records.notes: The augmentative suffix -ина adds contemptuous intensification over блядь; can be directed at men as a general-contempt insult. One of the strongest single-word insults targeting female sexual conduct in Russian.

records.definition: A promiscuous or easy woman; a slut; somewhat less severe than блядь or шлюха, implying sexual looseness and unreliability rather than outright prostitution.
records.notes: Etymology uncertain, possibly from шалить (to misbehave / fool around); perceived as slightly milder than блядь in insult force, making it more usable in heated speech without fully escalating to maximum register.

records.definition: From давать (to give / to put out); a woman who readily gives sex to anyone who asks; an easy lay.
records.notes: Structurally transparent to any Russian speaker: the feminine agent noun of 'to give.' Focuses on sexual availability rather than moral condemnation; slightly milder in insult force than блядь or блядина.

records.definition: Literally 'bedding' or 'floor-mat'; used as an insult for a woman who is sexually used by many men and treated as an object without dignity or agency.
records.english_term: sexual doormat / mattress (slang for promiscuous woman)
records.notes: The object metaphor (something you lie on) captures the dehumanizing dimension effectively; implies not just promiscuity but being passively used without agency. Occasionally applied to weak-willed men in a non-sexual sense.

records.definition: A whore or slut; also used as a general expletive; borrowed into Russian from Polish/Ukrainian, where курва/kurwa is a ubiquitous all-purpose expletive equivalent to 'fuck.'
records.notes: In Polish and Ukrainian the word has largely lost its sexual meaning and functions like 'fuck' or 'shit'; in Russian it retains the 'whore' meaning more strongly. Perceived as slightly foreign/coarser due to the Slavic loanword origin.

records.definition: From Church Slavonic 'creature / created being'; used as a strong insult for a vile, despicable, or treacherous person of either sex.
records.notes: Not directly derived from sexual vocabulary — the etymology is religious/archaic. Less crude than core mat but carries intense moral contempt. Associated with Dostoyevsky ('тварь дрожащая' — 'trembling creature') and contemporary political speech. Severity is moderate compared to хуй/пизда derivatives.

records.definition: Literally 'female dog'; the primary Russian general-purpose insult for a treacherous, despicable, or promiscuous person; equivalent to 'bitch' in English.
records.notes: One of the most versatile and commonly used insults in Russian; applied to both sexes in its general-contempt sense. In Russian criminal/prison jargon (феня), 'сука' specifically denotes a prisoner who collaborates with authorities — a grave insult in that subculture.

records.definition: Past participle of ёбнуть used as an adjective; meaning crazy, nuts, or unhinged — someone whose mind has been metaphorically 'fucked' loose.
records.notes: Similar formation to English 'fucked up' but specifically refers to mental state (craziness) rather than general disorder. 'Ты что, ёбнутый?' = 'Are you crazy / nuts?' Common in everyday speech to express incredulity at bizarre behavior.

records.definition: Crude compound insult from 'khuy' (penis) and 'plyesti' (to weave/braid); labels someone a bullshitting liar, smooth-talking scoundrel, or generally contemptible person.
records.notes: The 'weaving' root implies fabricating nonsense rather than pure stupidity; distinguishes it from simple stupidity insults; penis derivation aligns it with the prick-insult family.

records.definition: Compound crude insult from 'manda' (vulgar for vagina) and 'voshka' (diminutive louse/nit); denotes a small, contemptible, irritating person.
records.notes: Literally 'pubic louse'; the diminutive -ка suffix gives a contemptuous but comically small-scale quality; used for someone petty and annoying rather than grandiose evil; манда is a non-standard vulgar vagina term distinct from пизда.

records.definition: Strong crude insult derived from 'pizda' (the most taboo Russian word for vagina) with the contemptuous suffix -юк; means a contemptible, stupid, or worthless person.
records.notes: Despite the female anatomical root, applied without strong gender targeting; the suffix -юк creates a distinctive contemptuous diminutive form characteristic of Russian morphological insult-building.

records.definition: Compound crude insult from 'dolbit'' (to drill/pound) and the root of 'yebat'' (to fuck); the standard Russian epithet for a complete, irredeemable idiot.
records.notes: One of the most widespread Russian insults for extreme stupidity; the 'drilling' component implies mindless repetitive action; widely recognized across all age groups and social registers.

records.definition: Two-word compound expletive: 'yobanaya' (fucking, past passive participle of yebat') plus 'skotina' (beast/brute/bastard); means 'you fucking animal,' one of the harshest common Russian insults.
records.notes: Скотина alone is already a strong insult for a brutish contemptible person; ёбаная intensifies to near maximum; скотина is grammatically feminine but applied to any gender; two-word structure is common in Russian for emphatic abuse.

records.definition: Crude хуй-derived verb meaning to do something forcefully or excessively: to beat someone up, to pile on a huge amount, or to do something aggressively and sloppily.
records.english_term: to fuck up / to beat the crap out of
records.notes: Not a noun insult but a penis-derived intensifier verb; the prefix на- adds a sense of completion or excess; semantics are context-dependent; less recognized than the base word хуй itself.

records.definition: The standard Russian word for a female prostitute or sex worker.
records.notes: Borrowed from Latin via Western European languages; used in law, journalism, and everyday speech; carries social stigma but is not itself considered extremely crude; no formal or less-stigmatizing Russian equivalent exists.

records.definition: Borrowed from Italian 'puttana' (whore); in Russian implies a higher-class or more glamorous prostitute than проститутка.
records.notes: Entered Russian in the late Soviet/post-Soviet period; became widespread in the 1990s when Italian organized crime and fashion culture were influential in Russia; the Italian/European provenance lends a slightly elevated connotation.

records.definition: Borrowed from French 'cocotte'; an archaic term for a demi-mondaine, kept woman, or fashionable courtesan at the margins of 19th-century European high society.
records.notes: Primarily known from 19th-century Russian literature (Chekhov, Tolstoy era); rarely used in contemporary speech; recognition mainly among educated readers; peak_year omitted as the historical peak predates living memory.

records.definition: From ancient Greek 'hetaira'; refers to the educated, independent female companions and courtesans of ancient Greek society who moved in male intellectual and political circles.

records.notes: More frequent than the Cyrillicized мильф in Russian internet contexts; retained in Latin script as a direct borrowing from English pornographic taxonomy.

records.definition: Sexual activity between close biological relatives; a universal taboo concept borrowed into Russian from Latin via European languages.
records.notes: Clinical loanword with no competing native Russian term in common use; appears in legal, psychological, and pornographic contexts; the pornographic subcultural sense is layered onto the universal taboo term without softening it.

records.definition: A sexological term for primary sexual attraction directed at oneself; describes individuals who find themselves more erotically compelling than any external partner.
records.notes: Used in Russian sexological literature; distinct from mere masturbation in that it denotes a primary erotic orientation toward the self as object; rarely encountered outside clinical or academic contexts.

records.notes: Retains full psychological meaning of narcissism while in a kink/paraphilia context denoting specifically sexualized self-focus; more widely recognized than аутосексуализм because narcissism entered general Russian vocabulary via popular psychology.

records.definition: Deliberate restriction of breathing during sexual activity to heighten arousal; the standard Russian descriptive clinical compound for erotic asphyxiation.
records.notes: Literally 'erotic strangling/suffocation'; used in journalism, sexology, and forensic contexts; the more accessible of the two Russian terms for this practice, the other being the technical асфиксиофилия.

records.definition: The clinical sexological term for a paraphilia in which sexual arousal is derived from asphyxia or oxygen deprivation; the technical Greek-derived form of erotic asphyxiation.
records.notes: Encountered almost exclusively in Russian academic sexology and forensic medicine; maps to the same concept as эротическое удушение but at a far higher technical register; recognition low outside specialist audiences.

records.definition: Sexual stimulation achieved by inserting objects into the urethral canal; the Russian clinical descriptor for the kink practice known in English as 'sounding.'
records.notes: Bridges medical and kink registers; the English kink community uses 'sounding' while Russian retains a fully descriptive compound; recognized mainly by kink community members and medical professionals.

records.definition: Oral stimulation of the anus; Russian loanword from English 'rimming,' now more common than the clinical Latin-derived аниллингус.
records.notes: Arrived in Russian via internet pornography in the 2000s and largely displaced native circumlocutions; the dominant colloquial term for this act in Russian pornographic and casual usage.

records.definition: The process by which a sexual predator builds trust and emotional dependency with a potential victim — typically a minor — in order to facilitate sexual exploitation.
records.notes: Borrowed from English in its predatory/safeguarding sense; widely adopted in Russian media, law enforcement, and child protection discourse through the 2010s; recognition growing alongside online-safety awareness campaigns.

records.definition: Literally 'home video'; a widespread Russian euphemism for amateur sexual recordings or self-produced pornography.
records.notes: Functionally parallel to English 'home video' as a sex-tape euphemism; used in classified ads, pornographic site taxonomy, and everyday speech; the euphemistic valence depends entirely on context.

records.definition: Amateur pornography; non-professional sexual content produced by private individuals, as distinguished from studio-produced material.
records.notes: Direct calque of 'amateur pornography'; more explicit in register than домашнее видео and carries no euphemistic coating; standard taxonomy label on Russian-language pornographic platforms.

records.definition: Travel undertaken primarily to access sex workers, typically internationally and exploiting economic disparities; the Russian calque of 'sex tourism.'
records.notes: Used in Russian journalism, academic writing, and criminal law; carries strongly negative and exploitative connotations in Russian public discourse.

records.definition: The missionary position; face-to-face penetrative sex with one partner supine and the other lying atop; the standard Russian term.
records.notes: Direct calque of the English term; universally known and used comfortably in both casual conversation and health-education contexts.

records.definition: Vulgar Russian slang for the doggy-style sex position; literally the instrumental case of рак (crayfish), evoking the bent-forward posture.
records.notes: One of the most widely used crude sexual terms in Russian; the crayfish metaphor is opaque to non-native speakers but instantly recognizable to any Russian speaker; significantly cruder in register than the English 'doggy style.'

records.definition: Literally 'on all fours'; a neutral positional descriptor for the doggy-style sex position, less crude than раком and also usable in non-sexual contexts.
records.notes: Context-dependent: ordinary in non-sexual usage (a child crawling, an animal); in sexual contexts defaults to doggy-style; chosen over раком when lower register is desired.

records.definition: Literally 'horsewoman / equestrienne'; the Russian term for the cowgirl sex position, in which the typically female or receptive partner straddles and rides the supine partner.
records.notes: Horseback-riding metaphor parallel to English 'cowgirl'; the feminine noun grammatically presupposes a female-presenting on-top partner, though usage extends to any person in the straddling role.

records.definition: The reverse cowgirl position; the on-top partner straddles the supine partner facing away; Russian compound of обратная (reverse/inverted) and наездница (horsewoman).
records.notes: Direct calque of the English pornographic taxonomy term; less widely known than наездница; обратная literally means reversed or backward.

records.definition: Literally 'from above / on top'; a positional descriptor for the partner in the upper or active straddling role during sex, most commonly evoking the cowgirl or rider-on-top position.
records.notes: Gender-neutral spatial adverb pressed into service as positional shorthand; maps most naturally to cowgirl_position when context implies the receptive partner riding on top, but can describe either partner being above in any position.

records.definition: Literally 'from below / on the bottom'; a positional descriptor for the partner in the supine or receptive underneath role, most commonly associated with the missionary position.
