records.notes: Gender-neutral spatial adverb used as positional shorthand; paired with сверху (on top); context-dependent and not position-specific, but defaults to missionary-position imagery for the receptive supine partner.

records.definition: Sixty-nine spelled out in full Russian; simultaneous mutual oral sex between two partners, named for the visual resemblance of the digits 6 and 9 to two interlocked bodies.
records.notes: Full written form; less frequent than the numeral '69' in casual usage but used in speech contexts or for deliberate emphasis.

records.definition: The numeral shorthand for the sixty-nine mutual oral sex position; universally recognized in Russian-speaking internet and casual discourse.
records.notes: Written in Arabic numerals, which are universal across scripts; the dominant form of this term in Russian digital communication; effectively a loanword from international pornographic taxonomy.

records.definition: Literally 'spoon'; the Russian term for the spooning sex position, lateral rear-entry with both partners lying on their sides curled together.
records.notes: Same spoon metaphor as English; the word is also the ordinary kitchen-utensil noun, so context disambiguates; both languages independently produced the same visual metaphor for this position.

records.definition: Literally 'standing'; a positional descriptor for sex performed with at least one partner in a standing position.
records.notes: Adverbial participle of стоять (to stand); functions as a single-word shorthand for any standing-position sexual act; grammatically a verbal adverb repurposed as a positional noun in sexual taxonomy.

records.definition: Literally 'against the wall / at the wall'; the Russian descriptor for sex performed with one partner pressed against a wall, typically in a standing position.
records.notes: Prepositional phrase (у = near/at/against, стены = genitive of стена, wall); used as positional shorthand in Russian pornographic taxonomy and informal sexual discourse.

records.definition: On one's knees; used as a positional descriptor in sexual contexts, typically implying a kneeling receptive position during intercourse or oral sex.
records.notes: Literal meaning is simply 'on one's knees'; sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent. May reference doggy-style intercourse or kneeling for oral sex; the ambiguity makes it a plausible euphemism in non-explicit speech.

records.definition: To sleep with someone; the standard Russian euphemism for having sex, implying an overnight stay rather than naming the act.
To lie down with someone; a Russian euphemism for having sex, slightly more physically suggestive than 'спать с кем-то' but equally indirect.
records.notes: Less common than 'спать с кем-то' in everyday speech; has a slightly more deliberate or literary feel. The perfective form 'лечь' implies a single completed act.

records.definition: Closeness, intimacy; used as a broad euphemism for sexual intimacy or intercourse, emphasizing emotional and physical closeness between partners.
records.notes: Widely used in press, literature, and formal speech to avoid explicit terminology; can refer to the act of sex or to the general dimension of physical intimacy in a relationship; the word carries no vulgarity whatsoever.

records.definition: Intimate life; a Russian euphemism for one's sex life, referring to the sexual dimension of a person's relationships and overall activity.
records.notes: Refers to the ongoing pattern or dimension of sexual activity rather than any single act or relationship; frequently used in journalism, health contexts, and relationship advice; 'интимный' is the standard polite adjective for anything sexual in Russian.

records.definition: To make love; the standard romantic Russian euphemism for having sex, foregrounding emotional and romantic connection over the physical act.
records.notes: A parallel development to or calque of the English 'make love'; became dominant in Soviet and post-Soviet Russian as a polite literary alternative; 'заниматься' (to occupy oneself with / to engage in) treats love-making as an activity.

records.definition: To do it; the vaguest possible Russian euphemism for sexual activity, relying entirely on shared context to convey meaning.
records.notes: Universal across registers and age groups; the demonstrative 'это' (it/this) carries no inherent sexual meaning and requires context; commonly used in parent-child conversations and comedy.

records.definition: Intimate relations; a Russian euphemism for a sexual relationship or sexual activity between partners, used in formal and journalistic registers.
records.notes: Standard in official, journalistic, and legal contexts to avoid explicit language; slightly more formal than 'интимная жизнь'; often appears in court proceedings and medical intake forms.

records.definition: To jump into bed with someone; a Russian idiom for having a hasty or casual sexual encounter, emphasizing impulsiveness or eagerness.
records.english_term: to jump into bed with someone
records.notes: The perfective 'прыгнуть' (to jump once) adds a sense of quickness or rashness; often used critically to describe ill-considered sexual decisions or reckless romantic behavior.

records.definition: To climb or maneuver into bed with someone; a Russian euphemism implying a sexual encounter, with a connotation of deliberate or surreptitious maneuvering into a situation.
records.english_term: to get into bed with someone
records.notes: 'Залезть' (to climb into / clamber into) suggests more deliberate or possibly covert action compared to 'прыгнуть в постель'; can imply calculated seduction rather than mutual spontaneity.

records.definition: To know someone biblically; a Russian calque of the English ironic euphemism referencing the biblical use of 'to know' as sexual intimacy.
records.notes: Used in Russian typically with irony or literary humor; the biblical 'познать' draws on the Old Testament (Genesis, etc.) where 'to know' (Hebrew yada) denotes sexual union; the English phrase appears to have re-entered Russian via translation culture rather than independently.

records.definition: To live together; primarily literal, but in Russian social contexts commonly understood as a euphemism for an unmarried cohabiting sexual partnership.
records.notes: Often paired with 'гражданский брак' (civil marriage, colloquially used for unmarried cohabitation); the phrase does not name sex explicitly but is frequently used as a soft disclosure of a sexual partnership outside formal marriage.

records.definition: To share a bed with someone; a Russian euphemism for having sex or sleeping with a partner, referencing the shared bed rather than the act itself.
records.notes: More literary than colloquial; often found in fiction and journalism to describe a sexual relationship without explicit language; the perfective 'разделить' implies a completed singular event.

records.definition: To be naughty or mischievous; in sexual contexts, to engage in light sexual play, flirtatious transgression, or marital infidelity.
records.english_term: to fool around / to be naughty
records.notes: Primary meaning is innocent childhood mischief; sexual meaning is secondary but well-established; can imply anything from playful flirting to adultery depending on context and tone; often used with a winking or accusatory register.

records.definition: To spin or conduct a romance; a Russian idiom for having a love affair or romantic liaison, implying ongoing romantic and typically sexual activity.
records.english_term: to have a romance / to carry on an affair
records.notes: The verb 'крутить' (to twist/spin/manage) suggests deliberate cultivation of the romance rather than passive passion; does not necessarily imply infidelity the way 'affair' often does in English — can describe a legitimate relationship.

records.definition: To make love; the reflexive-reciprocal form of любить (to love), used in literary or elevated registers to mean engaging in sexual intercourse with mutual romantic feeling.
records.notes: More explicitly sexual in many literary contexts than 'заниматься любовью'; retains a romantic literary register; common in 19th–20th century Russian prose; rare in casual modern speech; the reciprocal morphology encodes mutuality.

records.definition: To caress and be tender with each other; a Russian literary term for affectionate physical intimacy including kissing, embracing, and gentle touching, typically stopping short of intercourse.
records.english_term: to cuddle and caress / to be affectionate
records.notes: From 'милый' (dear, sweet, darling); associated with tender romantic rather than explicitly sexual contexts; less common in contemporary speech than in 19th–20th century Russian literature; connotes sweetness rather than heat.

records.definition: To take; used in Russian slang to mean to have sex with someone, with a strong connotation of masculine dominance or sexual conquest.
records.notes: Standard Russian verb 'to take' repurposed as sexual slang; directional and asymmetrical — the man 'takes' the woman, encoding a power asymmetry; semantic complement to 'дать'; not maximally vulgar but clearly sexual in context.

records.definition: To give; in Russian sexual slang, for a woman to consent to and engage in sex, framed as providing sexual access to a male partner.
records.english_term: to put out / to give it up
records.notes: Semantic complement to 'брать': the man 'takes,' the woman 'gives.' Used in phrases like 'она ему дала' (she gave it to him). Not maximally vulgar but clearly sexual in context; frames sex as a commodity provided by women and extracted by men; widely understood across all demographics.

records.definition: To touch or feel up; in sexual contexts, to touch a partner's body or genitals with the hands for erotic purposes.
records.notes: Literally just 'to touch once' (perfective); sexual meaning is context-dependent; can imply unauthorized groping as readily as consensual manual stimulation; lacks the specificity of genital-only contact.

records.definition: To embrace and kiss passionately; a Russian colloquial term for making out, involving sustained kissing and close physical contact stopping short of intercourse.
records.notes: From 'обжать' (to press around / hug tightly); implies more physical intensity than a simple embrace; commonly used among teenagers and young adults; does not necessarily imply genital contact; often describes couples in public places.

records.definition: To fondle and squeeze each other; a Russian colloquial term for mutual groping and heavy petting, typically implying breast or genital contact stopping short of intercourse.
records.english_term: to grope each other / heavy petting
records.notes: From 'тискать' (to squeeze, to press firmly); implies more physical intensity and genital proximity than 'обжиматься'; often used to describe youthful sexual exploration or foreplay that does not progress to intercourse.

records.definition: To be tender and gentle with each other; a Russian colloquial term for soft, affectionate physical intimacy including light touching, cuddling, and caressing.
records.notes: From 'нежный' (tender, gentle, soft); the softest entry in the physical intimacy spectrum — rarely implies intercourse; suggests sweet, playful affection and emotional warmth rather than explicitly sexual contact.

records.definition: Fornication, lechery, or sexual immorality broadly; an Old Church Slavonic-derived term denoting illicit sexual activity with heavy moral and religious condemnation.
records.notes: Root of 'блудница' (harlot), 'блудить' (to fornicate / to err / to wander), and 'заблудиться' (to get lost — same root, showing how 'wandering' and 'sexual straying' were conceptually linked); found primarily in Orthodox religious texts, older literature, and ironic contemporary usage; broader in scope than English 'fornication' — can encompass all illicit sexuality.

records.definition: Adultery; the Church Slavonic and formal Russian legal-theological term for sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse.
records.notes: Mapped to 'fornication' as the closest registry concept, though прелюбодеяние specifically denotes adultery (at least one party married), not sex outside marriage generally; appears in the Seventh Commandment ('Не прелюбодействуй'), in pre-revolutionary Russian law, and in Orthodox canon law; the 'пре-' prefix (beyond/excess) combined with 'любо' (love) encodes 'love transgressed beyond its proper bounds.'

records.definition: An adulterer; a man who commits sexual infidelity against his marriage vows, derived from Church Slavonic and central to Orthodox moral theology.
records.notes: More specific than 'fornicator': прелюбодей denotes transgression within marriage (пре- = across a boundary), not merely sex outside marriage. Core vocabulary of Russian Orthodox moral discourse and Bible translation.

records.definition: A harlot or sexually immoral woman; the feminine form of блудник, used extensively in biblical texts and Church Slavonic literature.
records.notes: Most recognizable as the блудница who anoints Christ's feet in the Gospels. From блуд (fornication/straying). Carries heavy biblical weight; not merely a prostitute but a woman whose entire identity is defined by sexual sin and moral ruin.

records.definition: Licentiousness or dissolute behavior; habitual sexual promiscuity and moral looseness combined with indulgence in earthly pleasures.
records.notes: The surname Rasputin (Распутин) is derived from this root, making the word culturally loaded. Slightly more focused on promiscuity and loose living than разврат, which connotes active moral corruption. Used in literary and journalistic contexts.

records.definition: Lust; intense carnal desire; one of the seven deadly sins in Orthodox theology, denoting uncontrolled sexual appetite.
records.notes: Core term in Russian Orthodox moral theology; appears throughout Church Slavonic Bible translations and remains widely recognizable. Slightly more specific to sexual desire than страсть (passion), which is broader and not exclusively sexual.

records.definition: Fornication; illicit sexual intercourse between unmarried persons; a Church Slavonic compound carrying strong moral and religious condemnation.
records.notes: Compound of люб- (love/pleasure) + деяние (act/deed). More specifically ecclesiastical than блудодеяние; appears primarily in pre-20th century religious texts and biblical translations. Effectively extinct in modern spoken Russian.

records.definition: The sin of Sodom; a phrase explicitly framing sodomy as a biblical transgression deserving divine punishment, drawing on the destruction of Sodom in Genesis.
records.notes: Carries heavier moral condemnation than the standalone legal term мужеложство by invoking divine retribution. Used in Orthodox homiletics and conservative political rhetoric. Loads the act with eschatological weight beyond mere legal prohibition.

records.definition: Male homosexual intercourse; the legal and religious term used in Soviet criminal law (Article 121) that criminalized sex between men until 1993.
records.notes: Literally 'man-lying' (муж=man, ложство from ложе=bed). Unlike the broader English 'sodomy,' мужеложство is restricted specifically to male-male sex. Decriminalized in 1993 but remains the formal legal-historical term and appears in contemporary conservative religious rhetoric.

records.definition: Chastity; sexual purity; the virtue of refraining from sinful sexual conduct, a core concept in Orthodox Christian ethics.
records.notes: Literally 'whole-wisdom' (цело=whole/intact + мудрость=wisdom); implies both sexual purity and mental integrity — not merely abstinence but the positive virtue of sexual self-mastery. Widely used in contemporary Russian Orthodox discourse and conservative political rhetoric.

records.definition: Maidenhood; the archaic literary term for the state of female virginity, emphasizing the social and moral condition of the unmarried virgin girl.
records.notes: Concept mapped (defloration) describes the act of losing virginity; this word describes the prior state — no registry concept covers virginity-as-state. More poetic and archaic than девственность; emphasizes the maiden's social role and honor. Frequent in folk tales, byliny, and 18th–19th century literature.

records.definition: Virginity; the standard literary and semi-clinical Russian term for the state of never having had sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Concept mapped (defloration) describes the act of losing virginity; this word names the prior state. The standard modern term — more clinical and less archaic than девство. Commonly used in education, literature, and public health; unlike other words in this section it remains in active use.

records.definition: Obscenity or indecency; sexually offensive or morally objectionable behavior; an archaic legal and religious term for sexual misconduct.
records.notes: Literally 'un-need-ness' (не + потреба = need/use); behavior that should not exist or be tolerated. Used in pre-revolutionary Russian law. Now sounds dated; superseded by непристойность in modern usage.

records.definition: Shamelessness; brazen sexual or moral indecency performed without any sense of shame; a grave social failure in Russian honor culture.
records.notes: Literally 'without-shame-ness' (без=without, стыд=shame). Its force comes from the honor-shame framework central to traditional Russian culture: стыд is a moral regulator, its absence signals total degradation. The English concept 'indecency' is only approximate — the Russian specifically names the honor-culture violation.

records.definition: The genitals; literally 'shame parts,' a euphemistic plural noun for the external genitalia of either sex, common in religious and pre-modern texts.
records.notes: Срам (sram) = shame in Old Slavonic; shame-based naming of genitalia is widespread across Slavic and biblical traditions. Parallel to Latin pudenda (things to be ashamed of). Appears in Bible translations, folk medicine, and 19th-century literature. Now archaic.

records.definition: Licentious or lecherous; the adjective form of блуд, meaning characterized by sexual or moral waywardness and sinful straying.
records.notes: Universally recognizable via 'блудный сын' (the prodigal son), which skews connotation toward 'wayward/straying' rather than purely 'lustful.' The specifically sexual sense is more present in other блуд- compounds. In isolation, typically read as 'promiscuous' or 'licentious.'

records.definition: Debauchery; moral and sexual corruption and depravity; actively used in modern Russian journalism and political rhetoric to denote sexual licentiousness.
records.notes: Unlike most archaic words in this section, разврат remains in vigorous contemporary use — appearing in news media, political rhetoric (particularly about 'Western разврат'), and casual speech. One of the most universally recognized words in this set; bridges archaic and contemporary registers.

records.definition: Voluptuousness or lustfulness; the archaic literary term for deep, sustained surrender to carnal and sensual pleasures.
records.notes: Compound of люб- (love/pleasure) + страсть (passion). More literary and elevated than похоть (lust); implies sustained wallowing in pleasure rather than acute desire. Common in 18th–19th century Russian prose, poetry, and translations of French libertine literature.

records.definition: The loins; the area of the hips and lower abdomen biblically associated with reproductive power and physical strength.
records.notes: Church Slavonic borrowing; direct equivalent of biblical 'loins.' Appears in phrases like 'от чресел своих' (from one's loins = one's offspring) and 'препояши чресла' (gird your loins). Not inherently crude — purely poetic and archaic. The genitalia concept is approximate; чресла denotes the entire loin region, not specifically the genitals.

records.definition: The womb, bosom, or lap; in literary and archaic use, a euphemism for the female genital region.
records.notes: Primary meanings: (1) bosom/lap of nature ('на лоне природы'); (2) womb; (3) in explicit literary use, the vulva or vaginal area. Still widely recognized due to common figurative use. The vulva concept is the most sexually proximate registry match, though лоно primarily means womb or bosom.

records.definition: Flesh; the physical, carnal body as opposed to the spirit; in religious contexts specifically denotes the sinful sexual and bodily nature of humanity.
records.notes: Derived from Church Slavonic; central to Orthodox theology ('грехи плоти' = sins of the flesh; 'умерщвление плоти' = mortification of the flesh). The carnal_desire concept is approximate — плоть is the body itself, not a state of desire — but no registry concept covers 'carnal flesh' as a theological entity.

records.definition: The pleasures of the flesh; carnal or sensual gratification; a literary phrase for sexual and bodily pleasure viewed through a morally censorious lens.
records.notes: Утеха (comfort, consolation, pleasure) + плоти (genitive of плоть = flesh). Used in 19th-century literature to describe characters who surrender to bodily pleasures, always with an ironic or condemnatory undertone. The phrase persists in contemporary conservative religious rhetoric.

records.definition: The fall into sin; in secular literary use, a moral or sexual downfall, particularly a woman's first act of sexual transgression.
records.notes: Primarily refers to the biblical Fall of Adam and Eve (грех=sin, падение=fall). In literary Russian applied to sexual ruin — especially a young woman's first extra-marital sexual act. The sexual sense is heavily gendered: a man's грехопадение is moral; a woman's is specifically sexual ruin and social death.

records.definition: Fornication; illicit sexual intercourse; a Church Slavonic compound used primarily in religious law and moral theology.
records.notes: Combines блуд (fornication/straying) + деяние (act/deed); parallel to любодеяние but with slightly more emphasis on the concrete deed. Appears in Russian Orthodox canon law and pre-revolutionary moral texts. Effectively extinct in modern spoken Russian.

records.definition: A voluptuous or wantonly sensual woman; a woman who surrenders excessively to sexual and sensual pleasure.
records.notes: From сладострастие (sweet-passion): сладо- (sweet) + страсть (passion/lust). More literary than pejorative — 19th-century prose uses it for femmes fatales and morally fallen women. The nymphomania concept is approximate; сладострастница implies willing pleasure-seeking, not clinical compulsion. The 'sweet' etymology gives it a more seductive than pathological connotation.

records.definition: A sensualist or libertine; a man who dedicates himself to the pursuit of sexual and sensual pleasure; the masculine counterpart to сладострастница.
records.notes: From любострастие (see above). Used in 18th–19th century literature, often in translations of French libertine novels. The female form сладострастница is more common in Russian literary tradition, reflecting the culture's tendency to focus moral censure on women. The English 'libertine' emphasizes moral defiance; любострастник emphasizes pleasure-seeking.

records.definition: To live in fornication; to conduct one's life in a persistent state of sexual sin outside of marriage; a biblical phrase for ongoing sexual immorality.
records.notes: Жить (to live) + в блуде (in fornication/straying). Implies an ongoing sinful state rather than a single act. The English idiom 'living in sin' is approximate — the Russian explicitly names блуд (fornication) rather than sin generically. Used in Orthodox Church contexts and pre-revolutionary folk speech.

records.definition: Archaic Russian crude verb meaning to have sex, derived from the primary sense of scraping or abrading a surface; used to describe coital friction in pre-Soviet colloquial speech.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'to scrape/plane'; sexual sense is dialectal and archaic, rarely documented but attested in pre-revolutionary colloquial sources.

records.definition: Archaic Russian euphemism meaning literally 'to become friends with someone,' used as a polite circumlocution for becoming sexually intimate with a person.
records.notes: The sexual reading is entirely contextual and has largely vanished from modern usage; recognized mainly in 19th-century literary and epistolary texts.

records.definition: Reflexive Russian verb meaning to copulate or engage in sexual intercourse; the standard formal-archaic term for coitus in pre-Soviet and early Soviet medical and literary texts.
records.notes: Still found in older Russian dictionaries and legal documents; displaced in clinical use by 'половой акт' and in colloquial use by cruder terms; non-reflexive 'сношать' also attested.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning 'unclean' or 'impure' in a moral and spiritual sense; applied in religious contexts to persons, acts, or desires considered sexually or morally defiling.
records.notes: Not exclusively sexual; in Orthodox Christian rhetoric 'нечистые помыслы' (unclean thoughts) specifically connotes sexual sin; also a common epithet for the devil ('нечистый' = the unclean one).

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning 'ungodly' or 'impious'; used in religious and literary contexts to condemn persons guilty of sexual or moral sin against divine law.
records.notes: More specifically religious in tone than 'нечистый'; emphasizes violation of sacred law rather than ritual impurity; common in Church Slavonic-influenced prose and sermons.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning 'immodest' or 'indecent'; applied to behavior, dress, or speech that transgresses sexual propriety norms, particularly in 19th- and early 20th-century literary usage.
records.notes: Still intelligible to modern speakers but feels dated; 'нескромный взгляд' (immodest glance) and 'нескромные намёки' (immodest hints) are typical collocations in period literature.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning 'immoral'; used broadly to condemn behavior that violates accepted moral norms, with frequent application to sexual misconduct in literary and journalistic discourse.
records.notes: Fully current and not archaic despite its section placement; included due to formal register; heavily used in Soviet-era moral-didactic texts and remains standard in contemporary Russian public discourse.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning 'indecent' or 'obscene'; applied to sexual content, language, gestures, or behavior that violates standards of public decency.
records.notes: 'Непристойные жесты' (indecent gestures) and 'непристойные выражения' (obscene expressions) are typical collocations; remains in active legal and journalistic use.

records.definition: Archaic Russian adjective derived from 'срам' (shame/disgrace), meaning 'shameful' or 'disgraceful' in a specifically sexual or bodily sense; 'срамные части' was the standard archaic euphemism for genitalia.
records.notes: Directly embeds the honor/shame frame: genitalia and sexuality are linguistically coded as inherently shame-bearing; rooted in Orthodox moral culture and Old Church Slavonic tradition; 'срамота' (shameful deed) is a related noun.

records.definition: Russian adjective meaning 'carnal' or 'of the flesh'; refers to physical, especially sexual, desires and pleasures as contrasted with spiritual ones.
records.notes: 'Плотские грехи' (carnal sins) and 'плотские желания' (carnal desires) are standard collocations; the binary 'плотское vs. духовное' (carnal vs. spiritual) is central to Russian Orthodox moral theology.

records.definition: Russian literary phrase meaning 'carnal pleasures'; refers to physical and sexual gratifications of the body, typically deployed with a moralistic or ironic tone in literary and religious texts.
records.notes: A lexicalized phrase rather than a free combination; common in 18th–19th-century Russian prose and religious writing; sounds distinctly dated in modern speech.

records.definition: Russian noun meaning 'pleasures' or 'delights'; used in literary and poetic contexts as a gentle euphemism for sexual pleasures or erotic gratification.
records.notes: Not inherently sexual; acquires sexual meaning entirely from context; common in pre-revolutionary romantic and erotic poetry; the word is transparent but the sexual euphemism reading requires register awareness.

records.definition: Archaic Russian transitive verb meaning 'to cause to copulate' or 'to join in sexual union'; the non-reflexive form found in scientific, theological, and literary texts.
records.english_term: to copulate / to join in coitus
records.notes: The reflexive 'совокупляться' is more common and means simply 'to copulate'; the non-reflexive implies an external agent causing the union; found in zoological and theological texts.

records.definition: Russian internet slang verb for male masturbation, borrowed directly from English 'fap' (an onomatopoeic term); widely used on imageboards such as 2ch.hk and in Russian social media.
records.notes: Direct phonetic borrowing from English internet slang; the noun form 'фап' is also used; associated with chan culture and meme formats around compulsive masturbation to pornography.

records.definition: Russian crude slang noun derived from 'дрочить' (to masturbate); literally 'one who masturbates compulsively'; used widely as a general internet insult for a pathetic, contemptible, or sexually obsessed person.
records.notes: Functions on two levels: literal (compulsive masturbator) and figurative (loser/contemptible person); the figurative use has largely overtaken the literal in internet discourse; closely parallel to British English 'wanker'.

records.definition: Russian colloquial and internet abbreviation of 'порнография' (pornography); used in casual digital communication, search queries, and social media.
records.notes: Direct phonetic truncation matching English 'porn'; fully transparent to Russian speakers; crude rating is lower than the acts it names because the word itself has been neutralized through saturation.

records.definition: Russian Cyrillic transliteration of Japanese 'hentai' (変態); refers to sexually explicit Japanese animation or manga, widely distributed and discussed in Russian-language online anime communities.
records.notes: Borrowed from Japanese via English-language internet; in Japan 'hentai' broadly means 'pervert/abnormal'; in Russian internet usage, exclusively denotes explicit anime or manga pornography.

records.definition: Abbreviation for Japanese 'netorare' (寝取られ, literally 'to be taken while sleeping'); an erotic fiction and doujin genre in which a character's romantic partner is seduced or sexually taken by another person, with narrative focus on the betrayed partner's anguish or gradual corruption.
records.notes: Distinct from Western cuckolding: NTR typically lacks the cuckold's consent and centers psychological distress or coerced arousal rather than exhibitionist pleasure; common subcategory label in Russian-language hentai forums and doujin sites; the Latin acronym is used even in otherwise Cyrillic-script contexts.

records.definition: Russian transliteration of English 'sexting'; refers to the exchange of sexually explicit text messages, photographs, or videos via mobile devices or messaging applications.
records.notes: Entered Russian mainstream vocabulary around 2013–2015 alongside smartphone adoption; now standard in journalism, legal discourse around minors, and teen safety education campaigns.

records.definition: Russian colloquial phrase meaning literally 'sex by correspondence/messaging'; used for sexting or text-based erotic exchange, with a broader and more neutral framing than 'секстинг'.
records.notes: Emphasizes the textual/messaging medium and implies ongoing erotic dialogue rather than image exchange; predates the loanword 'секстинг' and is more transparent to older or less internet-native speakers.

records.definition: Russian calque of English 'swipe right', the Tinder UI gesture indicating romantic or sexual interest in a displayed profile; colloquially used to mean expressing attraction or giving approval to a person.
records.notes: Entered Russian from Tinder's UI vocabulary around 2014–2015; also deployed metaphorically outside dating-app contexts to mean 'I approve of that person' or 'I'd date them'; 'свайп влево' is the rejection antonym.

records.definition: Russian phonetic borrowing of English 'cumshot'; refers to the pornographic depiction of visible external male ejaculation onto a partner's body, regarded as the climactic and commercially required shot in professional pornography.
records.notes: Primarily confined to pornographic and adjacent internet contexts; speakers unfamiliar with porn vocabulary may not recognize it; the alternate spelling 'камшотт' also appears.

records.definition: Russian phonetic borrowing of English 'creampie'; refers to internal vaginal or anal ejaculation without a condom, or the visible display of semen leaking from the orifice afterward; a pornographic category label and act descriptor.
records.notes: More niche recognition than 'камшот'; known primarily to regular consumers of English-language pornography and Russian internet subcultures; the borrowing preserves the English pronunciation closely.

records.definition: Russian transliteration of 'deepfake'; refers to AI-generated synthetic video or imagery in which a real person's face is realistically superimposed onto explicit sexual content without their consent.
records.notes: Not exclusively sexual — deepfakes include political disinformation — but in popular Russian discourse the term is strongly associated with non-consensual sexual imagery of celebrities and private individuals; included here for the sexual-context usage.

records.definition: Russian phonetic spelling of 'OnlyFans'; refers to the subscription-based content platform widely used by sex workers and amateur creators to sell explicit sexual material directly to paying subscribers.
records.notes: Blocked in Russia by Roskomnadzor but widely accessed via VPN; the term remains in active use in Russian social media and mainstream media coverage of digital sex work and creator economics.

records.definition: Webcam-based sex work; performing sexual acts live via webcam for a paying online audience.
records.notes: Loanword from English 'webcam'; used as a noun (работать на вебкаме) and modifier; often refers specifically to the cam sex industry rather than webcam technology in general.

records.definition: A nude photograph or sexually explicit image, typically shared online; singular loanword from English 'nude.'
records.notes: Singular form; used primarily by younger Russian internet users; less common than the plural ноуды in practice.

records.definition: Nude photographs or sexually explicit images, typically shared online; plural loanword from English 'nudes.'
records.notes: Plural of ноуд; more commonly used than the singular; standard term in Russian internet requests and discussions around intimate image sharing.

records.definition: A leak of private or intimate content; nude images or videos distributed without the subject's consent.
records.notes: Primary meaning is any data or document leak; in sexual contexts refers specifically to leaked intimate content; common in phrases like 'слив с OnlyFans.'

records.definition: Leaked content; neuter substantivized adjective from слить, referring to stolen or privately obtained intimate media distributed without consent.
records.notes: Used as a standalone noun ('смотреть слитое' = 'to watch leaked content'); specifically implies intimate or sexual material when used without further qualification.

records.definition: Literally 'to fuck in the mouth'; used both as a literal descriptor of dominant oral penetration and as a general strong expletive or exclamation.
records.notes: Core mat vocabulary; dual register as literal sex-act descriptor and expletive intensifier; 'в рот' alone can function as a standalone expletive; among the most transgressive phrases in Russian obscene speech.

records.definition: To hook up with someone or pursue a casual romantic-sexual liaison; implies ongoing flirtation or a developing sexual connection rather than a strictly one-off encounter.
records.english_term: to hook up with / to mess around with
records.notes: Literally 'to stir' or 'to muddy'; in youth slang covers the spectrum from flirting to casual sex; 'мутить с кем-то' = 'to be seeing or casually hooking up with someone.'

records.definition: To get glued to or obsessively consume online content; in adult internet contexts, to binge or trance-watch pornography for extended periods.
records.notes: General internet slang meaning 'to get hooked on something'; applied to pornography in adult online communities; less specific than English 'gooning' and does not necessarily imply deliberate edge-play.

records.definition: To masturbate to or over someone or something; 'дрочить' is the base crude verb for masturbation, 'на' specifies the object of arousal.
records.english_term: to jerk off to / to wank over
records.notes: 'На' + accusative specifies the fantasy object; дрочить alone is the base masturbation verb; also used figuratively for any obsessive fixation on something.

records.definition: Erotica; sexually stimulating literary, artistic, or audiovisual material, often contrasted with hardcore pornography.
records.notes: Standard Russian word for erotica as a genre category; 'лёгкая эротика' ('light erotica') commonly used for softcore content; borrowed from Greek via European languages.

records.definition: Erotic text-based role-play conducted in online chat; phonetic Cyrillic transliteration of the English abbreviation 'RP,' understood as erotic in context.
records.notes: Specific to text-based erotic roleplay on VKontakte, Discord, and Telegram communities; 'устроить эрпэ' = 'to do an ERP session'; sometimes loosely applied to any online sexual text exchange.

records.definition: Colloquial diminutive of 'ролевая игра' (role-playing game); in online adult communities, refers specifically to an erotic text-based roleplay session.
records.notes: Diminutive suffix -ка on роль-; used in general gaming contexts but in adult communities denotes erotic RP; overlaps with эрпэ in meaning, slightly more informal.

records.definition: An anonymous internet user; on adult imageboards and forums, refers to anonymous participants in sexual discussions, subjects of leaked images, or anonymous partners sought for casual encounters.
records.notes: Direct borrowing of English 'anon'; central to Russian imageboard culture (dvach/2ch); in sexual contexts used for requests about or posts of anonymous women's images, anonymous sexual hookup solicitations, and content-sharing by pseudonymous users.

records.definition: Gay pornography; sexually explicit material depicting male homosexual sex acts.
records.notes: Compound of гей (borrowed from English 'gay') and порно; standard colloquial label used as a content category tag on adult platforms and in casual conversation.

records.definition: Lesbian pornography; sexually explicit material depicting female homosexual sex acts.
records.notes: Compound of лесби (truncated from лесбиянка, lesbian) and порно; standard colloquial label; consistently among the most-searched pornographic categories in Russian-language adult platforms.

records.definition: Zoopornography; sexually explicit material depicting sexual acts between humans and animals.
records.notes: Compound of зоо- (from зоология) and порно; production and distribution criminally prohibited in Russia under Article 242 of the Criminal Code.

records.definition: An interactive paid session with a cam performer in which the viewer directs the action in real time via tips or private commands.
records.notes: General word for 'interactive content' repurposed as a specific paid service tier on Russian-language cam platforms; typically contrasted with free public shows; implies viewer control over performer's actions.

records.definition: A private one-on-one paid show with a cam sex worker; the exclusive paid session tier on camming platforms where no other viewers are present.
records.notes: Loanword from English/German 'private'; industry-specific term in Russian cam culture; 'идти в приват' = 'to go into private' (to initiate a private session); priced at premium above group or free chat.

records.definition: Tits; the most common crude-but-not-mat slang term for female breasts in Russian.
records.notes: Not classified as mat (hard obscenity) but firmly crude; used extremely widely in casual speech, internet content, and even advertising; diminutive сисечки carries affectionate or playful tone.

records.definition: Fuck; crude noun for sexual intercourse, derived from the verb трахать/трахаться.
records.notes: Root трах- yields трахать (to fuck, transitive), трахаться (to fuck, reflexive/intransitive), трахнуть (perfective); less extreme than mat хуй-based vocabulary but firmly in the crude register.

records.definition: Ass; the standard crude colloquial term for the buttocks; also used figuratively in idioms meaning disaster or a hopeless situation.
records.notes: Not classified as mat but solidly crude; extremely versatile — 'полная жопа' means 'total disaster'; as an insult it is mild; widely used including in broadcast media and print.

records.definition: Cock; the primary mat obscenity for penis in Russian and one of the most taboo words in the language.
records.notes: Core mat vocabulary — one of three or four foundational Russian obscenities; considerably more taboo than English 'cock' or 'dick'; forms numerous compound expletives (похуй, нихуя, хуйня, etc.); ubiquitous in colloquial speech despite extreme formal vulgarity.

records.definition: Big Beautiful Woman; a pornographic category acronym for sexually explicit content featuring larger-bodied or obese women.
records.notes: Used unchanged from English as a content tag on Russian-language adult platforms; recognized by Russian adult-content consumers familiar with category taxonomy without necessarily knowing the full English expansion.

records.definition: MILF; objectifying label and pornographic category for a sexually attractive woman who is a mother; borrowed directly and unchanged from English.
records.notes: Used unchanged from English; widely recognized by Russian internet users through pornographic content and broader internet culture; full expansion ('mother I'd like to fuck') not always known but meaning is understood from context.

records.definition: Anime wanker; pejorative compound for a person obsessively addicted to anime and hentai pornography and masturbation.
records.notes: Compound of аниме (from Japanese via English) and дрочер (from дрочить 'to masturbate'); дрочер alone means wanker; the compound specifically mocks consumers of animated pornography; Russian internet equivalent of the English 'coomer' applied to the anime subculture.

records.definition: In Russian prison culture, to forcibly sodomize an inmate as a ritual act of social degradation, permanently demoting the victim to the lowest-caste 'petukhi' status with all attendant prohibitions and ostracism.
records.notes: The demotion is considered permanent and irreversible within prison culture; no subsequent act restores prior caste standing. Widely referenced in Russian crime literature, prison memoirs, and television drama.

records.definition: Nominalization of опустить; the ritual process of forcible sexual assault in Russian prison culture that permanently strips a victim of social standing and relegates them to the pariah caste.
records.notes: Used both for the discrete act and the broader social process of caste demotion. Appears in criminological and sociological literature on Russian prison subculture.

records.definition: Prison slang label for an inmate at the very bottom of the caste hierarchy — below ordinary петухи in some regional prison systems — connoting extreme degradation and untouchable status.
records.notes: Primary civilian meaning is 'gnat' or 'biting midge,' evoking pestilential worthlessness. Regional variation exists: in some institutions synonymous with петух, in others designates a distinct sub-caste below it.

records.definition: Collective noun for the 'petukhi' caste — the sexually degraded inmates at the bottom of Russian prison hierarchy; also used loosely for any gathering of despised or worthless people.
records.notes: Formed from петух (rooster) + collective suffix -ня. 'Rooster' in Russian prison slang designates a male who has been anally penetrated, hence the lowest-status caste; the collective form denotes them as a group.

records.definition: The designated cell or section of a prison block reserved for 'petukhi' inmates; pariah-caste members are segregated here to enforce their exclusion and to limit contact with higher-caste prisoners.
records.notes: Literally 'rooster coop'; the physical embodiment of caste segregation. Segregation is enforced both by guards and by inmate social pressure; petukhi who leave their area risk violence from other castes.

records.definition: The prison caste ranks or 'suits' — the formal social strata of Russian prison culture, typically воры, мужики, козлы/обиженные, and петухи — each governed by strict behavioral codes and sexual taboos whose violation triggers forced caste demotion.
records.notes: From масть (suit in cards; coat color in horses). The sexual dimension is definitional: a prisoner's caste status is determined partly by who they will and will not have sex with, and in what role. Crossing a caste boundary sexually results in immediate and permanent demotion.

records.definition: The formalized caste system of Russian prisons (понятия), in which social position is determined largely by sexual conduct and coded prohibitions; sexual contact across caste lines triggers permanent downward reclassification.
records.notes: A descriptive phrase borrowed from anthropology; used by academics, journalists, and inmates alike. Has no Western equivalent because the sexual dimension — who penetrates whom — is the primary axis of social stratification rather than wealth or violence alone.

records.definition: A specific prison caste label for inmates who perform menial and degrading tasks (cleaning latrines, running errands for higher castes) and are considered tainted, but who have not been sexually penetrated and thus rank above the petukhi.
records.notes: The sexual distinction is crucial: чёрты have avoided forced penetration and therefore retain marginally more dignity than petukhi, though they are still below мужики. The term is everyday Russian for 'devil.' Regional usage varies; in some prison systems the category does not exist or is merged with обиженные.

records.definition: Literally 'lowered into the roosters'; the formulaic phrase describing a prisoner's completed sexual demotion to the pariah caste, functioning simultaneously as a description of the assault and as a permanent identity label.
records.notes: Past passive participial construction. Once this label applies, the person is barred from sharing food, utensils, or physical space with higher-caste inmates. The phrase appears in legal testimony, prison memoirs, and journalism about the Russian penal system.

records.definition: Literally 'lower'; slang for the receptive partner in anal intercourse, used in both gay and prison contexts; in prison culture carries strong stigma because it implies low caste or forced submission.
records.notes: Contrasts with верхний (upper/top). In prison culture, being the нижний is not a preference but a caste marker implying either voluntary subordination or coerced submission; the word imports none of that stigma in consensual gay usage.

records.definition: The receptive partner in anal intercourse; used in gay slang as a neutral role identifier and in prison slang as a stigmatizing identity label; also appears in personal ads and dating profiles.
records.notes: Borrowed from Latin via technical vocabulary. In consensual gay culture, пассив is a neutral self-description; in prison culture it implies either forced penetration or caste membership in the petukhi. Contrasted with актив.

records.definition: The insertive and active partner in anal intercourse; in prison culture this role carries no stigma and does not lower the actor's caste status; in gay community usage it is a neutral role self-identifier.
records.notes: A key asymmetry of Russian prison sexual ethics: a higher-caste prisoner who penetrates a петух does not demote himself; only the receptive role triggers caste demotion. This asymmetry is absent in consensual gay culture, where the role is simply a preference.

records.definition: The insertive role in sexual intercourse, especially anal; the role that is socially neutral or valorized in Russian prison culture and a neutral preference marker in consensual gay discourse.
records.notes: More clinical and descriptive than the bare adjective активный; used in sexology, gay-community discussions, and prison sociology. The phrase mirrors the formal language of Soviet-era sexological writing.

records.definition: The receptive role in sexual intercourse, especially anal; in prison culture, accepting this role results in permanent caste demotion; in consensual gay contexts, a neutral preference self-identifier.
records.notes: More clinical and formal than пассив alone; found in sexological literature, gay-community educational materials, and prison sociological research alongside the subculture usage.

records.definition: Prison bunk bed; the primary site of clandestine and forced sexual activity in Russian prisons, metonymically associated with the power relations and sexual coercion enacted there.
records.notes: The word itself is not sexual — it denotes a prison-issue bunk — but is included in this corpus because prison sexuality discourse uses it as the metonymic site of sexual contact. The term is opaque to speakers without prison exposure; recognized primarily through crime drama and prison literature.

records.definition: A hidden spot or concealed stash in prison; used for hiding contraband and for conducting clandestine sexual activity away from guard observation and rival inmates.
records.notes: Like шконка, not inherently sexual but functions in this corpus as a site term for covert prison sex. Diminutive form, connoting smallness and concealment. Recognized mainly through crime fiction and prison journalism.

records.definition: Immoral; in Soviet and post-Soviet usage applied to persons or behaviors that violate sexual propriety norms — extramarital sex, homosexuality, public lewdness — and marked the subject as unfit for collective life.
records.notes: In Soviet bureaucratic language 'аморальный поступок' (immoral act) was a formal charge at workplace committees; conviction could cost Party membership, promotion, or employment. The word remains in active everyday use but has lost its institutional teeth post-1991.

records.definition: Soviet-era colloquial for a formal charge of sexual immorality leveled at a person by a work brigade, Komsomol cell, or party committee; also the collective hearing at which such a charge was adjudicated.
records.notes: Unique to the Soviet institutional practice of collective moral oversight with no Western equivalent. A confirmed аморалка could result in expulsion from the Party, public shaming at a general meeting, job loss, or housing deprivation. Survives post-1991 in ironic and nostalgic usage.

records.definition: Sexual and moral dissolution; the state of being loosened from social and sexual restraint; used by Soviet ideologues to condemn Western permissiveness and by Russian conservatives to criticize contemporary sexual mores.
records.notes: From распустить ('to let loose/unravel'); the implication is that social bonds have been allowed to slacken, releasing the person from appropriate sexual constraint. Ideologically loaded in Soviet discourse as a charge against bourgeois Western influence.

records.definition: Immodesty; the violation of standards of sexual and social propriety through dress, speech, or behavior, particularly applied to women in Soviet-era moral discourse as evidence of compromised moral character.
records.notes: Negation of скромность (modesty); in Soviet moral discourse, нескромность in dress or sexual behavior was a strike against a woman's моральный облик that could be raised at a collective meeting. Applies to both sexual and non-sexual conduct but the sexual dimension is primary in this corpus.

records.definition: Chaste; sexually pure in thought and action; in both Orthodox Christian theology and Soviet moral ideology, the valued state of sexual restraint before marriage, particularly for women.
records.notes: Etymology: цело (whole/intact) + мудрость (wisdom); literally 'whole-wisdom' or 'intact-wisdom,' framing chastity as cognitive and moral integrity rather than merely physical virginity. The word is more elevated and literary than its Soviet-era deployment might suggest.

records.definition: Modesty; the valued quality of restraint and decorum in sexual matters, dress, and self-presentation; a central Soviet moral virtue for women that encompassed sexual unavailability, unprovocative dress, and reluctance to discuss personal sexuality.
records.notes: One of the most common and broadly positive words in Russian; in the sexual dimension, скромность means projecting sexual unavailability and discretion — the antonym of распущенность. English 'modesty' covers multiple senses; the sexual-restraint dimension is what this corpus captures.

records.definition: Literally 'moral image' or 'moral profile'; the Soviet concept of a person's publicly assessed moral standing, including sexual conduct, family stability, and collective behavior, used by party committees to evaluate fitness for promotion, Party membership, or positions of trust.
records.notes: Sexual behavior was a primary component: extramarital affairs, homosexuality, or promiscuity were formal strikes against one's моральный облик. The concept presupposes a collective body with authority to evaluate and discipline private sexuality — an institutional structure without a Western equivalent.

records.definition: Moral decay or decomposition of customs; the Soviet and conservative Russian phrase for the decline of sexual and social morality, typically attributed to Western capitalist influence, permissiveness, or deliberate ideological subversion.
records.notes: Разложение means decomposition or putrefaction, applied to нравы (customs/mores); the metaphor frames sexual permissiveness as biological rot. Standard Soviet ideological formulation used to condemn homosexuality, pornography, and rock music alike; still deployed by Russian Orthodox Church spokespeople.

records.definition: Anti-social behavior; the Soviet legal and moral catch-all phrase applied to behaviors deemed harmful to socialist society, including homosexuality, prostitution, public drunkenness, and sexual promiscuity.
records.notes: In Soviet law, male homosexuality was classified under this category alongside hooliganism until Russia decriminalized it in 1993. The phrase remains in active conservative and legal discourse as a condemnation of sexual nonconformity; approximate match only because the English phrase lacks the Soviet legal-punitive weight.

records.definition: Soviet moral-legal category meaning 'social parasitism' — living without socially useful labor — deployed against those whose lifestyles (including sex workers and homosexuals) were deemed incompatible with socialist norms.
records.notes: Primarily a work-ethics and ideological term, not intrinsically sexual; included in sexuality indices because it was used to prosecute prostitutes, gay men, and the sexually dissolute under the 1961 anti-parasitism decree. Joseph Brodsky was famously convicted under it. Recognition higher among adults 40+ who lived under the Soviet system.

records.definition: Sexual licentiousness or moral looseness; a condemnatory compound phrase used in both Soviet official discourse and Orthodox moral teaching to denounce unrestrained sexual behavior.
records.notes: Распущенность alone means 'lack of discipline/moral looseness'; the compound specifies the sexual domain. Stilted and formal — never street slang. Heard in official speeches, church homilies, and moralizing journalism.

records.definition: Free love; the early-Soviet revolutionary ideology, most associated with Alexandra Kollontai, that rejected bourgeois marriage as a property institution and advocated sexual relationships based on desire and mutual consent alone.
records.notes: Prominent in 1917–1930 Bolshevik sexual politics before Stalin reversed course in the 1930s and reimposed conservative family norms. Now used historically, ironically, or in leftist discourse. Mapped to ethical_non_monogamy as closest concept, though free love carries an explicit anti-institutional ideological charge absent from ENM.

records.definition: Bourgeois morality; Marxist-Leninist shorthand for the sexual and family ethics of the capitalist class — monogamy, premarital chastity, property-based marriage — condemned in Soviet thought as ideological tools of class oppression.
records.notes: Ironic historical arc: early Soviets condemned bourgeois sexual conservatism, yet by the 1930s Soviet society became more sexually conservative than what it mocked. Still heard in contemporary leftist or satirical discourse. Recognition skews older.

records.definition: Decadentism; Soviet critical term for the perceived cultural and moral degeneration of bourgeois society, encompassing sexual permissiveness, aesthetic excess, nihilism, and despair.
records.notes: Derived from упадок (decline/decay). In Soviet literary criticism it targeted Symbolist and Decadent artists; in moral discourse it condemned Western sexual and cultural excess as evidence of capitalist collapse. Very low recognition among speakers under 40.

records.definition: Fornication or sexual immorality; in Orthodox Christian theology one of the eight capital passions, encompassing all non-marital sexual acts and regarded as a sin against God and the body.
records.notes: Church Slavonic root word from which блудница (harlot), блудный (prodigal/lecherous), and распутство derive. Distinct from прелюбодеяние (adultery specifically). Carries both theological weight and mild everyday crudeness — used colloquially to mean 'lechery' without religious framing.

records.definition: Adultery; in Orthodox theology and pre-revolutionary Russian law, sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse — a more specific and more severely condemned sin than блуд.
records.notes: Strictly means adultery (violation of marital fidelity); the registry's 'fornication' concept covers pre-marital sex and is not exact. In Orthodox confession, прелюбодеяние and блуд are enumerated as distinct sins. Formal, ecclesiastical register — never colloquial.

records.definition: The sin of fornication or lust; a set phrase from Orthodox moral theology naming sexual immorality as a sin against both God and the temple of the body.
records.notes: Compound phrase: блудный (lecherous/fornicating — same root as 'prodigal' in блудный сын, the Prodigal Son) + грех (sin). Common in Orthodox confessional and homiletic contexts. Slightly higher crude score than блуд alone due to the explicit 'sin' framing intensifying the moral charge.

records.definition: Sinful; adjective applied in Orthodox and broader Russian cultural discourse to characterize sexual desires, thoughts, or acts as contrary to divine law and spiritually corrupting.
records.notes: General religious adjective. Applied to sexuality to frame desire as inherently morally suspect — e.g., греховные мысли (sinful thoughts), греховные желания (sinful desires). Widely used outside strictly religious contexts in everyday moralizing speech.

records.definition: Sin; in sexual contexts, the Orthodox and broader Russian cultural framing of sexual desire and non-marital sex as a transgression against divine law — the foundational moral category governing all sexuality in religious discourse.
records.notes: Extremely high-frequency word with many non-sexual applications. Sexual meaning is the dominant application in Orthodox moral theology, activated by collocations: грехи плоти (sins of the flesh), введение в грех (leading into sin). Mapped to carnal_desire as the closest available registry concept.

records.definition: Ritual and moral impurity; in Orthodox theology, a state of spiritual uncleanness caused by sexual acts, menstruation, nocturnal emission, or other bodily events, requiring prayer and abstinence before full participation in worship.
records.notes: Encompasses both ritual impurity (temporary, cleansable through prayer) and moral impurity (sinful). Has strong Hebrew Bible antecedents (טָמֵא / tāmēʾ) transmitted through the Septuagint. Broader and more theologically precise than the registry's 'indecency,' which implies public-decency violation rather than ritual uncleanness.

records.definition: Chastity or sexual purity; in Orthodox Christianity, a cardinal virtue encompassing pre-marital virginity, marital fidelity, and the disciplined subordination of sexual desire to spiritual order.
records.notes: Etymology: целый (whole/intact) + мудрость (wisdom) — 'wholeness of mind.' Broader than mere abstinence: it is an attitude of integrated purity governing the whole person. Highly esteemed in Orthodox monastic and lay ascetic tradition. Closer to the Latin 'castitas' than to simple virginity.

records.definition: Carnal sin or sin of the flesh; Orthodox phrase for any sin rooted in bodily appetite, predominantly applied to sexual transgressions.
records.notes: Плотский derives from плоть (flesh). Nearly interchangeable with блудный грех in common use but technically broader — can include gluttony and other physical sins — though the sexual application is overwhelmingly dominant in confessional and homiletic contexts.

records.definition: Sodomy; in Russian Orthodox and historical legal usage, anal intercourse or other non-procreative sexual acts, historically criminalized and strongly condemned as a sin against nature and God.
records.notes: Borrowed from the biblical city of Sodom via Church Slavonic and Latin. Criminalized in Russia under Soviet Article 121 until 1993. Prominently revived in contemporary Russian anti-LGBT rhetoric since 2013; recognition has risen accordingly. Carries both theological condemnation and legal-historical register.

records.definition: Sodomite; in Orthodox theology and traditional Russian public discourse, a man who practices anal sex — used almost exclusively as a condemnation of homosexual men.
records.notes: Religious-legal pejorative. Usage has intensified sharply in Russian public discourse since the 2013 'gay propaganda' law, deployed by conservative commentators and clergy as an alternative to gay/homosexual that carries maximum moral-historical condemnation. Crude score reflects its function as a slur.

records.definition: Harlot or fornicatrix; in Orthodox usage, a woman guilty of sexual immorality — encompassing both prostitutes and promiscuous women who commit блуд.
records.notes: Feminine form derived from блуд. Famous from the Gospel narrative of the sinful woman (traditionally conflated with Mary Magdalene). Distinct from проститутка (prostitute) by its theological-moral rather than transactional framing. Carries the dual sense of sexual sinner and fallen woman; the condemnation is moral, not merely commercial.

records.definition: Fallen woman; a 19th-century Russian literary and social euphemism for a woman who has lost her sexual virtue through seduction, coercion, or poverty-driven prostitution, framed as a social tragedy rather than purely moral condemnation.
records.notes: Peak in Russian realist literature: Dostoevsky's Sonya Marmeladova, Tolstoy's Katyusha Maslova. The 'fall' (падение) implies a descent from social respectability. Carries more pathos and class-critical nuance than блудница, which is purely condemnatory. The term shaped 19th-century reform movements around rescuing такие женщины.

records.definition: Repentance or penance; in Orthodox Christianity, the sacramental and psychological process of confessing, regretting, and committing to turn away from sexual sin — the prescribed institutional response to блуд and плотский грех.
records.notes: Not inherently sexual but central to Orthodox sexual ethics as the culturally enforced mechanism for processing and renouncing sexual transgression. Mapped to sexual_repression because the institutional requirement of покаяние is a primary vehicle through which Russian religious culture internalizes guilt about sexuality. Distinct from Catholic penance: Orthodox покаяние emphasizes inner transformation over prescribed acts.

records.definition: Spiritual delusion (prelest); in Orthodox ascetic theology, a dangerous state of self-deception where a person believes demonic or carnal temptations — including sexual ones — to be divinely inspired, leading to spiritual pride and destruction.
records.notes: CRITICAL DISAMBIGUATION: The common modern Russian word прелесть means 'charm/beauty/delight' (recognition ~99%) — this is an entirely different, unrelated sense. The Orthodox theological meaning documented here is known primarily by monastics, theologians, and the Orthodox educated (~28%). In ascetic texts, sexual temptation is a primary gateway into прелесть. The English transliteration 'prelest' exists in Orthodox theological writing but has no common secular equivalent. Proposed slug: orthodox_spiritual_delusion.

records.definition: Temptation; in sexual contexts, the experience of being drawn toward sexual sin — understood in Orthodox theology as a trial of the soul and an opportunity to choose virtue or fall into блуд.
records.notes: Extremely common word with many non-sexual applications (temptation to steal, to lie, etc.). Sexual temptation is the most culturally prominent application in Orthodox and general Russian religious discourse. Mapped to lust as the closest registry concept for the sexual valence, though искушение denotes the external allure more than the internal craving.

records.definition: Sweetness of sin; a theological phrase acknowledging the seductive pleasure of sexual transgression, used in Orthodox homiletics to explain why believers succumb and to underscore the mortal danger of carnal desire.
records.notes: Phrase from Orthodox homiletic and confessional literature. Notable for its phenomenological honesty: the сладость (sweetness/pleasure) is acknowledged as real, not dismissed, making the warning more sophisticated — the pleasure is the trap. Found in patristic texts translated into Church Slavonic and in 19th-century Russian religious writers.

records.definition: Flesh; in Orthodox and biblical usage, the corporeal nature of the human being with its appetites and passions — especially sexual desire — understood as the domain of carnal temptation opposed to the spirit.
records.notes: Church Slavonic word distinct from the neutral тело (body). The biblical antithesis плоть vs. дух (flesh vs. spirit) is foundational to Orthodox sexual ethics. Key collocations: грехи плоти (sins of the flesh), похоти плоти (lusts of the flesh), умерщвление плоти (mortification of the flesh). Not crude in itself — its gravity is theological.

records.definition: Mortification of the flesh; the Orthodox and broader Christian ascetic practice of deliberately suppressing bodily appetites — through fasting, cold exposure, sleep deprivation, and physical austerities — as a discipline against sexual desire and carnal passion.
records.notes: Умерщвление = 'killing off/deadening.' Goes well beyond sexual abstinence to include active physical self-punishment. Central to Orthodox monasticism and advocated in patristic ascetic literature (Evagrius, John Climacus). Mapped to sexual_abstinence as closest registry concept, though the practice is markedly more physically demanding and involves deliberate bodily suffering rather than mere restraint.

records.definition: Lustful or lascivious; an archaic adjective, influenced by Church Slavonic, applied to people, thoughts, or glances characterized by intense carnal sexual appetite.
records.notes: Archaic form; the modern equivalent is похотливый (same meaning, fully current). Derived from похоть (lust/carnal desire). Found primarily in religious texts, 18th–19th century literature, and deliberately archaizing registers. Recognition among speakers under 35 is low; older speakers recognize it readily from religious or literary exposure.

records.definition: Shameless; applied in Orthodox moral discourse and everyday Russian speech to someone — especially a woman — who displays sexual behavior without remorse, guilt, or social concealment, violating the shame-based norms that regulate sexuality.
records.notes: Literally без (without) + стыд (shame) → бесстыжий. Shame (стыд) functions as the primary internal regulator of sexual behavior in Russian honor-shame culture; бесстыжий names its absence. Applied with particular severity to women who display sexuality publicly or without apparent guilt. Still actively used in colloquial Russian — not archaic. The 'approximate' translation quality reflects that 'shameless' in English has largely lost its specifically sexual sting.

records.definition: Moral shame or sexual disgrace; in Orthodox usage also a euphemism for the genitals ('shameful parts').
records.notes: Derives from Proto-Slavic *sormŭ; in Church Slavonic and Orthodox homiletics. Phrase 'срамные места' = genitals.

records.definition: A disgraceful or shameful state of affairs, especially in sexual or moral matters; used exclamatorially to express moral outrage.
records.notes: Nominalised intensification of срам; exclamatory use predominates in folk and colloquial speech ('какая срамота!').

records.definition: Honor; in sexual contexts specifically a woman's chastity and sexual reputation as a socially enforced patriarchal and Orthodox moral value.
records.notes: Primary Russian word for honor in all senses; in sexual discourse means female chastity as a family-owned social commodity. Loss of честь is a central plot driver in 19th-century Russian literature.

records.definition: Dishonor; in sexual contexts the formal social category of a woman having lost her chastity and consequently her standing in community and family.
records.notes: Antonym of честь; a grave social and legal category in pre-Soviet Orthodox Russia. The concept frames sexual dishonor as an irreversible status change, not merely a reputation problem.

records.definition: Public disgrace or scandal; in sexual contexts the public humiliation of a person, especially a woman, for violating sexual norms.
records.notes: General-purpose word for shame/disgrace, not inherently sexual; mapped to slut_shaming here because in the honor-shame economy it functions as the mechanism of social enforcement against sexual transgressors.

records.definition: To publicly disgrace or shame someone, typically by exposing sexual misconduct or destroying their reputation.
records.notes: Perfective verb (single completed act of disgracing); can apply to any public dishonoring but is frequently used in sexual honor contexts.

records.definition: To disgrace oneself; to bring shame upon oneself through illicit or sexually indecent behavior.
records.notes: Reflexive counterpart of опозорить; the self-directed version of public sexual shaming; implies the subject's own conduct caused the disgrace.

records.definition: To stain or taint someone's honor; to destroy a woman's sexual reputation through seduction, rape, or public revelation of sexual misconduct.
records.notes: Metaphor of staining/sullying fabric; 'запятнать' = to spot, to blot; used in 19th-century literature and folk speech for sexual violation or scandal that destroys female honor.

records.definition: Slut, whore; the primary Russian crude insult for a sexually promiscuous woman.
records.notes: One of the most common sexual insults in Russian; used as a serious character attack and as casual hyperbole. Etymology uncertain; possibly from Polish 'szluja'. Near-mat register.

records.definition: A loose or promiscuous woman; literally 'the one who walks around (sexually)'; derived from гулять (to walk, to revel, to fool around).
records.notes: Traditional folk/colloquial pejorative; less offensive than шлюха but still stigmatizing. Also appears in historical and literary texts for women of easy virtue.

records.definition: To sleep around, to engage in promiscuous extramarital sex; literally 'to accumulate by walking/roving about.'
records.notes: Prefix на- = accumulative result; гулять = to walk/revel/fool around. Used in phrases like 'нагулялась в молодости' (she slept around in her youth). Always implies extramarital context.

records.definition: To conceive and bear a child out of wedlock through promiscuous sexual behavior; literally 'to walk a child into existence.'
records.notes: Extension of нагулять with direct object (ребёнка = child); always pejorative, attributing the pregnancy to the woman's promiscuity; the father is typically unnamed or unknown.

records.definition: Illegitimate; born outside of marriage; the formal legal and bureaucratic term for a bastard in pre-Soviet Russian civil and church law.
records.notes: Compound: незаконно (unlawfully) + рождённый (born); purely clinical/legal register with no inherent insult force, unlike байстрюк or бастард. Used in official documents and 19th-century literature.

records.definition: Bastard; a derogatory folk and dialectal term for an illegitimate child, used primarily in Ukrainian and South Russian speech.
records.notes: Primarily Ukrainian; enters Russian through Babel, Bulgakov, Southern dialects. Etymology disputed: possibly Polish 'bęckart' or Yiddish. Largely obsolete in contemporary standard Russian.

records.definition: Bastard; an illegitimate child or general insult for a contemptible person; a direct loanword from French/English.
records.notes: Used in historical (noble genealogy, heraldry) and literary contexts, and also as a general modern insult. Less emotionally loaded in Russian than in English; slightly bookish.

records.definition: A fallen woman; a woman who has lost her virtue through sexual sin; used in Orthodox moral discourse and 19th-century Russian literature.
records.notes: From пасть (to fall); strong Orthodox moral framing equating sexual sin with a spiritual fall from grace. Used by Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, et al. Not crude — literary and religiously charged. Russian equivalent of Victorian 'fallen woman'.

records.definition: A spoiled or corrupted woman; one who is no longer sexually pure or virtuous; used as a pejorative for a sexually experienced or morally compromised woman.
records.notes: Literally 'corrupted' or 'spoiled' (as food spoils); the sexual meaning is implicit and applied almost exclusively to women. The metaphor treats virginity as a commodity that degrades on contact.

records.definition: A slut; crude colloquial insult for a sexually promiscuous woman who is 'dragged around' between sexual partners.
records.notes: From потаскать/потащить (to drag around repeatedly); implies the woman has been physically passed from partner to partner. Diminutive suffix -ушка moderates form but not force.

records.definition: Whoring, gross sexual debauchery, promiscuity as a way of life; abstract noun derived from блядь (whore/slut); also used hyperbolically for any contemptible or dishonest conduct.
records.notes: Near-mat word; broad extended meaning covers any morally reprehensible behavior beyond sexuality ('это политическое блядство'). The -ство suffix makes it an abstract/collective concept rather than a single act.

records.definition: Shame; in the Russian sexual honor economy, the internalized negative affect that enforces sexual norms and polices individual behavior from within.
records.notes: Distinguished from позор (external public disgrace) by being internal and self-directed. 'Как не стыдно' (have you no shame?) is a primary social sanction. The Russian honor-shame system treats стыд and позор as complementary enforcement mechanisms.

records.definition: To shame oneself; to behave in a sexually or morally disgraceful manner; to make a public spectacle of one's own shameful conduct.
records.notes: Reflexive of срамить (to shame someone else); implies acting in a way that invites moral condemnation. More archaic than опозориться; primarily encountered in religious and folk literary contexts.

records.definition: A shameless woman; a woman who lacks sexual or moral shame and flaunts her behavior openly.
records.notes: Feminine noun; без-стыд-ница = without-shame-woman; less severe than шлюха; often used by older generations scolding younger women perceived as sexually immodest. Masculine form бесстыдник exists but is less charged.

records.definition: To dishonor someone; in historical and literary contexts specifically to rape or seduce a woman, thereby destroying her sexual honor and social standing irreversibly.
records.notes: From обес-честить (to strip of honor); in 19th-century Russian literature typically a euphemism for rape or seduction-unto-ruin. Cf. usage in Pushkin, Dostoevsky, Ostrovsky. Modern usage more broadly means to disgrace in any context.

records.definition: A girl's honor; the specific set phrase denoting female virginity and sexual purity as a socially and morally valued patriarchal commodity in Russian culture.
records.notes: Fixed phrase; 'защитить честь девушки' = to defend a girl's honor; 'лишить чести' = to take her honor. The concept frames female virginity as an asset belonging as much to the family as to the individual woman.

records.definition: Female breasts; slang term used in Russian criminal argot (fenya) and some informal colloquial speech.
records.notes: Origin unclear; possibly reduplicative baby-talk (childish diminutive pattern) or borrowed via Romani into fenya. Restricted primarily to fenya speakers and users of urban criminal slang; low recognition outside that subculture.

records.definition: A sexually promiscuous or loose woman; used as a harsh insult meaning slut or cheap prostitute in criminal argot and broad colloquial speech.
records.notes: Crossed from феня into general colloquial use; one of the most widely deployed Russian female-targeted sexual insults.

records.definition: Literally 'mare'; criminal argot for a large, coarse, or sexually available woman — dehumanizes by equine comparison.
records.notes: The horse metaphor implies both sexual availability and physical coarseness; in prison slang sometimes denotes a female inmate used as a sexual object by others.

records.definition: Intensified augmentative of сука (bitch); a maximally contemptuous insult for a vile or despicable woman.
records.notes: The -ара suffix is a pejorative intensifier; considerably stronger than сука alone; common in criminal argot and street speech.

records.definition: A whore or sexually promiscuous woman; a strong insult borrowed from Polish/Ukrainian kurwa.
