records.definition: 'ĐM'; internet abbreviation for 'địt mẹ' (motherfucker), the most common profanity abbreviation in Vietnamese online spaces.
records.notes: Extremely common in Vietnamese internet comments, gaming, and social media; universally understood as the abbreviated expletive.

records.definition: 'ĐMM'; internet abbreviation intensifying 'đm', stands for 'địt mẹ mày' (fuck your mother/you); stronger variant.
records.notes: More intensified form than 'đm'; 'mày' = you; the addition of the second person makes it more direct and confrontational.

records.definition: 'VCL'; internet abbreviation for 'vãi cái lồn' (fucking hell / incredible cunt); a versatile profane exclamation.
records.notes: One of the most common Vietnamese internet expletives; used as a versatile intensifier/exclamation like English 'WTF'.

records.definition: 'CC'; internet abbreviation for 'con cặc' (fucking cock) or 'cái cặc' (the cock/dick); used as a profane exclamation.
records.notes: Common Vietnamese internet profanity abbreviation; 'cặc' = vulgar penis; used in gaming and social media.

records.definition: 'VL'; abbreviation for 'vãi lồn' (fucking incredible); a profane exclamation of disbelief or amazement.
records.notes: 'Vãi' = spill/scatter (intensifier), 'lồn' = vulgar vagina; used as reaction/exclamation; widely used Vietnamese internet slang.

records.definition: 'Ecstatically good'; the feeling of intense sexual pleasure or orgasmic satisfaction.
records.notes: 'Phê' = high/ecstatic (originally from drug context), 'sướng' = pleasure/satisfaction; used for both sexual and drug highs.

records.definition: OnlyFans; the subscription-based adult content platform where creators sell access to sexually explicit content.
records.notes: English platform name used directly; known among Vietnamese internet users; some Vietnamese creators use it from abroad.

records.definition: Cam girl; a woman who performs sexual acts on webcam for online viewers, either live-streamed or recorded.
records.notes: English loanword; used in Vietnamese internet discussions; Vietnam has a growing cam sex industry.

records.definition: Cam boy; a man who performs sexual acts on webcam for online viewers.
records.notes: English loanword; less common than 'camgirl' in Vietnamese discourse but recognized by internet-savvy users.

records.definition: Live streamed sex; sexual activity performed live on internet streaming platforms for viewers.
records.notes: Growing issue in Vietnam; police have prosecuted livestream sex cases; 'livestream' from English is widely used in Vietnamese.

records.definition: 'Booking services'; a euphemism for ordering sexual services online or by phone.
records.notes: 'Đặt dịch vụ' = to book/order services; in sex work context, a recognized euphemism for arranging a sex worker.

records.definition: 'Booking a girl'; to arrange/order a sex worker; the common colloquial expression for booking a female sex worker online.
records.notes: 'Đặt' = to book/order; 'gái' = girl (in this context = sex worker); extremely common in Vietnamese online sex work discourse.

records.definition: Gay male performer in 'cải lương' (southern Vietnamese reformed opera); a culturally recognized gay male theatrical role.
records.notes: 'Bóng' = gay man, 'cải lương' = southern Vietnamese traditional theater; historically some 'bóng' found acceptance in theatrical arts.

records.definition: Spirit medium; a person (often feminine-presenting male) who enters trance states and is 'possessed' by spirits in Vietnamese folk religion.
records.notes: Central to Vietnamese folk religion (thờ Mẫu / Mother Goddess worship); many 'con đồng' are gay or gender-nonconforming men.

records.definition: Male spirit medium; a man who serves as a ritual spirit medium in Vietnamese Mother Goddess religion (Đạo Mẫu).
records.notes: 'Ông' = Mr./male honorific, 'đồng' = spirit medium; often effeminate men; a culturally tolerated gender-nonconforming role.

records.definition: Female spirit medium; a woman who serves as a ritual spirit medium in Vietnamese Mother Goddess religion.
records.notes: 'Bà' = Mrs./female honorific; female practitioners are also common; some are lesbian or gender-nonconforming.

records.definition: Spirit possession ritual; the trance ceremony in Vietnamese Mother Goddess religion where the medium is possessed by spirits.
records.notes: 'Hầu' = to serve; 'đồng' = medium; UNESCO recognized 'thực hành tín ngưỡng thờ Mẫu' including hầu đồng in 2016.

records.definition: Person who 'mounts the spirit'; a spirit medium who enters trance possession; a descriptive term for any gender.
records.notes: Neutral descriptive phrase; 'lên đồng' = to mount the trance; less identity-based than 'con đồng'.

records.definition: A southern Vietnamese gay male ritual entertainer who performs at religious festivals and funerals; a culturally accepted gender-nonconforming role.
records.notes: Unique to southern Vietnam (Nam Bộ); 'bóng rỗi' perform theatrical shows at Goddess temples and funerals; culturally tolerated.

records.definition: 'Flower bóng'; a term for a gentle, effeminate gay man; a relatively neutral subtype within the 'bóng' spectrum.
records.notes: 'Hoa' = flower; contrasts with more visible/flamboyant types; Vietnam has elaborate internal classifications within gay communities.

records.definition: Master spirit medium; a senior practitioner who trains others in the spirit possession tradition.
records.notes: 'Đồng thầy' = master/teacher medium; holds high ritual authority; often long-term gender-nonconforming practitioners.

records.definition: Kathoey; Thai transgender woman or feminine gay man; borrowed term used in Vietnam due to proximity to Thailand.
records.notes: Thai loanword; known in Vietnam due to tourism and media; often used for Thai transgender women specifically.

records.definition: Ladyboy; transgender woman or feminine-presenting male, especially from Southeast Asian context.
records.notes: English term widely used in Vietnam; often refers specifically to Thai transgender women in Vietnamese tourism context.

records.term: người đồng tính nữ (lesbian - community term)
records.definition: Lesbian (formal community term); a woman attracted to other women; the respectful full-form term.
records.notes: Full formal designation; 'người' = person, 'đồng tính nữ' = same-sex female; contrasts with slang terms like 'les' or 'tom'.

records.term: người đồng tính nam (gay - community term)
records.definition: Gay man (formal community term); a man attracted to other men; the respectful full-form designation.
records.notes: Full formal designation; used in advocacy, journalism, and official reporting; preferred over slang in respectful contexts.

records.definition: LGBT; acronym for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender; the standard abbreviation for sexual and gender minority communities.
records.notes: Universally known in Vietnam via media; Vietnam is relatively progressive on LGBT issues in Southeast Asian context.

records.definition: The LGBT community; the collective community of lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people in Vietnam.
records.notes: Standard phrasing in Vietnamese journalism, advocacy, and policy discussions about sexual minority rights.

records.definition: 'Rainbow'; the rainbow symbol of LGBT pride; used in Vietnam to represent LGBT identity and community.
records.notes: The rainbow flag symbol is well-known in Vietnam; 'cầu vồng' = rainbow; used in pride events and LGBT advocacy.

records.definition: Gender reassignment surgery; medical procedures to change a person's physical sex characteristics.
records.notes: Vietnam legalized gender reassignment in 2015 but implementing regulations were slow; active medical tourism to Thailand exists.

records.definition: Hormone therapy; medical treatment using hormones to change secondary sex characteristics for transgender people.
records.notes: Used in transgender healthcare contexts; Vietnamese trans individuals often self-administer hormones due to limited healthcare access.

records.definition: Estrogen; the primary female sex hormone; used in transgender hormone therapy for feminization.
records.notes: Medical term used directly from English/Latin; known among healthcare providers and transgender communities in Vietnam.

records.definition: Testosterone; the primary male sex hormone; used in transgender hormone therapy for masculinization.
records.notes: Medical term used directly; known in healthcare and transgender contexts; also discussed in sports doping contexts.

records.definition: Chest surgery; surgical alteration of the chest for transgender people (breast augmentation for trans women, mastectomy for trans men).
records.notes: Used in transgender healthcare; both breast augmentation and mastectomy in gender-affirming contexts.

records.term: phẫu thuật tạo hình âm đạo
records.definition: Vaginoplasty; surgical construction of a vagina, typically as part of gender reassignment surgery for trans women.
records.notes: Medical term; the formal Vietnamese description of the procedure; known mainly to medical professionals and transgender individuals.

records.term: phẫu thuật tạo hình dương vật
records.definition: Phalloplasty; surgical construction of a penis, typically as part of gender reassignment surgery for trans men.
records.notes: Medical term; known mainly to medical professionals and transgender individuals; uncommon topic in mainstream Vietnamese discourse.

records.definition: Chastity/virtue; sexual purity, especially pre-marital virginity in women; a central Confucian social value.
records.notes: Core Confucian concept in Vietnamese culture; 'trinh' = chaste/pure, 'tiết' = integrity/moral standing; still highly valued.

records.definition: Virgin girl/woman; an unmarried woman who has not had sexual intercourse.
records.notes: 'Trinh' = chaste/virgin, 'nữ' = female; standard term for a virgin woman; used in medical and social contexts.

records.definition: Loss of virginity; the act of losing one's virginity; literally 'losing chastity'.
records.notes: 'Thất' = to lose/fail; 'trinh' = chastity; used in medical, social, and literary contexts about first sexual experience.

records.definition: To lose one's virginity; more colloquial than 'thất trinh'; commonly used in everyday speech.
records.notes: 'Mất' = to lose; more everyday form than 'thất trinh'; both still imply significant social meaning in Vietnam.

records.definition: 'Bad girl'; a girl or woman who has transgressed sexual norms, especially by having premarital sex.
records.notes: 'Hư' = spoiled/bad/naughty; used by parents, community, and conservative media for women who violate sexual norms.

records.definition: 'Bad girl'; a woman who breaks sexual norms; slightly more pejorative than 'con gái hư'.
records.notes: Shorter, more colloquial form; often implies sexual promiscuity; used in gossip and social media discussions.

records.definition: Whore; the most vulgar single-word term for a promiscuous woman or prostitute; a severe sexual insult.
records.notes: The core Vietnamese sexual slur for women; 'đĩ' alone is extremely offensive; the root of many compound insults like 'con đĩ'.

records.definition: A coquettish, flirtatious, or sexually loose woman; implies disregard for feminine virtue norms.
records.notes: 'Lẳng lơ' implies a woman who flirts or behaves seductively beyond social norms; milder than 'đĩ' but still pejorative.

records.definition: Promiscuous woman; a woman who is sexually liberal or seen as morally loose; a stronger term than 'lẳng lơ'.
records.notes: More strongly pejorative than 'lẳng lơ'; implies active sexual behavior deemed shameful; used in family and community condemnation.

records.definition: Promiscuous; having multiple sexual partners; engaging in romantic/sexual activity outside committed relationships.
records.notes: Can apply to men and women; less gender-biased than 'lẳng lơ'; used for infidelity or general promiscuity.

records.definition: 'Not upright/proper'; a person (especially woman) who does not conform to sexual moral standards.
records.notes: Indirect moral condemnation; 'đứng đắn' = proper/upright; 'không đứng đắn' = the opposite; used by conservative family members.

records.definition: 'Ruined body, lost virtue'; a strong condemnation for a woman who has violated sexual norms; fallen woman.
records.notes: Classical moral judgment; 'hư thân' = ruined person, 'mất nết' = lost virtue; historically devastating social consequence.

records.definition: 'Lost virtue'; lacking moral discipline in sexual matters; applied to women who transgress sexual norms.
records.notes: Abbreviated form of 'hư thân mất nết'; used in conservative discourse to condemn female sexual behavior.

records.definition: 'Failed virtue'; lacking moral integrity; used to describe sexual or moral transgressions that bring shame.
records.notes: 'Thất' = to lose/fail; 'đức' = virtue; applied to moral failures including sexual ones; used in family and community condemnation.

records.definition: Disgrace and shame; the state of social dishonor brought upon someone by sexual transgression.
records.notes: Sino-Vietnamese; 'ô' = dirty, 'nhục' = shame; often applied to families whose daughter has sexual scandal; honor-shame culture.

records.definition: Unchaste; not virginal; having had sex before marriage (applied to women); the opposite of 'trinh'.
records.notes: 'Bất' = not/without; 'trinh' = chaste/virgin; a severe moral judgment in traditional Vietnamese society.

records.definition: Virtue and moral character; especially female moral excellence including sexual chastity and fidelity.
records.notes: Confucian virtue concept; one of the four female virtues (tứ đức); includes sexual chastity as a core component.

records.definition: Preserving chastity; maintaining sexual purity, especially for widows who remained celibate after their husband's death.
records.notes: 'Thủ' = to guard/keep; archaic concept central to patriarchal Vietnamese gender norms; still referenced critically in feminist discourse.

records.definition: 'Good girl' (longer form); a well-behaved, sexually chaste young woman who upholds family honor.
records.notes: Used by parents and community elders to describe ideal female behavior; implies sexual propriety and obedience.

records.definition: 'Pure white virginity'; the quality of being innocent, untouched, and sexually pure.
records.notes: 'Trắng' = white (purity symbol); literary metaphor for virginal innocence; common in Vietnamese poetry and romantic literature.

records.definition: Clean/pure; morally and sexually uncorrupted; free from sexual sin or scandal.
records.notes: 'Trong sạch' = clean and clear; a common moral-sexual evaluation; 'con gái trong sạch' = a sexually pure girl.

records.definition: Scandal; notoriety from disreputable behavior, often sexual; bringing shame through widely known transgression.
records.notes: 'Tai tiếng' = bad reputation; applies to sexual scandals especially; common in media coverage of celebrity or political scandals.

records.definition: Scandal; a shocking and disgraceful event, including sexual misconduct or affairs made public.
records.notes: Common term for any major scandal; frequently used for sexual scandals involving public figures in Vietnamese media.

records.definition: 'Tomtomming'; to have a secret affair or illicit sexual involvement; implies sneaking around.
records.notes: Colloquial and somewhat humorous; 'tòm tem' is onomatopoeic, suggesting stealthy secret meetings; used in gossip.

records.definition: Boyfriend/girlfriend or lover; a romantic partner (not spouse); can imply an extramarital partner.
records.notes: Extremely common in Vietnamese; 'bồ' can mean legitimate partner or secret lover; context determines which; universally understood.

records.definition: 'Small girlfriend'; a young mistress or secret lover of a married man; the 'other woman' in an affair.
records.notes: 'Bồ' = lover, 'nhí' = small/young; widely used in Vietnamese to describe a young secret mistress; common tabloid topic.

records.definition: Lover; a person with whom one has a romantic and sexual relationship; often implies a non-marital partner.
records.notes: Literary/romantic register; 'người' = person, 'tình' = love/feeling; used in novels, songs, and romantic discourse.

records.definition: 'Little third'; the third party in an affair who breaks up a couple; the 'other woman/man'.
records.notes: Borrowed from Chinese internet slang '小三'; very popular in Vietnamese social media discussion of infidelity; mainly post-2015.

records.definition: Lover; a romantic-sexual partner, often in the context of an extramarital or secret relationship.
records.notes: 'Tình' = love, 'nhân' = person; slightly more formal than 'người tình'; used in romance novels and news reporting.

records.definition: Jealousy; the emotion of jealousy in romantic/sexual contexts; to feel jealous of a partner's behavior.
records.notes: One of the most commonly used emotional words in Vietnamese; sexual jealousy is a major theme in Vietnamese media and culture.

records.definition: Intense jealousy; the strong, consuming feeling of jealousy in romantic relationships; more intense than 'ghen' alone.
records.notes: 'Tuông' intensifies 'ghen'; often implies jealousy leading to conflict or confrontation; frequent theme in Vietnamese drama.

records.definition: Vital essence/energy; in Taoist-influenced Vietnamese medicine, the fundamental life energy including sexual essence retained through controlled ejaculation.
records.notes: Sino-Vietnamese Taoist concept; 'tinh' = semen/essence, 'khí' = energy; sexual conservation is seen as health-preserving.

records.definition: Kidney Yang; in traditional Vietnamese/Chinese medicine, the warming/active principle of kidney energy, linked to male sexual vitality.
records.notes: TCM concept fundamental to Vietnamese traditional medicine; low kidney yang = sexual dysfunction; treated with warming herbs.

records.definition: Kidney Yin; in traditional medicine, the cooling/nourishing principle of kidney energy; imbalance causes sexual dysfunction.
records.notes: Paired with thận dương; yin-yang balance in the kidneys is considered central to sexual health in Vietnamese traditional medicine.

records.definition: 'To tonify the kidney'; traditional medicine treatment to strengthen kidney function, primarily for sexual vitality and potency.
records.notes: Major Vietnamese traditional medicine practice; 'bổ thận' remedies are widely sold for male sexual dysfunction and infertility.

records.definition: 'Fortifying Yang'; traditional medicine treatments to enhance male sexual vitality and potency by strengthening Yang energy.
records.notes: Core traditional medicine concept; 'tráng dương' products (wines, tonics, herbs) are a large market in Vietnam and Vietnam-China trade.

records.definition: 'To supplement Yang'; tonic treatments to enhance Yang energy and male sexual performance.
records.notes: Closely related to 'tráng dương'; used interchangeably in traditional medicine marketing for male sexual health products.

records.definition: 'Physiology'; shorthand in Vietnamese for sexual capacity, performance, or drive; 'nhu cầu sinh lý' = sexual needs.
records.notes: 'Sinh lý' literally means physiology but is commonly used in everyday speech specifically for sexual function/libido.

records.definition: 'Tonify kidney and fortify Yang'; the combined traditional medicine treatment for male sexual vitality.
records.notes: The most common traditional medicine phrase for male sexual enhancement; found on countless herbal product labels in Vietnam.

records.definition: 'Supplement vital essence'; treatment to replenish sexual essence (tinh khí) consumed through sexual activity or illness.
records.notes: Traditional medicine practice; related to Taoist concepts of conserving and restoring jing; found in tonic wine and herbal formulas.

records.definition: Physiological impotence; inability to achieve or maintain erection; erectile dysfunction in traditional medicine framing.
records.notes: Combines traditional ('sinh lý' = physiology) with clinical ('bất lực' = inability); used in traditional medicine and clinical contexts.

records.definition: 'Internal power'; in Taoist tradition, the cultivation of internal energy including sexual energy for health and spiritual purposes.
records.notes: Martial arts and Taoist cultivation concept; sexual energy cultivation is one aspect of the broader nội công practice.

records.definition: 'Heart-kidney disconnection'; a TCM diagnosis describing disharmony between heart-fire and kidney-water, causing sexual and emotional dysfunction.
records.notes: Specific TCM syndrome; known mainly to traditional medicine practitioners; linked to sexual and sleep dysfunction.

records.definition: Kidney deficiency; the most common TCM diagnosis for sexual dysfunction, fatigue, and decline in sexual vitality.
records.notes: One of the most commercially exploited TCM diagnoses in Vietnam; 'thận hư' products (tonics, herbs) are a huge market.

records.definition: Missionary position; the sexual position with partners face to face, man on top; literally 'missionary preaching position'.
records.notes: Direct translation of 'missionary position'; well-known in Vietnam via online content and sex education materials.

records.definition: 'Dog position'; doggy style; the sexual position where the receiving partner is on all fours.
records.notes: 'Tư thế' = position, 'chó' = dog; the standard Vietnamese colloquial term for this position; crude but widely used.

records.definition: 'Doing it from behind'; a neutral-ish description of rear-entry sexual positions including doggy style.
records.notes: More neutral than 'tư thế chó'; descriptive phrase; used in sex advice and online discussions.

records.definition: 'Woman on top'; the cowgirl sex position where the woman straddles and rides her partner.
records.notes: Literal description; Vietnamese sex education and advice content uses this phrase; 'cowgirl' loanword also used sometimes.

records.definition: Facesitting; a sexual act where one partner sits on the other's face for oral stimulation.
records.notes: 'Ngồi' = sit, 'mặt' = face; the direct Vietnamese description; crude in context; known from online content.

records.definition: 'Position sixty-nine'; the 69 sexual position where both partners simultaneously perform oral sex on each other.
records.notes: Full Vietnamese name for the 69 position; 'sáu chín' = sixty-nine; also known simply as '69'.

records.definition: Sixty-nine; shorthand for the 69 position of mutual oral sex.
records.notes: 'Sáu' = six, 'chín' = nine; the number form of the 69 position name; equivalent to just writing '69'.

records.definition: 69; the numerically written shorthand for the sexual position involving simultaneous mutual oral sex.
records.notes: Universal symbol; used in Vietnamese internet discussions; the number shape represents two people in the 69 position.

records.definition: Informal term for someone assigned female who presents or identifies as male; 'pretending to be male'.
records.notes: Used in everyday Vietnamese speech; less stigmatizing than some other terms but still informal.

records.definition: Vietnamese slang for a butch or masculine-presenting lesbian; from English 'les' (lesbian) and 'tom' (tomboy).
records.notes: Widely used in Vietnam's LGBT community; contrasts with 'năng' (femme lesbian). Compound of borrowed terms.

records.definition: Clinical/formal Vietnamese term for bisexuality; literally 'dual-sex romantic attraction'.
records.notes: More formal than simply saying 'bi'; used in academic and medical contexts.

records.definition: Feminization; the process of acquiring or emphasizing feminine characteristics, used in medical or social contexts.
records.notes: Used in medical contexts (hormone feminization) as well as social commentary on gender expression.

records.definition: Extremely crude expletive literally meaning 'fuck your mother'; used as a general intensifier or insult.
records.notes: One of the strongest expletives in Vietnamese; extremely common in angry speech. Variant of 'địt mẹ'.

records.definition: Crude insult using the vulgar word for penis; roughly 'you dick' or 'you prick'.
records.notes: 'Đồ' is a classifier meaning 'you [derogatory]'; combined with 'cặc' (crude penis term) forms a strong insult.

records.definition: Chastity and virtue; the combination of sexual purity and moral integrity; a core Confucian female virtue.
records.notes: Classical compound; appears in classical texts about the four female virtues; more formal than 'trinh tiết'.

records.definition: 'Good girl'; a woman who conforms to sexual and social norms; the positive counterpart to 'gái hư'.
records.notes: 'Ngoan' = obedient/good; 'gái ngoan' implies sexual chastity and social conformity; highly valued in Vietnamese conservative culture.

records.definition: Pure/clean; innocent and sexually uncorrupted; used for both sexual and general moral purity.
records.notes: 'Trong' = clear/transparent, 'trắng' = white; the pairing emphasizes moral and sexual cleanliness.

records.definition: Adulteress/licentious woman; a classical pejorative for a woman who is sexually unfaithful or licentious.
records.notes: Sino-Vietnamese; 'dâm' = lewd, 'phụ' = woman; classical condemnation term; used in historical literature and conservative discourse.

records.definition: Romantic jealousy; jealousy specifically in the context of romantic love and sexual fidelity.
records.notes: 'Tình' = love/romance; specifies the romantic context of the jealousy; used in discussions of relationship dynamics.

records.definition: Vital force/energy; the physical and sexual energy of a person; in traditional medicine, linked to sexual potency.
records.notes: 'Khí' = energy/breath, 'lực' = strength; general life force concept with sexual health dimension in traditional medicine.

records.definition: 'Benefiting the essence'; traditional medicine concept of preserving and enriching sexual essence (tinh) for health and longevity.
records.notes: Taoist-influenced concept; reducing ejaculation to preserve jing/essence for health; practiced in traditional Vietnamese healing.

records.definition: Yang energy; the active, warm, male principle of energy; linked to sexual vitality and masculine potency.
records.notes: Fundamental Taoist concept; 'dương khí' strengthening is central to male sexual health in traditional Vietnamese medicine.

records.definition: 'Yin-Yang harmony'; the balance between male and female energies, including in sexual relationships; ideal state in traditional medicine.
records.notes: The ideal sexual-energetic state in Taoist medicine; harmonious sexual union is seen as health-promoting.

records.definition: 'Excess fire'; a TCM syndrome where excessive heat/fire energy causes sexual hyperactivity or dysfunction.
records.notes: TCM diagnostic term; relevant to sexual health (excessive desire, nocturnal emissions); treated with cooling herbs.

records.term: bệnh lây truyền qua đường tình dục
records.definition: Sexually transmitted infection; the full clinical phrase for diseases passed through sexual contact.
records.notes: Full official medical term; used in Vietnamese healthcare and public health campaigns; often abbreviated in practice.

records.definition: Sexual disease; common shorthand for sexually transmitted infections; literally 'love/sex disease'.
records.notes: Colloquial shorthand; 'bệnh' = disease, 'tình dục' = sexual; universally understood; less clinical than full term.

records.definition: 'Flower-willow disease'; classical/literary term for venereal diseases; a euphemistic reference to the world of pleasure (flowers and willows).
records.notes: Sino-Vietnamese; 'hoa' = flower (female), 'liễu' = willow (female beauty); alludes to sex work context of disease transmission.

records.definition: Gonorrhea; the bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
records.notes: Standard Vietnamese medical term; high awareness due to public health campaigns; common STI in Vietnam.

records.definition: Syphilis; the bacterial STI caused by Treponema pallidum; historically significant in Vietnam.
records.notes: 'Giang mai' = river plum; possibly from older naming conventions; the standard Vietnamese medical term for syphilis.

records.definition: Genital herpes; the viral STI caused by herpes simplex virus causing sores in the genital area.
records.notes: Standard Vietnamese medical term; 'mụn rộp' = blistering rash/herpes; 'sinh dục' = genital; clinical terminology.

records.definition: Genital warts; the STI caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) causing cauliflower-like growths on genitals.
records.notes: 'Sùi mào gà' = 'cauliflower growth of a rooster's comb'; vivid Vietnamese name; HPV vaccination awareness growing.

records.definition: HIV; Human Immunodeficiency Virus; the virus that causes AIDS; massive public health focus in Vietnam since 1990s.
records.notes: English acronym used directly worldwide including Vietnam; major public health issue; Vietnam has effective treatment programs.

records.definition: AIDS; Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome; the advanced stage of HIV infection; universally known in Vietnam.
records.notes: English acronym used directly; Vietnam had significant HIV/AIDS epidemic; massive awareness campaigns since 1995.

records.definition: Chlamydia; the bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.
records.notes: International term used directly; known to healthcare providers; awareness lower among general public than HIV or gonorrhea.

records.definition: Trichomonas/trichomoniasis; the protozoan STI caused by Trichomonas vaginalis; common but often overlooked.
records.notes: Medical term used directly; relatively low public awareness in Vietnam despite being common; mainly known to healthcare workers.

records.definition: Vaginal yeast infection; fungal infection of the vagina; 'nấm' = fungus, 'âm đạo' = vagina.
records.notes: Common in Vietnam; well-known due to widespread advertising for antifungal treatments; standard clinical term.

records.definition: Vaginitis; inflammation of the vagina, which can be caused by bacterial, fungal, or other infections.
records.notes: Clinical term; 'viêm' = inflammation, 'âm đạo' = vagina; frequently encountered in Vietnamese women's health contexts.

records.definition: 'Three-handed'; a threesome; sexual activity involving three people simultaneously.
records.notes: 'Tay' = hand (counting metaphor for persons); 'ba' = three; common in Vietnamese descriptions of three-way sex.

records.definition: 'Trio'; a group of three; in sexual context, a threesome or three-way sexual encounter.
records.notes: 'Bộ' = set, 'ba' = three; used for threesomes in online content; also the normal word for trio/set in non-sexual contexts.

records.definition: Group sex; sexual activity involving multiple participants; the clinical-neutral Vietnamese phrase.
records.notes: 'Nhóm' = group, 'tình dục' = sexual; used in public health research and sex education contexts.

records.definition: 'Three people'; a neutral euphemistic way to refer to a threesome sexual encounter.
records.notes: Extremely neutral on its surface; 'ba người' = three people; in sexual context understood as a threesome.

records.definition: 'Four people'; a neutral way to refer to a four-way sexual encounter.
records.notes: Neutral number-based reference; 'bốn người' = four people; used in explicit online content discussions.

records.definition: Gangbang; a sexual act involving multiple people having sex with one person; extremely crude.
records.notes: 'Đụ' = fuck (vulgar), 'tập thể' = collective/group; very crude compound; known mainly from online pornographic content.

records.definition: Group sexual relations; a more neutral term for group sex; 'quan hệ' = relations/relationship.
records.notes: More neutral phrasing than 'đụ tập thể'; used in news reporting about group sex cases and online discussions.

records.definition: 'Young lover'; a younger romantic partner, especially of an older married person; implies an affair.
records.notes: Common in discussions of age-gap affairs; 'người tình' = lover, 'trẻ' = young; often in tabloid reporting.

records.definition: Secret lover; a romantic-sexual partner kept hidden from others, typically from a spouse or family.
records.notes: 'Bí mật' = secret; used in gossip, tabloid reporting, and romance novels about hidden affairs.

records.definition: Lover; specifically an extramarital lover or mistress; 'nhân' = person, 'tình' = love/feeling.
records.notes: 'Nhân tình' implies an illicit relationship; used in legal contexts for extramarital affairs and in literary works.

records.definition: 'Small wife'; a secondary wife or concubine; in pre-modern Vietnam, wealthy men maintained multiple wives in a hierarchy.
records.notes: Historical institution; polygamy was legal in South Vietnam until 1975; 'vợ bé' contrasts with 'vợ cả' (first/main wife).

records.definition: Secondary wife; a concubine or secondary spouse in the traditional Vietnamese polygamous family structure.
records.notes: More formal/archaic than 'vợ bé'; appears in historical literature and legal discussions of pre-1975 family law.

records.definition: 'Wives and concubines'; the collective term for all of a man's wives and concubines in the traditional polygamous household.
records.notes: Classical Sino-Vietnamese; 'thê' = primary wife, 'thiếp' = concubine; found in historical novels and Confucian texts.

records.definition: Concubine; a secondary wife of lower status than the primary wife in a traditional polygamous household.
records.notes: Classical term; in pre-modern Vietnam, thiếp had specific legal rights but lower status; also a humble self-reference for women.

records.definition: Handmaiden-concubine; a woman who served as both attendant and concubine to a noble or royal household member.
records.notes: Classical term for female attendants-cum-concubines in aristocratic and royal households; seen in historical films and literature.

records.definition: Female household servant; a maid who may have also served sexual functions in historical aristocratic households.
records.notes: Historical term; 'hầu' = to serve, 'gái' = girl; in elite households often implied potential sexual availability to master.

records.definition: Female entertainer; a female performer in traditional Vietnamese theater or entertainment, often with associated sexual availability.
records.notes: Short for 'ả đào' (traditional female entertainer); 'đào' can also mean 'peach' in non-sexual contexts.

records.definition: Traditional female entertainer; a woman trained in singing, music, and the arts who entertained patrons, sometimes sexually.
records.notes: Associated with 'ca trù' (chamber music) tradition; 'ả đào' were highly skilled but socially marginal; protected by French-era tolerance.

records.definition: 'Male whore'; a crude insult calling a man a prostitute or sexually servile male; applied to effeminate or gay men.
records.notes: 'Thằng' = male (derogatory classifier), 'đĩ đực' = male whore; a severe gender-normative insult targeting gay/effeminate men.

records.definition: 'Male prostitute/whore'; a gender-crossing insult for a man behaving like a female prostitute; applied to gay or submissive men.
records.notes: 'Con' = child/female classifier (derogatory for males), 'đĩ đực' = male whore; compounds the insult by using female classifier.

records.definition: 'Lecherous goat'; a crude insult for a sexually predatory or excessively lecherous man.
records.notes: 'Dâm' = lewd, 'dê' = goat (symbol of lechery in Vietnamese); 'thằng' = male (derogatory); common male sexual insult.

records.definition: 'Licentious woman'; a strong insult for a sexually promiscuous or immoral woman.
records.notes: 'Con' = female classifier (derogatory), 'dâm phụ' = lewd woman; classical pejorative compound now used in heated arguments.

records.definition: 'Pack of sexual deviants'; a group insult condemning multiple people as sexually depraved or corrupt.
records.notes: 'Lũ' = pack/gang, 'dâm ô' = sexual misconduct; used to condemn groups engaged in or associated with sexual wrongdoing.

records.definition: 'Sexual pervert/degenerate'; a condemnatory insult for someone engaged in immoral or excessive sexual behavior.
records.notes: 'Dâm loạn' = sexual chaos/perversion; 'đồ' = derogatory classifier; used to strongly condemn sexual behavior.

records.definition: 'Lecherous old goat'; a strong insult for an older man who is sexually predatory or inappropriately lustful.
records.notes: 'Lão' = old man, 'dê' = goat (lechery symbol), 'tình dục' = sexual; combines age and sexuality in the insult.

records.definition: 'Lustful wretch'; an insult for someone driven by excessive sexual desire; a lecherous person.
records.notes: 'Háo' = craving, 'sắc' = beauty/sex; 'đồ' = derogatory; used to condemn sexually predatory or obsessive behavior.

records.definition: 'Sex-obsessed man'; an insult for a man who is perverted or obsessively interested in sex.
records.notes: 'Hiếu' = fond of, 'dâm' = lewd; 'thằng' = male derogatory; applied to sexually predatory or perverse men.

records.definition: 'Virtue-lost wretch'; an insult condemning someone for lack of sexual or moral virtue.
records.notes: 'Mất nết' = lost virtue; applied primarily to women; 'đồ' = derogatory classifier; conservative moral condemnation.

records.definition: 'Virtue-lost creature'; a gendered insult (using female classifier 'con') for a woman who has lost sexual/moral virtue.
records.notes: 'Con' = child/female classifier (derogatory), 'mất nết' = lost virtue; the female-classifier version emphasizes gender.

records.definition: 'Unchaste sort/kind'; a derogatory categorization of someone as sexually impure or morally fallen.
records.notes: 'Loại' = type/sort (derogatory), 'bất trinh' = unchaste; used in conservative family discourse to condemn premarital sex.

records.definition: 'Sexually shameless wretch'; a strong insult for someone with no sexual shame or moral restraint.
records.notes: 'Vô liêm sỉ' = without shame/conscience; 'tình dục' = sexual; a compound condemning total sexual shamelessness.

records.definition: The standard clinical Mandarin term for the penis, used in medical, educational, and formal public-health contexts.
records.notes: Standard term in PRC medical education and anatomy textbooks; essentially zero vulgarity but avoided in polite casual speech due to the anatomical subject matter.

records.definition: Formal clinical Mandarin phrase meaning 'male reproductive organ(s),' covering the entire external male genital apparatus; used in medical texts and sex-education curricula.
records.notes: More formal and broader in scope than 阴茎; often preferred in official health communications to avoid singling out the penis specifically.

records.definition: Common Mandarin term for the glans penis, literally 'turtle head,' describing the rounded tip of the penis; used in both clinical explanations and crude speech.
records.notes: Straddles clinical and everyday registers; the turtle-head imagery is acknowledged as mildly humorous even in formal usage. Used freely in urology consultations.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the foreskin, literally 'wrapping skin'; used in medical discussions of circumcision and hygiene.
records.notes: Elevated recognition due to widespread public discourse around infant circumcision debates and health campaigns in mainland China.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin anatomical term for the corpus cavernosum, the paired columns of erectile tissue in the penis that engorge with blood to produce erection.
records.notes: Highly specialized; recognition confined to medical students, clinicians, and health-literate laypersons. Not encountered in everyday speech.

records.definition: Standard clinical Mandarin term for the urethra, the duct carrying urine from the bladder and semen during ejaculation in males.
records.notes: High recognition partly because urinary-tract infections and related conditions are commonly discussed; the term carries no sexual charge on its own.

records.definition: Standard clinical Mandarin term for the prostate gland; recognition boosted by widespread prostate-health public-health campaigns targeting older men.
records.notes: Awareness elevated by PSA-testing campaigns and traditional Chinese medicine discourse on male reproductive health.

records.definition: The most common and most vulgar Mandarin crude slang for the penis; broadly equivalent in register and frequency to English 'cock' or 'dick.'
records.notes: Ubiquitous across mainland China, Taiwan, and diaspora communities; heavily censored on PRC platforms, which is why internet numeronym variants like J8 proliferate.

records.definition: Crude Mandarin slang for the penis; also widely deployed as a general expletive, intensifier, and dismissive term, mirroring the versatility of English 'dick.'
records.notes: More versatile than 鸡巴 as an expletive; 屌丝 ('dick silk') became a major internet self-deprecating identity term circa 2012, illustrating how the term's usage extends far beyond anatomy.

records.definition: Crude Mandarin slang for the penis, literally 'meat stick' or 'meat rod'; common in pornographic writing and erotic fiction.
records.notes: Strongly associated with the pornographic register; the compound meat + stick emphasizes physical presence and hardness. Frequently appears in Chinese-language erotic fiction (小说).

records.definition: Crude Mandarin slang for the penis, literally 'meat gun,' emphasizing phallic shape and thrusting function; used in pornographic and erotic writing.
records.notes: Less common than 肉棒 but from the same pornographic register; the gun metaphor doubles down on penetration imagery.

records.definition: Common Mandarin euphemism for the penis, literally 'number two' or 'the second one'; a playful, relatively inoffensive coded reference usable in mixed company.
records.notes: The 'second' framing may derive from ranking among siblings or simply from coded numbering to avoid naming the organ directly. Tone is humorous rather than obscene.

records.definition: Deliberately vague Mandarin euphemism for the penis (or genitals generally), literally 'that thing'; maximally evasive, allowing the speaker to imply without naming.
records.notes: The -儿 erhua suffix marks northern Mandarin / Beijing register; functions similarly to English 'it' or 'down there.' Preferred by older and more conservative speakers.

records.definition: Mild Mandarin euphemism for the penis, literally 'little brother'; used when speaking to or about children, and by adults in self-deprecating or playfully modest contexts.
records.notes: Standard vocabulary in Taiwanese and mainland parenting contexts for teaching body-part names to toddlers. Adults invoking it signal deliberate coyness or humor.

records.definition: Child-register Mandarin term for the penis (or genitalia generally), literally 'little chicken'; used by and with young children and carrying essentially no adult vulgar charge.
records.notes: Note that 鸡鸡 (jījī) can refer to either male or female child genitalia in some family contexts; the reduplication and diminutive 小 together signal the child register strongly.

records.definition: Mandarin metaphorical slang for the penis, literally 'gun'; exploits shape and penetration imagery; used in erotic writing and ribald speech but requires context to be unambiguous.
records.notes: Context-dependent: 枪 primarily means 'gun' in standard speech; the penile reading emerges only when the surrounding text or conversation makes it explicit.

records.definition: Mandarin metaphorical slang for the penis, literally 'stick' or 'rod'; relies on phallic shape association; also independently means 'great' or 'awesome,' enabling deliberate double entendres.
records.notes: The coincidence with the standard-speech meaning 'terrific/awesome' (你真棒 = 'you're great') makes it a favored vehicle for innuendo; context is essential.

records.definition: Mandarin metaphorical slang for the penis, literally 'root'; used in erotic literary and folk contexts, evoking organic, primal imagery rather than mechanical or violent analogies.
records.notes: Appears in classical erotic literature as well as modern online fiction; the 'root' metaphor connotes depth of penetration as well as shape.

records.definition: Mandarin metaphorical slang for the penis, literally 'snake'; the elongated reptilian form maps onto phallic shape, and the snake's movement suggests thrusting.
records.notes: Cross-cultural phallic archetype; in Chinese folk belief, snakes also carry associations with potency and cunning, enriching the metaphor beyond mere shape.

records.definition: Crude Mandarin slang for the penis, literally 'meat club' or 'meat cudgel,' emphasizing mass, hardness, and blunt force; used in pornographic writing.
records.notes: 棍 (club/cudgel) is slightly more menacing than 棒 (stick/rod), pushing this into a harder pornographic register than the milder shape-metaphors.

records.definition: Mandarin slang for the penis, literally 'big bird'; a humorous extension of 鸟 (bird) as a penis euphemism, with 大 (big) added for both size emphasis and comic effect.
records.notes: The 大 intensifier adds size braggadocio; also irresistibly evokes the Sesame Street character for younger speakers, which is leveraged for humor.

records.definition: Mandarin slang for the penis, literally 'bird'; one of the oldest and most widely understood penis euphemisms in Chinese, with documented use in classical texts.
records.notes: 鸟 as penis euphemism has classical roots; some Chinese surnames and place names historically containing 鸟 were subject to embarrassed avoidance. The character 屌 (diǎo) is a graphic compound of 鸟 + 尸, reinforcing the etymological link.

records.definition: Internet-era Mandarin abbreviation for 鸡巴 (jībā), using the Roman letter J for the initial syllable and the digit 8 (bā) to phonetically represent the second syllable; created to evade automated content filters on PRC platforms.
records.notes: 8 substitutes for 巴 via tonal homophony (both bā). Widely used on Weibo, Douyin, and Bilibili to bypass keyword filtering. Script tagged mixed_jp because the record contains a Latin letter and an Arabic numeral alongside Chinese context, though the language is Mandarin.

records.definition: Standard clinical Mandarin term for the vagina, the internal muscular canal extending from the cervix to the vulva; used in medical, educational, and formal public-health contexts.
records.notes: Like 阴茎 for the penis, this is the clinical default; avoided in casual speech not because it is vulgar but because Chinese social norms treat female anatomy as more taboo to name even clinically.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the external female genitalia (vulva), literally 'outer yin'; covers the labia, clitoris, and vaginal opening collectively.
records.notes: Lower recognition than 阴道 because the vulva/vagina distinction is poorly understood in lay Chinese usage, mirroring the pattern in many languages. 外阴 is the term used in PRC gynecology and sex-education curricula.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the labia, the paired skin folds surrounding the vaginal opening; used in medical and educational contexts.
records.notes: Composed of 阴 (yin/female/genital) + 唇 (lip); the collective term covering both labia majora and minora when unspecified.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the labia majora, the outer pair of skin folds forming the outer boundary of the vulva.
records.notes: Literally 'big yin-lips'; standard anatomical term in Chinese medical education; lower recognition than 阴唇 due to anatomical specificity.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the labia minora, the inner pair of skin folds surrounding the vaginal opening and urethral meatus.
records.notes: Literally 'small yin-lips'; paired anatomical term with 大阴唇; recognition is lower than the collective term 阴唇.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the mons pubis, the fatty tissue mound over the pubic symphysis; rarely encountered outside medical contexts.
records.notes: Composed of 阴 (yin/female) + 阜 (mound/hillock); a low-frequency anatomical term not widely known among the general public; poor sex education in China depresses lay recognition of sub-labia anatomical terms.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the hymen; literally 'virgin membrane,' embedding the virginity concept directly into the anatomical name.
records.notes: Literally 'virgin film/membrane' (处女 = virgin + 膜 = membrane); the etymology encodes cultural obsession with female virginity into the anatomical terminology itself, unlike the neutral Latin-derived English 'hymen'; extraordinarily high recognition relative to most anatomical terms due to the heavy cultural weight placed on female virginity in Chinese society.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the vaginal opening, the external entrance to the vaginal canal.
records.notes: Composed of 阴道 (vaginal canal) + 口 (opening/mouth); the 口 (mouth) component is widely used in Chinese anatomical terminology for tubular openings; standard term in gynecological and sex-education contexts.

records.definition: The most common and versatile crude Mandarin slang for the female genitalia (vulva/vagina); functions as both anatomical descriptor and general insult.
records.notes: Phonetically identical to the dedicated character 屄; because 屄 is blocked by content filters, the common character 逼 (to press/force) is used as a homophonic substitute in writing; ubiquitous in internet slang, insults, and casual crude speech; arguably the single most important vulgar word in Mandarin.

records.definition: The dedicated Chinese character for the female genitalia; the most morphologically explicit and taboo anatomical character in the Chinese writing system.
records.notes: One of a small set of dedicated 'dirty characters' (秽字) in Chinese orthography; the character structure is iconically anatomical; routinely blocked by content filters, search engines, and social media platforms, driving users to write 逼 as a substitute; recognition is high among literate adults but the character almost never appears in standard published text.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina, literally 'cave' or 'hole'; the second most prevalent crude vagina term after 逼, especially common in erotic fiction.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'cave,' 'acupoint,' or 'hollow'; because the character has abundant non-sexual meanings, content filters catch it less reliably than 屄, making it popular in online erotic writing; often appears in compounds such as 小穴 or 嫩穴 (tender hole).

records.definition: Crude compound slang for the vagina, literally 'little hole'; the dominant term for vagina in Chinese-language pornographic writing and erotic fiction.
records.notes: The diminutive 小 (little) adds an infantilizing or affectionate register typical of Chinese erotic discourse; this compound is overwhelmingly the most frequent vagina-slang in published erotic fiction on Chinese platforms.

records.definition: Extremely vulgar compound meaning 'lewd/smelly cunt'; functions both as a crude anatomical descriptor and as a highly offensive insult directed at women.
records.notes: 骚 (sāo) means sexually wanton, lewd, or emitting a fishy/musky odor; the compound insult is used primarily against women; in erotic contexts it describes the vulva approvingly or dismissively depending on register; equivalent in offense level to the most severe English genital insults.

records.definition: Universal deictic euphemism for the genitals, literally 'that place' or 'down there'; used to avoid naming genitals directly in polite or mixed company.
records.notes: Applies to both male and female genitalia depending on context; the most common avoidance strategy across all age groups; used in mainstream media, medical advice columns, and everyday conversation; southern Mandarin speakers may use 那里 (nàlǐ) as a regional variant.

records.definition: Infantilizing euphemism for the female genitalia, literally 'little sister'; used primarily when discussing female anatomy with or among young children.
records.notes: The corresponding male euphemism is 小弟弟 (xiǎo dìdi, 'little brother') for the penis; widely used in parent-child contexts and early sex education; the same phrase appears in erotic writing with a fetishizing infantilizing tone, creating a stark register split between innocent child-directed usage and explicit adult usage.

records.definition: Gender-neutral euphemism for the genitals, literally 'private place'; the dominant polite term in health journalism, sex education, and everyday conversation.
records.notes: Standard term in Chinese sex-education curricula, medical advice media, and news reporting on sexual assault; applies to both male and female anatomy; preferred over clinical terms in non-clinical written Chinese because it is simultaneously informative and inoffensive.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vulva, literally 'slit,' 'crack,' or 'seam'; refers to the external cleft appearance of the female genitalia.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'seam,' 'crack,' or 'gap'; the sexual meaning is understood contextually by most adults; appears in erotic writing and crude speech; less common than 逼 or 穴 but widely recognized; less taboo than those terms because the character has abundant non-sexual meanings.

records.definition: Crude slang for the vagina, literally 'hole' or 'cave'; emphasizes the penetrable orifice rather than external anatomy.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'cave,' 'hole,' or 'tunnel' in everyday language; in sexual slang specifically implies the vagina as a receptive orifice; somewhat less taboo than 穴 because 洞 is even more multipurpose in standard usage; also used crudely for the anus in some sexual contexts.

records.definition: Indirect slang for the female genitalia using the fish as a metaphor, drawing on a cross-cultural olfactory association between fish odor and vaginal secretions.
records.notes: The fish-vagina association appears cross-culturally; used in Chinese internet slang and regional crude expressions; recognition as a sexual metaphor is lower than 逼 or 穴 because it requires cultural context to decode; the metaphor can be used approvingly or derogatorily depending on speaker intent.

records.definition: Slang for the female genitalia using 'cat' as a metaphor, directly analogous to English 'pussy'; recognition has grown with exposure to English internet culture.
records.notes: Directly parallels the English 'pussy' slang metaphor; usage has increased among younger internet-literate speakers who consume English-language content; less dominant than 逼 or 穴 in native Mandarin erotic writing but growing in currency among younger cohorts.

records.definition: Literary and erotic euphemism for the female genitalia, using 'flower' as a metaphor for the vulva; rooted in classical Chinese erotic poetry and prose.
records.notes: The flower metaphor for female genitalia has deep roots in Ming and Qing dynasty erotic literature; in modern usage it appears primarily in literary or softcore romantic-erotic writing; far less charged than crude slang terms; recognition as a sexual metaphor among younger speakers may be declining as classical-erotic literacy decreases.

records.definition: The standard clinical Mandarin term for the clitoris; used in medical, anatomical, and formal sex-education contexts.

records.definition: The most widely recognized non-clinical Mandarin term for the clitoris, literally 'little bean'; the dominant lay term used in health communication, feminist media, and everyday conversation.
records.notes: The bean metaphor refers to the rounded shape of the clitoral glans; recognition significantly exceeds that of the clinical term 阴蒂 because of its accessible, non-threatening register; prominently used in Chinese feminist online communities, mainstream media health segments, and women's magazines; 'little bean' clitoris metaphors also appear in Japanese and other East Asian lay discourse.

records.definition: Shortened form of 小豆豆; casual slang for the clitoris using the 'bean' shape metaphor; slightly less frequent than the full 小豆豆 form.
records.notes: Functionally interchangeable with 小豆豆; the doubling of 豆 maintains a playful, cutesy register; also doubles as a common personal nickname and general diminutive for small round objects, giving it plausible deniability in ambiguous contexts.

records.definition: Crude compound slang for the clitoris, literally 'little meat bean'; more explicitly anatomical than 小豆豆 by inserting 肉 (flesh/meat).
records.notes: Less common than 小豆豆 in mainstream usage; the addition of 肉 (flesh) makes the term more graphically anatomical and shifts it toward a crude register; found primarily in erotic fiction and pornographic writing rather than health communication; recognition is lower because it lacks the mainstream feminist and health-media context that boosted 小豆豆.

records.definition: The standard clinical and colloquial Mandarin term for the anus; used in medical, hygiene, and everyday contexts with relatively low taboo.
records.notes: Composed of 肛 (a dedicated character for the anus) + 门 (gate/door); unusually high recognition for a clinical anatomical term because it appears routinely in digestive health, hygiene, and toilet-training contexts; significantly less taboo in Chinese than comparable genital terms, likely because it is associated more with digestion than sexuality in standard discourse.

records.definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the rectum, the terminal section of the large intestine leading to the anal canal.
records.notes: Literally 'straight intestine'; 直肠子 (one who speaks bluntly and thoughtlessly) is a common Mandarin idiom etymologically derived from this term but carrying no sexual meaning; the clinical anatomical term appears in colorectal cancer awareness, gastroenterological contexts, and is relevant to discussions of anal sex; lower recognition than 肛门 due to greater anatomical specificity.

records.definition: The short terminal segment of the large intestine connecting the rectum to the anal opening; standard clinical anatomical term in Mandarin medicine.

records.definition: Literally 'chrysanthemum flower'; the most widespread Mandarin slang for the anus, derived from the visual resemblance of the flower's radial petals to the anal sphincter.

records.definition: Literally 'fart hole'; a widely used crude Mandarin slang term for the anus.

records.definition: Literally 'butt hole'; crude Mandarin slang for the anus, compounding 屁股 (buttocks) with 眼 (hole).

records.definition: Literally 'back door'; a widely understood Mandarin euphemism for the anus in sexual contexts.

records.definition: The standard clinical Mandarin term for the scrotum, the external skin pouch enclosing and protecting the testicles.

records.definition: Literally 'egg'; the most common everyday Mandarin slang for testicle(s), mirroring the English metaphor 'ball'.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'egg' (food). Generates compound insults: 混蛋 (bastard), 王八蛋 (son of a bitch). One of the most culturally embedded terms in Mandarin.

records.definition: Reduplicated form of 蛋 (egg); affectionate or childlike slang for testicles, slightly softer in register than plain 蛋.
records.notes: Reduplication in Mandarin typically connotes diminutive or affectionate tone; widely used in both internet and everyday colloquial speech.

records.definition: Literally 'egg/ovum'; crude slang for testicles in mainland Mandarin (and penis in Taiwanese/Southern dialect usage), also functions as a general crude dismissive expletive.
records.notes: In mainland Mandarin, primarily testicles; in Taiwanese Hokkien-influenced usage, more often penis. Also a general crude dismissive (我卵才管 ≈ 'I don't give a shit'). Has a classical Chinese neutral meaning of 'egg.'

records.definition: Compound of two slang terms for testicles (卵 + 蛋); a crude, semantically emphatic designation for the testicles.
records.notes: The compound is redundant by design, for emphasis. Less frequent than either component alone; more common in Southern Chinese dialects.

records.definition: Literally 'two pieces/grains' (using the classifier 颗 for small round objects); a purely deictic euphemism for the testicles that avoids naming them directly.
records.notes: Entirely context-dependent; without surrounding context refers to any two small round objects. 颗 is the standard classifier for pills, seeds, and pearls — the choice of classifier implies round, small anatomy. Lowest crude score in this set due to total indirection.

records.definition: Literally 'egg/ball ache'; primarily used on the Chinese internet as a crude expletive meaning something is annoying, pointless, or frustrating; secondarily refers to literal testicular discomfort.
records.notes: Mapped to blue_balls as the closest anatomical concept, but dominant modern usage is a general frustration expletive (≈ English 'pain in the ass'), not specifically post-arousal testicular discomfort. Became a major internet meme circa 2010–2015.

records.definition: The standard clinical and literary Mandarin term for the female breast, used in medical, educational, and formal written contexts.
records.notes: 乳 relates to milk/lactation (cf. 母乳 = breast milk); 房 means room or chamber. Neutral and formal; not used in casual or sexual conversation.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin term for the nipple; used in both clinical and everyday contexts, with moderate crude potential in sexual contexts.
records.notes: Literally 'milk head.' Crosses clinical and everyday registers more fluidly than 乳房 — it is the default term with no common crude substitute in widespread use.

records.definition: The clinical Mandarin term for the areola, the pigmented circular ring of skin surrounding the nipple.
records.notes: Primarily used in medical, dermatological, and obstetric contexts. Less widely recognized outside educational or health contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'chest region'; the standard neutral term for the chest, widely used as a polite euphemism for female breasts in everyday and media contexts.
records.notes: Anatomically refers to the thorax in both sexes; in female-specific contexts defaults to meaning breasts. Preferred in formal and public-facing media over crude terms.

records.definition: Crude slang for female breasts; one of the most common vulgar terms for breasts in Mandarin Chinese.
records.notes: Derived from 奶 (milk) + nominalizer 子. Ubiquitous in erotic literature, internet discourse, and crude speech. Functionally equivalent to English 'tits' in register and vulgarity.

records.definition: Clipped form of 奶子; slang for female breasts; also the standard Mandarin word for milk — context determines the active meaning.
records.notes: Primary meaning is 'milk/dairy' (牛奶 = cow's milk; 奶茶 = milk tea). Sexual meaning activated entirely by context. Less crude than 奶子 due to the everyday milk association softening the register.

records.definition: Reduplicated childlike slang for female breasts; the soft sound evokes cuteness and a mildly coy rather than aggressively sexual register.
records.notes: 咪咪 also represents the sound a cat makes (meow). The dual meaning (cute/cat sound + breasts) reinforces the playful, infantilizing register. Used in flirtatious or teasing contexts more than in explicit sexual speech.

records.definition: Cantonese-origin slang for female breasts (Cantonese: 波 bō, 'ball/wave'), recognized across Mandarin media via Hong Kong cultural influence.
records.notes: In Mandarin, 波 means 'wave'; the breast meaning is purely Cantonese-derived. Crossed into mainland awareness via Hong Kong films, TV, and internet. Recognition peaked during peak Hong Kong media influence on mainland China (roughly 1990s–2000s).

records.definition: Literally 'big waves/balls'; Cantonese-origin slang specifically for large breasts, recognized across Mandarin contexts via Hong Kong media.
records.notes: Compound of 大 (big) + 波 (Cantonese breast slang). Appears in 大波妹 (busty girl). Recognition follows the same trajectory as 波 — tied to the Hong Kong cultural export era.

records.definition: Literally 'chest'; the most versatile Mandarin term for the chest/breast area, used neutrally for anatomy in both sexes and as a mild euphemism for female breasts in sexualized contexts.
records.notes: Unlike 胸部, the bare morpheme 胸 skews younger and more internet-native in sexualized usage (胸大 = big-chested; 胸控 = breast fetishist). Lower crude than 奶子 or 奶 because it is also the default clinical/everyday word for chest.

records.definition: Playful reduplication slang for female breasts, conveying a cute or infantile register; widely used across Chinese-speaking regions.
records.notes: Reduplication lends a childlike tone; used comfortably by adults in casual or intimate speech; common in both Mainland China and Taiwan.

records.definition: Crude compound slang for female breasts, literally 'milk balls/spheres,' emphasizing roundness in an objectifying way.
records.notes: 奶 (milk/breast) + 球 (ball/sphere); more vulgar and objectifying than reduplication forms like 波波; common in online and male peer-group speech.

records.definition: Soft, affectionate euphemism for female breasts based on their tactile quality; primarily an internet and intimate register term.
records.notes: Literally 'soft-soft'; reduplicated adjective repurposed as a noun; low recognition outside online contexts; provides plausible deniability due to its generic adjectival meaning.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical term for the uterus, the hollow muscular pelvic organ in which the fetus develops.
records.notes: Literally 'child palace'; no crude connotations; used in medical, school biology, and everyday health discourse without euphemistic pressure.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical term for the ovaries, the paired female gonads producing ova and sex hormones.
records.notes: Literally 'egg nest'; entirely clinical; widely recognized through health education and media coverage of ovarian cysts and polycystic ovary syndrome.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical term for the fallopian tubes, the paired ducts conveying ova from the ovaries to the uterus.
records.notes: Literally 'transport-egg tube'; no registry match found — proposed slug 'fallopian_tube'; lower recognition than ovaries or uterus because fallopian tube anatomy surfaces mainly in infertility and ectopic pregnancy discussions.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical term for the seminal vesicles, the paired glands producing the majority of seminal fluid volume.
records.notes: Literally 'essence/sperm sac'; specialized anatomy known mainly to medical professionals and educated laypeople; recognition spikes in prostate/reproductive health contexts.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical term for the vas deferens, the duct transporting sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.
records.notes: Literally 'transport-sperm tube'; highly specialized; general-population recognition is low but rises among men considering vasectomy (输精管结扎).

records.definition: Mandarin adoption of 'G-spot,' referring to the anterior vaginal wall region associated with heightened arousal and potential female ejaculation.
records.notes: Mixed script: Latin letter 'G' + Chinese character 点 (point/spot); a direct structural loanword rather than a Chinese coinage; widely recognized through popular health media and women's magazine coverage.

records.definition: The primary Mandarin clinical and legal term for sexual intercourse, equivalent to 'coitus' or 'sexual intercourse' in English.
records.notes: 性 (sex) + 交 (join/exchange); used in medical, legal, and journalistic registers; slightly higher crude score than pure anatomy terms because it names the act directly rather than the organ.

records.definition: A formal literary and classical Mandarin term for sexual copulation, used in pre-modern medical texts and literary prose.
records.notes: 交 (join) + 媾 (mate/marry); more archaic and formal than 性交; appears in classical novels such as Jin Ping Mei and traditional Chinese medicine texts; understood by educated readers but rarely produced in everyday speech.

records.definition: A literary Mandarin term for sexual union, emphasizing the joining of two bodies; found in classical texts and traditional medicine.
records.notes: 交 (join/intersect) + 合 (combine/unite); softer and more poetic than 交媾; used in Taoist and traditional medical discourse about the harmony of yin and yang energies during intercourse.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical phrase for 'sexual behavior' or 'sexual act,' broader than intercourse alone; the default neutral term in public health, legal, and research discourse.
records.notes: 性 (sex) + 行为 (behavior/conduct); technically covers all sexual acts, not only penetrative intercourse; preferred register for policy documents, sex education curricula, and academic research.

records.definition: Neutral-to-positive Mandarin term for lovemaking or sexual love, combining the physical and emotional dimensions; the everyday equivalent of 'making love.'
records.notes: 性 (sex/nature) + 爱 (love); warmer connotation than 性交; widely used in popular novels, film, and everyday speech; lacks clinical coldness and crude vulgarity.

records.definition: A domestic euphemism for sexual intercourse, especially within marriage; literally 'bedroom affairs,' common in traditional Chinese medicine and popular health writing.
records.notes: 房 (room/chamber) + 事 (affairs/matters); associated with TCM discussions of marital health and sexual restraint; carries a slightly conservative or older-generation register; still widely recognized but less produced by younger speakers.

records.definition: Clinical and neutral Mandarin phrase for a sexual relationship or the act of having sexual relations with someone.
records.notes: 性 (sex) + 关系 (relationship); the standard journalistic formulation '发生性关系' (to enter a sexual relationship / to have sex) is ubiquitous in news reporting on sexual assault, affairs, and legal cases.

records.definition: Euphemistic Mandarin phrase for a sexual/carnal relationship; frames intercourse in terms of physical flesh rather than the clinical or romantic registers.
records.notes: 肉体 (flesh/body) + 关系 (relationship); 肉体 carries a more carnal, occasionally pejorative nuance absent from 性关系; often implies an illicit, transactional, or purely physical arrangement rather than a loving one.

records.definition: The most common Mandarin crude verb meaning 'to fuck'; used both as a transitive verb for sexual intercourse and as a standalone expletive expressing anger or surprise.
records.notes: Homophonous with 操 (to operate/drill/exercise), enabling deliberate spelling substitution online; functions as both a sex verb and a general profanity; the single most frequently used Mandarin expletive across all age groups.

records.definition: The graphically explicit character for 'to fuck,' composed of 入 (enter) over 肉 (flesh); the etymologically correct vulgar character for the sex act.
records.notes: Distinct from the homophone 操 (operate); 肏 is consistently blocked by Chinese content filters, driving much lower digital-text frequency despite high recognition among educated users; its visual composition makes its meaning self-evident to literate readers.

records.definition: Polysemous Mandarin verb meaning 'to do/work' in standard usage and 'to fuck' in crude sexual contexts; one of several standard-character sex euphemisms.
records.notes: Standard meaning is entirely non-sexual; sexual sense activated by context; lower crude score than 操 because the character itself is neutral and plausible deniability is high; common in Northern spoken Mandarin.

records.definition: Originally 'grass/straw'; adopted as a phonetically similar substitute for 操 (cào) to evade internet censorship filters, and now used as a standalone crude expletive.
records.notes: Tonal difference from 操 (3rd tone vs 4th tone) provides minimal cover; rose to dominance in the 2010s alongside the expansion of Chinese social media censorship; also functions as a pure exclamation of shock or displeasure independent of sexual meaning.

records.definition: A versatile Mandarin verb meaning 'to do/handle/deal with' in standard use; used as a mild euphemism for having sex in spoken and written sexual contexts.
records.notes: One of the most common neutral-to-crude euphemisms for sex; strong plausible deniability from its non-sexual standard meaning; '搞在一起' ('got together') can mean began a romantic or sexual relationship.

records.definition: Standard Mandarin preposition and verb meaning 'above/on/to go up'; used crudely to mean 'to have sex with,' implying the active mounting role.
records.notes: Encodes positional dominance — the active partner 'goes on top of' the passive; '上了她' literally 'went up on her'; standard meaning is entirely non-sexual, giving high deniability; framing implies male or dominant-party agency.

records.definition: Mandarin verb meaning 'to play with/handle/manipulate'; used as a mild euphemism for sexual activity, encompassing foreplay and intercourse depending on context.
records.notes: Standard meaning is entirely non-sexual; softer register than 操 or 干; contextually ambiguous between foreplay and full intercourse; common in intimate spoken language and literary fiction.

records.definition: Crude Mandarin slang for 'to fuck,' using the standard character for 'sun/day' (rì) as a homophone substitution; predominantly Northern Chinese usage.
records.notes: Phonetically identical to 日 meaning 'sun/day'; sexual meaning is predominantly a Northern Mainland Chinese phenomenon (especially Henan, Shaanxi, Shandong dialects); understood but rarely produced in Southern China and Taiwan; functions as both a transitive sex verb and a general expletive in Northern speech.

records.definition: Crude slang for sexual intercourse or a single sex act; literally 'cannon'; functions as both noun ('a fuck') and verb ('to fuck'), typically implying vigorous or casual sex.
records.notes: Appears in compounds 打炮 and 干炮; homophonous with but distinct from 泡 (pào, to pursue/seduce), which uses a different character.

records.definition: Crude slang verb meaning to have sex; literally 'fire a cannon'; typically framed from the perspective of the active or initiating partner.
records.notes: 打 (to strike/do) + 炮 (cannon/fuck); slightly more verb-oriented than bare 炮; common in casual male-register speech and online forums.

records.definition: Onomatopoeic internet slang for sexual intercourse; the triple syllable mimics the rhythmic sound of skin contact during sex; emphatic variant of 啪啪.
records.notes: Triple form adds emphasis relative to the double 啪啪; proliferated on Weibo and WeChat-era Chinese internet; relatively playful register that evades content filters more readily than explicit terms.

records.definition: Onomatopoeic internet slang for sexual intercourse; mimics the sound of skin slapping during sex; the dominant casual shorthand for sex in contemporary mainland Chinese internet discourse.
records.notes: Probably the single most-used casual euphemism for sex on Chinese internet platforms; onomatopoeic ambiguity makes it difficult for automated content moderation to suppress; less vulgar than 炮 or 干.

records.definition: Euphemistic idiom for having sex; literally 'roll the sheets'; evokes tangled bedsheets during intercourse as an indirect image of the act.
records.notes: Widely used in entertainment media, drama recaps, and casual speech as a humorous and relatively inoffensive reference to sex; structurally similar to English 'hit the sheets.'

records.definition: Euphemistic use of 'to do' for having sex; gains sexual meaning entirely from context, parallel to English 'do it'; too ambiguous to carry sexual meaning in isolation.
records.notes: Most commonly appears as 做爱 (zuò'ài, 'make love'); bare 做 requires unambiguous sexual context to be read sexually; the lightest and most deniable register in this set.

records.definition: Euphemistic use of 'to sleep' for having sex with someone; typically takes a grammatical object, as in 睡了她 ('slept with her').
records.notes: Near-universal cross-linguistic metaphor; the parallel to English 'sleep with' is exact in both form and register; among the mildest and most socially acceptable Mandarin euphemisms for sex.

records.definition: Slang verb meaning to pursue and seduce someone for sex; literally 'to soak/immerse'; emphasizes the flirtation and pursuit process rather than the sex act itself, as in 泡妞 ('pick up girls').
records.notes: Distinct character from 炮 (pào, cannon/fuck) despite identical romanization; 泡 focuses on the social seduction process rather than the act; implies eventual sexual success without naming it explicitly.

records.definition: Crude slang meaning to successfully have sex with someone; literally 'to do/mess onto someone'; the directional 上 marks completion of a goal, framing sex as a conquest.
records.notes: 搞 (gǎo) alone means 'to handle/mess with'; 上 as a directional complement signals achieved outcome; comparable to English 'to score' or 'to get into bed with'; implies prior pursuit followed by success.

records.definition: Extremely crude compound for having sex; stacks two independent crude sex terms (干 'to fuck' + 炮 'fuck/cannon') for intensified vulgarity; implies aggressive or vigorous intercourse.
records.notes: 干 (gàn) is itself a standalone crude verb for sex with broad recognition; combining it with 炮 doubles the vulgarity; among the highest-crude-register Mandarin terms for intercourse.

records.definition: Standard clinical term for oral sex; literally 'mouth intercourse'; applies to both fellatio and cunnilingus and is the dominant medical and educational term.
records.notes: Used in sex education curricula, public health campaigns, and mainstream media; does not distinguish fellatio from cunnilingus without additional specification; the go-to neutral term.

records.definition: Highly clinical term for fellatio; literally 'penis oral sex'; specifies oral stimulation of the penis as distinct from cunnilingus.
records.notes: 阴茎 (yīnjīng) is the clinical/anatomical term for penis; this compound appears in medical and sexological literature but is rarely used in everyday speech; low general-public recognition due to clinical register.

records.definition: Formal clinical term for oral sex; literally 'oral cavity sexual intercourse'; more technically precise than 口交 and encountered primarily in medical or legal documents.
records.notes: 口腔 (kǒuqiāng) denotes the anatomical oral cavity; the full compound is the most formally verbose Mandarin rendering of oral sex; general-public recognition is lower than 口交 due to its bureaucratic register.

records.definition: Euphemistic slang for fellatio; literally 'blow the xiao (a vertical bamboo flute)'; the wind-instrument metaphor for oral stimulation of the penis parallels English 'blow job.'
records.notes: 箫 is a traditional Chinese end-blown bamboo flute; the metaphor is widely understood; carries a faintly classical or literary register because the instrument is associated with traditional music and poetry.
