records.notes: 娼 (prostitute) makes the transactional object explicit. Used in PRC legal code (《治安管理处罚法》 Article 66) and police reports. English 'soliciting' technically refers to the sex worker's offer, not the client's purchase, making this an approximate mapping.

records.definition: A client or customer who pays for sex; a john; one who patronizes sex workers.
records.notes: Compound of 嫖 (to patronize a sex worker) + 客 (customer/guest). The standard neutral term for a sex-work client; used in law enforcement, journalism, and public health contexts without significant additional stigma beyond the implied act.

records.definition: A pimp or procurer: a person who manages, recruits, or finds clients for sex workers, typically taking a cut of their earnings and often exercising control or coercion over them.
records.notes: Literally 'leather-strip customer'; the etymology of 皮条 (leather strip) likely refers to a leash or restraint, though folk etymologies vary. The standard modern term; used in legal contexts and journalism. Can extend to anyone acting as a middleman facilitating sexual transactions for profit.

records.definition: Slang for a sex worker, primarily female, derived from the Cantonese and Mandarin word for 'chicken'; the double meaning is widely understood across mainland China and Chinese diaspora communities.
records.notes: The chicken-sex worker equation likely originates in Cantonese street slang, possibly from the pecking motion of soliciting or from phonetic proximity to 妓 (jì). Can refer to male sex workers (男鸡) in some contexts. Context reliably disambiguates from the literal poultry meaning.

records.definition: Literally 'young lady' or 'Miss,' the standard polite address for a young woman; became a widely understood euphemism for sex worker in mainland China from the 1990s due to its adoption as a professional title in karaoke bars and massage parlors.
records.notes: One of the most striking semantic shifts in contemporary Mandarin: a standard polite address acquired strong sex-work connotations in mainland China through adoption in commercial entertainment venues. In Taiwan, 小姐 retains its polite meaning without stigma. Mainland speakers frequently substitute 女士 (lady) or 姑娘 (girl) in formal contexts to avoid the double meaning.

records.definition: Literally 'street-standing woman'; the standard Mandarin term for a female sex worker who solicits clients on public streets.
records.notes: Transparent descriptive compound: 站 (to stand) + 街 (street) + 女 (woman); neutral in register compared to more pejorative synonyms.

records.definition: Compensated dating in which typically young women provide companionship or sexual services to older men in exchange for money or gifts; borrowed from Japanese 援助交際 (enjo kōsai).
records.notes: Abbreviated from Japanese 援助交際; more prevalent in Taiwan and Hong Kong than mainland China; the power-age dynamic is more foregrounded than in the English 'sugar dating' gloss.

records.definition: To financially maintain a person — typically a younger woman — as a kept mistress or live-in partner in exchange for sexual availability; also the resulting arrangement itself.
records.notes: The word has a non-sexual meaning of 'to provide for / maintain' (e.g., dependents, pets); sexual reading is entirely context-dependent; extremely high recognition across all Mandarin-speaking regions.

records.definition: Literally 'second milk/wife'; a man's live-in mistress or informal second wife, especially one who is financially maintained — distinct from a casual affair by its domestic and economic permanence.
records.notes: Originally Cantonese slang popularized during the 1990s Hong Kong–Guangdong economic boom when men kept second households across the border; now universal in Mandarin. 二 (second) + 奶 (informal 'wife/woman').

records.definition: Literally 'little three'; the third party in a romantic triangle who is having an affair with someone already in a committed relationship; implies home-wrecking.
records.english_term: the other woman / the other man
records.notes: One of the most commonly used relationship insults in contemporary Mandarin; distinct from 二奶 (which implies a stable kept arrangement) — 小三 emphasizes the disruption of an existing couple; gender-neutral in principle but applied overwhelmingly to women.

records.definition: Slang for a male sex worker or gigolo who services female or male clients for payment; derived by analogy with 鸡 (chicken) as slang for female sex workers.
records.notes: The 鸡 (chicken) = female sex worker pairing spawned 鸭 (duck) = male sex worker; widely understood though usage is concentrated in urban slang and entertainment industry contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'wild pheasant/chicken'; crude slang for a prostitute or sexually available woman; also used metaphorically for anything counterfeit or unlicensed.
records.notes: The 鸡 (chicken) euphemism for sex workers is extended here with 野 (wild/undomesticated) to convey lack of class or control; the dual meaning (prostitute / fake/unofficial) creates deliberate ambiguity in some contexts.

records.definition: Literally 'to sell spring'; a literary-euphemistic expression for engaging in prostitution or selling sexual services, where 春 (spring) stands as the classical Chinese metaphor for eroticism.
records.notes: 春 (spring) as a euphemism for sexuality appears throughout classical Chinese literature and opera; less morally weighted than 卖淫 because the substitution softens the register; occasionally used in formal journalism for stylistic variation.

records.definition: Literally 'to sell lewdness'; the standard legal and official Mandarin term for prostitution; appears in criminal law, police reports, and formal journalism.
records.notes: This is the formal legal term — the relevant PRC law targets 卖淫嫖娼 (prostitution and soliciting) as a paired offense; 淫 (lewdness/licentiousness) carries Confucian-legal moral condemnation; high crude score despite clinical use because 淫 itself is a charged character.

records.definition: Literally 'yellow film'; the most widely used Mandarin slang term for pornographic video or film; 黄 (yellow) is the Chinese color-code for obscene/pornographic content.
records.notes: In Chinese cultural coding, 黄色 (yellow) = pornographic/obscene, analogous to English 'blue' for adult content; used universally across mainland China, Taiwan, and diaspora communities; the 黄 prefix applies broadly (黄书, 黄色笑话, etc.).

records.definition: Abbreviation for 'Adult Video'; in Chinese usage specifically denotes Japanese pornographic film productions (JAV); borrowed directly from Japanese industry terminology.
records.notes: Though technically an English abbreviation, AV in Mandarin/Chinese internet contexts connotes specifically the Japanese adult film industry and aesthetic; more culturally specific than generic 黄片; pronounced in Chinese as A-V (ēi-vī) or ài-wēi.

records.definition: Literally 'A-film'; common informal Mandarin term for pornographic video, using the Latin letter A to signal adult-only content.
records.notes: Mixed-script term (Latin 'A' + Chinese 片 film/disc); the 'A' borrows from film rating conventions suggesting adult-only; interchangeable with 黄片 in most contexts; A片 may have a slightly stronger association with East Asian (especially Japanese) productions.

records.definition: Literally 'adult film'; the most neutral and polite Mandarin term for pornographic or sexually explicit film, used in regulated and semi-official contexts.
records.notes: 成人 (adult / grown person) + 片 (film); preferred in legal, educational, and media contexts where 黄片 would be inappropriate; also used on age-gated platforms to describe their content category.

records.definition: Literally 'Category III film'; refers to films carrying Hong Kong's Category III (adults-only, 18+) film rating; colloquially used across Chinese-speaking regions to mean any pornographic or extremely sexually explicit film.
records.notes: Derives from Hong Kong's four-tier film classification (Category I / IIA / IIB / III); the Category III boom of 1990s Hong Kong cinema — featuring softcore and later explicit content — gave this term pan-Chinese cultural salience well beyond Hong Kong's borders. Recognition_pct_peak reflects 1990s cultural dominance.

records.definition: Literally 'hair film'; crude mainland Chinese slang for pornographic video, with 毛 (hair) referencing pubic hair as a metonym for sexual content.
records.notes: The pubic hair reference makes this cruder in feel than 黄片 despite identical denotation; particularly prevalent in mainland China internet slang and BBS culture from the early 2000s onward; less common in Taiwan and Hong Kong usage.

records.definition: Literally 'yellow book'; Mandarin slang for pornographic or obscene printed material — books, magazines, or illustrated publications with sexual content.
records.notes: Applies the 黄 (yellow = pornographic) prefix to 书 (book); usage has declined alongside physical print media; recognition remains high among adults who lived through the pre-internet era when physical 黄书 circulated underground.

records.definition: Literally 'licentious/lewd book'; a classical and literary term for pornographic or obscene written material, carrying explicit Confucian-moral condemnation via the character 淫.
records.notes: The character 淫 (lewdness/licentiousness) appears in imperial-era censorship edicts and legal codes; distinguished from 黄书 by its more classical register; often used in historical or literary-critical contexts discussing traditional erotica.

records.definition: Literally 'spring palace picture'; traditional Chinese erotic paintings or illustrations; the classical term for any form of erotic visual art.
records.notes: 春宫 (spring palace) is a classical Chinese euphemism for erotic content, analogous to the Japanese shunga ('spring pictures') which shares the same poetic metaphor; 图 (picture/diagram); these were historically produced for elite consumption and are now collected as art; the term can also be used informally to refer to any erotic image.

records.definition: Literally 'erotic/pornographic film'; the standard semi-formal Mandarin term for pornographic film or video, used in journalism, legal contexts, and everyday speech.
records.notes: 色情 (erotic/pornographic) is the standard formal compound used by Chinese media and law; 色情 alone functions as the adjective 'pornographic' across many compound terms (色情网站 = pornographic website, etc.); more neutral than 黄片 but less clinical than 成人片.

records.definition: Literally 'old bustard (bird)'; the traditional Chinese term for a brothel madam who manages female sex workers, collects earnings, and oversees the establishment.
records.notes: 老 (old/experienced) + 鸨 (great bustard, a bird associated with licentiousness in classical texts due to folk beliefs about the species); the term appears in classical Chinese literature and opera (《金瓶梅》, etc.); still the default word for the concept despite brothels being illegal in the PRC.

records.definition: Literally 'red light district'; a direct calque of the English term for an urban neighborhood concentrated with sex work, strip clubs, and adult entertainment venues.
records.notes: A loan-translation from English 'red light district'; so transparent a calque that it requires no specialist knowledge; widely used in news reporting, travel writing, and fiction across all Mandarin-speaking regions.

records.definition: Literally 'kiln sister'; an archaic Mandarin slang term for a prostitute, historically associated with brothels housed in cave-like or kiln-like structures in northern China.
records.notes: 窑 (kiln / cave dwelling, especially the yaodong cave houses of the Loess Plateau) + 姐 (older sister / woman); documents a historical period when such dwellings housed illicit establishments; mainly encountered in historical fiction, period dramas, and older literature today.

records.definition: Literally 'hidden door'; an archaic term for a clandestine, unlicensed brothel or a prostitute operating through hidden or back-alley premises.
records.notes: 暗 (hidden/dark/secret) + 门子 (small door / establishment); describes informal sex work venues that operated covertly without official licenses in pre-modern China; largely obsolete in active speech but appears in historical fiction and Republican-era literature.

records.definition: Literally 'to spend money to buy spring'; a euphemistic phrase for paying for sexual services from a sex worker, combining the financial transaction with the classical 春 euphemism for sex.
records.english_term: to pay for sex / to buy sex
records.notes: 花钱 (to spend money) + 买春 (to buy spring/sex); the retention of 春 (spring) as a classical euphemism gives the phrase a slightly literary or ironic quality compared to more direct equivalents; occasionally used in journalism covering sex-tourism or enforcement stories.

records.definition: Literally 'to look for a Miss/young lady'; a widespread euphemism for seeking out a female sex worker, exploiting the dual meaning of 小姐 as both a polite honorific and sex-worker slang.
records.notes: 找 (to look for) + 小姐 (Miss / young lady); in mainland China from the 1990s onward, 小姐 became so strongly associated with sex workers in service-industry contexts that many professional women actively avoid the title — a semantic shift with real social consequences; the phrase is low-crude precisely because its euphemistic cover remains largely intact.

records.definition: A full-service sex work package in which all sexual acts are performed within a single session; literally 'one dragon' (one complete set).
records.notes: The dragon metaphor implies completeness and unbroken continuity; circulates in mainland Chinese sex work slang and is understood mainly by male consumers of commercial sex.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin term for condom; literally 'contraception sleeve'; used across medical, educational, and everyday registers without euphemistic charge.
Colloquial shorthand for condom; the primary word meaning 'sleeve, cover, or sheath' in general Chinese, repurposed as a near-universal informal synonym for 避孕套.
records.notes: Highly polysemous; requires context for sexual interpretation; also means 'set' or 'series' in unrelated uses.

records.definition: Standard term for condom used in public health and government campaigns; literally 'safety sleeve'; emphasizes dual protection against STIs and pregnancy.
records.notes: Preferred in official materials and health-sector communications; virtually synonymous with 避孕套 in practice.

records.definition: Internet-generation slang for condom derived from the Jissbon 'TT' branded condom line, now used generically by younger Mandarin speakers in online and casual contexts.
records.notes: Brand-derived generic; predominantly recognized among users under 35 and in social media contexts; the brand itself remains the dominant association.

records.definition: Mandarin phonetic transliteration of the Durex brand name; the dominant condom brand in China, frequently used as a genericized synonym for condom in everyday speech.
records.notes: Durex's Chinese social media presence is aggressively witty, reinforcing brand recognition; genericization parallels 'Xerox' in English.

records.definition: Informal term for emergency contraceptive pill; literally 'after-the-event medicine'; used openly in online discussions and among young adults without significant stigma.
Clinical euphemism for induced abortion; abbreviated from 人工流产 (artificial evacuation); used in hospital settings and general discourse with minimal explicit moral loading.
records.notes: Short for 人工流产 (rén gōng liúchǎn); the clinical framing deliberately mutes the moral charge that 堕胎 carries; the predominant term in medical contexts.

records.definition: Induced abortion with morally pejorative overtones; the character 堕 (to fall, degenerate) frames the act as a moral transgression.
records.notes: More stigmatizing register than 人流; favored in conservative, religious, and anti-abortion rhetorical contexts; the character 堕 also appears in words for depravity and corruption.

records.definition: Crude verb meaning to take someone's virginity or to lose one's own virginity; literally 'break the virgin state'; applies to both female and male first intercourse.
records.notes: Can be used transitively (破她的处, 'deflower her') or intransitively (她破处了, 'she lost her virginity'); the bluntness of 破 (to break) gives it a higher crude score than the act itself warrants clinically.

records.definition: A woman who has never had sexual intercourse; a female virgin; also used figuratively for anything untouched, first-of-its-kind, or brand-new (e.g., 处女作, debut work).
records.notes: Registry match is imperfect: the nearest slug (defloration) denotes the act of removing virginity, whereas 处女 denotes the state of having it; used in both sexual and non-sexual figurative contexts.

records.definition: A man who has never had sexual intercourse; male virgin; a back-formation from 处女 (female virgin) substituting 男 (male) for 女 (female).
records.notes: Back-formation; male virginity carries minimal social stigma in Chinese culture compared to female virginity, so the term is often used with irony or mild teasing rather than condemnation.

records.definition: A man's fixation on requiring his female partner to be a virgin; the cultural insistence on female premarital chastity as a prerequisite for marriage or serious commitment.
records.notes: Widely debated in Chinese feminist and social media discourse as a sexist double standard; the English phrase 'virgin complex' exists but lacks the same mainstream critical discourse salience; frequently cited alongside discussions of the hymen restoration surgery industry in China.

records.definition: The supposedly 'safe period' in the menstrual cycle when pregnancy risk is lower; colloquially used to mean the rhythm or calendar method of contraception.
records.notes: Medical consensus holds it unreliable as contraception; nevertheless widely relied upon in China, especially in lower-income or rural contexts; no single-slug registry match — closest available is generic contraception.

records.definition: Internal ejaculation (ejaculating inside a partner's vagina or anus without a condom); a direct loanword from Japanese adult video slang 中出し (nakadashi).
records.notes: 中 = inside, 出 = ejaculate/come out; borrowed wholesale from the Japanese AV industry and now prevalent in Chinese online pornography communities and hookup culture discourse; recognition skews heavily male and online.

records.definition: External ejaculation; the withdrawal method of contraception in which the penis is removed from the vagina before ejaculation; literally 'outside-body ejaculation'.
records.notes: The clinical phrasing is used in sex education and medical contexts; everyday speakers typically say 不带套 or colloquial equivalents rather than this term.

records.definition: Colloquial phrase for having sex without a condom; literally 'not wearing a sleeve'; common in casual conversation, hookup app messaging, and negotiation of sexual encounters.
records.notes: Less subculture-specific than 裸套; used across heterosexual and gay contexts; frequently appears in hookup negotiations on apps such as Blued and Tinder.

records.definition: Slang for bareback sex (intercourse without a condom); an oxymoronic compound of 裸 (bare/naked) + 套 (condom), meaning effectively 'no condom at all'.
records.notes: Paradoxical formation: 'bare condom' = absence of condom; more prevalent in Chinese gay male online communities than in heterosexual discourse; recognition skews toward users of gay hookup apps.

records.definition: Abbreviation for sadomasochism (S&M); in Chinese internet and subculture usage, broadly denotes BDSM practices including power exchange, bondage, and pain play.
records.notes: More prevalent than the full BDSM abbreviation in Mandarin contexts; used seriously within the kink community and ironically in popular culture to describe any situation involving control or suffering.

records.definition: To train or condition a submissive partner through instruction, reward, and punishment; in BDSM contexts, the dominant shaping the submissive's behaviors and responses over time.
records.notes: General meaning is 'to train or discipline' (animals, children, subordinates); sexual meaning derives from D/s subculture; also used ironically on social media to mean coercively correcting someone's behavior.

records.definition: To bind or tie up; in sexual and BDSM contexts, refers to physical restraint using rope, cuffs, or other materials for erotic power exchange.
records.notes: Near-universal general-vocabulary recognition because 捆绑 simply means 'to tie/bind' in everyday Chinese; the sexual meaning is context-dependent and does not inherently signal BDSM.

records.definition: Rope bondage in the aesthetically deliberate Japanese-influenced style; implies technically structured and artistic binding rather than simple functional restraint.
records.notes: More specific than 捆绑; preferred term in Chinese shibari and rope bondage communities; recognition is lower due to niche subculture origin; frequently appears alongside Weibo and Bilibili rope-art content.

records.definition: Dominance or control; in BDSM contexts, the role of the partner who exercises authority, directs the scene, and commands the submissive.
records.notes: General-vocabulary word (e.g., economic dominance, dominant species); sexual and BDSM meaning requires explicit context; recognition figure reflects the BDSM-specific sense.

records.definition: Submission or obedience; in BDSM contexts, the act of yielding control and complying with the commands of a dominant partner.
records.notes: General-vocabulary word for compliance or obedience (military, institutional); BDSM meaning requires context; often paired with 支配 (dominance) in D/s community discussions.

records.definition: Master or owner; in BDSM contexts, the honorific used by a submissive to address or refer to their dominant partner, implying absolute ownership and authority over the submissive.
records.notes: Everyday word meaning master, owner, or host (e.g., homeowner, employer); sexual meaning is exclusively context-dependent; submissives address their dominant as 主人 as a core expression of the D/s dynamic; the ownership connotation is stronger than the English 'dominant' but matches 'Master' in formal D/s usage.

records.definition: Literally 'queen'; in Chinese BDSM and kink communities, the dominant female role equivalent to a dominatrix or femdom figure.
records.notes: Mainstream word repurposed for kink; widely used in Chinese BDSM online communities; the base word carries no inherent vulgarity, lowering the crude score relative to Western 'dominatrix'.

records.definition: Literally 'slave'; in BDSM contexts, denotes the submissive or slave role in a power-exchange dynamic, typically paired with a dominant female (女王).
records.notes: Classical Chinese word for slave repurposed for BDSM; the historical weight of the word adds severity not present in casual English 'sub'; often appears in compound forms like 脚奴 (foot slave) or 财奴 (financial slave).

records.definition: Literally 'pet'; in BDSM contexts, the person who adopts an animal persona under an owner or handler in pet play dynamics.
records.notes: Entirely neutral in everyday use; kink meaning is purely context-dependent; the term covers any pet-play animal persona (puppy, kitten, pony) without specifying species.

records.definition: Literally 'to trample or tread on'; in kink contexts, the fetishistic practice of a dominant partner stepping on or walking over a submissive, typically while wearing high heels.
records.notes: Trampling is a discrete kink not specifically named in the canonical registry; mapped to sensation_play as the nearest umbrella; frequently associated with high-heel fetishism (高跟鞋) and female dominance communities in Chinese kink spaces.

records.definition: Literally 'foot infatuation'; the Chinese term for foot fetishism, denoting sexual arousal from feet, socks, or related footwear.
records.notes: Morphologically transparent compound (恋=infatuation + 足=foot); widely recognized across mainland, Taiwan, and Hong Kong internet communities; one of the most commonly named kinks in Chinese online discourse.

records.definition: Literally 'role play'; in sexual contexts, refers to erotic roleplay where participants adopt personas such as teacher-student, doctor-patient, or fantasy characters during sexual activity.
records.notes: Entirely neutral in gaming and theatrical contexts; in sexual discourse kink meaning is activated by context; no specific erotic-roleplay concept exists in the canonical registry so bdsm_play is the nearest umbrella; commonly abbreviated as RP in Chinese internet slang.

records.definition: Literally 'beast person'; in Chinese internet and kink culture, refers to anthropomorphic animal characters and by extension to the community or fetishistic interest centered on such figures.
records.notes: Entered Chinese internet culture partly through gaming (World of Warcraft orcs = 兽人) and Japanese doujinshi; the kink dimension overlaps with Western furry fandom but the term is broader and more neutral; distinct from 兽交 (bestiality).

records.definition: Literally 'beast intercourse'; sexual contact or intercourse between a human and an animal; the Chinese term for bestiality and zoophilia.
records.notes: Morphologically transparent compound (兽=beast + 交=intercourse/sexual contact); illegal in most Chinese jurisdictions; heavily censored on Chinese internet platforms; considered among the most taboo sexual terms in the language.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical and journalistic term for pedophilia; sexual attraction to prepubescent children.
records.notes: Morphologically transparent (恋=infatuation + 童=child + 癖=pathological habit/paraphilia); used in medical, legal, and news contexts; high public recognition driven by media coverage of child sexual abuse cases in China.

records.definition: Literally 'to expose or reveal'; in kink contexts, refers to exhibitionism — the practice of exposing one's body or genitals in public or semi-public settings for sexual gratification.
records.notes: Borrowed kink usage from Japanese 露出 (roshutsu), where it is a well-established term; in everyday Chinese 露出 simply means 'to emerge or reveal' with no sexual connotation; kink meaning is primarily known among communities with exposure to Japanese adult content.

records.definition: Literally 'to peek secretly'; in kink contexts, refers to voyeurism — sexual gratification from secretly watching others undress, have sex, or engage in intimate activities.
records.notes: High recognition extends well beyond kink communities due to widespread use in crime reporting and criminal law covering unauthorized filming; the everyday pejorative meaning (peeping Tom) coexists with the kink-positive sense.

records.definition: Literally 'self-abuse or self-torment'; in kink contexts, refers to masochism — erotic gratification from experiencing pain or humiliation, whether self-inflicted or delivered by a partner.
records.notes: Commonly used non-sexually in everyday Chinese as a mild self-deprecating expression (e.g., binge-watching sad dramas is 'such 自虐'); the kink meaning is a subset of the broader sense; less clinically precise than English 'masochism' as it implies self-direction.

records.definition: Literally 'to abuse or maltreat'; in kink contexts, denotes sadism — sexual gratification from inflicting pain, humiliation, or domination on a consenting partner.
records.notes: Primary meaning is non-consensual abuse used extensively in news, law, and social work; the consensual BDSM meaning requires explicit context; very high recognition but overwhelmingly in the non-sexual sense; the kink meaning is a secondary register.

records.definition: Literally 'silk stockings'; in kink contexts, refers to fetishistic sexual arousal from stockings or nylon hosiery, one of the most prominent clothing fetishes in Chinese internet kink culture.
records.notes: Near-universal recognition as the everyday term for nylon stockings; the kink community around 丝袜 is large on Chinese internet platforms; closely associated with trampling (踩踏) and high-heel (高跟鞋) fetish communities; recognition of the kink meaning is much lower than the everyday word.

records.definition: Literally 'uniform'; in kink contexts, refers to uniform fetishism — sexual arousal from specific uniforms including schoolgirl outfits, nurse costumes, police uniforms, or military dress worn by a sexual partner.
records.notes: Entirely neutral everyday word; the kink dimension is heavily influenced by Japanese AV culture; schoolgirl uniforms (JK制服 / 学生制服) are particularly prominent; one of the most commonly depicted kinks in Chinese-language adult content.

records.definition: Phonetic borrowing from Japanese ロリ (loli), ultimately from Nabokov's 'Lolita'; in Chinese internet culture, denotes young-looking or petite girls (real or animated), and in kink contexts connotes sexual interest in such figures.
records.notes: Used in non-sexual contexts in anime fandom for the aesthetic of small, cute, young-looking girls; in kink sections carries pedophilic implications for animated content depicting minors; mapped to ephebophilia rather than pedophilia because the term is also widely applied to adult petite women in everyday Chinese internet usage; heavily censored in mainland China.

records.definition: Phonetic borrowing from Japanese ショタ (shota), originally the given name Shōtarō; refers to young-looking or feminine boys (real or animated), and in kink contexts denotes sexual interest in prepubescent-appearing male figures.
records.notes: Male counterpart to 萝莉; less mainstream recognition than 萝莉 in Chinese internet culture; primarily encountered in anime and doujinshi contexts; carries pedophilic implications for content depicting prepubescent male characters; mapped to pedophilia rather than ephebophilia because shota characters are typically depicted younger than loli characters.

records.definition: Literally 'group P' (P being Chinese internet crude slang for sexual intercourse); refers to group sex or an orgy involving multiple participants.
records.notes: Part of the Chinese internet NP shorthand system where N = number of participants and P = sex act; the term mixes a Hanzi character (群=group) with a Latin letter; P as slang for sex is derived from internet euphemism culture; 群P implies three or more participants without specifying configuration.

records.definition: Chinese internet slang for a sexual threesome; '3' = three participants, 'P' = crude internet slang for sexual intercourse; a widely used shorthand in Chinese online sexual discourse.
records.notes: Part of the Chinese internet NP system (3P = threesome, 4P = foursome, 群P = orgy); written entirely in Arabic numeral and Latin letter rather than Chinese characters; romanization is null since the term is already in Latin script; widely recognized among Chinese internet users under 40.

records.definition: Literally 'wife exchange'; the Chinese term for wife swapping, in which consenting couples exchange sexual partners with other couples.
records.notes: Carries inherent patriarchal framing — wives (妻) are the grammatical objects of exchange while husbands are implicit agents; associated with underground 换妻群 (wife-swap groups) organized via chat apps; legally ambiguous and socially taboo in China; a corresponding term for husband-swapping is essentially absent from Chinese vocabulary.

records.definition: Literally 'asphyxiation or suffocation'; in kink contexts, refers to breath play — the BDSM practice of controlled breathing restriction through choking, smothering, or strangulation for erotic arousal.
records.notes: Standard medical and everyday word for asphyxiation with no inherent kink connotation; in sexual contexts covers both consensual breath play and erotic asphyxiation; the word does not encode consent, creating legal and semantic ambiguity; recognized in kink meaning primarily among BDSM-adjacent communities.

records.definition: Literally 'candle'; in BDSM kink contexts, a synecdoche for wax play — the erotic practice of dripping hot candle wax onto a partner's skin for heat sensation.
records.notes: Entirely neutral everyday word; the kink meaning requires explicit BDSM framing to be understood; recognized mainly among BDSM-adjacent communities; the low crude score reflects the banality of the word itself rather than the practice it encodes.

records.definition: Literally 'high-heeled shoes'; in kink contexts, refers to fetishistic sexual arousal from high heels, commonly incorporated into trampling play, femdom scenarios, and foot fetishism.
records.notes: Universal recognition as the everyday term for high heels; foot_fetish is the closest registry match because the definition explicitly includes footwear; closely linked to 踩踏 (trampling) and 丝袜 (stocking) fetish communities in Chinese kink spaces; also appears in financial domination contexts where tribute is framed around buying the dominant's heels.

records.definition: Literally 'underwear or innerwear'; in kink contexts, refers to lingerie fetishism — sexual arousal from underwear, bras, panties, or similar intimate garments whether worn or used as objects of fixation.
records.notes: Entirely neutral everyday word with near-universal recognition; the kink dimension is large on Chinese internet; also surfaces in criminal news coverage of stolen-underwear cases (内衣偷窃), which inadvertently raises public awareness of the fetish.

records.definition: The standard Mandarin clinical term for fetishism; a paraphilia in which sexual arousal is triggered by a specific object, body part, or material not typically considered inherently sexual.
records.notes: Morphologically transparent (恋=infatuation + 物=object/thing + 癖=pathological habit/paraphilia); used in psychology texts and journalism; serves as the umbrella term under which specific Chinese kink communities such as 恋足 (foot fetish) and 丝袜 (stocking fetish) fall; the only clinical-register term in this batch.

records.definition: Sexual sadism and masochism; the practice of deriving erotic gratification from inflicting or receiving pain and humiliation; also used for non-consensual sexual abuse.
records.notes: Ambiguous: covers both consensual BDSM S/M play and criminal sexual abuse depending on context; the 虐待 component (maltreatment/torture) gives a stronger negative framing than the English acronym 'BDSM.'

records.definition: A butt plug; an anal sex toy with a flared base designed for rectal insertion and retention during sexual activity.
records.notes: Literally 'anal stopper/plug'; straightforward descriptive compound; used in sex-shop retail and online adult content contexts.

records.definition: A vibrator; a rod-shaped vibrating device used for sexual stimulation, typically clitoral or vaginal.
records.notes: Literally 'vibrating stick/rod'; the standard Mandarin term for a wand-style vibrator; widely recognized due to e-commerce platforms listing such products.

records.definition: A bullet or egg-shaped vibrator; a small egg-shaped vibrating sex toy used for clitoral, vaginal, or anal stimulation, often remote-controlled.
records.notes: Literally 'jumping egg'; form-specific term distinct from the wand-style 振动棒; remote-controlled versions are common in public-play fetish contexts; no single direct English equivalent.

records.definition: A sex toy; a generic term for any object designed for sexual stimulation or pleasure.
records.notes: Proposed slug 'sex_toy_generic'; the registry contains specific toy entries (vibrator, butt_plug, dildo) but no umbrella category; the concept has a direct English equivalent but no registry match.

records.definition: Adult novelties or erotic products; the standard polite retail and marketing term for sex toys and related adult products sold in adult stores and online.
records.notes: Literally 'romance-interest use-items'; significantly more euphemistic than 性玩具 — 情趣用品 appears on product packaging and retail signage where 性玩具 would not; register distinction is commercially and socially meaningful.

records.definition: Black stockings or thigh-highs as a fetish aesthetic; in Chinese internet and ACG culture, shorthand for the erotic appeal of women wearing black hosiery.
records.notes: Literally 'black silk'; dominant fetish category in Chinese ACG communities; 黑丝控 means a black-stockings fetishist; carries a seductive adult connotation contrasted with the purer aesthetic of 白丝.

records.definition: White stockings or thigh-highs as a fetish aesthetic; in Chinese internet and ACG culture, associated with an innocent or pure erotic appeal contrasting with the more seductive 黑丝.
records.notes: Literally 'white silk'; counterpart to 黑丝; the purity/innocence coding is central to its appeal in moe and loli-adjacent ACG aesthetics; lower crude score than 黑丝 reflects that register.

records.definition: Condomless sex; having vaginal or anal intercourse without a condom.
records.notes: Literally 'without sleeve/cover'; standard terminology on Chinese hookup apps and sex forums for both straight and gay contexts; frequently listed in personal ad profiles.

records.definition: Chaotic or indiscriminate sex involving multiple partners; can refer to group sex or broadly promiscuous sexual mixing.
records.notes: Literally 'chaotic intercourse'; the 乱 (disorder/chaos) component connotes moral disorder and transgression; also used as a pornographic category label, partly borrowed from Japanese AV terminology.

records.definition: Sexual promiscuity; indiscriminate sexual activity with many different partners over time.
records.notes: Literally 'excessive/unrestrained intercourse'; 滥 means excess or uncontrolled abuse; always pejorative; emphasizes a pattern of many partners over time rather than the simultaneous group-sex implied by 乱交.

records.definition: Sex involving multiple participants; group sex with more than two people.
records.notes: P is shorthand for 人 (person); numerical variants: 三P=threesome, 四P=foursome, 多P=five or more; internet and hookup-app slang; script mixes a Simplified Chinese character with a Roman letter P.

records.definition: A northern Mandarin euphemism for sex; literally 'that matter/thing,' with Beijing-dialect er-hua suffixation used to avoid naming sexual activity directly.
records.notes: The 儿化 (er-hua) suffix marks this as distinctly northern/Beijing Mandarin; essentially absent in southern dialects and Taiwan Mandarin; the same construction is used for menstruation and other bodily taboos.

records.definition: A vague deictic euphemism for genitalia or sexual activity; literally 'that one/thing,' used to avoid naming the genitals or the sex act directly.
records.notes: Highly polysemous: can reference genitalia, the sex act, menstruation, or any unnameable topic; 那个 also functions as the standard Mandarin hesitation filler equivalent to English 'um/uh,' producing frequent accidental double entendres.

records.definition: To have sex; a universal Mandarin phrasal euphemism meaning 'do that thing,' one of the most common circumlocutions for sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Adds the verb 做 (do/make) to 那个; near-universal comprehension across Mandarin speakers; used in family, medical, and everyday contexts where naming the act directly would be taboo.

records.definition: To make love; a cute, affectionate euphemism for sexual intercourse formed by reduplicating the character 爱 (love).
records.notes: Reduplication imparts a childlike or coy tone; extremely common in internet and texting contexts; the register implies affectionate sex between partners rather than casual or transactional encounters.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; a classical Chinese literary metaphor for sex derived from the imagery of clouds and rain, originally from the legend of the Goddess of Mount Wu.
records.notes: Shortened form of the chengyu 巫山云雨; widely encountered in historical novels and TV dramas; recognition declining among speakers under 30 with limited classical literary exposure.

records.definition: Sexual intercourse; a classical four-character chengyu alluding to the erotic dream-encounter between King Xiang of Chu and the Goddess of Mount Wu, as recorded in Song Yu's 'Gaotang Fu' (c. 3rd century BCE).
records.notes: Full form of 云雨; used in high literary, formal, and historical drama registers; the cultural allusion is untranslatable to English though the underlying concept is intercourse_generic; a canonical chengyu.

records.definition: To have conjugal sex; a formal or dated term for sexual intercourse between spouses, frequently used in traditional Chinese medicine literature to advise on sexual frequency.
records.notes: Literally 'perform/act in the bedroom'; standard in TCM texts on 房事 (bedroom matters); sounds clinical or old-fashioned to contemporary speakers under 40; still found in medical and formal literary contexts.

records.definition: To have sex; literally 'share a room,' used as a circumlocution for sexual intercourse, especially conjugal sex.
records.notes: The sexual implication is sufficiently entrenched that 同房 is understood as sexual intercourse even without explicit context; common in news reporting, medical consultations, and polite speech; parallels English 'sleep together.'

records.definition: The joy of sexual intimacy between a harmonious couple; a classical four-character phrase likening the union of lovers to fish in water.
records.english_term: conjugal bliss / pleasures of the marriage bed
records.notes: Literally 'fish-water joy'; the fish-in-water image (鱼水情) emphasizes natural mutual harmony and compatibility; foregrounding the relational joy over the physical mechanics; rare in contemporary spoken Mandarin, found mainly in classical novels and formal prose.

records.definition: To get a hotel room for sex; a modern Mandarin euphemism implying a sexual hookup by reference to checking into a hotel.
records.english_term: get a room / check in to hook up
records.notes: Literally 'open a room'; the sexual connotation is so dominant that 开房 without further context is universally understood as a sexual hotel visit; ubiquitous in dating app discourse and everyday colloquial speech.

records.definition: To successfully have sex with someone after pursuit; literally 'to take down/capture,' framing sexual success as conquest.
records.notes: Primary meaning is military/competitive 'to capture or overcome'; the sexual sense is derived metaphor; male-coded conquest framing; used without stigma in peer speech; equivalent to English 'score.'

records.definition: To pick up girls; to pursue women romantically or sexually with the goal of initiating a relationship or sexual encounter.
records.english_term: hit on girls / pick up girls
records.notes: Literally 'soak/steep girls'; 泡 implies a slow, patient softening process (like steeping tea); 妞 is informal for young women; emphasis on the pursuit phase rather than the outcome; peak during early PUA culture adoption in mainland China circa 2008–2012.

records.definition: To seduce or pick up girls; specifically associated with PUA (pickup artist) subculture and the systematic application of seduction techniques.
records.notes: Literally 'control/handle little sister'; 把 implies deliberate manipulation or taking control of a person; 妹 (younger sister/girl) is informal for young women; peak usage aligned with PUA culture's height in Chinese internet communities circa 2010–2015; more methodology-focused than the process-oriented 泡妞.

records.definition: Internet slang meaning to arrange a casual sexual hookup with someone, typically via messaging apps or dating platforms; 炮 (pào, 'cannon') is crude slang for sex.
records.notes: 炮 as slang for sex is crude; 约炮 is ubiquitous on Chinese dating apps such as Momo. Predominantly mainland Chinese usage; Taiwanese speakers use different vocabulary.

records.definition: Literally 'one-night love/feeling'; the standard Mandarin term for a one-night stand with no expectation of ongoing contact.
records.notes: Emotional neutrality is slightly softened by 情 (feeling/love), giving it a faintly romantic framing absent from the English 'one-night stand'; otherwise a direct conceptual calque.

records.definition: Literally 'bedroom kung fu'; colloquial for sexual skill, stamina, and technique in bed, applicable to any gender.
records.notes: Maps imperfectly to sexual_potency (which centers on erectile function); the Chinese term emphasizes artistry and technique broadly. Plays on 功夫 (gōngfu, 'skill/martial arts') as a metaphor for sexual proficiency. Usually complimentary.

records.definition: Literally 'spring night'; a poetic and literary euphemism for a night of romantic or sexual intimacy, often evoking a wedding night or a passionate encounter.
records.notes: Derived from the Song-dynasty line 春宵一刻值千金 ('a spring night's moment is worth a thousand gold'). Connotations are romantic rather than crude; widely recognized through classical education and period drama.

records.definition: Literally 'to steal something fishy/rank-smelling'; colloquial for a married person sneaking out to have illicit sex; 腥 (fishy smell) is a crude oblique reference to sex.
records.notes: The fishy-smell allusion gives a mildly crude flavor to an otherwise casual idiom. Emphasizes stealth and illicitness over moral condemnation. Distinct from 出轨 in focusing specifically on the physical sexual act rather than the relational betrayal.

records.definition: Literally 'to go off the (train) rails'; the dominant modern Mandarin term for marital or relationship infidelity, covering both emotional and sexual cheating.
records.notes: Extremely common across all media and age groups. The railway metaphor implies straying from an established correct path. Applies to both emotional and sexual infidelity, unlike narrower terms.

records.definition: Literally 'a red apricot blossom grows over the garden wall'; a classical Chinese idiom specifically for a married woman committing adultery.
records.notes: From Song-dynasty poet Ye Shaoweng. Gender-specific: conventionally applied only to women; using it of a man is incongruous or ironic. Widely recognized through classical education and popular culture.

records.definition: Literally 'to steal a person'; colloquial for having a secret illicit sexual affair, with a stronger emphasis on physical (sexual) betrayal than 出轨.
records.notes: More vivid and slightly cruder than 出轨; common in vernacular speech and regional dialects. The 'stealing' framing implies both secrecy and active transgression. More likely to connote the sexual act itself.

records.definition: Literally 'nourishing to the eyes'; a compliment meaning someone or something is visually pleasing or attractive, often with implicit sexual or aesthetic appeal.
records.notes: Can be applied to people, scenery, or objects; when used of a person it implies attractiveness that may be sexual but need not be explicitly so. Very positive in connotation, essentially never offensive.

records.definition: Literally 'that thing'; a coy, evasive euphemism for the genitals — most commonly the penis — used to avoid naming the organ directly.
records.notes: The 儿 (er) retroflex suffix is a Northern Chinese (especially Beijing) dialectal marker, less common in southern dialects. Defaults to male genitalia but can refer to female genitalia in context. Used in a humorous or embarrassed register.

records.definition: 'Intimate relationship'; a semi-clinical euphemism used in media, public health, and everyday speech to refer to a romantic and/or sexual partnership without naming sex directly.
records.notes: Standard polite register for sex-inclusive partnerships; widely used by psychologists, journalists, and in formal writing. In legal or medical contexts can denote a single sexual act rather than an ongoing relationship.

records.definition: Literally 'to roll'; in sexual contexts an abbreviation of 滚床单 (gǔn chuángdān, 'to roll the sheets'), a crude colloquial euphemism for having sex.
records.notes: The primary meaning of standalone 滚 is an imperative ('get out / fuck off'). The sexual meaning is derived from the compound 滚床单 and requires explicit context to be read sexually. Recognition of the sexual-specific reading is substantially lower than overall recognition of the character as an expletive.

records.definition: Literally 'indescribable / cannot be described'; a Chinese internet euphemism for sexually explicit content or acts, deployed to evade content filters and censorship algorithms.
records.notes: Peaked circa 2013–2015 during early Weibo/WeChat censorship games. The irony is universal legibility: every reader knows exactly what is being alluded to. Functionally equivalent to NSFW but posed as mock modesty. Applies to any censored content, not only sexual.

records.definition: Literally 'you know (what I mean)'; a winking internet phrase used to imply sexual or otherwise sensitive content without stating it, relying on shared understanding between speaker and audience.
records.english_term: you know what I mean; wink wink
records.notes: Often followed by ellipsis or a knowing emoji. Applies to any sensitive topic but sexual implication is by far the most common usage. Low crude score because the referent is gestured at, not named.

records.definition: Literally 'those who know, all know'; a broader, slightly more exclusive version of 你懂的, implying that sexual or taboo content is self-evident to the initiated without spelling it out.
records.notes: More in-group than 你懂的; implies a community of knowing readers while excluding the uninitiated. Common in comment sections under ambiguously suggestive posts to signal sexual subtext while maintaining plausible deniability against content moderation.

records.definition: 'Ambiguous/flirtatious'; a state of romantic or sexual tension between two people who are undefined — neither a couple nor simply friends — characterized by pleasurable uncertainty and flirtatious signals.
records.notes: One of the most culturally loaded terms in modern Mandarin romance vocabulary; English lacks a single-word equivalent. Can describe the relationship status (处于暧昧, 'to be in an ambiguous state') or a specific flirtatious act (发暧昧, 'to send ambiguous signals'). Tone is usually positive or wistful rather than pejorative.

records.definition: Literally 'hidden rules'; an established Chinese term for the unwritten quid-pro-quo expectation that career advancement in entertainment, media, or business requires sexual compliance with power figures.
records.notes: Unlike the English 'casting couch' (individual predation), 潜规则 implies a normalized, systemic institutional arrangement in which the coercion is structural and widely understood. Reached peak salience during Chinese #MeToo discussions around 2018. Connotes both the predatory behavior and the complicit culture that sustains it.

records.definition: Literally 'inner meaning / connotation'; in Chinese internet usage, a genre tag for content containing hidden sexual meaning or double entendre perceptible only to the knowing reader.
records.notes: Primary meaning in standard Mandarin is 'depth of character / implicit meaning'; the sexual-subtext usage is a deliberate ironic repurposing by internet culture. Content tagged 内涵 typically appears innocent on the surface and relies on a shared code of references.

records.definition: Literally 'the closeness of skin touching skin'; a classical four-character euphemism for physical and sexual intimacy, implying naked bodily contact of a deeply intimate or sexual nature.
records.notes: The chengyu (four-character phrase) structure marks it as literary-classical register. Widely used in romance novels and period dramas to imply sex without explicit description. Does not necessarily imply full intercourse — can refer to any significant intimate skin contact.

records.definition: Literally 'the affection of fish in water'; a classical metaphor for the harmonious, mutually pleasurable sexual and emotional bond between a married couple — fish being perfectly at home in water.
records.notes: Classical in register; associated with traditional ideals of marital sexual harmony. Also appears extensively in Maoist political rhetoric (军民鱼水情, 'soldier-people fish-water affection'), which has diluted the specifically sexual connotation in modern usage.

records.definition: 'Secret/private liaison'; a clandestine sexual affair, typically adulterous or pre-marital, conducted in secret; carries connotations of moral and legal transgression.
records.notes: More formal or literary than 出轨; also carries a second meaning of 'secretly communicating with the enemy' (treason) in military/political contexts. The sexual meaning is older; both senses share the core notion of forbidden clandestine contact.

records.definition: Literally 'bedroom arts'; the classical Chinese (especially Taoist) tradition of sexual cultivation practices — including regulated intercourse, breath retention, and semen retention — believed to promote health, longevity, and spiritual development.
records.notes: A culturally distinct concept without a true English equivalent; Western 'tantric sex' is analogous but from an entirely different tradition. Referenced in texts such as 素女经 (Classic of the Plain Girl) and 玉房秘诀 (Secret Instructions of the Jade Chamber). Not a euphemism for sex — it is a genuine esoteric practice system with its own technical vocabulary.

records.definition: Classical Chinese: the act of an emperor sexually visiting and favoring a concubine or consort; the emperor 'gracing' a woman with his sexual attention, simultaneously conferring status upon her.
records.english_term: (imperial) to favor sexually; to be graced by the emperor
records.notes: Rooted in the Chinese imperial harem (后宫) system with no English equivalent. 'To bed a concubine' misses the unilateral power conferral — 幸 frames sex as a gift bestowed downward from absolute authority. The woman's consent or experience is structurally absent from the classical usage of the term.

records.definition: Literally 'to approach and favor'; classical Chinese for the emperor personally coming to a concubine's quarters for sex; 临 (to approach, condescend to be present) amplifies the power differential beyond standalone 幸.
records.english_term: (imperial) to personally favor sexually; to condescend with a sexual visit
records.notes: More specific than 幸 alone; 临 stresses the physical act of the emperor's arrival at a lesser person's location, further underscoring rank asymmetry. Found in imperial court records, historical annals, and period fiction. Shares the novel concept slug imperial_sexual_bestowal with 幸.

records.definition: Classical Chinese for lascivious over-familiarity or lecherous intimacy; taking unseemly sexual liberties with someone; blends contemptuous over-familiarity with sexual impropriety.
records.notes: Single-character classical term virtually absent from contemporary speech; encountered in classical texts and historical fiction. Appears in compounds such as 狎昵 (xíání, 'lascivious closeness') and 狎妓 (xiájì, 'to consort with prostitutes'). Low recognition reflects purely classical usage restricted to educated readers.

records.definition: Sexual licentiousness or debauchery; dissolute and promiscuous behavior regarded as morally corrupt.
records.notes: Still used in contemporary Chinese as a moral judgment; appears in PRC legal codes governing obscenity offenses; both literary and journalistic.

records.definition: Obscene or indecent; filthy and lewdly offensive to public morality.
records.notes: Archaic compound; 秽 means foul or filthy, 亵 means to profane or treat with irreverence; appears in imperial legal and moral texts; rarely used in modern speech but still read in classical contexts.

records.definition: Prostitute; a woman who sells sexual services; an archaic standard term for a female sex worker.
records.notes: Distinguished from 妓 by implying lower-class street prostitution rather than courtesan status; survives in compounds like 娼妓 and 卖娼; still widely recognized.

records.definition: Classical term for traveling entertainers — singers, actors, and dancers — who occupied the lowest social caste in imperial China and were frequently also sexual laborers.
records.notes: Can be male or female; imperial law grouped 优伶 with prostitutes, barring them and their descendants from sitting the civil examinations; the primary identity is performer, not sex worker, but the association was structural and enforced.

records.definition: Idiom for illicit sexual assignations, derived from the licentious music and secret trysts said to occur in the mulberry groves by the Pu River in ancient Wei state, condemned in the Classic of Rites.
records.notes: From 礼记: 桑间濮上之音 designated debauched music associated with sexual license; became a literary shorthand for premarital or adulterous encounters; recognizable mainly to readers of classical Chinese today.

records.definition: Pillow and sleeping mat; a classical euphemism for sharing a bed and having sexual intercourse.
records.notes: Metonymic; the two objects together denote the shared sleeping space; appears in classical poetry and prose to imply intimacy without naming the act; gentle enough for court literature.

records.definition: Reed-pipe music and singing; a literary synecdoche for the festive pleasures of the courtesan quarter — music, wine, and female company — evoked without naming sex directly.
records.notes: Not inherently sexual; functions as atmosphere-shorthand for the commercial entertainment and sex trade ecosystem; appears in Tang and Song poetry; still used in contemporary literary prose to evoke nostalgia for that world.

records.definition: Spring pictures; traditional Chinese erotic woodblock prints or paintings depicting sexual acts, analogous to Japanese shunga.
records.notes: 春 (spring) is a classical Chinese metaphor for sexuality and vitality; spring pictures were produced from the Song dynasty onward and were commonly given as wedding gifts or sold at markets; widely recognized across all Chinese-speaking communities.

records.definition: To sexually violate someone, or to engage in illicit sexual intercourse; in classical and legal usage covers both rape and consensual adultery or fornication.
records.notes: 奸 = to violate or wrong; 淫 = licentious or excessive; the compound appears in imperial legal codes and classical moral texts; in modern usage the primary meaning has narrowed toward sexual assault and rape.

records.definition: In archaic usage, sexual union or conjugal consummation; 媾 denotes sexual joining, especially within a marital or clan-alliance context.
records.notes: The modern compound 媾和 overwhelmingly means 'to conclude a peace treaty' in contemporary usage; the sexual sense of 媾 belongs entirely to classical texts including the Book of Changes and early poetry; recognition figures here reflect the archaic sexual reading only, which most contemporary speakers are unaware of.

records.definition: Lewd words and licentious songs; a classical idiom for bawdy or sexually suggestive literature and music.
records.notes: 淫词 = licentious words; 艳曲 = sensual or glamorous songs; the idiom appears in moral critiques of popular entertainment from the Song dynasty onward and in imperial censorship edicts targeting dissolute texts.

records.definition: To frequent prostitutes; to consort with or patronize sex workers, typically in a habitual or intimate manner.
records.notes: 狎 implies illicit familiarity and licentiousness; 妓 = prostitute; verb used predominantly of male clients in classical and Republican-era literature and in vernacular fiction like Jin Ping Mei.

records.definition: To sleep among flowers and lodge with willows; a classical idiom for habitually visiting prostitutes and spending nights in brothels.
records.notes: 花 (flowers) and 柳 (willows) are the canonical classical metaphors for female sex workers and brothel neighborhoods respectively; the idiom emphasizes leisurely repeated indulgence rather than a single transaction; compare with the more common 寻花问柳.

records.definition: To seek flowers and inquire about willows; a classical idiom for visiting brothels and seeking the company of prostitutes.
records.notes: More common and more widely recognized than the near-synonym 眠花宿柳; still used in contemporary Chinese as a literary or gently humorous euphemism for brothel patronage; appears in historical drama and fiction.

records.definition: Wind and moon establishment; a classical euphemism for the pleasure quarter or the broader commercial world of romantic and sexual entertainment.
records.notes: 风月 (wind and moon) is a classical metaphor for romantic and sexual pleasures; 场 (field or establishment) gives it institutional scope; occasionally still used in contemporary media to describe the sex trade with literary distancing.

records.definition: Land of smoke and flowers; a literary euphemism for a brothel or district of prostitution.
records.notes: 烟花 (smoke and flowers) was a classical metaphor for the ephemeral, glamorous world of courtesans; must be distinguished from the modern meaning of 烟花 as fireworks; used in historical novels and period drama.

records.definition: Land of tenderness; a classical metaphor for the paradise of feminine warmth and sexual pleasures that ensnares a man and causes him to neglect his duties.
records.notes: Conventionally traced to the Tang historian's description of Emperor Xuanzong's obsession with Yang Guifei; the phrase carries a built-in moral valence — the pleasure is real but the dereliction of duty is the implied condemnation; widely recognized and still used in modern Chinese.

records.definition: Classical Chinese entertainment venue of the Song and Yuan dynasties functioning as a combined theater and pleasure house where dramatic performances and sexual services coexisted.
records.notes: Literally 'curved railing,' referring to the fenced performance areas in urban entertainment districts; functionally combined theater, brothel, and tavern; appears extensively in Water Margin and Jin Ping Mei; primarily a historical-literary term today.

records.definition: Blue-green tower; the canonical classical Chinese term for a high-class courtesan house where literary men socialized with educated courtesans.
records.notes: Originally meant any stately mansion with painted blue-green balconies; the sexual association solidified in the Southern Dynasties period; by the Song dynasty it exclusively denoted high-class establishments where cultural exchange and sex were intertwined; one of the most widely recognized classical sexuality terms in modern Chinese.

records.definition: Flower streets and willow lanes; a classical idiom for the red-light district or the urban neighborhood concentrated with brothels and sex workers.
records.notes: 花 (flowers) and 柳 (willows) are the canonical classical metaphors for sex workers and brothels respectively; the idiom is still understood and used in contemporary Chinese to describe red-light districts both historical and modern.

records.definition: Woman of wind and dust; a literary euphemism for a prostitute or fallen woman who drifts through life without a fixed home or social standing.
records.notes: 风尘 (wind and dust) connotes a hard, wandering life exposed to the elements; the idiom typically implies sympathy as much as condemnation; widely used in Republican-era fiction and contemporary film to describe sex workers with narrative complexity.

records.definition: Ancient Chinese term for a female entertainer and prostitute, especially a singing girl or dancer who provided sexual services in the Zhou through Han dynasties.
records.notes: Predates 妓 as the dominant term; in Zhou and Han texts, 倡 (female) and 优 (male) together designated the performer-prostitute caste; distinct from the homophone character 娼 though the meanings overlap heavily; now only encountered in classical texts.

records.definition: Consort, concubine, or female entertainer; originally the clan name of the Zhou royal house, later generalized to mean a beautiful woman of noble or semi-noble status kept as a companion or concubine.
records.notes: Polysemous across history: Zhou texts use it for noble ladies; later texts use it for concubines and kept women; in contemporary slang it is sometimes used as a euphemism for 鸡 (jī, prostitute) via homophony, but this colloquial usage is entirely separate from the classical literary sense documented here.

records.definition: Beauty and artistic skill; the integrated professional repertoire of a courtesan, encompassing physical attractiveness, musical performance, poetry composition, and cultivated conversation.
records.notes: 色 = physical beauty and sexuality; 艺 = artistic accomplishment; a courtesan judged high on 色艺 commanded elevated social status and fees; the compound underscores that classical Chinese courtesans were evaluated as cultural performers, not merely as sexual commodities.

records.definition: A good match or desirable mate; the ideal romantic and sexual partner as expressed in the Confucian literary tradition.
records.notes: From 关雎, the opening poem of the Book of Songs: 窈窕淑女，君子好逑 ('A fair and gracious lady is the good match of a gentleman'); 逑 means mate or companion; this is the earliest classical Chinese formulation of the ideal romantic union and is still cited in modern discourse on love and marriage.

records.definition: A graceful, elegant, and virtuous maiden; the classical Chinese ideal of feminine beauty and moral character, from the opening stanza of the Book of Songs.
records.notes: From 关雎 in the Classic of Poetry (诗经); not sexually explicit but denotes idealized feminine desirability for courtship and marriage. Widely quoted in modern usage as a literary allusion.

records.definition: To masturbate; derived from the stroking hand motion; primarily refers to male masturbation and is ubiquitous in Chinese internet slang.
records.notes: Literal meaning is to slide or strip something along the hand (e.g., pulling leaves off a branch). The sexual meaning dominates in internet discourse. Also appears in 撸管 (lū guǎn, lit. 'stroke the pipe').

records.definition: Literally 'old driver'; a person, usually male, celebrated as experienced in sexual matters and skilled at steering conversations or content into sexually explicit territory through innuendo.
records.notes: Anchors an extended driving metaphor: 开车 (making innuendo), 车速太快 (content too explicit). Combines valorized experience with plausible-deniability euphemism. Peaked 2014–2016 on Weibo and WeChat. No English concept captures the specific compound of sexual expertise and innuendo skill held in esteem.

records.definition: Literally 'to drive'; euphemism for making sexual innuendo, steering a conversation into sexually suggestive territory, or producing sexually charged content.
records.notes: The driving metaphor implies skill and control: the 老司机 (old driver) navigates to explicit content while bystanders are nominally unaware. Peaked alongside 老司机 circa 2014–2016.

records.definition: Literally 'the car is going too fast'; exclamation that sexual content or innuendo is escalating too quickly or has become too explicit for the context.
records.notes: Used as mock alarm or genuine warning when online discourse crosses from suggestive into overtly explicit. Extension of the 开车/老司机 driving metaphor; implies the speaker is uncomfortable with the pace of escalation.

records.definition: Literally 'welfare' or 'benefits'; internet euphemism for sexually suggestive or nude images shared by a creator as a treat or reward for their followers.
records.notes: Completely asexual in standard Mandarin (government benefits, employee perks). The sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent. Ranges from mildly suggestive selfies to explicit nude sets depending on community.

records.definition: Literally 'meat anime'; slang for sexually explicit animated pornography, typically Japanese-style hentai.
records.notes: 肉 (meat/flesh) functions as a crude intensifier for explicitly sexual content; 番 typically denotes an anime episode or series. Contrasts with 普通番 (regular/non-explicit anime).

records.definition: Content rating tag indicating sexually explicit material restricted to adults aged 18 and over; borrowed from Japanese doujinshi and game classification conventions.
records.notes: Directly borrowed from Japanese convention (Comiket R-18 designation, CERO-Z for games). More specific than NSFW—it explicitly signals sexually explicit content rather than merely inappropriate or violent material. Used widely in Chinese ACG communities.

records.definition: A visual cipher representing the Japanese word エロ (ero, meaning erotic); the characters 工 and 口 together approximate the katakana エ and ロ in appearance, used as a censorship-evading label for erotic content.
records.notes: Originated in Japanese internet culture as a text-filter workaround. Somewhat archaic among younger Chinese users who prefer newer evasion terms. Understood primarily within ACG (anime, comics, games) communities.

records.definition: Borrowed from Japanese エッチ (ecchi, the letter H); an adjective or noun labeling sexually lewd or suggestive content, milder than explicit pornography.
records.notes: In Japanese, H is a euphemistic reading derived from 変態 (hentai) via its romaji initial. Adopted into Chinese ACG internet culture. Slightly archaic among Gen Z Chinese users who tend to prefer 涩 or 色.

records.definition: Sexually explicit or pornographic images; uses 涩 (astringent) as a near-homophone substitute for 色 (lustful/sexual) to evade automated content moderation.
records.notes: The character swap (涩 for 色) is a standard Chinese internet censorship-evasion technique called 谐音梗 (homophonic substitution). 涩 has no inherent sexual meaning; the evasion is transparent to human readers while defeating keyword filters.

records.definition: Sexually explicit or pornographic images; 色 here directly means lustful or sexual.
records.notes: The direct form of 涩图; 色 carries unambiguous sexual meaning in this compound. Both 色图 and 涩图 are functionally synonymous, but 涩图 is preferred on platforms with keyword filtering.

records.definition: Literally 'booklet' or 'notebook'; slang for doujinshi—self-published fan comics, often sexually explicit, typically based on characters from existing anime, manga, or games.
records.notes: The term is completely euphemistic—本子 alone simply means any small booklet. Sexual meaning is entirely context-dependent. Borrowed from the Japanese doujinshi scene via Chinese ACG fandom.

records.definition: Literally 'without mosaic'; pornographic content, especially Japanese AV, that lacks the legally required pixelation censoring genitalia.
records.notes: Paired antonym of 有码. Japanese law (Penal Code Article 175) requires genital mosaic in domestically distributed adult video; uncensored versions are technically illegal to produce in Japan but widely distributed abroad and online.

records.definition: Literally 'with mosaic'; pornographic content, especially Japanese AV, that includes the legally mandated pixelation censoring genitalia.
records.notes: Paired antonym of 无码. Less searched than 无码 by obvious preference. The 码 (code/mosaic) refers to the pixelated blur applied to genitalia per Japanese obscenity law.

records.definition: A packaged set or collection of photographs, typically nude or sexually explicit, released together as a series.
records.notes: 套 (set/suit/matched collection) is neutral in standard Chinese; the sexual connotation is entirely contextual. Commonly used for model shoots, amateur nude sets, and leaked content collections.

records.definition: Literally 'private shoot'; non-professional self-produced nude or sexually explicit photographs or video, typically shared privately or circulated after leaking.
records.notes: 私 (private/personal) distinguishes it from professionally produced content. Carries an illicit or intimate flavor; frequently associated with leaked material from personal devices or private messaging apps.

records.definition: An online content creator whose primary niche is exhibitionist content: nude or sexual self-exposure in semi-public or public settings, shared on social media or adult platforms.
records.notes: 露出 is also the standard Chinese translation for the Japanese AV niche 露出 (public nudity fetish/outdoor exposure). The term blends Japanese kink vocabulary with Chinese social media influencer culture (博主 = blogger/KOL).

records.definition: Literally 'car flip'; internet slang for a public figure or person being exposed or caught in a scandal; in sexual contexts refers to leaked intimate content or revealed sexual hypocrisy.
records.notes: Primarily a general scandal/failure term, not exclusively sexual; mapped here for its frequent deployment in sexual exposure contexts. Concept covers leaked nudes, exposed infidelity, and public sexual hypocrisy equally.

records.definition: Literally 'edge ball' (a table tennis shot grazing the table edge); content that is sexually suggestive or provocative while technically remaining within platform or legal content rules.
records.notes: The table tennis metaphor captures deliberate exploitation of content-moderation grey zones. Describes a strategy as much as a content type. No clean English concept equivalent; bawdy_humor is the nearest registry entry but misses the regulatory-gaming dimension.

records.definition: Literally 'sex/gender transformation'; primarily refers to fan fiction and art in which a character changes biological sex or gender; secondarily used informally for transgender or gender-nonconforming identity.
records.notes: Primary context is anime/manga fandom (equivalent to English 'genderbend' or Rule 63). cross_dressing is the nearest registry concept but 性转 specifically implies biological sex transformation, not only clothing change. Also used colloquially in transgender discourse in mainland China.

records.definition: Literally 'paper person'; a 2D animated or illustrated fictional character from anime, manga, or games who is the object of romantic or sexual attachment, contrasted with a real ('3D') person.
records.notes: Tone ranges from self-deprecating to affectionate. The term names the character as the object of desire, distinct from naming the person who is attracted. Analogous to Japanese 二次元 (2D world) culture and the 'waifu' phenomenon but more neutral and broader in scope.

records.definition: Literally 'veteran/old sex maniac'; a pejorative, or affectionately self-applied, term for an older male who is obsessively and publicly focused on sex.
records.notes: 老 (old/veteran) intensifies the base 色批. Used as genuine insult or ironic self-label in online male communities. The 'veteran' reading of 老 implies experienced, which softens it slightly compared to pure condemnation.

records.definition: A person, typically male, who is obsessively and inappropriately fixated on sex; a pervert or lecher; frequently self-applied with ironic humor in online communities.
records.notes: 批 functions as a crude collective-noun or intensifier suffix; 色 (lustful/sexual) is the root. Harsher than 好色 (fond of sex) but softer than a serious insult; widely embraced as a self-deprecating label in ACG and male internet subcultures.

records.definition: Literally 'face shot'; ejaculating onto a partner's face.
records.notes: The compound has a pseudo-clinical structure (颜/face + 射/shoot-ejaculate) that reads more technical than most crude slang. Predominantly used in pornographic content discussion and adult forums; not used in polite conversation.

records.definition: Female live streamer or broadcaster, typically on platforms like Douyin, Bilibili, or Huya; connotes a young woman who leverages physical attractiveness or suggestive behavior to attract viewers and virtual gifts.
records.notes: Not explicitly sexual in all contexts but heavily sexualized in internet subculture; 女 = female, 主播 = anchor/broadcaster; the virtual gifting economy incentivizes sexual performance without requiring explicit content.

records.definition: Live streaming; in sexual contexts refers to live broadcast of sexually suggestive or explicit content on platforms or private channels.
records.notes: Entirely neutral in mainstream use; sexual meaning is context-dependent; platforms nominally prohibit explicit 直播 but enforcement is inconsistent; often used in compound phrases like 直播造人 (live-streaming sex).

records.definition: Private message or DM; in sexual contexts, the act of sliding into someone's private messages with romantic or sexual intent, often after interacting with their public suggestive content.
records.notes: Neutral term for any private message; 私 = private, 信 = message/letter; sexual meaning entirely determined by content of the message sent; often the step that follows claiming 沙发 in adult forum culture.

records.definition: Compensated dating; an arrangement in which a typically young woman accompanies a man for money or gifts, with sexual activity implied or expected; borrowed and adapted from Japanese enjo-kōsai (援助交際).
records.notes: Shortened from Japanese 援助交際 (enjo-kōsai); carries stronger connotations of youth and exploitation than Western sugar dating; widely associated in Chinese internet moral panics of the early 2000s with teenage girls; 援 = aid/assist, 交 = intercourse/exchange.

records.definition: Neutral verb meaning to make an appointment or invite someone; in sexual internet slang, to arrange a casual sexual encounter; context or pairing with 啪 makes the sexual meaning explicit.
records.notes: Ordinary word for 'to arrange/invite' that acquired strong sexual meaning in dating-app and hookup culture; alone it is ambiguous; combined as 约啪 it is explicit; also appears in 约炮 (same meaning, rawer register).

records.definition: Literally 'lewd fucking operation'; internet slang for a wild, audacious, or sexually transgressive act or maneuver; 骚 implies sexual lewdness, 操 literally means 'to fuck,' 作 means move or action.
records.notes: 骚 (sāo) = lewd/sexually provocative; 操 (cāo) = to fuck (crude); the phrase has been partially desexualized in general internet use to mean any surprising or clever tactic, retaining a latent sexual undertone from its constituent morphemes.

records.definition: Literally 'take me flying'; euphemism for bringing a partner to orgasm or sexual ecstasy; also used as a request for an experienced partner to initiate or guide one into new sexual territory.
records.english_term: take me to the stars / make me come
records.notes: Heavily dual-use: in gaming contexts means 'carry me to a higher rank'; in sexual contexts means 'bring me to orgasm'; peak use during 2015–2017 gaming-sexual humor crossover period on platforms like Bilibili and Weibo.

records.definition: The 2D dimension; refers to the anime and manga cultural world; in sexual contexts encompasses hentai, erotic doujinshi, and the fan communities that produce and consume them; contrasted with 三次元 (the real, 3D world).
