records.notes: Not inherently sexual; 二次元 refers to the entire otaku/anime cultural dimension; sexual meaning arises in compound phrases like 二次元黄图 (2D erotic image); the term carries the full spectrum of Japanese-origin otaku sexuality into Chinese internet culture.

records.definition: Literally 'old driver, please guide me'; 老司机 (experienced driver) is a metaphor for a sexually experienced person; the full phrase requests sexual initiation or tutelage from an older, more experienced partner.
records.english_term: show me the ropes / take me under your wing
records.notes: 老司机 originally referred to experienced internet users who could navigate to pornographic or illicit content in Chinese forums; evolved into a broader metaphor for sexual expertise; 带带我 = guide/carry me along; peak use in gaming-sexual humor crossover circa 2014–2016.

records.definition: AV actress; a female performer in adult video productions, primarily the Japanese AV industry; the dominant term in Chinese internet culture for a professional female pornographic performer.
records.notes: AV = adult video, borrowed directly from Japanese industry terminology; 女优 = actress; the Japanese AV industry overwhelmingly shapes Chinese-language sexual vocabulary and pornographic consumption patterns; many performers are known to Chinese audiences by Japanese stage names.

records.definition: Goddess; in internet slang, an idealized and extremely attractive woman placed on a pedestal by male admirers; implies unattainable beauty, sexual desirability, and an untouchable purity that makes direct pursuit feel impossible.
records.notes: Correlates strongly with simp culture in Chinese internet; men who 女神ify a woman often feel they cannot pursue her directly; can be used sarcastically; the goddess framing simultaneously sexually objectifies and desexualizes by elevating the woman beyond reach.

records.definition: Literally 'female dog'; used as an extremely derogatory term for women, implying sexual submissiveness, promiscuity, and animal-level degradation; appears both as a misogynistic insult and as a consensual BDSM degradation label in sexual role-play.
records.notes: 母 = female (of animals), 狗 = dog; more explicitly dehumanizing than English 'bitch' because it foregrounds the animal's reproductive/breeding role; in BDSM contexts used as consensual humiliation language; as a street insult it is near maximally offensive to Chinese women.

records.definition: Sexy blogger or social media influencer; a content creator whose primary appeal is sexual attractiveness; posts suggestive or revealing photos and videos to attract followers and monetize their image.
records.notes: 性感 = sexy/sensual, 博主 = blogger/content creator; spans a range from mildly suggestive lifestyle influencers to semi-explicit creators; does not inherently imply explicit content or commercial sex work.

records.definition: Not Safe For Work; English acronym adopted verbatim in Chinese internet culture as a content warning tag for sexually explicit, graphic, or otherwise inappropriate material.
records.notes: Used without translation in Chinese internet discourse; recognized primarily by younger, English-literate users; often paired with the native euphemism 福利 (fúlì, 'welfare content') which serves the same signaling function for monolingual Chinese audiences.

records.definition: Literally 'large scale'; euphemism for sexually explicit or very revealing content in film, photography, or performance; ranges in practice from mildly provocative exposure to near-pornographic material.
records.notes: 大 = large/great, 尺度 = scale/degree/permissible boundary; 尺度 alone refers to the limits of acceptable content; degree of explicitness is highly contextual and may mean anything from a swimsuit to softcore; used in film criticism and on content platforms to signal restricted material.

records.definition: Literally 'indecent video'; refers to leaked or secretly recorded sexual footage, typically involving a celebrity or private individual; the standard media euphemism for a sex tape in Chinese news reporting.
records.notes: 不雅 = indecent/unseemly, 视频 = video; implies the content was not intended for public circulation; the term is preferred by Chinese media over explicit alternatives; frequently deployed in celebrity scandal coverage; non-consensual distribution is the dominant real-world context.

records.definition: Literally 'masturbate until dry'; describes masturbating compulsively and exhaustively until sexually depleted; hyperbolic expression for marathon or addictive self-gratification.
records.notes: 撸 (lū) = to stroke/pull (crude masturbation slang), 干 (gān) = dry/empty; implies total depletion of semen and vitality; related to 撸管 (masturbation) and intersects with Chinese 色戒 (sexual abstinence) and NoFap discourse about compulsive pornography use.

records.definition: Literally 'to rush/charge'; internet slang for masturbating to sexually arousing content; posting 冲 as a comment under explicit images signals that the viewer is aroused and about to masturbate.
records.notes: Single character used as shorthand in adult forum and Weibo comments; functionally equivalent to posting 'fapping' or 'cooming' in Western internet culture; also used in gaming to mean 'rush/attack,' making the sexual meaning entirely context-dependent.

records.definition: Literally 'shot/fired'; crude past-tense expression meaning 'ejaculated' or 'came'; 射 (shè) is the standard Chinese crude verb for male ejaculation, drawing on a shooting/projectile metaphor.
records.notes: 射 = to shoot/fire/jet; 了 marks completed action; 射 alone is the verb, 射了 confirms the act is done; also posted as a comment under pornographic content to announce orgasm; one of the most widespread crude ejaculation terms in Mandarin across all demographics.

records.definition: To arrange a casual sexual encounter; 约 = to make an appointment, 啪 = onomatopoeia for the sound of sex; together meaning 'to hook up for sex.'
records.notes: 啪 (pā) is an onomatopoeia evoking the slapping or smacking sound of sex; the compound makes the sexual intent of 约 fully explicit; widely used on Chinese dating apps such as Tantan and Momo and in casual sex culture discussions.

records.definition: Literally 'cannon friend'; a fuck buddy or friend with benefits; a person one has sex with regularly without a formal romantic relationship or emotional commitment.
records.notes: 炮 (pào) = cannon/firecracker; crude slang for sex, drawing on the same explosive/ejaculation metaphor as 射 (to shoot/ejaculate); 友 = friend; the metaphor parallels English military-weapon-based sex slang; one of the most common and widely understood crude relationship terms in Mandarin.

records.definition: Literally 'sofa/couch'; in Chinese internet forums, claiming the first-comment position on a post; in adult content forums, posting 沙发 signals one is first to view and engage with explicit material and may imply priority sexual interest in or access to the poster.
records.notes: Neutral internet convention for claiming first-comment status, analogous to Western 'first!'; sexual implication is indirect and context-dependent; in adult forums, being 沙发 confers priority status and an implicit first right of engagement with the content creator.

records.definition: Literally 'open the box'; Chinese internet slang for doxxing — publicly exposing someone's real identity, private information, or sexual content without consent; the box metaphor references cracking open what is deliberately kept hidden.
records.notes: 开 = open, 盒 = box; in sexual contexts specifically targets revealing private nude images, sexual history, or alternate online identities; used as a harassment and public shaming tactic, frequently directed against women and LGBTQ+ individuals as punishment for perceived transgressions.

records.definition: Literally 'private goods/merchandise'; in sexual internet slang, refers to privately held or leaked explicit content — nudes, sex tapes, or exclusive material — of celebrities or private individuals not intended for public circulation.
records.notes: 私 = private, 货 = goods/merchandise; originally means contraband or smuggled goods; repurposed in internet slang for exclusive or leaked sexual content; obtaining someone's 私货 implies intimacy, privilege, or violation depending entirely on consent context.

records.definition: PY deal; PY = abbreviation of 屁眼 (pìyǎn, anus); refers to a corrupt or shameful illicit exchange involving sexual favors, leaked intimate content, or degrading transactions in return for resources, career advancement, or social media exposure.
records.notes: PY = 屁眼 (pìyǎn = anus); 交易 = transaction/deal; the anus reference frames the exchange as inherently degrading and shameful; in internet contexts often describes trading sexual content or sexual access for clout, platform followers, job opportunities, or material benefit.

records.definition: Taoist sexual cultivation practice in which a male practitioner absorbs yin essence from female partners during intercourse to replenish and strengthen his own yang vitality.
records.notes: Core technique of 房中术 (fángzhōng shù, 'bedroom arts'); asymmetric by design — the female partner loses finite vital essence while the male practitioner gains; historically criticized as a rationalization for sexual exploitation of women.

records.definition: Taoist sexual cultivation practice in which a female practitioner absorbs yang essence from male partners during intercourse to strengthen her own yin vitality; the female-practitioner counterpart to 采阴补阳.
records.notes: Far less commonly discussed than its male-directed counterpart; associated with female Taoist adepts and occasionally framed in popular texts as a form of female sexual vampirism draining male vitality.

records.definition: Taoist practice of retaining semen at the point of orgasm and redirecting that vital essence upward through the spine to nourish the brain, believed to prolong life and enhance cognitive and spiritual capacity.
records.notes: One of the most cited concepts in 房中术 literature; has modern echoes in internet NoFap discourse, though the Taoist framing is medico-spiritual rather than moral; the technique typically involves perineal pressure or visualization at the moment of orgasmic inevitability.

records.definition: Taoist sexual cultivation technique in which a male practitioner systematically engages with multiple women in sequence, absorbing yin essence from each while retaining his own yang, accumulating vital force.
records.notes: Literally 'governing/managing women'; appears in classical texts including 素女经 (Classic of the Plain Girl) and 玉房秘诀; the term frames women instrumentally as reservoirs of yin energy to be strategically harvested; no Western parallel exists for multipartner sex explicitly framed as male spiritual cultivation.

records.definition: The harmonious merging of yin (female) and yang (male) principles — cosmologically and sexually — whereby male and female partners unite in intercourse to achieve spiritual and vital equilibrium.
records.notes: Primarily a cosmological and philosophical term widely used in non-sexual contexts; in 房中术 specifically applied to sexual union as a means of achieving cosmic balance; mild in register and not considered crude when used in its philosophical sense.

records.definition: The three fundamental life forces of Taoist cosmology — jīng (sexual/vital essence, including semen), qì (vital breath/energy), and shén (spirit) — whose cultivation and preservation are the core goal of internal alchemy and Taoist health practice.
records.notes: Extremely widely known across Chinese culture; only 精 (jīng) is inherently sexual (equated with semen in males, vital essence in females), and the full compound is not considered a sexual term; included here because sexual retention practices explicitly aim to conserve and transform 精 into the higher forces.

records.definition: Taoist internal alchemy practice of refining sexual essence (jīng, including semen) into vital breath (qì) through breathing exercises, meditation, and sexual retention, representing the first stage of the inner alchemical ascent.
records.notes: Part of the standard neidan sequence: 炼精化气 → 炼气化神 → 炼神还虚 → 炼虚合道; specifically involves redirecting the energy of sexual arousal and near-ejaculation upward through the governing vessel (督脉) rather than expelling it.

records.definition: Taoist internal alchemy: the comprehensive system of meditative, breathwork, and sexual energy practices aimed at transforming bodily essences upward through the three treasures (jīng → qì → shén) to achieve spiritual transcendence or immortality.
records.notes: Contrasted with 外丹 (wàidān, external alchemy using physical substances); in sexual cultivation contexts the transformation of 精 (jīng, sexual essence) through retention and redirection is the foundational first step; 内丹 traditions vary in whether sexual partner practice or solo meditation is used.

records.definition: Taoist 'dual cultivation': a spiritual practice in which male and female partners cultivate together through sexual union, with each partner advancing their respective inner alchemical development simultaneously during intercourse.
records.notes: Distinct from mere sex in that both partners are notionally cultivating simultaneously; in practice, classical critics noted the practice often devolved into the male absorbing yin while the female partner was simply used as a vehicle; also invoked in modern qigong communities and some Westernized Tantric frameworks.

records.definition: The overarching Taoist principle and practice of absorbing vital essence from a sexual partner during intercourse to replenish one's own vital energy; the general term subsuming both 采阴补阳 and 采阳补阴.
records.notes: The metaphor is explicitly agricultural: 采 means 'to pick/harvest (fruit or crops)'; the image frames the partner's body as a resource field and the practitioner as harvester, underscoring the transactional and asymmetric character of the practice.

records.definition: Taoist practice of retaining semen at the point of ejaculation and redirecting that vital essence internally rather than expelling it, believed to restore and amplify the practitioner's vitality and longevity.
records.notes: Short form of 还精补脑; techniques include perineal occlusion (闭精), muscular restraint (忍精), and visualized redirection up the spine; medically this achieves retrograde ejaculation or simple orgasm suppression; the Taoist rationale is that semen embodies finite life force and each ejaculation shortens lifespan.

records.definition: Taoist technique of physically sealing the ejaculatory pathway at the moment of orgasm by applying external pressure to the perineum or base of the penis, preventing semen expulsion while the orgasmic sensation occurs.
records.notes: A mechanical approach within semen retention practices; distinct from 忍精 which relies on muscular willpower without physical occlusion; the physical pressure technique achieves retrograde ejaculation (semen diverted into the bladder), which carries urological risks not acknowledged in classical texts.

records.definition: Taoist practice of withholding ejaculation through sustained muscular contraction and mental focus at the point of orgasmic inevitability, retaining semen by willpower alone rather than external obstruction.
records.notes: 忍 means 'to endure, forbear, suppress'; the distinction from 闭精 is the means (internal willpower vs. external pressure); both serve the same 还精 goal; in practice the two are often combined and not strictly separated in classical texts.

records.definition: In Taoist sexual cultivation theory, the vital yin essence intrinsic to the female body — encompassing vaginal secretions and a broader metaphysical female life force — which male practitioners of 采阴补阳 seek to absorb during intercourse.
records.notes: Encompasses but is not reducible to vaginal lubrication; in Taoist physiology, 阴精 is considered inexhaustible in women in some texts (contrasted with the supposedly finite 阳精 of men), a belief that rationalized unrestricted harvesting from female partners.

records.definition: In Taoist sexual cultivation theory, the vital yang essence of the male body — primarily semen — understood as a finite and precious life force whose loss through ejaculation depletes longevity and vitality.
records.notes: Functionally equivalent to semen in classical texts but carries additional metaphysical weight as the primary vehicle of a man's vital force; its conservation is the central preoccupation of 房中术; the belief in its finite and irreplaceable nature is the theological engine driving all semen retention practices.

records.definition: Taoist sexual principle meaning 'intercourse without emission': the male practitioner engages in sexual union to the point of orgasm while retaining semen, achieving the cultivational benefits of sexual contact without the perceived loss of vital essence.
records.notes: A four-character classical idiom expressing the ideal outcome of 房中术 practice; corresponds structurally to the Western clinical term coitus reservatus but is embedded entirely in a Taoist cultivation rationale rather than a contraceptive one; the phrase appears across multiple classical bedroom-arts manuals as the core prescription.

records.definition: The traditional Confucian virtue of female sexual chastity and fidelity, encompassing premarital virginity, marital sexual exclusivity, and post-widowhood lifelong sexual abstinence; the foundational concept of the Chinese honor/shame economy of female sexuality.
records.notes: While 'chastity' exists in English, 贞节 carries institutional enforcement mechanisms absent from the English concept: failure to maintain it could result in family violence, legal sanction, or social erasure; widows were subject to particular scrutiny; the Neo-Confucian dictum 饿死事小，失节事大 ('starvation is a small thing, losing chastity is a great thing') formalized its absolute priority.

records.definition: Chastity, sexual virtue, and moral integrity — primarily applied to women — emphasizing the intrinsic personal quality of sexual purity; slightly more formal and literary in register than 贞节, and applicable across unmarried, married, and widowed contexts.
records.notes: 贞操 and 贞节 are near-synonyms often used interchangeably; 贞操 foregrounds the inner moral quality (操 = personal conduct, moral character) while 贞节 foregrounds the social institution; 贞操观 ('view of chastity') remains a contemporary phrase used in discussions of gender attitudes.

records.definition: A woman celebrated in Confucian moral tradition for preserving her chastity through extreme self-sacrifice — typically suicide after sexual assault, death upon a fiancé's death before marriage, or self-mutilation or death to resist forced remarriage.
records.notes: Historical chastity martyrs were commemorated in official local gazetteers (地方志), eulogized in 烈女传 collections, and honored with 贞洁牌坊 arches; the category collapses rape victims and voluntary martyrs into a single honorific without distinguishing agency; no Western institution exists that celebrates women's deaths as proof of sexual virtue.

records.definition: The lifelong observance of sexual fidelity to a deceased husband by a widow, enacted through refusal to remarry and sustained sexual abstinence; considered the highest expression of wifely virtue in traditional Confucian society.
records.notes: Specifically applies to widows rather than unmarried women; pressure to 守节 could be exerted by in-laws who stood to lose a daughter-in-law's labor if she remarried; government endorsement through 牌坊 and official gazetteering created structural incentives for compliance; a widow who remarried was said to 失节 (lose virtue).

records.definition: The loss of female sexual chastity — whether through rape, seduction, or consensual premarital sex — treated as a catastrophic and irreversible moral failure bringing shame upon the woman and her family, regardless of whether she was a victim or a willing participant.
records.notes: The phrase deliberately erases the consent/coercion distinction: a rape victim who 失节 was subject to the same social consequences as a woman who chose sex outside marriage; historically both could face family violence, forced suicide, or marriage to the perpetrator; this conflation is what makes the concept culturally specific and not reducible to Western 'loss of virginity.'

records.definition: A decorative stone or wooden memorial arch erected by imperial or local government decree to publicly honor women who exemplified chastity virtues — principally widows who refused remarriage, or women who died to preserve their virtue.
records.notes: Physical structures still standing across China; erection required formal petition, investigation of the woman's conduct, and government approval — making the arch an official state endorsement of her sexual behavior; they functioned simultaneously as community moral advertisements and family prestige objects; no Western institutional equivalent exists that converts female sexual self-denial into state-sponsored public architecture.

records.definition: Widow; a woman whose husband has died; within the Chinese honor/shame economy, a woman expected to observe 守节 (perpetual chastity) and subject to intense social surveillance of her sexual behavior.
records.notes: While 'widow' is a universal concept with a direct English equivalent, 寡妇 is included here because the term carried specific sexual-honor baggage absent in English: widows were assumed to be a sexual threat to male neighbors and a target of male predation; the folk saying 寡妇门前是非多 ('much gossip in front of a widow's gate') reflects anxious male projection onto unsupervised female sexuality; remarriage by a widow was stigmatized as moral failure.

records.definition: 'Broken shoe': a highly derogatory slang term for a sexually promiscuous woman, implying she has been 'worn out' and made worthless by many men, like a shoe used by multiple feet until it falls apart.
records.notes: The shoe metaphor is layered: shoes are functional objects worn by many; a broken shoe is useless and discarded; the term therefore encodes both sexual promiscuity and a verdict of resulting worthlessness specific to the agricultural and working-class cultural contexts where it is most prevalent; more viscerally contemptuous than 荡妇 due to the disposability imagery.

records.definition: 'Licentious/dissolute woman': a highly derogatory term for a sexually wanton or promiscuous woman; one of the most cutting Mandarin insults directed at female sexual behavior, carrying connotations of moral degradation beyond mere promiscuity.
records.notes: 荡 means 'dissolute, licentious, unrestrained'; 妇 means 'woman/wife'; the compound is slightly more literary and carries more historical Confucian moral weight than 破鞋 but is equally vicious; frequently intensified in speech as 臭荡妇 ('stinking slut') or 死荡妇 ('dead slut'); widely used in internet arguments as a misogynistic epithet; recognition slightly higher than 破鞋 due to broader literary and media circulation.

records.definition: Idiom for a woman who is sexually promiscuous and emotionally fickle; literally 'having the nature of water and willow catkins,' both of which drift without anchorage.
records.notes: Always gendered female; the natural metaphor frames sexual looseness as moral weightlessness rather than explicit conduct.

records.definition: 'A beautiful face is water that brings calamity'; idiom attributing disaster to female attractiveness, blaming women for the downfall of men who desired them.
records.notes: No English equivalent captures both the beauty-as-weapon framing and the explicit blame-displacement onto women for male downfall; used to excuse male failures from historical emperors to modern men.

records.definition: Idiom condemning a group as utterly morally bankrupt; literally 'the men are thieves and the women are prostitutes,' applying the worst gendered moral failure to each sex simultaneously.
records.notes: The prostitution accusation (女娼) is the more damaging half in Confucian moral framing; the compound insult targets couples, families, or political factions.

records.definition: 'Green hat'; the canonical Chinese symbol for cuckoldry — a man said to be wearing a green hat has been sexually betrayed by his wife or partner.
records.notes: Green as the cuckold color derives from Yuan/Ming dynasty sumptuary law requiring male relatives of prostitutes to wear green headgear; now ubiquitous in internet memes and everyday idiom.

records.definition: 'Rotten goods'; a crude misogynistic slur for a sexually promiscuous woman, framing her body as spoiled merchandise.
records.notes: The commodity metaphor (货 = goods/merchandise) is central, treating female sexual value as a physical asset depleted by use; also applied as a general insult for any morally debased person.

records.definition: 'Integrity and shame'; the Confucian virtue of having an appropriate capacity for moral shame, especially regarding sexual conduct; most commonly invoked negatively (没有廉耻) to accuse someone of brazen indecency.
records.notes: English has no equivalent for the positive value of feeling sexual shame appropriately; Chinese moral philosophy treats this capacity as a prerequisite for ethical personhood, not an inhibition to overcome.

records.definition: 'Shameless'; brazenly lacking any sense of moral shame, especially regarding sexual conduct or social propriety.
records.notes: Applicable across all moral domains; in sexual contexts specifically targets conduct that openly violates norms of modesty without remorse.

records.definition: 'Shame'; the subjective experience of sexual or moral shame, especially regarding conduct that violates social norms of modesty or chastity.
records.notes: Captures the internal emotional dimension of Confucian shame culture; distinct from 耻辱, which emphasizes external social disgrace; the concept bridges personal guilt and communal accountability.

records.definition: 'Disgrace and humiliation'; the state of being publicly shamed for sexual misconduct, encompassing the social condemnation and the loss of standing it produces.
records.notes: More externally oriented than 羞耻; implies visible social consequences and witnesses; commonly the outcome of the community's moral condemnation of sexual behavior deemed improper.

records.definition: 'Unchaste'; the state of being sexually unfaithful or impure, especially applied to women who have violated expectations of marital or pre-marital chastity.
records.notes: Inherently gendered — chastity (贞) is coded as a female virtue in traditional Chinese morality, so its negation almost always indicts women; rarely applied to men.

records.definition: 'Lewdly disordered'; extreme sexual promiscuity or moral disorder, implying that unrestrained lust has corrupted one's character and social life.
records.notes: 淫 alone signals sexual excess; 乱 (disorder/chaos) amplifies this to systemic moral breakdown; used in legal and official contexts for sexual misconduct serious enough to warrant punishment.

records.definition: 'Improper conduct and character'; a formal accusation of moral character defects encompassing sexual misconduct, dishonesty, and violations of social virtue.
records.notes: Functions as a bureaucratic condemnation in workplace, school, and legal contexts; sexual misconduct is among the most common specific triggers in Chinese institutional settings.

records.definition: 'Damaging customs and corrupting public morals'; a formal condemnation of behavior — typically sexual — judged to undermine community values and social order.
records.notes: Used in legal, media, and official contexts to justify censorship and punishment of sexual content or behavior; the concept directly underpins Chinese obscenity law enforcement.

records.definition: 'Disgracing the family tradition'; to bring shame upon the entire family lineage through sexual misconduct, treating the family's moral reputation as a multigenerational asset that can be damaged.
records.notes: The concept of 门风 (family tradition/wind) is specifically Chinese — sexual misconduct reflects not just on the individual but dishonors the lineage across generations; no English equivalent captures this collectivist multigenerational shame structure.

records.definition: 'Privately born child'; an illegitimate child born outside of marriage, carrying the social stigma of its parents' unsanctioned sexual union.
records.notes: More neutral in register than 野种; in contemporary usage appears in legal, journalistic, or clinical contexts; associated stigma has diminished in urban China but persists in more traditional communities.

records.definition: 'Wild breed'; a crude contemptuous slur for an illegitimate child, framing the child as biologically and morally inferior due to being born outside of marriage.
records.notes: Significantly cruder and more dehumanizing than 私生子; the 野 (wild, uncivilized) component implies a perceived hereditary moral taint alongside the illegitimacy.

records.definition: 'The fondness of the cut sleeve'; a classical literary allusion to male homosexuality, from Emperor Ai of Han (r. 7–1 BCE) who cut his sleeve rather than disturb his sleeping male favorite, Dong Xian.
records.notes: Most widely recognized of the Chinese classical allusions to homosexuality; 断袖 alone suffices as a shorthand in literary contexts; the low crude score reflects its elegant literary framing.

records.definition: 'The preference of Lord Longyang'; a classical allusion to male homosexual love from the Warring States period (c. 3rd century BCE), involving Lord Longyang and the King of Wei.
records.notes: Less recognized than 断袖之癖 among general audiences; 龙阳 alone functions as a classical shorthand for a gay man; standard in scholarly and historical discussions of pre-modern Chinese sexuality.

records.definition: 'Half-eaten peach'; a classical allusion to male homosexual affection, from Mizi Xia sharing a half-eaten peach with Duke Linggong of Wei as an expression of love.
records.notes: Among the more obscure of the classical allusions in modern awareness; typically appears paired with 断袖 in the compound 分桃断袖; conveys the tenderness of male love more than its sexual dimension.

records.definition: 'Sharing the peach, cutting the sleeve'; a compound classical allusion combining the two most famous Chinese literary symbols of male same-sex love (余桃 and 断袖) into a single idiom.
records.notes: More recognizable than 余桃 alone; used in scholarly, literary, and increasingly in historical fiction and danmei (男男 romance) contexts to signal male same-sex desire with classical gravitas.

records.definition: 'Male custom'; a Ming dynasty term for male homosexuality, referring to the practice as a social phenomenon (风, custom/wind) rather than framing it clinically or morally.
records.notes: Homophone of 南风 (nánfēng, 'southern wind') but uses 男 (male) rather than 南 (south); more historically descriptive while 南风 is more euphemistic; both refer to male same-sex practice.

records.definition: 'Rabbit deity'; in its historical sexual sense, a term for young male sex workers in imperial Beijing who served male clients; distinct from its modern identity as a beloved Beijing folk-art clay figure.
records.notes: The word today overwhelmingly evokes the endearing Mid-Autumn Festival clay rabbit deity; the historical sexual meaning is largely unknown outside historical scholarship; recognition score reflects awareness of the sexual meaning only, not the folk figure.

records.definition: Historically, young male Peking opera performers who supplemented their income through sexual services to male patrons; the same word now means 'mister' or, in some dialects, a wife's affectionate term for her husband.
records.notes: The sexual meaning (male theatrical prostitute) is archaic and unrecognized by most modern speakers; in the Qing dynasty, 相公 houses were the male equivalent of brothels; recognition score reflects the historical sexual meaning, not the word's dominant modern meanings.

records.definition: 'Beautiful/graceful boy'; a boy kept for sexual use by an adult male patron; the Chinese equivalent of the Latin catamite, describing the historical institution of powerful men maintaining young male sexual servants.
records.notes: Distinct from modern clinical concepts (pedophilia/ephebophilia) in describing a historically normalized social institution with economic and social dimensions; appeared in legal codes, poetry, and social commentary throughout Chinese history.

records.definition: 'Southern wind'; a classical euphemism for male homosexuality, possibly referencing regions of China where it was considered more socially prevalent.
records.notes: Exact homophone of 男风 (nánfēng, 'male custom') using 南 (south) rather than 男 (male); the sexual meaning is almost entirely archaic and unrecognized by modern speakers without literary training; recognition score reflects awareness of the historical sexual meaning only.

records.definition: Historical South Chinese institution of male sworn brotherhood that functioned as a formalized same-sex domestic and romantic partnership, documented primarily in Fujian and Guangdong.
records.notes: Distinct from ordinary sworn brotherhood (结拜兄弟) by its romantic and sometimes sexual dimensions; participants cohabited and maintained lifelong bonds akin to marriage.

records.definition: Historical Cantonese institution of female sworn sisterhood in which women pledged celibacy from men and formed exclusive domestic partnerships, sometimes with erotic dimensions; literally 'golden-orchid covenant.'
records.notes: Prevalent in the Pearl River Delta silk industry where economically independent women could sustain such partnerships; closely related to the 自梳女 (self-combing women) tradition; the 金兰 phrase derives from the I Ching metaphor for two hearts in sympathy.

records.definition: Classical Chinese euphemism for tribadism or vulva-to-vulva sexual contact between women; literally 'polishing/grinding mirrors,' with the mirror as a conventional metaphor for the vulva.
records.notes: Found in Qing dynasty erotic fiction including 品花宝鉴; the mirror metaphor derives from the vulva's symmetrical, reflective shape; the term is entirely archaic and would confuse most modern speakers without context.

records.definition: A castrated male servant of the Chinese imperial court; eunuchs occupied a distinct social and gender category with privileged access to the emperor and imperial family's private quarters.
records.notes: The institution ended with the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912; universally recognized through compulsory history education and period dramas; the last imperial eunuch, Sun Yaoting, died in 1996; differs from 'eunuch' in implying a specific imperial bureaucratic role.

records.definition: Classical and formal Mandarin term for a castrated male official serving in the imperial court; more literary and bureaucratic in register than the colloquial 太监.
records.notes: Used in formal histories and classical texts; 宦 originally referred to court service generally, not castration; the castration requirement became standard during the Han dynasty; less familiar to non-scholarly speakers than 太监.

records.definition: Pejorative or colloquial Mandarin term for a transgender woman or male-to-female gender-nonconforming person, especially a performer; literally 'human demon/monster.'
records.notes: Widely applied to Thai kathoey performers in Chinese media; carries strong stigmatizing connotation in mainland PRC; partially reclaimed in entertainment and nightlife contexts; offensiveness is roughly parallel to English 'tranny.'

records.definition: Internet and anime subculture term for a biological male who presents convincingly as female through dress and mannerism; literally 'fake girl/woman'; analogous to 'femboy' in Anglophone internet culture.
records.notes: Popularized through anime fandoms and Chinese BBS culture circa 2010–2018; generally neutral to appreciative in online communities; culturally distinct from 人妖 in implying voluntary aesthetic performance rather than transgender identity; recognition declining as younger users prefer newer terms.

records.definition: Common Mandarin colloquial term for a tomboyish girl or young woman who adopts masculine dress, behavior, or interests; literally 'fake boy/lad'; does not inherently imply lesbian identity.
records.notes: Generally neutral to affectionate in tone; lacks the explicit lesbian connotation 'butch' carries in English; frequently applied to sporty or adventurous girls in casual speech and fiction.

records.definition: Mandarin colloquial term for a masculine-presenting or mannish adult woman; carries mild pejorative connotation; literally 'man-woman'; applied to adults rather than girls.
records.notes: Slightly more pejorative than 假小子; implies a grown woman who fails to conform to feminine gender expectations; may or may not imply lesbian identity depending on context; 婆 (old woman) adds a slightly contemptuous edge absent in 假小子.

records.definition: Mandarin term for a gender-neutral or androgynous person; in Chinese usage often describes people with androgynous physical appearance rather than necessarily claiming a non-binary gender identity in the Western sense.
records.notes: 中性 literally means 'neutral/neuter'; the term gained currency with K-pop and Chinese androgynous male idol aesthetics (小鲜肉 era); the Western non-binary identity framework does not map cleanly onto Chinese 中性 usage, which is more aesthetic than political.

records.definition: Mandarin term for an intersex person; a person born with sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary male or female definitions; literally 'dual-sex person.'
records.notes: More colloquial than the medical term 间性人 (jiānxìng rén); 双性 also means 'bisexual' in some compounds (双性恋), so context is required to distinguish intersex from bisexual meaning.

records.definition: Classical Chinese literary term for a pleasure house or upscale brothel where courtesans entertained clients with music, poetry, and sexual services; literally 'blue/green tower.'
records.notes: The 'blue/green' color originally referred to painted roof tiles of entertainers' residences; the term evokes the cultivated, aestheticized nature of Tang-Song dynasty courtesan culture and is far more literary and less crude than direct words for brothel; widely recognized through classical poetry and period dramas.

records.definition: Classical Chinese four-character idiom for the entertainment and prostitution quarter; literally 'flower streets and willow alleys'; both flower and willow are conventional classical poetic symbols for courtesans.
records.notes: A chengyu (成语); 花 and 柳 are classical erotic metaphors making this highly euphemistic; still appears in modern literary writing and journalism as a literary shorthand for red-light areas.

records.definition: Classical Chinese literary euphemism for a prostitute or courtesan; 烟花 (fireworks/smoke and flowers) is a classical metaphor evoking fleeting beauty and the transient pleasure-quarter world.
records.notes: Encodes both the allure and transience of the courtesan's life through the fireworks/smoke metaphor; found throughout classical poetry and vernacular fiction; the 烟花 element also evokes the colloquial 烟花场所 (entertainment venues) in modern regulatory language.

records.definition: Literary Chinese euphemism for a woman living outside respectable society through sex work or social disgrace; literally 'wind and dust woman,' evoking itinerancy and moral marginalization.
records.notes: 风尘 (wind and dust) evokes the nomadic, exposed existence of the social margins; used in contemporary literary writing to describe both historical and modern sex workers with distancing sympathy; less specific than 妓女 and more implicitly compassionate in tone.

records.definition: Song and Yuan dynasty enclosed entertainment venue housing theatrical performances, acrobatics, storytelling, and associated sex work; literally 'hooked railing,' referring to the fence enclosing the performance area.
records.notes: Primarily an entertainment complex rather than a dedicated brothel; sex work was embedded in the broader entertainment economy; the concept sits between 'theater' and 'brothel' with no precise English equivalent; contained within the larger 瓦子 entertainment district.

records.definition: Song dynasty commercial entertainment district containing theaters, marketplaces, storytellers, and entertainment venues including sex work; literally 'tile market'; a precursor to modern red-light and entertainment districts.
records.notes: More general than a red-light district — encompassed legitimate commerce and performance alongside sex work; 勾栏 theaters were located within 瓦子; term is primarily of historical interest, known mainly to students of Song dynasty history and classical literature.

records.definition: Classical Chinese term for a female singing entertainer who also provided social and often sexual companionship to patrons; a singing courtesan skilled in music, poetry, and conversation.
records.notes: 妓 (jì) in classical Chinese meant 'entertainer,' not strictly 'prostitute'; semantic narrowing to 'prostitute' is a modern development; 歌妓 were analogous to Japanese geisha in providing musical and social companionship, though sexual services were common; frequent figures in Tang and Song dynasty poetry.

records.definition: Classical Chinese term for a female dancing entertainer who provided social and often sexual companionship to patrons; a dancing courtesan skilled in performance dance.
records.notes: Parallel to 歌妓 with dance as the primary skill rather than song; both terms appear as emblems of pleasure-quarter culture in Tang and Song dynasty poetry; less recognized by modern speakers than 歌妓.

records.definition: Imperial Chinese term for a state-registered courtesan required to serve at official government banquets and entertainments; literally 'government courtesan'; legally distinct from private prostitutes.
records.notes: 官妓 were registered with and supervised by local governments; required to entertain officials at public functions without fee, permitted to accept private clients otherwise; the institution was formally abolished during the Ming dynasty but persisted informally; the public/private distinction had legal and tax implications.

records.definition: Imperial Chinese term for a private or unlicensed prostitute operating outside the official courtesan registry; literally 'private prostitute'; contrasted with the state-registered 官妓.
records.notes: The official/private distinction carried legal and fiscal implications; 私妓 operated without sanction and were subject to periodic crackdowns; the term is largely unknown outside specialist historians of imperial Chinese social history.

records.definition: Ming and Qing dynasty term for young women purchased from poor Yangzhou-area families, intensively trained in refined arts and etiquette, and sold at high prices to wealthy men as concubines or high-class courtesans; literally 'Yangzhou thin horse.'
records.notes: The 'thin horse' metaphor evokes the lean, elegant physique cultivated through strict diet and physical training; documented in detail by Zhang Dai's 陶庵梦忆; represents a commodified grooming pipeline from poverty to concubinage with no precise English equivalent; distinct from both sex trafficking and ordinary concubinage.

records.definition: Pejorative historical slang for a heavily made-up woman of easy virtue or a prostitute; literally 'powder head,' with thick cosmetics as a classical marker of the courtesan or promiscuous woman.
records.notes: The powder/cosmetics association links to the classical trope of heavy makeup as a signal of sexual availability; largely archaic in current use, surviving mainly in historical fiction and period drama; would confuse most speakers under 50 without context.

records.definition: The most acclaimed and highest-ranking courtesan in a brothel or pleasure district, selected by reputation, artistic skill, and beauty; literally 'flower champion/leader'; analogous to the Japanese oiran.
records.notes: 花魁 were celebrated cultural figures attracting literary men and wealthy patrons; appears in famous classical stories including 卖油郎独占花魁; sits between 'courtesan' and 'celebrity sex worker' with no single English equivalent; recognized through classical literature education and period drama.

records.definition: Crude Mandarin slang for a pimp or the husband who profits from his wife's prostitution; the most dishonored male role in the traditional Chinese honor-shame economy; literally 'turtle duke/gentleman.'
records.notes: The turtle (龟/王八) carries exceptional cultural weight in Chinese insult culture, uniquely combining cuckoldry, cowardice, and moral degradation in one symbol; 龟公 implies both the pimping function and the dishonor of tolerating and profiting from one's wife's sex work; related compound 王八蛋 ('turtle egg') is among the most common Chinese expletives.

records.definition: A female madam or manager of a nightclub, karaoke bar, or brothel who oversees sex workers and handles client relations; borrowed from English 'mommy'.
records.notes: Entered Chinese via Hong Kong and Cantonese-influenced entertainment industry vocabulary; still actively used in contemporary vice parlance across mainland, Taiwan, and Southeast Asian Chinese communities.

records.definition: A pimp or male manager who controls and profits from female sex workers; compound of 鸡 (jī, chicken — slang for female prostitute) and 头 (tóu, head or boss).
records.notes: The slang term 鸡 (chicken) for female sex worker originates in Cantonese rhyming slang and spread into Mandarin usage; 鸡头 thus literally means 'chicken head,' i.e., the boss who runs the chickens.

records.definition: A concubine; a woman held in a legally subordinate marital position below the primary wife (正妻), with fewer inheritance rights and lower social status, recognized within the formal Confucian household hierarchy.
records.notes: Also functioned as a humble first-person pronoun for women in classical texts; the specific legal and Confucian hierarchical dimensions — and the sharp distinction from 正妻 — have no true English counterpart.

records.definition: A concubine (diminutive or informal form); 小 (xiǎo, small or little) emphasizes the concubine's subordinate position or can reflect the speaker's condescending or possessive framing.
records.notes: More colloquial than 妾 alone; frequently appears in historical dramas and vernacular fiction; the 小 prefix sometimes functions affectionately but always encodes social inferiority relative to the primary wife.

records.definition: The formal act of taking a concubine; to add a woman to one's household in a subordinate marital capacity according to established social rites.
records.notes: 纳 (nà) means to formally receive or incorporate; the term describes the ritualized institutional act of acquisition rather than mere cohabitation, carrying connotations of social legitimation and ceremony.

records.definition: A kept mistress maintained in a separate household outside the official family residence; literally 'outer or external room or dwelling'.
records.notes: Distinct from 妾 (concubine within the household); 外室 implies physical and social separation from the official family, often greater independence for the woman but less legal protection and no formal marital status.

records.definition: A female household servant granted sexual access to the male master, occupying an informal status between domestic servant and concubine — sexually available but not formally elevated in social rank.
records.notes: 通房 literally means 'through-room' or 'room with unrestricted access'; 丫头 is a female servant or girl; the institution is specific to imperial and feudal Chinese household structure and does not map cleanly to any Western equivalent.

records.definition: A colloquial and relatively polite term for a concubine, especially in the Republican-era Chinese household; literally 'aunt-wife' or 'second-rank wife', used as a euphemistic social address form.
records.notes: Peak usage in the Republican era (1912–1949) when concubinage was still widely practiced among wealthy families; 姨 (yí, maternal aunt) was used as a polite address for a woman of subordinate marital status; still widely recognized through historical drama and literature despite concubinage being abolished by PRC Marriage Law in 1950.

records.definition: A classical four-character idiom (chéngyǔ) describing a man who lavishes favor and affection on his concubine(s) to the neglect or active harm of his primary wife; literally 'favor the concubine, destroy or oppress the wife'.
records.notes: Describes a specific moral-social transgression in the Confucian household order, where the hierarchy of wife above concubine was ideologically mandated; no English concept captures this particular inversion of marital hierarchy as a named moral failing.

records.definition: A euphemism for a sexual partner, concubine, or person with whom one shares the inner chamber; literally 'person within the room or chamber'.
records.notes: Classical and literary euphemism; 房 (fáng) refers to the private bedchamber rather than a public room, implying ongoing sexual intimacy without specifying the woman's marital or social status.

records.definition: The act of a male master formally claiming a female servant or lower-status woman as a sexual partner by granting her access to his bedchamber; literally 'to take into the room'.
records.notes: Describes the asymmetric power act of sexual incorporation specific to the Chinese feudal household system; distinct from 纳妾 (taking a socially contracted woman as concubine) in that it typically involves a servant already within the household being 'received' upward into sexual availability without full concubine status.

records.definition: Slang for defloration — to take a person's virginity for the first time; literally 'to open the bud or pod', a botanical metaphor for the hymen or first penetration.
